answers.title: Report — Proposing Onboard HFO Sample Testing (Properties & Operational Benefits)
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer, write a report to the vessel's owners proposing the adoption of (16) onboard HFO sample testing, explaining which properties would be tested and the operational benefits which may be achieved. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**To**: Owners / Fleet Technical Superintendent
**From**: Chief Engineer Officer, MV [Vessel Name]
**Date**: [Date]
**Subject**: Proposal for Adoption of Onboard HFO Sample Testing

**1. Purpose**

This report proposes the adoption of an onboard heavy fuel oil (HFO) sample-testing programme, setting out which fuel properties would be tested and the operational benefits this would provide.

**2. Background**

At present, fuel quality is confirmed only by shore laboratory analysis of the MARPOL retained sample, with results typically returned some days after bunkering — by which time a significant quantity of the fuel may already have been consumed. An onboard rapid-test kit would allow screening within hours of receipt, before the fuel is committed to service.

**3. Properties that would be tested onboard**

- **Density** (kg/m³ at 15°C) — needed to correctly set purifier gravity discs and to reconcile bunkered mass against volume delivered.
- **Kinematic viscosity** (cSt at 50°C) — confirms the correct heating and pumping requirements for the injection system.
- **Water content** (% by volume, e.g. crackle test or portable distillation kit) — high water content risks injector damage, corrosion, and combustion instability.
- **Compatibility/stability** (spot test) — detects incompatibility between the new bunker and existing tank residuals, which can precipitate asphaltenes and choke filters/purifiers.
- **Total sediment** — an early indicator of sludge formation and filter-blocking tendency.
- **Sulphur content** (rapid test strip or portable analyser) — critical for MARPOL Annex VI/ECA compliance verification before the fuel is burned.
- **Flash point** — a safety-critical check confirming the fuel is safe to store and handle per SOLAS requirements.
- **Catalytic fines (Al + Si)** — abrasive refinery-catalyst contaminants that cause severe wear to injectors, fuel pumps, piston rings and liners if not adequately removed by purification.

**4. Operational benefits**

- **Early detection before full consumption**: off-spec or incompatible fuel can be identified within hours rather than days, allowing the suspect batch to be segregated before it reaches the engine.
- **Protection of machinery**: early warning of high water content, cat fines or poor stability allows purifier settings to be adjusted (reduced throughput, increased temperature) before the fuel is burned, reducing the risk of injector, pump, piston and liner damage.
- **Regulatory compliance support**: immediate sulphur confirmation protects against MARPOL Annex VI violations, particularly before ECA entry, and supports verification against the Bunker Delivery Note.
- **Reduced dependency on shore laboratories**: valuable on long ocean passages or at ports with limited laboratory turnaround, reducing schedule risk while awaiting results.
- **Cost avoidance**: the cost of a single injector, pump or turbocharger failure from contaminated fuel typically far exceeds the cost of a testing kit and consumables, and avoids unplanned off-hire time.
- **Fleet-wide quality trending**: logged results can be shared with the Technical Superintendent to identify recurring problem suppliers or ports over time.

**5. Recommendation**

It is recommended that the vessel be supplied with an onboard fuel test kit (covering at minimum density, viscosity, water content, compatibility and cat-fines screening), that testing be carried out at every bunkering, and that results be logged with any adverse finding reported immediately to the Technical Superintendent before the fuel is committed to service tanks.

answers.title: Heavy-Weather Power Loss/Misfire from Water in Fuel — Immediate Actions, Sources & Standing Orders
answers.question_as_set:
While operating in heavy weather the main engine loses power and misfires. Investigation shows considerable quantities of water in the fuel.

(a) As Chief Engineer Officer explain the immediate actions which should be taken to ensure safe (6) operation of the ship.

(b) State, with reasons, the possible sources of water entering the fuel storage, handling and (5) supply system.

(c) As Chief Engineer Officer write the standing orders that would be issued with respect to (5) operation of the fuel storage, handling and supply system. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Immediate actions to ensure safe operation of the ship (6)**

- Inform the Bridge/Master immediately of reduced engine reliability; in heavy weather, request a reduction in speed and/or a course alteration to ease motion and reduce propulsion demand.
- Reduce engine load to a safe, stable level to minimise further misfiring, black smoke, or a complete loss of propulsion.
- Drain water from the day tank/settling tank drain cocks and check any fuel oil water separators/coalescers.
- Change over to a clean or alternative fuel source (a different tank, or MDO/MGO) if available, to restore reliable combustion.
- Increase purifier desludging frequency and verify the gravity disc/bowl setting is correct for the degree of contamination.
- Check fuel filters (likely blocking rapidly with water/sludge) and change over to the standby filter if differential pressure is rising.
- Monitor exhaust temperatures per cylinder and indicator/power cards for continuing misfire; be prepared to reduce load further or stop if the situation worsens.
- Once safe to do so, inform the Engineering Superintendent; if in coastal/restricted waters, advise the Bridge to have anchors ready and consider requesting sea room or tug standby in case of complete propulsion loss.

**(b) Possible sources of water entering the fuel storage, handling and supply system, with reasons (5)**

- **Contaminated bunker supply** — water already present in the fuel as delivered, from poor housekeeping of shore/barge tanks or water drawn up from the bottom of a bunker barge tank during delivery.
- **Condensation in storage/service tanks** — warm, humid air entering through tank vents condenses on the tank walls with temperature cycling; being denser than fuel, water settles at the tank bottom and can be drawn into suction if tanks are not regularly sounded/drained.
- **Leaking heating coils** in settling or service tanks — a failed steam or thermal-oil heating coil allows the heating medium to enter the fuel directly.
- **Deck/weather ingress** — in heavy weather, green seas over the deck can force water through poorly sealed air-pipe heads, sounding-pipe caps, or tank access covers if not properly secured before the weather deteriorated — a strong candidate given the heavy-weather context of this scenario.
- **Purifier heater/cooler leaks** — internal leaks in plate heat exchangers allowing the water side to mix into the fuel side.
- **Incorrect valve line-up during maintenance** — a flushing or test-water line inadvertently left connected to a fuel system after work.

**(c) Standing orders regarding operation of the fuel storage, handling and supply system (5)**

- All fuel tanks to be sounded and drained (water-checked) at least once per watch, with results logged.
- Air-pipe heads, sounding-pipe caps and tank access covers to be confirmed secure before any anticipated heavy weather, with draining frequency increased following any period of green seas on deck.
- Purifiers to be run continuously with desludge intervals reviewed and shortened whenever fuel quality is in doubt; treated-fuel water content to be checked and logged each watch.
- Fuel samples to be tested for water content at every bunkering and periodically thereafter, with results logged.
- Fuel filters to be inspected and changed over promptly on any rise in differential pressure, with a clean standby filter always ready.
- Any water detected in fuel to be reported immediately to the duty engineer/Chief Engineer, with the affected tank isolated from service until the cause is investigated and cleared.
- Heating-coil integrity to be checked periodically, with any suspect coil isolated and repaired at the earliest opportunity.

answers.title: High Exhaust Temperature on a 4-Stroke Generator Engine (Single vs Multiple Cylinders) + Why Multiple Valves Are Fitted + Operating Arrangement
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain the possible causes and actions to be taken in the event of a high exhaust temperature on a 4-stroke generator engine at :

(i) a single cylinder; (3)

(ii) more than one cylinder. (3)

(b) Explain why multiple air inlet and exhaust valves are fitted to highly rated 4-stroke engines. (4)

(c) Describe an arrangement for operating multiple valves from a single cam, explaining how the (6) "tappet" clearance is set for both valves. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Possible causes and actions for high exhaust temperature at a single cylinder (3)**

Causes: a leaking or burnt exhaust valve; a faulty or worn fuel injector causing poor atomisation or dribbling (late/incomplete combustion); incorrect fuel pump timing on that unit; low compression from worn rings, liner wear, or a valve not seating; a partially blocked fuel supply to that injector.

Actions: reduce load; check the indicator/power card and compression for that cylinder; inspect the injector and exhaust valve at the next opportunity; isolate/cut out the cylinder if the condition is severe; continue close monitoring.

**(a)(ii) Possible causes and actions for high exhaust temperature at more than one cylinder (3)**

Causes (common-mode faults, since more than one unit is affected): turbocharger fouling or damage reducing overall air supply; charge air cooler fouling raising intake air temperature; increased exhaust back-pressure from a fouled economiser/silencer; general engine overload; poor fuel ignition quality affecting several cylinders; a governor or load-sharing fault causing sustained overload.

Actions: reduce overall engine load; check turbocharger boost pressure and charge air temperature; inspect air filters and charge air cooler; check fuel quality/viscosity; reduce load further or shut down if temperatures continue to rise; investigate common systems (turbocharger, air supply, fuel quality) rather than individual injectors.

**(b) Why multiple air inlet and exhaust valves are fitted to highly rated 4-stroke engines (4)**

A highly-rated engine (high BMEP, high speed) needs a large total valve-flow area to admit sufficient air and expel exhaust gas within the very short valve-open duration available per cycle at high rpm. A single valve of adequate flow area would need to be large and heavy — increasing valve and spring inertia to the point of valve bounce/float at high speed — and would leave too little cylinder-head material around a single large seat for adequate cooling passages and structural strength. Two (or more) smaller valves per function give the same or greater total flow area with much lower individual valve mass, reducing dynamic loading on the valve gear and permitting reliable high-speed operation without bounce, while also allowing better cooling around each smaller valve seat (reducing the risk of thermal cracking or hot-corrosion burn-out) and freeing up space at the centre of the cylinder head for a centrally-mounted fuel injector, improving combustion chamber symmetry and fuel spray distribution.

**(c) Arrangement for operating multiple valves from a single cam, and how tappet clearance is set for both valves (6)**

**[Sketch]** A single cam lobe drives a rocker arm (or pushrod-and-rocker arrangement), which bears down on a **valve bridge** (also called a valve yoke or crosshead) — a rigid bridge piece sitting across the tops of both valve stems for that function (e.g. both exhaust valves). The bridge is held in alignment by a central guide pin/spigot, with a central adjustable pivot screw allowing the two valves to be set to operate in unison from the single cam/rocker input, so that both valves open, close and lift together.

**Setting tappet clearance**: with the engine on turning gear and the piston for that cylinder brought to TDC on its firing (compression) stroke — confirmed against the flywheel/timing marks, with both valves fully closed and the cam on its base circle — the bridge's own central adjusting screw is first set using a feeler gauge between the bridge and each individual valve stem tip, so that both valves carry an equal, correct clearance relative to the bridge itself. This equalises the load between the two valves so that neither is held slightly open by the other. With the bridge centralised and both valves individually equalised, the main tappet clearance — between the rocker arm and the top of the bridge — is then set to the maker's specified clearance using a feeler gauge, and the rocker adjusting screw locknut is tightened to the correct torque. The engine is then barred over by hand to confirm smooth valve operation before the rocker cover is closed up.

answers.title: Why Multiple Exhaust Valves Are Fitted to Medium-Speed Engines + Tappet Clearance Setting + Checking Procedure
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain why multiple air inlet and exhaust valves are fitted to some medium speed diesel (4) engines.

(b) Explain how the valve actuator (tappet) clearance is set for multiple valve installations. (4)

(c) Write a procedure for checking the valve operating mechanisms of a medium speed engine. (8) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why multiple air inlet/exhaust valves are fitted to some medium-speed diesel engines (4–6)**

Medium-speed engines run at higher rotational speeds than large slow-speed crosshead engines, so each valve has only a very short time window per cycle in which to admit air or expel exhaust gas. A single large valve capable of passing the required flow would need to be heavy, and the resulting valve-and-spring inertia risks valve bounce or float at higher speeds, along with excessive seating loads that accelerate seat wear and burning. Fitting two (or more) smaller valves per function gives the same or greater total flow area at much lower individual valve mass, permitting reliable high-speed operation, reducing dynamic loading on the valve train, and giving better cooling around each smaller valve seat (reducing the risk of thermal cracking and hot-corrosion burn-out) — while also leaving room in the cylinder head for a centrally-positioned fuel injector, improving spray distribution and combustion symmetry.

**(b) How valve actuator (tappet) clearance is set for multiple-valve installations (4)**

The two valves for a given function (e.g. both exhaust valves) are linked by a rigid **valve bridge** (yoke/crosshead) that sits across both valve stem tips and is kept aligned by a central guide pin. With the engine on turning gear, the cylinder brought to TDC on its firing stroke (cam on the base circle, both valves closed), a feeler gauge is used at the bridge's own adjusting screw to set each valve's individual clearance to the bridge equally, so neither valve is held slightly open by the other. Only once the bridge is correctly centralised and equalised is the main tappet clearance — between the rocker arm and the top of the bridge — set to the maker's specification using a feeler gauge, with the rocker adjusting screw locknut then tightened to the correct torque.

**(c) Procedure for checking the valve operating mechanism of a medium-speed engine (6–8)**

1. Stop the engine, engage turning gear, and isolate per a permit to work.
2. Bar the engine to bring the cylinder under test to TDC on its firing (compression) stroke, confirmed against timing marks/flywheel, with the cam on its base circle.
3. Visually inspect the valve bridge, rocker arms, pushrods and cam followers for wear, cracking, or looseness.
4. Check the valve bridge guide pin for excessive wear or play, and confirm the bridge sits square and level across both valve stems.
5. Using a feeler gauge, check and, if necessary, adjust the individual valve-to-bridge clearance for each valve, equalising both before locking the bridge adjusting screw.
6. Check and, if necessary, adjust the main tappet (rocker-to-bridge) clearance to the maker's specification using a feeler gauge, tightening the rocker adjusting screw locknut to correct torque.
7. Visually check valve spring condition (corrosion, cracking) and, if fitted, confirm valve rotators are functioning correctly (checked by observing witness marks rotating between inspections).
8. Repeat the above for each valve/cylinder in the firing order.
9. Bar the engine through a complete cycle, listening and observing for smooth, correct valve operation with no unusual noise, before closing up the rocker covers.
10. Record all clearances measured and any adjustments made in the engine log/PMS.

answers.title: Starting Air Reservoir — Safety Devices, Preparing for Internal Inspection & Defects Found
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to main starting air reservoirs:

(a) state, with reasons, FOUR safety devices fitted; (4)

(b) write a procedure in order to prepare a reservoir for internal inspection; (6)

(c) describe an internal inspection, stating TWO defects which may be found and the possible (6) causes of such defects. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) FOUR safety devices fitted to a starting air reservoir, with reasons (4)**

- **Safety/relief valve** — set to lift slightly above working pressure, relieving overpressure from a faulty compressor or unloader before the shell is overstressed.
- **Bursting disc or fusible plug** (older designs) — a secondary/backup overpressure protection, rupturing at a set pressure should the relief valve fail to lift.
- **Pressure gauge** — allows continuous monitoring, giving early warning of abnormal pressure build-up or loss.
- **Isolating/non-return arrangement on the outlet** — prevents backflow of combustion gases into the reservoir in the event of a starting valve fault, and allows the reservoir to be isolated for maintenance.

**(b) Procedure to prepare a reservoir for internal inspection (6)**

1. Reduce reservoir pressure to zero via the drain valve and/or a vent cock — never rely on the gauge reading alone.
2. Isolate the reservoir from the starting air system by shutting and locking/tagging the inlet and outlet valves.
3. Confirm isolation by reopening the drain and checking for any residual pressure.
4. Obtain a Permit to Work/Enclosed Space Entry Permit as appropriate, and carry out a risk assessment.
5. Remove the manhole door/cover using correct tools and lifting arrangements given its weight.
6. Ventilate thoroughly and test the atmosphere (O2 ~20.8%, no flammable/toxic gas) before entry; only enter once confirmed safe.

**(c) Internal inspection — TWO defects which may be found, with possible causes (6)**

- **Internal corrosion/pitting of the shell** — caused by moisture carried over from the compressor (inadequate after-cooling/draining) accumulating inside the reservoir over time.
- **Oil/carbon deposit build-up on internal surfaces** — caused by compressor lubricating oil carryover (worn piston rings/seals in the compressor), creating a fire/explosion risk if ignited by a hot spot or spark.

answers.title: Cutting Out and Hanging Up a Two-Stroke Crosshead Cylinder Following Crosshead Pin Failure
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of sketches, the procedure for cutting out and "hanging-up" an engine (12) cylinder of a two-stroke crosshead engine in the event of complete failure of the crosshead pin such that the crosshead pin cannot be operated and no replacement is immediately available.

(b) State, with reasons, the factors which may inhibit starting and limit the operating speed of the (4) engine with a cylinder cut out. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Procedure for cutting out and hanging up an engine cylinder following complete crosshead pin failure with no replacement available, with sketches (12)**

1. Stop the engine and engage turning gear; isolate starting air, fuel and cylinder lubrication to the affected unit.
2. Cut off fuel to the affected unit (lift the fuel pump roller / set VIT to zero per maker's procedure) so no fuel is injected to that cylinder.
3. Where a hydraulic override/blocking arrangement is fitted, keep the exhaust valve for that unit closed; otherwise isolate its operation per maker's instructions.
4. Isolate the starting air supply to that unit (blank or shut its starting air valve) to prevent air admission to the disabled cylinder.
5. Bring the affected unit to the position specified by the maker (typically around TDC) where the piston/crosshead assembly can be safely supported.
6. Since the crosshead pin itself has failed and cannot be operated, and no replacement is available, lift the piston/crosshead assembly clear using maker-supplied lifting screws/gear and secure it in the raised (hung-up) position with substantial chocks and lashings so it cannot descend under gravity or vibration - this isolates the crankpin/connecting rod from any load or contact with the piston assembly.
7. Disconnect the connecting rod at the appropriate point per maker's instructions and secure it clear of the crankshaft so it cannot foul moving parts.
8. Protect exposed running surfaces (crankpin, guide) from contamination with clean, lint-free covers.
9. Close up the crankcase, reinstate lubrication to the remaining units, and bar the engine over by hand to confirm free rotation with no fouling before restarting.
10. Restart on the remaining cylinders and increase load gradually, closely monitoring vibration, bearing temperatures and cylinder power balance.

**(b) Factors which may inhibit starting and limit the operating speed with a cylinder cut out, with reasons (4)**

- Reduced starting torque/turning effort - with one fewer cylinder contributing starting-air impulses, the engine may be harder to start (particularly against resistance from a cold engine or high friction), and starting-air consumption per successful start rises.
- Increased torsional/mechanical vibration - the uneven firing pattern from a missing cylinder excites torsional vibration in the shafting, typically requiring a reduced maximum RPM (avoiding barred/critical speed ranges) to keep vibration within safe limits.
- Reduced maximum available power - the remaining cylinders carry a higher relative load to compensate for the lost cylinder, but overall power is reduced and RPM is normally limited to avoid overloading the remaining units and bearings.
- Increased thermal/mechanical stress on remaining units - sharing propulsion load among fewer cylinders raises the load per cylinder, requiring closer monitoring, which in practice caps the safe operating speed.

answers.title: Crosshead Bearing Inspection - Risk Assessment Points, Lifting Equipment Fitness & Defects Found
answers.question_as_set:
(a) State, with reasons, SIX points that should be covered by a risk assessment for the inspection (6) of a main engine crosshead bearing.

(b) State how it can be ensured that the lifting equipment used for the inspection of a crosshead (4) bearing is fit for the purpose intended.

(c) List THREE defects which might be detected during inspection of a crosshead pin and bearing, (6) stating the probable cause of such defects. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) SIX points that should be covered by a risk assessment for the inspection of a main engine crosshead bearing (6)**

1. Isolation and lock-out of the engine (turning gear engaged and locked, starting air isolated) to prevent inadvertent movement during the work.
2. Enclosed/confined space entry considerations if crankcase entry is required (atmosphere testing, ventilation, standby person).
3. Manual handling and lifting hazards - bearing shells, keeps and associated tools are heavy, requiring correctly assessed lifting equipment and technique.
4. Hot surfaces/residual heat - the bearing and surrounding structure may still be hot from recent running; a cooling-down period must be allowed and confirmed before hands-on work.
5. Sharp edges/pinch points - risk of cuts or crushing injuries from the bearing shell, crankpin, or adjacent moving-part clearances.
6. PPE requirements and competency of personnel - appropriate protective equipment and ensuring only trained, competent persons carry out the task.

**(b) How it can be ensured that the lifting equipment used for the inspection is fit for the purpose intended (4)**

Lifting equipment (chain blocks, slings, shackles, lifting beams) must be selected from the vessel's Register of Lifting Appliances and Loose Gear, confirming each item's safe working load (SWL) is adequate for the load; each item must carry a current, valid test certificate (thorough examination by a competent person - typically within the last 12 months for loose gear, or 5 years for appliances) and be visually inspected before use for wear, corrosion, deformation or damage. Any item found defective, uncertified, or without a legible SWL marking must be withdrawn from use immediately and not substituted with unapproved alternatives.

**(c) THREE defects which might be detected during inspection of a crosshead pin and bearing, stating the probable cause of such defects (6)**

- Wiping/scoring of the white metal bearing surface - caused by lubrication failure (oil starvation, contaminated oil, or incorrect clearance) leading to breakdown of the hydrodynamic oil film.
- Excessive bearing clearance beyond maker's limits - caused by normal progressive wear over running hours, or accelerated wear from misalignment or inadequate lubrication.
- Cracking or fatigue damage to the crosshead pin or bearing shell - caused by cyclic loading over an extended service life, often initiated at a stress concentration (oil holes, fillets) or by a prior overload event.

answers.title: Main Engine Fresh Water Cooling System (HT/LT) + Charge Air Supply System
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a main engine fresh water cooling water system, (10) incorporating HT and LT systems.

(b) Describe the charge air supply system for a turbocharged engine, explaining the purpose of (6) each main part. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Main engine fresh water cooling water system incorporating HT and LT systems, with a sketch (10)**

**[Sketch]** HT circuit: jacket water pump → cylinder jackets, cylinder heads, exhaust valve cooling → HT cooler → back to jacket pump, with a thermostatic three-way valve maintaining jacket outlet at a set temperature (typically ~80-90°C) and a preheater for standby/starting conditions. LT circuit: LT pump → charge air cooler, lube oil cooler → LT cooler (central seawater-cooled heat exchanger) → back to LT pump, typically operating at a lower temperature (~25-36°C) than the HT circuit.

The HT (jacket) system circulates fresh water through the cylinder jackets, cylinder heads and exhaust valve cages to remove combustion heat, operating at a relatively high, closely controlled temperature to minimise thermal shock and maintain efficient combustion. A three-way temperature control valve blends cooled and uncooled water to hold the jacket outlet temperature within a narrow band regardless of load. The LT (low-temperature) system runs at a lower temperature, primarily cooling the charge air cooler and lubricating oil cooler, since these components need a lower coolant temperature to achieve their cooling duty efficiently (e.g. maximising charge air density, keeping LO viscosity in range). Both circuits ultimately reject heat to a central seawater-cooled heat exchanger (or a central cooler system), keeping seawater away from direct contact with engine components and reducing corrosion risk.

**(b) Charge air supply system for a turbocharged engine, explaining the purpose of each main part (6)**

Air is drawn from the engine room (or a dedicated intake) into the turbocharger compressor, where it is compressed, raising both its pressure and temperature. The compressed air then passes through the **charge air cooler**, which removes the heat of compression (using LT cooling water), increasing air density and therefore the mass of oxygen delivered to the cylinders for a given volume — improving combustion efficiency and power output. A **water separator** downstream of the cooler removes condensate formed as the air is cooled, preventing water from entering the cylinders. The cooled, dried air then passes into the **scavenge air receiver/manifold**, which acts as a buffer evening out pressure pulsations before the air enters each cylinder through the scavenge ports (two-stroke) or inlet valves (four-stroke). On some installations, an **auxiliary blower** supplies scavenge air at low load/starting, when exhaust gas energy is insufficient to drive the turbocharger effectively.

answers.title: HT/LT Cooling Water Systems for a Combined Pair of Medium-Speed Engines + Shutdown-Engine Temperature Maintenance
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the HT and LT cooling water systems for a combined pair of (12) medium speed engines in an installation.

(b) For the system described in part (a), explain how a shut-down engine is maintained at the (4) correct temperature for immediate starting when the associated engine is also stopped and when the associated engine is running. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) HT and LT cooling water systems for a combined pair of medium-speed engines in an installation, with a sketch (12)**

**[Sketch]** Two medium-speed engines (e.g. a running engine and a standby/shut-down engine) sharing common HT and LT cooling water circuits via a manifold arrangement, with cross-connection valves, common coolers, and a keep-warm circulation line to the stopped engine.

Where two or more medium-speed engines share a common cooling water system, each engine has its own HT (jacket) and LT circuit, but these connect to shared header/manifold pipework so that either engine's pumps and coolers can serve the installation, and so that a stopped engine can still receive circulated warm water from the running engine's system. Isolating valves at each engine allow individual engines to be taken out of the common circuit for maintenance without affecting the other. Common HT and LT coolers (heat exchangers to seawater or a central cooling system) serve both engines, sized for combined running load. Standby pumps are cross-connected so that either engine's pump can supply the whole system if one engine's own pump is unavailable.

**(b) How a shut-down engine is maintained at the correct temperature for immediate starting, both when the associated engine is also stopped and when it is running (4)**

When the associated (running) engine is operating, its own HT system circulates warm jacket water through the shared header, and a keep-warm branch line (with a small circulating pump or by natural thermosiphon, depending on design) draws some of this warm water through the stopped engine's jacket, keeping it at an elevated standby temperature without the stopped engine needing its own heater running. This allows the stopped engine to be started quickly without thermal shock, since its jacket is already close to normal operating temperature. When both engines are stopped (neither running), an electric jacket-water heater and a small circulating pump maintain the shared HT water — and hence both engines' jackets — at a preheat temperature (typically 60–70°C) so that whichever engine is called upon can be started promptly without excessive cold-start wear or thermal stress, in line with standard standby-generator/engine keep-warm practice.

answers.title: Crosshead Bearing & Guide Clearances — How Checked + Procedure for Checking Bottom-End Bearing Surface Condition
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe how crosshead bearing and guide clearances can be checked. (6)

(b) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the procedure for checking the condition of a crosshead (10) engine bottom end bearing surface. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) How crosshead bearing and guide clearances can be checked (6)**

With the engine stopped and on turning gear, the piston/crosshead for the unit under test is barred to the appropriate position specified by the maker (typically with the crosshead at or near the bottom of its stroke, where access is best). Crosshead **guide clearance** is checked by inserting feeler gauges between the crosshead shoe and the guide face at top and bottom (or port/starboard, depending on design), comparing the measured clearance against the maker's specified limits; this can also be checked using a dial gauge to measure lateral movement of the crosshead when a lever/jack is used to rock it against the guide. Crosshead **bearing (pin) clearance** is typically checked by lifting the crosshead slightly with a jack while a dial gauge records the vertical lift — the reading corresponds to the bearing clearance — or by removing the bearing cap/keep and directly measuring the shell-to-pin clearance with feeler gauges or lead-wire crush method (a soft lead wire is placed across the bearing, the cap re-torqued, then removed and the flattened wire measured with a micrometer to give the clearance).

**(b) Procedure for checking the condition of a crosshead engine bottom-end bearing surface, with a sketch (10)**

**[Sketch]** Bottom-end (crankpin) bearing assembly — bearing cap, upper and lower shells, crankpin, retaining bolts/studs.

1. Stop the engine, engage turning gear, and isolate starting air/fuel per permit to work; allow the unit to cool if recently run.
2. Drain or isolate the lubricating oil supply to the bearing as required, and open the crankcase per the enclosed-space entry procedure if entry is needed.
3. Remove the bearing cap retaining bolts/studs in the sequence specified by the maker, and carefully lift off the cap, noting its orientation for correct reassembly.
4. Withdraw the lower bearing shell (and, where design permits, roll out the upper shell) for inspection.
5. Visually examine the white-metal (or equivalent bearing) surface under good lighting for wiping, scoring, pitting, discolouration (bluing from overheating), or fatigue cracking.
6. Inspect the crankpin journal surface for scoring, corrosion, or heat damage, checking for smoothness and roundness.
7. Measure the bearing shell thickness (e.g. with a ball micrometer at the crown) and compare against the maker's minimum permissible thickness.
8. Measure the running clearance using feeler gauges or the lead-wire method, comparing against the maker's specified limits.
9. Check the journal for ovality/taper using a micrometer at several circumferential and axial positions.
10. If within limits and serviceable, clean and reassemble with fresh lubricating oil, torque the bearing cap bolts to the maker's specification in the correct sequence, and confirm free rotation on turning gear before returning the unit to service. If defects are found beyond acceptable limits, renew the shells and/or refer the crankpin for reconditioning as appropriate.

answers.title: Checking/Adjusting Fuel Injection Pump Timing — Restored (Previously Removed as Pre-2016-Only)
answers.answer_text:
**Checking/adjusting FI-pump timing (spill method)**

Stop, lock out and allow the engine to cool; refer to the maker's timing specification in degrees BTDC; turn the engine on turning gear to the timing mark (flywheel/dial gauge); slacken the HP pipe and rotate until fuel just spills, comparing against the specification. Adjust via camshaft/cam-follower repositioning or shims (mechanical systems) or via the ECU (electronic systems); tighten, bleed, test-run and check exhaust/power; document the work.

**Power balance**

All cylinders should contribute equally: set equal fuel per pump/injector, ensure uniform compression (valve clearance, ring condition), and monitor EGT and load-indicator (Pmax/Pcomp) cards — electronic engines trim automatically via the ECU. This is essential to avoid overloading individual units, excess vibration/bearing stress, and to keep SFC/emissions low.

answers.title: Crankcase Explosion — Probable Events, Effects & Hazards + OMD Standing Orders — Restored (Previously Removed as Pre-2016-Only)
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Outline the events leading to a crankcase explosion, describing the affects and hazards. (12)

(b) As a Chief Engineer Officer state the standing orders regarding the activation of the oil mist (4) detector. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Probable events leading to a crankcase explosion, effects and hazards (12)**

*Stage 1 — hot spot formation*: defective/overheated bearing (main, crankpin or crosshead); piston rod/stuffing box blow-past; misaligned or seized running gear; inadequate lubrication.

*Stage 2 — oil mist generation*: hot spot (typically >200°C) vaporises LO droplets; vapour condenses on cooler surfaces into fine white oil mist, initially too rich to ignite.

*Stage 3 — explosive mixture formation*: as mist density increases and disperses, it reaches the LEL and becomes ignitable — white mist may be seen escaping from crankcase doors/vents.

*Stage 4 — ignition (primary explosion)*: the hot spot (or a spark) ignites the mixture; pressure wave blows open crankcase relief doors, which then reseat.

*Stage 5 — secondary explosion*: rush of fresh air into the crankcase mixes with remaining oil mist/vapour, creating a second, far more violent explosion — the main cause of catastrophic damage.

*Effects*: crankcase doors blown off/relief valves lifted; crankcase structure fractured/distorted; engine room fire from ejected burning oil/gases; damage to bearings, con-rods, crank webs; engine rendered unserviceable.

*Hazards*: fire/explosion risk to personnel; burns and blast injuries; fatalities from the (far more lethal) secondary explosion; structural damage to the ship; loss of propulsion endangering the vessel; engine room flooding risk if sea water systems are damaged.

**(b) Standing orders — OMD activation (4)**

OMD must be in continuous operation whenever the main engine runs. Any alarm is to be treated as a crankcase explosion risk — do not investigate immediately. On activation: reduce engine load and inform the bridge to stop the engine at the earliest safe opportunity; do not open crankcase doors for a minimum of 20 minutes after shutdown (allow cooling); keep all personnel clear of the doors. The OMD must be tested/calibrated per manufacturer schedule; defective units reported and repaired immediately, with enhanced manual rounds required if operation continues with a non-functional OMD. Every activation is logged in the engine room logbook with actions taken.

answers.title: Turbocharger Surging on a Two-Stroke Engine with Two Turbochargers — Checking & Rectifying
answers.question_as_set: Outline the actions to be taken for checking and rectifying surging at one of two main engine (16) turbochargers on a two-stroke engine. You must include actions to be taken in order to investigate the cause of the surging and to return the turbocharger and engine to normal safe operating condition. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Actions to be taken for checking and rectifying surging at one of two main engine turbochargers on a two-stroke engine (16)**

**Recognising and confirming surging**: surging is heard as a repetitive, cyclic banging/rumbling from the affected turbocharger, often accompanied by fluctuating scavenge air pressure, fluctuating exhaust gas temperature on the associated cylinders, and possible momentary drops in engine RPM or vibration. Confirm which of the two turbochargers is affected by listening/feeling at each unit and comparing scavenge pressure and speed readings between them.

**Immediate action**: reduce engine load — surging is far more likely at low load/light running where the compressor operates close to its surge line, so reducing load (or, if load cannot be reduced, closely monitoring for escalation) is the first step to move the operating point away from the surge region. Increase monitoring of exhaust temperatures across all cylinders, since surging disturbs air distribution and can cause temporary overheating or incomplete combustion on the affected cylinders.

**Investigating the cause — checks to carry out**:
- **Air-side fouling**: inspect and clean the compressor side (salt, oil, dust deposits reduce effective flow area and shift the compressor's operating point toward surge); check air filters for blockage.
- **Gas-side fouling**: inspect and clean the turbine side (carbon deposits on the nozzle ring/turbine blades restrict and unbalance gas flow, altering the turbocharger's operating point).
- **Charge air cooler condition**: check for fouling or blockage, which raises resistance on the air side and can push the compressor toward surge.
- **Uneven cylinder loading**: check indicator cards/power balance — if one or more cylinders are under-fuelled or over-fuelled, the resulting uneven exhaust gas flow can upset turbocharger operation and provoke surging even when the turbocharger itself is clean and undamaged.
- **Mechanical condition of the turbocharger**: check for bearing wear, rotor imbalance, or blade damage, any of which can alter the compressor's stable operating range.
- **Load-sharing between the two turbochargers**: on a twin-turbocharger arrangement, check for uneven distribution of exhaust gas or scavenge air between the two units (e.g. a partially blocked crossover duct or manifold), which can overload one turbocharger relative to the other and induce surging in the more heavily loaded unit.

**Rectification**: clean the fouled compressor and/or turbine side (water-washing on the compressor side while running, or grit-blasting/manufacturer-approved cleaning on the turbine side, as applicable); clean or renew air filters and clear any charge air cooler fouling; rebalance cylinder fuelling/power via indicator cards if uneven loading is found; if the turbocharger itself is mechanically defective (worn bearings, damaged blades, rotor imbalance), plan for overhaul or renewal of the affected components at the earliest opportunity, operating at reduced load in the meantime to avoid worsening the condition; correct any ducting/manifold restriction causing uneven load-sharing between the twin turbochargers.

**Follow-up**: after rectification, gradually increase load while monitoring scavenge pressure, exhaust temperatures and for any recurrence of surging noise/vibration; log the incident, findings and corrective action taken, and update the planned maintenance schedule if fouling or wear is found to be recurring.

answers.title: Procedure - Changing a Cylinder Liner (Cover Removal Through Liner Replacement) - Restored (Previously Removed as Pre-2016-Only)
answers.answer_text:
**As Chief Engineer Officer, outline a procedure for the changing of a cylinder liner in a large crosshead diesel engine, from removal of the cylinder cover to replacement of the liner (16)**

1. **Preparation**: stop and cool the engine; shut fuel/LO/CW to the unit; drain cooling water; ventilate and clear the area. Disconnect HP fuel pipes, indicator cocks, CW connections; remove the exhaust valve and its connections.
2. **Cover**: slacken nuts gradually in a crisscross pattern; use certified gear on designated lifting points; lift vertically and smoothly; land on a clean, stable surface.
3. **Piston**: disconnect piston-cooling oil pipes; fit the piston lifting tool; draw the piston upward through the liner; protect it on a clean bench.
4. **Liner removal**: remove holding rings/clamps and old sealing rings; secure the liner lifting tool; apply slight upward crane force to break the seating (heat the block if needed); lift slowly and vertically; land in prepared storage.
5. **Preparation of the seating**: clean and inspect the block seating for carbon, cracks and wear; clean the CW passages; fit new rubber sealing rings with the recommended lubricant.
6. **New liner installation**: lower slowly and evenly; align and seat; measure liner protrusion against maker's spec; secure with retaining rings/clamps.
7. **Reassembly**: piston (mind ring orientation) -> cooling connections -> cover (crisscross torque) -> fuel/CW/LO pipes, checking for no leaks.
8. **Checks and restart**: slow-turn the engine to confirm free movement; CW pressure test; area cleared; start at low RPM, monitoring temperatures, pressures, vibration and lubrication of the new liner.
9. **Closing**: monitor liner wear with calibrated tools, CW flow and cylinder lubrication, and carry out timely piston/ring maintenance.

answers.title: Exhaust-Gas Steam Generation System — No Bypass, Steam-Dump Condenser
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch an exhaust gas steam generation system in which the exhaust gas economiser (8) comprises of a steam generation unit and a water/steam drum; there is no exhaust gas bypass arrangement but the steam system has a steam dump condenser. The sketch must show the exhaust gas flow as well as the feed water and steam flows. Soot blowing arrangements and the steam dump condenser system must be included. The Steam drum, which is supplied with feed water, is located above the exhaust gas economiser.

(b) Describe the operation of the steam generation system sketched in the answer to part (a). The (8) description must explain how the steam pressure is regulated and how the feed water system operates to maintain water flow through the economiser steam generation unit. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
The system is a single-pressure, natural-circulation exhaust gas boiler designed to recover waste heat from the main or auxiliary engine **without any exhaust gas by-pass arrangement**.

Hot exhaust gases from the engine enter the bottom of the boiler, flow vertically upward over finned or bare generating tubes and leave via the funnel. There is no by-pass damper; all exhaust gas is therefore forced through the heat transfer surface at all engine loads.

Feed water is pumped from the hotwell/cascade tank by the feed water pump and is discharged directly into the water/steam drum, which is mounted above the generating tube bank. Because the drum is located at the highest point, natural circulation is established as follows:

- Relatively cool water from the drum flows down the large-diameter downcomer pipes (usually at the sides of the boiler casing) to the bottom header of the generating bank.
- Inside the generating tubes the water absorbs heat from the upward-flowing exhaust gas, partially evaporates and becomes a steam/water mixture of lower density.
- This lighter mixture rises naturally through the riser tubes back to the steam drum, where steam is separated from water in the steam space and by the baffles/cyclone separators.
- The continuous density difference between downcomer and riser circuits maintains steady circulation without the need for a circulating pump.

**Steam pressure regulation and excess steam disposal**

Saturated steam leaves the drum through the main steam stop valve to heating services, tank heating, fuel oil heaters, accommodation heating, etc.

Because there is no exhaust gas by-pass, the steam generation rate is directly proportional to engine load. When the engine load (and therefore exhaust gas temperature/flow) increases, more steam is produced than may be required by the consumers.

To prevent excessive pressure rise in the drum, an automatic pressure-controlled dump valve (surplus steam valve) is fitted on the steam outlet line from the drum. This valve is set to the required working pressure (usually 6–9 bar). As long as consumer demand keeps drum pressure below the set value, the dump valve remains closed.

When consumer demand falls and drum pressure tends to rise, the dump valve opens automatically and diverts excess steam to the atmospheric surplus condenser (steam dump condenser). The surplus steam is condensed by sea water cooling and the condensate drains back to the hotwell, thus maintaining constant drum pressure irrespective of variations in engine load or consumer demand.

**Feed water regulation and level control**

The water level in the steam drum is maintained automatically by a conventional feed water regulator (single- or two-element control) acting on the feed pump discharge valve or on the speed of the feed pump (if turbine-driven). A low water level would expose the generating tubes and risk overheating, while a high level would carry water over into the steam lines.

Periodic soot blowing (steam or compressed air) is carried out on the gas side to remove soot deposits and maintain high heat transfer efficiency.

Thus the system provides fully automatic, safe steam generation over the full engine load range with no exhaust gas by-pass, using natural circulation and an atmospheric dump condenser for pressure control.

**[Sketch]** WHR unit using an oil-fired boiler as the steam-collecting drum; pressure controlled by atmospheric/dump steam condenser returning condensate to the hot well.

answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe the symptoms and possible causes of an exhaust gas boiler/economiser fire. (5)

(b) Describe the procedure for inspecting and cleaning the gas side of an exhaust gas boiler/ (5) economiser.

(c) Explain how the main engine and auxiliary steam plant may be operated in the event of an (6) exhaust gas boiler/economiser suffering severe damage rendering it inoperable. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Symptoms of an exhaust-gas boiler/economiser fire (5)**

- Sparks, glowing soot or flames from the funnel
- Rapid rise in exhaust gas temperature after economiser and high differential pressure across it
- Turbocharger surging / hunting
- Smoke or burning smell from uptake / paint blistering on casing
- Abnormal increase in steam pressure (if composite boiler)

**Causes**

- Accumulation of oily/sooty deposits due to poor combustion, faulty injectors, leaking fuel valves or excessive cylinder oil
- Failure to carry out regular soot blowing or water washing
- Low water circulation leading to hot spots and ignition of soot
- Prolonged low-load operation allowing unburnt fuel to deposit
- Backflow of fuel into the uptake during starting/air running of engine

**(b) Procedure for inspection and cleaning the gas side (5)**

1. Stop main engine, open exhaust gas bypass damper (if fitted) or blank the uptake
2. Stop circulating pumps, fully drain the water side, open vents and hand-hole doors to prevent pressure build-up
3. Allow complete cooling, carry out risk assessment and issue enclosed-space entry permit
4. Soot blow thoroughly (if still possible) then water-wash the tube bank using the fixed washing system or portable high-pressure jets; drain all soot/water to soot tank/bilges
5. Enter with proper PPE and lighting; inspect tubes, fins, headers and baffles for corrosion, erosion, cracking, soot deposits and clear any blockages; check condition of sacrificial anodes if fitted
6. On completion, close up, remove blanks/bypass, test soot blowers and confirm free operation of bypass damper before returning to service

**(c) Operating the main engine and auxiliary steam plant if the economiser is rendered inoperable (6)**

- Inform Master immediately, enter defect in log book and suspend UMS operation – revert to manned engine room 24 hrs
- Isolate and fully drain the damaged economiser on water side; keep vents and drains open, remove hand-hole doors and safety valve easing gear to prevent pressure build-up
- Thoroughly water-wash gas side to remove all soot and prevent secondary fire
- If exhaust bypass damper is fitted – close damper to economiser and route exhaust through bypass
- If no bypass is fitted – maintain engine on reduced load, keep exhaust temperature after economiser as low as practicable (usually <180–200°C if heavily damaged) to prevent further damage
- Light off and run auxiliary/oil-fired boiler to maintain full steam pressure for fuel heating, accommodation, purifiers and other essential services
- Monitor funnel continuously for sparks/smoke, keep fire team and boundary cooling ready, gradually increase load while closely watching temperatures and prepare defect report for classification society / port state

answers.title: Oil-Fired Boilers — Fuel & Pilot-Ignition System, Cold Flash-Up & HFO Changeover, Combined Air/Fuel Control
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to oil fired boilers:

(a) describe, with the aid of a sketch, the fuel system including the pilot ignition system; (6)

(b) explain how the boiler whose fuel system is described in part (a) is flashed up from cold on (6) diesel oil and changed over to heavy fuel operation;

(c) explain how the air and fuel supplies are controlled together in order to produce optimum (4) combustion at all loads. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Oil-fired boiler fuel system (6)**

**[Sketch]** Service tank, filter, FO supply pumps, pressure-regulating/recirculation, fine filter, heaters, ignition pump, pneumatic valves, pilot burner & main burner; diesel-oil supply line for flash-up.

**(b) Flashing up from cold on diesel oil and changeover to heavy fuel (6)**

- Carry out pre-light-off checks: water level normal, all mountings free, circulation pumps tested, no leaks, forced-draught fan OK, fuel pumps tested on recirculation.
- Select MDO mode at the control panel. Ensure fuel supply 3-way valve to MDO, return 3-way valve to MDO (both supply and return must be to diesel to prevent contamination).
- Start fuel supply pump and circulate MDO through the system for at least 30–60 minutes to warm the fuel lines, burner, and furnace (warming-through period). Check pressure at burner is normal (20–30 bar).
- Start forced-draught fan, purge furnace for minimum 3–5 minutes (or as per maker's instruction) to remove any explosive mixture.
- Light off automatically or manually on pilot burner → main burner ignites on low fire. Raise steam pressure very slowly (maximum 3–4 bar per hour) to avoid thermal stress. Keep firing intermittent at low rate until working temperature is approached.
- When steam pressure reaches approximately 6–8 bar and HFO tracing/heating lines are fully warmed: gradually open HFO heater steam inlet valve to raise HFO temperature to correct viscosity (11–14 cSt, usually 120–140°C).
- When HFO temperature and viscosity are correct, change over supply first, then return to HFO (supply before return to maintain pressure).
- Increase firing rate as required. Confirm stable combustion, no smoke, correct atomisation.

**(c) How air and fuel supplies are controlled together for optimum combustion at all loads (4)**

The air and fuel supplies are controlled together by a fully modulating combustion control system with air/fuel ratio control and oxygen trim:

- The steam pressure transmitter senses boiler steam pressure and sends a demand signal to the master controller.
- The master controller compares actual pressure with set pressure and outputs an increasing or decreasing signal to both the fuel control valve and air damper servo motor simultaneously.
- A characterised cam (or electronic mapping) in the controller ensures that the air damper opens slightly in advance of the fuel valve (air-lead) and closes after the fuel valve (fuel-lead) — this is called cross-limiting and prevents black smoke during load changes.
- A flue gas oxygen analyser continuously measures O₂ content in the uptake and automatically trims the air damper position (oxygen trim) to maintain optimum excess air (usually 3–5% O₂) at all loads, compensating for changes in fuel quality, atmospheric conditions, or fouling of the burner.

This system ensures optimum combustion, minimum smoke, and maximum efficiency at all firing rates from low fire to high fire.

**[Sketch]** Combined air/fuel control — jackshaft (master drive unit) linking combustion-air damper and fuel valve, with automatic adjustment on the blower side of the shaft.

answers.title: Economiser Gas-Side Cleaning — Engine Running (Sootblowing) & Stopped (Water Washing), Running Dry
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to an economiser:

(a) write a procedure for the cleaning of the gas side of an economiser when the associated main engine is:

(i) running; (5)

(ii) stopped. (5)

(b) write a procedure for operation of the main engine when the associated economiser cannot be (6) operated due to tube failure. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Engine RUNNING — Sootblowing procedure (5)**

1. Inform bridge of your intentions to sootblow (ask permission) — wind direction/ship position is important.
2. Ensure engine is at full load, for high gas velocity to carry away dislodged soot.
3. Open steam supply to sootblowers, and warm through associated lines, slowly.
4. Commence sootblowing — whether automatic or manual, the lowest sootblowers should be operated first, then work your way upwards.
5. Once sootblowing is complete, close steam supply, and inform bridge.
6. Check uptake temperatures before and after economiser. Temperature differential should increase after successful sootblowing, proving heat transfer is now improved within the unit.

**(a)(ii) Engine STOPPED — Water washing procedure (5)**

1. Safety sequence (risk assessment, engine isolation, enclosed space permit).
2. Open access doors, allow sufficient time to cool.
3. Stop circulating pumps.
4. Open drain line from economiser to soot tank (for wash water).
5. Start water washing with FW using dedicated washing line.
6. Once soot removed, enter for visual inspection, ensuring gas paths clear, remove any remaining soot build-up, proceed with caution if using pressure washer.
7. Clear any residues in the base of economiser.
8. Return back to normal and replace door gaskets if necessary.
9. Leave to dry, check no leakage from doors when next running up engine.

**(b) Operating the main engine with the economiser inoperable — Running Dry (6)**

- Safety considerations (risk assessment, engine shut down, isolated).
- Stop and isolate circulating pumps.
- Isolate and drain economiser unit. Close and lock inlet/outlet valves, open drain and vent. Economiser must be completely drained and dried out.
- Inlets and outlets should be blanked and all mountings removed to ensure that no moisture could accumulate within the tubes. Remove safety valves and ensure pressure is zero.
- Increased use of sootblowers should be considered and regular inspections carried out to ensure that there is no build-up of soot. Full water washing procedure beforehand for removal of soot deposits.
- The Classification Society should be informed, in writing, if the intention is to run the unit dry. Consult with superintendent, original equipment manufacturer, etc.
- Run on low load according to original equipment manufacturer recommendations. Keep eye on uptake temperatures. Implement full watchkeeping and ensure aux. boiler coping with steam demand.

*Supplementary source note (second worked version of running-dry, kept alongside the first per the standing verbatim rule):*

- When shutting off the water circulation, the main engine should also be shut down so the exhaust gas boiler can cool down and any smouldering soot deposits on the boiler tubes can die out.
- The heating surface should be inspected carefully for soot deposits, and water washing performed, both for cleaning and cooling.
- Make every effort to re-establish the water circulation to the boiler and thereby reduce the dry running period to a minimum.
- Boiler manufacturers allow dry running of exhaust gas boilers only in the case of emergency and with a clean boiler. In addition they emphasise that every possible precaution must be observed to prevent soot fire.

answers.title: Engineer-Manager Standing Instructions — In-Service Gas-Side Cleaning & Uptake Fire
answers.question_as_set:
(a) As the Engineer Manager write standing instructions for the in-service cleaning of the gas side (8) of a waste heat recovery steam generator unit.

(b) As the Engineer Manager write standing instructions for the action to be taken in the event of (8) an uptake fire in the waste heat recovery steam generating unit and action to be taken to enable operation of the engine after the fire has been extinguished if there is a leak in the tube nest and no exhaust gas bypass is fitted. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Standing instructions — in-service (online) gas-side cleaning of exhaust gas boiler/economiser (8)**

*I. Soot blowing (using steam or air soot blowers)*

- Only carry out soot blowing when main engine load is ≥65–70% MCR (or as per maker's instruction) to ensure sufficient exhaust gas velocity to carry soot clear of the funnel.
- Inform Bridge at least 10 minutes before commencing – request course alteration to keep wind 15–20° on either bow to prevent glowing soot falling on deck or superstructure.
- Warm through soot blower steam supply lines for minimum 15–30 minutes to prevent thermal shock and water carry-over.
- Open drain traps on steam supply lines and confirm dry saturated steam at correct pressure (usually 7–12 bar).
- Open main soot blower steam isolating valve slowly.
- Start automatic soot blowing sequence from control panel: sequence always starts from lowest soot blower (economiser section) and progresses upwards to prevent re-deposition; each blower rotates and retracts automatically.
- Monitor exhaust gas temperature drop across economiser: a drop of 15–30°C after soot blowing indicates effective cleaning; record inlet/outlet temperatures and differential pressure before and after.
- After completion, close steam isolating valve and inform Bridge "Soot blowing completed".
- Whenever possible, perform final soot blow immediately before stopping main engine (best cleaning effect due to high load and temperature).

Frequency: Normally every 24–48 hours at sea when on HFO, or as per PMS / maker's recommendation.

*II. Out-of-service (offline) water washing of gas side*

Only to be carried out when main engine is stopped for more than 24 hours (e.g., in port, dry-dock or extended stoppage).

- Stop main engine and open exhaust gas bypass damper (if fitted) OR blank the uptake.
- Stop economiser circulating pumps, fully drain water side, open vents and hand-hole doors to release pressure.
- Allow complete cooling (minimum 12–24 hours) until gas-side temperature <40°C.
- Carry out risk assessment and issue Enclosed Space Entry Permit.
- Test atmosphere inside uptake for O₂ ≥20.8%, LEL = 0%, no toxic gases.
- From outside, visually inspect extent of soot deposits on tubes and fins.
- Open bottom drains to soot collection tank / bilges.
- Water wash from top downwards using fixed water-washing nozzles (preferred), OR portable high-pressure fresh water jets (150–200 bar) with approved chemical detergent if heavily fouled with oily soot.
- Wash section by section, ensuring all soot is flushed downwards.
- After washing, allow complete draining and drying.
- Enter with proper PPE and carry out detailed inspection: tube walls and fins for corrosion, erosion, cracking, pitting; headers and baffles for leakage; soot blower lances and nozzles for wear, blockage, alignment; sacrificial anodes (if fitted) – replace if <50% remaining; confirm all gas passages are clear.
- Test soot blowers (live steam test) if accessible.
- Close up all doors, remove blanks, refill water side, vent properly.
- Enter completion in Planned Maintenance System and Official Log Book.

**Never water-wash online with engine running** – risk of thermal shock, tube rupture, and steam explosion.

**(b) Standing instruction — uptake fire in exhaust gas boiler/economiser & subsequent engine operation, no bypass damper fitted (8)**

*I. Immediate actions on discovery of uptake fire*

- Inform Bridge immediately – request reduction of main engine load to absolute minimum possible or stop engine if fire is severe.
- Stop economiser circulating pumps.
- Fully isolate and drain the economiser on the water side – open all vents, drains and hand-hole doors.
- Remove all hand-hole doors and safety valve easing gear to ensure no possibility of pressure build-up from residual water turning to steam.
- Boundary cooling – start fire pump and apply external cooling water to casing and bulkheads if fire is intense.
- Thoroughly water-wash the gas side as soon as temperature permits to remove all burning and unburnt soot.
- After fire is fully extinguished, inspect for tube damage/leakage and record findings.

*II. Continued main engine operation after uptake fire (known tube leak, no exhaust bypass damper fitted)*

Decision to continue operation is at Master's and Chief Engineer's discretion only after full risk assessment and with Class/Flag approval if required.

- Inform Master and enter defect in Official Log Book – suspend UMS notation immediately.
- Maintain economiser completely isolated and drained on water side at all times – keep all vents, drains and hand-hole doors open.
- Restart main engine at dead slow or minimum controllable RPM and gradually increase load while strictly monitoring: exhaust gas temperature after economiser (must not exceed manufacturer's limit for dry operation, typically 180–220°C maximum for short periods; never exceed 250°C); funnel for sparks or re-ignition; casing and bulkhead temperatures.
- Operate auxiliary oil-fired boiler continuously to supply 100% of ship's steam demand (FO heating, accommodation, tank cleaning, etc.).
- Establish continuous manned watch in engine room (24 hours) – no UMS operation permitted.
- Regularly inspect economiser gas side (every watch) for hot spots, glowing soot or re-ignition.
- Reduce engine load immediately if any rise in exhaust temperature after economiser is observed.
- Prepare defect report for classification society and port-state authorities at next port.
- Plan permanent repair (tube plugging or renewal) at earliest opportunity – prolonged dry running with leak will cause severe tube erosion and possible catastrophic failure.

**Warning:** Running the main engine with exhaust gases passing through a leaking, dry economiser is an emergency measure only and must be limited to the minimum time necessary to reach a port of refuge or repair.

answers.title: Waste-Heat System — Water/Steam Circulation, Circulating Pump Cooling, Prolonged Low Load, Boiler Water Condition
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to waste heat steam generation systems:

(a) describe, with the aid of a sketch, the economiser circulation system; (5)

(b) explain how the economiser circulation pumps are kept cool; (3)

(c) describe how the boiler water is maintained in a condition which minimises scale formation and (8) system corrosion. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Water/steam circulation system for the waste-heat recovery section (5)**

The system is a composite steam plant consisting of an exhaust gas economiser installed in the main engine uptake and an oil-fired auxiliary boiler sharing a common steam and water drum.

- Feed water is drawn from the feed water tank (atmospheric or pressurised) by the boiler feed pumps.
- Feed water passes through the economiser where it is preheated by main engine exhaust gases (exhaust gas IN → OUT).
- Preheated water leaves the economiser and enters the water side of the auxiliary boiler.
- In the auxiliary boiler, water is heated and boiled by the oil burner when required. Any additional heat required to maintain steam pressure is supplied by firing the auxiliary boiler.
- Saturated steam is taken from the common steam space of the auxiliary boiler and supplied to ship's services (accommodation heating, fuel oil heating, tank cleaning, etc.).
- After use, steam condenses and drains are led to the atmospheric drain tank / hotwell via observing tank and drain condenser.
- A condensate recirculation line with control valve maintains minimum flow through the feed pumps and prevents overheating.
- Make-up water or excess condensate is transferred between the hotwell and the feed water tank to maintain correct level.

**[Sketch]** Composite plant: economiser in ME uptake + oil-fired auxiliary boiler sharing common steam/water drum; feed-water tank, feed pumps, saturated steam to services.

**(b) How the economiser circulation pumps are kept cool (3)**

Modern economiser circulating pumps are canned-motor type (or magnetically-driven sealless type) specifically designed for high-temperature boiler water (up to 160–180°C).

- The pump and electric motor are a single sealed unit – the rotor and impeller are immersed in the pumped water inside a corrosion-resistant stainless-steel can.
- The circulating boiler water itself flows around the motor rotor and stator can, cooling the motor directly and eliminating the need for shaft seals or external cooling.
- Heat from the motor windings is transferred to the circulating water, which then carries it away to the boiler – no separate cooling water system or fan is required.

This design ensures zero leakage, high reliability at high temperature, and prevents cavitation or flashing of the hot water.

**(c) How system steam pressure is maintained at prolonged reduced load (8)**

When the main engine operates at prolonged low load (typically below 30–40% MCR), exhaust gas temperature and mass flow drop significantly, reducing heat transfer in the economiser so the waste heat recovery system alone cannot maintain required steam pressure. The composite system then operates as follows:

- Steam pressure transmitter on the common steam line senses falling pressure and sends a demand signal to the master steam pressure controller.
- The auxiliary oil-fired boiler automatically lights off (or increases firing rate if already running) and supplies the shortfall in steam production, becoming the primary steam generator.
- Economiser circulating pumps remain running continuously at normal speed to maintain forced circulation through the economiser tubes and prevent steaming, hot spots or thermal stress, even though steam generation from exhaust gas is minimal.
- Exhaust gas temperature after economiser drops (often to 130–160°C at low load), increasing the risk of acid dew-point corrosion (sulphuric acid) and heavy soot deposition.
- Soot blowing frequency must be increased (sometimes every 8–12 hours instead of 24–48 hours) to prevent excessive soot build-up, high back pressure and uptake fire risk.
- If an exhaust gas bypass damper is fitted, it may be partially or fully opened at very low loads (<20–25% MCR) to raise exhaust temperature and reduce cold-end corrosion; when fully bypassed the auxiliary boiler supplies 100% of demand.
- Steam pressure is maintained automatically by the auxiliary boiler burner modulating in parallel with the reducing contribution from the waste heat section until full pressure is restored.

Result: normal steam services continue with no loss of pressure, but specific fuel oil consumption rises because the auxiliary boiler now consumes fuel that would otherwise have been "free" waste heat.

*Supplementary source content — boiler water condition (not directly attributed to a marked sub-part on the confirmed October 2022 paper; see note below):*

Boiler water condition is maintained by external pre-treatment of make-up water together with internal chemical treatment, regular testing and blowdown: mixed-bed ion-exchange/mineraliser treatment of make-up water; deaeration to <0.02 ppm O₂; hydrazine or approved oxygen scavenger dosing (15–30 ppb reserve); pH 10.5–11.0 with P-alkalinity 100–200 ppm via caustic soda/coordinated phosphate treatment; phosphate dosing (20–50 ppm) to precipitate hardness as sludge; polymer/starch dispersants to keep solids in suspension; daily testing of pH, alkalinity, phosphate, hydrazine reserve, chloride (<200 ppm) and conductivity/TDS (<1500 µS/cm); bottom and continuous surface blowdown to remove solids and prevent priming/carry-over.

answers.title: Water Hammer — Causes, Avoidance & Port Emission-Compliant Boiler Fuel System
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to boilers and steam generation systems:

(a) explain the term water hammer, stating how it is caused and describing the possible (4) consequences of it;

(b) explain how water hammer can be avoided; (4)

(c) describe, with the aid of a sketch, how the boiler fuel system may be operated in port to comply (8) with local emission control regulations. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) The term water hammer, how it is caused and its possible consequences (4)**

Water hammer occurs when condensate accumulates in steam systems and is then carried along by the steam flow. The steam flow causes ripples in the condensate until waves are formed, then slugs of condensate strike obstacles such as pipe bends, valves, etc. This can result in severe vibration, damaging pipelines, support brackets and causing wear on materials; it can also damage gaskets and valves and cause leakages.

**(b) How water hammer can be avoided (4)**

- Draining condensate regularly, not allowing it to accumulate within systems.
- Efficient steam trap operation.
- Warming through steam systems slowly.
- Avoiding sudden high pressure increases.

**(c) How the boiler fuel system may be operated in port to comply with local emission control regulations (8)**

**[Sketch only in source]** HFO/MDO single-burner fuel supply system with re-circulation (3-way valves, cooler fitted on the MDO return line) — the sketch shows the arrangement for switching the burner supply between HFO and low-sulphur MDO ahead of port/ECA entry, with 3-way changeover valves on supply and return and a cooler on the MDO return line to protect the return-line components from residual heat.

answers.title: Waste-Heat Steam Generating System with Separate Oil-Fired Boiler & ME Exhaust-Gas Economiser
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a waste heat steam generating system incorporating (10) separate oil fired boiler and diesel engine exhaust gas heat recovery unit (economiser).

(b) Explain how the system described in part (a) operates to ensure that the correct steam (6) pressure is maintained during variations in engine load and steam consumption. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Waste-heat steam generating system incorporating a separate oil-fired boiler and diesel-engine exhaust-gas heat-recovery unit (economiser) (10)**

- Distilled water fills the hotwell, which is maintained at 80°C to remove oxygen & prevent thermal shock when entering the boiler.
- Boiler fires to meet steam demand and its water is circulated by pumps through the economiser.
- Here, it is heated by exhaust gas from the running engine.
- Water then returns to the boiler where steam separates, and is fed to consumers.
- Clean condensate returns back to the hotwell via a condenser (cooled by sea water).
- Condensate from oil heaters returns via the observation tank, which allows clear indication of contamination.
- Auto dump valve operates according to steam supply & demand, preventing excessive pressure.
- Cross-connections to/from other boilers & economisers available for isolation and redundancy purposes.

**[Sketch]** Economiser, boiler, circulating pump, condenser, observation tank, hotwell, feed pumps, auto dump valve, cross-connections.

**(b) How the system maintains correct steam pressure during variations in engine load and steam consumption (6)**

During steady condition at 85% load:

- System is normally capable of meeting steam supply from exhaust gas heat recovery alone.

If load drops, or steam demand increases:

- Boiler fires automatically, then load varies to meet the steam demand.

If steam demand drops or too much steam is produced:

- Automatic dump valve opens and regulates, sending excess steam through the dump condenser, returning as condensate to the hotwell.

All of the above operates automatically, with manual control available when required.

**[Sketch]** Steady 85% load, boiler firing on load/demand change, auto dump valve & dump condenser returning condensate to hotwell.

answers.title: Combined Gas/Steam Turbine Waste-Heat Recovery for Electrical Generation
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a waste heat recovery system for electrical generation using (8) main engine exhaust gas in combined gas/steam turbine systems.

(b) Describe the operation of the waste heat recovery system described in part (a) whilst the (8) associated main engine is running. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Waste-heat recovery system for electrical generation using main-engine exhaust gas in combined gas/steam turbine systems (8)**

- System consists of a gas (power) turbine driven by engine exhaust, geared to a steam turbine driven by superheated steam.
- Superheated steam is generated from waste heat recovery — steam produced from the boiler and economiser system.
- Condensate from the steam turbine and excess steam dumps to a condenser.
- Exhaust gas returns to the engine uptake after passing through the gas turbine.
- Turbines are geared to an alternator.

**[Sketch]** Power (gas) turbine driven by ME exhaust geared with a steam turbine driven by superheated steam from boiler/economiser; turbines geared to an alternator; bypass valve to prevent turbo surging at high loads.

**(b) Operation of the system whilst the associated main engine is running (8)**

- Operation is controlled by automatic valves & a control system, regulating the flow of steam and exhaust gas accordingly.
- Only when engine load is high enough can exhaust gas be spared for the power turbine — at lower loads it is needed for the main turbocharger.
- A bypass valve is available for when the turbine is not running, to prevent turbocharger surging at high loads.
