answers.title: Camshaft Chain Drive System — Inspection Process, Possible Defects & Correct Chain Tension
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to the use of camshaft chain drive systems on diesel engines:

(a) describe the inspection process and the possible defects that may be found; (8)

(b) describe how correct chain tension is maintained, stating the effects of incorrect tension. (8) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Inspection process and possible defects that may be found (8)**

With the engine isolated and permit to work and enclosed space entry permit obtained, carry out the inspection as follows:

- The entire length of the chain should be checked, with close inspection of individual links.
- Check the chain for cracks on rollers, which might be caused by overloading or vibration; pitting on rollers may have been caused by deterioration of the lubricating oil.
- Check that the chain rollers can run freely and that the chain links can move freely on the pin and bushing (i.e. not "seized" between the pin and the bushing) — this might be caused by lack of lubrication.
- The tightness of the chain has to be checked. A slack chain will change the injection and exhaust valve timings, causing poor efficiency of the engine; if found slack, tightening should be done according to maker's instructions.
- Check for bright marks on the side plates and wheel sides — caused by misalignment of the chain.
- Inspect the lube oil jet nozzles for possible stoppages or deformations.
- Examine the rubber track of the guideways for cracks or other damage.
- Make a general inspection for loose bolts and screws, which might have been caused by insufficient tightening torque or excessive vibration.
- Check the teeth of the chain wheels; if abnormal wear is found, take measurement.

**(b) How correct chain tension is maintained, and the effects of incorrect tension (8)**

Correct chain tension is maintained by running the engine within limits — i.e. not overloading — and maintaining a routine inspection of the chain drive. The tension is checked by turning the engine with turning gear in the astern direction, so that the longest side of the chain is the slack side. After stopping the turning gear, the chain is pulled back and forth by hand, and the transverse movement should be between 1/2 and 1 link. If outside these limits, adjustment is carried out by tightening or slackening the adjustment nuts on the tensioner.

If the chain tightness is too high, there will be a high load on the chain wheel bearings, leading to early failure; excessive loading on the chain can also lead to excessive wear and damage to the chain links, rollers and sprocket wheel teeth.

If the chain is too slack, the timing of the fuel pump and exhaust valve will change, leading to poor efficiency of the engine. The chain will also vibrate, causing cyclic stress, excessive wear on the sprocket teeth, and can destroy the rubber liner guide bars.

answers.title: Load-Sensing Governor for an Alternator-Driven Auxiliary Diesel Engine — Description, Response to Load Increase & Droop
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to a load sensing governor for an alternator driven by an auxiliary diesel engine:

(a) describe, with the aid of a sketch, such a governor; (8)

(b) describe the action of a governor in response to a large increase in electrical load; (4)

(c) explain EACH of the following:

(i) the necessity for droop; (2)

(ii) how droop is effected. (2) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Description of a load-sensing governor, with a sketch (8)**

**[Sketch]** Mechanical-hydraulic speed-sensing and electro-hydraulic load-sensing governor, labelled: Speeder spring, Ballhead, Centring spring, Needle valve, Receiving piston, H.P. oil supply, Speed pilot valve, Transmitting piston, Speed power valve, Increase-fuel output, Load computer, Load pilot valve, Solenoid, Load power piston.

The governor combines a mechanical-hydraulic speed-sensing element and an electro-hydraulic load-sensing element, and the two sensing elements are independent of each other. Since the load change is sensed prior to any speed change, the primary governing action is achieved by the load-sensing element; in this respect, the speed-sensing element can be considered both a fine-correction facility and a back-up system for the load-sensing element.

**(b) Action of the governor in response to a large increase in electrical load (4)**

During increased load, load sensing is achieved by an electronic computing circuit which controls a solenoid-operated pilot valve in direct proportion to the load change. The measured value may be either an electrical output from the generator or a signal from a torque-measuring circuit.

**(c) (i) The necessity for droop (2)**

Droop is necessary for parallel operation of the machines if stable operation is to be achieved. When two diesel engines are synchronised, either electrically or mechanically (geared), the speeds must obviously be constant with one another.

**(c) (ii) How droop is effected (2)**

As the load on the generator is increased from no load to full load, the actual speed of the engine tends to decrease (droop). To increase the power output in this mode, the engine speed setting is increased, and hence the fuel to the engine is increased.

answers.title: Crankcase Explosion Sequence + Oil Mist Detector Description & Accuracy Check
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe the sequence of events that may lead to a crankcase explosion. (6)

(b) Describe an oil mist detector, explaining how it operates. (8)

(c) State how an oil mist detector operation is checked for accuracy. (2) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Sequence of events leading to a crankcase explosion (6)**

1. **Hot spot formation** — a friction source develops (wiped bearing, ring blow-by, misaligned components), reaching ~200–300°C.
2. **Primary mist formation** — heat vaporises lubricating oil, condensing into a white oil mist that builds up in the crankcase atmosphere.
3. **Flammable mixture** — mist concentration enters the LEL (~40 mg/L) to UEL range, making the atmosphere ignitable.
4. **Primary explosion** — ignition at the hot spot causes a moderate-pressure deflagration; crankcase relief valves lift and vent the burning gases.
5. **Secondary (major) explosion** — fresh air rushes back in through the relief valves as pressure drops, mixing with remaining rich mist for a far more violent explosion — this causes structural damage, blown-off crankcase doors, and fatalities.

**(b) Oil mist detector — description and operation (8)**

**[Sketch]** Oil Mist Detector — rotating sampling disc feeds each bay in turn; measuring tube (mist) compared optically against a clean-air reference tube via photo-electric cells.

Sampling pipes lead from multiple crankcase compartments to a rotating sampling disc/sequential valve, drawing samples via an extraction pump. A reference cell (clean air) and measuring cell (crankcase sample) are compared optically: a light source projects a beam through the sample; oil mist particles scatter/attenuate the light; a photoelectric detector measures the reduction in intensity versus the reference, expressed as % obscuration. When this exceeds the alarm threshold (~2.5% or as set), an alarm triggers, with visual/audible alarm on bridge and engine room, automatic slowdown/shutdown on modern systems, and identification of the affected compartment via sequential sampling. Additional features: self-monitoring for lamp failure/blocked pipes, and temperature compensation to avoid false alarms from normal mist levels.

**(c) Checking OMD accuracy (2)**

A calibrated test filter (neutral density filter of known obscuration value) is inserted into the optical path; the reading is checked against the known filter value, which must fall within manufacturer tolerance. Some detectors have a built-in test button simulating a set obscuration level electronically to verify alarm activation, confirming the alarm set point triggers at the correct threshold.

answers.title: Crankshaft Deflections — Why Taken, Procedure & Out-of-Limit Action
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain why crankshaft deflections are taken. (4)

(b) Write a procedure for the taking of main engine crankshaft deflections. (8)

(c) Explain the action to be taken if some crankshaft deflection readings are outside acceptable (4) limits. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why crankshaft deflections are taken (4)**

To check crankshaft alignment — detecting hogging, sagging, or athwartship misalignment of main bearings; to identify worn/damaged main bearings causing the crankshaft to drop; to prevent crankshaft fatigue cracking or failure from excessive bending stress; and to confirm alignment is within builder's/class limits — required periodically and after dry-docking, grounding, or heavy weather.

**(b) Procedure for taking main engine crankshaft deflections (8)**

*Preparation*: obtain the builder's deflection record and acceptable limits; shut down the engine, engage turning gear, isolate starting air, issue a permit to work; confirm engine temperature (warm readings preferred); fit the dial gauge into the split-pin hole at each crank web cheek, correctly zeroed.

*Taking readings (per unit)*: rotate to BDC — zero/note the reading (B1); rotate to port (90°) — record P; rotate to TDC — record T; rotate to starboard (270°) — record S; return to BDC — note reading (B2); repeat for every crank unit in sequence.

*Recording*: record readings as +/- relative to the BDC reference; calculate vertical deflection T−(B1+B2)/2 (sagging/hogging) and horizontal deflection P−S (athwartship); compare against class-approved limits and previous trend records.

**(c) Action if readings are outside acceptable limits (4)**

Do not operate the engine — risk of crankshaft cracking or bearing failure. Notify the Chief Engineer, Class Surveyor and ship's management. Investigate the probable cause: worn/damaged/wiped main bearing (inspect and renew); soft foot or shifted engine seating (check and re-chock); hull deflection (verify loading/ballast condition, re-measure afloat and in dock). Drop the relevant main bearing keep and measure clearances with feeler gauge/lead wire. After remedial work, re-take deflections to confirm return within limits before restarting, and record all findings in the engine log and Class survey report.

answers.title: Report — Bottom-End Bearing Check After High-Temperature Alarm & Return to Full Service
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer, write a report for the engineering superintendent regarding the checking of (16) a bottom end bearing on a crosshead type main diesel engine, after a high temperature alarm was activated at sea, and the subsequent return to full service of the engine. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Report on checking a bottom-end bearing on a crosshead main diesel engine after a high-temperature alarm, and return to full service (16)**

**1. Incident details**: high-temperature alarm on the unit's bottom-end bearing LO outlet; alarm set point and recorded temperature noted; vessel position/weather logged; Master informed, logged in Engine Room and Deck Logs.

**2. Immediate actions**: engine speed reduced progressively (Full Away → Slow Ahead → Dead Slow); standby generator online, electrical load transferred; LO parameters checked; engine stopped when temperature kept rising, turning gear engaged.

**3. Pre-entry checks & safety**: crankcase ventilated per maker's instructions, allowed to cool to safe entry level; enclosed-space entry procedure followed (O₂/HC/CO tested); risk assessment and permit to work issued; non-sparking tools used, extinguisher stationed.

**4. Crankcase inspection**: doors opened, interior inspected for overheating/wiping/mist residue; affected bearing cap removed; shell surfaces inspected for wiping/scoring/overlay loss; crankpin journal inspected for scoring/blueing; oil feed hole checked for blockage; clearance measured (feeler gauge) and shell thickness measured (micrometer).

**5. Findings & root cause**: minor wiping on the lower shell; slight, repairable crankpin scoring; oil feed hole partially blocked with carbonised deposit — restricted LO flow, elevated friction, and thermal alarm activation; no crack/fracture found.

**6. Remedial actions**: feed hole cleared (approved cleaning agent, compressed air); oil passages flushed and confirmed clear; wiped shell renewed as a matched pair; crankpin polished and re-measured; new shells fitted with clearance confirmed to maker's data; cap torqued to spec in sequence; locking device fitted.

**7. Post-repair checks**: crankcase confirmed clean, all tools/materials accounted for, doors secured; turned on turning gear for abnormal noise/resistance check; slow-turned on air; LO primed, temperature/flow monitored; started on low load, run at slow/half ahead, re-entered after initial run for a satisfactory re-check.

**8. Return to full service**: progressively loaded per maker's running-in procedure; Full Away resumed after graduated loading with all parameters (bearing temp, LO pressure, EGT, cylinder pressures) confirmed normal.

**9. Recommendations**: LO filters/strainers cleaned and inspected at next port; increased crankcase inspection frequency as precaution; all unit oil feed holes inspected at next scheduled maintenance; LO analysis records reviewed; incident reported under ISM Code non-conformity/near-miss system.

**10. Supporting documents**: Engine Room Log extract, bearing clearance record, torque record sheet, LO outlet temperature trend, enclosed-space entry permit, risk assessment, PMS job card, photograph record.

answers.title: Two Automatic Slowdown + Two Automatic Shutdown Parameters, With Testing
answers.answer_text:
**(a) TWO automatic slowdown parameters (4)**

- **Low lubricating oil pressure (main/crosshead)**: applied to reduce engine load and bearing friction heat before seizure occurs, giving time to investigate without a full shutdown.
- **High jacket cooling water (JCW) temperature**: applied to reduce heat input from combustion, allowing the cooling system to recover and preventing liner cracking, piston seizure, or thermal stress damage.

**(b) TWO automatic shutdown parameters (4)**

- **Crankshaft overspeed**: exceeding ~10–15% above MCR RPM risks catastrophic mechanical failure of con-rods, crankshaft and pistons — immediate fuel cut-off is the only safe response.
- **Low-low lubricating oil pressure**: pressure falling critically below the slowdown set-point indicates imminent bearing failure — shutdown prevents crankshaft/bearing seizure and engine destruction.

**(c) Testing each parameter for correct operation (8)**

- *Slowdown — low LO pressure*: throttle the LO supply valve gradually, or use the pressure transmitter's test cock, or the AMS/IAS simulation function, to simulate falling pressure. Confirm alarm activates → slowdown signal → engine reduces to preset RPM; restore pressure and reset.
- *Slowdown — high JCW temperature*: use the temperature transmitter/AMS test function (or a calibrator at low load). Confirm alarm → slowdown command → RPM reduces; restore cooling flow and reset.
- *Shutdown — overspeed*: with the engine stopped/dead slow, manually actuate the mechanical overspeed trip (test button on governor) or simulate via the electronic safety-system test panel without raising actual RPM. Confirm fuel cuts off immediately, engine stops, alarm/shutdown logged; reset trip and confirm the engine won't restart until manually reset.
- *Shutdown — low-low LO pressure*: continue reducing pressure past the slowdown set-point (test cock or AMS simulation) to the shutdown set-point. Confirm shutdown signal → fuel cut-off → engine stops, logged on AMS; restore pressure and verify a manual reset is required before restart.

answers.title: Minimising Scavenge Residue Buildup + Scavenge-Fire Damage
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain how the build up of residue in the scavenge space of a large slow speed two stroke (10) engine is minimised by design, operation and maintenance.

(b) Explain the possible damage which could be caused by a scavenge fire. (6) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Minimising residue buildup in the scavenge space by design, operation and maintenance (10)**

*Sources of residue*: cylinder oil blow-past from worn rings; crankcase oil migrating up the piston rod past the stuffing box; condensate from scavenge air coolers; carbon particles and unburnt fuel.

*By design*: piston rod stuffing box fitted with scraper/wiper rings preventing crankcase oil migrating upward, with a drain-back arrangement to sump; scavenge box with self-draining pipes and water-seal traps; moisture separators after scavenge air coolers; scavenge spaces enclosed by diaphragm plates to contain drainage zones.

*By operation*: maintain correct cylinder lubrication feed rates (avoid over-lubrication); control scavenge air temperature (higher temp reduces condensation); maintain correct fuel injection to prevent dribbling/poor atomisation; avoid prolonged low-load/slow-steaming (promotes incomplete combustion and blow-past); monitor stuffing box drain quantity/appearance; clear scavenge drains during watches.

*By maintenance*: periodically inspect/clean scavenge spaces via access covers; clear scavenge ports of carbon deposits; renew worn piston rings; renew stuffing box seals/scraper rings at recommended intervals; clean air coolers and renew moisture-trap elements; inspect/clear scavenge drain piping.

**(b) Damage caused by a scavenge fire (6)**

Stuffing box damage (seals/scraper rings burned, crankcase no longer protected); piston rod damage (scoring, distortion, loss of surface hardness); piston rings seizing in grooves (blow-past, liner damage); scavenge trunk/diaphragm distortion from sustained heat; scavenge relief valves lifting (engine room fire risk if venting there); air cooler element damage (fouling/corrosion from heat and soot); turbocharger damage (contaminated hot air degrading blading, possible surging); crankcase explosion risk (if fire penetrates the stuffing box, hot gases/burning oil enter the crankcase); bearing damage (heat conducted through the piston rod degrading crosshead/bottom-end bearing lubricant film).

answers.title: Oil Mist Alarm — Full Procedure From Activation to Return to Normal Operation
answers.question_as_set: Write a procedure for the actions to be taken in the event of an engine oil mist detector alarm (16) being activated, stating the reasons for EACH action. The procedure must cover the period from activation of the alarm to return of the engine to normal operation. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Procedure for actions on activation of an engine oil mist alarm, covering activation to return to normal operation, with reasons for each action (16)**

**Phase 1 — Immediate actions on activation**: inform the bridge immediately (so they can reduce speed/manoeuvre clear/prepare for propulsion loss); reduce engine load/speed (lowers crankcase pressure differential and mist-generation rate, reducing explosion risk); activate slow-turn/standby (safe transition, no sudden shutdown); identify the triggered OMD cell (localises the fault to a compartment); do NOT open crankcase doors (hot mist + oxygen = explosion risk — allow cooling first).

**Phase 2 — Controlled shutdown**: stop the engine (eliminates continued mist generation and heat source); keep LO circulating pumps running (continues cooling bearings/running gear, prevents seizure, removes heat from the hot spot); keep turning gear engaged after stopping (prevents shaft bow, allows even cooling); allow a minimum 20 minutes cooling (ensures mist disperses, no hot spot capable of ignition remains); post a fire watch/have CO2 ready (precaution in case of crankcase fire on opening).

**Phase 3 — Inspection of crankcase**: check for white smoke/smell before opening (indicates internal fire/continued vaporisation); open doors carefully and partially at first (pressure equalisation — sudden full opening risks flashback); inspect the identified bay for overheated/wiped bearings, discoloured/scored crankpin or journal, excessive carbonisation or burnt smell, damaged piston/con-rod.

**Phase 4 — Fault rectification**: record findings in the engine log (ISM Code defect reporting/root cause analysis); renew or recondition the damaged bearing (removes the mist-generating heat source); check the LO system (sample for contamination, verify pressure/cooling to the affected bearing); inspect and clean OMD cells (oil deposits cause spurious alarms — must be verified clean and functional before restart); verify crankcase relief valves are operational (last line of defence against crankcase explosion; SOLAS requires them in good order).

**Phase 5 — Return to normal operation**: test the OMD and confirm no alarm; start on no-load/slow speed, monitoring oil pressure, temperature and OMD readings before loading; gradually increase to normal RPM, watching OMD, bearing and exhaust temperatures at each step; inform the bridge the engine is available; complete the defect/near-miss report (required under ISM Code SMS, triggering a PMS review of the OMD and bearings).

answers.title: Fatigue — S/N Curve for Steel, Design Avoidance & Poor Maintenance/Operation Causes
answers.answer_text:
**(a) S/N curve for steel, with fatigue limit and two stress-cycle conditions (4)**

**[Graph]** S/N (Wöhler) curve — Curve A = steel with a clear Endurance Limit (Sₑ); Curve B = non-ferrous material with no defined endurance limit; two representative stress-cycle conditions marked on Curve A (one at ~10⁴ cycles/high stress/short life, one at the endurance plateau ~10⁶–10⁷ cycles).

**(b) Designing to avoid fatigue failure using the S/N curve (4)**

The endurance limit (Sₑ) is identified as the stress level below which steel endures infinite cycles without failure; the component is designed so maximum operating stress stays below Sₑ with an adequate safety factor. Stress concentration factors (notches, keyways, holes) are accounted for so actual local stress still falls below Sₑ. For a finite design life, the corresponding fatigue strength at that cycle count is read off the curve and operating stress kept below it. Surface finish, heat treatment and material selection are chosen to raise fatigue strength, effectively lifting the S/N curve.

**(c) How poor maintenance and operation cause fatigue failure below the design limit (8)**

*Poor maintenance*: corrosion/pitting (surface pits act as stress raisers, pushing local stress above Sₑ even if nominal stress is below it); fretting corrosion (micro-movement at joints/bearings removing protective oxide, creating crack sites); improper fastening tightness (loose bolts introduce unaccounted cyclic bending); worn/misaligned bearings (added dynamic loads and vibration); undetected cracks (propagate under cyclic load, extreme stress concentration at the crack tip); inadequate lubrication (increased friction/heat/surface damage initiating cracks).

*Poor operation*: overloading (pushes stress above the endurance limit); running at/near critical/resonant speed (vibration amplification, dynamic stresses far exceeding steady-state design values); frequent start/stop cycles (each is a high-stress cycle — fatigue accumulates faster per Miner's Rule if underestimated in design); shock loading/water hammer (transient stress spikes on top of the cyclic baseline); thermal cycling (thermal stresses combine with mechanical cyclic stress, accelerating crack growth); operating in a corrosive environment without protection (corrosion fatigue significantly lowers the effective endurance limit used in design).

answers.title: Fatigue — S/N Curve Relationship, Stress Raiser Definition & Fatigue Limit
answers.question_as_set:
(a) With the aid of sketches, explain the term "fatigue" as applicable to engineering components. (12) State what is meant by the term "fatigue limit".

(b) Explain the term "stress raiser" with respect to fatigue, giving THREE examples and stating (4) how stress raisers reduce the fatigue life of a component. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) S/N curve — relationship between applied stress and cycles to failure (5)**

The S/N (Wöhler) curve plots stress amplitude (S) against cycles to failure (N, log scale) — as applied stress increases, cycles-to-failure decrease (inverse relationship). Curve A (ferrous metals, e.g. steel) flattens at the Endurance Limit (Sₑ), below which the material can theoretically withstand infinite cycles. Curve B (non-ferrous, e.g. aluminium, copper) never flattens — fatigue strength is instead quoted at a specific cycle count (N₁). Crack propagation follows three stages: initiation → propagation → final fracture, all driven by cyclic stress above the endurance/fatigue limit.

**(b) Stress raiser — definition, examples, influence on crack propagation (5)**

A stress raiser (stress concentrator) is a geometric discontinuity or surface irregularity causing localised stress amplification far exceeding nominal stress. Examples: keyways, splines, shaft shoulders; holes, notches, grooves; corrosion pits and surface scratches; weld toes/undercuts; threaded sections (bolt roots); sharp internal corners/insufficient fillet radius. Stress at the raiser tip can be 2–4× (or more) the nominal stress (Stress Concentration Factor, Kt); fatigue cracks almost always initiate at a raiser, and once initiated, the crack tip itself becomes a new stress raiser, accelerating propagation until sudden fracture. Smooth, well-radiused transitions and polished surfaces reduce Kt and extend fatigue life significantly.

**(c) Fatigue limit definition, and how poor maintenance/operation cause cracking below the design limit (6)**

The Fatigue (Endurance) Limit is the maximum stress amplitude below which a ferrous material can endure infinite cycles without failure — but a component designed below it assumes ideal, unchanging conditions.

*Poor maintenance*: corrosion/corrosion fatigue (can reduce the fatigue limit by 25–50% in a corrosive environment like seawater); fretting corrosion at press-fitted/bolted interfaces (removes the protective oxide layer); worn/loose bearings (shaft whip and vibration adding unplanned cyclic bending); inadequate lubrication (surface wear, heat, micro-cracks); improper repairs (weld repairs without stress relief introducing residual tensile stress and weld-toe raisers).

*Poor operation*: running at critical speed/resonance (dynamic stresses many times nominal, far exceeding the endurance limit); overloading/shock loading (a single overload event can initiate a crack that normal cyclic loading then propagates); thermal cycling/thermal fatigue (repeated heating/cooling adding cyclic thermal stress); propeller cavitation (high-frequency stress fluctuations from bubble collapse); misalignment (additional cyclic bending moment every revolution, raising effective stress amplitude above design value).

answers.title: Crankcase Oil Mist Eliminator/Oil Box + Trunk-Piston Crankcase LO Properties & Maintenance
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe the purpose of a diesel engine crankcase oil mist eliminator / oil box, explaining how (6) such a system operates.

(b) Describe, with reasons, the properties required of a trunk piston diesel engine crankcase (10) lubrication oil stating how the LO is maintained in good condition over an operating period. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Purpose and operation of a crankcase oil mist eliminator/oil box (6)**

The crankcase contains oil mist, vapour and air from churning rotating parts and hot surfaces; if mist concentration reaches the LEL, an ignition source (hot bearing/spot) can cause a crankcase explosion. The eliminator removes oil mist particles from the crankcase atmosphere, keeping concentration below explosive levels and preventing pressure build-up.

Operation: a motor-driven extraction fan continuously draws crankcase gases through the system; gases pass through a coalescing/demisting element (mesh pads, baffles, or centrifugal separator) where oil droplets coalesce and drain back to the sump; cleaned air is discharged back into the crankcase (closed loop) or to a safe external location; a flame trap/gauze at inlet and outlet prevents flame propagation on ignition; a separately-fitted OMD triggers alarm and automatic slowdown/shutdown if mist rises above threshold; the oil box/drain pot collects separated oil, draining back to the sump by gravity.

**(b) Properties required of trunk-piston crankcase LO, and maintaining it in good condition (10)**

*Properties and reasons*: correct viscosity (SAE 30–40, forms a hydrodynamic film across the operating temperature range — too thin causes film breakdown, too thick causes poor circulation/pumping losses); high viscosity index (minimises viscosity change cold-start to full load); detergency (keeps combustion deposits/carbon/lacquer in suspension); dispersancy (keeps soot/contaminants finely dispersed for filter removal rather than agglomerating into sludge); alkalinity/TBN (neutralises acidic combustion by-products blowing past rings, matched to fuel sulphur content); anti-wear/EP additives (protect bearing and cam/follower surfaces under boundary lubrication); oxidation resistance (inhibits oxidation from high crankcase temperature, 80–90°C); corrosion inhibitors (protect bearing metals from acidic attack); anti-foam additives (prevent aeration from churning, which weakens the oil film); good demulsibility (sheds water from condensation/coolant leaks rather than emulsifying).

*Maintaining LO condition*: regular sampling/analysis (viscosity, TBN, water content, metal particles, soot/insolubles — trend monitoring); continuous filtration (full-flow 10–25µm filters plus bypass depth filters, changed on condition/hours); centrifugal purification (continuous slip-stream removal of water, sludge, fine particles); LO temperature control (thermostatic cooler, ~40–45°C inlet to bearings — excess temperature accelerates oxidation/viscosity loss); water detection/removal (crackle test/sampling, purifier removal of free water); top-up with correct grade only; monitoring TBN (renewal if it drops below half the new-oil value or maker's limit); crankcase inspections (sludge, strainer condition, dilution signs); oil renewal based on condition monitoring or running-hour interval, whichever is sooner, with the crankcase flushed before refilling.

answers.title: Torsional Vibration Causes/Effects + Critical Speed + Fatigue Cracking Factors
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to diesel engine crankshafts:

(a) explain the causes and effects of torsional vibration; (4)

(b) explain the term critical speed, stating why the engine should not be continuously operated at (6) this speed;

(c) explain the term fatigue cracking, stating, with reasons, TWO factors which have an influence (6) on the likelihood of fatigue cracking. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Causes and effects of torsional vibration (4)**

*Causes*: each power stroke applies a sudden, periodic torque impulse to the crankshaft; the elastic crankshaft twists and untwists with each impulse (torsional oscillation); when impulse frequency matches the shaft system's natural frequency, resonance amplifies the vibration; multi-cylinder engines produce multiple impulse sources that can combine and reinforce.

*Effects*: cyclic stress reversals causing fatigue cracking at stress-concentration points (fillets, oil holes); excessive vibration risking crankshaft fracture; damage to coupling, flywheel and driven machinery (pumps, alternators); gear tooth damage on timing/PTO drives.

**(b) Critical speed — definition and why continuous operation must be avoided (6)**

Critical speed is the engine speed at which torsional impulse frequency coincides with the natural frequency of the crankshaft-flywheel system, causing resonance — energy is fed into the vibration at the same rate it oscillates, so amplitude builds rapidly since system damping (oil films, friction) can't absorb the input. Continuous operation must be avoided because oscillation amplitude is greatly magnified, stress levels far exceed design limits, and prolonged running causes crankshaft fatigue failure. Critical speeds are identified by the maker and marked as barred/restricted ranges on the telegraph/governor — brief transit through is permitted, but sustained running within the barred range is prohibited.

**(c) Fatigue cracking — definition and two influencing factors (6)**

Fatigue cracking is progressive crack growth under repeated cyclic loading at stress below the material's ultimate tensile strength: initiation at a stress concentration → slow propagation with each cycle → sudden brittle fracture.

*Factor 1 — stress concentration points*: oil holes, fillet radii, keyways and surface defects create localised stress amplification; cracks always initiate here. Sharper fillets or rough finish raise stress concentration and fatigue risk — makers specify minimum fillet radii and surface finish to reduce it.

*Factor 2 — mean stress level/engine loading*: higher mean stress (combustion loads, firing pressure, misalignment) raises the working stress range; per the Goodman diagram, higher mean stress reduces the allowable alternating stress before fatigue occurs. Overloading or a bent/misaligned crankshaft increases mean stress, accelerating crack propagation; poor main bearing alignment concentrates bending stress at specific journals, compounding the risk.

answers.title: Torsional Vibration Definition/Effects + Engine Deterioration Risk + TV-Alarm Reasons
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Define the term Torsional Vibration with respect to an engine crankshaft, stating the effect that (6) high levels can have on an engine crankshaft.

(b) Explain how engine deterioration influences the risk of Torsional Vibration, stating what can be (4) done to minimise that risk.

(c) Explain TWO possible reasons for the activation of a Torsional Vibration alarm after an engine (6) has been started if there had been no previous history of such an alarm and if no maintenance had been undertaken on the engine whilst it was stopped. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Torsional vibration — definition and effects on the crankshaft (6)**

Torsional vibration is the oscillatory twisting/untwisting of the crankshaft about its longitudinal axis, caused by cyclic, uneven torque impulses from successive power strokes; between impulses the crankshaft elastically springs back, superimposing torsional oscillation on normal rotation. Resonance occurs when impulse frequency matches the crankshaft's natural torsional frequency, greatly amplifying twist amplitude.

Effects of high torsional vibration: fatigue cracking at stress concentrations (fillet radii, oil drillings, crankpin/journal transitions); crankshaft fracture (often sudden, at crankpin or main journal fillets); severe bearing damage from fluctuating dynamic loads; damage to the torsional vibration damper; damage to flexible couplings, PTO drives and driven machinery.

**(b) How engine deterioration increases TV risk, and minimisation measures (4)**

Deterioration effects: worn injectors/pumps (poor atomisation/mistimed injection → uneven combustion torque impulses → increased excitation); worn rings/liner (blow-past → uneven cylinder pressures → torque imbalance); misfiring cylinders (irregular impulse pattern, higher excitation amplitude); degraded/worn TV damper (reduced damping, increased resonance amplitude).

Minimisation: regular indicator card analysis (confirm even cylinder power distribution); maintain fuel injection equipment in good condition; scheduled TV damper inspection/replacement; observe barred speed ranges; maintain flexible coupling elements.

**(c) TWO reasons for a TV alarm activating after start with no prior history and no maintenance during the stop (6)**

- **Change in fuel oil grade/quality (bunkered while stopped)**: a different fuel batch (viscosity, density, ignition quality) alters combustion characteristics and torque impulse profile, potentially exciting a torsional resonance mode not previously encountered.
- **Propeller fouling or damage during the stop**: marine growth, debris, or impact damage alters the mass-elastic system of the shafting (effective inertia of the driven end), shifting the natural torsional frequency into resonance with the firing impulse frequency at normal operating speed.

answers.title: Secondary Crankcase Explosion Sequence + CEO Management to Minimise Risk & Effects
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to main engine crankcase explosions:

(a) explain the sequence of events leading to a secondary crankcase explosion; (6)

(b) as Chief Engineer Officer, explain how an engine should be managed in order to minimise the (10) risk of a crankcase explosion and the effects of a crankcase explosion should one occur. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Sequence of events leading to a secondary crankcase explosion (6)**

1. **Hot spot formation** — overheated bearing, piston/liner seizure, or defective piston rod gland; contacting LO vaporises into fine oil mist.
2. **Primary explosion** — mist concentration rises within the LEL and ignites at the hot spot, a small primary explosion consuming oxygen and creating a localised pressure surge; crankcase relief doors lift and reseat momentarily.
3. **Conditions for secondary explosion** — the opening of relief doors draws fresh air (oxygen) back in while hot, partially-burned oil residue and fresh mist are still present, re-entering the explosive range.
4. **Secondary explosion** — a far larger, more violent explosion occurs; relief doors may fail to contain the blast; burning gases and flame are ejected outward, causing structural damage and crew casualties — the principal cause of severe crankcase casualties.

**(b) Management as Chief Engineer Officer — minimising risk and managing effects (10)**

*Minimising risk — monitoring/detection*: maintain and regularly test the OMD (calibrate per maker's instructions, never bypass alarms); continuous bearing temperature monitoring; monitor piston cooling oil outlet temperature (rise indicates a developing hot spot); regular crankcase inspections at anchorage/slow speed (bearing clearances, dipper clearances, piston rod gland blow-past).

*Maintenance*: maintain crankcase ventilation (slight negative pressure, clean flame traps); ensure relief doors are in good condition, move freely and reseat correctly; maintain piston rod gland packing (prevents hot gas ingress); keep LO in correct condition (sampled, correct viscosity/cleanliness); prevent excessive crankcase oil spray.

*Operational practices*: never ignore OMD alarms — treat every alarm as genuine until proven otherwise; investigate and rectify abnormal running parameters promptly; train crew in crankcase explosion procedure.

*Managing the effects if an explosion occurs*: on OMD alarm/explosion indication, immediately reduce to dead slow or stop; do NOT open crankcase doors (secondary explosion risk); sound the general alarm, muster crew, keep personnel clear of the doors; allow at least 20 minutes cooling before any approach; ensure no personnel stand in front of relief doors (they operate automatically to vent pressure); after safe cooling, cautiously crack open doors with CO2 extinguisher ready; identify and isolate the hot spot before any restart attempt; enter the crankcase only after enclosed-space entry procedures; report the incident under ISM Code (non-conformity/near-miss) and to flag state authority.

answers.title: CEO Standing Instructions — High-Temperature Scavenge Alarm During UMS Operation
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer, write instructions for the actions to be taken in the event of a high (16) temperature scavenge alarm being activated, due to a rapid rise in temperature, during a period of UMS operation, stating the reasons for EACH action. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Standing instructions for actions on a high-temperature scavenge alarm (rapid rise) during UMS operation, with reasons for each action (16)**

*Immediate actions*: acknowledge the alarm and proceed to the ECR (UMS means no watchkeeper is present — the on-call engineer must attend immediately to assess severity); inform the Bridge, requesting reduced engine load/speed (lowers combustion pressure and heat input, limiting scavenge fire spread and further temperature rise); cancel UMS mode and man the engine room (the situation requires continuous human monitoring).

*Investigative actions*: identify the affected unit(s) from the alarm panel (localises the problem); carefully check scavenge inspection covers from a safe distance for smoke/sparks/oil mist (confirms whether a scavenge fire is present); check indicator cocks and bar the engine slowly if safe (detects blow-past of combustion gases into the scavenge space); inspect turbocharger and air cooler outlet temperatures (elevated charge air temperature can raise scavenge trunk temperature — faulty cooler or fouled T/C may be the root cause); check cylinder exhaust temperatures for the affected unit (high EGT indicates poor combustion/late injection/faulty injector causing afterburning into the scavenge space); check crankcase OMD readings (scavenge fire can transfer heat to the crankcase — early mist detection prevents explosion risk).

*If scavenge fire is confirmed*: shut cylinder lubrication to the affected unit (removes a combustible fuel source); increase scavenge air flow if possible without opening inspection covers (starves the fire of oxygen — opening covers introduces fresh air and risks flare-up); activate a fixed smothering system or inject steam if fitted; cut off fuel to the affected unit; continue running at reduced load to maintain airflow through the scavenge space (sudden stop traps heat and gases, worsening the situation).

*Post-incident/recovery*: allow cooling before opening inspection covers (prevents rush of air into a hot space causing re-ignition/flare-back); inspect for damage (burnt deposits, ring condition, ports, diaphragm seals); log the event and raise a Non-Conformity Report under ISM Code; notify the Company/DPA and flag state if damage is significant (statutory obligation under SOLAS/ISM).

*Common root causes to investigate*: blow-past of piston rings (high EGT + crankcase mist); faulty fuel injector (irregular combustion, high EGT); excess cylinder lubrication (oil accumulation in the scavenge space); fouled/choked scavenge ports (restricted airflow, uneven temperatures); defective air cooler (elevated charge air temperature).

answers.answer_text:
**(a) Standing instructions for the watchkeeping engineer — failure of the engine room monitoring and alarm system (8)**

*Immediate actions*: notify the Chief Engineer and Master immediately; inform the OOW on the bridge; log the time and nature of the failure in the Engine Room Log.

*Manning/watchkeeping*: revert to manual watchkeeping (continuous engine room attendance); post additional watchkeepers as directed; suspend UMS/AMS operation until restored.

*Monitoring*: manually check and record all critical parameters at regular intervals (minimum every 30 minutes or as directed) — main/auxiliary engine temperatures, pressures, RPM; boiler levels/pressures; bilge levels; fuel oil and LO pressures/temperatures — using local gauges, sight glasses and thermometers.

*Safety*: maintain a strict fire and flooding watch; never leave the engine room unattended; monitor all alarms locally.

*Communication/documentation*: report system status to the Chief Engineer regularly; record all manual readings; inform the Chief Engineer immediately of any parameter deviation.

*Restoration*: do not attempt repairs beyond competence; the system must be fully tested and certified restored before reverting to UMS, with Chief Engineer sign-off required.

**(b) Procedure for repeated activation of an OMD alarm (8)**

*First activation*: reduce engine load/speed immediately; notify the bridge (request permission to reduce speed/stop); notify the Chief Engineer.

*On repeated activation*: shut down the main engine — do not continue running; engage turning gear once at rest, do not enter the crankcase immediately; allow at least 20 minutes cooling; maintain forced ventilation if fitted, keep crankcase doors closed during this period; keep ignition sources clear.

*Investigation (after cooling)*: open crankcase doors carefully, standing clear of the opening; inspect all bearings (main, crankpin, crosshead) for overheating signs (blued/wiped metal, carbonisation); check crankcase oil mist concentration with a portable detector if available; identify the hot bearing or defective component; check the OMD unit itself for contamination or malfunction (dirty sampling tubes, faulty detector head).

*Rectification*: if a hot bearing/defect is found, do not restart until repaired; if the OMD unit is faulty, replace/clean and re-test to ensure a genuine fault isn't masked; record findings and notify the Chief Engineer.

*Restart conditions*: only restart on the Chief Engineer's authority; continuous manual monitoring of the crankcase area during initial restart; increase load gradually, monitoring OMD readings closely.

answers.title: Balance Weights (Medium-Speed Engine) — Purpose, Maintenance Checks & Composite Pistons
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain, with the aid of sketches, the purpose of balance weights fitted to the crankshaft of a (8) medium speed engine.

(b) Describe the maintenance checks required for detachable balance weights. (4)

(c) Explain why composite pistons may be fitted to medium speed engines, stating the reasons for (4) the materials used. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Purpose of balance weights fitted to a medium-speed crankshaft (8)**

**[Sketch]** Balance weight positioned diametrically opposite the crankpin; its centrifugal force resolves into a vertical component Vc (opposing the primary inertia force F1) and a horizontal component Hc (a residual, unavoidable trade-off).

The crankshaft has rotating unbalanced masses (crankpin, crank webs, big-end bearing) and reciprocating unbalanced masses (piston assembly, upper con-rod), the latter generating primary (1st order) and secondary (2nd order) inertia forces. Balance weights, positioned diametrically opposite the crankpin, fully counteract the rotating masses and partially counteract the primary reciprocating inertia force — the weight's centrifugal force splits into a vertical component (opposing the primary force) and an unavoidable residual horizontal component; a single counterweight cannot fully balance reciprocating forces without introducing this new horizontal imbalance. Without balance weights: high main bearing loads and accelerated wear, excessive vibration transmitted to the hull/structure, crankshaft/bedplate fatigue cracking, and increased noise. Multi-cylinder crank-throw arrangement also helps forces/couples from different cylinders cancel each other.

**(b) Maintenance checks for detachable balance weights (4)**

Fastening bolts (check torque to spec, inspect for stretch/thread damage, replace stretch bolts exceeding limits); locking arrangements (lock wire, tab washers, thread-locking devices — renew every overhaul); mating/contact faces (check for fretting corrosion, scoring, micro-movement marks); NDT inspection (dye penetrant or MPI on the weight body and fastening holes for cracks); dowels/keys (check wear, deformation, looseness); mass verification (weigh and confirm against the stamped/recorded value — no material added or removed); correct reassembly (refit in the same marked position/orientation).

**(c) Composite pistons in medium-speed engines — why, and material reasons (4)**

A composite piston joins a steel/nodular cast iron crown to an aluminium alloy skirt/body. Crown material reasons: exposed to high combustion temperature (~400–450°C) and pressure — steel retains strength at temperature, resists thermal fatigue/cracking, allows machining of an oil cooling gallery, and better resists ring-groove wear under high ring loads. Skirt material reasons: aluminium is lightweight (reduces reciprocating mass, hence inertia forces and bearing loads — critical at medium-speed RPM), has good thermal conductivity and bearing properties against the liner, and is cost-effective/easy to machine. Composite rather than single material: aluminium alone can't withstand crown temperatures (would soften/crack/suffer ring-groove collapse); steel alone would be too heavy (raising inertia loads, bearing wear and vibration) — the composite gives crown thermal strength plus skirt low mass, with differential thermal expansion accounted for in the joint design.

answers.title: Cylinder Liner Calibration, Two Forms of Abnormal Wear & Prevention
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe a procedure for cylinder liner calibration, indicating how the readings are recorded to (6) allow for easy recognition of liner wear.

(b) Describe TWO forms of abnormal cylinder liner wear, explaining how EACH is recognised. (6)

(c) Explain how abnormal cylinder liner wear may be prevented. (4) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Procedure for liner calibration, and how readings are recorded (6)**

**[Sketch]** Calibration tool & template in the liner — liner template with holes; liner calibration gauge.

Gauge at regular intervals per the maintenance manual; keep records per cylinder and calculate wear rate. Clean and inspect the liner before gauging. Liner and micrometer must be at the same temperature, or a correction factor is applied. Measure using a standard template with strategically positioned holes — the micrometer is placed in each hole for readings at fixed heights, taking Port–Starboard and Forward–Aft measurements at every position; the difference between directions gives ovality. Wear is greatest in the top one-third (highest combustion temperature and pressure). Normal rate is approximately 0.1mm/1000 hours, rising if overloaded; renew the liner at approximately 0.6–0.8% of bore, or per maker's limit.

**(b) TWO forms of abnormal wear and how recognised (6)**

- **Oval wear** — non-uniform elliptical wear from piston side thrust; recognised at calibration by a significant thrust-vs-non-thrust diameter difference, leading to poor ring sealing and blow-by, high oil consumption.
- **Scuffing (micro-seizure)** — localised welding and tearing from lubrication failure/friction; recognised as deep vertical scratches/scoring visible via scavenge ports, leading to ring wear, high oil use, poor compression.

**(c) How abnormal wear is prevented (4)**

Correct cylinder oil grade and BN, evenly distributed via the lubricators; proper cooling water flow/temperature to avoid localised overheating/distortion; avoid prolonged low-load running; correct start/stop procedures; periodic liner and ring inspection with regular calibration for predictive maintenance.

answers.title: Abnormal & Excessive Liner Wear — Cause/Detection, Effects & Prevention
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to abnormal and excessive cylinder liner wear:

(a) explain how it may be caused, stating how it is detected; (6)

(b) explain the effects and consequences of excessive cylinder liner wear; (5)

(c) explain how abnormal cylinder liner wear may be prevented. (5) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Causes and detection (6)**

Causes: poor lubrication (metal-to-metal contact → scuffing); improper combustion (bad timing, poor fuel, prolonged low load → glazing and carbon); contaminants (cat fines/abrasives, excess cylinder-oil deposits, cooling water leaks eroding the surface); distortion/misalignment (poor installation, uneven cooling → uneven wear).

Detection: liner calibration (internal micrometer/bore gauge at set positions); increased blow-by (smoke, low compression); high LO consumption; abnormal patterns visible at scavenge port inspection.

**(b) Effects and consequences (5)**

Reduced ring sealing → blow-by → efficiency loss, higher fuel/LO use; loss of compression → poor combustion, carbon deposits; increased clearance → ring flutter → breakage/sticking; in severe cases, liner cracking → cooling water entering the combustion chamber; uneven wear → piston misalignment and scuffing.

**(c) Prevention (5)**

Correct oil grade and feed rate; maintain cooling water flow and temperature; load management (running at higher loads periodically prevents glazing); fuel quality and injection timing control; routine calibration and scavenge inspections for early detection.

answers.title: Cylinder Liner Scuffing — Cause/Detection, Effects & Treating Minor Scuffing
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to cylinder liner scuffing:

(a) explain how it is caused, stating how it is detected; (6)

(b) explain the effects of cylinder liner scuffing: (4)

(c) explain how minor scuffing may be treated in order to avoid the need for liner replacement. (6) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Cause and detection (6)**

Cause: metal-to-metal contact between rings and liner when the oil film breaks down — inadequate lubrication, contaminated oil, wrong surface finish; overheating (poor cooling/overload → local thermal expansion, lost clearance); piston misalignment or worn rings giving uneven pressure.

Detection: raised EGT on the unit (friction); higher liner/piston temperatures; excessive blow-by with rising LO consumption; scavenge port inspection showing discoloured, rough or smeared surfaces.

**(b) Effects (4)**

Loss of ring-liner sealing → blow-by, power/efficiency drop; friction → higher temperatures → further deterioration; severe cases → deep grooves requiring liner renewal; metal debris → abrasive particles in the LO; extreme cases → piston seizure.

**(c) Treating minor scuffing to avoid liner replacement (6)**

Raise the cylinder oil feed rate to re-establish the film; run at higher load for a period so the rings polish the surface; plateau honing at maintenance (light machining removes high spots, restores the oil-retaining finish); localised lapping with abrasive paste/controlled running-in; for more severe cases, renew rings with softer or chrome-plated rings — if scuffing still progresses, full liner replacement is needed.

answers.title: Medium-Speed Liners — Polishing & Glazing, Anti-Polishing Ring & Effective Lubrication
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to medium speed diesel engine cylinder liners:

(a) explain the cause and effects of liner polishing or glazing; (6)

(b) explain the action of an anti-polishing ring during the operation of the engine; (5)

(c) describe how effective cylinder lubrication is achieved. (5) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Cause and effects of polishing and glazing (6)**

**Polishing** — excessive/poor-quality lubrication produces a smooth, mirror-like liner surface with no asperity contact, so the liner can't retain oil: friction rises, sealing falls, and rapid ring wear follows. **Glazing** — incomplete combustion leaves unburnt fuel and oil residues forming a hard, varnish-like layer, typical of prolonged low-load running where combustion temperatures are never reached, leading to poor oil-film retention, blow-by, low compression and high oil consumption. Both, unaddressed, lead to severe liner/ring wear, efficiency loss and maintenance cost.

**(b) Action of an anti-polishing ring (APR) (5)**

**[Sketch]** Anti-polishing ring at the liner top, proud of ring travel, scraping the piston top-land.

The APR is a carbon scraper ring at the top of the liner. On each up-stroke it scrapes carbon off the piston top-land/crown edge, stopping deposits reaching the rings and liner — keeping ring-liner contact correct (preventing polishing/glazing), maintaining ring sealing (less blow-by/oil use), and removing insulating deposits that would otherwise cause local overheating. The APR should be inspected and maintained regularly.

**(c) How effective cylinder lubrication is achieved (5)**

Correct oil selection plus a controlled feed rate (tribo pack) and optimal distribution onto the liner; the right quantity (avoiding both starvation and over-lubrication/carbon/glazing); correct BN to neutralise acids; honing cross-hatch to retain the film; ongoing monitoring of liner wear, ring condition and lube performance.

answers.title: Thermal Stress in the Cylinder Liner — How Induced, Why Damaging, Avoiding at Full Power
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain, with the aid of a sketch, Thermal Stress, stating how thermal stress is induced in the (8) cylinder liner when the engine is operating.

(b) Explain why thermal stress may be damaging to an engine cylinder. (4)

(c) Explain how thermal stress may be avoided in an operating engine without reducing engine (4) power output. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) How thermal stress is induced when operating, with a sketch (8/10)**

**[Sketch]** Bar under constant heating vs original unheated condition — hot side in tension/compression pattern across the section.

A large temperature difference (ΔT) exists between the inner and outer liner surfaces — the inner face sees combustion gas, the outer is water-cooled. The inner face expands more, creating internal stress as different parts of the liner try to expand/contract at different rates. This is worst at the upper liner (longest gas exposure). Repeated heating/cooling cycles cause thermal fatigue, leading to cracks/deformation; effects are intensified by sudden load changes, inefficient cooling, and poor lubrication.

**(b) Why this is damaging (4)**

Uneven expansion/contraction causes cracking, distortion and fatigue failure; micro-cracks propagate, leading to coolant leakage, compression loss and ring wear; local overheating and deposits cause scuffing and seizure.

**(c) How thermal stress is avoided without reducing power / how it is minimised (4/6)**

**[Sketch]** ME cooling-water system (cooler, FW generator, preheater, expansion tank, main & standby circulating pumps) plus a load-dependent liner cooling temperature graph.

The cooler regulates cooling water temperature; even circulation eliminates hot spots; the expansion tank absorbs volume change for steady pressure and no thermal shock; the preheater warms the engine before starting (avoiding cold-start shock at load); main and standby circulating pumps guarantee flow; load-dependent cooling keeps liner wall temperature optimal across the load range. Operationally: avoid rapid load changes, maintain quality coolant, and inspect the cooling system regularly.

answers.title: Thermal Stress + Fatigue of the Cylinder Liner — How Combined, and Minimising Operation
answers.question_as_set:
(a) With reference to an engine cylinder liner explain the term "Thermal Stress", indicating how (4) and why it occurs during operation of an engine.

(b) Explain how the upper part of a cylinder liner is subjected to fatigue during engine operation. (4)

(c) Explain how thermal stress and fatigue combine and can lead to failure of a cylinder liner (4) during engine operation.

(d) Describe how an engine should be effectively operated in order to minimise the risk of failure (4) due to the combined effects of fatigue and thermal stress. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) What "thermal stress" is, and how/why it occurs in a liner (4)**

Internal stress arises from temperature variation: the hot inner face (combustion) versus the cooled outer face causes uneven expansion, building internal stress through repeated expansion/contraction — intensified by rapid load change, poor cooling, and temperature fluctuation.

**(b) How the upper liner is subjected to fatigue (4)**

Every cycle combines thermal cycling (heat-cool) with the mechanical stress of combustion pressure; repeated cycles start micro-cracks at stress concentrations, particularly near cooling ports and flame-impingement zones.

**(c) How thermal stress and fatigue combine to cause failure (4)**

Thermal micro-cracks become weak points; mechanical combustion stress widens and deepens them, leading to fractures, scuffing and hot spots; cracks can penetrate the wall, causing coolant leakage or total breakdown.

**(d) How to operate the engine to minimise the combined risk (4)**

Gradual load changes; uniform coolant flow and correct cooling water temperature; correct cylinder oil selection/distribution; regular inspection (borescoping, crack detection); keeping combustion parameters (Pmax, injection timing) at recommended values; considering improved liner materials/coatings.

answers.title: FOUR Defects Found During Piston/Liner Inspection via Scavenge Ports
answers.question_as_set: Describe FOUR defects which may be found during a piston/liner inspection via cylinder (16) scavenge ports, explaining the possible causes and the action which should be taken to prevent their re-occurence. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
Four defects, their causes, and preventive action:

1. **Liner scuffing** — rough/scored surface. Cause: insufficient lubrication, improper combustion, thermal stress leading to metal-to-metal contact. Prevention: proper cylinder lubrication, correct injection timing, avoid overloading.
2. **Ring breakage/excessive wear** — broken, worn or stuck rings. Cause: poor fuel quality, poor ring lubrication, excessive combustion pressure, leading to lost seal, blow-by and increased oil use. Prevention: regular ring inspection/renewal, high-quality cylinder oil, proper fuel treatment.
3. **Carbon/deposit build-up on crown and liner**. Cause: incomplete combustion, excessive cylinder-oil feed rate, poor-quality fuel, leading to increased thermal stress and poor ring sealing. Prevention: maintain the injection system, optimise feed rate, periodic crown decarbonisation.
4. **Crack formation on liner or piston crown**. Cause: high thermal stress, improper cooling, mechanical overload — potentially catastrophic if unchecked. Prevention: monitor cooling for even heat dissipation, avoid excessive load, routine NDT for early detection.

answers.title: Two-Stroke Piston — Thermal Stress & Crown Cracking, Labelled Sketch, Crown Burning & Carbon in Cooling Spaces
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to two stroke, slow speed engine pistons:

(a) explain what is meant by the term thermal stress and how this can cause cracking of crown (4) surfaces;

(b) sketch a cross-section of a piston, labelling the main components and indicating coolant flow; (8)

(c) state a cause of EACH of the following defects:

(i) burning of the crown upper surfaces; (2)

(ii) carbon deposits in the cooling spaces. (2) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) "Thermal stress" and how it cracks crown surfaces (4)**

Uneven temperature across the crown — the top face sees combustion gas, the underside is oil/water-cooled — creates thermal gradients and uneven expansion/contraction. Repeated cycles cause thermal fatigue; once stress exceeds the fatigue limit, cracks form at high-stress points such as edges, cooling holes and ring grooves. This is accelerated by poor cooling flow, excessive combustion temperatures, and prolonged high load.

**(b) Piston cross-section sketch, labelling main components with coolant flow**

**[Sketch]** Moly-chrome steel crown (withstands heat) · Nozzle · Short cast-iron skirt · Centre line for studs · Hardened steel piston rod · Path of cooling oil (arrows up through the rod → crown underside → return).

**(c) A cause of EACH: (i) burning of crown upper surfaces (2); (ii) carbon deposits in the cooling spaces (2)**

(i) Crown burning: localised overheating from poor combustion (bad injection timing/atomisation/low-grade fuel), cooling failure, or excessive load pushing combustion temperatures beyond the material limit.

(ii) Carbon in cooling spaces: oil contamination/thermal degradation of the cooling oil leaving carbon residue; inefficient cooling flow creating hot spots where oil burns; poor maintenance (passages not cleaned at overhaul).

answers.title: Exhaust Valve Burn-Out — Indications, Causes & Minimising Practices
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to diesel engine cylinder head exhaust valves:

(a) state, with reasons, the indications of valve burn out; (4)

(b) state the causes of burnt out valves; (4)

(c) state the onboard procedures and practices that would minimise valve failure. (8) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Indications of valve burn-out, with reasons (4)**

Rise in EGT on the unit (hot gas leaks past the valve, often the highest EGT of all cylinders); loss of power on the unit (compression down, incomplete combustion, low MEP); exhaust smoke change (black = incomplete combustion, bluish = oil, sparks/afterburning if severe); abnormal noise (hissing on compression, irregular running/vibration, turbocharger surging from uneven gas flow); compression pressure drop with irregular firing, detected by EGT pyrometers, MIP systems, scavenge pressure and visual/audible checks.

**(b) Causes of burnt-out valves (4)**

High-temperature (hot) corrosion — vanadium, sodium and sulphur in residual fuel form low-melting vanadates/sulphates attacking seat metal above ~450–500°C; poor seating/leakage from deposits (soot, carbon, cat-fines) holding the valve off its seat, creating a hot-gas jet and local burning; impact damage/mechanical wear from too-fast/hard seating; overheating from low-load/slow-steaming, fouled turbocharger, or poor bore-cooling of the seat; poor fuel quality/treatment; inadequate maintenance (infrequent overhaul, wrong seating pressure/velocity, sealing-oil system neglect).

**(c) Minimising practices (8)**

Monitoring/trending EGT per cylinder and indicator/compression cards; fuel management (low-vanadium/sodium fuel, purifiers/filters against cat-fines and water, avoid prolonged <40–50% load, periodic load-up to 80–85% MCR every 1–2 days to burn deposits off); valve operation checks (correct timing/closing velocity, daily sealing-oil checks, spindle rotation verification); scheduled overhauls per maker's TBO (inspect spindle/disc/seat for deposits, burning, dents; measure seat burn-away; regrind/renew); exhaust system maintenance (clean EGB/turbocharger, check manifold for soot); cylinder lubrication and temperature control (correct feed rate/TBN, optimal scavenge/exhaust temperatures, efficient cooling); crew training so early symptoms are recognised.

answers.title: Cracked Cylinder Head (Combustion Chamber ↔ Water Space) — Symptoms, Actions & Report
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Symptoms, with reasons (4)**

Cooling-water contamination (oil/combustion gas entering the CW — colour change, foul odour, frothing in the expansion tank); loss of cooling water (unexplained level drop from water entering the combustion space); white smoke/steam in the exhaust (water vaporising in the chamber); fluctuating cylinder temperatures and pressures (irregular combustion from coolant ingress).

**(b) Actions if the engine cannot be immediately stopped (6)**

Reduce load (lowers Pmax and temperature, slowing crack growth); continuously monitor the CW system (level drop, temperature, pressure); isolate the cylinder — cut fuel if the design permits (reduces water ingress); temporarily increase cylinder lubrication; regularly inspect the scavenge space for water/oil emulsification and ring damage; prepare a controlled shutdown at the earliest safe opportunity, with the crew informed and alert.

**(c) Report to the Superintendent — probable cause and prevention (6)**

*Incident*: white smoke, fluctuating head temperatures, CW level drop — probable crack between head and water space. *Immediate*: load reduced, fuel cut to the unit, CW parameters maintained, scavenge space inspected. *Probable cause*: thermal fatigue from high localised temperature, improper CW flow, or previous overheating — fatigue starting at stress concentrations such as injector pockets and valve seats. *Preventive*: replace the head at the earliest port opportunity, carry out metallurgical inspection, check/clean CW flow across all heads, tighten temperature monitoring and alarm limits, reinforce gradual load-change procedures to avoid thermal shock.

answers.title: Lifting a Cylinder Cover — Procedure, Risks & Lifting-Gear Certification
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of sketches, the procedure for lifting a cylinder cover from a slow speed (6) crosshead engine, explaining how the lifting gear is attached to the cover.

(b) State the risks that may be associated with lifting a cylinder cover using the procedure (4) described in part (a).

(c) Describe the arrangements which must be in place to ensure that all lifting equipment has a (6) current test certificate and is fit for operation. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Procedure for lifting a cylinder cover from a slow-speed crosshead engine, with sketches (6)**

Inform port authorities the engine is immobilised; at the FWE bring the telegraph/fuel lever to zero, take controls at the ECR; stop pumps, shut fuel/exhaust-valve-air/start-air/LO/jacket valves, fit "Do not operate" tags; engage turning gear. Remove CW piping, HP fuel pipes to injectors, the exhaust-valve air pipe, LO hydraulic pipe, and drain pipes. Clean stud threads, fit the hydraulic tensioning device over the studs (nut elongated by hydraulic pressure, supplied at one point or via pump and flexible hoses to each nut), back nuts off with a tommy bar, release pressure, remove nuts. Screw in lifting eye-bolts, hook the crane, lift the cover clear (with a small water jacket), and land it on wooden blocks. Discard the sealing gasket; cover the liner bore; lap the fuel/start/exhaust valve bores; fit new seal rings and CW connection gaskets on reassembly.

**(b) Risks of the lifting operation (4)**

Dropping/uncontrolled fall (sling/shackle/hook failure, wire snap, lifting-eye shear — a 1–2 tonne cover onto the block/liner/personnel); personnel struck by a suspended load (sway from ship motion or uneven hoisting causing crushing); damage to engine components (striking the exhaust-valve housing/injectors/studs, damaging the liner top face, misalignment on landing); crane/gear failure (SWL exceeded, limit-switch failure, tool misuse) — all heightened in the confined, low-headroom engine room, requiring risk assessment, a toolbox talk, and exclusion zones.

**(c) Arrangements ensuring lifting equipment has a current test certificate and is fit for use (6)**

Testing/thorough examination by a competent person before first use and at least every 5 years, with accessories/loose gear thoroughly examined every 12 months (and re-tested after modification/damage/repair). A competent person's certificate confirms SWL, test details and fitness. A Register of Lifting Appliances lists all items, ID marks, SWL, test dates and certificates, available to flag/port state/class. Certificates are obtained within 28 days and retained for at least 2 years; gear is permanently marked with SWL, ID and last-test date. Planned maintenance includes pre-use visual checks, lubrication, and function tests (limit switches, brakes) — defective gear is taken out of use until re-certified, with class/flag compliance verified via the SMS before heavy lifts.

answers.title: Report — Piston Cracking in One Unit, Then a Second Unit
answers.question_as_set: Write a report to the superintendent engineer concerning an incident of cracking which was (16) discovered in one piston of a main diesel engine and the subsequent discovery of cracking in another piston of the same engine. The report must include information about the immediate action taken to prevent further damage to the engine, the subsequent action to remedy the fault and recommendations to prevent subsequent future similar incidents. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Report to the superintendent concerning piston cracking in one unit, then a second unit (16)**

*Detection*: a rise in EGT plus abnormal knocking on one unit prompted slowing the engine; scavenge port inspection revealed crown cracking; a precautionary inspection then found a similar crack in another piston.

*Immediate*: load reduced; temperatures/pressures monitored on all units; affected units isolated with fuel cut off; crankcase and scavenge spaces inspected; CW/LO parameters maintained; bridge and office informed.

*Remedy*: controlled stop; heads, pistons and liners removed and examined; cracks confirmed, with metallurgical analysis identifying thermal fatigue as the primary cause; replacement pistons fitted to maker's spec (fitment/clearances); injectors serviced to confirm correct spray pattern (no localised overheating); cooling passages cleared; reassembled per the manual; slow-turned before restart; gradual restart with monitoring.

*Recommendations*: regular crown inspections for thermal fatigue/stress cracks; periodic borescope of combustion chambers; EGT/pressure differential monitoring; injection timing/atomisation checks; a cooling-system routine for uniform crown temperatures; gradual load changes; metallurgical testing of pistons at overhauls; guidance requested from the office on replacement intervals.

answers.title: Report — Crosshead Engine Bottom-End (Crankpin) Bearing Failure at Sea
answers.question_as_set: You are Chief Engineer Officer on board a vessel with a single, 6 cylinder, two-stroke crosshead (16) propulsion engine which has two turbochargers. One turbocharger suffers failure due to a seized bearing at the turbine end which damages the turbocharger shaft so that the turbocharger cannot be operated. Write a report for the Engineering Superintendent detailing the failure and its cause, explaining how the failure happened and procedures which should be instituted throughout the fleet so that similar failures cannot occur. In the report explain, with reasons, the steps taken by you to ensure that the associated engine can be operated at reduced power. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Report on a crosshead engine bottom-end (crankpin) bearing failure at sea (16)**

*Detection*: an oil-mist detector high-level alarm on the unit, escalating to a general crankcase OMD alarm; knocking/hammering from the crankcase; bearing temperatures rising; increased vibration; LO pressure falling with rising differential across the LO filters; visually, metallic particles/white metal in the sump and on magnetic filters. After stopping and barring over, opening the crankcase doors revealed severe wiping, scoring, partial break-up of the lower shell, and white metal transferred to the crankpin journal — no full seizure.

*Immediate*: dead slow then stop per the emergency procedure; fuel rack to zero/spill valve tripped; start air isolated; no crankcase entry until the oil mist dissipated, with ventilation running; bridge informed, steerage kept on reduced power; engineers mustered.

*Continuing passage*: the cylinder was cut out per maker's procedure — fuel pump deactivated, exhaust valve kept closed (hydraulic override on ME engines), lubricator quill blanked, CW in/out closed; scavenge checked for gas leaks; the piston was left in place (too risky to lift at sea); restart at 60–70% MCR avoiding critical speeds; crankcase checks every 4 hours, frequent oil samples, temperatures/pressures/vibration watched; bridge kept advised; an emergency-towing contingency prepared; the vessel arrived safely.

*Probable cause*: lubrication failure causing oil-film breakdown, overheating, wiping and white-metal damage — contributing factors included partial restriction of the oil supply bore (sludge), marginally low viscosity (high temperature or minor water ingress), localised overload (uneven cylinder loads or geometrical irregularity), and cat-fines or water contamination abrading/corroding the overlay; full root-cause analysis to follow in drydock alongside a review of oil-analysis trends.

*Other checks*: all other bottom-end, crosshead and main bearings inspected (clearances normal); crankshaft deflections within maker's limits; LO system flushed, filters changed, magnetic plugs re-checked; oil samples sent ashore (acceptable BN, slight Fe/particle rise); turbocharger, scavenge spaces and piston cooling verified; cylinder loads re-balanced via indicator cards/MIP.

*Recommendations*: in drydock, open the bearing and journal fully, renew shells, clean oil bores; reminders on oil analysis, filter differentials and crankcase inspections. Enclosures: logbook pages, OMD records, LO lab reports, photographs.

answers.title: Report — Cylinder Liner Cracking With Water Leakage Into the Cylinder
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer, write a report to the engineering superintendent regarding the (16) failure of a main engine cylinder liner due to cracking which resulted in water leakage from the cooling space into the cylinder. The report must explain how the defect was detected, the immediate action taken, the rectifying action taken to ensure that the engine could be operated and the checks made on the engine before and after restarting. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Report on liner cracking with water leakage into the cylinder (16)**

*Detection (5 signs)*: drop in CW pressure with rising water consumption; water contamination visible in the scavenge space at port inspection; white exhaust smoke; unstable performance with high EGT on the unit; higher-than-normal liner temperature.

*Immediate*: load reduced; visual check via scavenge ports plus CW samples taken for testing; CW supply to that liner isolated; bridge and office notified, emergency repairs prepared.

*Rectify*: engine stopped and cooled; head removed; liner inspected, revealing a longitudinal crack; liner renewed with a spare per maker's instructions; rings/components checked for water damage; CW channels flushed; LO checked for water and samples analysed.

*Before restart*: new liner seating and alignment confirmed; torqued to spec; CW system pressure-tested; LO inspected; piston movement/clearance verified.

*After restart*: parameters monitored, confirming no further leakage; exhaust colour/temperatures normal; LO re-tested clean; load increased gradually. Closing recommendations: reinforce inspections/PM schedule; spare-parts and condition-monitoring recommendations to follow.
