answers.title: Report — Replacement of a Damaged Cylinder Cover at Sea
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer outline a procedure for the changing of a cylinder liner in a large (16) crosshead diesel engine after the removal of the cylinder cover to the replacement of the liner. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Report on replacing a damaged cylinder cover at sea (16)**

*Detection*: abnormal EGT rise, irregular knocking, raised CW temperature on the unit; scavenge-port inspection revealed gas leakage around the cover joint, confirmed by a compression-pressure drop and soot around the head.

*Likely cause*: thermal stress and fatigue from repeated heat/cool cycles; uneven CW flow from partly blocked cooling passages causing local overheating and cracking; combustion-pressure fluctuation from poor injection or worn parts; incorrect torque or gasket failure at a previous maintenance, eroding the sealing face via blow-by.

*Action*: controlled shutdown; CW drained, components isolated; bolts slackened in sequence to avoid distortion; cover lifted with proper gear; the block's seating surface inspected; new cover fitted with alignment and torque to spec; cooling passages cleaned; lubrication and injector settings verified; gradual restart watching for leaks, temperatures and pressures.

*Prevention*: routine cleaning of cooling passages; torque verification at overhauls; EGT condition monitoring; injector inspection/calibration and timing checks; correct gaskets and tightening procedure.

answers.title: UMS Call-Out — Slowdown From High Cylinder Exhaust Temperature
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Write a procedure for the action a duty engineer should take on being called to the engine room (6) during a UMS period in the event of an engine slowdown due to a high cylinder exhaust temperature on the main propulsion engine.

(b) State, with reasons, the possible causes of a high exhaust temperature on a single cylinder of a (5) main propulsion engine.

(c) Explain why a defect resulting in a high exhaust temperature on one cylinder can cause engine (5) damage if the engine is not slowed down when the fault initially occurs. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Duty engineer's procedure on a UMS slowdown for high cylinder EGT (6)**

Acknowledge the alarm and inform the bridge; assess using engine room logs and alarm records; carry out a visual inspection for leaks and vibration; verify EGT readings and identify the affected cylinder; slow the engine gradually; investigate and rectify the cause (fuel issue, valve problem) before returning to normal operation.

**(b) Causes of high EGT on a single cylinder, with reasons (5)**

Leaky exhaust valve (hot gas escape, incomplete combustion); leaky fuel injector (excess fuel causing afterburning); incorrect fuel-pump timing; increased piston/ring clearance causing blow-by (low compression, incomplete combustion); scavenge fire (uncontrolled combustion in the scavenge space).

**(c) Why the defect damages the engine if not slowed down at once (5)**

High temperatures rapidly degrade components — the exhaust valve can burn/warp; ring and liner wear accelerates; continued running allows overheating to spread to the turbocharger and engine block, hence the requirement to slow down immediately.

answers.title: Consequences of Poor Maintenance Technique — Four Named Components
answers.question_as_set:
A significant number of machinery failures are due to poor maintenance techniques. State, with reasons, the possible consequences of poor maintenance techniques on EACH of the following:

(a) main engine lubricating oil self cleaning filters; (4)

(b) cylinder liner honing; (4)

(c) auxiliary engine bottom end bearing overhaul; (4)

(d) fitting of piston compression and oil control rings. (4) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Consequences of poor maintenance technique, with reasons, for each of:**

**(a) Main engine LO self-cleaning filters (4)**

Ineffective filtration allows contaminated oil (sludge, metal, combustion products) to circulate, causing premature bearing/ring wear; blocked discs cause oil starvation, risking bearing seizure and crankshaft damage. Fix: regular inspection, proper disc cleaning, timely renewal of worn parts.

**(b) Cylinder liner honing (4)**

Too smooth (over-honed or wrong cross-hatch) gives no oil retention, causing friction and scuffing; excessive honing causes high oil consumption and carbon; uneven honing causes uneven wear and shortened liner life. Fix: hone to the maker's surface-finish specification.

**(c) Auxiliary engine bottom-end bearing overhaul (4)**

Wrong reassembly, improper torque, or missed defects cause uneven load, friction and bearing failure; dirty surfaces or unchecked clearances cause oil starvation, overheating and crankshaft damage. Fix: precise torques, clearance measurement, thorough shell and journal inspection.

**(d) Fitting of piston compression and oil control rings (4)**

Wrong gap alignment or reversed orientation causes poor sealing (low compression, blow-by, high oil use, power loss, liner wear); wrong size or worn rings cause overheating and early failure. Fix: fit per maker's instructions — correct alignment, gap clearance, and orientation.

answers.title: CEO Report — Slow-Turning Failure & Water at the Cylinder Head Gasket
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer, write a report to the engineering superintendent regarding failure of (16) a four-stroke main engine, to complete a slow turning procedure and the discovery of water around a cylinder head gasket after the failed slow turning attempt. The report must outline possible causes of the problem and the steps taken to identify the exact cause. The report must also explain the measures taken to rectify the defect(s) and the steps taken to prevent similar future incidents. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Report on a four-stroke main engine's failure to complete slow turning, and water discovered around a cylinder head gasket (16)**

*Detection*: pre-departure slow turning per standing orders and maker's instructions failed to complete — the turning gear stopped/stalled mid-rotation, indicating hydraulic lock. An immediate stop was issued and turning gear isolated; inspection revealed water weeping around the No. 5 unit's cylinder head gasket; starting was aborted and departure delayed.

*Possible causes*: failed/deteriorated cylinder head gasket allowing jacket cooling water into the combustion space; cracked cylinder head (thermal fatigue/mechanical stress across water passages); cracked cylinder liner (upper collar/flange near the cooling jacket); leaking head cooling-water O-rings/sealing rings; leaking water-cooled fuel valve/injector sleeve; leaking air-start valve (less likely to cause full lock); air cooler/heat-exchanger leakage.

*Identifying the exact cause*: indicator cocks opened on all cylinders confirmed water ejection from No. 5; the head was removed after depressurising/draining the CW system; visual inspection plus dye-penetrant testing of the fire face and water passages; hydraulic pressure test of the head at 1.5× working pressure; the gasket was found compressed/damaged with a wash-out track; liner top land/collar inspected with DPI; block mating face checked for distortion; the CW pressure/level log reviewed, confirming slow pressure loss over the previous watch; a CW sample analysed (CO₂ test) confirming combustion-gas cross-contamination; crankcase inspected for milky (water-contaminated) LO, sample sent for analysis. Root cause: the No. 5 head gasket failed due to inadequate clamping load — two studs found with reduced clamping force from thermal-cycling fatigue.

*Rectification*: head sent ashore for crack testing and refacing, new OEM gasket fitted; two damaged studs renewed, block mating face checked for flatness; head refitted and torqued to maker's sequence/values/angle; liner O-rings renewed preventively; CW system refilled, vented and pressure-tested with no leaks; engine slow-turned with indicator cocks open confirming no further water ejection; started and run at low load with all parameters within limits; LO renewed and system flushed following confirmed contamination.

*Prevention*: PMS updated to add cylinder-head stud-torque verification; standing instruction revised so slow turning is always performed with indicator cocks cracked open; jacket CW pressure-trend logging made mandatory, with any unexplained drop triggering investigation; CW inhibitor concentration checked; remaining heads scheduled for stud-torque checks; crew briefed on hydraulic-lock hazards and gasket-failure warning signs.

answers.title: Fuel-Water Emulsification (FWE) to Reduce Diesel Engine NOx Emissions
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to Fuel Water Emulsification to reduce diesel engine NOx emissions:

(a) describe, with the aid of a sketch, such a system; (12)

(b) explain the disadvantages of this method. (4) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Fuel-Water Emulsification system, with a sketch (12)**

**[Sketch]** Fuel-Water Emulsification system — D.O. and HFO tanks, supply pumps, emergency air-driven pump, homogenizer with H₂O feed, circulating pump, pre-heater, safety tank, venting box, full-flow filter, water sensor, main engine, fuel oil drain tank.

The FWE system reduces NOx emissions by introducing controlled amounts of water into the fuel before combustion. Fuel (D.O. or HFO) is pumped from storage tanks by supply pumps, with an emergency air-driven pump ensuring supply during pump failure. The fuel passes through a homogenizer, where water is added and mixed to form a stable, uniform emulsion, then fed to the circulating pump for consistent flow and pressure. Before entering the engine, the emulsified fuel is preheated to the desired viscosity and passes through a full-flow filter and a water sensor monitoring water content. Excess fuel returns to the system, with separated water drained to the fuel oil drain tank; a venting box and safety tank manage pressure fluctuations.

The NOx-reduction mechanism is the micro-explosion effect: as fuel droplets reach the high-temperature combustion chamber, the water inside rapidly vaporises, causing the droplets to break into finer particles (improving air-fuel mixing) while absorbing latent heat and lowering local combustion temperature. Since NOx formation is highly temperature-dependent, this reduces NOx significantly; the water also promotes slower, more uniform combustion, preventing the localised hot spots that are primary NOx sources, and reduces particulate-forming fuel-rich zones. Overall, FWE can reduce NOx emissions by 30–50%.

**(b) Disadvantages of this method (4)**

Engine efficiency may be affected, as water addition reduces the fuel's energy content, causing a slight rise in fuel consumption for the same power output. Corrosion and wear risk on fuel system components is higher due to water presence, accelerating oxidation and erosion. Maintaining a stable emulsion requires precise monitoring and control — poorly mixed emulsions cause incomplete combustion, increased carbon deposits, and potential engine damage. The system also requires additional equipment and modifications, raising installation and maintenance costs.

answers.title: SOx Exhaust Gas Cleaning — Monitored Parameters & Sea-Pollution Prevention
answers.answer_text:
**(a) System parameters monitored, monitoring device location, data storage & availability to regulators (10)**

Key parameters: the SO₂/CO₂ ratio (gas analysers in the exhaust duct, verifying SOx stays within permissible limits); pH level of discharge water (measured at the washwater discharge outlet, to prevent acidic effluent harming marine life); turbidity (suspended particles in discharge water, for opacity compliance); polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) concentration (sensors in the washwater discharge line, to prevent oil pollution from scrubber effluent); temperature (at the washwater discharge point, to prevent thermal pollution); washwater flow rate (flow meters, ensuring adequate water for SOx removal); pressure drop across the scrubber (differential pressure sensors, detecting blockages/inefficiency); and, for open-loop systems, alkalinity at the scrubber inlet (ensuring effective SOx absorption and pH control).

Data is stored in the ship's onboard EGCS data recording system, typically integrated with the ship's automation system, continuously logged and accessible via digital logs, printouts or electronic submissions. Flag states, port state control and classification societies require this data available for inspection; modern installations may also feature remote monitoring for real-time compliance tracking.

**(b) How SOx cleaning systems can pollute sea water, and prevention (6)**

*Pollution causes*: acidification (open-loop scrubbers discharge acidic washwater, lowering sea pH and affecting ecosystems); heavy-metal contamination (vanadium, nickel, lead in discharge); oil/PAH pollution (hydrocarbons mixing into washwater); increased turbidity (particulate matter reducing light penetration for aquatic life); thermal pollution (discharge significantly warmer than ambient seawater).

*Prevention*: pH neutralisation (alkaline dosing, e.g. sodium hydroxide, to keep discharge pH above regulatory limits); filtration and treatment (washwater filtration and sludge removal to capture metals/particles); PAH monitoring (sensors ensuring hydrocarbon levels stay within limits); closed-loop or hybrid systems (recycling washwater instead of direct discharge, or switching modes); and compliance with MARPOL Annex VI via regular inspection and documentation of washwater quality.

answers.title: SCR Chemical Supply System — Safety/Pollution Avoidance & NOx Reduction Chemistry
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a diesel engine NOx reduction system using chemical supply, (12) explaining the safety and pollution avoidance systems required.

(b) Explain chemical reactions involved in the NOx reduction system described in part (a) of the (4) question. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Diesel engine NOx reduction system chemical supply — sketch, safety & pollution avoidance (12)**

**[Sketch]** SCR chemical supply system — Controller, Safety Valve, Evap, dosing pump, Ammonia tank, flow-rate/temp/NOx/ammonia sensing lines, air <LEL, static mixer, receiver, ME, T/C, bypass, SCR.

SCR reduces NOx via controlled injection of ammonia (or urea solution) into the exhaust, reacting with NOx over a catalyst to form harmless N₂ and H₂O, meeting IMO Tier III. The reagent is stored in a dedicated tank and pumped through double-skinned pipe (safety); an evaporator and dosing pump prepare the correct quantity for engine load/exhaust conditions. A static mixer blends ammonia into the exhaust stream, with air supplied below the Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) to eliminate combustion risk; the mixed gas passes through a receiver before the SCR reactor. A bypass valve allows exhaust to skip the SCR unit if needed, for continuous engine operation during a system fault.

Safety/pollution-avoidance features: double-skinned piping (prevents ammonia leaks); flow-rate, temperature, NOx and ammonia-slip sensors (performance/compliance monitoring); a safety valve (releases excess pressure); and dynamic injection-rate adjustment (limits ammonia slip — unreacted ammonia that would otherwise pollute the atmosphere). Proper temperature control and flow regulation optimise catalyst efficiency for effective NOx reduction under MARPOL Annex VI.

**(b) Chemical reactions involved (4)**

Urea thermally decomposes to ammonia and CO₂:

CO(NH₂)₂ + H₂O → 2NH₃ + CO₂

Ammonia then reacts with NOx over a vanadium/titanium/zeolite-based catalyst. For NO:

4NO + 4NH₃ + O₂ → 4N₂ + 6H₂O

For NO₂:

6NO₂ + 8NH₃ → 7N₂ + 12H₂O

Where the exhaust contains a mix of NO and NO₂, the optimal 1:1 reaction is:

NO + NO₂ + 2NH₃ → 2N₂ + 3H₂O

The system minimises ammonia slip — excess unreacted ammonia released to atmosphere as secondary pollution — through continuous monitoring of NOx levels, temperature and injection rate.

answers.title: Why Efficient Engines Produce More NOx + SCR Unit Description + Monitoring Exhaust Flows
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain why highly efficient diesel engines tend to produce more NOx than low performance (4) diesel engines.

(b) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) unit for a marine (8) propulsion diesel engine.

(c) Explain why accurate monitoring of the exhaust gas flows entering and leaving a Selective (4) Catalytic Reduction unit are required and how these readings are used to control the reduction chemical supplied to the SCR unit. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why highly efficient diesel engines tend to produce more NOx (4)**

Higher efficiency comes from higher combustion temperatures and pressure ratios, and NOx formation is directly temperature-dependent — nitrogen and oxygen react at high temperature to form NO/NO₂. Advanced fuel injection and turbocharging improve air-fuel mixing, raising peak combustion temperature; efficient engines also run leaner (excess oxygen), further promoting NOx formation. Environmental regulation therefore requires after-treatment technologies such as SCR to offset this trade-off.

**(b) SCR unit for a marine propulsion diesel engine (8)**

**[Sketch]** Selective Catalytic Reduction unit — Controller, Safety Valve, Evap, dosing pump, Ammonia tank, flow-rate/temp/NOx/ammonia lines, air <LEL, static mixer, receiver, ME, T/C, bypass, SCR.

(As described in the SCR chemical-supply canonical: ammonia/urea stored and dosed via evaporator and pump, mixed into the exhaust via a static mixer with sub-LEL air, reacted over the catalyst, with a bypass valve for system faults.) Efficiency depends on accurate reagent dosing and maintaining the SCR's optimal temperature range (typically 250–450°C) for effective NOx conversion, ensuring IMO Tier III compliance under MARPOL Annex VI.

**(c) Why exhaust gas flow monitoring in/out of the SCR is required, and how readings control chemical dosing (4)**

Flow rate, temperature and NOx concentration are measured at both SCR inlet and outlet. These readings set the precise reagent dose: too little reagent leaves NOx reduction incomplete (excess emissions); too much causes ammonia slip (unreacted ammonia released to atmosphere, a pollution and compliance risk). The SCR control unit adjusts injection rate in real time based on these readings and changing engine load/fuel type, keeping the system within IMO Tier III limits while minimising ammonia-related pollution.

answers.title: External NOx Reduction System (SCR) — Chemistry, Urea vs Ammonia, Exhaust-Gas-Quality Monitoring
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, an external system for reducing engine NOx emissions, (8) explaining the chemistry of the process.

(b) Explain why Urea is used in the Selective Catalytic Reduction process instead of ammonia. (4)

(c) Explain why the exhaust gas quality must be monitored before and after the Selective Catalytic (4) Reduction unit, stating how such monitoring influences operation of the SCR unit. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) External NOx reduction system (SCR), with chemistry (8)**

**[Sketch]** External NOx reduction system (SCR) — Controller, Safety Valve, Evap, dosing pump, Ammonia tank, flow-rate/temp/NOx/ammonia lines, air <LEL, static mixer, receiver, ME, T/C, bypass, SCR.

Ammonia solution, stored in a dedicated tank and pumped via double-skinned pipe, is prepared by an evaporator and dosing pump and injected via a static mixer into the exhaust stream (with sub-LEL air for safety), before passing through a receiver into the SCR reactor. A bypass valve allows exhaust to skip the unit if needed. Reaction chemistry: 4NO + 4NH₃ + O₂ → 4N₂ + 6H₂O and 6NO₂ + 8NH₃ → 7N₂ + 12H₂O.

**(b) Why urea is used instead of ammonia (4)**

Ammonia is toxic and hazardous, requiring specialised pressurised or refrigerated storage. Urea (CO(NH₂)₂) is a stable, non-toxic solid or aqueous solution that is easily stored and transported; injected into the exhaust, it thermally decomposes to release ammonia in a controlled way: CO(NH₂)₂ + H₂O → 2NH₃ + CO₂ — reducing ammonia-slip and environmental-hazard risk versus direct ammonia handling.

**(c) Why exhaust gas quality is monitored before and after the SCR unit, and how this affects operation (4)**

Sensors measure NOx concentration, temperature and ammonia level. Pre-SCR monitoring determines the correct reagent dose (too little → incomplete NOx reduction; too much → ammonia slip and pollution). Post-SCR monitoring confirms compliance with IMO Tier III and that no excess ammonia is released. This closed-loop monitoring optimises reagent consumption, maintains catalytic efficiency, and prevents damage from unreacted-ammonia deposits.

answers.title: SCR + Fuel Sulphur Content Effects & Turbocharger Interaction — Dual-Path System
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Influence of fuel sulphur content on SCR operation, with a graph (4)**

**[Graph]** Temperature upstream of SCR (250–370°C) vs sulphur content (0–4.0%).

High-sulphur fuel combustion produces SO₂ and some SO₃, which react with the ammonia injected for NOx reduction, forming ammonium bisulphate (NH₄HSO₄) and ammonium sulphate ((NH₄)₂SO₄):

SO₃ + NH₃ + H₂O → NH₄HSO₄
SO₃ + 2NH₃ + H₂O → (NH₄)₂SO₄

These sulphate deposits condense at relatively high temperature (250–300°C), blocking and fouling the SCR catalyst and reducing effectiveness over time, increasing cleaning/maintenance costs. Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) formation from SO₃ and water condensation can also corrode the turbocharger, economiser and SCR reactor housing, especially if exhaust temperature drops too low at low engine load. Mitigations: exhaust gas heating to keep temperature above 300–350°C (preventing bisulphate deposition), and/or an SOx scrubber upstream of the SCR to cut sulphur content before it reaches the catalyst.

**(b) How turbocharger operation can detrimentally affect the SCR unit when burning high-sulphur fuel (4)**

High-sulphur fuel raises SOx, which can react with SCR ammonia injection to form ammonium bisulphate; if exhaust temperature is low, this condenses on the turbocharger turbine blades, causing corrosion/fouling that reduces turbocharger efficiency and can lead to surging or eventual failure. Turbochargers also reduce exhaust gas temperature (especially at lower loads), which can fall below the SCR's optimal range (250–450°C), further increasing bisulphate deposition risk on both SCR catalyst and turbocharger components. Mitigations include engine tuning adjustments, exhaust gas bypass systems, or waste-heat-recovery modifications to keep exhaust temperature adequate for SCR operation while protecting the turbocharger.

**(c) A system maintaining good turbocharger performance and good NOx reduction when burning high-sulphur fuel, meeting the conflicting conditions (8)**

**[Sketch]** Dual-path SCR/turbocharger arrangement — Controller, Safety Valve, Evap, dosing pump, Ammonia tank, sensing lines, air <LEL, static mixer, receiver, ME, T/C, bypass, SCR.

A dual-path exhaust arrangement combines: an **SCR bypass system** (allows exhaust to partially/fully bypass the SCR at low load, when temperatures are too low to prevent bisulphate formation); an **exhaust gas heater/heat-retention system** (waste-heat recovery or exhaust gas burner raising temperature before the SCR reactor, reducing sulphate-deposition risk); a **turbocharger protection mechanism** (dedicated heat exchanger or air bypass regulating turbocharger-inlet gas temperature, preventing condensation of corrosive sulphur compounds on turbine blades); an **SOx scrubber upstream of the SCR** (removing most sulphur oxides before the SCR reactor); and an **intelligent ammonia-injection control system** (adjusting dosing based on real-time exhaust temperature and sulphur content, optimising NOx reduction while avoiding excess ammonia slip).

answers.title: Diesel Engine NOx Emissions & Control — EGR/DWI CO2 Trade-Off + Selective Catalytic Reduction System
answers.answer_text:
**(a) How EGR and Direct Water Injection reduce NOx but raise specific CO2 emissions (6)**

In EGR, a portion of exhaust gas is recirculated into the intake air, reducing available oxygen and peak combustion temperature; since NOx formation is highly temperature-dependent, this suppresses thermal NOx. However, reduced oxygen causes less complete combustion, lowering engine efficiency and raising specific fuel consumption (SFC) — and since CO₂ is directly tied to fuel burned, specific CO₂ emissions rise per unit power.

Direct Water Injection similarly injects water into the combustion chamber/intake to absorb heat and lower peak temperature, suppressing NOx — but also reduces combustion completeness/thermal efficiency, requiring more fuel for the same power output and again raising CO₂ per kWh.

Both methods trade NOx reduction for efficiency, requiring careful optimisation to balance emissions control against fuel economy.

**(b) Selective Catalytic Reduction system, with monitoring/control systems required**

**[Sketch]** Selective Catalytic Reduction system — Controller, Safety Valve, Evap, dosing pump, Ammonia tank, flow-rate/temp/NOx/ammonia lines, air <LEL, static mixer, receiver, ME, T/C, bypass, SCR.

SCR chemically converts NOx to N₂ and H₂O using ammonia as the reducing agent, meeting IMO Tier III. Key components: ammonia tank, pump/evaporator, static mixer (thorough blending before the reactor), receiver, and SCR reactor, with a bypass for low-load/fault conditions.

Monitoring/control required: NOx sensors at SCR inlet and outlet (verify emissions stay within regulatory limits); ammonia-slip sensors (detect unreacted ammonia before atmospheric release); exhaust temperature monitoring (the catalyst has an effective operating range — too low reduces conversion efficiency, too high risks catalyst damage); and a controller that adjusts ammonia injection rate in real time against NOx level and engine load, backed by pressure-relief/safety valves for safe ammonia handling. All data is logged for real-time diagnostics and compliance reporting (verifiable at port inspections under MARPOL Annex VI).

answers.title: Hybrid SOx Scrubber Systems — Open/Closed Loop Fluids, When Used, Closed-Loop Effectiveness & Sea-Pollution Avoidance
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Fluids used in open and closed loops, and how controlled to meet scrubbing demand (6)**

In open-loop mode, seawater is the scrubbing medium — its natural alkalinity neutralises SOx; seawater is drawn in, used for scrubbing, then discharged overboard once meeting discharge limits. In closed-loop mode, freshwater dosed with an alkaline additive (usually sodium hydroxide, NaOH) is continuously recirculated with minimal discharge. Scrubbing efficiency is controlled by adjusting fluid flow rate, NaOH dosing and water pH against engine load — higher loads producing more SOx require higher flow/dosing, lower loads less.

**(b) When Open Loop vs Closed Loop scrubbing is used (2)**

Open-loop scrubbing is used in open seas, where seawater alkalinity is high and regulations permit discharge of treated washwater. Closed-loop scrubbing is used in Emission Control Areas (ECAs) and ports, where discharge regulations are strict and open-loop discharge is restricted.

**(c) Maintaining closed-loop neutralising effectiveness over long periods, and avoiding sea pollution (8)**

As SOx reacts with NaOH, the fluid's alkalinity falls over time, so additional NaOH is dosed to maintain effective scrubbing, with pH and NaOH concentration continuously monitored and adjusted. To prevent pollution, a water treatment unit removes sludge and particulate matter before any treated washwater is discharged; sludge (containing sulphates and impurities) is collected in holding tanks for shore disposal, ensuring no acidic or contaminated discharge reaches the sea, per IMO regulations.

answers.answer_text:
**(a) Describe EITHER an Open Loop OR a Closed Loop SOx scrubber system (10)**

**[Sketch]** Open Loop — scrubber exhaust, exhaust gas in, seawater in, washwater treatment, separated residue, scrubber overboard.

An Open Loop system uses seawater's natural alkalinity to neutralise SOx: exhaust gas is directed into a scrubber tower where sprayed seawater dissolves SO₂ (forming sulfurous acid, further oxidising to sulphuric acid), which the seawater's alkalinity neutralises into calcium sulphate and other harmless salts. Treated exhaust is released to atmosphere; washwater passes through a treatment unit separating solids/sludge for port disposal, with remaining treated water discharged overboard under MARPOL Annex VI limits (pH, turbidity, PAH). Advantages: no chemical additives, lower complexity/cost. Limitations: reduced efficiency in low-alkalinity waters, and many ports/ECAs restrict or ban open-loop discharge.

**[Sketch]** Closed Loop — exhaust gas, scrubber, NaOH unit, fresh water, process tank, water treatment, sludge tank, holding tank, cooler, pumps.

Alternatively, a Closed Loop system recirculates fresh washwater dosed with NaOH, reacting with SO₂ to form dissolved sodium sulphate; washwater passes to a process tank for filtration/treatment, is recirculated, with sludge sent to a holding tank for port disposal (any overboard discharge must still meet MARPOL Annex VI). A cooling system maintains scrubber temperature. Advantages: works in low-alkalinity/ECA waters where open-loop is restricted, minimal direct discharge. Trade-offs: NaOH replenishment, sludge-related maintenance, higher operating cost.

**(b) Systems to monitor to ensure IMO compliance (6)**

Exhaust gas emissions (continuous emission monitoring systems measuring SO₂/CO₂ ratio against the 0.50% global or 0.10% ECA sulphur cap); washwater quality (pH ≥6.5 at the overboard discharge point, turbidity, PAH concentration); scrubber flow rate (accurate pumping/recirculation control for effective SOx removal); in closed-loop systems, NaOH concentration (proper neutralisation); and sludge/residue management (logged collection and disposal to port reception facilities). All monitoring data is logged and made available to port state control for compliance verification.

answers.answer_text:
**(a) Open loop system for reducing SOx, explaining operation whilst the vessel is in open waters (6)**

Seawater is pumped into the scrubber and sprayed over the exhaust gas; its natural alkalinity in open ocean waters neutralises the dissolved SO₂/sulphuric acid into harmless salts, with treated washwater discharged overboard — viable specifically because open-water seawater alkalinity is high enough for effective, compliant neutralisation without chemical additives.

**(b) Closed loop scrubber system for removing SOx, and stating when it would be used (10)**

A closed-loop system recirculates freshwater dosed with an alkaline additive (NaOH) to neutralise SO₂ into dissolved sodium sulphate, with the washwater treated and recirculated rather than continuously discharged; sludge is collected for port disposal, and a cooling system keeps the scrubber within operating temperature limits. answers.title: NOx Formation Mechanism + ONE External Reduction Method (Efficiency Trade-Off)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) How NOx is formed, and why the aim of high engine efficiency increases the problem (6)**

NOx forms from the high-temperature combustion process: intake air (~78% N₂, 21% O₂) reacts above ~1,300°C via the Zeldovich mechanism, which is strongly temperature-dependent. Higher efficiency is typically achieved by raising combustion temperature and pressure (better fuel atomisation, higher thermal efficiency) — but this directly intensifies NOx formation, and efficient engines' leaner air-fuel mixtures (excess oxygen) further promote it. So while higher efficiency cuts fuel consumption and CO₂, it worsens NOx, creating an inherent efficiency/NOx trade-off.

**(b) ONE external means of reducing NOx to meet current regulations (10)**

Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR): ammonia or a urea-based solution is injected into the exhaust upstream of a catalytic reactor. Urea decomposes to ammonia at high temperature; the ammonia then reacts with NOx over the catalyst (4NO + 4NH₃ + O₂ → 4N₂ + 6H₂O; 6NO₂ + 8NH₃ → 7N₂ + 12H₂O), converting it to harmless nitrogen and water and meeting IMO Tier III limits. SCR operates optimally within a specific exhaust temperature range (roughly 270–450°C), making temperature monitoring essential; NOx sensors, ammonia-slip monitors and exhaust-temperature control regulate injection and prevent excess ammonia escaping. SCR is widely used in marine applications, capable of NOx reductions up to ~90%, but requires careful maintenance (urea consumption monitoring, preventing injection-system crystallisation, catalyst condition) to remain effective.

answers.title: Diesel Engine Exhaust Emissions — Causes & Effects of CO, CO2, Hydrocarbons & Particulate Matter
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to diesel engine exhaust emissions, describe the causes and effects of EACH of the following:

(a) carbon monoxide; (4)

(b) carbon dioxide; (4)

(c) hydrocarbons; (4)

(d) particulate matter. (4) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Carbon Monoxide (CO) (4)**

Produced by incomplete combustion when insufficient oxygen is available (poor air-fuel mixing, low excess-air ratio, faulty injectors). Highly toxic — reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, causing CO poisoning; in the atmosphere it contributes to ground-level ozone formation, harming air quality.

**(b) Carbon Dioxide (CO2) (4)**

A natural product of complete combustion (carbon in fuel fully reacting with oxygen). CO₂ output is directly proportional to fuel consumption. Its major effect is contribution to global warming/climate change as a greenhouse gas trapping atmospheric heat.

**(c) Hydrocarbons (HC) (4)**

Unburned hydrocarbons result from incomplete combustion (poor fuel atomisation, low combustion temperature, malfunctioning injectors). They react with NOx in sunlight to form photochemical smog, harmful to health and the environment; some hydrocarbons are also carcinogenic.

**(d) Particulate Matter (PM) (4)**

Soot — fine carbon particles, metal oxides and unburned hydrocarbons from incomplete combustion, associated with poor fuel quality, excessive load, or inefficient combustion. Fine particles penetrate deep into the lungs, causing respiratory disease (asthma, lung cancer), and contribute to atmospheric haze reducing visibility.

answers.title: Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) System — Sketch, Operating & Thermal Efficiency Problems
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, an exhaust gas recirculation system, explaining how the (12) system reduces the level of NOx in the engine exhaust gas.

(b) Explain the operating and thermal efficiency problems associated with Exhaust Gas (4) Recirculation systems. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) EGR system, with a sketch, and how it reduces NOx (12)**

**[Sketch]** Exhaust Gas Recirculation system — turbocharger, exhaust, intake, scrubber with sea-water inlet/outlet, gas cooler for EGR with S.W. inlet/outlet, EGR blower, cylinder, air cooler.

Exhaust gas leaves the cylinder and passes through the turbocharger; part is diverted through a control valve into the EGR system, entering a scrubber where seawater removes SOx and particulate matter. The scrubbed gas passes through a gas cooler (seawater-cooled) before the EGR blower, which recirculates the cleaned, cooled gas into the engine's air intake, through the air cooler, and into the cylinder for combustion. By diluting intake air with cooled exhaust gas, the system lowers oxygen concentration and peak combustion temperature — since NOx formation is highly temperature-dependent, this significantly suppresses thermal NOx formation, helping meet IMO Tier III limits.

**(b) Operating and thermal-efficiency problems with EGR (4)**

- **Increased soot/carbon deposits**: recirculated exhaust raises unburned hydrocarbon/particulate levels in the combustion chamber, fouling the turbocharger and intake valves, raising maintenance costs and reducing performance.
- **Reduced combustion efficiency**: lower intake oxygen reduces combustion efficiency, raising fuel consumption for the same power output — indirectly increasing CO₂ emissions.
- **Higher exhaust/thermal stress**: recirculating exhaust increases heat retention, raising thermal stress on components and potentially shortening part life/reducing cooling-system efficiency.
- **Potential power loss**: less available oxygen can reduce power output, particularly at high load, requiring fuel-injection strategy adjustments that can further hurt fuel economy.

answers.title: Dual-Fuel Four-Stroke Combustion Process (Pilot Injection) + Exhaust Gas Recirculation Explained
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain, with the aid of sketches, the gas combustion process in a dual fuel medium speed main (10) engine, operating with pilot injection.

(b) Explain what is meant by exhaust gas recirculation and how this may be effective in reducing (6) air pollution. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Gas combustion process in a dual-fuel medium-speed main engine with pilot injection (10)**

**[Sketch]** Dual-fuel gas combustion process — intake of air and gas / compression of air and gas / ignition by pilot diesel fuel.

A dual-fuel four-stroke engine uses both gaseous fuel (e.g. natural gas) and a small pilot quantity of liquid diesel to guarantee reliable ignition, across the standard intake/compression/power/exhaust strokes. During intake, the intake valve opens first for scavenge air; once air flow is positive, the gas admission valve opens to introduce gaseous fuel, ensuring proper mixing and preventing manifold gas accumulation. Near the end of induction, the gas valve closes first, then the intake valve, for precise fuel control.

During compression (both valves closed), the piston compresses the air-fuel mixture; since the gaseous fuel doesn't auto-ignite at this temperature, a small pilot diesel injection just before TDC ignites under high pressure/temperature, and this flame front then ignites the gas-air mixture — the power stroke. During exhaust, the exhaust valve opens and burnt gases are expelled before the cycle repeats.

The fuel control system continuously balances gas and pilot-fuel quantity for optimal power/emissions, and can automatically switch to diesel-only mode if gas supply is interrupted; electronic control optimises delivery for load and operating conditions.

**(b) What Exhaust Gas Recirculation means, and how it reduces air pollution (6)**

EGR recirculates a controlled portion of exhaust gas back into the intake, diverted from the exhaust manifold and mixed with fresh air (typically cooled via an EGR cooler) before combustion. This dilutes intake oxygen and lowers peak combustion temperature — since NOx formation rises sharply with temperature, the cooler, slower burn significantly reduces NOx output, helping the engine meet emission regulations.

answers.title: Cylinder Power Balance — Why Essential, Damaging Effects, Checking & How Achieved
answers.question_as_set: Explain why cylinder power balance is essential for a diesel engine and how cylinder power (16) balance is achieved. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Why cylinder power balance is essential**

Cylinder power balance means each cylinder in a multi-cylinder engine develops approximately the same indicated power (MEP) under the same operating conditions. This matters for several reasons:

- **Prevention of mechanical overload/damage** — an overloaded cylinder sees higher peak pressures and thermal/mechanical stress on piston, rings, liner, head, con-rod and crankshaft, risking cracking, scuffing, ring breakage or seizure; underloaded cylinders suffer incomplete combustion, fouling and cold corrosion.
- **Reduction of torsional vibration and crankshaft stress** — uneven firing impulses excite torsional vibration in the shafting system, risking fatigue cracking (especially at crankshaft fillets), coupling fretting, and bearing stress.
- **Optimal fuel efficiency (SFC)** — uneven power distribution causes inefficient combustion in some cylinders, raising SFC by 1–3 g/kWh or more; balance minimises unburnt fuel, smoke and emissions while maximising thermal efficiency.
- **Control of exhaust gas temperature (EGT)** — imbalance causes high EGT in overloaded cylinders (risking exhaust valve/turbocharger/economiser damage) and low EGT in underloaded ones (deposits, after-burning). Balance keeps EGT within safe limits (typically <480–520°C, ±10–15°C spread).
- **Smooth running, reduced maintenance** — imbalance raises vibration, noise and bearing loads, complicates scavenge air distribution and cylinder lubrication, risking liner polishing or excess oil consumption.
- **Compliance with maker/class limits** — engine makers specify maximum allowable power deviation (e.g. ±5% MEP); imbalance can void warranties or breach class rules.

**How cylinder power balance is achieved**

1. **Monitoring and measurement**: take indicator diagrams (power/compression cards) via mechanical indicator or electronic MIP system; calculate IMEP/MIP per cylinder; record per-cylinder EGT (pyrometers); monitor scavenge air pressure and peak/firing pressures. Target uniform MIP (±3–5% or maker limit, e.g. ±2–3 bar) and EGT spread ±10–20°C.
2. **Adjustment of fuel quantity**: in camshaft-controlled engines (e.g. MAN B&W MC-C), adjust individual fuel-pump VIT/spill timing (small changes, e.g. 0.5–1mm rack movement); in electronically controlled engines (ME-C/ME-B, WinGD RT-flex/X), adjust via the ECS interface (automatic balancing functions exist but manual fine-tuning is often needed). Adjust one cylinder at a time, run 15–30 minutes to stabilise, re-measure, repeat.
3. **Secondary checks**: verify equal cylinder lubrication feed rates; check scavenge port condition and air cooler efficiency; confirm turbocharger performance is normal; adjust exhaust valve timing/VIT profile where fitted.
4. **Frequency/best practice**: balance after overhaul, fuel change, prolonged low-load running, or on imbalance alarms; perform at steady load (70–90% MCR); follow maker guidance; use calibrated tools, and never adjust during manoeuvring.

**Checking cylinder performance/power** (asked as a separate sub-part in some sittings): indicator diagrams (pressure variations reveal fuel injection/compression issues), compression pressure test (sealing efficiency of rings/liner/valves), exhaust gas temperature monitoring (uneven EGT signals over-fuelling, misfiring or afterburning), and a power balance test comparing each cylinder's contribution.

answers.title: Performance Determination, Defective Fuel Injection Detection & Afterburning Causes
answers.question_as_set:
(a) As Chief Engineer Officer, explain how the performance of a main diesel engine may be (6) determined, indicating how the information collected is analysed to assess the performance of an individual cylinder in relation to the overall engine performance.

(b) Explain how defective fuel injection may be detected, stating, with reasons, the causes of (6) defective cylinder fuel injection.

(c) Explain the causes of afterburning in a single cylinder of a diesel engine, stating how this may (4) be brought to the attention of the duty engineer. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) How main engine performance is determined, and how information is analysed per cylinder vs overall (6)**

Continuous trend-analysis logging of SFC, exhaust gas temperatures, cylinder pressures and compression pressures identifies gradual deterioration before it becomes critical. The indicator diagram is the primary tool — a pressure-crank-angle/pressure-volume graph revealing combustion timing and mechanical-loss issues per cylinder; deviations flag late injection, poor atomisation or compression loss. Power balance tests compare each cylinder's contribution to ensure even load distribution. SFC trending (rising SFC signals inefficient combustion, incorrect timing or mechanical losses) and EGT monitoring (abnormal temperature vs other cylinders can indicate afterburning, over-fuelling or poor air intake) complete the picture, alongside compression pressure tests (ring/liner/valve sealing) and turbocharger performance checks. All data is compared to maker specification and historical trend, allowing targeted maintenance (injection timing adjustment, pump/injector overhaul, component replacement).

**(b) Detecting defective fuel injection, and its causes (6)**

Symptoms: abnormal indicator diagrams (delayed pressure rise, erratic combustion curve); higher EGT in the affected cylinder vs others; rising SFC with reduced power; excessive smoke (black = incomplete combustion, white = fuel dribbling).

Causes: clogged/eroded injector nozzles (poor atomisation, incomplete combustion); incorrect injection pressure (too high or low, poor fuel distribution); worn fuel pump plungers/barrels (inconsistent delivery); faulty injector needle seating (dribbling, afterburning, carbon deposits); incorrect fuel viscosity from temperature variation (over-fuelling or poor atomisation).

**(c) Causes of afterburning in a single cylinder, and how it is brought to the duty engineer's attention (4)**

Causes: poor fuel atomisation (delayed/incomplete combustion); late injection timing (fuel ignites too late, burning into the expansion stroke); low compression pressure (worn rings, liner wear, valve leakage) reducing combustion efficiency.

Detected via: black smoke (incomplete combustion); higher EGT in the affected cylinder; knocking sounds from irregular combustion pressure; excessive carbon deposits on exhaust valve/piston crown. Regular monitoring of EGT, injection performance and indicator diagrams allows early detection, enabling injector cleaning, pump adjustment and compression checks before the problem worsens.

answers.title: Indicator-Diagram Fault Library — Reference Set of Combustion & Valve-Timing Signatures
answers.answer_text:
Reference material underpinning any indicator-diagram fault question (irregularities common to all units point to a shared fault — fuel oil system, intake air, turbocharger, air cooler, exhaust; irregularities confined to one unit point to that cylinder's injector, fuel pump, or exhaust valve):

**Early Ignition** — abnormally high peak pressure at the top of stroke; knocking from shock loads on running gear; raises thermal efficiency but exhaust temperature falls (combustion starts early) while vibration/shock damages the engine. Causes: mistimed fuel pump, faulty fuel valve/injector, wrong fuel quality, overheated cylinder parts.

**Late Ignition** — low peak pressure after TDC; combustion continues into the expansion stroke (incomplete combustion, energy loss, elevated EGT, black smoke); reduced power. Causes: faulty injector or over-tight injector spring, poor fuel quality, mistimed/leaking fuel pump, under-cooled cylinder parts, incorrect atomisation, low compression, insufficient combustion air.

**After Burning** — rise in the expansion line late in the stroke; continued burning raises EGT/pressure and causes black smoke; unburnt carbon fouls the exhaust system, damaging valves/seats, causing turbocharger surge and uptake-fire risk in the economiser; elevated cylinder temperature breaks down lubrication and increases liner/ring wear, can burn the piston crown. Causes: slow fuel combustion, poor fuel quality, low fuel temperature (high viscosity).

**Leaky Fuel Injector** — reduced power in the affected unit, high EGT, black smoke; possible knocking/pressure waves in the injection system; sudden ups-and-downs on the injection/expansion side of the diagram; afterburning from incomplete combustion. Causes: leaking injector, choked spray holes causing poor atomisation and dripping.

**Partly Choked Fuel Valve** — low EGT in the unit; loss of engine power. Causes: fuel oil contamination/improper purification, carbon formation at the injector tip, carbon deposits on the fuel valve from overheating.

**Low Compression** — low pressure on the indicator card; reduced power. Causes: improper combustion, insufficient combustion air, ring/liner wear allowing air leakage past the piston during compression.

**Exhaust Valve Opening — Early/Late (light-spring diagram)** — *Early opening*: elevated EGT, exhaust-system fouling, power loss. *Late opening*: reduced blow-down effect and scavenging efficiency, poor exhaust gas quality reaching the turbocharger.

**Choked Exhaust** — power loss, increased EGT, turbocharger surging, adversely affected scavenging efficiency.

answers.title: One Engine Showing Higher SFC in a Multi-Engine Installation — Causes & Detection
answers.question_as_set:
In a multi engine installation one engine is showing higher Specific Fuel Consumption (SFC) than the other engines. All engines take fuel oil from the same fuel oil service tank and each engine has an individual dedicated fuel supply unit of the same make and type.

(a) Explain with reasons the possible causes for one engine having a higher specific fuel (8) consumption than the other engines.

(b) State with reasons how the cause of the higher SFC can be detected (8) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Possible causes of one engine having higher SFC than identical sister engines on a shared fuel service tank (8)**

Fuel injection system issues (improper pump timing, worn injector nozzles, incorrect injection pressure); faulty governor setting (incorrect fuel delivery for the load); lower compression pressure (worn piston rings, liner wear, leaking head valves) requiring more fuel for the same power; turbocharger performance variation (fouled/damaged unit reducing air supply, causing incomplete combustion); air filter blockage or intake leaks (reduced air-to-fuel ratio); bearing/component wear (higher mechanical/frictional losses); incorrect fuel rack setting or control-system calibration; and cooling-system inefficiency (malfunctioning jacket cooling affecting combustion efficiency).

**(b) How the cause of higher SFC can be detected (8)**

- Indicator diagram analysis — compare P-V/P-θ diagrams against the other engines for injection timing, combustion efficiency and pressure-rise differences.
- Compression pressure test — check for worn rings, liner wear, leaking head valves.
- Fuel pump and injector testing — pump timing, injection pressure, atomisation quality.
- Turbocharger performance check — air pressure, fouling, efficiency.
- Air intake inspection — filters and ducts for blockage/leaks.
- Governor and fuel rack setting comparison against the other engines.
- Mechanical losses evaluation — bearings, lubrication, moving components.
- Cooling system efficiency check — coolant temperatures, jacket cooling, heat exchanger performance.

answers.answer_text:
**(a) How information gathered from a cylinder is analysed (4)**

Trend analysis and comparison against baseline data across indicator diagrams, peak/compression pressure, EGT, fuel injection timing and SFC. A normal indicator diagram shows a smooth pressure rise; delayed or premature combustion signals faulty injection or compression loss. Compression readings assess sealing efficiency; EGT signals combustion quality (high = over-fuelling/afterburning, low = misfiring/under-fuelling). Power balance tests confirm equal cylinder contribution — a consistently low-power cylinder suggests defective injection, compression loss, or mechanical wear.

**(b) Recognising defects from the gathered data, and how they influence cylinder power (6)**

Low peak pressure vs other cylinders → late injection, worn rings, or leaky exhaust valves (reduced effective power). High EGT in one cylinder → over-fuelling, poor atomisation, or afterburning (inefficient combustion, added thermal stress). Low EGT → misfiring, under-fuelling, or insufficient air (incomplete combustion, power loss). Power imbalance detected via performance testing → underperformance from injection issues, compression loss, or mechanical inefficiency. Disproportionately rising SFC in one cylinder → excessive frictional resistance from worn bearings or mechanical losses.

**(c) Rectifying the identified defects (6)**

Fuel injection faults (late injection, poor atomisation) → test, recalibrate, or replace pumps/injectors. Compression loss (worn rings, liner wear, valve leakage) → overhaul or replace affected components. High EGT/afterburning → inspect and clean injector nozzles for proper spray/atomisation. Turbocharger/air intake problems → check for fouling/damage, clean or replace air filters. Increased SFC from mechanical losses → lubrication checks, alignment corrections, bearing inspection. Also assess cooling system performance to keep cylinder temperatures within optimal limits.

answers.title: 2-Stroke Engine Load Diagram — Operating/Limit Lines, Clean vs Fouled Hull, MAN B&W Reference
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain, with the aid of a graph, a large 2 stroke diesel engine load diagram, labelling the (12) operating and limit lines.

(b) On the graph sketched in part (a), with the vessel fully ballasted, at constant load and in calm (4) weather, mark point 'x' to show the position if the hull was clean and point 'y' to show the position if the hull was fouled. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Large 2-stroke diesel engine load diagram — operating and limit lines (12)**

**[Graph]** Load diagram — Engine Power (%) vs Engine RPM, numbered operating/limit lines 1–9.

- **Line 1 — Optimum propeller curve**: ideal matched engine/propeller condition for efficient fuel consumption and minimal mechanical stress.
- **Line 2 — Heavy running line**: engine under heavier-than-normal load (fouled hull, adverse weather, high resistance) — increased fuel consumption and overload risk.
- **Line 3 — Maximum speed line**: highest permissible RPM at full load; exceeding it risks overspeed, excess wear and damage.
- **Line 4 — Torque/thermal limit**: maximum torque without excessive thermal stress; exceeding it risks piston overheating and thermal damage.
- **Line 5 — Maximum MEP line**: crossing it stresses pistons, liners and bearings, accelerating wear.
- **Line 6 — Light running line**: under-loaded conditions (small propeller, light ship, favourable current); prolonged running below it risks incomplete combustion, turbocharger surging, carbon deposits.
- **Line 7 — Maximum power line**: absolute highest power; sustained operation near it raises wear, fuel consumption and failure risk.
- **Line 8 — Thermal overload line**: beyond this, EGT rises excessively, risking piston seizure, liner scuffing, turbocharger damage.
- **Line 9 — Mechanical overload line**: structural limit; beyond it, catastrophic failure of major components (con-rods, crankshaft, bearings) is possible.

The load diagram optimises fuel consumption (stay near the optimum propeller curve), prevents overloading (avoid thermal/mechanical limits), ensures efficient propulsion (adjust to sea conditions), and improves longevity (avoid low-load carbon buildup) — regular monitoring against it allows early detection of abnormal conditions.

**(b) Marking clean-hull and fouled-hull points, fully ballasted, constant load, calm weather (4)**

**[Sketch]** Load diagram with the vessel fully ballasted at constant load in calm weather — point positions for clean hull and fouled hull marked on the operating lines. A clean hull sits closer to the light-running line (Line 6); as the hull and propeller foul over time, the propeller curve moves left (heavier running, toward Line 2), requiring extra power for the same speed — the extent of this shift indicates the need for hull cleaning/propeller polishing.

---

**Reference: MAN B&W Diesel A/S Service Letter SL91-287/OG (August 1991) — Load Diagram, MC Engines**

Two diagram families are defined: Diagram II for ships delivered up to and including 1991, Diagram I for later installations. In both, the key recommendation is not exceeding the diagram's left-hand limitation (torque-rich operation). Operators should regularly plot the observed speed/power combination against the diagram, and plot the actual clean-hull/calm-weather propeller curve (actual Line 6) and design point for reference.

*Limits for continuous operation* — bounded by four lines: Line 3 (max continuous speed); Line 4 (torque/speed limit set by available air supply for combustion); Line 5 (max continuous MEP); Line 7 (max continuous power). Continuous operation without limitation is allowed only within the area bounded by lines 3, 4, 5 and 7.

*Limits for overload operation* — Line 8 marks the overload boundary; the area between lines 4, 5, 7 and line 8 is available for overload only for limited periods (1 hour per 12 hours).

The area between lines 1 and 4 is available for non-steady running (shallow water, heavy weather, acceleration) without an explicit time limit, though lines 4 and 5 must not be exceeded except during limited overload. As the hull and propeller foul with time in service, the propeller curve moves left from line 6 toward line 2 (heavier running), signalling the need for hull/propeller cleaning. Point A is the 100% speed/power reference; Point M (normally equal to A) may sit to the right of A on line 7 if a shaft generator is fitted.

answers.title: Top Bracing — Purpose, Hydraulic Unit, Checking Instructions
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain why top bracing is used for large crosshead engines. (4)

(b) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a hydraulic top bracing unit for a large crosshead engine (6) indicating where the top bracing is fitted and how it operates.

(c) Write instructions for the checking of a large crosshead engine hydraulic top bracing system (6) and a holding down system. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why top bracing is used for large crosshead engines (4)**

Top bracing is provided at the top of taller engines to stiffen the upper part and resist twisting forces imposed by the crosshead guide forces. Without top bracing, these forces would cause fatigue in the "A" frame, leading to cracks and misalignments. By adding top bracing, the rigidity of the engine to the ship is increased, raising the natural frequency of the engine and ship vibration, which helps to reduce resonance between the engine structure and the ship. Since the distance between the crosshead guide and the holding-down arrangement is large, it results in a large moment that places significant stress on the "A" frame and holding-down bolts. The top bracing helps to reduce this stress, ensuring better structural integrity and prolonging the engine's operational life.

**(b) Hydraulic top bracing unit — sketch and operation (6)**

**[Sketch]** Hydraulic top bracing — hull side / engine side, solenoid bypass valve, HI-SET / LO-SET pressure release, manual adjustment, spherical bearing, NRV, oil inlet from accumulator, oil drain to accumulator unit.

A hydraulic top bracing unit is installed at the top of a large crosshead engine, connecting the engine entablature to the ship's hull. It is designed to reduce transverse vibrations and increase structural stability by damping the forces generated by the reciprocating components of the engine. The top bracing unit consists of a hydraulic cylinder, a spherical bearing, and a manual adjustment mechanism to accommodate movement and ensure proper alignment.

The hydraulic top bracing is particularly useful for vessels experiencing high rates of hull/engine deflection while loading and discharging. The spherical bearing absorbs relative vertical and longitudinal movement between the hull and the engine, ensuring flexibility without compromising stability. Hydraulic forces control the bracing force through the main high-set relief valve. Oil is supplied from an accumulator, which maintains pre-tension in the system. When engine vibrations cause movement in the bracing unit, the oil pressure increases; once it reaches the set point of the high relief valve, the piston locks, preventing further engine movement.

A low-set pressure relief valve is activated when the engine is stopped, ensuring that any vibrations from the hull are not transferred to the engine structure. The non-return valve (NRV) allows oil to flow into the system while an oil drain line directs used oil back to the accumulator. By providing controlled resistance to transverse forces, the hydraulic top bracing system enhances engine stability, reduces resonance, and minimises structural fatigue.

**(c) Checking instructions — top bracing system and holding-down system (6)**

*Top bracing system:*
1. Inspect the overall condition of the top bracing arrangement for any visible damage or misalignment.
2. Check the position indicator on the indication band to ensure it is within the acceptable range.
3. Verify the accumulator pressure by reading the pressure gauge and ensuring it is within the specified limits.
4. Inspect for hydraulic oil leaks around the cylinder, valves, and connections.
5. Check the tightness of bolts securing the arrangement to both the hull and the engine.
6. Observe the operation during engine running, ensuring proper damping and stability without excessive movement or abnormal vibrations.

*Holding-down arrangement:*
1. Examine the overall condition for any signs of wear, corrosion, or misalignment.
2. Inspect for fatigue cracks in the structure and around the bolt areas.
3. Use a feeler gauge to check if the nut is flush with the surface, indicating proper seating.
4. Check the condition of the chocks, ensuring they are intact and free from damage.
5. Verify bolt tightness according to the Planned Maintenance System (PMS) schedule when the engine is not running.

**Hydraulic vs friction top bracing (asked as an addition in one sitting):** the hydraulic type maintains a constant, self-adjusting pre-load and accommodates hull/engine deflection through its accumulator and spherical bearing, whereas a friction type relies on a static friction grip that can slip or loosen over time and cannot follow movement — so the hydraulic type gives more reliable, consistent bracing with less maintenance.

answers.title: Fatigue Cracking — Causes, Propagation & Cylinder-Head Holding Studs
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain fatigue cracking, stating its causes and propagation. (8)

(b) Explain how the risk of fatigue cracking of cylinder head holding studs is liable to be increased (8) by poor maintenance and engine overload. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Fatigue cracking — causes and propagation (8)**

Fatigue cracking is a progressive failure that occurs in materials subjected to repeated cyclic loading, even when the applied stress is below the material's ultimate tensile strength. Over time, these repeated stress cycles cause small cracks to develop, which gradually propagate until catastrophic failure occurs.

The primary causes of fatigue cracking include cyclic loading, which continuously weakens the material, and stress concentrations due to sharp edges, machining defects, or poor design. Material defects, such as impurities and microstructural flaws, further reduce fatigue resistance. Corrosion fatigue also accelerates crack initiation, especially in marine environments where moisture and combustion gases are present. Additionally, thermal cycling, caused by repeated heating and cooling, results in expansion and contraction that contributes to fatigue crack formation.

The process occurs in three distinct stages. First, crack initiation begins at surface imperfections or stress concentration points. Next, crack propagation continues with each stress cycle, gradually extending deeper into the material. Finally, once the remaining cross-section can no longer support the applied load, sudden fracture occurs, leading to complete failure of the component.

**(b) Cylinder-head holding studs — risk from poor maintenance and engine overload (8)**

Cylinder head holding studs are critical components that secure the cylinder head to the engine block, experiencing high cyclic loads due to combustion pressure and mechanical vibrations. Poor maintenance and engine overload can significantly increase the risk of fatigue cracking, leading to structural failure.

Improper maintenance practices, such as incorrect torque application, result in uneven stress distribution, making some studs more prone to failure. Similarly, lack of lubrication can cause dry or corroded threads, leading to localised stress concentrations where cracks initiate. If routine inspections are neglected, small fatigue cracks may go undetected, eventually propagating into full fractures. Additionally, corrosion damage from exposure to moisture and combustion gases accelerates fatigue crack growth, especially in high-temperature conditions.

Engine overload further exacerbates the issue by increasing combustion pressure, subjecting the studs to higher tensile and cyclic stresses. Overloading also generates excessive heat, causing thermal expansion that places additional strain on the studs. Furthermore, increased vibrations amplify stress variations, while sudden load changes, such as rapid acceleration or emergency stops, impose mechanical shock loads that accelerate crack propagation.

To minimise the risk of fatigue cracking, it is essential to follow proper maintenance procedures, including correct torque application, regular lubrication, and thorough inspections. Additionally, avoiding engine overload ensures that cylinder head studs operate within their designed stress limits, enhancing engine reliability and longevity.

answers.title: Tie Rods — Sketch, Why Fitted (Crosshead vs Trunk-Piston), Checking
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Draw a labelled sketch through a section of a crosshead type engine, showing the location and (4) fitting of tie rods.

(b) Explain why tie rods are fitted in crosshead engines and are not required for trunk piston (6) engines.

(c) As Chief Engineer Officer, write instructions for the checking of tie rods fitted in an engine, (6) stating the equipment to be used. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Labelled sketch through a crosshead engine showing tie rods (4)**

**[Sketch]** Section through crosshead engine showing tie rods — exhaust valve housing, cylinder head, gas pressure, entablature (compressive load), tie rods (tensile load), coupling (tie rods are in two parts because the cylinder part moves too much), 'A' frame, pinching screw and groove detail, jack bolts, main bearing, bedplate (compressive load), crankshaft, tank top (compressive load); right-hand detail: entablature, frame, tie bolts, bed plate.

**(b) Why tie rods are fitted in crosshead engines but not required in trunk-piston engines (6)**

Tie rods are long, high-tensile bolts that run through the main structural components of a crosshead engine, connecting the bedplate, frame, and cylinder block into a single rigid unit. They are essential in crosshead engines because these engines experience high tensile and compressive forces due to their two-part construction, where the piston and crosshead are separate. The tie rods absorb and distribute the firing forces from the cylinder block down to the bedplate, preventing misalignment, reducing structural stresses, and maintaining engine integrity.

In contrast, trunk-piston engines do not require tie rods because they have an integrated engine block design, where the cylinder block, crankcase, and bedplate are cast as a single unit. The entire structure is more compact and inherently rigid, allowing it to withstand the forces generated during combustion without requiring additional reinforcement. The absence of a crosshead mechanism also means that bending stresses and misalignment risks are significantly lower, eliminating the need for tie rods.

**(c) Checking tie rods — equipment used (6)**

- **Visual inspection**: examine the tie rods for signs of corrosion, cracks, or deformation; look for any misalignment or displacement that could indicate loosening.
- **Torque checking**: using a hydraulic torque wrench or calibrated torque multiplier, verify that the tie rod nuts are tightened to the specified torque (or specified tightening pressure in the case of hydraulically-tightened nuts) per the engine manual. Uneven tightening can lead to structural stress imbalances.
- **Ultrasonic testing (UT)**: conduct ultrasonic flaw detection using an ultrasonic thickness gauge or flaw detector to check for internal cracks or material fatigue, which may not be visible externally.
- **Strain measurement**: use a dial gauge or strain gauge to measure any elongation or stretching beyond acceptable limits, indicating potential failure.
- **Engine running observations**: monitor for abnormal vibrations, knocking sounds, or excessive movement of the cylinder block, which could indicate loosened tie rods.
- **Log and report findings**: record all inspection data, including torque values, visual observations, and test results, in the maintenance log. Report any irregularities for corrective action.

answers.title: Holding-Down Arrangement — Design Features That Limit Stud Stress
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a main engine holding down system explaining how the (8) design features help prevent excessive stress in the holding down studs.

(b) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, an engine top bracing arrangement, explaining why they are (8) fitted and checked for operational performance. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Main engine holding-down system — design features preventing excessive stud stress (8)**

**[Sketch]** Main engine holding-down arrangement — bolt/stud, nut, distance tube, clearance hole, side chock, support chock, bracket, bedplate, tank top, spherical washer, spherical nut.

The engine holding-down arrangement is designed to securely fix the main engine to the ship's hull structure while minimising excessive stress on the holding-down studs. The bedplate of the engine is mounted on the tank top, with a chock in between to provide a solid and level surface for proper load distribution. These components are held together using holding-down bolts and nuts, ensuring that the engine remains firmly in position.

A key design feature is the **distance tube**, which encloses the holding-down bolt. This tube helps in maintaining proper bolt tension and prevents excessive bending stress on the bolts by ensuring axial loading rather than lateral forces — for a set loading, the effective length of the stud (stud length plus tube length) gives a very large radius of bending, so the induced stress is kept low.

Additionally, a **spherical washer and spherical nut** are used at the bottom of the bolt. These elements allow for self-alignment, compensating for minor misalignments between the engine and the ship's structure, which in turn reduces the risk of fatigue failure in the bolts.

The **side chocks and brackets** further assist in preventing lateral movement of the engine, ensuring that vibrations and dynamic loads are evenly distributed.

By incorporating these design elements, the holding-down system effectively absorbs the forces generated during engine operation, reducing the risk of excessive stress, bolt loosening, and structural failure.

answers.title: Trunk-Piston Medium-Speed Engine — LO Properties & Lubrication System
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the lubrication systems of a crosshead type slow speed diesel (8) engine.

(b) Explain the properties required by the lubricating oil in EACH of the systems described in part (8) (a), stating how these properties compare with those of a lubricating oil used in the crankcase of a trunk piston type diesel engine. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Properties required of a lubricating oil for a trunk-piston medium-speed engine, and why some differ from a crosshead crankcase oil**

A lubricating oil for a trunk piston type medium-speed engine must have the following properties:

- **High detergency and dispersancy**: trunk-piston engines often burn residual fuels, generating carbon, soot and deposit formation; the oil must keep these contaminants in suspension to prevent sludge formation.
- **Adequate alkalinity (high TBN, 20–40)**: to neutralise acidic combustion by-products, particularly with high-sulphur fuel.
- **High thermal stability and oxidation resistance**: medium-speed engines run hot, so the oil must resist thermal breakdown and oxidation that form sludge and varnish.
- **Wear protection / load-carrying ability**: a strong oil film to minimise metal-to-metal contact, reducing wear on rings, liners and bearings.
- **Viscosity stability**: maintains viscosity over time and under varying load/temperature for a reliable film.
- **Good water separation and anti-foaming properties**: marine engines pick up water from combustion/condensation; the oil must shed water and resist foaming to maintain lubrication efficiency.

*Why it differs from crosshead crankcase oil*: a crosshead crankcase oil only lubricates bearings and running gear and never contacts combustion products, so it does not need high detergency or high TBN. The trunk-piston oil uses one charge for both cylinder and crankcase duties, so it must carry better detergency, higher TBN and stronger wear protection all at once.

**(b) Lubrication system of a trunk-piston medium-speed engine, with automatic standby**

**[Sketch]** 4-stroke trunk engine lubrication system — LO sump (60°C), LO pump (4.5 bar) + pre-lube pump, LO duplex filter, TCV, LO cooler (55°C), oil gallery to gears, camshaft bearings, cams & roller guides, rocker arms, fuel pump, main/bottom-end/gudgeon-pin bearings, piston cooling & liner splash (through con-rod).

The lubrication system ensures continuous oil supply, cooling, and impurity removal, with an automatic standby capability to enhance reliability. Lubricating oil is stored in the LO sump, where it is drawn by the main LO pump and pressurised to approximately 4.5 bar. This oil then passes through a duplex filter, ensuring continuous filtration even during maintenance. The thermostatic control valve (TCV) regulates the oil temperature, directing it either through the LO cooler for cooling or bypassing it when cooling is not required. The cooled oil at 55°C is then distributed through the main oil gallery to different engine components.

From the oil gallery, lubrication is supplied to main bearings, bottom-end bearings, and gudgeon pin bearings. Oil also travels through the connecting rod to cool and lubricate the piston crown. Simultaneously, the oil is supplied to camshaft bearings, cams, roller guides, rocker arms, and the fuel pump. Gears and liner splash lubrication further ensure proper lubrication of the valve train and cylinder walls.

Impurities are removed via the duplex filter (continuous filtration, cleanable during maintenance without stopping flow) and, in most installations, a centrifugal purifier taken on a slip-stream from the sump to remove water, sludge and fine solids continuously.

The system has an automatic standby pump, activated when the main pump fails or oil pressure drops below a set limit. Sensors continuously monitor oil temperature and pressure, triggering an alarm and switching to the standby pump when necessary. The lubrication system operates at an optimal sump temperature of 60°C to maintain viscosity and prevent excessive wear.

answers.title: Trunk-Piston Auto-Standby Lubrication System + Crosshead Separate Cylinder LO System
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a lubrication system for a trunk-piston engine which has an (8) automatic standby capability.

(b) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a cylinder lubrication system for a cross-head engine, (8) explaining why a separate cylinder LO system is fitted. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Lubrication system for a trunk-piston engine with automatic standby capability (8)**

**[Sketch]** 4-stroke trunk engine lubrication system — LO sump (60°C), LO pump (4.5 bar) + pre-lube pump, LO duplex filter, TCV, LO cooler (55°C), oil gallery to gears, camshaft bearings, cams & roller guides, rocker arms, fuel pump, main/bottom-end/gudgeon-pin bearings, piston cooling & liner splash (through con-rod).

The lubrication system of a trunk piston medium-speed engine ensures continuous oil supply, cooling, and impurity removal, with an automatic standby capability to enhance reliability. Lubricating oil is stored in the sump, drawn by the main LO pump and pressurised to approximately 4.5 bar, passing through a duplex filter (continuous filtration even during maintenance) and a thermostatic control valve/cooler arrangement before distribution at 55°C through the main oil gallery to main, bottom-end and gudgeon-pin bearings, the piston (via the con-rod), camshaft bearings, cams, roller guides, rocker arms and the fuel pump. An automatic standby pump activates on main pump failure or low oil pressure, with sensors continuously monitoring temperature and pressure and triggering an alarm on switchover.

**(b) Cylinder lubrication system for a cross-head engine, and why a separate cylinder LO system is fitted (8)**

**[Sketch]** Crosshead cylinder lubrication (total-loss) — cylinder lubricating-oil service/day tank, cylinder lubrication box, distribution manifold, pumps, filters, strainer, seawater cooler, lubricating-oil drain tank.

A crosshead engine physically separates combustion (cylinder) from the running gear (crankcase) via the diaphragm/stuffing box, so it needs two independent oils. The cylinder lubrication system is supplied from a cylinder lubricating oil (CLO) day tank positioned above the engine for gravity feed. Cylinder lubricators (an Alpha-type electronically-controlled system on modern engines) inject small, precisely timed quantities of high-TBN (70–100) cylinder oil directly onto the cylinder liner and piston rings, synchronised to piston position via tacho/index signals. This oil is designed to withstand extreme combustion temperatures, reduce friction and neutralise the strongly acidic sulphuric-acid by-products of combustion. Unlike crankcase oil, cylinder oil is not reused — it is a total-loss/once-through system, and the oil is burnt and expelled with the combustion gases as sludge.

A separate system is essential because cylinder oil and crankcase oil have fundamentally different duties: cylinder oil needs high alkalinity to counteract sulphuric acid at high temperature and is consumed in use, while crankcase oil (recirculated, filtered, cooled and purified) needs good oxidation stability, water separation and long-term wear protection at a much lower, more stable operating temperature. Mixing the duties in one oil (as a trunk-piston engine must) would compromise both.
