answers.title: Bacterial Attack on LO Sumps — Chief Engineer's Report
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer write a report to the company superintendent engineer concerning (16) bacterial attack of lubricating oil in the sumps of the main engine and one of the generator engines. The report should explain how the attack was detected, damage found in the engines, investigations into the possible cause of the attack, how the immediate problem was resolved and how future incidents may be prevented. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**As Chief Engineer Officer, report to the company superintendent engineer concerning bacterial attack of lubricating oil in the sumps of the main engine and one of the generator engines (16)**

To: Superintendent Engineer
From: Chief Engineer Officer
Subject: Report on Bacterial Attack in Lubricating Oil Sumps of Main Engine and Generator Engine

This report outlines the detection, investigation, and resolution of a bacterial attack on the lubricating oil in the sumps of the main engine and one of the generator engines, together with recommendations to prevent future occurrences.

**Detection**: the issue was first detected during routine oil analysis, where increased acidity, emulsification, and the presence of sludge were noted in samples from both sumps. Visual inspection revealed milky, cloudy oil with an unusual odour, indicating microbial contamination. Increased filter clogging and degradation of oil viscosity were also observed.

**Damage found**: the main engine exhibited signs of bearing wear, blocked oil passages, and corrosion in the oil cooler, with reduced lubricity leading to abnormal friction and increased bearing temperatures. In the generator engine, filters were heavily clogged with sludge, reducing oil flow and increasing wear on piston rings and bearings, with reduced efficiency in heat dissipation raising operational temperatures.

**Investigation into cause**: water ingress was identified as the primary factor, with traces of cooling water leakage into the sump providing a favourable environment for microbial growth. Extended oil change intervals and low operating temperatures in the generator sump contributed to bacterial proliferation. Poor ventilation and stagnation of the oil further accelerated growth, and prior contamination during storage or filling may have introduced bacteria into the system.

**Immediate action taken**: contaminated oil in both engines was drained and disposed of per environmental regulations. The system was flushed with biocide-treated flushing oil to eliminate bacterial residue. Clogged filters were replaced and oil coolers inspected for residual contamination. Water leakage points were identified and repaired. Fresh, antimicrobial-treated lubricating oil was refilled, and the engines run at higher temperature for a period to eliminate remaining moisture and microbial presence.

**Prevention of future incidents**: regular oil sampling and analysis to detect early contamination; strict monitoring of water ingress with immediate rectification of leaks; use of biocide-treated lubricants in humid/high-risk environments; frequent cleaning and draining of sumps to remove water accumulation and sludge; proper ventilation and optimal oil operating temperatures to prevent stagnation and microbial growth; and adherence to proper oil storage/handling procedures.

Chief Engineer Officer, [Ship Name]

answers.title: Crosshead Separate LO Systems — Properties Compared with Trunk-Piston
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Lubrication systems of a crosshead-type slow-speed diesel engine (8)**

**[Sketch]** Crosshead main-engine (crankcase) LO system — sump tank, main LO pumps, ME/E LO cooler, auto back-flush & bypass filters, sludge checker, distribution manifold to main/crosshead/camshaft/thrust bearings, piston-cooling oil outlet, drain to purifier & storage tanks.

**[Sketch]** Crosshead cylinder lubrication (total-loss) — cylinder lubricating-oil service/day tank, cylinder lubrication box, distribution manifold, pumps, filters, strainer, seawater cooler, lubricating-oil drain tank.

The lubrication system of a crosshead-type slow-speed diesel engine maintains two separate systems for the crankcase and the cylinder liners, due to their very different operating conditions. The crankcase (main engine) system draws oil from an LO sump tank via main LO pumps, through filters and an LO cooler, to the main bearings, crosshead bearings, camshaft bearings and thrust bearings; a sludge checker and bypass filters remove contaminants, the piston-cooling oil outlet cools the piston, and used oil drains back to the sump for purification and reuse.

The cylinder lubrication system is independent, supplied from the CLO day tank positioned above the engine for gravity feed. Alpha-controlled cylinder lubricators inject small quantities of high-TBN cylinder oil directly onto the liner and rings; this oil is designed for high-temperature, high-alkalinity duty and — unlike crankcase oil — is not reused, being expelled as sludge with the combustion gases.

**(b) Properties required in each system, compared with a trunk-piston crankcase oil (8)**

The cylinder lubrication system requires oil with high alkalinity (TBN) to neutralise acidic combustion by-products, particularly sulphuric acid from fuel sulphur, plus excellent high-temperature stability given exposure to combustion heat and pressure, and adequate detergency/dispersancy to prevent carbon/deposit buildup on the liner and rings. Since cylinder oil is consumed during operation, it does not need long-term oxidation stability or water-separation properties.

The crankcase lubrication system requires good oxidation stability and water-separation properties since it operates in a cooler environment. It should have a lower TBN than cylinder oil, as it is not exposed to combustion gases, but needs high film strength and anti-wear properties to protect bearings and moving parts, and excellent demulsibility for a long service life.

By comparison, the lubricating oil used in the crankcase of a **trunk-piston** engine must perform both cylinder and crankcase duties in one unified system: moderate TBN to handle acidic combustion by-products while maintaining oxidation stability for prolonged use, plus strong anti-wear and detergent properties to protect rings, liners and bearings simultaneously — balancing high-temperature resistance and long-term stability in a single, more complex formulation, unlike the two specialised oils of a crosshead engine.

answers.title: Crosshead Separate LO Systems — Cylinder LO When Changing Between Fuels
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the lubrication systems for a crosshead engine, explaining (10) the properties required for the lubricating oil in each system.

(b) Describe a system which may be used to ensure that the cylinder lubricating oil properties are (6) available for a crosshead engine when changing between fuels (including between fuel oil and gas), stating why it is not desirable to use the same cylinder LO for different fuel specifications (including gas). Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Lubrication systems for a crosshead engine, and the properties required in each (10)**

**[Sketch]** Crosshead main-engine (crankcase) LO system — sump tank, main LO pumps, ME/E LO cooler, auto back-flush & bypass filters, sludge checker, distribution manifold to main/crosshead/camshaft/thrust bearings, piston-cooling oil outlet, drain to purifier & storage tanks.

**[Sketch]** Crosshead cylinder lubrication (total-loss) — cylinder lubricating-oil service/day tank, cylinder lubrication box, distribution manifold, pumps, filters, strainer, seawater cooler, lubricating-oil drain tank.

As in the paired canonical on crosshead LO systems, the crankcase and cylinder systems are entirely separate: the crankcase system recirculates cooled, filtered oil to the main/crosshead/camshaft/thrust bearings, while the cylinder system is a gravity-fed, total-loss supply of high-TBN oil injected onto the liner and rings by Alpha-controlled lubricators, consumed and expelled as sludge.

**(b) Ensuring cylinder LO properties are available when changing between fuels (including fuel oil and gas), and why the same cylinder LO should not be used across fuel types (6)**

Using the same cylinder LO for both high-sulphur and low-sulphur fuels (including gas) is undesirable because of differences in acid formation, lubrication requirements and deposit control:

- High-sulphur fuels generate sulphuric acid, requiring high-TBN oil (70–100 mg KOH/g) to neutralise acidity and prevent liner corrosion.
- Low-sulphur fuels and gas produce minimal acidic by-products, making low-TBN oil (15–40 mg KOH/g) more suitable.
- Using high-TBN oil with low-sulphur fuel leads to excessive calcium deposit buildup, causing ring sticking and abrasive wear.
- Using low-TBN oil with high-sulphur fuel results in insufficient acid neutralisation, leading to corrosion.
- Gas engines operate at higher combustion temperatures, requiring low-ash oils to prevent pre-ignition and fouling.

To manage this, modern engines use automated cylinder oil blending systems, automatically adjusting the TBN of the delivered cylinder oil to match the fuel sulphur content in use at any given time, ensuring the correct oil grade is always applied through a fuel change-over.

answers.title: Cylinder Lubricant Properties for HFO + Electronically-Controlled (Alpha) Cylinder Lubrication
answers.question_as_set:
(a) State, with reasons, THREE properties required of a cylinder lubricant for a main engine (6) operating on HFO.

(b) Describe, with the aid of sketches, an electronically controlled cylinder lubrication system, (10) stating how the timing and quantity of cylinder lubricant is regulated and set. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Three properties required of a cylinder lubricant for a main engine operating on HFO (6)**

- **High alkalinity (high TBN)**: HFO contains sulphur, and its combustion produces sulphuric acid which corrodes cylinder liners and piston rings; the cylinder lubricant must have a high TBN to neutralise these acidic by-products and prevent excessive liner wear and damage.
- **Thermal and oxidation stability**: the lubricant must withstand high combustion temperatures without breaking down or forming deposits, maintaining its lubricating properties and minimising ring sticking or scuffing under extreme conditions.
- **Detergency and dispersancy**: strong detergent/dispersant properties keep combustion residues, soot and ash in suspension, preventing deposits on liners, piston rings and ring grooves and ensuring proper sealing.

**(b) Electronically-controlled (Alpha) cylinder lubrication system — timing and quantity regulation (10)**

**[Sketch]** Electronically-controlled (Alpha) cylinder lubrication — per-cylinder lubricators with solenoid valves + accumulator, sensors, pump station with standby pump & pump control unit, Alpha Cylinder Lubricator Control Unit (tacho & index signals, switchboard/backup/monitor units, alarm & safety systems), HMI panel.

Lubricating oil is stored in a sump tank and circulated by a pump station, which includes a standby pump for redundancy. Oil is distributed to per-cylinder lubricators, which inject it onto the liner. The Alpha Cylinder Lubricator Control Unit regulates oil flow based on signals from the engine's tacho and index sensors, synchronising injection precisely with piston position. Solenoid valves on each lubricator control the exact quantity of oil delivered per injection.

Lubrication rates (measured in g/kWh or g/bhp·h) are set through the HMI panel, and the system automatically adapts oil injection based on fuel type, sulphur content and engine load — modifying feed rate and, where a dual-oil system is fitted, the TBN of oil supplied, to prevent both under- and over-lubrication. In case of a control-unit failure, a backup control unit ensures continued operation, with an alarm system alerting the crew to any faults for timely maintenance. Electronic control of this kind improves feed-rate accuracy compared with fixed mechanical lubricators, extending liner life and reducing oil wastage.

answers.title: Crankcase LO Bacterial/Microbial Attack — Causes, Detection & Return to Service
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe the causes and effects of bacterial attack on crankcase lubricating oil. (6)

(b) Explain how bacterial attack on crankcase oil may be detected. (4)

(c) Describe how a crankcase lubricating oil system may be returned to service following bacterial (6) attack of the lubricating oil. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Causes and effects of bacterial attack on crankcase lubricating oil (6)**

Bacterial attack is primarily caused by contamination with water and organic matter, creating an environment suitable for microbial growth. Poor maintenance — ineffective water separation, infrequent oil changes, inadequate heating — promotes bacterial proliferation. Condensation, fuel dilution, or coolant leaks further contribute. Hydrocarbon-degrading bacteria thrive at oil-water interfaces, forming biofilms and sludge within the crankcase.

Effects include degradation of lubricating oil properties through microbial metabolic activity — increased acidity, reduced viscosity, loss of anti-wear additives. Slime and deposit formation clogs filters, restricts oil flow, and increases friction, leading to bearing damage, overheating, or even engine seizure. Hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) and organic acids produced by bacteria accelerate corrosion of metal surfaces.

**(b) How bacterial attack may be detected (4)**

Visual inspection may reveal sludge deposits, darkened oil, or biofilm in the crankcase, on filters and in piping. A rotten-egg (H₂S) or musty odour often indicates microbial activity. Oil analysis is the most reliable method — laboratory testing for low TBN, reduced viscosity, presence of water, and microbial growth. Microbial culture tests or ATP (adenosine triphosphate) bioluminescence tests specifically confirm bacterial contamination. Frequent filter clogging and increased bearing wear rates are further indicators.

**(c) Returning a crankcase LO system to service following bacterial attack (6)**

Drain the contaminated oil completely and remove all sludge deposits from the crankcase, sump, filters and pipelines. Flush the system with a cleaning agent or detergent-based flushing oil to dissolve residual biofilms; if severe, a biocide treatment may be required to eliminate bacterial spores. Once thoroughly cleaned, dry the system and refill with fresh, treated lubricating oil of correct viscosity, TBN, and water content below acceptable limits. Restart the engine at idle with gradual load increases, monitoring oil pressure, temperature and filter condition. Sample the oil regularly to confirm microbial contamination has been eliminated. Preventive measures: maintain oil temperature above 50°C, improve water separation and filtration, conduct routine oil analysis, and consider periodic biocide dosing in high-risk conditions.

answers.title: Crankcase LO Analysis — Water, Metal Particles & Falling Alkalinity/Antioxidant Reserve
answers.question_as_set: A slow speed diesel engine crankcase lubricating oil analysis report indicates a substantial (16) presence of fresh water, metal particles and a reduction of BOTH alkalinity and anti-oxidant reserve. Explain the possible causes of EACH of these changes, and how they may be found. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**A slow-speed diesel engine crankcase LO analysis report shows fresh water, metal particles, and reduced alkalinity AND antioxidant reserve — causes and how each is found (16)**

**Fresh water** can result from leaking cooling water systems (cracked cylinder liners, defective O-rings, faulty heat exchanger) or condensation from poor crankcase ventilation / inadequate draining of separators. Detected via visual inspection (milky/emulsified oil), pressure testing of the cooling system, monitoring expansion-tank levels for unexplained losses, and Karl Fischer titration or hot-plate tests to quantify water content.

**Metal particles** suggest abnormal component wear: bearing wear releases lead, tin or copper; piston/liner scuffing introduces iron and aluminium; gear-train, camshaft or turbocharger bearing damage adds further metal contamination. Detected via spectrometric oil analysis (identifies specific metal elements), magnetic-plug or filter inspections for metallic debris, and vibration-based bearing condition monitoring for early-stage failures.

**Reduced alkalinity (TBN depletion)** is commonly caused by fuel contamination, combustion by-products, and extended oil service life — sulphuric acid from fuel combustion reacting with and depleting the alkaline additives, raising corrosion risk. Detected via TBN testing, fuel-dilution analysis by gas chromatography, and monitoring cylinder drain oil for excessive acidity.

**Reduced antioxidant reserve** occurs from high operating temperatures, prolonged oil use, fuel or water contamination, and exposure to catalytic metals like copper. Excessive oxidation leads to viscosity changes, sludge formation and increased acid content. Detected via oxidation-index measurement using infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), viscosity testing, and total acid number (TAN) analysis.

Regular oil analysis, system-parameter monitoring, and scheduled maintenance allow early detection and prevention of major failures; where contamination is found, corrective actions include oil replacement, system flushing, and mechanical repairs to restore optimal lubrication performance.

answers.title: Electronically-Controlled & Common-Rail Fuel Injection — Layout, Quantity & Timing Control
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a main engine electronically controlled fuel injection system. (6)

(b) Explain how fuel injector quantity and timing is changed in the fuel injection system sketched (6) in part (a).

(c) State why it may be necessary to change engine fuel injection timing. (4) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**System layout and the two fluid rails**

**[Sketch]** Electronically-controlled common-rail system: control oil rail, rail valves, injection control valves, fuel oil rail and fuel-quantity piston generating the fuel-quantity signal.

Modern slow-speed engines (MAN B&W ME, WinGD/Sulzer RT-flex/X) replace the cam-driven jerk pump with a common-rail system keeping fuel pressurised independently of engine speed. Two separate rails are used: the fuel oil rail (high-pressure accumulator feeding the injectors) and the control/servo oil rail (≈200 bar) that actuates the valves.

**How fuel quantity is changed**: the ECU reads engine load and speed, sending a signal to the fuel quantity piston, which adjusts the volume of fuel delivered to the injectors.

**How injection timing is changed**: rail valves and injection control valves open/close according to ECU commands, deciding when fuel is sent to the injectors; timing can be advanced or retarded dynamically based on speed, load and fuel quality.

**Why fuel injection timing is changed**: different fuels have varying ignition delays (especially low-sulphur or alternative fuels); higher load calls for advanced timing (better power/efficiency), lower load for retarded timing (reduced fuel consumption/emissions); retarding timing lowers peak cylinder temperature and reduces NOx; cold-start conditions call for retard, high-speed operation for advance, for smooth performance.

**Key numbers**: common-rail injection pressure 1000–2200 bar (up to 2500); control/servo oil ≈200 bar; start of injection ≈5–15° BTDC held to ±0.5–1° crank angle; peak firing pressure ≈180–220 bar in modern engines.

answers.title: Fuel Injection Fundamentals — Excess Air, Droplet Size & Injection Timing
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain why a diesel engine cylinder is supplied with excess air. (4)

(b) Explain why fuel droplet size produced during injection has to be within narrow limits in order (4) to enable good cylinder combustion to be achieved.

(c) Explain how the desired fuel droplet size is produced by fuel injectors. (4)

(d) State why fuel injection timing has to be controlled within narrow limits to enable economic (4) engine operation without bearing overload. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Why diesel engine cylinders are supplied with excess air (air-fuel ratio 20:1–60:1 vs stoichiometric ≈14.5:1)**

Ensures complete combustion (diesel is injected late with limited mixing time, so surplus O₂ burns all droplets, reducing smoke/soot/HC); dilutes the charge to control peak flame temperature and reduce thermal NOx; allows load variation without throttling (diesel is quantity-governed by fuel alone, so excess air prevents over-rich mixtures and black smoke at high load); improves scavenging and cools cylinder components (liner, piston crown, exhaust valves), especially important in 2-stroke engines.

**Why fuel droplet size must be within narrow limits (target Sauter Mean Diameter ≈10–50µm, most droplets 5–100µm)**

Too large (>50–100µm): slow evaporation, poor mixing, long ignition delay, incomplete combustion, high smoke/soot/carbon deposits, wall-wetting (liner washing, oil dilution). Too small (<5–10µm): excessive penetration loss, short spray reach, poor distribution in large-bore cylinders, wall impingement, possible knock or high NOx from over-rapid evaporation. The correct size balances evaporation rate against penetration depth for consistent ignition delay, controlled heat release, low emissions and high thermal efficiency.

**How fuel injectors produce the desired droplet size**

High injection pressure (1000–2200 bar in common-rail systems) creates high velocity/shear across the nozzle holes, breaking fuel into fine droplets; nozzle geometry (8–12 holes, 0.2–0.5mm diameter, optimised length-to-diameter ratio, sac-less/mini-sac design) shapes the spray; controlled needle-lift dynamics and internal turbulence/cavitation further improve atomisation.

**Why fuel injection timing must be controlled within narrow limits**

*Economic operation*: correct timing places peak cylinder pressure near TDC for maximum crankshaft leverage, highest thermal efficiency, lowest SFC, and complete combustion before the expansion stroke. *Avoiding bearing overload*: too-advanced timing creates excessively high peak firing pressure and rapid pressure-rise rate, overloading the piston, con-rod, crosshead and main bearings (wiping/fatigue risk); too-retarded timing causes late burning, high EGT and after-burning, indirectly stressing components.

answers.title: Fuel Injector Nozzle Cooling — Why Needed & How Achieved
answers.question_as_set:
Wih reference to engine fuel injector nozzle cooling:

(a) explain why fuel injector nozzle cooling is necessary; (4)

(b) describe, with the aid of a sketch, the operation of a nozzle cooling system for a generator (8) engine;

(c) explain how fuel injector nozzles are cooled on engines which are not fitted with a separate (4) nozzle cooling system. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why fuel injector nozzle cooling is necessary (4)**

To prevent overheating and burning of the nozzle tip from the high combustion flame temperature, to maintain correct fuel viscosity at the nozzle for good atomisation, and to reduce carbon deposit formation on the tip.

**(b) Operation of a nozzle cooling system for a generator engine, with a sketch (8)**

A dedicated cooling circuit (water or oil) circulates around the nozzle holder. The cooling medium enters and leaves through separate pipes, carrying heat away from the tip area — kept independent of the main jacket-water circuit so cooling can continue even if the engine is stopped.

**(c) How nozzles are cooled on engines not fitted with a separate cooling system (4)**

The fuel itself acts as the coolant. Leak-off fuel or excess circulating fuel absorbs heat from the nozzle tip and returns to the fuel tank or mixing column, providing continuous cooling as fuel flows through the injector body.

answers.title: Fuel Injector Nozzle Burning — Causes, Investigation & Prevention
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to failure of fuel injector nozzles due to burning:

(a) state, with reasons, THREE possible causes; (6)

(b) write a procedure to be used when investigating the cause of fuel injector nozzle burning; (6)

(c) describe a maintenance system which should be operated in order to minimise the risk of future (4) fuel injector nozzle burning. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Causes of fuel injector nozzle burning**

Poor atomisation (worn/clogged nozzle producing large droplets, incomplete combustion, localised overheating and tip burning); incorrect injection timing (too advanced/retarded causing flame impingement and excess heat on the tip); high EGT (turbocharger, charge-air-cooler or air-fuel fault raising exhaust temperature, causing thermal fatigue and tip erosion); contaminated fuel (cat-fines, water, deposits causing abrasive wear/carbon, degrading the spray); improper cooling (blocked/inefficient nozzle cooling causing prolonged high temperature, burning or failure).

**Investigation → prevention**

*Investigate*: visual inspection of the tip for burn/erosion/deposits; fuel-quality check (water, viscosity, sulphur, cat-fines); verify injection timing and pressure; review EGT trends; inspect cooling passages; examine the combustion chamber/piston crown for related damage.

*Prevent*: precise electronic fuel-injection monitoring and control; EGT monitoring; efficient nozzle cooling; fuel treatment (heating/viscosity control of HFO); ISO 8217 fuel-quality checks; scheduled ultrasonic cleaning and calibration of injectors.

answers.title: Main Engine Fuel-Oil Circulating System & HFO/MGO Fuel Changeover
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer write instructions for the main and auxiliary engine fuel change- over (16) procedures to be followed when a vessel is due to move into an Emission Control Area. Approximate timings must be mentioned to ensure that the vessel does not infringe any regulations and the instructions must mention steps required to avoid cross- contamination of fuel in service tanks, where MGO is carried as the low sulphur fuel. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**The circulating system — flow and valves**

**[Sketch]** Main-engine fuel-oil circulating system — MGO/HFO service tanks, 10µ auto & bypass filters, supply pumps (4–5 bar), heaters, gas-oil cooler, viscometer, circulating pumps (8–10 bar), mixing column and tank return.

Fuel is drawn from MGO/LSFO or HFO service tanks via a common manifold, through supply pumps (4–5 bar) and 50µ inlet filters, into a mixing column (buffer/de-aeration), then circulating pumps (8–10 bar), through heaters (HFO) or a gas-oil cooler (MGO), a viscometer (controls heating to target viscosity), and to the engine. Excess fuel returns to the mixing column; a pressure-regulating valve set at ≈8 bar prevents over-pressure.

**HFO → LSFO/MGO changeover — timed procedure**

*Pre-changeover (≈24 hours before)*: confirm LSFO quality/quantity and sulphur content; inspect filters, strainers and pumps; plan the compliance time (before ECA entry) and work backwards.

*Initiating changeover (4–6 hours before)*: reduce HFO temperature gradually (≈10°C per 15–20 minutes) to avoid pump cavitation and thermal shock; watch viscosity/pressure/temperature at the viscometer; watch pumps for vibration.

*Switching tanks (2–3 hours before)*: open the LSFO outlet while HFO remains open initially; gradually close the HFO valve; redirect the mixing-column return to the LSFO tank before shutting HFO (prevents cross-contamination and sulphur-limit breach); turn off the heater once LSFO circulates; keep the PRV at 8 bar.

*Post-changeover (up to 1 hour after)*: check engine performance, EGT and emissions; inspect the 50µ inlet filters; log start/stop times, consumption and compliance in the Engine Log and Fuel Oil Changeover Record.

**ECA/MARPOL Annex VI cross-contamination control**: complete the main engine changeover 1–2 hours before the ECA boundary, auxiliaries 3–4 hours before (switching one at a time to avoid blackout); use dedicated service tanks, fully drain/flush HFO before refilling MGO, flush fuel lines and change filters after transition; log time/date/position of changeover.

**Generators to MDO while the main engine stays on HFO**: separate MDO service/flushing pumps let generators run clean MDO while the main-engine loop keeps HFO hot and circulating (booster pumps/heaters running) for quick reactivation; a mixing unit and compressed-air purge prevent cross-contamination. Revert by re-introducing HFO while throttling MDO, purging MDO before restart.

answers.title: Two-Stroke Gaseous Fuel Injection System — Why Injected Direct, Not Premixed
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a system for burning gaseous fuel in a two-stroke diesel (12) engine, indicating safety features fitted and explaining why the gas has to be injected into the cylinder rather than mixed with the combustion air outside of the cylinders.

(b) Define the term Methane Slip, explaining how it occurs and why it is undesirable. (4) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Gaseous fuel system for a two-stroke diesel engine, with a sketch (12)**

**[Sketch]** Two-stroke gaseous-fuel injection system — 300-bar gas supply, gas accumulator, window valve, gas injectors, FIVA, ELGI/ELWI valves, blow-off & purge valves, hydraulic-oil actuation and silencer vent.

High-pressure gas (≈300 bar) is stored and buffered in a gas accumulator, metered by a window valve, and injected directly into the cylinder by electronically-timed ELGI (gas) and ELWI valves; a FIVA valve controls the pilot diesel. Safety devices: blow-off valve (over-pressure protection), purge valve (clears residual gas at shutdown/transition), hydraulic-oil actuation, and a vent to a silencer.

**Why gas is injected directly into the cylinder rather than premixed with combustion air outside (4)**

Premixing gas with air before the cylinder risks pre-ignition or knocking, since the gas-air mixture can ignite prematurely from high compression temperatures. In a two-stroke engine specifically, intake and exhaust overlap during scavenging, so a premixed charge would blow straight through to exhaust (fuel loss, uncontrolled exhaust combustion) — direct injection avoids this while giving precise control of timing and quantity, improving combustion efficiency and significantly reducing methane slip.

**Methane slip — definition and why undesirable**

Methane slip is unburned methane escaping to atmosphere through the exhaust, caused by incomplete combustion (poor mixing, low-load operation, leaking exhaust valves) — more common in low-pressure premixed systems. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas (global warming potential >25× CO₂), so even small amounts significantly erode the climate benefit of using gas fuel. Mitigated by optimised injection timing, improved air-fuel mixing, high-pressure direct injection, and oxidation catalysts in exhaust after-treatment.

answers.title: Dual-Fuel 4-Stroke Engine — Gas & Liquid Fuel Systems at the Cylinder, Controller I/O & Gas-Piping Safety
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the arrangement of the gas and liquid fuel systems at the (12) cylinder of a dual fuel 4-stroke engine, stating the input and output signals at the controller.

(b) Describe the arrangement of the gas fuel piping system used for a 4-stroke dual fuel engine, (4) stating the safety features incorporated. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Gas and liquid fuel systems at the cylinder of a 4-stroke dual-fuel engine, with controller signals**

**[Sketch]** Dual-fuel 4-stroke cylinder arrangement — common fuel rail and common gas rail with solenoid-actuated valves; controller fed by crankshaft-RPM and crank-angle-encoder signals.

A common diesel fuel rail and a common gas rail feed solenoid-operated valves. Gas admits into the intake air with fresh scavenge air; near TDC, a small pilot diesel injection ignites the charge, since gas cannot auto-ignite due to its high ignition temperature.

*Controller (ECU) inputs*: crankshaft RPM sensor, crank-angle encoder, fuel pressure sensor, gas pressure sensor, EGT sensor, knock sensor, oxygen (O₂) sensor. *Outputs*: control signals to the gas admission solenoid valve (timing and duration) and pilot diesel injector; the ECU also trims the air-fuel ratio and triggers alarms/emergency shutdown on abnormal conditions (excessive knock, gas leak, etc.).

**Gas fuel piping system safety features**

Double-wall gas piping (an inner-pipe failure is contained and detected); gas leak detection sensors at critical points (supply line, engine inlet) with automatic alarms and shutdown; ventilation system plus inert gas (nitrogen) purging to disperse leaks and eliminate oxygen; explosion-proof electrical components in hazardous areas; continuous temperature/pressure monitoring plus an Emergency Shutdown (ESD) system.

**Why a 2-stroke engine can't premix gas with air but a 4-stroke engine can**

In a 2-stroke, intake and exhaust overlap during scavenging, so a premixed charge would blow straight through to exhaust (fuel loss, uncontrolled combustion downstream). A 4-stroke has separate intake and compression strokes, so a premixed charge stays in the cylinder — port injection/fumigation is practical and efficient there.

answers.title: Direct Injection of Liquid Gas (LNG) into Cylinders — Advantages Over Conventional Gaseous Admission
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a diesel engine fuel system which employs direct injection of (12) liquid gas into engine cylinders.

(b) Explain the advantages of this type of gas injection system compared with the use of gaseous (4) fuel in the form of gas. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Diesel engine fuel system employing direct injection of liquid gas into engine cylinders, with a sketch**

**[Sketch]** Direct liquid-gas (LNG) injection for a 2-stroke — gas accumulator, FIVA controlling pilot diesel, ELWI & ELGI valves and gas injectors, with blow-off/purge/window valves and hydraulic-oil control.

High-pressure LNG accumulator (~300 bar) feeds through a window valve and ELGI/ELWI valves to direct gas injectors in the combustion chamber; pilot diesel is supplied via the FIVA valve when needed. Safety devices: blow-off valve, purge valve, silencer; the ECU controls injection timing and quantity.

**Advantages of direct liquid gas injection compared with low-pressure gaseous fuel admission**

Higher energy density — liquid LNG has much higher energy per unit volume than compressed gas, allowing smaller tanks or greater range for the same power output; better combustion efficiency — high-pressure liquid injection gives superior atomisation and more complete combustion than low-pressure gas admission; lower methane slip — much less unburned methane escapes, since the fuel is injected directly and burns more completely; and it allows higher gas substitution rates with a better overall performance/emissions profile.

answers.title: LNG Engine Installations — Gas Valve Unit, Ventilation/Inert Gas & Pilot Injection
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to LNG diesel engine installations:

(a) describe, with the aid of a sketch, a Gas Valve Unit, explaining its purpose and indicating where (8) it is located in the gas train;

(b) explain why ventilation and inert gas systems must be installed with the engine fuel gas system; (4)

(c) state why pilot injection must be provided when burning fuel gas, explaining how a pilot (4) injection system operates. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Gas Valve Unit (GVU) — purpose and location (8)**

**[Sketch]** Gas Valve Unit in the LNG gas train — bunker line, gas tank, pressure build-up unit, evaporator, glycol heating, double-walled pipe, GVU and supply piping to the cylinder gas valves.

The GVU is the final control unit located between the high-pressure gas supply and the engine's fuel injection system. It regulates and stabilises gas pressure, controls gas flow to match engine demand, acts as a safety shut-off valve (emergency stop), and facilitates purging/venting of the system. It contains shut-off valves, pressure regulators, venting lines and sensors.

**(b) Why ventilation and inert gas systems must be installed with the engine fuel gas system (4)**

LNG is cryogenic — any leak rapidly vaporises and forms flammable gas-air mixtures. Without ventilation, these mixtures can accumulate in enclosed spaces and create an explosion hazard; the ventilation system continuously disperses leaked gas. The inert gas system (nitrogen or CO₂) replaces oxygen in tanks, lines and spaces so that even if gas leaks, it cannot ignite, and is also used to purge lines before maintenance or shutdown.

**(c) Why pilot injection must be provided, and how it operates (4)**

Natural gas has a high ignition temperature and poor auto-ignition properties, so it will not reliably ignite by compression alone in a diesel engine. A small quantity of pilot diesel (MDO/MGO, typically 1–5% of total fuel energy) is injected first; it ignites under compression, creating the high-temperature flame kernel needed to ignite the main gas charge. The pilot injector is electronically controlled, with timing and quantity adjusted by engine load — ensuring stable combustion, preventing misfiring/knocking, and enabling smooth dual-fuel operation.

answers.title: Otto vs Diesel Cycle Dual-Fuel Operation & Problems Burning Gaseous Fuel
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe with the aid of sketches the operation of a four-stroke dual fuel engine, explaining (10) how the correct amount of gaseous and liquid fuels are supplied to the cylinders to meet the power requirement and how the cylinder charge is ignited.

(b) State, with reasons, three problems associated with the burning of gaseous fuels in a diesel (6) engine, indicating how these problems may be overcome. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Otto (premixed, low-pressure) vs Diesel (direct high-pressure gas injection) dual-fuel cycles**

**[Sketch]** Diesel-cycle (direct high-pressure gas injection) dual-fuel arrangement — gas accumulator, ELWI/ELGI valves, FIVA, gas injectors and window/blow-off/purge valves.

In the Otto-cycle approach, gas is mixed with air before compression and a pilot injection ignites the premixed charge — giving high thermal efficiency and low NOx (lower peak temperature) but being more prone to knock and methane slip. In the Diesel-cycle approach, gas is injected late at high pressure with no premixing, again ignited by a pilot — giving a higher effective compression ratio, better efficiency/power and lower methane slip, but higher NOx due to higher peak temperature.

**THREE problems with burning gaseous fuel, and fixes**

- **Methane slip** — mitigated by high-pressure gas injection and oxidation-catalyst after-treatment.
- **Knock/pre-ignition** (high auto-ignition temperature, incorrect air-fuel ratio) — mitigated by electronic fuel injection, optimised pilot timing, EGR or charge-air cooling.
- **Power/efficiency loss at low load** (unstable combustion, misfire risk) — mitigated by raising the pilot fuel ratio, or running diesel-only at low load.

answers.title: Methanol as a Marine Fuel — Properties, Hazards/Handling & Four-Stroke Use
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain why methanol can be used as a fuel for marine diesel engines, indicating the properties (2) of methanol which make it useful as a fuel.

(b) Explain why methanol must be treated with caution when used on board a ship, stating how it (4) should be stored and prepared for use.

(c) Describe how methanol may be used in a marine fuel in four-stroke diesel engines. (10) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Why methanol can be used as fuel — key properties**

High oxygen content (≈50% by mass) promoting complete combustion with very low soot/PM/HC/CO; low cetane number (<5) but high octane (≈109), requiring ignition assistance (pilot diesel or glow plugs); zero sulphur, eliminating SOx emissions and helping meet IMO 2020 and future regulations; liquid at ambient temperature (boiling point ≈65°C), so it's easy to store and bunker like conventional fuels without cryogenic handling; high hydrogen-to-carbon ratio giving lower CO₂ emissions per unit energy (lifecycle impact depends on green/e-methanol production).

**Why methanol must be treated with caution — storage and preparation**

*Hazards*: highly toxic (ingestion, inhalation or skin absorption can cause blindness or death); wide flammable range (6–36.5% in air); low flash point (≈11–12°C); burns with a nearly invisible flame; corrosive to aluminium, zinc and some plastics/rubbers; very low lubricity.

*Storage*: dedicated tanks with nitrogen inert-gas blanketing; methanol-resistant tank coating (epoxy or stainless steel); flame arrestors on vents; located away from accommodation; spill containment to slop tanks; alcohol-resistant AFFF foam for firefighting.

*Preparation for use*: filtration plus addition of lubricity improvers and ignition enhancers (typically 200–500 ppm); double-wall fuel lines with leak detection; strict PPE, gas detection, emergency showers/eyewash, and crew training per IGF Code interim guidelines for low-flashpoint fuels.

**Use in four-stroke marine diesel engines**

Mainly used in dual-fuel mode because of the low cetane number, via two methods: **Port Fuel Injection (PFI)/fumigation** — methanol injected into the intake manifold as a premixed charge, with a small pilot diesel injection (5–50% energy share, often 10–20%) near TDC igniting the mixture; **direct injection dual-fuel** — high-pressure methanol injected directly into the cylinder late in compression, allowing higher methanol substitution (up to 95% in tests) with better knock control. Engine modifications required: corrosion-resistant pumps/injectors, an additional methanol rail, retained pilot diesel system, modified ECU mapping, and knock sensors. Benefits: 50–85% NOx reduction, near-zero SOx/PM, good efficiency at many loads, and seamless switch to 100% diesel if needed. Challenges: knock risk at high loads (mitigated by timing retard, EGR or water addition), ~2–2.5× larger fuel tanks needed due to lower energy density, and cold start may require diesel-only mode.

answers.title: Poor Ignition-Quality Fuel (Low Cetane) — Effects on Slow-Speed vs Medium-Speed Engines & Mitigation
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to poor ignition quality fuel:

(a) explain how it can affect combustion in BOTH slow speed and medium speed diesel engines; (8)

(b) explain how the effects on BOTH diesel engine types in part (a) can be reduced. (8) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**How poor ignition quality fuel affects combustion**

*Slow-speed (2-stroke crosshead) engines*: long ignition delay causes late combustion, high peak pressures, and possible knocking/detonation; incomplete combustion raises exhaust gas temperature, smoke, soot and SFC; thermal overloading of the piston crown, rings and liner risks scuffing and hot spots; reduced power output and efficiency, with higher maintenance from carbon deposits.

*Medium-speed (4-stroke trunk) engines*: more pronounced knocking due to higher engine speed and shorter time for combustion; higher thermal and mechanical loading on valves, pistons and bearings; risk of turbocharger surging or overload from irregular combustion; increased NOx/particulate emissions and potential after-burning in the exhaust.

**Mitigation (both engine types)**

Use fuel additives/ignition quality improvers (cetane boosters); slightly advance injection timing to compensate for the longer delay; ensure fuel is heated to correct viscosity for good atomisation; maintain high injection pressure and good nozzle condition for fine droplets; improve air supply (turbocharger, charge air cooler) to aid combustion; use pilot fuel injection or switch to better-quality fuel where possible; carry out regular maintenance of the fuel treatment plant (purifiers, filters) to remove water/contaminants; keep cylinder-oil BN and feed rate correct to neutralise acids and limit liner polishing.

answers.title: Report — HP Fuel Pump Unit Failure on an Electronically Controlled Engine
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer write a report to the engineering superintendent regarding the (16) failure of a high pressure fuel pump unit on an electronically controlled engine. The report must explain the nature of the failure, how the failure was detected and the immediate action taken. The report must also explain the actions taken to replace the pump and the steps taken to minimise the risk of future similar fuel pump failures. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Report on failure of a high-pressure fuel pump unit on an electronically controlled engine**

*Nature of failure*: seizure, internal leakage, loss of pressure, erratic operation, or complete breakdown of the HP fuel pump.

*Detection*: alarms (low fuel pressure, injection deviation), performance monitoring (high EGT on affected units, power loss, unusual vibration/noise), ECU fault codes.

*Immediate action*: reduce engine load/speed; isolate the affected pump if possible; switch to standby or manual mode if available; monitor remaining units closely; inform the bridge and superintendent.

*Replacement actions*: prepare the spare pump; follow the maker's procedure for safe isolation and removal; bleed air from the system; calibrate the new pump; test on the engine at low load first.

*Preventive measures*: regular inspection of pump internals during overhaul; strict fuel-quality control (water, particles); proper lubrication/cooling of the pump; timely replacement per running hours; monitoring of fuel-pressure trends.

**Report on fuel injector replacement due to erosion and burning**

*Detection*: routine performance monitoring showed increased exhaust temperatures, fluctuating cylinder pressures, and poor combustion; during maintenance, visual inspection revealed eroded nozzle holes, burned tips, deposits and pitting.

*Likely causes*: poor atomisation (worn nozzles); contaminated fuel (water, catalytic fines); excessive injection pressure; inadequate injector cooling; extended service life beyond recommended hours.

*Actions taken*: replaced damaged injectors with new OEM units; checked and improved fuel filtration/treatment; reviewed and adjusted injection pressure settings; inspected and maintained the injector cooling system; revised the overhaul schedule.

*Preventive measures instituted*: continuous performance monitoring (cylinder pressure, EGT); periodic fuel-quality testing plus enhanced filtration; strict adherence to maker's service intervals; routine cooling-system checks; crew training on early signs of injector problems.

answers.title: Electronically Controlled Engines — Fuel, Exhaust Valve & Starting Air Control Mechanisms
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to electronically controlled engines:

(a) describe how fuel injection quantity and timing is adjusted; (6)

(b) describe how the exhaust valve timing may be varied; (5)

(c) describe how starting air valves are regulated. (5) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Fuel injection quantity and timing adjustment**

The ECU uses inputs from multiple sensors (engine load, speed, fuel rail pressure, EGT, crank angle, etc.), calculating and controlling Start of Injection (SOI), injection duration, and rail pressure. This enables multi-stage injection (pilot + main + post) for better combustion, lower emissions and smoother operation. Injection is independent of engine speed (unlike cam-driven systems), with real-time feedback allowing continuous optimisation.

**Variable exhaust valve timing**

Controlled by a hydraulic actuation system: the ECU signals a rail valve, high-pressure servo oil moves a slide rod, which actuates the exhaust valve piston; a position sensor provides feedback. The ECU varies opening/closing timing based on load and speed (e.g. earlier opening for better scavenging at high load, or a Miller-cycle effect for efficiency/emissions reduction at part load); spring air assists closing.

**Starting air valve regulation**

ECU-controlled via solenoid valves (pneumatic or hydraulic actuators) instead of mechanical cams. A crank-angle sensor tells the ECU exact cylinder positions, so air is directed only to the correct cylinders at the precise crank angle for smooth, efficient starting with minimal air consumption. Once the engine reaches self-sustaining speed, the ECU closes all starting air valves — preventing backfiring and starting-air explosions, and reducing wear.

answers.title: Report — Repeated Exhaust-Valve Failures on Medium-Speed Auxiliary Engines
answers.answer_text:
**Report to the Superintendent Engineer regarding a number of cases of severe damage to medium-speed engine exhaust valves in the previous 12 months, outlining probable cause and future steps to avoid similar incidents (16)**

**1. Introduction**: submitted following a number of severe exhaust-valve-related failures on auxiliary-engine units #1, #2, #4 and #6 during the past twelve months, to record the sequence of incidents, identify probable root causes, and recommend corrective measures — based on engine-room log entries, alarm records, overhaul reports and the onboard spare-gear inventory.

**2. Summary of incidents**:
- **Case 1 — Unit #4**: black smoke at the engine block activated the water-mist system; the engine was stopped and inspected. A broken exhaust-valve spring allowed the spindle to free-fall onto the piston crown, shattering the cylinder head and spindle and damaging the valve guide, with exhaust gas released into the engine room. The complete cylinder-head assembly was renewed with an overhauled spare.
- **Case 2 — Unit #1**: a knocking noise was detected; inspection identified excessive tappet clearance. The engine was stopped and clearance reset per the manufacturer's manual — no catastrophic damage, but incorrect valve setting accelerates seat wear and imposes impact stress on valve components.
- **Case 3 — Unit #6**: high exhaust gas temperature was recorded; inspection found a broken valve spindle leaking gas into the manifold. Owing to a shortage of new spindles, used spindles had been repeatedly lapped and reused; material fatigue and thermal stress on the aged component caused the failure. The cylinder-head assembly was renewed with an overhauled spare.
- **Case 4 — Unit #6 (a second incident)**: during routine tappet/timing adjustment the exhaust valve was found stuck in its guide. Dismantling revealed heavy carbon on the spindle, traced to an incorrectly "clocked" lube-oil drive line that formed an oil trap and contamination build-up. The head was decarbonised, the spindle bore cleaned, leak-tested and returned to service.
- **Pattern**: the failures share common threads — broken/aged valve components, incorrect clearances, deposit build-up and elevated exhaust temperatures — indicating a systemic cause (spares and maintenance management, plus operational loading) rather than isolated component defects.

**3. Probable causes**: inadequate critical-spare availability (insufficient stock of cylinder heads, spindles, springs and valve gear, delaying full renewals); repeated reuse of aged components (spindles repeatedly lapped and reused, reducing material strength and causing fatigue failure); incorrect valve setting (excessive tappet clearance causing impact loading and accelerated wear); improper lubrication-line configuration (mis-aligned oil drive line creating an oil trap, carbon accumulation and valve sticking); operational overloading (engines run under sustained overload, particularly while other units were under maintenance, raising thermal/mechanical stress — with high-temperature vanadium/sodium hot corrosion and cat-fines ruled out via fuel analysis). Collectively these indicate a combination of mechanical fatigue, thermal overloading, poor spare management and maintenance constraints.

**4. Recommendations** (linked to each cause above): procure and hold adequate onboard stock of genuine, manufacturer-approved critical spares (spindles, springs, guides, complete cylinder-head assemblies) and stop reusing over-lapped spindles; carry out a comprehensive major overhaul of the affected engines at the next dry dock, renewing all critical valve-train components; enforce PMS tappet-clearance and timing checks, verify valve-rotator operation, and correct the lube-oil drive-line alignment to prevent oil traps and carbon build-up; avoid sustained overload, verifying AVR/PMS load-sharing and governor balancing so load is shared smoothly; trend individual exhaust-gas temperatures, vibration and tappet clearances, arranging shore-specialist vibration/fatigue analysis to catch component stress early; improve maintenance planning and shore coordination so spares arrive and maintenance windows are honoured despite the operating schedule.

**5. Conclusion**: the repeated failures are primarily attributable to material fatigue, insufficient spare support, operational overloading and maintenance constraints; without a structured corrective plan, recurrence is likely and may lead to major engine breakdown and extended off-hire.

answers.title: Diesel Generator — Preparing & Selecting as Standby, and Post-Shutdown Checking Procedure
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain how a diesel generator is prepared and selected as a standby generator. (8)

(b) Write a procedure for checking a diesel generator engine after it has been shut down and (8) before it is returned to standby duty. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) How a diesel generator is prepared and selected as a standby generator (8)**

This assumes the engine is already mechanically fit (that is part b). The task here is to bring it to a state of armed readiness and select it at the board.

1. Confirm auxiliaries and pre-start state — sump oil level correct, jacket water level up and the jacket-water pre-heater ON (kept warm so it can accept load immediately), fuel service/day-tank level good and fuel valves open, starting-air receiver at pressure (or start batteries charged), governor set.
2. Keep-warm/pre-lubrication running — the standby set is held warm (heater) and, where fitted, the pre-lube/priming pump runs continuously or cyclically so there is an oil film on start, avoiding thermal and lubrication shock when it auto-starts onto load.
3. Test run — start the engine locally, warm it through and run at no load; check lube-oil pressure, cooling-water and exhaust temperatures, governor stability and that it reaches rated speed with no abnormal noise/leaks; then stop (or leave running to synchronise).
4. Prove the electrical end — confirm the AVR builds rated voltage at correct frequency, and that phase sequence/rotation is correct for paralleling.
5. Set up the breaker and controls — ACB racked into the service (connected) position, control/tripping fuses in, undervoltage relay healthy, synchronising unit set to auto.
6. Select to STANDBY/AUTO on the PMS or selector switch — arm the set so it will auto-start on demand (blackout, load-dependent start, or a heavy-consumer request), and set its start priority/sequence in the load-sharing order.
7. Confirm standby readiness — with keep-warm and pre-lube running, starting air/batteries topped up, the set is now able to start, synchronise and be on the bars within ~45 seconds, sharing kW (governors) and kVAr (AVR) automatically.

**(b) Procedure for checking a diesel generator engine after shutdown, before it is returned to standby duty (8)**

This is the physical engine round after it has been running or worked on, worked through methodically:

1. Make safe/tidy up — engine correctly stopped; if maintenance was carried out, confirm all tools and rags accounted for, guards and covers refitted, and any isolation removed.
2. Lubricating oil — check sump level and top up; check oil condition (no water/fuel contamination, correct colour/smell); check LO filter differential pressure and clean/change if due; sample if scheduled.
3. Cooling water — check jacket/expansion-tank level and top up with treated water; verify inhibitor/treatment concentration; check the header tank and confirm no leaks.
4. Fuel oil — check service/day-tank level, drain off any water, check/clean filters, confirm no leaks, and prime/vent the system so it is ready to fire.
5. Starting system — top up and drain the starting-air receiver of water/oil (or check battery charge and electrolyte); confirm air-start valves and pressure are correct.
6. Bar over/check for hydraulic lock — open the indicator (test) cocks, engage turning gear and bar the engine over one revolution (or blow through on air) to prove free rotation and that no water/oil has collected in a cylinder; then disengage turning gear and close the cocks.
7. Leak and integrity check — walk round for oil, water, fuel, air and exhaust leaks; check the turbocharger, and drain any water from the charge-air cooler.
8. Governor and linkages — check governor oil level and that the fuel-rack/control linkages move freely.
9. Protection and alarms — confirm trips and alarms are reset and healthy (LO low-pressure, HT high-temperature, overspeed), and instrumentation reads correctly.
10. Replenish and warm through — with all consumables topped up, pre-heater on and pre-lube running, the engine is now physically fit — then it can be prepared and selected to standby per part (a).

answers.title: Engine Cooling-Water Waste Heat Recovery — Electricity Generation (Organic Rankine Cycle) & Ship Heating Utilisation
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, an engine cooling water waste heat recovery system for (8) generating electricity, explaining how the system operates.

(b) Describe, with the aid of sketches if necessary, how waste heat recovered for diesel engine (8) cooling water can be utilised throughout the ship for different heating purposes, explaining how such heat recovery systems are operated. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Engine cooling-water waste heat recovery system for generating electricity, with a sketch, explaining how it operates (8)**

**[Sketch]** Organic Rankine Cycle recovering jacket cooling-water heat to generate electricity: evaporator → expander/generator → seawater condenser → feed pump, a closed loop.

The engine's jacket cooling water (~80–90°C) is the heat source. Because that temperature is far too low to boil water usefully, the system uses a closed Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) charged with a low-boiling-point organic fluid — a refrigerant such as R245fa or R134a, or a hydrocarbon like isopentane.

How it operates (a closed loop, like a fridge run as a heat engine):

1. **Evaporator** — the hot jacket water gives up its heat to the organic fluid, boiling it into a high-pressure vapour (the jacket water leaves cooler and returns to the engine/central cooler).
2. **Expander/turbine** — the high-pressure vapour expands through a turbine or screw expander, doing shaft work that drives a coupled generator/alternator, producing electricity fed to the main switchboard (through a converter/synchronising gear).
3. **Condenser** — the low-pressure exhaust vapour is cooled by seawater (or the central fresh-water cooler) and condensed back to liquid.
4. **Feed pump** — pumps the liquid back up to evaporator pressure, completing the cycle.

This recovers low-grade heat that would otherwise be dumped to sea, cutting diesel-generator load, fuel consumption and CO₂/EEDI. The ORC can be combined with scavenge-air and lube-oil cooler heat, or topped up by an exhaust-gas source, to boost output.

**(b) How waste heat recovered from diesel engine cooling water is utilised throughout the ship for different heating purposes, and how such systems are operated (8)**

**[Sketch]** Utilisation of recovered jacket cooling-water heat: a three-way control valve feeds the fresh-water generator, HVAC/accommodation, domestic hot water and oil heating, with surplus dumped through the central cooler.

The jacket water leaving the engine carries a large quantity of low-grade heat that would otherwise be rejected to sea. Dedicated heat exchangers tap this circuit; a three-way temperature-control valve gives the heating services first call on the heat, with the seawater central cooler removing only the surplus, so the jacket stays at its ~85°C set-point. Main uses:

- **Fresh-water (distilling) plant** — the biggest and classic use. Jacket water heats a vacuum evaporator: under vacuum, seawater boils at only ~40–60°C, so 80–85°C jacket water is hot enough to distil it. Vapour is condensed to distilled water; a salinometer dumps any off-spec water. Only run at sea, clear of the coast.
- **HVAC/accommodation heating** — jacket water (or a secondary hot-water loop it heats via an exchanger) feeds the air-heater batteries in the ventilation/AC plant and cabin heaters.
- **Domestic hot water** — heats a calorifier supplying washrooms and galley.
- **Fuel-oil and lube-oil tank heating** — base/tank-maintenance heating of HFO settling and service tanks to keep viscosity and pumpability (final heating to injection viscosity still needs steam or electric heaters).

Operating philosophy: temperature-controlled and load-dependent — recovery services are prioritised and the central cooler dumps the balance. At low engine load, or in port, there may be too little heat, so a steam or electric heater (auxiliary/composite boiler) backs up the services. The cooled jacket water returns to the engine, keeping cylinder-liner temperatures stable.

answers.title: Report — Turbocharger Failure: Seized Turbine-End Bearing & Shaft Damage, Fleet-Wide Preventive Measures
answers.answer_text:
**As Chief Engineer Officer on a vessel with a single 6-cylinder two-stroke crosshead propulsion engine and two turbochargers, one of which fails (seized turbine-end bearing, damaged shaft, inoperable): report for the Engineering Superintendent detailing the failure and cause, explaining how it happened, fleet-wide preventive procedures, and the steps taken to operate the engine at reduced power (16)**

**1. Introduction**: the affected turbocharger (one of two identical units supplying scavenge air in parallel) failed without prior major alarm — first indication was a sudden rise in exhaust gas temperature on several cylinders, a drop in scavenge air pressure, and unusual noise/vibration from the turbocharger. The turbine end bearing was found seized, with the shaft scored, bent/distorted and possibly fractured, rendering the unit inoperable. Load was reduced immediately to protect the remaining turbocharger and engine.

**2. Cause of the failure and how it happened** — root cause: lubrication failure to the turbine end bearing, leading to overheating, seizure and mechanical destruction of the shaft. Sequence:

1. **Initial lubrication deficiency** — partial or complete loss of LO supply/pressure to the turbine end bearing, possibly from blockage/restriction in the supply line or orifice, failure of the T/C lube oil pump or choked filters, oil contamination (water ingress, fuel dilution, metallic particles), or bearing clearance increased beyond limits from normal wear (allowing excessive oil leakage and starvation under load).
2. **Overheating and seizure** — without adequate oil film, the bearing overheated rapidly under high exhaust gas temperature and rotational speed; the bearing material softened/melted, seizing the shaft journal within the housing.
3. **Shaft damage** — once seized, the continuing drive from exhaust gases caused the shaft to twist, score heavily and suffer mechanical damage (possible bending/cracking), making it impossible to rotate the rotor safely.
4. **Secondary effects** — the sudden loss of one turbocharger caused an immediate drop in scavenge air pressure, leading to richer combustion, rising exhaust temperatures and increased thermal loading on the remaining turbocharger and engine. No prior major vibration or bearing-temperature-trend alarm was recorded, indicating the failure developed rapidly once lubrication was compromised.

**3. Actions taken onboard to operate at reduced power**:

- **Isolation of the damaged turbocharger** — shut down and isolated on both exhaust gas and air sides (where design permits); the rotor secured against rotation to eliminate risk of exhaust gas leakage, vibration transmission, or further mechanical failure.
- **Controlled reduction of engine power** — load gradually reduced, currently operated at approximately 55–65% of MCR (subject to confirmation from Superintendent and Class), because the remaining turbocharger cannot supply sufficient scavenge air for full-load combustion (risking very low air-fuel ratio, incomplete combustion, excessive exhaust temperatures, thermal overload of pistons/exhaust valves/liners); to protect the remaining turbocharger from overspeed/overload; to maintain stable combustion within acceptable exhaust temperature margins; and to comply with the engine builder's emergency operating instructions for single-turbocharger operation.
- **Enhanced monitoring and control** — continuous monitoring of all cylinder exhaust temperatures (kept as balanced as possible), scavenge air pressure, remaining turbocharger speed/vibration/bearing temperatures; fuel rack position limited manually or via the load limiter; increased frequency of scavenge space inspections; auxiliary systems (cooling water, lube oil) operated with extra margins; Bridge informed and speed adjusted for safe navigation.

**4. Recommendations for fleet-wide preventive measures**:

1. **Turbocharger bearing inspection and replacement policy** — strict adherence to OEM-recommended running hours (typically 20,000–30,000 hours or earlier based on condition); mandatory boroscopic inspection of turbine and compressor ends at every major overhaul or on any abnormal symptom.
2. **Lubricating oil management** — enhanced LO analysis programme for turbocharger systems (particle count, water content, viscosity, metal content); regular cleaning/replacement of T/C lube oil filters and strainers; verification of correct oil type and pressure at the T/C inlet under all load conditions.
3. **Condition monitoring upgrade** — continuous vibration monitoring/trending on all turbochargers; bearing temperature sensors with trending and pre-alarm settings (not just high-high shutdown); regular review of exhaust gas temperature spreads and scavenge pressure trends as early indicators.
4. **PMS review** — update turbocharger PMS jobs to include more frequent checks of oil supply lines, orifices and drains; include "turbocharger distress" troubleshooting in the Chief Engineer's standing orders.
5. **Training and awareness** — fleet-wide training on early detection of turbocharger problems (noise, vibration, oil consumption, temperature rise); ensure all engineers are familiar with single-turbocharger emergency operation procedures for each engine type in the fleet.
6. **Spares and emergency preparedness** — review stock levels of critical turbocharger spares (bearings, shaft seals, etc.) across the fleet; consider carrying one complete spare turbocharger or major rotating assembly for vessels with critical single-engine propulsion.

**5. Conclusion**: the failure was caused by lubrication starvation leading to bearing seizure and shaft damage. Prompt action allowed the engine to be safely operated at reduced power on the remaining turbocharger, preventing more serious damage to the main engine.

answers.title: Starting Air System — Description, Components & Safety Devices
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a main engine starting air system, stating the safety devices (8) which are incorporated.

(b) In the event of the main engine failing to turn over on air even though there was suffficient air (8) pressure in the starting air receivers, explain the procedure for tracing the cause of the failure. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a main engine/diesel engine starting air system, stating the safety devices incorporated (8)**

**[Sketch]** Main engine starting air system with safety devices — air bottle, auto/main valve, distributor, NRV, slow-turning valve, per-cylinder air-start valves, with bursting disc, relief valve and flame arrester on the manifold.

**System components**: Air bottle (stores starting air at ~30 bar); Start block valve (7 bar, supplies the control circuit); Auto/Main valve (pneumatically operated master valve admitting high-pressure air to distributor and starting air valves); NRV (prevents back-flow of combustion gases into the air line); Distributor (timed to the crankshaft, sequences air to the correct cylinder starting air valves in firing order); Starting air valves (on each cylinder head, admit high-pressure air at the correct timing); Slow turning valve (allows slow rotation before full start, checking for hydraulic lock); Block valve for main valve (controls pilot air); Fuel pump puncture valve (holds fuel pumps off-load during air start); Local/Remote control panel; T/G interlock (prevents starting if turning gear engaged).

**Safety devices fitted**: Bursting disc (ruptures to relieve manifold overpressure); Relief valve (limits manifold/pipeline pressure); Flame arrester (prevents flame propagating back into the air-start valve and pipework); NRV (prevents combustion-gas backflow into the distributor/main air line); Fuel pump puncture valve (cuts fuel if an air-start valve leaks, preventing combustion gas entering the air line); Distributor stop valve (isolates the distributor for maintenance); T/G interlock (prevents the start signal if turning gear is engaged).

**Key fact**: the air bottle sits at ~30 bar; the control circuit runs on the 7 bar start block valve; the distributor is timed to the crankshaft and sends air-start pulses to each cylinder in firing order.

answers.title: Slow Turning System — Why Fitted, When It Operates, How It Works
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to an engine air starting system:

(a) explain why a slow turning system is fitted; (4)

(b) state, with reasons, when a slow turning system operates; (4)

(c) describe, with the aid of a sketch, an air starting system, explaining how the slow turning (10) system operates. Check against the original paper. The part marks as supplied sum to 18, but every question on this paper carries 16. One allocation above is likely mis-stated; the question text itself is unaffected. Total 18 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why a slow turning system is fitted (4)**

Before starting, a cylinder may have accumulated liquid (water from condensation, fuel, or lube oil). If the engine is barred over slowly first, any hydraulic lock is detected — liquid cannot be compressed and will cause catastrophic damage (bent connecting rod, cracked cover) if a full air start is applied directly. It confirms free rotation of the engine and that no mechanical obstruction exists, protecting the crankshaft, bearings and cylinder covers from damage.

**(b) When slow turning operates (2)**

After a prolonged shutdown (port stay, repairs, standby periods) — liquid ingress risk is highest. It is automatically triggered when the engine has been stationary for a set period (typically 30 minutes on modern engines) — the interlock requires the engine to complete slow turning before full start air is admitted.

**(c) How the slow turning system operates, with a sketch (10)**

**[Sketch]** Air starting system with slow turning arrangement — the slow turning valve admits a small, controlled flow directly to the manifold, bypassing the main distributor.

Sequence: start signal received (bridge or local) → T/G interlock checked, blocking the start if turning gear is engaged → slow turning valve opens, admitting a small controlled flow of air directly to the starting air manifold, bypassing the main distributor → engine rotates slowly (one full revolution or as set) → if rotation is free with no hydraulic lock detected, indicator cocks are closed → the slow turning interlock clears, energising the Auto/Main valve → full starting air is admitted via the distributor, sequenced to cylinder air start valves in firing order → engine fires and accelerates to running speed → fuel admitted, starting air cut off, engine runs on fuel.

**Key fact**: slow turning uses a small controlled flow that bypasses the distributor; the main start is interlocked behind a successful slow turn.

answers.title: Air Start System Explosion — How It Occurs & CEO Prevention
answers.answer_text:
**(b) How an explosion in a diesel engine air start system might occur (4)**

A leaking or seized-open air start valve allows high-temperature combustion gases to flow back into the air start manifold. Lubricating oil mist present in compressed air (from the compressor) accumulates in the manifold. Hot gases or sparks from the cylinder ignite the oil/fuel mist in the manifold, causing an explosion. Separately, if slow turning is not done and a cylinder has accumulated fuel/water (hydraulic lock), sudden admission of air can cause a pressure explosion.

**(c) Chief Engineer actions to avoid explosion (4)**

*Operational precautions*: always slow-turn the engine before a full air start (checks for hydraulic lock, purges cylinders); verify flame arresters are clean and in place before starting.

*Maintenance regime*: regularly overhaul and test air start valves for leakage (a leaking valve is the primary cause); inspect and maintain NRVs to ensure correct seating; drain air start lines and bottles regularly to remove moisture/oil; keep air compressors well maintained to minimise oil carryover.

*Checks and procedures*: check the bursting disc and relief valve condition regularly; ensure the distributor stop valve is closed when the engine is on standby for maintenance; follow SMS/PMS schedules; brief watchkeepers on correct starting procedures.

**Key point**: the primary cause is a leaking air-start valve — it is the component to overhaul and test first, since it is what lets hot combustion gas back into an oil-laden manifold.

answers.title: Engine Fails to Start/Turn Over on Air — Fault-Finding & Avoidance
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain why an engine may fail to start on air when the start air receiver is fully charged and (10) the air receiver outlet to the engine is open.

(b) Describe how problems with air starting systems may be avoided. (6) Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Why an engine may fail to start on air when the receiver is fully charged and outlet is open (10); how such problems are avoided (6); tracing the cause of a failure to turn over on air (8)**

*Main air supply path faults*: main start air valve not opening (solenoid fault, seized valve, control air failure); starting air distributor faulty (not sending timed pulses); control air pressure too low (below ~7 bar).

*Cylinder faults*: start air valves seized/stuck closed (carbon deposits, corrosion, spring failure).

*Timing/control faults*: remote start signal not reaching the main valve (broken circuit, faulty solenoid); telegraph/ECR selector in the wrong position; reversing servo failure (start interlock remains active).

*Safety interlocks preventing start*: overspeed trip not reset; low LO pressure interlock active; OMD or bearing high-temperature alarm active; turning gear engaged interlock; open cylinder cocks (start inhibit on some engines).

*Mechanical faults*: hydraulic lock; broken/jammed piston; excessive exhaust back pressure.

*Air system specific*: faulty control/pilot air (no pilot signal, blocked strainer/filter, corroded/blocked pipework).

**Fault-finding trace (step-by-step)**: 1) check air bottle pressure (min ~17–20 bar, normal 30 bar); 2) check start block valve (7 bar) fully open; 3) check auto/main valve pilot air signal; 4) check NRV not stuck closed; 5) check turning gear interlock fully withdrawn; 6) check slow turning valve operates; 7) check the distributor receiving air with correct timing; 8) check individual cylinder starting air valves (crack the airline to test); 9) check for hydraulic lock (crack indicator cocks, bar manually); 10) switch to local control — if it starts, the fault is in the remote/telegraph system.

**Avoiding air start problems**: regular overhaul of the main valve, distributor and cylinder valves; daily draining of air receivers; test/overhaul automatic drain traps; regularly test safety interlocks; inspect valve seats for erosion; test control/pilot air pressure; service compressors regularly (worn rings cause oil carry-over); fit/maintain oil-water separators and filters; ensure turning gear is disengaged and interlocked before starting; open indicator cocks and bar the engine before starting after a prolonged shutdown; fit flame/bursting disc arrestors per SOLAS.
