answers.title: Dangers of the Starting Air System, Failure to Fire on Fuel & Transfer to Local Control
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe the dangers associated with a main engine starting air system, explaining how these (9) dangers are mitigated.

(b) State, with reasons, THREE causes of an engine failing to fire on fuel after successfully turning (3) over on starting air.

(c) Explain how the engine is transferred to local (engine side) control in the event of failure of the (4) main engine remote control system. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Dangers associated with a main engine starting air system, and mitigations (9)**

1. **Starting air line explosion/blowback** — a misfiring fuel-injected cylinder passes burning gases back through the open starting air valve into the line; fuel/oil contamination creates an explosive mixture. *Mitigations*: bursting discs on the main line, flame traps/NRVs on branch lines, automatic drain valves, relief valves, regular draining and inspection.
2. **Air receiver over-pressure** — compressor malfunction or blocked relief path. *Mitigations*: safety relief valves set to SWP, fusible plugs, pressure gauges and high-pressure alarms.
3. **Main starting valve leakage (weeping)** — hot combustion gases enter the manifold during firing strokes, risking manifold fire/explosion. *Mitigations*: valve overhaul and seat lapping at intervals, non-return features on individual valves, temperature monitoring.
4. **Hydraulic lock** — water ingress from a leaking head/liner jacket accumulates in the cylinder; starting causes catastrophic failure (bent con-rod, cracked head). *Mitigations*: always crack indicator cocks and turn on air first ("gas free" turn), inspect cocks before starting, maintain cooling joints and liner O-rings.
5. **Inadvertent starting/uncontrolled movement** — the engine can turn over unexpectedly if pressurised during maintenance. *Mitigations*: turning gear interlock, shut/vent the manifold during maintenance, lock-out/tag-out (ISM Code).
6. **High-pressure air injury** — leaks from HP connections (up to 30 bar) are a direct hazard. *Mitigations*: regular hydraulic pressure testing per class survey, proper jointing/torquing, PPE, no standing in line with flanges during pressurisation.

**(b) THREE causes of failing to fire on fuel after a successful air turn-over (3)**

Fuel supply issues (faulty pumps, blocked lines, insufficient pressure); incorrect fuel injection timing (faulty camshaft timing, sticking pump racks, improper governor settings); air in the fuel system (recent maintenance, line leakage, or inadequate priming introducing air, preventing proper atomisation).

**(c) Transfer to local (engine-side) control on remote control failure (4)**

1. Contact the bridge and request main engine stoppage. 2. Proceed to the local control station and confirm bridge communication. 3. Switch the control transfer changeover valve/cock from "remote" to "local". 4. Engage the clutch changeover mechanism (anti-clockwise), disengaging fuel rack control from the governor and connecting the manual hand control. 5. Unlock the local hand control lever, setting it to zero-fuel/start position. 6. On bridge telegraph orders, select ahead/astern via the selector switch, confirming direction via indicator lights. 7. Press the start button manually at the local station, adjusting fuel quantity with the hand control lever as required.

answers.title: Starting Air Receiver — Entry, Inspection, Survey & Closing Up
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe the procedure for entry into, and inspection of, the inside of a starting air receiver, (12) stating the types of defects which may be present with their possible causes.

(b) Describe the procedure of closing up the air receiver and the initial pressurisation to working (4) pressure. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Procedure for entry into and inspection of a starting air receiver, stating defects and causes (12); closing up and initial pressurisation (4); preparing for survey (6)**

**Pre-entry procedure**: isolate the receiver (shut all inlet/outlet valves, lock off/tag out; depressurise fully, open drain/vent, confirm zero on the gauge; blank-flange all connections); obtain an Enclosed Space Entry Permit and appoint a standby man; test the atmosphere with a calibrated gas detector (O₂ 20.8%, range 19.5–23.5% acceptable; CO/hydrocarbon within safe limits); ventilate for a minimum of 15 minutes before entry; entry team in PPE (no naked flames), continuous atmosphere monitoring, harness/lifeline if needed.

**Inspection points and defects, with causes**: internal corrosion/pitting (moisture carried over with compressed air, ineffective separator/auto-drain, salt-laden intake); scale/rust deposits (long-term moisture accumulation, infrequent draining); oil contamination/carbon deposits (compressor piston-ring blow-past, excessive cylinder lubrication, unloader oil carryover); cracking at welds/seams (fatigue from pressure cycling, poor original weld quality, corrosion-assisted cracking); blistering of paint/lining (moisture beneath coating); thinning of shell walls (corrosion wastage — requires UT gauging); defective/corroded drain valve seat (condensate erosion); distortion/dents (overpressure event, mechanical impact); cracked/deteriorated manhole gasket or seat (age, thermal cycling). Measure shell thickness with a UT gauge against original/class minimum, recording and photographing findings; notify the class surveyor if wall thinning or cracking is found.

**Preparing for survey**: inspect shell/end plates for corrosion, pitting, cracking, deformation; check welds/seams; inspect manhole/flange facings and gasket condition; check the safety relief valve (correct set point, lifts freely, reseats, certification date); check the drain valve, pressure gauge, and fusible plug if fitted; note oil contamination as a compressor piston-ring/seal failure indicator (fire/explosion risk).

**Closing up and initial pressurisation**: ensure the interior is clean and dry, all tools/rags/equipment removed (toolbox check); renew the manhole gasket if deteriorated; fit the manhole cover, tighten bolts evenly in a cross pattern to correct torque; remove all blanks/spades; leave the drain valve cracked open initially; crack open the inlet valve slowly, raising pressure in stages (25%→50%→75%→100% working pressure), checking for leaks with soapy water/leak detector and listening for hissing/creaking at each stage; once satisfied, close the drain valve, bring to full working pressure, confirm the safety/relief valve lifts and reseats correctly, and log the inspection.

**Key fact**: O₂ 20.8% (range 19.5–23.5%), minimum 15 minutes ventilation before entry, staged pressurisation 25→50→75→100% with leak checks at each stage; oil inside a receiver indicates compressor blow-past — a fire/explosion risk.

answers.title: Compressor Inter-Stage & After-Cooling, Condensate Drainage
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to diesel engine starting air systems:

(a) write instructions for the checking of the starting air system in order to determine the reason (6) for an engine failing to turn over when the starting air system is activated;

(b) describe the procedure for checking and preparing a starting air receiver for survey; (6)

(c) explain why cooling is required between the compressor stages and after the final stage, (4) stating the arrangement used for draining condensate from the coolers. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Why cooling is required between compressor stages and after the final stage, and the condensate drainage arrangement (4)**

Air temperature rises significantly at each compression stage (adiabatic heating); without cooling, temperatures entering subsequent stages would be dangerously high. Cooling protects compressor components — excess heat breaks down lubricating oil, causing carbon deposits and increased fire/explosion risk in the air lines, and can seize components (piston, rings) or cause liner wear. Inter-stage cooling reduces air volume before the next stage works on a denser charge, approaching isothermal (more efficient) compression. The after-cooler cools final delivery air before the receiver, reducing thermal stress on the receiver/pipework and minimising moisture carryover.

As hot compressed air cools, moisture condenses at each cooler; each inter-cooler and after-cooler has a separator/moisture trap at its lowest point. Condensate is removed via automatic float-operated drain traps (opening when water accumulates, discharging to a safe drain) and manual drain cocks (opened periodically as watchkeeping routine). Drains lead to a safe location — not directly to bilge, due to oil-contamination risk — typically to an oily water separator or holding tank.

answers.title: Local Control of the Main Engine — Following Failure of the Automatic Control System
answers.question_as_set: With reference to the local control of a main engine following failure of the automatic control (16) system, explain how the engine can be monitored and controlled. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Following failure of the automatic control system, explain how the main engine can be monitored and controlled locally (16)**

*Context*: the automatic control system provides remote manoeuvring, automatic governing/load programs, sequencing of starts/reversals, and automatic monitoring/alarm/slowdown/shutdown. On failure, control transfers to the local (emergency) manoeuvring stand, and monitoring reverts to manual reading of local instruments plus physical checks, with increased manning.

**1. Change-over and manning**: inform the bridge immediately, agreeing manoeuvres will be slower; notify the Chief Engineer and muster additional engineers (local control is labour-intensive); establish reliable communications (engine-room telegraph with backup, sound-powered telephone, agreed bell/repeat system); suspend UMS and man the engine room continuously.

**2. Local control of the main engine** — *starting and reversing*: manual control of the starting-air master/automatic valve and distributor; for direct-reversing engines, shift the camshaft/reversing servo manually, confirming fuel cam and air-start timing before admitting air; use manual interlocks/blocking correctly since automatic sequencing is lost. *Speed and fuel control*: control speed via the local fuel regulating handwheel/lever, keeping the mechanical/hydraulic governor in service for speed holding; set speed in steps, letting parameters settle; apply slow, graduated load changes to avoid thermal shock/overload without automatic load programs. *Supporting auxiliaries*: start and control locally the normally auto-sequenced services (LO pumps, jacket/piston cooling water pumps, fuel supply/booster pumps, cylinder lubricators), confirming correct pressure before and during running; confirm independent protective devices (overspeed trip, low LO pressure trip, emergency stop) remain effective, ready to trip manually since automatic slowdown/shutdown may be inoperative.

**3. Manual monitoring**: read local instruments at frequent intervals — LO pressure/temperature, jacket/piston cooling water pressures/temperatures, fuel pressure/temperature/viscosity, scavenge/charge-air pressure, turbocharger speed, per-unit exhaust temperatures (local pyrometer), engine RPM, cylinder peak pressures if time permits, bearing/thrust temperatures where gauges exist. Physical rounds: listen for knocking, feel bearing housings/crankcase doors for heat, observe exhaust colour/haze, check drains and sight-glass flows/gauge-glass levels. Log all readings and times, trending by eye since alarm coverage is reduced.

**4. Responding to bridge manoeuvres**: repeat back each telegraph order, set speed/direction locally, confirm achieved RPM to the bridge; keep one engineer on telegraph/comms and another on fuel/speed control, with others on monitoring rounds.

**5. Restoration**: do not revert to automatic/remote control until fully repaired, tested and certified by the Chief Engineer; log the fault, actions and restoration; raise a defect/PMS entry.

answers.title: CEO Report — Failure to Start in Reverse During Port Manoeuvring
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer write a report to the Engineering Superintendent regarding TWO (16) incidents of failure of the main propulsion engine to start in the reverse direction during a recent manoeuvring session whilst entering port. The report must cover details of the manoeuvring control situation at the time of the incidents and the immediate action taken to ensure the safety of the ship. The report must also detail the actions taken by the Chief Engineer to ensure that the cause of the problem was detected and rectified. Details must be included in the report about the actions you, as Chief Engineer, have taken to minimise future similar occurrences. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Report on two incidents of the main propulsion engine failing to start in the reverse direction during port manoeuvring (16)**

*Details*: two separate incidents during the same port-entry manoeuvre; calm weather, congested waters, reduced speed under bridge control preparing for pilot boarding/berthing. The engine was under remote bridge control in manoeuvring mode — multiple ahead/astern commands succeeded before failure. On both occasions, an astern command from the bridge telegraph produced no astern rotation, despite adequate starting air pressure and successful ahead commands immediately prior — pointing the fault at the reversing/direction-selection path rather than the air supply.

*Immediate actions for ship safety*: bridge informed immediately of the failure and loss of standby propulsion; anchor prepared for immediate deployment; control transferred from bridge to ECR for manual operation; engine successfully started ahead under local control and held at minimal RPM to maintain position pending tug assistance; engine-room staff on emergency standby.

*Investigation and rectification*: starting air system confirmed within limits (30 bar, receivers/valves operational) — the distributor responded for ahead but wasn't triggering cylinder air valves for astern, isolating the fault from the air supply. The reversing camshaft actuator was inspected — the reversing control signal wasn't fully engaging the astern position. A faulty electro-pneumatic solenoid valve responsible for shifting the reversing mechanism was identified as intermittently sticking — the root cause. The valve was replaced with an onboard spare, with full functional testing of the reversing mechanism and starting in both directions verified satisfactory.

*Preventive measures*: all electro-pneumatic valves and control-air components cleaned, lubricated and tested under load, with the full starting-air/reversing system tested through simulated manoeuvring cycles; a checklist introduced to verify camshaft position feedback before critical manoeuvres, with local ahead/astern responsiveness tests before every port entry; watchkeeping engineers briefed on emergency procedures, with joint bridge/engine drills for propulsion-loss scenarios; critical solenoid valves flagged for the critical-spare inventory, with a closer PM check frequency for electro-pneumatic control units.

answers.title: Slow Turning System — Checking & Routine Monitoring Instructions
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer, write instructions for the checking of the engine slow turning system and (16) subsequent routine monitoring of the engine slow turning system. The instruction must take account of problem areas which may be linked to the need for slow turning of an engine whilst selected for standby and prior to an actual start. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Instructions for checking the slow turning system and subsequent routine monitoring, covering standby and prior to starting (16)**

*Purpose*: the slow turn proves the engine is free to rotate and vents any liquid accumulated above a piston before full starting air is admitted.

**Part 1 — Functional check** (before standby, after work on cylinders/cooling/fuel/air systems, and at PMS intervals): obtain bridge permission before rotating the engine, confirming the propeller/shaft is clear and no personnel are on moving parts; confirm turning gear is disengaged and prove its interlock by attempting a slow turn with T/G engaged (must be blocked); confirm starting/control air is available within limits, draining condensate/oil first; confirm the automatic slow-turn function is enabled with the correct stopped-time threshold; open all indicator cocks so liquid can vent and be seen; initiate a slow turn and confirm at least one complete revolution; watch every indicator cock throughout, confirming no water/oil/fuel discharge and listening for abnormal knocking; confirm the slow turn completes within the set time and the system then permits (or correctly blocks) a normal start; confirm the slow-turn air valve/solenoid reseats with no leakage; record the test, pressures and result in the log.

**Part 2 — Routine monitoring on standby**: keep the slow-turn function auto-enabled at all times, never bypassed to save time; maintain air pressure within limits, draining receivers/main at the start of each standby and at intervals; perform/confirm a slow turn with cocks open before each manoeuvring period or start once stopped beyond the set time; monitor the jacket cooling-water expansion tank level (a falling level indicates internal leakage — treat as a liquid-lock risk); watch for leak sources (jacket water past O-rings/cracked liner, dribbling fuel valve, over-lubrication, leaking exhaust-valve/cover cooling), isolating a suspect unit's fuel if a leaking injector is suspected; keep indicator cocks free and clear; confirm the turning-gear interlock remains healthy; keep compressors/air system ready so slow turn isn't left incomplete through low pressure; log each standby (time stopped, slow-turn completion, air pressures, any liquid observed); on UMS standby, confirm interlocks/alarms are functional, reporting any defect immediately.

**Part 3 — Problem areas, required response**: if liquid is ejected at slow turn — DO NOT START; keep cocks open, turn slowly to expel the liquid, identify and isolate the source, inform the bridge, rectify before clearing (starting against a liquid lock can crack the cover, bend the con-rod, and damage the crosshead/bearings). If the engine fails to rotate or the slow turn doesn't complete — do not force a start; investigate low air pressure, distributor fault, turning gear still engaged, or mechanical seizure. Treat any cylinder that repeatedly discharges liquid as defective, keeping it under investigation. Report all findings to the Chief Engineer with appropriate log/defect entries.

answers.title: Turbocharger Performance Monitoring & Assessment of Condition
answers.answer_text:
**(a) How performance is monitored and how information is used to assess performance (8)**

Performance is monitored through a range of operational parameters reflecting the health and efficiency of both turbine and compressor stages: turbocharger speed (proximity sensor/tachometer — a drop or sudden increase may suggest fouling, bearing failure or imbalance); compressor inlet/outlet air pressure and temperature (a reduction in scavenge air pressure or rise in outlet temperature can indicate compressor-side fouling or clogged filters); exhaust gas temperature and pressure at turbine inlet (high values point to turbine-blade fouling or combustion issues); differential pressure across filters and gas paths (rising pressure drop indicates choking); vibration monitoring (bearing wear, rotor imbalance, blade damage); and, where fitted, lube oil pressure/temperature and surge-detection features.

All readings are logged in engine monitoring systems and compared against baseline/design data. Trend analysis supports preventive maintenance planning, fault detection, performance optimisation, and avoidance of major failures.

**(b) Arrangements for maintaining the system in good condition (8)**

Routine cleaning of both compressor side (fouling from salt, dust, oil mist — manual or water-washing methods) and turbine side (carbon deposits — grit blasting or manufacturer in-service cleaning). Air intake filters are periodically cleaned/replaced. On turbochargers with independent lube oil systems, oil level, temperature, pressure and cleanliness are checked regularly, and oil seals inspected to prevent leakage into the air path. Bearings are inspected for wear, vibration and overheating, and renewed during planned overhauls. After major maintenance or blade repair the rotor is dynamically balanced. Proper warm-up/cool-down procedures reduce thermal stress on casing and rotor. Overhauls occur at manufacturer-recommended intervals, examining and renewing seals, bearings and blades as necessary. Detailed maintenance logs and trend records (vibration levels, cleaning intervals, component replacements) support long-term condition monitoring and preventive scheduling.

answers.title: Why Turbochargers Are Fitted — Installation, Monitoring & In-Situ Cleaning
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain why turbochargers are fitted to some diesel engines and describe how they efficiently (6) achieve that aim.

(b) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a turbocharger installation showing the paths of engine (10) exhaust gas, charge air and cooling water. State the monitoring systems provided for the system, explaining why they are fitted, how they operate and how their functioning is checked. Explain how turbochargers can be cleaned without dismantling. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why turbochargers are fitted and how they efficiently achieve that aim (6)**

Turbochargers use otherwise-wasted exhaust gas energy to compress intake (scavenge) air, allowing more air (and therefore more fuel) to be burned per cycle than a naturally-aspirated engine could manage, substantially raising power output and efficiency for a given cylinder size without the parasitic power loss of a mechanically-driven blower.

**(b) Installation, monitoring, and in-situ cleaning (10)**

**[Sketch]** Turbocharger installation — exhaust gas, charge-air and cooling-water paths; T/C, air cooler, scavenge & exhaust manifolds.

A typical installation has a turbine side connected to the exhaust manifold and a compressor side connected to the air intake. Exhaust gas from the cylinders enters the turbine casing, rotating the turbine blades, and exits to the uptake/economiser. The turbine shaft drives the compressor impeller, which draws in atmospheric air, compresses it, and delivers it to the charge air cooler; cooled, compressed air then enters the scavenge manifold. A cooling-water system (fresh water through the charge air cooler) removes compression heat to maintain optimal air density.

Monitoring systems include: turbocharger speed (tachometer), exhaust gas temperature at turbine inlet, charge air pressure and temperature, bearing lube oil pressure (if fitted), and vibration monitoring — detecting fouling, imbalance, overheating or bearing failure. Functioning is checked through regular calibration, alarm testing, and observing operational trends.

In-situ cleaning without dismantling: on the compressor side, water washing injects a fine mist of water into the air intake while the engine runs at steady load, washing deposits from the blades. On the turbine side, dry particulate blasting or chemical cleaning systems (carbon-removing granules or cleaning fluids injected via dedicated turbine-side connections) dislodge soot and carbon deposits — reducing the need for frequent dismantling.

answers.title: Electric Scavenge Blowers, Disabling a Failed Turbocharger & Running with T/C Inoperative
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to slow speed diesel engine turbocharging:

(a) explain why electrically driven scavenge air blowers are fitted; (4)

(b) describe how a turbocharger may be disabled to allow for operation of the main engine in the (8) event of failure of the turbocharger rotor;

(c) describe the procedure for running an engine in the event of a turbocharger not being (4) operational. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why electrically driven scavenge air blowers are sometimes fitted (4)**

A turbocharger depends on sufficient exhaust gas energy, only produced at moderate-to-high engine load. At very low loads, starting, manoeuvring or idling, exhaust gas volume/energy is insufficient to drive the turbocharger effectively, so the engine relies on electrically driven auxiliary blowers for adequate scavenge air. These typically operate automatically below a set load threshold (often ~30% MCR) and switch off once the turbocharger becomes effective, ensuring smooth transition and maintaining overall efficiency.

**(b) Disabling a turbocharger to allow operation after rotor failure (8)**

The turbocharger bypass isolation method diverts exhaust gas away from the turbocharger and supplies combustion air via the auxiliary scavenge blowers instead. Exhaust gas bypass valves redirect exhaust away from the turbine inlet directly to the uptake/economiser; turbine inlet and outlet are blanked and the compressor side isolated from the scavenge manifold, fully isolating the unit from both gas and air sides. Electrically driven scavenge blowers are brought online to supply charge air, the engine control system is adjusted to match fuel injection to the reduced air supply, and lube oil lines to the turbocharger are isolated. Sensor alarm thresholds for the isolated unit are adjusted to avoid false alarms. This allows the engine to continue at a de-rated power level, generally 25–40% MCR.

**(c) Procedure for running with the turbocharger inoperative (4)**

The engine is run de-rated using electrically driven scavenge blowers, typically in a "blower mode"/"manual scavenge air" mode adjusting fuel injection to match reduced air. Load is restricted to a safe margin (typically 25–40% MCR depending on engine make/class). Starting air and fuel injection timing may be manually or automatically adjusted for low-air operation. Frequent monitoring of exhaust temperatures, cylinder pressures and scavenge air pressure is essential. This is a temporary emergency measure only, pending repair or replacement of the turbocharger.

answers.title: Turbocharger Jet-Assist System & Waste-Gate/Air-Bypass Arrangement
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Turbocharger jet-assist system — how and why it is used (10)**

**[Sketch]** Jet-assist system: 1 regulating arm · 2 switch · 3 piston · 4 jet solenoid valve · 5 lambda cylinder · 6 shutdown solenoid valve.

The jet-assist system is an auxiliary device improving turbocharger performance during low-load conditions or transient operations (rapid acceleration, sudden load changes), by injecting compressed air directly onto the turbine to temporarily increase its speed and boost compressor output when exhaust gas energy alone is inadequate.

When the fuel index increases, the regulating arm (1) rotates, activating the switch (2), which pushes the piston (3) forward. This completes an electrical circuit, triggering the jet solenoid valve (4), which opens to allow compressed air from the ship's compressed-air system onto the compressor side, rapidly accelerating it. This raises charge air pressure, which acts on the lambda cylinder (5), returning the piston (3) to its original position; once the required lambda (air-fuel) ratio is achieved, the system deactivates automatically, with the shutdown solenoid valve (6) ensuring safe interruption. Jet assist typically activates during load increases above ~50% MCR and stays active 3–8 seconds; if active over 10 seconds, the solenoid closes and a jet-assist failure alarm triggers. This reduces turbo lag and ensures optimal combustion under dynamic loads.

**(b) Waste-gate and air-bypass system — why fitted (6)**

**[Sketch]** Waste-gate (upstream of turbine) and air-bypass arrangement across exhaust & scavenge receivers.

Exhaust gas from the cylinders enters the exhaust receiver, distributing flow to the turbine. To prevent turbine over-speed and compressor over-boosting at high load, a waste-gate valve upstream of the turbine allows a portion of exhaust gas to bypass the turbine entirely, straight to the uptake — protecting both turbocharger and engine. An air-bypass valve between the scavenge air receiver and compressor outlet allows a portion of compressed air to bypass the receiver and recirculate, used during transient conditions for fine air-delivery control. Both valves operate on control signals based on engine load, air pressure or turbocharger speed, maintaining efficiency, avoiding surge, reducing thermal stress, and ensuring stable operation across the load range.

answers.title: Turbocharger Lubrication System, Bearing Replacement & Return-to-Service Checks
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the lubrication system for a turbocharger. (6)

(b) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the replacement of a turbocharger bearing, stating the (10) checks which must be made before the turbocharger is returned to service. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Lubrication system for a turbocharger (6)**

**[Sketch]** T/C lubrication system: main LO storage/engine sump → T/C LO supply pumps → LO cooler → LO filter → bearings → drain back to sump.

Lubricating oil is drawn from the main engine sump or a dedicated LO storage tank by turbocharger LO supply pump(s), passes through an LO cooler (temperature control) and LO filter (removes contaminants), and is routed under pressure to the turbocharger bearings, forming a protective film that reduces friction and dissipates heat at the very high rotational speeds involved. Oil then drains back via a return line to the main sump for recirculation. Redundancy features (standby pumps, cooler bypass for cold conditions) are typically provided.

**(b) Replacement of a turbocharger bearing, and checks before return to service (10 — note: guide shows this part as 4, see instance note)**

**[Sketch]** Bearing/rotor work — removing the rotor: lifting bracket, gas casing, air-inlet casing, guide plate & axial lock, centering tube, rotor sling, guide tube, holding pin.

After isolating the turbocharger and allowing it to cool, the air-inlet and exhaust-gas casings are removed to expose the rotor assembly. Using a lifting bracket or rotor sling, the rotor is carefully lifted after removing the guide plate, axial lock and centering/guide tubes, then placed on a support stand. The bearing housing is accessed and old bearings removed; the housing and shaft are cleaned and journals inspected for wear, pitting or scoring. New bearings are fitted, with clearances measured against manufacturer limits. Oil passages are checked clear and the rotor manually rotated to confirm smooth movement before reinsertion, alignment and torquing of all components.

**Checks before returning to service**: lube oil system connected and flow-checked for leaks; lube oil pressure, bearing temperature and vibration monitored during startup; rotor free rotation and proper alignment confirmed manually.

answers.title: Two-Stroke Exhaust-Gas & Charge-Air Flow, Water Separator Operation & Consequences
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the exhaust gas and charge air flow system through an (6) engine cylinder and turbocharger of a two-stroke engine, indicating the cooling and water separation systems.

(b) Describe how a water separator removes water droplets from a charge air flow. (4)

(c) Explain the possible consequences of not removing water droplets from engine charge air and (6) draining the water separator unit. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Exhaust-gas and charge-air flow through a two-stroke engine cylinder and turbocharger, with cooling and water-separation (6)**

**[Sketch]** Two-stroke exhaust-gas/charge-air flow: T/C, air cooler (LT FW in/out), water separator & drain, scavenge manifold, exhaust manifold.

Exhaust gas exiting the engine drives the turbine side of the turbocharger; the turbine shaft drives a compressor drawing in and compressing fresh air from the engine room. This is directed through the charge air cooler (cooled by LT fresh water) before entering the scavenge manifold and cylinders. As the air is cooled, moisture condenses and is collected by the water separator and drained off before the air reaches the cylinders. After combustion, exhaust gas exits through the exhaust manifold back to the turbocharger, completing the cycle.

**(b) How a water separator removes water droplets (4)**

As hot, humid compressed air cools in the charge air cooler, water vapour condenses into droplets. The separator uses inertia and deflection: internal baffles/vanes force an abrupt change of airflow direction; heavier water droplets cannot follow the rapid direction change (due to inertia) and are flung against the separator walls, where they coalesce and collect at the bottom for draining, leaving only dry, clean air to reach the cylinders.

**(c) Consequences of not removing/draining water droplets (6)**

Water entering the cylinders can corrode liners, piston rings and other internal components, reducing service life. It disrupts combustion (lower combustion temperature, poor ignition quality), causing incomplete combustion, carbon deposits and fouling. Water can wash away lubricating oil from critical surfaces (piston rings, liners), increasing friction and wear. In extreme cases, water ingress can cause hydraulic locking, leading to mechanical failure or deformation of engine parts. Regular draining is therefore essential for safe, efficient operation.

answers.title: Charge-Air Coolers — Purpose, In-Service Checks, Consequences of No Condensate Drain
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain why charge air coolers are fitted to turbocharged diesel engines, stating the possible (6) effects on engine operation and performance if they are not maintained in good condition.

(b) As Chief Engineer Officer, write instructions for the routine in-service checking of charge air (6) cooler performance and cleanliness together with the checking of condensate draining.

(c) State, with reasons, the possible consequences if condensate is not drained from the charge air (4) cooler. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why charge-air coolers are fitted, and effects if not maintained (6)**

Charge air coolers increase intake air density after turbocharger compression (which heats the air, reducing density and available oxygen). Cooling the air restores density, allowing more oxygen into the cylinders — improving combustion efficiency, power output and fuel economy while reducing emissions. If not properly maintained, fouling on the cooling surfaces reduces heat transfer, raising intake air temperature; this can cause poor combustion, increased SFOC, higher exhaust temperatures, greater risk of thermal overload on exhaust valves and piston crowns, engine knocking, and a general drop in performance.

**(b) Chief Engineer's instructions for routine in-service checks (6)**

- **Air temperature monitoring**: regularly record charge air temperature before/after the cooler; a rising outlet temperature or reduced differential indicates fouling.
- **Pressure drop monitoring**: increased pressure drop across the cooler signals clogging, requiring cleaning.
- **Cooling water parameters**: monitor LT cooling water inlet/outlet temperature and ensure adequate flow/pressure.
- **Drain inspection**: check the water separator drain daily and keep it clear; excessive water may indicate a leaking cooler tube.
- **Visual inspection/borescope**: periodically inspect externally for leaks and internally (borescope) for fouling or corrosion.
- **Scheduled cleaning**: plan regular chemical/manual cleaning per manufacturer recommendation, especially during overhauls, with all observations logged.

**(c) Consequences if condensate is not drained (4)**

Accumulated water can be carried into the combustion chambers with the charge air, causing corrosion of cylinder liners, piston rings and other internal parts. Water ingress disrupts combustion, leading to knocking, power loss and increased emissions. In severe cases, hydraulic locking can occur — incompressible liquid in the cylinder causing mechanical failure or deformation of engine parts.

answers.title: Water Separators — Operating After CAC Damage & After T/C Bearing Failure
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to slow speed diesel engine turbocharging:

(a) explain why water separators are fitted; (4)

(b) describe how an engine may be operated in the event of a charge air cooler being damaged (6) beyond immediate repair;

(c) describe how an engine may be operated in the event of a turbocharger bearing failure which (6) cannot be repaired immediately. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why water separators are fitted (4)**

Water separators remove condensed moisture from the scavenge air after it passes through the charge air cooler. As compressed air cools, water vapour condenses into droplets; if not removed, this water can enter the combustion chamber, corroding piston rings and cylinder liners, interfering with combustion efficiency, and in extreme cases causing hydraulic lock. The separator ensures only clean, dry air enters the cylinders.

**(b) Operating with a charge air cooler damaged beyond immediate repair (6)**

If design permits, the charge air cooler can be bypassed, allowing hot compressed air directly into the engine — but due to high intake temperatures, the engine must be de-rated to reduce thermal load and prevent abnormal combustion or high exhaust temperatures. Scavenge air temperature, exhaust gas temperature and other key parameters are closely monitored; cooling systems (jacket water, LO) may be run harder, rapid load changes avoided, and in some designs water injection used temporarily to lower intake air temperature. This is an emergency measure only, pending port repairs.

**(c) Operating after an unrepairable turbocharger bearing failure (6)**

The faulty turbocharger is isolated (locked or bypassed per engine design) to prevent further mechanical damage from a seized/imbalanced rotor. Auxiliary electrically driven scavenge blowers automatically start to supply charge air, though at lower volume/pressure than the turbocharger provided. The engine is de-rated to a reduced load, typically not exceeding 30–40% MCR, with fuel index adjusted to match the reduced air supply and prevent over-fuelling (incomplete combustion, black smoke, exhaust fouling). Scavenge pressure, exhaust temperature and the scavenge space are monitored closely; this arrangement is strictly temporary, pending proper repair.

answers.title: Assessing Turbocharger Operating Performance & Performance-Degrading Defects
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to turbochargers:

(a) explain how the operating performance of a turbocharger system may be assessed; (10)

(b) state, with reasons, defects which adversely affect the operating performance of a (6) turbocharger. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**(a) How turbocharger operating performance may be assessed (10)**

Assessed through continuous/periodic monitoring of: turbocharger rotor speed, scavenge air pressure, air cooler differential pressure, exhaust gas temperature before/after the turbocharger, and charge air temperature — logged routinely and compared against engine performance curves or manufacturer baseline data. Rising exhaust gas temperature or falling scavenge air pressure at a given load indicates poor performance. Air cooler pressure-drop trends reveal fouling; turbocharger speed directly indicates how effectively exhaust energy is being used. On multi-turbocharger engines, comparing exhaust temperatures between units helps identify imbalance or an underperforming unit. Visual inspections during overhauls (carbon deposits, bearing-seal oil leakage, blade damage) also contribute. Trending this data over time supports predicting and rectifying performance degradation.

**(b) Defects that adversely affect performance, with reasons (6)**

- **Fouling of turbine/compressor blades** (carbon deposits, salt/oil contamination) — causes imbalance and reduced airflow, lowering turbocharger speed and air delivery efficiency.
- **Blade damage** (erosion, cracking, deformation) — reduces performance and can cause vibration.
- **Oil leakage from the bearing housing** into the compressor/turbine side — contaminates and fouls the airflow, and may signal impending bearing failure.
- **Blocked/leaking charge air coolers and clogged air filters** — increase air-path resistance, reducing charge air pressure and affecting combustion.
- **Defective sensors/instrumentation** — give misleading readings, hindering accurate assessment.

Unaddressed, these defects cause poor combustion, increased fuel consumption and higher emissions.

answers.title: Single-Turbocharger Engine — Impeller Vane Breaks Off and Strikes the Charge-Air Cooler
answers.question_as_set: With reference to a slow speed diesel engine fitted with a single turbocharger, describe, with (16) reasons, the possible action which could be taken to enable the main engine to be operated, if whilst on oceanic passage, a small portion of one of the impeller vanes breaks off and impacts with the charge air cooler. Total 16 marks
answers.answer_text:
**Action to enable main engine operation after a small impeller vane fragment breaks off and impacts the charge-air cooler, on a slow-speed engine with a single turbocharger (16)**

Immediate action is needed to assess damage extent and determine if safe operation remains possible, given the risk of further deterioration of the turbocharger's rotating assembly and impaired charge-air-cooler air delivery/cooling.

- Reduce engine load and stabilise at lower power output to minimise further stress on the turbocharger.
- Fully inspect the charge air cooler for punctures, deformation or internal fin damage affecting pressure/temperature or causing air leakage and loss of scavenge efficiency.
- Recover any fragments and thoroughly clean the scavenge space to prevent further debris ingestion into the cylinders.
- If the cooler is leaking, apply temporary sealing (approved repair compounds, epoxy, or isolating damaged rows) to maintain partial functionality.
- Closely monitor charge air temperature and pressure to keep them within acceptable limits.
- Evaluate turbocharger performance: rpm, vibration (if sensors fitted), abnormal noise or temperature rise, especially near the bearing housings.
- If the turbocharger remains operational but at reduced efficiency, run at reduced load (typically not exceeding 40–50% MCR), relying on auxiliary scavenge blowers to supplement charge air, with fuel index reduced accordingly to prevent over-fuelling and incomplete combustion.
- If the turbocharger shows further signs of failure, bypass it altogether and operate in natural-aspiration mode assisted solely by auxiliary blowers — this limits output significantly and requires constant monitoring of exhaust gas temperature and scavenge pressure, since excessive load in this condition risks poor combustion, fouling and thermal damage.
- Maintain close coordination with the company's technical team and class society; log a full damage report and prepare spares for replacement at the next port.

Such temporary operation is only intended to allow the vessel to reach a safe haven for proper repair.

answers.title: Pump Selection for Ship's Services
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to pump selection, state TWO types of pump for EACH of the following applications, stating why they are suitable:

(a) bilge pumping; (2)

(b) lubricating oil circulating; (2)

(c) sea water circulating; (2)

(d) sewage sludge; (2)

(e) steering gear. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Bilge pumping**
Reciprocating (positive-displacement) pump — self-priming with a good suction lift, so it can draw from a low or partly dry bilge and handle dirty, solids-laden water.
Centrifugal pump (with priming aid) — moves large volumes for rapid dewatering; robust and simple, and with an open/non-clog impeller can pass small debris.

**(b) Lubricating oil circulating**
Screw pump — gives smooth, pulsation-free delivery ideal for viscous oil and maintains steady pressure to the bearings.
Gear pump — positive displacement provides constant delivery against system resistance and copes well with high L.O. viscosity.

**(c) Sea water circulating**
Centrifugal pump — suited to large volumes of low-viscosity water at the low/moderate heads of cooling circuits; reliable for continuous duty.
Axial-flow (propeller) pump — delivers very high flow at low head, well matched to large SW circulating duties such as condenser/cooler cooling.

**(d) Sewage sludge**
Progressive cavity (mono) pump — handles thick, viscous, solids-laden sludge with a gentle, non-clogging action and steady delivery.
Diaphragm pump — self-priming, tolerates abrasive/stringy solids and dry running, with no fine clearances to jam. (A non-clog/vortex-impeller centrifugal is an acceptable alternative.)

**(e) Steering gear**
Variable-delivery axial-piston pump (swash-plate) — gives infinitely variable, reversible flow for proportional rudder control at the high pressures the rams need.
Variable-delivery radial-piston pump (Hele-Shaw) — provides variable, reversible delivery from a constant-speed motor, suited to the high-pressure hydraulic steering circuit.

**Logic:** match positive-displacement pumps to viscous, self-priming, suction-lift or high-pressure duties (L.O., sludge, steering, bilge suction); match centrifugal/axial pumps to high-volume, low-viscosity duties (SW circulating, bulk bilge dewatering).

answers.title: Double-Entry Impeller; Two-Speed vs Throttling
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to centrifugal pumps:

(a) sketch a double entry impeller showing directions of flow; (3)

(b) explain why double entry impellers are fitted; (2)

(c) explain, with the aid of a Head versus Flow diagram, why a two speed pump is preferable to throttling where high and low capacities are demanded for a large sea water circulating pump. (5)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Double-entry (double-suction) impeller — sketch**
*Sketch instructions: draw a horizontal shaft with a central boss. On both sides of the boss draw a curved impeller eye (suction inlet). Show arrows entering axially from left and right into the two eyes, turning 90° inside the impeller, then discharging radially outward at the outer diameter into the volute casing. Label: Suction inlet (both sides), Shaft, Impeller vanes, Discharge (radial) to volute.*
Water enters the impeller axially from both ends (one suction eye on each side of the shaft), turns through 90° inside the impeller, and is discharged radially at the outer diameter into the common volute.

**(b) Why double-entry impellers are fitted**
The dominant reason is **axial-thrust balance**: the two eyes face in opposite directions, so the axial forces cancel and the thrust bearing is relieved. Splitting the flow into two halves also lowers the inlet velocity and the NPSH required, reducing cavitation risk and allowing a higher total capacity — suited to large-throughput duties such as main sea-water circulating.

**(c) Two-speed operation versus throttling**
A centrifugal pump's duty is set by where its characteristic curve meets the system resistance curve (friction head, which rises roughly with flow squared). A lower flow can be obtained either by throttling a valve or by reducing pump speed.

*Head/Flow diagram: at full speed (curve N1) the pump runs at point A (high capacity). Throttling partly closes the discharge valve, steepening the system curve, so the duty slides up curve N1 to point B: low flow but still high head — the surplus head between B and what the pipework actually needs (point C) is dropped across the valve and wasted as heat, while the pump keeps absorbing nearly full power. Reducing speed drops the whole pump curve to N2, meeting the original system curve at point C — the same low flow at a much lower head.*

By the affinity laws Q ∝ N, H ∝ N² and crucially P ∝ N³, so halving the speed cuts power to about an eighth. For a large SW circulating pump whose demand swings between high capacity (full power / warm water) and low capacity (part load / cold water), the cube-law power saving makes two-speed operation clearly preferable to wasting power continuously across a throttle valve. The only limitation is that two fixed speeds give two operating points rather than infinite control — adequate for a two-level cooling duty.

answers.title: Impeller & Volute Function; Impeller Features
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to centrifugal pumps:

(a) explain the function of EACH of the following:

(i) the impeller; (2)

(ii) the volute; (2)

(b) state why some pumps may have EACH of the following:

(i) a double entry impeller: (2)

(ii) a diffuser ring; (2)

(iii) more than one impeller. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) The impeller**
The impeller is the rotating element that puts energy into the liquid. Liquid enters at the eye and is flung outward by the curved vanes; the rotation accelerates it, raising its velocity (kinetic energy) and giving it centrifugal head. It converts the mechanical energy of the shaft into kinetic energy in the fluid, delivered at high velocity to the impeller periphery.

**(a)(ii) The volute**
The volute is the spiral casing passage surrounding the impeller, of increasing cross-section toward the discharge. As the high-velocity liquid passes through this expanding passage its velocity falls and, by Bernoulli, kinetic energy is converted into pressure energy. The volute therefore turns velocity head into useful pressure head while collecting and guiding the flow to the outlet.

**(b)(i) A double-entry impeller**
Chiefly to balance axial thrust (the two eyes face opposite ways so axial forces cancel). It also splits the flow, lowering inlet velocity and NPSH required and allowing higher capacity — e.g. main sea-water circulating.

**(b)(ii) A diffuser ring**
A ring of fixed guide vanes around the impeller forming gradually widening passages. It converts velocity to pressure more efficiently and uniformly than a plain volute, recovers more head, and by guiding the flow symmetrically gives balanced radial pressure (reducing radial thrust). Typical of high-head and multi-stage pumps.

**(b)(iii) More than one impeller (multi-staging)**
To develop a high total head a single impeller could not. Impellers in series on one shaft each feed the next, so the heads add together, giving high delivery pressure (e.g. boiler feed) while keeping each impeller's diameter, tip speed and stress at efficient values.

answers.title: Gear-Type Pump — Principle, Materials, Application
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the principle of operation of a gear type pump, indicating the direction of flow of the fluid. (6)

(b) State the materials that gear type pump components may be manufactured from. (2)

(c) State an application that is suitable for the employment of gear pumps, and why they are suited. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Principle of operation**
A gear pump is a positive-displacement pump. Two close-meshing gears — a driving gear and a driven (idler) gear — run in a casing with very small tip and end clearances. On the suction side the teeth continuously come out of mesh, so the enclosed space increases and a partial vacuum draws liquid in. The liquid is trapped in the pockets between the teeth and the casing wall and carried around the outside (periphery) of each gear — not through the centre. On the discharge side the teeth come back into mesh, the volume reduces, and the liquid is positively displaced out under pressure. The line of meshing teeth seals against back-flow. Delivery is near-constant per revolution, so a relief valve is always fitted.
*Sketch instructions: draw two meshing gears side by side in a close-fitting casing. Grey arrows show gear rotation (opposite directions where they mesh); blue arrows trace the liquid path — in at the suction side, around the outer periphery of each gear in the tooth pockets, out at the discharge side. Label suction (in), discharge (out), driving gear, driven/idler gear, and the meshing point where back-flow is sealed.*

**(b) Materials of construction**
Casing/body — cast iron or cast steel for oil duties; bronze or gunmetal for corrosive/seawater service; aluminium for light duty.
Gears — case-hardened alloy steel (most common); cast iron or bronze for lighter/corrosive service; sometimes one non-metallic gear (Tufnol/phenolic) to reduce wear and noise.
Shafts — hardened/alloy steel.
Bushes, bearings, end (wear) plates — bronze, gunmetal or white-metal; needle or ball bearings on some designs.
Shaft seal — mechanical seal or lip seal.

**(c) Suitable application and why**
Lubricating-oil circulating/transfer (equally fuel-oil and hydraulic duties). As positive-displacement units they deliver a steady, near-constant volume against varying back-pressure (keeping bearing oil pressure stable), are self-priming, give relatively smooth low-pulsation delivery, handle viscous oils well and can develop the high pressures required, while remaining compact, simple and reliable.

occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; the sketch trap to watch for is showing liquid flowing through the centre of the meshing gears rather than around the outer periphery of each gear in the tooth pockets.

answers.title: Operating Principle; NPSHa Definition & Temperature Effects
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to centrifugal pumps and pumping systems:

(a) explain the principle of operation of a centrifugal pump; (4)

(b) define net positive suction head available (NPSHa); (2)

(c) state the effects of temperature on NPSHa; (2)

(d) describe how the effects of temperature can be overcome. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Operating principle**
Liquid enters axially at the eye of a rotating impeller. The curved vanes fling it radially outward and accelerate it, so it leaves the periphery at high velocity (kinetic energy). It then passes into the volute or diffuser — a passage of increasing area — where the velocity falls and that kinetic energy is converted into pressure energy, delivering the liquid at a useful outlet pressure. Continuous removal of liquid from the eye keeps the pressure there low, drawing in fresh liquid and maintaining steady flow. As it relies on imparting velocity, it is not self-priming and its delivery varies with the head against which it works.

**(b) NPSH available (NPSHa)**
NPSHa is the total suction head actually available at the impeller eye above the vapour pressure of the liquid, expressed as a head of that liquid — the margin of pressure energy at the suction over the liquid's vapour pressure that prevents it flashing into vapour as it enters the impeller. For cavitation-free running, NPSHa must exceed the pump's NPSH required (NPSHr).
NPSHa = absolute pressure head at the surface ± static suction head − suction-line friction losses − vapour-pressure head of the liquid.

**(c) Effect of temperature on NPSHa**
Raising the liquid temperature raises its vapour pressure. Since vapour-pressure head is subtracted, higher temperature reduces NPSHa (less margin above boiling) and increases cavitation risk — why hot-well, condensate and feed suctions are prone to cavitation. (A slight fall in density is a minor secondary effect; the rise in vapour pressure dominates.)

**(d) Overcoming the temperature effect**
Provide a positive (flooded) suction head — pump below the source, or tank raised; feed deaerator/hot-well mounted high above the feed pump.
Pressurise the suction source to raise the absolute pressure head at the surface.
Reduce suction-line losses — short, large-bore, smooth piping with minimal bends/fittings.
Reduce suction velocity / NPSHr — low-speed or double-entry first stage, or a booster pump.
Where possible, limit or sub-cool the suction temperature to lower the vapour pressure.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Operating Principle; NPSHa Definition & Temperature Effects
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: NPSHa is poorly understood across sittings even though it recurs frequently: candidates rarely link temperature to vapour pressure in part (c), and a common wrong answer for 'how the effects of temperature are overcome' in part (d) is simply 'fit a cooler' -- the fix is reducing suction losses/lift or raising suction head, not cooling the liquid.

answers.title: NPSHa versus NPSHr; Increasing NPSHa by Design
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to centrifugal pumps and pumping systems:

(a) explain, with the aid of a diagram, the distinction between Net Positive Suction Head available (NPSHa) and Net Positive Suction Head required (NPSHr); (8)

(b) explain how the NPSHa may be increased by design. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) NPSHa versus NPSHr**
NPSHa (available) is set by the system — the suction head actually delivered to the impeller eye above the liquid's vapour pressure (atmospheric/tank pressure ± static suction head − suction friction losses − vapour-pressure head). Friction losses grow with flow squared, so NPSHa falls as flow increases.
NPSHr (required) is set by the pump, fixed by its design and speed. As liquid accelerates into the eye its pressure drops below the flange value; NPSHr is the minimum margin above vapour pressure needed at the flange so the liquid does not flash at the lowest internal point. Entry losses rise with velocity, so NPSHr increases with flow (roughly with Q²).

*Diagram: plot NPSH (y-axis) against flow rate Q (x-axis). NPSHa is a curve falling as Q rises; NPSHr is a curve rising as Q rises. To the left of where the two curves cross, NPSHa > NPSHr (safe, no cavitation); to the right, NPSHr > NPSHa (cavitation). The crossing point marks the limiting flow.*

The rule is NPSHa > NPSHr (with a margin). To the left of the crossing the pump is safe; at the crossing they are equal — the limiting flow; to the right NPSHr exceeds NPSHa and the pump cavitates (loss of head, noise, vibration, impeller erosion). NPSHa is what the installation supplies; NPSHr is what the pump demands.

**(b) Increasing NPSHa by design**
Provide a positive (flooded) suction head — pump below the supply, or the tank raised (e.g. feed deaerator high above the feed pump).
Pressurise the suction vessel to raise the absolute pressure head on the surface.
Reduce suction-line losses — short, large-bore, smooth piping, few bends/fittings, full-bore valves.
Fit a booster pump on the suction.
Keep the suction temperature down (or slightly sub-cool) to lower the vapour pressure.

occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: The NPSHa-vs-NPSHr diagram is weakly answered across sittings -- sketches tend to be vague rather than clearly showing the margin between the two curves that defines the safety margin against cavitation.

answers.title: Principle & Relief Valve; Double Entry; Routine Overhaul
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to centrifugal pumps:

(a) explain the operating principle of a centrifugal pump, stating why it is unnecessary to fit a relief valve to it; (3)

(b) explain why some pumps have a double entry impeller; (2)

(c) describe a routine overhaul of a centrifugal pump, stating the inspections, measurements and possible replacement parts that may be required. (5)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Principle and why no relief valve is needed**
The impeller imparts velocity (kinetic) energy to the liquid, which is then converted into pressure energy in the volute/diffuser. A relief valve is unnecessary because the pump can only develop its fixed shut-off (maximum) head: if the discharge is closed or blocked the impeller merely churns the trapped liquid and the pressure rises no higher. Unlike a positive-displacement pump (which keeps displacing a fixed volume and would build dangerous pressure), the centrifugal is inherently self-limiting.

**(b) Why a double-entry impeller**
Mainly to balance axial thrust — a suction eye each side gives equal, opposite axial forces that cancel, relieving the thrust bearing. Splitting the flow also lowers inlet velocity and NPSH required, reducing cavitation risk and allowing higher capacity (e.g. main sea-water circulating).

**(c) Routine overhaul**
After isolating the pump electrically and mechanically, shutting the valves and draining it, uncouple the driver, remove the casing/cover and withdraw the rotating assembly; clean and inspect.

**Inspections:**
Impeller — vanes/shrouds for cavitation pitting, erosion, cracks, wear (especially eye and tips).
Wear (neck) rings — casing and impeller rings for wear and scoring (they control internal leakage).
Shaft — wear, scoring, bending, corrosion (under the sleeve and at journals).
Shaft sleeve — grooving/wear where the seal runs.
Casing/volute — erosion, pitting, corrosion.
Bearings — wear, pitting, discolouration, roughness.
Mechanical seal faces (or gland packing) — wear and damage.
Keys, keyways and fasteners — wear and security.

**Measurements:**
Wear-ring clearances — most important; compare with maker's limits (excess clearance causes recirculation and lost head/efficiency).
Shaft straightness/run-out (dial gauge); journal and sleeve diameters.
Shaft end-float/axial position and impeller setting.
On reassembly, coupling alignment (and check for soft foot).

**Likely replacement parts:** wear/neck rings; mechanical seal or gland packing; bearings; all joints, O-rings and gaskets; shaft sleeve; and the impeller or shaft if worn, cracked or badly eroded. Rebuild to correct clearances with new joints/seals, set the rotor, re-align the coupling, then refill, vent and run-test (discharge pressure/flow, leakage, vibration, noise, bearing temperature) before return to service.

answers.title: Condition Assessment; Misalignment Effects and Correction
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to centrifugal pumps:

(a) explain how the internal condition may be assessed without having to dismantle the pump; (3)

(b) state the effects of misalignment between the driving motor and the pump; (2)

(c) describe, with the aid of a sketch, how misalignment may be corrected. (5)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Assessing internal condition without dismantling**
Performance / head check — at known speed, read suction & discharge pressures (developed head) and flow; take motor current/power. A fall in head and flow for the same speed, or a low shut-off pressure, indicates internal wear (enlarged ring clearances, eroded impeller, recirculation).
Vibration analysis — frequency content reveals imbalance/erosion, worn bearings, misalignment and cavitation.
Bearing temperature and noise — high temperature indicates bearing distress; a gravelly rattle with fluctuating gauges indicates cavitation.

**(b) Effects of misalignment**
Heavy vibration, noise and increased power consumption; rapid wear and premature failure of bearings; mechanical seal damage and leakage; coupling wear/fretting; in severe cases shaft fatigue and fracture.

**(c) Correcting misalignment**
Misalignment is either parallel (offset) or angular (often combined). The pump is taken as fixed and the motor moved to suit.
*Sketch instructions: draw the pump (fixed) and motor (movable) connected by a coupling. Show a rim gauge (dial indicator) reading radial/parallel offset, and a face gauge reading angular error. Show shims under the motor feet for vertical/angular correction, and jacking screws at the base for horizontal correction.*

**Prepare:** isolate and lock off; clean feet, baseplate and coupling faces; check holding-down bolts; test for soft foot; set the coupling gap and allow for thermal growth if hot-running.
**Measure:** clamp dial indicators across the coupling (rim and face) or use laser alignment; rotate both shafts together and read at 0°, 90°, 180°, 270°. The rim (radial) gauge reveals parallel/offset; the face gauge reveals angular misalignment.
**Correct:** add/remove shims under the motor feet — equal shims for vertical offset, unequal front-to-back to tilt for angular; move the motor sideways with jacking screws for horizontal errors.
**Re-check:** re-read after each adjustment until within tolerance, tighten the bolts and check again (tightening can pull alignment off); on hot units, a final check at running temperature.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Condition Assessment; Misalignment Effects and Correction
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: A binary question -- candidates who know the dial-gauge alignment procedure and the effects of misalignment score well, others don't; there's little partial-credit middle ground.

answers.title: Raising Speed; Multi-Staging; Centrifugal vs PD for L.O.
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to centrifugal pumps:

(a) describe how EACH of the following improves pump performance:

(i) raising the speed of rotation; (2)

(ii) multi-staging. (2)

(b) explain the advantages of using centrifugal pumps instead of positive displacement pumps for lubricating oil circulating duties. (6)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Raising the speed of rotation**
A higher speed raises impeller tip velocity, imparting more kinetic energy and head. By the affinity laws flow rises with speed (Q ∝ N) and head with its square (H ∝ N²), so a given impeller develops much greater head and capacity, or the same duty is met by a smaller pump. (Penalty: power rises with the cube of speed, P ∝ N³, and NPSHr increases.)

**(a)(ii) Multi-staging**
Several impellers in series on one shaft, each discharging into the next, so the per-stage heads add up. The total head is roughly the single-stage head times the number of stages while flow stays that of one impeller — giving high delivery pressure (e.g. boiler feed) yet keeping each impeller's diameter, tip speed and stress at efficient values.

**(b) Centrifugal vs PD for L.O. circulating**
No over-pressurisation — limited to shut-off head; a choked filter or closed valve just makes it churn, so no relief valve is needed (a PD pump must have one).
Smooth, pulsation-free delivery — steady oil supply and film to bearings, less pipework fatigue and vibration.
High capacity, compact and simple — large volume at low head efficiently; only the impeller rotates, so smaller, lighter, cheaper and very reliable.
Tolerant of contaminants — open passages pass small wear particles without the scoring/jamming that fine PD clearances suffer.
Simple, safe control — output set by throttling without over-pressure danger.
Direct high-speed drive — couples straight to a motor, avoiding the reduction gearing a PD pump often needs.

**Trade-off:** not self-priming and delivery falls if head rises — not significant for a flooded-suction, low-head circulating duty, so the centrifugal is preferred.

answers.title: Principle & Relief Valve; Impeller Types; Cavitation
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to centrifugal pumps:

(a) state the operating principle of a centrifugal pump and why it is unnecessary to fit a relief valve to it; (2)

(b) state TWO impeller types, explaining which type of application EACH would be best suited for;

(c) explain why cavitation occurs, and how it is reduced by design. (4) (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Principle and relief valve**
The impeller imparts velocity to the liquid, converted to pressure in the volute/diffuser. No relief valve is needed because the pump can only develop its fixed shut-off head; if the discharge is closed it merely churns the liquid and cannot over-pressurise itself as a PD pump would.

**(b) Two impeller types and applications**
Open (or semi-open) impeller — little/no shrouding; unobstructed passages pass solids and fibres without clogging, so best for dirty or solids-laden liquids (bilge, sludge, sewage). Lower efficiency and more clearance-sensitive.
Closed (shrouded) impeller — vanes enclosed between shrouds give defined passages and minimal internal leakage; highest efficiency on clean liquids (sea-water and fresh-water cooling, L.O. service).

Other valid answers: double-entry (high capacity, e.g. main SW circulating) and multi-stage (high head, e.g. boiler feed).

**(c) Cavitation — why it occurs and how it is reduced**
**Why:** as liquid accelerates into the eye its pressure falls; if it reaches the liquid's vapour pressure the liquid flashes into vapour bubbles. Carried into the higher-pressure impeller, these bubbles collapse (implode), causing rattling noise, vibration, loss of head/flow and pitting/erosion of impeller and casing. It occurs whenever NPSHa falls below NPSHr.

**Reduced by design:**
Lower the pump's NPSHr — larger impeller eye, lower speed, or a double-entry impeller (halves inlet velocity); an inducer on critical duties.
Improve the suction installation to raise NPSHa — flooded suction, pressurised suction vessel, short large-bore low-loss piping.
Limit the liquid temperature where possible (lower vapour pressure = greater margin).

answers.title: Pump Selection (Including Cargo Oil Stripping)
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to pump selection, state TWO types of pump for EACH of the following applications, stating why they are suitable:

(a) bilge pumping; (2)

(b) cargo oil stripping; (2)

(c) sewage sludge; (2)

(d) lubricating oil circulating; (2)

(e) sea water circulating. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Bilge pumping**
Reciprocating pump — self-priming with good suction lift; handles dirty, solids-laden water.
Centrifugal pump (with priming aid) — large-volume dewatering; open/non-clog impeller passes small debris.

**(b) Cargo oil stripping**
Reciprocating pump — strongly self-priming, drawing the last residues from a nearly empty tank against an air/oil mixture.
Screw pump (PD) — maintains suction and steady delivery at the low flows/high suction lift of stripping, and handles viscous oil. (A self-priming centrifugal stripping pump is also used.)

**(c) Sewage sludge**
Progressive cavity (mono) pump — gentle, non-clogging handling of thick solids-laden sludge.
Diaphragm pump — self-priming, tolerates abrasive/stringy solids and dry running. (Vortex-impeller centrifugal acceptable.)

**(d) Lubricating oil circulating**
Screw pump — smooth pulsation-free delivery of viscous oil; steady bearing pressure.
Gear pump — constant delivery against system resistance; handles high viscosity.

**(e) Sea water circulating**
Centrifugal pump — large volumes of low-viscosity water at low/moderate head; reliable continuous duty.
Axial-flow (propeller) pump — very high flow at low head for large SW circulating duties.

answers.title: Two Priming Systems and Their Advantages
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe TWO systems of priming centrifugal pumps. (6)

(b) List the advantages of EACH of the priming methods described in part (a). (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Two priming systems**

**1. Central priming system (vacuum / air-pump type).** A single air-extraction system primes several pumps. A common priming main connects to the top of each pump casing, and a continuously available air pump — usually a liquid-ring (water-ring) type — maintains a vacuum in it. When a pump is to be primed, its connection opens (often automatically on start); the air pump draws air from the casing and suction line into the main, so the pressure falls and liquid is drawn up to fill the casing. A float-operated priming valve on each pump closes when water reaches it (preventing carry-over to the air pump) and reopens if air later collects, so the system re-primes automatically. The liquid-ring air pump uses a vaned rotor running eccentrically, the ring of sealing water forming moving "liquid pistons" that draw and expel air.

**2. Self-priming pump (recirculation type).** The casing retains a charge of water when stopped. On starting with air in the suction, the impeller mixes this air with the retained water into an emulsion, discharged into an internal separation chamber. There the velocity falls; air separates and escapes to discharge while the heavier water drops back and is recirculated to the eye to repeat the cycle. Each pass removes more air, progressively lowering suction pressure and drawing the liquid up; once solid liquid arrives, recirculation ceases and it runs as a normal centrifugal. The only requirement is the initial water charge.

**(b) Advantages of each**
**Central priming system:** one air pump serves many pumps — economical, no priming gear duplicated; standard high-efficiency (non-self-priming) centrifugals can be used. Primes quickly and re-primes automatically when air collects — well suited to air-prone duties (e.g. the bilge main) and lets pumps sit above the liquid without foot valves.
**Self-priming pump:** self-contained — no separate vacuum pump, priming main, float valves or foot valve; less to install, maintain and fail. Independent — unaffected by failure of any central system and recovers its own prime after losing suction; convenient for standalone or portable duties.
