answers.title: Performance Assessment; Aligning a Replacement Motor
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to centrifugal pumps:

(a) explain how the performance may be assessed without the need to dismantle the pump; (3)

(b) state the effects of misalignment between the driving motor and the pump; (3)

(c) describe, with the aid of a sketch, how on a new replacement motor, alignment is checked and adjusted. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Assessing performance without dismantling**
Developed head and flow — at known speed read suction/discharge pressures and flow; a fall for the same speed (or low shut-off pressure) points to internal wear.
Power/current — a change for a given duty indicates altered condition.
Vibration, noise and bearing temperature — reveal imbalance, worn bearings, misalignment, cavitation and bearing distress.

**(b) Effects of misalignment**
Heavy vibration, noise, higher power consumption; rapid bearing wear and premature failure; mechanical seal damage and leakage, coupling wear/fretting; in severe cases shaft fatigue and fracture.

**(c) Aligning the replacement motor**
The pump is fixed and the new motor moved to suit. Misalignment is parallel (offset) and/or angular, in both vertical and horizontal planes.
*Sketch instructions: draw the pump (fixed) and the new motor (to be moved) joined by a coupling. Show a rim gauge for radial offset (parallel) and a face gauge for angular error, mounted on the coupling. Show shims under the motor feet for vertical/angular correction and jacking screws for horizontal correction.*

**Prepare** — set the motor and coupling half; clean feet/baseplate/faces; bolts loosely fitted; check for soft foot; set the coupling gap; allow for thermal growth if hot-running.
**Check** — clamp dial gauges across the coupling (rim and face) or use laser; rotate both shafts and read at 0°, 90°, 180°, 270° (rim = parallel, face = angular).
**Adjust** — shims under the feet for vertical (equal = parallel, unequal = angular); jacking screws for horizontal.
**Re-check** after each move until within tolerance, tighten and re-check; final check hot where thermal growth is significant.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Performance Assessment; Aligning a Replacement Motor
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: The alignment-check sketch is the trap: the magnetic base must sit on the motor shaft with the dial pointer riding on the pump shaft, and the motor shaft is rotated by hand to read run-out. Mounting the gauge on the casing with the pointer on a shaft only proves that shaft isn't bent -- it doesn't check alignment between the two machines.

answers.title: Axial Piston Hydraulic Pump; Axial vs Radial Pressure
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a constant speed, uni-directional, axial flow pump suitable for hydraulic applications. (6)

(b) Explain, with the aid of a sketch, how the axial flow pump can achieve higher pressures than its radial flow counterpart. (4)
answers.answer_text:
In hydraulics the "axial flow" pump here is the axial piston pump; its "radial flow counterpart" is the radial piston pump — both positive-displacement.

**(a) Constant-speed, uni-directional axial piston pump**
A fixed-displacement (swash-plate) axial piston pump has a cylinder barrel carrying a ring of pistons arranged axially around and parallel to the drive shaft. The barrel is rotated by the shaft at constant speed; each piston's slipper bears on a stationary, inclined swash plate set at a fixed angle. As the barrel rotates, each piston is drawn out of its bore over half a revolution (suction) and pushed back in over the other half (delivery). A stationary port (valve) plate with two kidney ports connects each cylinder to inlet while filling and to outlet while discharging. With a fixed swash angle and one direction of rotation the pump delivers a constant flow in one direction. An odd number of pistons (e.g. 7 or 9) smooths delivery. It is compact, high-speed and high-pressure — suited to hydraulic power packs (steering gear, deck machinery).
*Sketch instructions: draw a rotating cylinder barrel with an odd number of pistons arranged parallel to a central drive shaft. Show the pistons' slippers bearing against a stationary swash plate set at a fixed angle. Show a stationary port plate with two kidney-shaped ports, one connected to suction (in), one to delivery (HP out). Label: drive shaft, swash plate (fixed angle), pistons, cylinder barrel (rotates), port (valve) plate, suction (in), delivery (HP out).*

**(b) Why the axial type achieves higher pressure**
Both are positive-displacement; what limits them is how the reaction to the piston's pumping force is carried by the running gear.
*Sketch instructions: two side-by-side diagrams. Axial piston: show the pumping force F = P×A acting as a direct end-thrust along the piston axis onto the swash plate, with only a small side load F·tanα. Radial piston: show the pumping force acting radially against a cam/reaction ring, generating a large radial reaction plus a tangential side load from rotation.*

In the axial piston pump the pumping force F = P×A acts along the piston as a direct end-thrust onto the swash plate, taken by a large thrust bearing, so the piston is loaded essentially in pure compression. The only transverse load is F·tanα (swash angle α ≤ ~18°, tanα ≈ 0.3), so the running gear is lightly side-loaded and can take very high pressures (commonly 300–400 bar).

In the radial piston pump the force acts radially against an eccentric cam/reaction ring through a small line contact; because the block rotates relative to that surface, each piston also carries a tangential side load, and the radial reactions combine into a large unbalanced side load on the eccentric/shaft bearing. The resulting bending and high contact stresses set a lower safe-pressure limit. Hence, for comparable size, the axial arrangement transmits the load as a well-supported axial thrust with minimal side loading, allowing higher working pressure.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Axial Piston Hydraulic Pump; Axial vs Radial Pressure
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: An often-avoided question -- many candidates sketch a hydraulic circuit rather than the pump itself. The mark-earning detail is that the swash (tilting) plate stays stationary while the cylinder block rotates, so the control lever attaches to the swash plate, not to anything on the rotating block.

answers.title: Affinity Laws; Impeller Trimming; Two-Speed vs Throttling
answers.question_as_set:
(a) State the affinity laws for a centrifugal pump. (3)

(b) State the effects on the pump affinity laws of fitting a slightly smaller diameter impeller. (2)

(c) Explain, with the aid of a Head versus Flow diagram, why a two speed pump is preferable to throttling where high and low capacities are demanded for a large sea water circulating pump. (5)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Affinity laws**
For a fixed impeller, relating performance to speed N:
Flow proportional to speed: Q ∝ N
Head proportional to speed squared: H ∝ N²
Power proportional to speed cubed: P ∝ N³
So doubling the speed doubles flow, quadruples head, and increases power eight-fold.

**(b) Fitting a slightly smaller diameter impeller**
The same relationships apply to impeller diameter D at constant speed: Q ∝ D · H ∝ D² · P ∝ D³
A slightly smaller (trimmed) impeller gives a modest reduction in flow, a larger reduction in head, and the greatest reduction in power — a permanent way to reduce capacity and head to suit a system without changing speed.

**(c) Two-speed operation versus throttling**
Duty is set where the pump curve meets the system resistance curve (friction head rising with flow squared). Lower flow comes either from throttling a valve or reducing speed.

*Head/Flow diagram: at full speed the duty is at point A. Throttling steepens the system curve and slides the duty up curve N1 to point B — low flow but high head, with the surplus head (B to C) wasted across the valve while the pump still absorbs near full power. Reducing speed drops the pump curve to N2, meeting the original system curve at point C — same low flow, much lower head.*

With P ∝ N³, halving speed cuts power to about an eighth. For a large SW circulating pump swinging between high and low capacity, the cube-law saving makes two-speed clearly preferable to continuous throttle losses; the only limitation is two fixed operating points, adequate for a two-level cooling duty.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Affinity Laws; Impeller Trimming; Two-Speed vs Throttling
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Parts (a)-(b) (affinity laws, effect of impeller trimming) are reliable marks; part (c) is where marks are lost -- candidates often fail to state clearly that throttling wastes power across the valve while the pump still absorbs near-full power, which is the actual reason two-speed operation is preferable for swinging high/low capacity duties.

answers.title: Laboratory Tests on Ship's Plate Steel + Brittle Fracture Features
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
(a) List the laboratory tests that may be carried out on specimens of steel for ships' plate, stating reasons for these tests. (6)

(b) Outline FOUR features of a fracture in a component which would assist in the verification that brittle fracture had occurred. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Laboratory tests on steel for ships' plate**
**Tensile test.** A standard test piece is pulled to failure to determine the yield stress, ultimate tensile strength (UTS), percentage elongation and reduction in area. This verifies the steel meets the specified strength requirements and gives a measure of its ductility.
**Bend test.** A specimen is bent cold (typically through 180° around a former). It checks ductility and soundness — the outer fibres must stretch without cracking, confirming freedom from surface defects, laminations or excessive brittleness.
**Notched-bar impact test (Charpy V-notch).** A notched specimen is struck and the energy absorbed in fracture is measured, usually over a range of temperatures. This establishes the toughness/notch ductility and the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature — critical for ship plate, which must resist brittle fracture in cold sea conditions.
**Hardness test (Brinell/Vickers).** Gives a quick indication of strength and, importantly, the uniformity of the material across the plate. Useful for checking heat-affected zones and weldability.
**Chemical analysis.** Confirms the composition (carbon, manganese, sulphur, phosphorus, etc.) lies within specified limits, since composition governs strength, weldability and resistance to brittle fracture.
**Metallographic examination & NDT.** Micro-examination reveals grain size, inclusions and segregation; ultrasonic testing detects internal flaws and laminations that would weaken the plate.

Any six of the above, with reasons, will cover the marks.

**(b) Four features confirming brittle fracture**
Absence of plastic deformation — little or no necking, thinning or reduction in cross-sectional area; the broken pieces fit back together almost exactly.
Bright, granular/crystalline appearance of the fracture face, rather than the dull, fibrous, torn appearance of a ductile failure.
Chevron (herringbone/arrowhead) markings on the surface, which point back towards the origin of the crack.
Fracture plane normal to the applied tensile stress — a flat, square-edged break with no shear lips, and evidence of rapid crack propagation (often initiated at a notch, defect or at low temperature).

answers.title: Stress/Strain Curve for Mild Steel
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a Stress/Strain curve for a mild steel test specimen. (2)

(b) With reference to the curve sketched in part (a), explain EACH of the following:

(i) modulus of elasticity; (2)

(ii) percentage elongation; (2)

(iii) ultimate tensile stress; (2)

(iv) yield stress. (2)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: plot stress (vertical) against strain (horizontal). Show the straight elastic line from the origin O to a proportional limit A, then elastic limit B, an upper yield point C (where load drops suddenly) and lower yield point D, rising to the ultimate (maximum) stress at E, then falling as necking occurs to fracture at F. Label O, A, B, C, D, E, F.*

**(b)(i) Modulus of Elasticity**
The slope of the straight-line portion O–A, where stress is directly proportional to strain (Hooke's Law). E = stress / strain (in the elastic region). A measure of the stiffness of the material — its resistance to elastic (recoverable) deformation. For mild steel E ≈ 200–210 GN/m². The steeper the line O–A, the stiffer the material.

**(b)(ii) Percentage Elongation**
A measure of ductility — how much the specimen stretches permanently before fracture (point F). % Elongation = (final gauge length − original gauge length) / original gauge length × 100. The two broken halves are fitted back together and the final gauge length measured. For mild steel this is typically around 20–25%. A high value indicates a tough, ductile material that gives ample warning before failing.

**(b)(iii) Ultimate Tensile Stress (UTS)**
Corresponds to the highest point on the curve, E — the maximum load the specimen carries divided by its original cross-sectional area. Beyond E, localised "necking" begins; the reduced area means the load falls off (E→F) even though the true stress in the neck is still rising, and the specimen finally fractures at F. UTS is the figure quoted for the strength of the steel.

**(b)(iv) Yield Stress**
The stress at which the material begins to deform plastically — permanent strain sets in. On the mild-steel curve this is the distinct yield region: an upper yield point C where the load drops suddenly, followed by a lower yield point D at which strain increases with little or no increase in stress. Below the yield stress the steel returns to its original length when unloaded; above it the deformation is permanent. It is the key design figure, as structures are kept safely below yield.

answers.title: Shipboard Applications of Metals
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
State a typical shipboard application for EACH of the following metals, explaining how their properties make them particularly suitable for the stated application:

(a) stainless steel; (2)

(b) grey cast iron; (2)

(c) titanium; (2)

(d) manganese bronze; (2)

(e) aluminium; (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Stainless Steel** — Application: galley equipment, food/freshwater storage tanks and pipework; also fresh/sea water pump shafts and valve spindles. Reason: high chromium content (≥12%) forms a self-healing passive oxide film giving excellent corrosion resistance to water, salt and foodstuffs; keeps surfaces hygienic and maintains good strength with an easily-washed finish.

**(b) Grey Cast Iron** — Application: engine cylinder liners, cylinder blocks, bedplates and pump/valve bodies. Reason: free graphite flakes give self-lubricating properties, excellent wear resistance and high damping capacity to absorb vibration; good compressive strength, cheap and easily cast into complex shapes — though brittle and weak in tension.

**(c) Titanium** — Application: plate-type heat exchangers and seawater cooler plates. Reason: outstanding seawater corrosion resistance combined with a very high strength-to-weight ratio, allowing thin plates with excellent heat transfer that resist erosion/corrosion with little maintenance, despite high initial cost.

**(d) Manganese Bronze** — Application: ship's propellers (especially smaller ones). Reason: a high-tensile brass offering good strength, toughness and ductility with excellent corrosion and cavitation-erosion resistance in seawater; casts well into large complex shapes and resists the fatigue stresses of the propeller's working environment.

**(e) Aluminium** — Application: superstructure, deckhouses, lifeboats and ladders. Reason: low density (about one-third that of steel) reduces topside weight, lowering the centre of gravity and improving stability, and cutting fuel consumption; forms a protective oxide film giving good marine-atmosphere corrosion resistance, with alloying restoring adequate strength.

answers.title: Creep and Fatigue (with graph)
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
Describe, with the aid of a graph, EACH of the following types of ferrous material failure, stating ONE practical example of EACH:

(a) creep; (5)

(b) fatigue. (5)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Creep**
Definition: creep is the slow, continuous plastic (permanent) deformation of a material under a constant load (stress) over a long period at elevated temperature, occurring even when the applied stress is well below the yield stress. For steels it becomes significant above roughly 0.4 × the melting temperature (absolute), typically above ~350–400°C.

*Graph: plot strain (vertical) against time (horizontal). Show an initial instantaneous strain step at t=0, then a Primary stage where the rate is high but falling, a Secondary stage that is the long straight portion at constant minimum rate, and a Tertiary stage that curves sharply upward to rupture.*

Primary (transient) creep: strain rate is initially high but decreases as the material work-hardens. Secondary (steady-state) creep: the rate is constant and minimum — work-hardening balanced by recovery; the longest stage, and its slope is the design figure used to predict service life. Tertiary creep: the rate accelerates rapidly as necking, voids and cracking develop, leading to rupture. The higher the temperature and/or stress, the steeper the curve and the sooner failure occurs.

**Practical example:** exhaust valves, exhaust valve spindles and superheater/boiler tubes — high temperature plus sustained pressure causes gradual stretching. Burnt boiler tubes that "bag" or balloon outwards are a classic creep failure.

**(b) Fatigue**
Definition: fatigue is failure under repeated, fluctuating or reversed (cyclic) loading at a stress below the ultimate tensile — often below the yield — stress. A tiny crack initiates at a stress concentration, propagates a little with each cycle, and the component finally fractures suddenly when the remaining cross-section can no longer carry the load.

*Graph: the S–N (Wöhler) curve — stress amplitude (vertical) vs number of cycles to failure on a log scale (horizontal). The curve falls as stress reduces, then flattens to a horizontal fatigue (endurance) limit, below which the material has effectively infinite life.*

Fracture face: a smooth area showing "beach marks"/conchoidal lines radiating from the origin, plus a rough crystalline area of final rapid fracture. Cracks start at keyways, sharp corners, threads, weld defects, corrosion pits or tool marks.

**Practical example:** crankshafts (at fillet radii between journals and webs), propeller-shaft failures, or fluctuating-load bolts. Generous fillet radii and polished surfaces are the main preventives.

**Key difference:** creep is time and temperature dependent (static load); fatigue is cycle dependent (dynamic/repeated load).

answers.title: Creep — Strain-Time Curve (Supplied)
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.answer_text:
The curve plots strain against time under a constant load at elevated temperature, and reads through four features: Initial strain (elastic + plastic) — the instantaneous strain produced the moment the load is applied, before any time-dependent creep begins. Primary (transient) creep — strain rate starts high but progressively decreases as the material work-hardens. Secondary (steady-state) creep — the long, straight portion of constant minimum slope, work-hardening balanced by thermal recovery; the most important region, since its slope (the steady creep rate) is used to predict service life. Tertiary creep — the rate accelerates rapidly as voids, necking and internal cracking develop, terminating at rupture.

**Key point:** creep is permanent plastic deformation occurring under a steady stress below the yield point, given enough time at temperature.
**Practical example:** superheater/boiler tubes and exhaust valves — sustained high temperature plus steady pressure causes gradual stretching (e.g. boiler tubes that "bag" outward over time).

answers.title: S–N (Wöhler) Fatigue Curve
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.answer_text:
Definition: fatigue is failure of a component under repeated, fluctuating or reversed (cyclic) loading, at a stress below the ultimate tensile — often below the yield — stress. A microscopic crack initiates at a stress concentration, propagates with each cycle, and the component fails by sudden fracture once the remaining cross-section can no longer carry the load.

Reading the graph: stress amplitude (S) is plotted against number of cycles to failure (N), with N on a logarithmic scale. As applied stress is reduced, cycles survived increase, so the curve falls steeply through the finite-life region. For ferrous metals the curve then becomes horizontal: this level is the fatigue (endurance) limit. Below it the steel endures an effectively infinite number of cycles. Designing below this limit prevents fatigue failure.

Fatigue fracture appearance: a smooth area with "beach marks"/conchoidal lines radiating from the crack origin (slow growth), plus a rough crystalline area where final rapid fracture occurred. Cracks start at stress raisers — keyways, sharp corners, threads, weld defects, corrosion pits or tool marks.

**Practical example:** crankshafts (failing at the fillet radii between journals and webs), propeller-shaft failures, or fluctuating-load bolts. Main preventives: reduce stress concentrations via generous fillet radii, polished surfaces and good surface finish.

answers.title: Fatigue — LCF/HCF and Finite/Infinite Life
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.answer_text:
Definition: fatigue is failure of a component under repeated, fluctuating or reversed (cyclic) loading, at a stress below the ultimate tensile — often below the yield — stress. A tiny crack initiates at a stress concentration, grows a little with each cycle, and the part fails by sudden fracture when the remaining section can no longer carry the load.

**High-stress/low-N end:** at high stress the material survives only a few cycles; the curve sits high and flat at top left. The region left of ~10³–10⁴ cycles is Low Cycle Fatigue (LCF) — large stresses (often into the plastic range), few cycles. Typical of occasional heavy overloads or thermal cycling.

**Falling portion:** as stress is reduced, cycles survived rise sharply; the curve sweeps downward. The region beyond ~10⁴–10⁵ cycles is High Cycle Fatigue (HCF) — lower stresses, very large numbers of cycles, essentially elastic. Covers most rotating/vibrating machinery.

**The horizontal fatigue (endurance) limit:** the curve flattens at ~10⁶–10^7 cycles and becomes horizontal. Above it is the finite-life zone (eventual failure after a calculable number of cycles); below it is the infinite-life zone — the steel endures effectively unlimited cycles.

Fracture appearance: a smooth area with "beach marks" radiating from the origin, plus a rough crystalline area of final rupture.

**Practical example:** crankshafts failing at journal/web fillet radii (also propeller-shaft and connecting-rod bolt failures). Preventives: generous fillet radii, good surface finish, removal of stress concentrations.

answers.title: Air Receivers — Corrosion, Prevention, Safe Interim Use
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to air recievers:

(a) explain why air receivers are prone to corrosion; (3)

(b) state how corrosion can be prevented; (3)

(c) if significant corrosion is detected during a regular inspection, explain how the air receiver may still be safely used in service until a permanent repair can be effected. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why air receivers are prone to corrosion**
The air delivered by the compressor contains moisture (water vapour). As the air is compressed and cools in the receiver, this moisture condenses out as water, collecting at the bottom. Liquid water in contact with the steel — together with oxygen in the compressed air — provides the classic conditions for electrochemical (wet) corrosion. In addition, the air carries traces of oil carried over from the compressor, and the moisture may be slightly acidic, accelerating attack. Corrosion concentrates at the bottom of the receiver and around the drain, worsened if the receiver is not drained regularly.

**(b) How corrosion can be prevented**
Drain the receiver regularly of accumulated water and oil — the single most important measure (automatic drain traps, routine manual draining, slight slope toward the drain).
Remove moisture before the air enters by fitting effective inter-/after-coolers with moisture separators (and air dryers where fitted) on the compressor delivery.
Protect the internal surfaces with a corrosion-resistant coating/paint or galvanising, inspected and maintained at survey.

**(c) Safe use in service until a permanent repair**
Establish the remaining metal thickness by ultrasonic thickness testing over the affected area, and calculate the wall thickness still required to contain the working pressure safely with an adequate margin.
Reduce the maximum working pressure — allow the receiver to remain in service at a reduced (de-rated) working pressure, with the safety valve re-set to the new lower pressure.
Re-set/verify safety devices and increase monitoring — confirm the safety valve lifts at the de-rated pressure, drain frequently, inspect the corroded area more often.
Obtain Classification Society/Surveyor agreement — continued use at reduced pressure must be documented and approved, clearly marked on the vessel, with a permanent repair carried out at the earliest opportunity.

**Principle:** since bursting pressure depends on wall thickness, reducing the working pressure in proportion to the lost thickness restores an acceptable safety margin until the vessel can be properly repaired.

answers.title: Metallurgical Processes — Induction Hardening, Nitriding, Case Hardening
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
Explain EACH of the following metallurgical processes:

(a) induction hardening; (3)

(b) nitriding; (3)

(c) case hardening. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Induction Hardening**
A surface-hardening process applied to medium/high-carbon steels. The component is surrounded by a water-cooled copper coil (inductor) carrying a high-frequency alternating current, inducing eddy currents that rapidly heat a thin surface layer above its upper critical temperature while the core stays cool. The surface is then immediately quenched. Result: a hard, wear-resistant martensitic surface layer over a tough, ductile core. Depth is controlled by current frequency and heating time. Rapid, localised, and well suited to gear teeth, crankshaft journals and cam surfaces.

**(b) Nitriding**
A surface-hardening process that introduces nitrogen, carried out on special alloy steels containing nitride-forming elements (aluminium, chromium, molybdenum — "Nitralloy" steels). The finished, heat-treated component is held at a relatively low temperature (~500°C) in an ammonia atmosphere for a prolonged period; the ammonia dissociates and nitrogen diffuses into the surface, forming extremely hard, wear-resistant nitrides. Advantages: low temperature and no quenching, so minimal distortion; the surface retains hardness at elevated temperature with good corrosion and fatigue resistance. Used for valve spindles, gears and crankshafts. Main drawback: the process is slow.

**(c) Case Hardening**
Produces a hard, high-carbon surface "case" on a tough, low-carbon steel core. Two stages: **1. Carburising** — heated to ~900–950°C in a carbon-rich medium (solid, liquid or gaseous) so carbon diffuses into the surface layer; longer time and higher temperature give a deeper case. **2. Hardening** — the carbon-enriched surface is heated above its critical temperature and quenched, transforming the high-carbon case into hard martensite while the low-carbon core stays soft and tough, often followed by a refining/tempering treatment. Result: a hard, wear-resistant outer case with a tough, ductile core — typical applications being gudgeon pins, gears, cams and bearing surfaces.

answers.title: Class 1 Pressure Vessel — Test Pieces and Tests
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of sketches, how the test pieces for a Class 1 pressure vessel are obtained. (6)

(b) List the tests which are carried out on the test pieces described in Q(a). (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) How the test pieces are obtained**
For a Class 1 (fusion-welded) pressure vessel, weld quality must be proved by destructive testing. Since specimens cannot be cut from the finished vessel, a separate test plate is welded on as a continuation of an actual production seam.
*Sketch instructions: draw a test plate (~300mm wide) butted up to and welded as an extension of a vessel's main longitudinal seam. Mark out and number the specimen locations across the weld: (1) a dog-bone profiled transverse tensile specimen; (2) two plain rectangular strips for bend tests (root bend, face bend); (3) a further reduced-section tensile/all-weld-metal specimen; (4) and (5) small notched strips for impact (Charpy) tests from the weld metal and HAZ. Mark a lower spare portion reserved for retests.*

**Preparing the test plate.** A test plate is butted up to and welded integrally with the end of one of the vessel's main (longitudinal) seams, forming a natural run-off extension. This guarantees identical conditions — same parent plate, edge preparation, welding procedure, consumables, welder, pre-heat and heat treatment.
**Heat treatment and NDT.** The test plate undergoes any stress-relieving/heat treatment given to the vessel, and is then radiographed (and/or ultrasonically examined) along with the seam to confirm soundness before specimens are cut.
**Retest material.** A lower portion is reserved spare material "for retests if necessary," so duplicate pieces can be cut from the same proven plate should any specimen fail or give a doubtful result.

**(b) Tests carried out**
Transverse tensile test — across the weld, to verify the joint meets specified UTS (ideally failing in the parent metal, not the weld).
Bend tests — a root bend and a face bend (and/or a side bend on thick plate), proving ductility and soundness.
Impact (Charpy V-notch) test — notched pieces broken to measure toughness/notch ductility of the weld metal and HAZ.
Macro-examination (and hardness) test — a section polished, etched and examined for penetration, fusion, freedom from cracks/porosity/slag and correct profile, often with a hardness survey across weld, parent metal and HAZ.

answers.title: Types of Stress and Strain; Tests on Ship's Side Plating
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Materials used for hull and machinery are subject to stress and strain in service. Define EACH of the following:

(i) THREE types of stress; (3)

(ii) TWO types of strain. (2)

(b) Describe the tests that may be carried out on steel to be used for ships side plating. (5)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Three Types of Stress**
Stress is the internal resistance per unit area set up against an applied load: stress = load ÷ cross-sectional area (N/m²).
Tensile stress — set up by a pulling (stretching) load along the axis, tending to lengthen the material. Example: a tie-bar, or the lower fibres of a sagging hull.
Compressive stress — set up by a pushing (squeezing) load, tending to shorten or crush. Example: a pillar/stanchion, or deck plating of a sagging hull.
Shear stress — set up when equal, opposite and parallel loads act across a section, tending to make one part slide over the adjacent part. Example: the cross-section of a rivet or bolt.

Bending and torsional/twisting stress are equally acceptable as a third type.

**(a)(ii) Two Types of Strain**
Strain is the deformation produced by the stress, expressed as a ratio (no units).
Direct (linear) strain — change in length per unit original length produced by tensile or compressive stress: strain = change in length / original length. Tensile strain is an extension; compressive strain a shortening.
Shear strain — the angular distortion produced by a shear stress, measured as the angle (radians) through which a face is displaced relative to the original right angle.

Volumetric strain (change in volume ÷ original volume) is an acceptable alternative.

**(b) Tests on steel for ship's side plating**
Tensile test — a machined test piece pulled to destruction to find yield stress, UTS, percentage elongation and reduction in area.
Bend test — a strip bent cold around a former to confirm ductility and soundness.
Impact (Charpy V-notch) test — notched specimens broken over a range of temperatures to establish the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature.
Chemical analysis — confirms composition within specified limits, governing strength, weldability and brittle-fracture resistance.
Hardness test and NDT/examination — hardness checks strength and uniformity; ultrasonic testing detects internal laminations/flaws.

answers.title: Cupro-Nickel, White Metal, Titanium + NAB/Stainless for Large Propellers (apart from corrosion/erosion)
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe the properties of EACH of the following alloys used in marine engineering, giving a practical example for which EACH are suited:

(i) cupro-nickel; (2)

(ii) white metal; (2)

(iii) titanium; (2)

(b) Apart from corrosion and erosion resistance, describe the properties of EACH of the following for use in the munufacture of large propellers;

(i) nickel aluminium bronze (2)

(ii) stainless steel. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Cupro-Nickel** — a copper-base alloy with nickel (typically 70/30 or 90/10), often with small iron and manganese additions. Outstanding resistance to seawater corrosion and erosion, particularly impingement attack by fast-flowing water, with good ductility and reasonable strength; resists biofouling. Example: seawater pipework and condenser/cooler tubes and tube plates.

**(a)(ii) White Metal** — a soft tin- or lead-based bearing alloy (Babbitt), with antimony and copper. Low coefficient of friction, good embeddability and conformability; bonds readily to a stronger backing shell. Example: lining of main and bottom-end (white-metalled) and crosshead bearings.

**(a)(iii) Titanium** — outstanding strength-to-weight ratio and exceptional seawater corrosion resistance from a stable, self-healing oxide film. Retains strength at temperature but costly and difficult to machine. Example: plate-type heat exchangers/seawater cooler plates.

**(b)(i) Nickel-aluminium Bronze** (apart from corrosion/erosion) — high strength-to-weight ratio with excellent toughness and ductility, so it withstands fluctuating (fatigue) loads and occasional impact without cracking. Good fatigue strength and cavitation resistance, and casts well into the large, complex curved blade shapes required.

**(b)(ii) Stainless Steel** (apart from corrosion) — propeller-grade (often cast martensitic/duplex) stainless steel provides high tensile strength and hardness, allowing thinner, more efficient blade sections for the same strength. Good toughness and fatigue resistance for cyclic loading, excellent cavitation-erosion resistance, and a hard surface that polishes smooth and is readily repaired by welding.

answers.title: Brittle vs Ductile Failure; Ductile-Brittle Transition; Charpy Test
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to steels used in shipbuilding and marine engineering:

(a) describe EACH of the following types of failure:

(i) brittle failure; (2)

(ii) ductile failure. (2)

(b) explain the term ductile to brittle transition stating the factor that determines ductile to brittle transition; (2)

(c) describe a test to determine the value of brittle fracture of a specimen test piece. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Brittle Failure**
A sudden, rapid fracture with little or no plastic deformation beforehand. The crack propagates very quickly, often at stresses below the yield point, giving no warning. The fracture face is bright, granular/crystalline, the break roughly square to the applied stress, and the pieces fit back together almost exactly (no necking). Promoted by low temperature, notches/stress raisers and shock loading.

**(a)(ii) Ductile Failure**
Occurs only after considerable plastic deformation. The material stretches, yields and necks down before tearing, absorbing a large amount of energy and giving plenty of visible warning. The fracture face is dull, fibrous and rough, often with a characteristic "cup-and-cone" shape and shear lips. The desirable, "safe" mode of failure.

**(b) Ductile-to-Brittle Transition**
Many steels are ductile and tough at higher temperatures but become brittle as temperature falls. The transition is the change in behaviour over a narrow temperature band: above it failure is tough and ductile (high energy); below it the same steel fails in a brittle manner (low energy). The determining factor is temperature — specifically the transition temperature. For ship steels this must be kept safely below the lowest expected service (seawater) temperature; composition (lower carbon, added Mn/Ni) and fine grain size are used to lower it.

**(c) Charpy Impact Test**
Specimen: a standard bar (10mm×10mm×55mm) with a V-notch machined at its centre to act as a controlled stress raiser. Apparatus: supported horizontally as a simple beam in the anvil of a pendulum impact-testing machine, notch on the face opposite the side to be struck. The test: a heavy pendulum/striker, released from a known height, swings down and breaks the specimen in one blow; the energy absorbed (joules) is read from the machine scale. Interpretation: a high energy value indicates tough/ductile behaviour, a low value brittle. Repeating over a range of temperatures and plotting energy vs temperature gives the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature.

answers.title: Properties of Materials — Strength, Hardness, Ductility, Toughness, Brittleness
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
Describe EACH of the following properties of materials:

(a) strength; (2)

(b) hardness; (2)

(c) ductility; (2)

(d) toughness; (2)

(e) brittleness. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Strength** — the ability to withstand an applied load without failing. Measured as the stress the material can carry, quoted as tensile, compressive or shear strength. Ultimate tensile strength is the maximum stress sustained before failure.

**(b) Hardness** — the ability to resist surface indentation, scratching, abrasion and wear. Measured by pressing a standard indenter into the surface (Brinell, Vickers or Rockwell). Hardness generally rises with strength but usually with reduced ductility. Important for wearing surfaces such as gear teeth and journals.

**(c) Ductility** — the ability to undergo considerable plastic deformation before fracture. Measured by percentage elongation and percentage reduction in area in a tensile test. Mild steel and copper are good examples.

**(d) Toughness** — the ability to absorb energy, particularly from shock or impact, without fracturing, by deforming plastically. Combines reasonable strength with good ductility and resists crack propagation. Measured by the energy absorbed in an impact (Charpy/Izod) test. Essential for shock-loaded parts such as crankshafts and gears.

**(e) Brittleness** — the tendency to fracture suddenly with little or no plastic deformation. A brittle material gives no warning, fails at low energy, and the broken faces fit back together almost exactly. Examples: grey cast iron, glass, hardened steel.

answers.title: Sea Water Pipelines, Strainers and Ship's Side Valves — Flooding Risk
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set: State the inspections, instructions and maintenance that should be carried out on main sea water pipelines, strainers and ship's side valves to minimise the risks of engine room flooding. (10)
answers.answer_text:
**Ship's Side Valves and Sea Chests.** Inspect the valves and surrounding shell plating for external corrosion, wastage, weeping, cracks and the condition of securing studs/flanges. At dry-dock, open up for survey: examine seats and faces, renew worn seats/discs, check the spindle, gland and valve body thickness (ultrasonic check). Confirm cathodic protection/sacrificial anodes in the sea chests are renewed and gratings/gridbars are secure and clear. Operate the valves fully open and shut at intervals so they do not seize, and keep remote/emergency closing arrangements free and tested. Ensure each valve is clearly labelled with clear open/shut indication.

**Sea Water Strainers/Filters.** Inspect and clean strainer baskets regularly (more often in shallow, muddy, weed- or ice-laden water). Check basket, body and cover for corrosion and erosion, renew wasted baskets, ensure cover joints/seals are sound. Where duplex (changeover) strainers are fitted, prove the changeover mechanism so one side can be cleaned while the other stays in service.

**Main Sea Water Pipelines.** Inspect pipework for external corrosion, wastage, pitting and leakage, paying attention to flange joints, bends, low points and high-flow areas (erosion-corrosion). Take ultrasonic thickness readings on suspect runs and renew wasted sections before they fail. Check pipe supports, hangers and clamps are secure, flange bolts tight and gaskets sound.

**Instructions and Operational Precautions.** Maintain up-to-date pipeline diagrams; valves clearly marked and labelled. Brief watchkeepers on the location and operation of all ship's side valves and emergency closing positions. Ensure bilge wells, level alarms and bilge pumps are tested and working, with the emergency bilge suction (direct to main SW circulating pump) proven. Keep engine room bilges clean and dry so a new leak is immediately obvious. After any maintenance, pressure-test/check for leaks before relying on the component.

**Aim:** keep the components most exposed to sea pressure sound (no wastage), operable (valves free, strainers changeable), leak-tight (good joints) and monitored (bilge alarms, regular inspection) — so any ingress is minimised, detected early and controlled.

answers.title: Fretting and Fretting Corrosion
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain EACH of the following metallurgical failure mechanisms:

(i) fretting; (3)

(ii) fretting corrosion. (3)

(b) State TWO shipboard examples where fretting may occur. (2)

(c) State TWO shipboard examples where fretting corrosion may occur. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Fretting**
A form of surface (wear) damage between two contacting, loaded surfaces subjected to slight relative movement — typically a small, repeated oscillatory slip of very low amplitude caused by vibration or fluctuating loads, rather than gross sliding. Although the surfaces are nominally clamped or a tight fit, the minute repeated movement causes the high spots (asperities) to weld together and shear off, producing fine wear debris and progressive damage. The result is surface pitting, scoring and loss of fit, and because the damaged surface acts as a stress raiser, it frequently initiates fatigue cracks (fretting fatigue), its most serious consequence.

**(a)(ii) Fretting Corrosion**
Fretting combined with a corrosive (oxidation) action — the more damaging form. The small oscillatory movement continually rubs away any protective oxide film and detaches fine metal particles, exposing fresh, clean metal at the interface. This freshly exposed metal immediately oxidises, and the repeated movement removes the new oxide as well, so the process is continuous. The fine debris is a hard oxide (on steel, a characteristic red-brown "cocoa" powder). This abrasive oxide accelerates wear and loosens the fit.

**(b) Two examples of fretting** — splined shaft couplings/keyed joints and gear-tooth contacts subjected to vibration; bearing housings and journals, or the mating faces of bolted joints under fluctuating load.

**(c) Two examples of fretting corrosion** — shrink-fitted/interference fits (e.g. propeller-shaft and crank-web/journal fits, or fitted coupling bolts); roller and ball bearing seatings on shafts, and spline/coupling joints of line shafting exposed to moisture.

answers.title: Cupro-Nickel, White Metal, Titanium + NAB/Stainless for Casting of Large Propellers
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe the properties of EACH of the following alloys used in marine engineering, giving a practical example for which EACH are suited:

(i) cupro-nickel; (2)

(ii) white metal; (2)

(iii) titanium. (2)

(b) Discuss the merits of EACH of the following alloys for use in the casting of large propellers:

(i) nickel aluminium bronze; (2)

(ii) stainless steel. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)** As per Q12 above — cupro-nickel (seawater pipework/condenser tubes), white metal (bearing linings), titanium (plate heat exchangers).

**(b)(i) Nickel-aluminium Bronze** — the most widely used propeller alloy; casts extremely well into the large, complex curved blade shapes required and finishes to a fine, smooth surface, giving a dense, sound casting. Combines a high strength-to-weight ratio with excellent toughness and ductility, outstanding seawater corrosion resistance and good cavitation-erosion resistance; relatively repairable by welding. Drawbacks: lower strength than steel (thicker sections needed) and high cost.

**(b)(ii) Stainless Steel** — cast (martensitic or duplex) stainless steels give higher tensile strength and hardness than NAB, allowing thinner, more hydrodynamically efficient blade sections and lighter propellers for a given strength. Good toughness and fatigue resistance, excellent cavitation-erosion resistance, and a hard surface taking a high polish and readily repaired by welding. Trade-offs: more difficult to cast soundly into large intricate blade forms (greater defect risk), can suffer crevice/pitting corrosion in stagnant seawater, and generally more expensive.

answers.title: MMA Electrode Storage; Edge Preparation; Three Arc-Welding Defects
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
(a) State the factors in the storage of Manual Metal Arc welding electrodes which will assist in producing good quality welds. (2)

(b) Explain the importance of edge preparation before welding. (2)

(c) Sketch THREE electric arc welding defects, stating the cause of EACH. (6)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Storage of MMA welding electrodes**
Electrodes must be kept dry and warm in a heated, ventilated store or holding oven so the flux coating does not absorb moisture (damp electrodes cause porosity, cracking and poor arc stability). Keep them clean and undamaged (coating intact), stored in sealed containers, used in date order, and re-baked to the maker's temperature if exposed, with low-hydrogen types held in a heated quiver at the workplace.

**(b) Importance of edge preparation**
Correct edge preparation (right bevel angle, root face and root gap, with clean edges) ensures full penetration and complete fusion right through the joint, so the weld develops its full strength with no unfused root or trapped slag. It also controls the volume of weld metal and heat input, giving a sound, defect-free joint of correct profile and minimising distortion.

**(c) Three electric arc welding defects**
*Sketch instructions: draw three butt-weld cross-sections. (1) Undercut — a groove melted into the parent plate at the toe of the weld. (2) Lack of penetration — the weld metal fails to reach and fuse the root, leaving an unfilled gap. (3) Porosity — gas holes (blowholes) trapped in the solidified weld metal.*

**Undercut** — caused by excessive welding current, too long an arc, too fast a travel speed or an incorrect electrode angle.
**Lack of (incomplete) penetration** — caused by current too low, travel too fast, too narrow a root gap/faulty edge preparation, or too large an electrode for the joint.
**Porosity** — caused by damp electrodes or moisture, a contaminated joint (oil, rust, scale, paint), or inadequate shielding/too long an arc.

Other acceptable defects: slag inclusions, lack of sidewall fusion, overlap, and cracking (hydrogen/hot cracking).

occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Storage answers stop at 'protect from moisture' without explaining why (moisture causes hydrogen embrittlement/porosity); welding-current faults must be stated as too high OR too low, not just 'incorrect amps'; and the arc-defect sketches are consistently weak.

answers.title: Creep Test — Strain-Time Diagram and Four Stages
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a Strain versus Time diagram, how a creep test is carried out to determine the strain rate of the material under test. (6)

(b) Explain EACH of the stages sketched in the diagram in part (a). (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) How a creep test is carried out**
A standard tensile test specimen is mounted in a creep-testing machine and enclosed in a thermostatically controlled electric furnace, holding it at a constant, accurately maintained elevated temperature. Once at uniform temperature, a constant axial load (constant stress) is applied — usually by a deadweight/lever system — and held unchanged for the test. The resulting extension is measured continuously by a sensitive extensometer, and strain is recorded against elapsed time (which may run for hundreds or thousands of hours). Plotting these readings produces the creep curve. The strain rate is the slope of this curve — the figure of interest is the slope of the long, straight secondary (steady-state) portion, since this governs the useful service life. The test is repeated at several stresses and temperatures so creep behaviour can be predicted for actual operating conditions.

*Diagram: strain (vertical) against time (horizontal), starting with a vertical step (initial strain) at t=0, then Primary, Secondary and Tertiary regions as below.*

**(b) The stages on the diagram**
Initial strain (elastic + plastic): the instantaneous strain when the load is applied, before time-dependent creep begins.
Primary (transient) creep: creep rate starts relatively high but progressively decreases as the material work-hardens.
Secondary (steady-state) creep: the long, straight region of constant minimum creep rate — the most important region; its slope is the strain rate used for design and life prediction.
Tertiary creep: the rate accelerates rapidly as voids, necking and cracking develop and the cross-section reduces, leading finally to rupture.

answers.title: Centrifugal Sea-Water Pump — Materials of Construction
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
State, with reasons, the materials used in EACH of the following components of a centrifugal pump for sea water circulating duties:

(a) casing; (2)

(b) impeller; (2)

(c) shaft; (2)

(d) wear rings; (2)

(e) mechanical seal. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**Casing** — Gunmetal/bronze (or cast iron with a corrosion-resistant lining on cheaper pumps; nickel-aluminium bronze on higher-duty pumps). Must resist seawater corrosion over a large, intricately cast shape; bronze/gunmetal casts readily into the volute and gives adequate strength to contain the pressure.

**Impeller** — Nickel-aluminium bronze (or gunmetal/bronze). Exposed to high-velocity seawater, so must resist erosion, cavitation and impingement attack as well as general corrosion; NAB combines this with high strength and toughness and casts well into the curved vane shape.

**Shaft** — Stainless steel (e.g. martensitic 13% Cr or duplex), or a high-strength steel shaft with stainless/bronze sleeves. Transmits driving torque and needs high tensile and fatigue strength, while resisting corrosion where it contacts seawater; renewable sleeves protect a cheaper steel shaft at the seal and bearing areas.

**Wear Ring** — Bronze/gunmetal (often leaded bronze). Renewable sacrificial components maintaining the running clearance between impeller and casing; made of a softer material so rubbing wears the cheap, easily-replaced ring rather than the expensive impeller or casing.

**Mechanical Seal** — A hard face of silicon carbide or tungsten carbide (or ceramic) running against a softer carbon (graphite) face, with stainless steel metal parts and synthetic rubber elastomer seals. The faces must be hard, wear- and corrosion-resistant with a low coefficient of friction to seal against seawater leakage with minimal wear; the carbon face is self-lubricating.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Centrifugal Sea-Water Pump — Materials of Construction
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: The casing material is the trap: plain grey cast iron corrodes quickly in sea water and is a wrong answer across colleges, yet keeps appearing. Bronze is the standard correct answer; Ni-Resist (nickel-alloyed) cast iron is an accepted alternative for high-reliability systems but is almost never mentioned. The rest of the question (impeller, shaft, wear ring, seal) is reliably full marks.

answers.title: Alloying Elements in Steel — Cr, Mn, Mo, Ni, V
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
Explain the effects of the addition of EACH of the following alloying elements to improve the characteristics of steels:

(a) chromium; (2)

(b) manganese; (2)

(c) molybdenum; (2)

(d) nickel; (2)

(e) vanadium. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Chromium** — increases hardness, strength and wear resistance and improves hardenability. Its most important effect is conferring corrosion and oxidation resistance — above ~12% it forms the self-healing passive oxide film that makes stainless steel. Forms hard, stable carbides improving high-temperature strength and abrasion resistance.

**(b) Manganese** — acts as a deoxidiser and desulphuriser during steelmaking. Increases strength, hardness, toughness and hardenability; in high percentages (Hadfield's manganese steel) produces an extremely tough, work-hardening, abrasion-resistant steel for impact/wear duties.

**(c) Molybdenum** — raises strength, hardness and hardenability, and is especially valued for improving strength and creep resistance at high temperatures (boiler, superheater and steam-turbine steels). Forms stable carbides, refines grain, and reduces temper brittleness.

**(d) Nickel** — increases strength and toughness without loss of ductility, and is particularly effective at improving toughness and impact resistance at low temperatures (lowering the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature). Improves hardenability and, with chromium, gives tough, corrosion-resistant austenitic stainless steels.

**(e) Vanadium** — a strong grain refiner that forms hard, stable carbides, giving increased strength, hardness, toughness and fatigue resistance. Improves resistance to softening at high temperature, so used in tool steels and high-strength spring/forged steels.

answers.title: Fatigue Crack Propagation to Total Failure
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set: With reference to machinery parts under cyclic loading, describe, with the aid of sketches, how the propagation of even the smallest of cracks can lead to total component failure. (10)
answers.answer_text:
Machinery parts under cyclic (fluctuating or reversed) loading — crankshafts, connecting rods, propeller shafts, gear teeth, bolts — can fail by fatigue at stresses well below yield. The mechanism is the slow growth of a crack from a tiny initial flaw until the remaining metal can no longer carry the load.

*Sketch instructions: draw a shaft cross-section in three stages. (1) A small initial crack at a surface stress-raiser (fillet, keyway, oil hole). (2) The crack progressing across the section, with curved "beach mark" lines showing successive crack-front positions. (3) Final failure — a small remaining crystalline overload zone where sudden fracture occurred.*

**Stage 1 — Crack Initiation.** Fatigue almost always begins at a point of stress concentration on the surface — a fillet, keyway, oil hole, thread, machining mark, corrosion pit, or sub-surface inclusion. Here the local stress is magnified well above the nominal stress, and with each cycle this point is repeatedly strained. Even though the average stress is below yield, the magnified local stress exceeds the material's limit, and after a number of cycles a microscopic crack forms at the surface.

**Stage 2 — Crack Propagation.** With every load cycle the crack opens slightly under the tensile part of the cycle and closes under the compressive part. Each cycle advances the crack tip a minute amount, so the crack grows progressively across the section. The repeated opening and closing rubs and burnishes the fracture faces smooth, leaving the characteristic curved "beach marks" radiating from the origin. As the crack grows the load-bearing cross-section is continuously reduced, so the stress on the remaining sound metal steadily rises.

**Stage 3 — Final Sudden Failure.** This continues until the remaining intact area becomes too small to carry the applied load. At that moment the stress in the remaining ligament reaches the ultimate strength and the component fractures suddenly and completely in a single overload — even though the loads never increased. This final fast-fracture zone has a rough, bright, granular/crystalline appearance, in clear contrast to the smooth, beach-marked fatigue zone.

**Why the smallest crack matters:** no warning by deformation is given — a crack invisibly small at the outset will, given enough cycles, propagate right across the section and cause total failure. This is why stress concentrations are minimised by generous fillet radii and good surface finish, components are designed to work below the fatigue (endurance) limit, and critical parts are subject to regular NDT crack detection.

occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: A well-defined, well-scoring question for candidates who understand the mechanism, but a clear split -- those who don't grasp how a fatigue crack initiates and propagates under cyclic loading to sudden final fracture score poorly rather than partially.

answers.title: Electrode Storage; Edge Preparation; Pipe Crack Repair (Repeat Sitting)
answers.topic: Materials, Failure Mechanisms, Welding & Auxiliary Systems
answers.question_as_set:
(a) State the factors in the storage of Manual Metal Arc welding electrodes which will assist in producing good quality welds. (2)

(b) Explain the importance of edge preparation before welding. (2)

(c) Sketch TWO methods of plate edge preparation. (2)

(d) A hairline crack is detected in a pipe, as Chief Engineer Officer, state the factors to be taken into account in reaching a decision on the method of repair. (4)
answers.answer_text:
Identical question to Q22/Q18 above, repeated at a later sitting; the model answer is unchanged.

**(a)/(b)/(c)** As per Q18/Q22 above.

**(d) Hairline crack in a pipe — factors in the repair decision**
Nature, location and cause of the crack — what fluid, pressure and temperature does the line carry, and is it part of an essential or class-surveyed safety system? Determine the true extent by NDT and identify the root cause — a sound repair must remove the cause, not just the symptom.
Pipe material, condition and weldability — governs whether welding is feasible; check for general wastage since a badly wasted pipe is better renewed than patched.
Resources, competence and class requirements — correct consumables, a qualified welder, and whether Classification Society/flag approval is needed, and whether the repair can be carried out at sea or must wait for port/dry-dock.
Type of repair and risk — permanent repair versus a temporary measure to reach port safely, weighing the consequences of failure and the time/cost of each option.

answers.title: Pneumatically Operated Control Valves — Positioner, Hysteresis, Fail Safe/Set
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to pneumatically operated control valves:

(a) state FOUR reasons for fitting a valve positioner; (4)

(b) explain valve hysteresis, stating how it affects the process; (2)

(c) state the immediate action to be taken to restore control upon failure of the positioner bellows;

(d) state the difference between fail safe and fail set. (2) (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Four reasons for fitting a valve positioner**
To overcome stem/gland friction and hysteresis — it ensures the valve plug takes up the exact position demanded by the controller signal.
To overcome unbalanced process forces — high or fluctuating differential pressure across the plug tends to push the valve off its demanded position; the positioner senses the error and corrects it.
To speed up the valve response — the positioner acts as a power relay with its own air supply, so the actuator responds faster (overcomes lag in long signal lines and large actuator volumes).
To modify the signal/travel relationship — allows split-range operation, action reversal, or a characterised (non-linear) relationship between signal and travel. (Also acceptable: to apply a higher actuator pressure than the 0.2–1.0 bar signal.)

**(b) Valve hysteresis and its effect**
Hysteresis is the difference in valve stem position obtained for the same controller signal depending on whether that signal is increasing or decreasing — chiefly caused by stem/gland friction and lost motion in the linkage. Its effect on the process is a deadband/lag: the valve does not respond to small signal changes, especially reversals, so the controlled variable wanders from setpoint, producing offset, sluggish correction and hunting (oscillation).

**(c) Immediate action on failure of the positioner bellows**
The bellows is the signal-receiving element, so its failure leaves the valve uncontrolled. Operate the positioner bypass so that the controller output air is fed directly to the actuator diaphragm — this restores control (less accurately). If no bypass is fitted, transfer the loop to manual until repairs are made.

**(d) Fail safe versus fail set**
Fail safe — on loss of air supply or signal, the valve is driven by spring action to a predetermined safe position (fully open or fully closed).
Fail set (fail-in-place/fail-fixed/fail-freeze) — on loss of air supply, the valve stays in its last position; air is trapped in the actuator by a lock-up valve.

answers.title: Capacitance Electrode Level Measuring Transmitter
answers.question_as_set: Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the principle of operation of a capacitance electrode level measuring transmitter. (10)
answers.answer_text:
**Basic principle.** The device works on the principle that electrical capacitance varies with the level of liquid in the tank. A capacitor is formed by two conductors separated by a dielectric (insulating) material: C = εa · A / d, where A is the facing area of the plates, d the distance between them, and εa the permittivity of the material between them. In a level transmitter the area and spacing are fixed by construction, so capacitance changes because the effective dielectric changes as liquid rises and falls.

*Sketch instructions: draw an insulated metal probe mounted vertically inside a stilling well/tube within the tank. Show the probe as one capacitor plate and the earthed tank wall/well as the other. Show a vent hole at the top and liquid-entry holes at the bottom of the stilling well. Label the high-frequency AC bridge circuit connected to the probe.*

**Construction.** An insulated metal probe (electrode) is mounted vertically in the tank, housed within a stilling well/tube that damps surface turbulence and sloshing. The probe forms one plate of the capacitor; the metal tank wall (or surrounding well) forms the earthed second plate. The probe carries an insulation sheath so the system still works with conductive liquids. A vent hole at the top and liquid-entry holes at the bottom of the stilling well allow the liquid inside the well to follow the true tank level.

**How level produces a capacitance change.** The space between the probe and the earthed wall is occupied partly by liquid (below the surface) and partly by vapour/air (above the surface). Liquid and vapour have very different dielectric constants, so as the level rises, more of the probe's length is surrounded by the higher-dielectric liquid and the overall capacitance increases proportionally with level. This capacitance forms part of a high-frequency AC bridge circuit; the bridge unbalance (proportional to level) is measured, amplified, and converted to a standard output signal (e.g. 4–20mA) calibrated directly in level/percentage full.

answers.title: Closed-Loop Control Circuit — Block Diagram
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch an annotated block diagram of a closed loop control circuit. (5)

(b) Describe how the control loop sketched in Q(a) operates. (5)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw boxes for Set point → Controller → Regulating unit (Actuator + Regulator/valve) → Process, with a Measuring unit (Detect → Measure → Display) taking a signal off the process output and feeding it back to the Controller via a feedback line.*

The essential blocks to label are: set point (desired value input); controller (comparator + control action); regulating unit = actuator + regulator (e.g. valve positioner/actuator and control valve); process (the plant being controlled); measuring unit = detect → measure → display (sensor/transducer, transmitter, indicator); and the feedback line carrying the measured value back to the controller.

**(b) How the control loop operates**
The purpose of the loop is to hold a process variable (the controlled condition) at a desired value.
**Set point.** The operator sets the desired value; this is the reference fed into the controller.
**Detection and measurement (feedback).** The detecting element senses the actual value of the controlled condition, converts it into a standard signal, and feeds it back to the controller.
**Comparison and error.** The controller compares the feedback with the set point; any difference is the error (deviation) signal. This comparison of output with input is what makes the loop "closed".
**Control action.** Acting on the error, the controller produces a corrective output signal according to its control mode (on/off, P, PI or PID), aiming to drive the error towards zero.
**Correction.** The controller output goes to the actuator, which moves the regulator (e.g. a control valve) to alter the manipulated variable into the process.
**Closing the loop.** The change in the manipulated variable alters the process; the new value is again detected and fed back, and the cycle repeats continuously, holding the controlled condition at set point despite disturbances.

In short: measure → compare with set point → calculate error → correct → re-measure, repeated continuously. Because the output is fed back and compared with the input, the system self-corrects without operator intervention — the defining feature of closed-loop control, in contrast to open-loop control which has no feedback.

answers.title: Control Systems Terminology — Two-Step, Offset, Gain, Proportional, Integral
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to control systems, explain EACH of the following:

(a) two-step action; (2)

(b) offset; (2)

(c) gain; (2)

(d) proportional action; (2)

(e) integral action. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Two-step action** — a control action in which the final control element can take up only two fixed positions, fully ON or fully OFF, with no intermediate setting. A small differential gap (deadband) is built in to prevent rapid switching (chatter), so the controlled condition continuously cycles (hunts) about the set point. Simple and cheap; suited to processes that tolerate cycling — e.g. domestic-type thermostats, calorifier heating, refrigeration.

**(b) Offset** — the sustained (steady-state) deviation between the controlled condition and the set point that remains after the process has settled following a load change. A characteristic of proportional control: because the controller needs a finite error to produce the new valve position demanded by the new load, the variable settles displaced from — not exactly at — the set point. Removed by adding integral action.

**(c) Gain** — the ratio of the change in controller output to the change in input (error) that produced it: Gain = Δoutput / Δinput. It is the inverse of the proportional band: Gain = 100 / PB(%). High gain (narrow band) gives fast, sensitive response but a tendency to instability; low gain (wide band) gives sluggish but stable response.

**(d) Proportional action** — the controller output is directly proportional to the magnitude of the error: output ∝ error (within the proportional band). Gives smooth, stable control, but leaves a residual offset after a load change.

**(e) Integral action** — the rate of change of controller output is proportional to the error, so the output keeps changing for as long as any deviation exists. Its function is to eliminate offset, continuing to adjust the final control element until the measured value returns exactly to set point. Always combined with proportional action (P+I).

occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Gain is the term candidates most often can't explain -- it needs to be stated as the ratio of change in output to change in input, not just described vaguely as 'sensitivity.'

answers.title: Pneumatic Control Valves — Positioner Reasons, Hysteresis Sketch, Design/Maintenance
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to pneumatically operated control valves:

(a) state the reasons for fitting a valve positioner; (4)

(b) describe, with the aid of a sketch, valve hysteresis, stating how it affects the process; (3)

(c) describe how design and routine maintenance can limit hysteresis. (3)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)** As per Q1 above (stem/gland friction, unbalanced process forces, speed of response, signal/travel modification).

**(b) Valve hysteresis with sketch**
*Sketch instructions: plot Flow (vertical, 0–100%) against Input signal (horizontal). Draw two curves — one for increasing signal, one for decreasing — that do not retrace the same path, forming a "loop." Mark the vertical gap between them as the hysteresis.*

Hysteresis is the difference in valve position (and hence flow) obtained for the same input signal, depending on whether that signal is increasing or decreasing. It is caused chiefly by stem/gland friction (stiction) and lost motion/backlash in the actuator linkage and packing. Effect on the process: the valve does not respond to small signal changes — especially when the signal reverses direction — so there is a deadband/lag in correction; the controlled variable drifts from set point, giving sluggish, inaccurate control with offset and hunting.

**(c) How design and routine maintenance can limit hysteresis**
**By design:** fit a valve positioner (the single most effective measure); use low-friction gland packing (PTFE/graphite); provide a stiff, well-engineered actuator and linkage with minimum free play/backlash, adequately sized to give thrust well in excess of friction forces.
**By routine maintenance:** adjust gland packing correctly (sealed but not over-tightened); lubricate and clean the stem, renewing worn/scored stems; check and take up wear/backlash in the linkage and positioner feedback mechanism, periodically calibrating the positioner and carrying out a valve signature/stroke test.

answers.title: Resistance Temperature Detector (RTD)
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a temperature measuring instrument that uses the principle of operation of a change in resistance with the application of heat. (6)

(b) Describe how the instrument sketched in part (a) is tested and calibrated. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Principle.** The instrument is a Resistance Temperature Detector (RTD). It works on the principle that the electrical resistance of a metal increases as its temperature rises — a near-linear, accurate and repeatable relationship: Rt = R0(1 + αθ), where R0 is the resistance at 0°C, α the temperature coefficient of resistance, and θ the temperature.

*Sketch instructions: draw the RTD as one arm of a Wheatstone bridge, supplied at Vs, with fixed resistors R1, R2, R3 as the other arms and a millivolt detector across the bridge. Show the RTD element as a fine platinum wire coil wound on a former, protected inside a stainless-steel sheath/thermowell.*

**Construction.** The sensing element is a fine coil of pure platinum wire, stable and corrosion-resistant with a high, repeatable, almost linear temperature coefficient. The standard is the Pt100 (100Ω at 0°C), wound on a former and protected inside a stainless-steel sheath/thermowell.

**Measurement.** The RTD forms one arm of a Wheatstone bridge. At a reference temperature the bridge is balanced (zero output). As the medium temperature changes, the RTD resistance changes, unbalancing the bridge, giving an out-of-balance voltage proportional to temperature, amplified into a standard output (e.g. 4–20mA).

Lead/cable compensation: a three- or four-wire connection cancels the resistance of the long connecting cable, which would otherwise add error.

**(b) Testing and calibration**
**Practical method:** place the RTD probe in a precision temperature source (bath or dry-well calibrator) alongside a certified reference thermometer; compare readings at a series of known temperatures and adjust zero/span so they agree.
**Model method:** immerse the probe in melting ice (0°C) and check resistance reads 100Ω for a Pt100; a second known point (e.g. boiling water, ≈138.5Ω) confirms the span.

answers.title: Electrical/Electronic vs Pneumatic Remote Monitoring and Control
answers.question_as_set: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of electrical remote monitoring and control systems compared to pneumatic systems. (10)
answers.answer_text:
**Advantages of electrical/electronic systems**
Speed of signal transmission — electrical signals travel at near the speed of light with no transmission lag, whereas pneumatic signals suffer significant lag in long small-bore lines.
Suited to long-distance/remote transmission — electrical signals travel long cable runs with little degradation; pneumatic transmission becomes impractical beyond roughly 100–300m.
Compatibility with computers, PLCs and data systems — integrate directly with microprocessors, PLCs, alarm/monitoring and IAS systems; pneumatic signals must be transduced (I/P or P/I converters) first.
No clean, dry air supply required — avoids the need for a treated instrument-air supply; pneumatic systems depend entirely on clean, oil-free, moisture-free air.
Higher accuracy and easier signal manipulation — easier to amplify, scale, linearise, sum and process, allowing complex control strategies (cascade, ratio, feedforward).
Lower maintenance of transmission medium — no air leaks to trace; more compact instruments with built-in diagnostics.

**Disadvantages of electrical/electronic systems**
Explosion/fire hazard in flammable atmospheres — sparks are a serious risk in hazardous zones; special (intrinsically safe, flameproof, pressurised) protection is needed, whereas pneumatic systems are inherently safe.
No inherent fail-safe energy store on power loss — a pneumatic actuator holds stored energy and spring-returns to a safe position on signal loss; electronic systems need reliable power/battery back-up.
Susceptible to electrical interference — EMI/RFI, earth loops and induced voltages require screened cable and correct earthing; pneumatic signals are immune.
Final correcting element still usually needs power conversion — most large valves remain pneumatically actuated, needing an I/P converter and air supply anyway.
Specialised skills and equipment to maintain — needs trained electronic/instrument technicians; pneumatic systems are simple, robust and easily repaired.
Sensitivity to environment — electronics can be affected by moisture, vibration, salt-laden atmosphere unless suitably protected.

**Conclusion:** electronic systems dominate modern ships for speed, range and integration with computerised control, but pneumatic systems retain advantages of inherent safety, simplicity and fail-safe action. Many installations are hybrid — electronic transmission with pneumatically actuated final control valves via I/P converters.
