answers.title: Control Terms (P/I) + Cascade Control — Jacket Cooling Water
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain EACH of the following control terms:

(i) proportional action; (2)

(ii) integral action. (2)

(b) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a control system that may be enhanced by the inclusion of cascade control. (6)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Proportional action** — the controller output is directly proportional to the error between measured value and set point: output ∝ error. Gives smooth, stable response but leaves a residual offset after a load change.

**(a)(ii) Integral action** — the rate of change of controller output is proportional to the error, so the output keeps changing for as long as any deviation exists. Its purpose is to eliminate the offset left by proportional action, continuing to adjust until the measured value returns exactly to set point.

**(b) Cascade control — main engine jacket cooling water example**
*Sketch instructions: draw MASTER (P+I) controller taking jacket water OUTLET temperature and feeding its output as the remote set point to a SLAVE (P) controller, which takes jacket water INLET temperature and drives a 3-way valve mixing cooler and bypass flow, which feeds the engine jackets and returns to outlet.*

Cascade control uses two controllers in series — a master (outer) and a slave (inner) — with two measuring elements. The master controller's output does not go to the valve directly; instead it acts as the set point for the slave controller, and only the slave drives the final control element.

**Master controller (P+I)** — senses the jacket water temperature leaving the engine (the outlet) — the true controlled condition. It compares this with the set point and computes the required jacket water inlet temperature, sent as the set point to the slave, not to the valve.

**Slave controller (P)** — senses the jacket water temperature at the engine inlet (downstream of the three-way valve) and drives the three-way valve to mix cooled and bypassed water to achieve the inlet temperature demanded by the master.

**Why cascade improves control:** disturbances (engine load changes, sea-water temperature variations) are corrected by the fast inner (slave) loop before they reach the engine and upset the outlet temperature, while the slow outer (master) loop only makes small set-point adjustments to hold the outlet steady — giving tighter, more stable control with less overshoot and hunting than a single loop could achieve.

answers.title: Control Air Dryer (Twin-Tower Desiccant)
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to pneumatic instrument and control systems:

(a) sketch a control air dryer as fitted downstream from the instrument air compressor or reducing valve; (6)

(b) explain the operation of the dryer sketched in part (a). (4)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw a twin-tower (duplex) heated desiccant dryer. Show air inlet with pressure gauge, a changeover/diverter valve directing wet air to whichever tower is drying, two desiccant-packed towers each with a heating element, non-return valves at each tower outlet, a humidity probe in the common dry-air outlet line, a restrictor/orifice with cross-connection for purge air to the off-line tower, and an air drain to atmosphere from the regenerating tower.*

**(b) Operation.** The dryer removes moisture from the instrument air so the control system receives clean, dry, oil-free air — wet air would corrode and freeze in orifices and cause faulty operation.

**Drying:** wet compressed air enters via the changeover valve and passes up through the on-line tower; moisture is adsorbed onto the desiccant, and dry air leaves through the non-return valve to the instrument-air system. The humidity probe monitors dryness of the delivered air.

**Regeneration:** while one tower dries, the other is regenerated — a small fraction of dried air is bled through the restrictor and passed down through the off-line tower (assisted by its heating element), carrying away the released moisture, exhausted to atmosphere through the air drain.

**Changeover:** the two towers are alternated automatically (on a timer, or when the humidity probe detects saturation), so the regenerated tower comes on-line while the saturated one is regenerated — giving a continuous supply of dry air without interruption.

answers.title: PID Control Terms — P, I, D and Why Combined
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain EACH of the following control terms:

(i) proportional action; (2)

(ii) integral action; (2)

(iii) derivitive action. (2)

(b) Explain why proportional, integral and derivative actions are combined in one controller (PID), stating an example where it may be used. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Proportional action** — output ∝ error; gives smooth, fast, stable response but leaves a residual offset.

**(a)(ii) Integral action** — output rate ∝ error, integrating the error over time; eliminates the offset left by proportional action.

**(a)(iii) Derivative action** — output ∝ rate of change of error, not its size. Gives a large, early corrective "kick" the instant the variable starts moving rapidly, anticipating the deviation and reducing overshoot on fast-changing processes. Has no effect on a steady error and cannot remove offset.

**(b) Why P, I and D are combined (PID)**
Each action has a weakness the others cover: Proportional provides the basic, immediate correction but leaves offset. Integral removes that offset but is slow and can cause overshoot/instability alone. Derivative anticipates rapid changes and damps overshoot but cannot remove offset by itself. Combined as PID, the controller responds quickly and proportionally (P), eliminates steady-state offset (I), and resists rapid deviations and overshoot (D) — giving fast, accurate, stable control that none of the actions could achieve alone.

**Example of use:** a process that suffers large, sudden load changes and must be held precisely at set point with no offset — e.g. main engine jacket cooling water temperature control, or boiler combustion/steam temperature and pressure control.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: PID Control Terms — P, I, D and Why Combined
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; the part (b) 'why combined' answer needs all three terms tied together -- proportional gives fast response but leaves offset, integral removes the offset but can overshoot/lag, derivative anticipates rate of change to dampen overshoot -- rather than describing each in isolation again.

answers.title: Explosimeter (Combustible Gas Detector)
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, an explosimeter for the detection of combustible gas. (6)

(b) Describe how the instrument sketched in part (a) is tested and calibrated. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Principle.** A catalytic-filament (pellistor) type explosimeter based on a Wheatstone bridge, measuring flammable gas/vapour concentration as a percentage of the Lower Explosive Limit (LEL). It works on the principle of catalytic combustion: the sample is burned on a heated catalytic filament, raising its temperature and hence its resistance, unbalancing a Wheatstone bridge.

*Sketch instructions: draw a Wheatstone bridge with a heated catalytic detector filament in a combustion chamber as one arm, a matched compensating filament as an adjacent arm, and two fixed resistors completing the bridge. Show a battery supply, a galvanometer (calibrated 0–100% LEL) across the bridge, and a sampling tube with hand aspirator drawing the sample over the filament.*

**Construction.** The sensing element is a fine platinum filament coated with a catalyst, mounted in a combustion chamber, forming one arm of the bridge; a matched, inactive/compensating filament in a sealed chamber forms an adjacent arm. A hand aspirator draws the atmosphere to be tested through a sampling tube over the filament.

**Operation.** The filament is heated and the bridge balanced (zero reading) in clean air. The aspirator draws the sample over the hot filament; combustible gas burns on the catalyst, releasing heat that raises the filament's resistance and unbalances the bridge. The out-of-balance current is proportional to gas concentration, read as % LEL.

**Important limitation:** relies on oxygen for combustion, so gives a false low/unreliable reading in oxygen-deficient or very rich atmospheres — unsuitable for inert or tank atmospheres.

**(b) Testing and calibration**
Function/response (bump) check: zero the instrument in clean air, confirm the filament heats and the sampling line is sound.
Span calibration: apply a certified test gas of known concentration (e.g. 50% LEL methane) and adjust the span control until the galvanometer reads the known value.
Zero in clean air: re-zero in fresh air with no contaminant, repeating zero/span until both are correct.

answers.title: Pneumatic Proportional Plus Integral Controller + Integral Saturation
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to automatic control:

(a) sketch a pneumatic proportional plus integral controller; (6)

(b) explain the term integral saturation; (2)

(c) explain the action to be taken by the operator in the event of integral saturation occurring. (2)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw a flapper-nozzle P+I controller. Show air supply at 1.4 bar through a fixed restrictor feeding a nozzle; a flapper positioned by a comparator (set point vs measured value); output signal 0.2–1.0 bar; a proportional (feedback) bellows fed from the output repositioning the flapper; and an integral (reset) bellows opposing it, fed through an adjustable integral restrictor.*

**Operation.** An error moves the flapper relative to the nozzle, changing nozzle back-pressure and hence output. The feedback bellows gives proportional action by repositioning the flapper in opposition to the input change. The integral bellows, fed slowly through the adjustable restrictor, continues acting on the flapper for as long as a deviation exists, driving the output on until the error is removed — eliminating offset.

**(b) Integral saturation.** Also called "integral wind-up," this occurs when a deviation persists for a long time and the integral action keeps integrating that error, driving the integral bellows (and controller output) hard up against its limit — the output goes fully to one extreme. This typically happens when the controller cannot correct the error, e.g. the plant is shut down, on standby, or the loop is in manual. When normal operation resumes, the output remains saturated until the integral action slowly unwinds, so the controller is slow to respond and overshoots badly.

**(c) Operator action on integral saturation.** Transfer the controller to manual and manually bleed off/reset the wound-up integral pressure (vent the integral bellows) so the output returns to a sensible mid-range value matching actual process demand. Bring the controller back towards the set point and switch back to automatic ("bumplessly") only when the measured value is at or near the set point.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Pneumatic Proportional Plus Integral Controller + Integral Saturation
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; integral saturation (reset windup) is the concept to nail -- the integral term keeps building while the final control element is already at its travel limit, and the operator action is to switch to manual/hold the output until the process re-enters the controllable range before returning to auto.

answers.title: Proportional Band Width
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to automatic control systems:

(a) explain the term proportional band width; (2)

(b) state how the proportional band may be adjusted on EACH of the following:

(i) motion balance controllers (2)

(ii) force balance controllers. (2)

(c) explain the consequences if the proportional band is set incorrectly. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Proportional band width.** The percentage change in the input (measured value/error) required to move the controller output through its full range — i.e. to drive the final control element from fully shut to fully open. It is the inverse of gain: Gain = 100 / PB(%).

**(b)(i) Motion balance controllers.** Adjusted by altering the lengths/ratio of the linkage (lever arms) between the input (measuring) element, the flapper and the feedback — i.e. moving the pivot/fulcrum position along the connecting lever, which changes how much flapper movement (and hence output change) results from a given input movement.

**(b)(ii) Force balance controllers.** Adjusted by altering the ratio of the effective areas of the bellows (or the position of the fulcrum/pivot on the force beam) on which the input and feedback pressures act, changing the balance of forces about the flapper for a given error.

**(c) Consequences of incorrect proportional band setting.**
Too narrow (gain too high): the controller becomes over-sensitive — a small deviation produces a large output change, over-correcting, causing overshoot and sustained hunting/oscillation about the set point, wearing the valve.
Too wide (gain too low): the controller is sluggish — a large deviation produces only a small correction, response is slow, and a large offset remains. Control is stable but poor and inaccurate.

The correct setting is a compromise — the narrowest band that still gives stable control without hunting, with any residual offset then removed by adding integral action.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Proportional Band Width
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: A rarely-attempted, poorly-answered question -- most candidates don't actually know what proportional band width means (the % change in input needed to drive the output/valve through its full range) despite it underpinning the whole P/PI/PID topic.

answers.title: Suitable Control Actions for Marine Processes
answers.question_as_set:
(a) State, with reasons, the control actions that may be suitable for EACH of the following processes:

(i) settling tank oil temperature; (2)

(ii) jacket water temperature; (2)

(iii) temperature of oil being purified. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Settling tank oil temperature.** Two-step (on/off) control is suitable. A settling tank has a large mass of oil with a very large thermal capacity (slow-responding) and no critical accuracy requirement. Because the temperature changes very slowly, the cycling inherent in on/off control is small and acceptable, so the simplest, cheapest action is adequate.

**(a)(ii) Jacket water temperature.** Proportional plus integral (P+I), often P+I+D, is suitable. The outlet temperature must be held accurately and steadily with no offset despite frequent engine load changes, so a modulating PID action is required, not on/off.

**(a)(iii) Temperature of oil being purified.** Proportional plus integral (P+I) is suitable. Correct, closely-held purification temperature is critical to viscosity and separation efficiency, so accurate offset-free modulating control is needed without the cycling of on/off control.

**(b) Block diagram (purifier heating loop example)**
*Sketch instructions: draw Set point → Controller (P+I) → Control valve (steam supply) → Heater (process), with a Temperature probe sensing the heated oil and feeding back to the controller.*

The temperature probe senses the oil temperature leaving the heater and feeds it back to the controller, which compares it with the set point. Any error produces a P+I output that repositions the steam control valve, adjusting steam flow to the heater. The probe re-measures continuously, holding the purified-oil temperature accurately at set point with no offset.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Suitable Control Actions for Marine Processes
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: A judgement-based question where reasoned answers (matching control action to how fast/slow and how much lag each process has) were marked generously as long as the reasoning was justified, rather than marked against one fixed 'correct' answer.

answers.title: Cascade and Split Range Control
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain EACH of the following control terms:

(i) cascade; (2)

(ii) split range. (2)

(b) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a control system that may be enhanced by the inclusion of cascade control. (6)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Cascade.** Uses two controllers in series — a master (primary/outer) and a slave (secondary/inner) — with two measuring elements and two feedback loops. The master's output provides the set point for the slave, and only the slave drives the valve. The fast inner (slave) loop corrects intermediate disturbances before they reach and upset the main controlled variable.

**(a)(ii) Split range.** One controller operates two (or more) final control elements in sequence over different parts of its output signal range — e.g. over a 0.2–1.0 bar signal one valve opens over the lower half and a second over the upper half. Used where one controller must control both heating and cooling of a process.

**(b) Cascade control — jacket cooling water example**
As per Q8 above: a three-way valve splits jacket water between cooler and bypass. The master (P+I) senses the jacket water outlet temperature and provides the set point for the slave (P), which senses the inlet temperature and drives the three-way valve. The fast inner loop absorbs disturbances (load, sea-water temperature) before they reach the outlet, while the slow outer loop makes only small set-point corrections — holding the jacket water temperature steady without large fluctuations.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Cascade and Split Range Control
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: The recurring confusion is answering part (b) with a split-range description (one valve for heating, one for cooling, both driven directly by the same controller) when the question specifically asks for CASCADE control, where a master controller (e.g. sensing jacket outlet temperature) resets the set point of a slave controller (e.g. on the SW valve) to hold the process steady against varying engine load and sea temperature.

answers.title: Pneumatic Control Valves — Positioner and Hysteresis (Examiner-Noted Variant)
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to pneumatically operated control valves:

(a) state the reasons for fitting valve positioners; (4)

(b) with the aid of a sketch, explain valve hysteresis and how it affects the process; (4)

(c) describe how the design and routine maintenance can limit hysteresis. (2)
answers.answer_text:
Same underlying content as Q1/Q5 above (valve positioner reasons; hysteresis definition, sketch and effect; design/maintenance measures to limit it), with marks re-distributed 4/4/2 rather than 4/2/2/2 or 4/3/3.

**(a)** Overcome stem/gland friction; overcome unbalanced/fluctuating process forces; speed up valve response; modify the signal/travel relationship (split range, action reversal, characterised response). Further valid reasons: supply higher actuator pressure than the signal; allow the valve to work against high process pressure.

**(b)** *Sketch instructions: Flow (vertical axis) against Input signal (horizontal axis), with separate increasing and decreasing curves and the gap between them labelled as the hysteresis.* Caused mainly by stem/gland friction and lost motion/backlash; effect is a deadband/lag giving offset and hunting about the set point.

**(c)** By design: fit a positioner; use low-friction gland packing; provide a stiff, well-aligned actuator/linkage with minimum backlash. By maintenance: correct gland packing adjustment, clean/lubricate the stem, take up wear/backlash in the linkage and periodically calibrate the positioner with a stroke test.

answers.title: Automatic Sprinklers — Fire Control vs Fire Suppression; Glass-Bulb Limitations
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to automatic sprinkler systems for fire fighting purposes:

(a) explain, with the aid of a Heat Release versus Time diagram, the difference between fire control and fire suppression; (6)

(b) state the limitations of using glass bulbs to activate sprinkler heads and suggest, with reasons, an alternative mechanism. (4)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: plot Heat Release Rate/HRR (kW, vertical) against Time (horizontal). Show three curves: an uncontrolled fire rising steeply throughout; a "fire control" curve that rises then flattens into a plateau; and a "fire suppression" curve that rises then falls sharply toward zero after the activation point. Label the activation point clearly.*

**(a) Fire control versus fire suppression**
Up to system activation, the fire develops along its natural growth curve and HRR rises steadily. The uncontrolled fire (no intervention) continues to climb steeply until all available fuel is burning or flashover occurs.

**Fire suppression** (curve falling to zero) is where the discharged water actually extinguishes the fire, or knocks it back so severely that HRR falls continuously toward zero. Water reaches the burning fuel surfaces in sufficient quantity to cool them below ignition temperature and remove heat faster than combustion generates it. The defining feature is that the curve turns downward immediately after activation and keeps decreasing.

**Fire control** (curve flattening into a plateau) is less complete. The water does not extinguish the fire but limits its growth: enough is applied to pre-wet adjacent combustibles and prevent spread, so HRR stops rising and holds roughly steady until the original fuel is consumed. It does not run away, but it is not extinguished either.

**Essential distinction:** suppression = a sharply decreasing HRR (the fire is being extinguished); control = a steady plateaued HRR (growth and spread halted, but burning continues until fuel is exhausted). In practice suppression demands a higher water application density delivered directly onto the seat of the fire, whereas control can be achieved with a lower density protecting the surroundings.

**(b) Glass-bulb limitations and an alternative**
Fixed temperature activation only (can be slow in some fire-growth scenarios); can be painted over or damaged during maintenance; single temperature rating per bulb.

**Better alternative:** quartzoid bulb or fusible link systems, or electronic detection combined with solenoid-operated heads, for faster and more reliable activation.

answers.title: Water Mist / Hi-Fog Systems — Containment, Droplet Size, Activation
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to fixed fire fighting systems employing fresh water in a high fog or mist form, explain EACH of the following:

(a) how the fire is contained and extinguished; (4)

(b) the importance of particle size and flow rate; (4)

(c) state the means by which the system may be activated. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) How the fire is contained and extinguished.** Very fine water droplets (high surface-area-to-volume ratio) provide rapid cooling, oxygen displacement (steam expanding ~1,600–1,700 times), and radiant heat blocking. Contained by radiant screening and cooling of surroundings; extinguished by cooling the burning material and local oxygen displacement. Excellent for machinery spaces with minimal water damage compared to traditional sprinklers, and effective on oil fires.

**(b) Importance of particle (droplet) size and flow rate**
**Droplet size:** must be small enough to present a very large total surface area and remain suspended long enough to penetrate the fire zone, flash to steam, and produce the smothering/radiant-blocking effects. Not so fine that they lack momentum to penetrate the fire plume's thermal up-currents (would be carried away or evaporate too soon). Large droplets fall out quickly, give poor evaporation and oxygen displacement, and behave like ordinary water spray. Governed by nozzle design and operating pressure.
**Flow rate:** must deliver enough water to absorb the heat released and generate sufficient steam; too low a flow will not control the fire. Because fine droplets are used efficiently, the total quantity of water required is far less than a conventional sprinkler/deluge system — minimising secondary water damage and free-surface/stability risk, and allowing smaller pumps and pipework. Must be matched to the size of the protected space and design fire load.

**(c) Means of activation.** Automatic — via fire detectors (smoke, heat/rate-of-rise, or flame) wired to the fire control panel, which opens the section/deluge valve and starts the pump; or by frangible glass-bulb spray heads opening individually at their set temperature (wet-pipe arrangement). Manual — by a manually operated valve or push-button/release station, located locally and/or remotely at a continuously manned control position.

answers.title: Accidental CO2 Release — Contractor Maintenance, Line Testing
answers.question_as_set:
Accidents have occurred due to premature or accidental release of CO2 into the machinery spaces.

(a) State the safety procedures that the Chief Engineer Officer should adopt with respect to maintenance being carried out on the system by shore contractors. (3)

(b) Explain why the Chief Engineer Officer and ship's staff should still have to check on work carried out by shore contractors. (2)

(c) State how the liquid levels in the CO2 bottles may be checked in situ and how often this test should be carried out. (2)

(d) Explain why ship's general service air should not be used for blowing through and testing CO2 operating lines and suggest a suitable alternative. (3)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Safety procedures for shore contractor maintenance**
**Permit to work and isolation** — issue a permit; make the system safe before work begins by isolating the discharge: disconnect/isolate the master valve and cylinder pilot/operating lines, remove or lock off the firing/control heads, and ensure safety locking pins are fitted so no cylinder can discharge.
**Competence, briefing, supervision and access control** — confirm contractors are competent/certified and brief them and ship's staff; ensure a responsible officer supervises throughout, control access to the CO2 room and protected space, post warning notices, confirm CO2-room ventilation is running.
**Restore and account afterwards** — confirm the correct number of cylinders are connected, all pilot/operating lines correctly reconnected, the system recharged as required, and only then remove isolations and pins to return the system to the armed, ready condition. Record the work.

**(b) Why ship's staff must still check the work.** Ultimate responsibility for the safety of the ship and the operational readiness of this critical, statutory life-safety installation remains with the C/E and command, not the contractor. Contractors may be unfamiliar with the specific installation, may make errors, or may leave lines cross-connected, valves shut, or pins left in/out. Independent verification ensures nothing is overlooked — the people who must operate and live alongside the system are the ones who confirm it is safe and ready.

**(c) Checking liquid levels in situ, and frequency.** Checked without removing or weighing the cylinders using a radioactive (gamma-ray) or ultrasonic liquid-level indicator, passed up and down the outside of each cylinder; the signal changes at the liquid/gas interface, marking the level. (Traditional alternative: disconnect and weigh.) Carried out at least annually; any cylinder that has lost more than about 10% of its charge must be refilled or replaced.

**(d) Why not ship's service air, and a suitable alternative.** General service air contains moisture and oil. Moisture can condense and cause corrosion (and could freeze) in the small-bore pipework, while oil and dirt deposit in lines, pilot connections and small orifices/nozzles, partially or wholly blocking them — so in a real fire the pilot signal or CO2 itself fails to reach where needed.

**Suitable alternative:** dry, oil-free gas — typically nitrogen from a bottle (or dry CO2/specially cleaned dry oil-free compressed air) — inert, dry and clean, proving the lines clear without introducing moisture or oil.

answers.title: Safety Equipment Survey — Fire Safety Examinations
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer, describe the examinations that would be carried out during a safety equipment survey with regard to fire safety. (10)
answers.answer_text:
A Safety Equipment Survey confirms the fire-safety arrangements required by SOLAS are present, complete, in good condition and operational.

**Fire detection and alarm systems.** Detectors (smoke, heat, flame) tested by simulating activation, confirming correct zone indication and audible/visual alarms; fault-monitoring and power-supply changeover verified; manual call points checked.

**Fixed fire-extinguishing installations.** Charge of the medium confirmed (weighing or in-situ level indication for CO2); cylinders, pipework, distribution valves, nozzles, operating/pilot lines, control/release cabinets, alarms and time-delay devices examined; pre-discharge alarm, ventilation and fuel/quick-closing-valve shutdowns confirmed to operate; pipework/nozzles confirmed clear.

**Portable and semi-portable extinguishers.** Examined for correct type, location, number, accessibility and condition, with charges, seals, pressures and service dates checked.

**Fire main, pumps, hydrants, hoses and nozzles.** Main and emergency fire pumps run and shown to deliver required pressure and jets; hydrants, valves, hoses, couplings and nozzles examined; international shore connection confirmed aboard.

**Fireman's outfits and breathing apparatus.** Protective clothing, boots, gloves, helmet, axe, safety lamp, lifeline examined; SCBA cylinder pressures, means of recharging, spare charges and EEBDs checked.

**Structural fire protection, closures and ventilation stops.** Fire doors and self-closing/release arrangements; fire dampers and ventilation closing; remote stops for ventilation fans, fuel and oil pumps; quick-closing valves on oil tanks.

**Means of escape.** Escape routes confirmed clear, unobstructed and marked, with low-location lighting/escape signing and emergency lighting tested.

**Other fire-safety items.** Fire control plan(s) confirmed correct, up to date and displayed as required, including the copy in a weathertight container outside the deckhouse.

The objective is to verify not only that equipment exists in the required quantity and locations but that it is properly maintained, correctly serviced and dated, and will function on demand.

answers.title: Inspections and Tests for Satisfactory FFE Condition and Operation
answers.question_as_set:
Describe the inspections and tests that should be carried out to ensure satisfactory condition and operation of the ship's fire fighting equipment. (10) Fire safety & CO2 systems Management, surveys & reports Verification and known flags What was checked before this file was issued.

• Every sitting from July 2016 to July 2026 present in the source was located and its Section A questions extracted — 328 questions in total, with no gaps in the sequence.

• Printed part-marks were summed for every question and compared against the 10-mark total each question carries. Exceptions are listed below rather than adjusted.

• Four sittings (July 2018, October 2018, March 2019, October 2019) exist in the source only as scanned pages with no text layer. These were rasterised at 300 dpi, read by OCR, and then checked against the page images. Their mark totals reconciling to 10 is the evidence the reconstruction is faithful.

• October 2024, December 2024 and March 2025 are likewise scan-only in the source and were transcribed from the page images.

• The four most recent sittings (October 2025, December 2025, March 2026, July 2026) were transcribed from screenshots supplied by the user rather than from the SQA papers. In those screenshots the questions are numbered Q1/Q2/Q3; they have been renumbered here to the paper's Q1/Q2/Q3. As an independent check, every earlier sitting that the source application flagged as a repeat was matched back against this compilation and agreed word-for-word.

• Second-source check on the four screenshot-sourced sittings. A second, independently supplied set of screenshots was compared question by question against October 2025, December 2025, March 2026 and July 2026 as printed here. Thirty of those thirty-two questions agreed in wording and in every printed part-mark. March 2026 Q7 and Q8 lie outside the second set and still rest on the original single transcription. Open flags — verify against your own copy of the paper. October 2018, Section C, Q13. The printed part-marks read (3), (2) and (3), which sum to 8, not 10.
answers.answer_text:
These checks form part of the ship's planned maintenance system and the SOLAS periodic testing regime, carried out at weekly, monthly, quarterly and annual intervals, with everything recorded.

**Fire main, pumps, hydrants, hoses and nozzles.** Main and emergency fire pumps run regularly to confirm they prime readily and deliver required pressure; the emergency pump proved to start and run independently of the main machinery space. Hydrants and isolating valves operated; hoses examined for perished/split lining; couplings and nozzles checked.

**Fixed fire-extinguishing installations.** Cylinder contents verified periodically; pipework and nozzles confirmed clear; distribution/master valves examined and operated; release cabinet, controls, pre-discharge alarm and time delay tested; associated trips (ventilation shutdown, fuel quick-closing valves, pump stops) confirmed to operate.

**Fire detection and alarm system.** Detectors tested by simulated activation; manual call points operated in rotation; fault and power-failure monitoring checked; changeover to emergency/battery supply proved.

**Portable and semi-portable extinguishers.** Each examined for type, charge, seals/pins, pressure and service date; a proportion discharged and recharged on a rotational basis.

**Fireman's outfits, breathing apparatus and EEBDs.** Outfits examined for complete, serviceable equipment; SCBA cylinders checked for full pressure; low-pressure/whistle alarms tested; EEBDs confirmed in number, location and date.

**Closures, ventilation stops and escape routes.** Fire doors and dampers operated; remote stops for ventilation fans and pumps tested to confirm trip and reset; escape routes walked to confirm clear, marked and lit.

**Records and drills.** Regular fire drills test the equipment in use and the crew's ability to operate it.

**In summary,** the regime confirms three things for every item: present and complete in the required quantity; in good material condition; and operates correctly on demand — the operational test being most important, since equipment that exists but fails to function gives a false sense of security.

answers.title: Major Machinery-Space Fire — Remote Shutdowns and Boundary Control
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to a major fire in the machinery space:

(a) explain why EACH of the following equipment is shut down remotely, stating how it is achieved;

(i) settling and service tank outlet valves; (2)

(ii) fuel transfer and supply pumps; (2)

(iii) mechanical and natural ventilation; (2)

(b) explain how the fire is brought under control using the facilities outwith the affected machinery space. (4)
answers.answer_text:
The common principle is starving the fire of fuel and air from a position of safety outside the space, since in a major fire the machinery space may be untenable.

**(i) Settling and service (quick-closing) tank outlet valves.** Shut remotely to cut off the supply of fuel and oil, since these tanks hold large quantities of heated, readily combustible oil above the machinery. Achieved by quick-closing valves held open against a spring, tripped from a remote release point outside the space (wire/cable, hydraulic/pneumatic trip), releasing the holding mechanism so the spring slams the valve shut.

**(ii) Fuel transfer and supply (booster) pumps.** Shut down remotely so oil is no longer pumped, often under pressure, toward or within the fire. Achieved by remote emergency stops (trip push-buttons/switches) outside the space, cutting the electrical supply to the pump motors.

**(iii) Mechanical and natural ventilation.** Shut down to cut off the air (oxygen) supply and prevent inrush of air feeding combustion; essential before releasing a fixed gas/mist system since the space must be sealed. Achieved by remote stops for supply and exhaust fans, together with closing ventilation openings (flaps, fire dampers, skylights, funnel/engine-room vent closures) from outside.

**(b) Bringing the fire under control from outside the space.**
Evacuate, account for personnel, isolate sources — confirm everyone is clear, then operate remote trips: shut the quick-closing tank outlet valves, stop fuel transfer/supply and oil pumps.
Seal the space — stop ventilation fans and close all openings, dampers, skylights, doors and funnel flaps.
Release the fixed system — with the space confirmed evacuated and sealed and the pre-discharge alarm/time delay operated, release the fixed installation (CO2, water mist) from the cabinet outside the space; keep the space sealed to prevent re-ignition.
Boundary cooling and monitoring — cool the boundaries with water/hoses from adjacent compartments to limit heat transfer and prevent spread; monitor boundary temperature; re-enter only later, once cooled and confirmed safe, by a team in BA.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Major Machinery-Space Fire — Remote Shutdowns and Boundary Control
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Part (a) (why each item is shut down remotely) is well answered, but part (b) (fighting the fire from outside the space) is surprisingly weak -- many candidates just repeat part (a) and assume the fire self-extinguishes once starved of fuel/air/ventilation, without describing active boundary cooling. The two frequently-missed actions are starting the emergency generator and the emergency fire pump to supply that boundary cooling.

answers.title: Fixed CO2 Smothering — Maintenance, Safe Release, Re-Entry
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to fixed CO2 smothering systems for ships machinery spaces:

(a) State the safety procedure that the Chief Engineer Officer should adopt with respect to maintenance being carried out on the system by contractors whilst the vessel is in port. (3)

(b) State the procedure prior to the safe release of CO2 into the machinery space in the event of a fire. (4)

(c) Describe the factors that should be considered prior to re-entry of the machinery spaces after the release of CO2 gas. (3)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)** As per Q3 above (permit/isolation, competence/supervision/access control, restore and account afterwards).

**(b) Procedure prior to safe release of CO2**
Evacuate and account for all personnel — raise the alarm, evacuate, muster and head-count to confirm nobody remains inside; CO2 is an asphyxiant and this is the single most critical step.
Isolate fuel and oil sources — shut quick-closing valves on settling/service tanks, stop fuel transfer/supply and oil pumps.
Seal the space — stop all ventilation and close all openings, dampers, skylights, doors and funnel flaps.
Operate the release — at the cabinet outside the space, opening it operates the alarm and time delay; after confirming the space is clear and sealed, operate the master/distribution valve then the cylinder release control in sequence to discharge the required cylinders.

**(c) Factors prior to re-entry**
Fire fully extinguished and space cooled — allow sufficient time for the fire to be completely out and the space/boundaries to cool, monitoring boundary temperatures.
Atmosphere safe to breathe — ventilate/purge, test for oxygen content and toxic/flammable gases, confirm safe before unprotected entry; any entry before that is by a team in SCBA.
Controlled, equipped entry with backup — a properly equipped team in BA and protective clothing, with charged fire hoses ready, communications and a backup/standby team, opening up gradually with means to re-seal and re-flood if the fire revives.

answers.title: Hydrocarbon Tanks — Flammability Terms and Safe Atmosphere
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to tanks containing hydrocarbon liquids and vapours:

(a) define EACH of the following terms:

(i) explosive limits; (2)

(ii) vapour pressure; (2)

(iii) flash point. (2)

(b) explain how the atmosphere in cargo tanks containing varying percentages of flammable gas can be maintained in a safe condition at all times. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Explosive (flammable) limits.** The range of hydrocarbon-vapour-to-air concentrations within which the mixture will ignite and burn/explode if a source of ignition is present. Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) — minimum concentration below which the mixture is too lean to burn. Upper Explosive Limit (UEL) — maximum concentration above which the mixture is too rich to burn (insufficient oxygen). Only between these limits is the mixture flammable.

**(a)(ii) Vapour pressure.** The pressure exerted by the vapour given off by a liquid when liquid and vapour are in equilibrium in an enclosed space at a given temperature. A measure of volatility — high vapour pressure means the liquid evaporates readily. Vapour pressure increases with temperature.

**(a)(iii) Flash point.** The lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off sufficient vapour to form a flammable mixture with the air immediately above its surface, such that it will momentarily flash when a source of ignition is applied. Used to classify the fire hazard of petroleum products.

**(b) Maintaining a safe tank atmosphere at all times.** The atmosphere is kept safe by inert gas (IG) — keeping oxygen content too low to support combustion regardless of hydrocarbon vapour present (below about 11% no mixture is flammable; tanks are maintained with oxygen below 8% for a safety margin).
**Inert the tank** — supply inert gas to reduce oxygen below 8%, so the atmosphere cannot support combustion whatever the vapour concentration.
**Maintain a positive pressure** — keep a slight positive IG pressure at all times so air cannot leak in and raise oxygen.
**Manage operations under inert conditions** — during discharge, feed IG in to replace outgoing cargo; monitor oxygen and hydrocarbon content continuously.
**Avoid the flammable region during gas-freeing/aeration** — do not ventilate straight from inerted to air; first purge with inert gas to bring hydrocarbon content well down, so introducing air moves from too-lean-and-inerted to fresh air without entering the flammable range.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Hydrocarbon Tanks — Flammability Terms and Safe Atmosphere
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Very poorly answered -- most candidates show little grasp of basic hydrocarbon flammability terms (explosive limits, vapour pressure, flash point) or how a tank atmosphere with varying flammable-gas percentage is kept safe (inerting to below the lower or above the upper explosive limit, not simply 'ventilating').

answers.title: CO2 Bottled System — Overpressure Protection and Periodic Maintenance
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to fixed installations for machinery space fires:

(a) sketch a CO2 bottled system; (5)

(b) explain how the system sketched in part (a) is protected from overpressure; (2)

(c) describe the periodic maintenance required. (3)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw the release cabinet (actuating handle, alarm switch, CO2-release and open-valve controls), operating bottle and piston, master valve, relief valve, the CO2 bottle bank connected via a manifold, and distribution nozzles into the protected space.*

**(b) Protection from overpressure**
**On the distribution/manifold pipework — the relief valve.** CO2 stored as liquid under pressure expands greatly if temperature rises; the relief valve on the common manifold lifts at a set pressure and vents the excess safely to atmosphere outside the CO2 room, preventing the pipework from bursting.
**On the individual cylinders — the bursting disc.** Each cylinder has a frangible bursting disc in its valve; if overheated (e.g. a fire in the CO2 room), the disc ruptures at a predetermined pressure and releases that cylinder's contents in a controlled manner, preventing the cylinder from exploding.

**(c) Periodic maintenance required**
Cylinder contents check (annually) — weighing or in-situ liquid-level indication; any cylinder that has lost more than about 10% of charge must be refilled or replaced; cylinders pressure-tested at longer survey intervals (typically every 10 years).
Pipework, nozzles and valves — periodically blown through with dry, oil-free air or nitrogen to prove clear; master/distribution valves examined and operated.
Operating, control and alarm gear — operating (pilot) bottle, actuating handles, linkages and locking pins checked; release alarm and time delay tested.

answers.title: Newly Acquired Vessel — FFE Inspections on Taking Over
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer appointed to a newly acquired vessel, describe the inspections that should be carried out to ensure satisfactory condition and operation of the ship's fire fighting equipment. (10)
answers.answer_text:
On joining a newly acquired vessel, the aim is a thorough initial survey to establish the true condition of every item, familiarise the C/E and staff with the installation, and identify any defects or shortfalls inherited from the previous owner.

**Documentation and familiarisation first.** Begin with the fire control plan, equipment certificates and records — PMS history, service/test records, dates of last servicing of extinguishers and BA, last weighing/level-check of CO2 cylinders, and survey/certificate status.

**Fire main, pumps, hydrants, hoses and nozzles.** Run the main and emergency fire pumps, confirming each primes and delivers required pressure; prove the emergency pump starts independently of the main machinery space.

**Fixed fire-extinguishing installation.** Verify cylinder charge, examine cylinders, pipework, valves, pilot lines, nozzles, release cabinet, alarms and time delay; confirm associated trips operate.

**Fire detection and alarm system.** Test detectors by simulated activation; operate manual call points; check power-failure monitoring.

**Portable extinguishers, fireman's outfits, BA and EEBDs.** Examine every item for correct type, condition, charge and in-date service.

**Closures, ventilation stops and escape routes.** Operate fire doors, dampers and remote stops for ventilation/fuel pumps; walk escape routes to confirm clear, marked and lit.

**Establishing the baseline.** The emphasis on a newly acquired ship is to confirm each item exists in the required quantity, is in good material condition and actually operates on demand — recording findings as a baseline, raising defects, and holding an early fire drill to test equipment and crew familiarity.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Newly Acquired Vessel — FFE Inspections on Taking Over
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; treat as the standard FFE-survey inspection question (Q5/Q16 pattern) framed as a first-week takeover check, so structure the answer around verifying condition/testing/certification of each item rather than describing equipment in the abstract.

answers.title: Inert-Gas Smothering — Sequence of Events and Recovery to Proceed
answers.question_as_set: Following a serious machinery space fire, the engine room was abandoned and an inert gas smothering agent used to extinguish the fire. Explain the sequence of events which led to this course of action and the subsequent actions taken to enable the vessel to proceed on passage. (10)
answers.answer_text:
**The sequence of events leading to release of the smothering agent**
Detection and raising the alarm — the fire is detected; the alarm is raised, the bridge informed and the crew mustered.
First-aid fire-fighting attempt — duty engineers tackle the fire early with local appliances, aiming to extinguish before it develops.
Fire grows beyond local control — despite efforts the fire spreads (typically an oil fire fed by a leak onto a hot surface); the space becomes untenable and the decision is taken to evacuate and fight by total flooding.
Evacuate and account for all personnel — muster/account for all by head-count; the gas is an asphyxiant so positive confirmation is essential.
Isolate fuel and oil sources — trip quick-closing valves, stop fuel/oil pumps, shut down the main engine.
Seal the space — shut down ventilation and close all openings.
Release the smothering medium — with the space confirmed evacuated and sealed, release the fixed system from the cabinet outside the space.
Hold sealed and cool boundaries — keep the space sealed to prevent re-ignition; cool boundaries and monitor temperature.

**Subsequent actions to enable the vessel to proceed on passage**
Allow time, then assess — leave sealed for a prolonged period so the fire is out and boundaries cooled before opening up.
Ventilate, test atmosphere and re-enter safely — purge and test oxygen/toxic/flammable gas content; re-enter by a team in SCBA with backup ready.
Investigate, make safe and assess damage — identify and rectify the cause, examine fire/smoke damage, isolate damaged circuits, clean down residue.
Restore essential services — recharge fire-fighting systems, restore power, cooling, lubrication, fuel and control systems, carefully restart the main engine and essential auxiliaries.
Confirm seaworthiness and proceed — once propulsion and essential services are proven, brief the crew, record defects and proceed on passage (or arrange assistance/tow if damage is too great).

answers.title: CO2 for Hold Fires — Combined Detection/Extinguishment; Gas Quantity Estimate
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw a sample-extraction smoke detection system sharing pipework with the CO2 flooding system. Show a detection cabinet (in the control station/wheelhouse) with a continuously running suction fan and a detector chamber (photo-electric cell/light beam), a change-over valve, a CO2 bottle bank with master valve, and distribution/sampling pipes running to nozzles in each cargo hold.*

**(a)** A sample-extraction (smoke) detection system shares its pipework with the CO2 flooding system — one set of pipes serves both purposes.

**Operation — detection (normal).** The fan continuously draws small air samples from each hold through the sampling lines into the detector chamber, and the air is returned to the holds. If a fire starts, combustion products drawn up the line become visible/obscure the light beam, raising the alarm and indicating which hold's line shows smoke.

**Operation — extinguishing (on detection).** Identify and confirm the affected hold; raise the alarm. Stop the detection fan, close the hold's ventilation, seal the hold, confirm no personnel inside. Operate the change-over valve so the CO2 bank is connected to the distribution lines instead of the fan. Open the master valve and release the required number of cylinders; gas travels down the same pipework to the nozzle, floods the hold, displaces oxygen and smothers the fire. Keep the hold sealed until confirmed cool.

**(b) Estimating the quantity of gas**
1. Free-gas volume required: at least 30% of the gross volume of the largest cargo space: required volume = 0.30 × (gross volume of largest hold).
2. Convert volume to mass: using CO2 specific volume ≈ 0.56 m³/kg (density ≈ 1.79 kg/m³): mass = required free-gas volume ÷ 0.56.
3. Convert to cylinders: divide by the charge per standard cylinder (typically 45 kg), rounding up.

(For machinery spaces the larger 40% figure and a rapid-discharge time limit apply; for cargo holds it is the 30%-of-largest-hold basis, and the discharge need not be as rapid.)

answers.title: CO2 Hold-Fire System (from Supplied Sketch) — Description and Gas Estimate
answers.answer_text:
Same underlying content as Q14 above, worked from a supplied sketch showing a fan motor box and diverting valve, smoke detection cabinet in the wheelhouse, low-pressure suction lines, CO2 room with cylinders and distribution valves, high-pressure CO2 lines, and a combined smoke collector/discharge head in each hold.

The detection side uses low-pressure suction lines to the wheelhouse detection cabinet (fan plus diverting valve); the extinguishing side is fed by high-pressure CO2 lines from the CO2 room. The combined collector/discharge head in each hold serves both functions — low-pressure suction draws sample air up for detection, high-pressure CO2 is driven down the same route for extinguishing, with the changeover made at the diverting valve and the CO2-room distribution valves.

**Gas quantity estimate:** as per Q14 — 30% of the gross volume of the largest hold, converted to mass via CO2 specific volume (≈0.56 m³/kg), then divided by the cylinder charge (typically 45 kg) to give the number of cylinders required.

answers.title: Safety Equipment Survey — Report to Superintendent Engineer
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer, write a report to the Superintendent Engineer naming the items and describing the examinations that were carried out during a safety equipment survey with regard to fire safety. (10)
answers.answer_text:
Same content as Q4 above, framed as a formal report. The examiner tests both report format (which carries marks) and survey content.

**REPORT**
To: Superintendent Engineer, [Company Name]
From: Chief Engineer Officer, MV [Ship's Name]
Date: [Date]   Reference: [Ref No.]
Subject: Examinations Carried Out During Safety Equipment Survey — Fire Safety

Sir, I report that the periodic Safety Equipment Survey in respect of the ship's fire-safety arrangements has been attended and completed. The items examined were as follows: 1. Fire detection and alarm system. 2. Fixed fire-extinguishing installation. 3. Fire main, pumps, hydrants, hoses and nozzles. 4. Portable and semi-portable extinguishers. 5. Fireman's outfits and breathing apparatus. 6. Structural fire protection, closures and ventilation stops. 7. Means of escape and fire control plan. [Each followed by the same detail as Q4's answer.]

All equipment was found present in the required quantity and locations, in satisfactory material condition and operational on demand, with the exception of the following defects raised for rectification: [list defects, or state "nil"]. The findings have been recorded and the planned maintenance system updated accordingly.
I respectfully submit this report for your information and further instruction.
Yours faithfully, [Name], Chief Engineer Officer, MV [Ship's Name]

**Report technique:** open with one line stating the purpose, present items as a numbered list, and close with a summary finding plus a defects/"nil" line — that closing sentence separates a report from a plain list and picks up the format marks.

answers.title: Standing Orders — Prevention and Detection of Machinery-Space Fires
answers.question_as_set: The company, with which you are employed, requests that all Chief Engineer Officers prepare standing orders regarding the prevention and detection of fires in the machinery spaces. Compile such a list of recommendations to be submitted to central office. (10)
answers.answer_text:
**A. Prevention — control of oil and fuel.** All oil leaks traced and repaired without delay; hot surfaces kept properly lagged and oil-tight; high-pressure fuel injection lines sheathed/double-walled with leak-detection alarms operational; tank tops, savealls and bilges kept clean; tanks not overfilled, quick-closing valves maintained operational.

**B. Prevention — housekeeping and storage.** Machinery space kept clean and tidy; oily rags kept in covered, self-closing metal containers; flammable liquids and gas bottles stored properly and isolated when not in use; escape routes kept clear.

**C. Prevention — ignition sources.** A strict hot-work permit system enforced (checked area, fire watch, extinguisher, post-work inspection); no smoking except designated areas; electrical equipment maintained in good order.

**D. Prevention — machinery operation and maintenance.** Planned maintenance of boilers, purifiers, incinerators and exhausts to prevent overheating/soot fires/oil leaks; crankcase oil-mist detectors and temperature alarms maintained and proven; watchkeepers to maintain vigilant regular rounds.

**E. Detection.** The fixed fire-detection system maintained, unobstructed and tested at PMS intervals; alarms annunciate at the engine control room and bridge; in UMS spaces the dead-man alarm and extension alarms maintained operational.

**F. General.** Regular fire drills and crew familiarisation held; all defects reported and rectified promptly. These standing orders to be displayed in the engine control room and brought to the attention of all engineer officers and ratings.

**Exam technique:** the two points most often specifically rewarded are the hot-work permit system and keeping oil off hot surfaces (lagging + shielding).

answers.title: Fresh-Water Hi-Fog — Sketch, Activation, Suitable Location
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to fresh water HI-FOG fire fighting systems:

(a) sketch such a system; (6)

(b) state how the system in part (a) is activated; (2)

(c) state, with a reason, a suitable location for the above system. (2)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw a water tank with a level switch, a solenoid-valve make-up connection from the fresh-water supply (with fire main back-up), main and standby pumps started from a pump starter box (operated by the fire detection system), discharging to sprinkler/mist heads.*

**(b) How the system is activated.** Automatic, initiated by the fire detection system: when detectors sense a fire, the fire detection system signals the pump starter box, which starts the main pump (with the standby pump cutting in automatically on a pressure drop or main-pump failure). The pumps draw fresh water from the tank and deliver it at high pressure to the sprinkler/mist heads. The tank level is monitored by a level switch and automatically replenished through a solenoid valve (with the fire main as back-up). The system may also be started manually.

**(c) Suitable location, with reason.** A machinery space/engine room (around the main engine, purifiers, boiler front and other oil-fuel hazards). Reason: these spaces present a high risk of oil fires on hot surfaces, where the water-mist system is particularly effective — it cools rapidly, the steam produced smothers the fire by displacing oxygen, and it uses only a small quantity of fresh water, minimising secondary water/salt damage and avoiding free-surface/stability problems.

answers.title: Plate vs Tubular Heat Exchangers — Why Plate Is Usually Superior
answers.question_as_set: With reference to the design, construction and materials used in the manufacture of plate type heat exchangers, explain why, in most cases, they are superior to tubular type heat exchangers. (10)
answers.answer_text:
**Design.** A plate heat exchanger is built from a stack of thin, pressed metal plates clamped together in a frame. Hot and cold fluids flow through alternate channels between adjacent plates in true counterflow, giving a very close temperature approach (~1°C vs ~5°C for tubular) — so seawater can be used effectively even when only slightly cooler than the medium being cooled. The plates are pressed with a corrugated chevron (herringbone) pattern; adjacent plates' corrugations cross over, inducing high turbulence at low velocity, raising the heat transfer coefficient and keeping surfaces self-cleaning.

**Construction.** The plates are very thin (~0.5–0.6mm), so conductive resistance is low and a large area is packed into a small volume — compact and light. The stack is clamped by tie bolts with gaskets sealing each channel, making the unit easy to open, clean mechanically and reassemble; capacity can be altered by adding or removing plates.

**Materials.** Plates are usually stainless steel (304/316) for general duty, or titanium where seawater is handled, since titanium resists chloride attack and erosion; because the plates are so thin, titanium remains economically viable. Gaskets are an elastomer (nitrile, EPDM or Viton).

**Why superior in most cases.** Together these give a heat transfer coefficient typically 3–5 times that of a shell-and-tube unit — a smaller, lighter cooler, closer temperature approach, lower fluid hold-up, easier maintenance, reduced fouling, flexible re-rating and economic use of titanium.

**Why "in most cases" and not always:** the gaskets limit the plate exchanger to moderate temperatures (~150–180°C) and pressures (~25 bar). Where high temperature, high pressure or steam is involved (e.g. feed-water heaters), the tubular type with its robust gasket-free pressure boundary remains the better choice.

answers.title: Heat Exchanger Flow Types — Parallel, Counter, Mixed
answers.question_as_set:
Describe EACH of the following heat exchanger types, stating a suitable application for EACH type:

(a) parallel flow; (3)

(b) contra flow; (3)

(c) mixed flow. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Parallel flow.** Both fluids enter at the same end and flow in the same direction. The temperature difference is large at the inlet and small at the outlet, giving a lower mean temperature difference — the least efficient arrangement, but produces rapid initial heat transfer and a more uniform wall temperature, limiting thermal stress. *Application:* bringing a fluid quickly to a moderate temperature without overheating, e.g. heating a viscous fluid where a high local wall temperature must be avoided.

**(b) Counter-flow.** The fluids enter at opposite ends and flow in opposite directions. The temperature difference is spread more evenly, giving the highest mean temperature difference and greatest efficiency — the cold outlet can approach the hot inlet temperature. *Application:* central cooling and heat recovery, e.g. jacket water and lube oil coolers, feed-water heaters.

**(c) Mixed (cross) flow.** The fluids flow at an angle to each other (typically ~90°), combining features of parallel and counter-flow; in a shell-and-tube unit one fluid passes through the tubes while the other is directed back and forth across the bundle by baffles. Efficiency lies between parallel and counter-flow; construction is compact and mechanically robust, with baffles supporting the tubes and promoting turbulence. *Application:* the common baffled, multi-pass shell-and-tube cooler, e.g. seawater-cooled jacket water or charge-air coolers.

*Sketch instructions: draw Temperature (vertical) vs Length (horizontal) profiles. Parallel flow: two curves starting far apart, converging but never crossing. Counter-flow: two curves running roughly parallel, giving near-uniform ΔT and a close approach.*

answers.title: Multi-Tubular Exchangers — Features That Aid Performance
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to multi-tubular heat exchangers, explain how EACH of the following contribute to satisfactory performance:

(a) tube wall thickness; (2)

(b) dense population of tubes in the tube plate; (2)

(c) tube materials selection; (2)

(d) coolant flow rates; (2)

(e) unimpeded passage of coolant at entry and exit from the tubes. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Tube wall thickness.** The wall is the conductive barrier, so thinner gives lower thermal resistance and better heat transfer, but must still withstand working pressure and give a corrosion/erosion allowance — as thin as strength and durability permit.

**(b) Dense population of tubes.** Packs the maximum heat transfer surface area within a given shell diameter, transferring more heat in a compact unit; keeps tube velocity high enough for good turbulence.

**(c) Tube materials selection.** Must combine good thermal conductivity with corrosion/erosion resistance, particularly from seawater; aluminium-brass or cupro-nickel resist chloride attack and impingement while conducting well.

**(d) Coolant flow rates.** A sufficiently high flow rate maintains turbulent flow, raising the coefficient and keeping surfaces self-cleaning, but must not be so high as to erode the tubes.

**(e) Unimpeded passage at entry and exit.** Smooth, unobstructed entry/exit gives even distribution across all tubes, minimises pressure loss, and avoids local turbulence/eddies at tube ends that would cause impingement attack and fouling dead spots.

answers.title: Plate-Type Cooler — Sketch, Design Reasons, Advantages
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to plate type heat exchangers:

(a) sketch a cross sectional view showing the plate design pattern and the directions of hot and cold fluid flow; (4)

(b) state TWO reasons for the plate design patterns; (2)

(c) state, with reasons, FOUR advantages of a plate cooler compared to shell and tube type. (4)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw a plate cross-section with four corner ports (hot in, hot out, cold in, cold out), chevron/herringbone corrugations, gasket around the edge shown dashed, and opposing hot/cold flow arrows (counterflow). Adjacent channels carry the opposite fluid.*

**(b) Two reasons for the chevron pattern.** (1) The corrugations of adjacent plates cross at many points, inducing high turbulence at low velocity, raising the coefficient and keeping surfaces self-cleaning. (2) The pattern of contact points gives the thin plates mechanical support against fluid pressure, stiffening the assembly so very thin plates can be used without distortion.

**(c) Four advantages over shell-and-tube**
Higher heat transfer/more compact — a coefficient several times that of a tubular unit, so a smaller, lighter cooler does the same duty.
Closer temperature approach — true counterflow lets the cold outlet approach within ~1°C of the hot inlet (vs ~5°C tubular).
Easier maintenance — the unit unbolts so plates can be slid apart, cleaned mechanically and reassembled, far quicker than withdrawing a tube bundle.
Flexible capacity — plates can be added or removed to re-rate the cooler, which a fixed tube bundle cannot offer.

answers.title: Design Aspects That Promote Heat Transfer
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to heat exchangers, describe how EACH of the following design aspects promote heat transfer:

(a) material selection; (5)

(b) flow patterns; (3)

(c) extended surface areas. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Material selection.** Balances thermal conductivity (copper alloys, aluminium, good steels give low resistance), corrosion/erosion resistance (especially seawater side — aluminium-brass, cupro-nickel or titanium keep the surface clean and intact), strength to allow a thin wall, and compatibility with the fluids without setting up galvanic action.

**(b) Flow patterns.** Counterflow spreads the temperature difference evenly, giving the highest mean ΔT and closest approach. Flow is also arranged to promote turbulence rather than laminar flow — breaking up the slow boundary layer at the surface (the main resistance to transfer). Baffles in shell-and-tube units, or corrugations in plate units, create this turbulence and help keep surfaces clean.

**(c) Extended surface areas.** Heat transferred is proportional to surface area, so fins greatly increase the effective area for a given size — used particularly on the side handling a gas or poorly-conducting fluid where the coefficient is low (e.g. the air side of a charge-air cooler or radiator), compensating for the poor coefficient with extra area.

answers.title: Material Selection for a Seawater-Cooled Multi-Tubular Cooler
answers.question_as_set: Discuss the factors that lead to the selection of materials for use in a sea water cooled, multi-tublar heat exchanger. (10)
answers.answer_text:
**The controlling problem: seawater.** An electrolyte rich in chlorides, carrying dissolved oxygen, silt and marine organisms at velocity. Materials must survive this for years while transferring heat efficiently and staying leak-tight.

**The governing factors.** Thermal conductivity (copper alloys give good transfer); corrosion resistance (rules out plain carbon steel for wetted surfaces); erosion/impingement resistance (tolerate design velocity without stripping the protective film); resistance to biofouling (copper alloys are mildly toxic to marine growth); mechanical strength; galvanic compatibility (dissimilar metals form a cell — sacrificial anodes fitted); cost and availability (titanium almost ideal but expensive).

**How these decide each component.** Tubes — aluminium-brass at moderate velocities, cupro-nickel (90/10 or 70/30) where higher velocity/corrosion resistance is needed, titanium for severe duty. Tube plates — commonly naval brass or similar copper alloy, galvanically close to the tubes. Shell & water boxes — coated or rubber-lined steel/cast iron, or suitable bronze, fitted with sacrificial anodes.

**Conclusion:** no single material satisfies every requirement, so selection balances conductivity, corrosion/erosion resistance, antifouling, strength, galvanic compatibility and cost.

answers.title: Modes of Heat Transfer; Promoting vs Retarding Transfer
answers.question_as_set:
(a) State THREE modes of heat transfer. (1)

(b) Describe how the design requirements of EACH of the following are met, detailing the materials used to promote or retard heat transfer:

(i) plate cooler in central cooling system; (3)

(ii) meat room in domestic provisions space; (3)

(iii) auxiliary steam system pipelines. (3)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)** Conduction, convection and radiation.

**(b)(i) Plate cooler in a central cooling system — promote transfer.** Many very thin plates (~0.5mm) for low resistance and large area, a chevron corrugation pattern creating turbulence, and counterflow for the closest approach. Plate material chosen for conductivity plus seawater corrosion resistance — stainless steel general, titanium for seawater.

**(b)(ii) Meat room — retard transfer.** Thick insulation of low conductivity (closed-cell polyurethane foam or cork), protected by a vapour-tight barrier so moisture cannot penetrate and condense. Inner lining is smooth, impervious and hygienic (galvanised/stainless steel or GRP), with insulated, well-sealed doors.

**(b)(iii) Auxiliary steam pipelines — retard heat loss.** Carbon steel (or alloy steel for higher temperatures) for the pressure boundary, lagged with low-conductivity insulation (mineral wool, glass fibre or calcium silicate), finished with protective cladding to keep the lagging dry (wet lagging conducts heat and accelerates corrosion).

answers.title: Shipboard Fresh Water Production — Evaporators & Reverse Osmosis
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to the on board production of fresh water for domestic purposes:

(a) explain the principles of operation of EACH of the following:

(i) low heat source evaporator; (2)

(ii) flash evaporator; (2)

(iii) reverse osmosis. (4)

(b) state the constraints placed on the installation and use of systems for shipboard production of fresh water. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Low heat-source evaporator.** Boils seawater at low temperature (~40–60°C) by holding the chamber under a vacuum maintained by an air/brine ejector; lowering the pressure lowers the boiling point so low-grade heat (engine jacket water) is hot enough to boil the feed. Vapour passes through a demister and is condensed into distillate.

**(a)(ii) Flash evaporator.** Feed is heated under pressure, then admitted to a chamber at lower pressure; because the water enters above the boiling point for that pressure, part of it "flashes" instantly to vapour without boiling on a heating surface. With no boiling on a hot surface, scale is greatly reduced.

**(a)(iii) Reverse osmosis.** Seawater is pumped against a semi-permeable membrane at a pressure above its osmotic pressure (~55–70 bar), forcing pure water through while dissolved salts are held back — giving fresh permeate and a concentrated brine reject. Needs no heat, only the high-pressure pump.

**(b) Constraints.** Evaporators must not run within a stated distance of the coast or in harbours, estuaries or polluted/shallow water. Distillate for drinking must be treated (hardened/mineralised and sterilised) since pure distilled water is flat, slightly acidic and aggressive.

answers.title: Domestic Water Treatment — Silver-Ion Sterilisation
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to the treatment of domestic water for potable use:

(a) describe the principle of operation of a steriliser that uses silver ions; (4)

(b) state the advantages of silver ion sterilisation over other methods; (2)

(c) state the inspections and maintenance that should be carried out on EACH of the following:

(i) fresh water tanks; (2)

(ii) calorifiers. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Principle.** Silver ions are oligodynamic — toxic to bacteria even in tiny concentrations. Water passes through a cell containing silver electrodes across which a small direct current is applied; the current makes the silver anode release silver ions by electrolysis, the dosing rate controlled by varying current in proportion to flow. The ions interfere with bacterial cell function and reproduction, killing them and preventing regrowth, giving a lasting residual effect.

**(b) Advantages over other methods.** Provides a lasting residual effect, protecting against re-contamination throughout storage and distribution (which UV does not); leaves no taste, odour or colour (unlike chlorination), and is harmless at the concentrations used.

**(c)(i) Fresh water tanks.** Inspect internally for cleanliness, coating condition and corrosion; drain, clean, recoat, refill and chlorinate before service. Ensure correct isolation from other systems and screened vents.

**(c)(ii) Calorifiers.** Inspect internally for scale, sludge and corrosion; examine the heating coil and sacrificial anode, renewing if wasted; check thermostat and relief valve, confirm water temperature discourages bacterial growth (e.g. Legionella).

answers.title: Harmful Bacteria in Water — Constraints, Maintenance, Sterilising
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to bacteria harmful to humans in drinking and washing water:

(a) state the constraints placed on the installation and use of systems for shipboard production of fresh water; (3)

(b) state the maintenance and treatment recommended for fresh water tanks; (3)

(c) describe how the entire fresh water system can be made free from bacteria; (3)

(d) state an acceptable residual value in the fresh water tanks to ensure the correct concentration of treatment in the system. (1)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Constraints.** Evaporators must not run within a defined distance of land or in harbours, estuaries, canals or shallow/polluted water. The system must have no cross-connection with seawater, sanitary, bilge or other non-potable systems. The distillate must be hardened/mineralised, sterilised and brought to potable standard.

**(b) Tank maintenance and treatment.** Inspect internally for cleanliness, corrosion and coating condition, cleaning and recoating as needed. Ensure tanks do not share boundaries with oil/sewage tanks. After entry, cleaning or repair, disinfect by super-chlorination and flush thoroughly before service.

**(c) Making the whole system free from bacteria.** Super-chlorinate the entire system — tanks, pipework, calorifiers and outlets — at a high concentration (~50 ppm), circulated through every tap and outlet so dead legs are exposed. Leave to stand for several hours, then drain and flush with fresh water until chlorine falls to the normal residual.

**(d) Acceptable residual.** A free chlorine residual of about 0.2 ppm in the tanks (with silver-ion dosing, of the order of 0.1 ppm silver).
