answers.title: Flash Evaporator — Sketch, Principle, Regulations
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a single stage flash evaporator, labelling the component parts and showing the directions of flow. (5)

(b) Explain the term flash evaporation. (2)

(c) State the regulations governing the operation of an evaporator if the distilled water is intended for human consumption. (3)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw the feed pump and feed heater feeding a flash chamber held under vacuum. Show vapour rising through a demister to a seawater-cooled condenser, with the distillate drawn off by a distillate pump and brine drawn off the bottom by a brine pump (overboard). Include the air ejector maintaining the vacuum.*

**(b) Flash evaporation.** Heated water entering a chamber held at a lower pressure suddenly "flashes" — part of it turns instantly into vapour without boiling on a heating surface. Because the chamber pressure corresponds to a saturation temperature below the feed temperature, the water is momentarily above its boiling point for that pressure, so the excess heat vaporises part of it immediately on entry. With no boiling on a hot surface, scale is greatly reduced.

**(c) Regulations for human consumption.** The evaporator must not run within a stated distance of the coast (commonly ~20 nautical miles) or in harbours, estuaries, canals or polluted/shallow water. The distillate, being pure, flat and slightly aggressive, must be treated before drinking — passed through a hardening/mineralising filter and sterilised (chlorination, silver-ion or UV), meeting the potable standard with a maintained residual disinfectant.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Flash Evaporator — Sketch, Principle, Regulations
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: A new-to-recent-diets question: part (a) catches candidates sketching a boiling-process (heated) evaporator instead of a FLASH evaporator, and part (b) shows very few candidates actually understand flash evaporation (rapid vaporisation of superheated liquid when pressure is suddenly reduced, rather than by adding more heat).

answers.title: Osmosis & Reverse Osmosis for Fresh Water
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain the principles of osmosis and reverse osmosis. (4)

(b) Describe how reverse osmosis is used for the production of fresh water on board ship. (4)

(c) State the limitation of the quality of the permeate in a single pass reverse osmosis system, describing how the quality of the permeate could be improved. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Osmosis and reverse osmosis.** Osmosis is the natural movement of water through a semi-permeable membrane from a weak (or pure) solution to a stronger solution until concentrations equalise; the pressure needed to just stop this flow is the osmotic pressure. Reverse osmosis reverses it: applying a pressure greater than the osmotic pressure forces water the other way, leaving the salts behind.

**(b) Reverse osmosis onboard.** Seawater is pre-treated (coarse/fine filters, sometimes chemical dosing) to protect the membranes. A high-pressure pump raises the feed above the osmotic pressure (~55–70 bar) and delivers it to the membrane modules (commonly spiral-wound). Permeate passes through and is collected as fresh water; salts leave as concentrated brine, discharged overboard. The plant needs only electrical power, so can run independently of the main engines.

**(c) Single-pass limitation and improvement.** The membranes do not reject 100% of dissolved salts — a small proportion passes into the permeate, so a single-pass product may not meet the lowest required salt content. Improved by a second pass (two-pass RO), treating the already-low-salinity permeate again to remove most remaining salts.

answers.title: Engine Room Fresh Water Central Cooling System
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch an engine room fresh water central cooling system, indicating the water temperatures at salient points on the system. (6)

(b) State, with reasons, FOUR advantages of the system sketched in part (a) compared to one which is totally sea water cooled. (4)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw three circuits. The seawater circuit runs from sea suction, through the SW pump, to the central coolers, then overboard (~32°C in, ~43°C out). The LT fresh water circuit runs from the central coolers (~36°C) through the LT pump to LT services (L.O., charge air, generator sets) and the jacket water cooler, returning at ~44°C. The HT fresh water circuit runs from the main engine jacket (~80°C out) through the HT pump and jacket water cooler, back to the engine at ~71°C, with an expansion tank on the HT circuit.*

**(b) Four advantages over a fully seawater-cooled system**
Greatly reduced corrosion/erosion — only the small seawater circuit up to the central coolers sees seawater; the rest of the engine room now carries treated fresh water.
Lower material cost — only the central coolers and short seawater pipework need expensive corrosion-resistant materials.
Reduced fouling/stable cooling — fresh water deposits little scale or growth, so surfaces stay clean with far less cleaning.
Less maintenance/higher reliability — fewer seawater-wetted components to clean and renew, and the closed circuit can be chemically treated.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Engine Room Fresh Water Central Cooling System
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Part (a) sketch quality was good where candidates drew genuine central cooling system layouts with temperatures marked at salient points; part (b) is the mark-loser -- 'state with reasons four advantages' needs an actual reason attached to each advantage (e.g. 'less corrosion because fresh water in the closed circuit needs no continuous seawater contact with the block'), not brief unsupported claims like 'less corrosion.'

answers.title: Vacuum Sewage System — Description, Advantages, Stagnation
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe a vacuum sewage system. (5)

(b) List the advantages of the system described in part (a). (4)

(c) State why untreated sewage should not be allowed to stagnate. (1)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Description.** A vacuum sewage (collection) system uses differential pressure rather than gravity or water volume to transport sewage and grey water from sanitary fittings to a central collection tank. The system maintains a partial vacuum (typically ~0.4–0.5 bar absolute) in a vacuum manifold/collecting main by means of vacuum pumps (commonly liquid-ring type). Each toilet is connected to the manifold through an interface valve; when flushed, the valve opens briefly and the pressure differential accelerates sewage and a slug of air at high velocity into the manifold, using only around 1 litre of water. Sewage collects in the vacuum tank; a discharge/sludge pump delivers it to the treatment plant, holding tank, or overboard per MARPOL Annex IV.

**(b) Advantages**
Low water consumption — ~1 L per flush vs several litres for gravity systems.
Pipework flexibility and space saving — small-bore pipes can run in any direction since flow doesn't depend on gravity gradients.
Reduced odour and improved hygiene — leaks draw air inward rather than letting sewage/gas escape.
Reduced blockage and self-cleaning action — high transport velocity scours the lines.

**(c) Why untreated sewage should not stagnate.** Stagnant sewage undergoes anaerobic decomposition, producing toxic hydrogen sulphide and flammable methane — a poisoning, asphyxiation and explosion hazard, plus foul odour, corrosion and health/bacterial risk.

answers.title: Biological Sewage Treatment Plant — Operation with Sketch
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set: (a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the operation of a biological sewage treatment plant. (10)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw a tank divided into three chambers: aeration chamber (with air diffusers at the bottom), clarification/settling chamber (with sludge return line), and chlorination/disinfection chamber. Show sewage inlet, screen, air supply from a compressor, surface scum return, and final discharge after chlorination.*

It works as a continuous-flow unit treating sewage by encouraging aerobic bacteria to digest organic matter, meeting MARPOL Annex IV and MEPC.227(64) standards.

**1. Screening and inlet.** Raw sewage enters and passes through a screen/comminutor, removing or breaking down large solids and rags.

**2. Aeration chamber.** Air diffusers at the bottom deliver a cloud of fine bubbles that supply dissolved oxygen to aerobic bacteria and keep the activated sludge ("floc") in agitation and intimate contact with the sewage. The bacteria oxidise organic matter into carbon dioxide, water and mineral salts. A retention time of 24 hours or more allows most of the BOD to be broken down.

**3. Clarification chamber.** Solids settle in this quiescent zone; clear water overflows to discharge, and some settled sludge is returned to the aeration chamber to maintain the bacterial population.

**4. Chlorination chamber.** Disinfects the clarified effluent to destroy harmful bacteria before discharge overboard.

answers.title: Biological Sewage — Anaerobic Conditions, Hazards, BOD
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe the principle of operation of a biological sewage treatment plant. (4)

(b) Explain how anaerobic conditions can occur within a sewage treatment plant, stating the hazards that may be encountered. (4)

(c) Explain the meaning and significance of the term biological oxygen demand. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)** As per Q4's principle below.

**(b) Anaerobic conditions and hazards.** If air supply fails or is insufficient (compressor failure, blocked diffusers) or the plant is overloaded, dissolved oxygen is depleted faster than it can be replaced, and the sludge turns septic; anaerobic (putrefactive) decomposition takes over. Hazards: toxic gas — hydrogen sulphide (H2S), poisonous and able to cause unconsciousness or death, and which dulls the sense of smell, removing the warning of its presence; flammable/explosive gas — methane accumulation creates fire/explosion risk; oxygen deficiency — an enclosed-space asphyxiation hazard; foul odour, corrosion of tank/pipework, and failure to meet the discharge standard.

**(c) Biological (Biochemical) Oxygen Demand.** BOD is the amount of dissolved oxygen (mg/L) consumed by aerobic bacteria breaking down organic matter in a sample over a set period and temperature (standard test: 5 days at 20°C, BOD5). A high BOD means a large amount of organic matter that will draw down oxygen in the receiving water, harming marine life; it is a key parameter limited under MARPOL Annex IV/MEPC.227(64), used to judge whether treated effluent is fit for discharge.

answers.title: Biological Sewage — Principle, Operational Factors, Bypass, BOD
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to biological sewage systems:

(a) describe the principle of operation of a biological sewage treatment plant; (4)

(b) state TWO operational factors that may adversely affect the operation of the plant and how the effects would be indicated; (2)

(c) explain why, on a long sea passage, it is inadvisable to bypass the unit. (2)

(d) explain the meaning and significance of the term biological oxygen demand. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Principle of operation.** Works on the aerobic activated-sludge principle, using a colony of aerobic bacteria to digest organic matter. After screening, sewage enters an aeration chamber where air is supplied through diffusers, providing dissolved oxygen and keeping the activated sludge in suspension and intimate contact with the effluent. Bacteria oxidise organic matter into carbon dioxide, water and mineral salts. The mixture passes to a settling/clarification chamber where sludge is recirculated to aeration, leaving clear effluent chlorinated before discharge.

**(b) Two operational factors and indication.** Loss/insufficiency of air supply (compressor failure, fouled diffusers) — indicated by reduced bubbling, a drop in compressor pressure, and a foul (rotten-egg) smell as the sludge turns septic. Hydraulic/organic overloading or chemical poisoning (detergents/excess chlorine killing the colony) — indicated by poor, cloudy effluent, sludge carry-over and a failed BOD/faecal-coliform result.

**(c) Why bypassing is inadvisable on a long passage.** The plant relies on a living bacterial colony that must be continuously fed and aerated. If bypassed for a long period, the bacteria starve, the sludge turns septic and the colony dies off — the plant then requires complete re-seeding and re-establishment, a slow process during which it cannot meet its discharge standard. Bypassed raw sewage also stagnates, producing toxic H2S and methane.

**(d)** As per Q3 above.

occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Generally good answers -- no strong recurring trap noted, though the bypass-on-long-passage reasoning (part c) and BOD significance (part d) are the parts most worth double-checking are genuinely explained rather than just stated.

answers.title: Membrane Bioreactor (MBR) Sewage Treatment Plant
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set: Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a Membrane Bioreactor type sewage treatment plant. (10)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw a two-stage aerated bioreactor system feeding into a membrane filtration module. Show a screen/filter press at the inlet, a first-stage bioreactor (with blower/diffusers), a transfer pump through an interstage filter to a second-stage bioreactor, a cross-flow pump drawing mixed liquor across the membrane module, a permeate tank/pump, and a turbidity meter monitoring the permeate before discharge.*

An MBR combines the conventional aerobic activated-sludge process with membrane ultra-/micro-filtration in place of gravity settling, producing a very high-quality, clear effluent (permeate) that comfortably exceeds MARPOL Annex IV/MEPC.227(64) standards.

**Operation.** Both black and grey water pass through a filter press/screen removing solids. The screened sewage enters the first-stage bioreactor (aerated by a blower) where aerobic bacteria begin digesting organic matter. Mixed liquor moves through an interstage filter to the second-stage bioreactor for further digestion. The cross-flow pump draws mixed liquor across the membrane surface at high velocity, continuously scouring it to limit fouling; the membrane physically separates clean permeate from the retained activated sludge (returned to the second-stage reactor). The permeate flows to a permeate tank, monitored by a turbidity meter, and is discharged overboard — often without chlorination since the membrane itself removes bacteria.

**Advantages over a conventional plant:** smaller footprint, much better and more consistent effluent quality, handles variable loads well, usually no chlorination required.

answers.title: Vibration in Main Propulsion Transmission Systems
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set:
(a) State,with reasons, FOUR causes of vibration in main propulsion transmission systems. (8)

(b) State the effects of vibration if allowed to continue without any intervention. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Four causes of vibration**
1. Mass imbalance of rotating components — manufacturing tolerance, uneven wear or damaged/cavitation-pitted propeller blades generate a rotating centrifugal force, producing a once-per-revolution vibration.
2. Misalignment of the shafting — poor installation, bearing wear or hull flexing forces the shaft to run bent/offset, imposing cyclic bending stresses and vibration often at twice shaft speed.
3. Torsional vibration from the engine's cyclic torque — each cylinder firing produces a fluctuating torque; when an exciting harmonic coincides with a natural torsional frequency, resonance occurs (hence a barred speed range).
4. Propeller-excited (blade-passing) vibration — each blade passing through the non-uniform wake field produces a fluctuating thrust at blade-passing frequency, aggravated by worn blades or cavitation.

**(b) Effects of vibration if allowed to continue.** Fatigue cracking and failure of shafting, couplings, gearing and holding-down bolts due to repeated cyclic stressing; accelerated wear and damage to bearings, gears and seals, loosening of fastenings, fretting, noise and discomfort, and ultimately loss of alignment leading to breakdown of the propulsion system.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Vibration in Main Propulsion Transmission Systems
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; the four causes of vibration typically drawn on are misalignment, unbalance, worn couplings/bearings, and torsional/critical-speed effects -- each needs a stated reason, not just a name, to pick up the 8 marks in part (a).

answers.title: Standing Orders — Gas Cutting and Gas Welding Equipment
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer, prepare standing orders for working with gas cutting and gas welding equipment, including the storage of spare bottles. (10)
answers.answer_text:
These orders are to be read, understood and complied with by all personnel before any gas cutting or welding work is undertaken on board.

**Authorisation and preparation.** No gas cutting or welding without a valid Hot Work Permit signed by the Chief Engineer (and Master where required), defining location, duration, precautions and the responsible person. Area to be checked gas-free, combustibles removed or shielded, and a fire watch with an extinguisher posted throughout and for a period after work.

**Equipment condition and use.** Cylinders secured upright, valves and regulators checked for leaks (soap solution, never a flame), flashback arresters fitted at both the regulator and torch ends, hoses in good condition and colour-coded correctly, and non-return valves maintained.

**Storage of spare bottles.** Stored in a dedicated, well-ventilated store, oxygen and acetylene/fuel gas cylinders kept separated, secured upright against falling, protected from heat/direct sunlight, with valve caps fitted when not in use and empty cylinders marked and segregated from full ones. A suitable fire extinguisher to be available at the store entrance.

**Personal protective equipment.** Correctly shaded welding goggles/face shield, leather gauntlets and apron, flame-retardant boiler suit and boots — specified by name and reason (radiation, spatter, burns), not a generic "use correct PPE."

These standing orders to be displayed and brought to the attention of all engineer officers and ratings.

answers.title: Familiarisation Training — Emergency Duties (New Engine Room Member)
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set:
(a) As a Chief Engineer Officer, compile a list of items included in familiarisation training for a new engine room department member with regards to emergency duties. (6)

(b) State the paperwork associated with part (a). (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Items to include**
The person's own muster station, lifeboat/liferaft station and specific emergency duties as shown on the muster list, together with the emergency alarm signals and what action each requires.
Escape routes from machinery spaces and the location/operation of emergency escape openings and EEBDs along them.
Location and operation of firefighting appliances — portable extinguishers, hoses, the fixed fire-extinguishing system, its release controls and the alarm/evacuation procedure before release.
Location and operation of engine-room emergency controls and remote shutdowns — fuel quick-closing valves, ventilation fan stops, oil transfer pump stops.
Emergency systems and equipment — emergency generator/switchboard, emergency fire pump, emergency air compressor, emergency steering gear and emergency lighting.
Location and use of personal and emergency safety equipment — lifejackets, immersion suits, BA sets, resuscitation equipment, bilge/dewatering arrangements, enclosed-space entry procedures, SOPEP gear and first aid.

**(b) Associated paperwork**
The ship's Muster List (Station Bill) detailing each crew member's emergency station and duties.
A familiarisation/induction checklist, signed by both the trainee and the responsible officer as documentary evidence, required before the seafarer is assigned duties (STCW/ISM).
The Safety Management System (SMS) manuals and emergency procedures/contingency plans under the ISM Code.
The training/drill record book, in which the individual's participation is logged, together with SOPEP/SMPEP and official log book entries.

answers.title: Procedure — Safety Precautions for Servicing Accommodation Lifts
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer, write a procedure listing recommendations for the safety precautions to be adopted when servicing accommodation lifts. (10)
answers.answer_text:
Accommodation lifts present particular hazards — falls into the lift shaft, crushing by a moving car or counterweight, and electric shock.

**Authorisation and isolation.** A Permit to Work raised and signed before servicing begins. Electrically isolate the lift at the main supply, lock off the isolator with a personal padlock and "Do Not Operate" tag. Prove the supply is dead with a test instrument before touching any conductor. Warning notices posted at every landing, with open landing doors barriered.

**Securing the car and counterweight.** The lift car physically secured against movement (chocked, or supported on safety gear) before entering the shaft — reliance on the brake alone is not acceptable. The counterweight's position known and accounted for. Where the car must be moved, use only the dedicated inspection/maintenance control at reduced "creep" speed.

**Working in the shaft/on the car top.** Adequate lighting provided. Car-top guard rail and inspection control station in use. Fall-arrest harnesses worn where there is risk of falling. Nothing dropped down the shaft. The shaft/pit treated as an enclosed space where appropriate, gas-tested before entry if in doubt.

**Communication and standby.** A second competent person in attendance with two-way communication; no one works alone in the shaft.

**Functional checks and return to service.** Check landing-door and car-door interlocks, the over-speed governor and safety gear, limit switches and buffer arrangements. Examine suspension ropes/chains for wear. Remove all tools and personnel, account for everyone, remove locks/tags only when satisfied work is complete, then test-run the lift through its full travel and log the work in the PMS/lift logbook.

answers.title: Pre-Port State Control Inspection — Engine Room Checks
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set: List TEN checks that a Chief Engineer Officer should make prior to a Port State Control inspection of the engine room and its equipment. (10)
answers.answer_text:
**Oily Water Separator (OWS) and 15ppm bilge alarm** — confirm operational, no illegal bypass ("magic pipe") arrangements, and the Oil Record Book fully completed and matching equipment/tank soundings (the single most heavily scrutinised item).
**Engine room bilges and tank tops clean and dry** — bilge high-level alarms tested and working.
**Fixed and portable firefighting equipment** — fixed system charged, controls in order; portable extinguishers in date; fire pumps tested.
**Quick-closing valves and remote/emergency stops** — proven to operate from remote stations.
**Emergency systems** — emergency generator starts on load; emergency steering gear operational.
**Steering gear** — proven operational with both power units; testing records up to date.
**Means of escape and EEBDs** — escape routes clear; EEBDs in date and properly stowed.
**Safety of machinery and housekeeping** — guards fitted, no significant leaks, lagging oil-free.
**Pollution-prevention equipment and records** — incinerator and sewage plant operational with valid records; SOPEP locker complete; Garbage Record Book up to date.
**Certificates, documentation and planned maintenance** — all statutory certificates valid; PMS up to date with no overdue critical jobs.

answers.title: IMO 2023 GHG Strategy — Reducing CO2 Emissions
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to the 2023 International Maritime Organisation (IMO) strategy on the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions from ships:

(a) state FOUR operating practices that may be adopted on board ship to comply with the IMO requirement to reduce CO2 emission levels; (4)

(b) explain what is meant by EACH of the following:

(i) CII; (2)

(ii) EEDI; (2)

(iii) EEXI. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Four operating practices to reduce CO2 emissions**
Speed reduction/"slow steaming" — fuel consumption (and CO2) rises roughly with the cube of speed, so reducing service speed gives a large reduction per voyage.
Voyage and weather-routeing optimisation — planning the most economical route, avoiding adverse weather and unnecessary "steam then wait" arrivals.
Optimum trim and hull/propeller condition — operating at optimum trim and keeping the hull and propeller clean and fouling-free reduces resistance and fuel burn.
Machinery efficiency measures — waste heat recovery, efficient auxiliary loading, and minimising unnecessary running of auxiliaries/boilers.

**(b)(i) CII (Carbon Intensity Indicator).** An operational, annually-calculated measure of a ship's CO2 emissions per unit of transport work (grams CO2 per deadweight-tonne-mile), rated A to E against a required trajectory that tightens each year.

**(b)(ii) EEDI (Energy Efficiency Design Index).** A design measure applied to new ships, expressing grams of CO2 per tonne-mile at the design stage based on installed power, capacity and speed, requiring new designs to meet progressively stricter efficiency levels.

**(b)(iii) EEXI (Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index).** The equivalent design-efficiency measure applied retrospectively to existing ships, a one-off calculation confirming the ship meets a required efficiency level, often achieved by engine power limitation (EPL) where necessary.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: IMO 2023 GHG Strategy — Reducing CO2 Emissions
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; be precise on the three acronyms -- CII (Carbon Intensity Indicator, an operational annual rating), EEDI (Energy Efficiency Design Index, for new-build ships), EEXI (Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index, retrofitted requirement for existing ships) -- since they're easy to blur together.

answers.title: Condition Monitoring System vs Other Maintenance Regimes
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Discuss the merits of a condition monitoring system compared to other maintenance regimes. (5)

(b) Describe how the data is gathered, stored and evaluated on a computer based vibration analysis system. (5)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Merits of condition monitoring compared to other regimes.** Compared to time-based (planned) maintenance, which opens up machinery on a fixed interval regardless of actual condition, condition monitoring bases maintenance on the machine's real, measured condition — avoiding unnecessary strip-downs of healthy equipment while catching developing faults early, before breakdown. Compared to breakdown (run-to-failure) maintenance, it avoids unplanned failures, consequential damage and lost production/off-hire. In practice a mixed strategy is normal: condition monitoring on important rotating machinery, planned maintenance on items not easily monitored, and run-to-failure on minor non-critical equipment.

**(b) Gathering, storing and evaluating data.**
**Gathering:** vibration is sensed by a transducer (commonly an accelerometer) placed at defined measuring points on bearing housings in horizontal, vertical and axial directions — either permanently mounted for continuous monitoring, or read on a route with a portable data collector.
**Storing:** the digitised readings are uploaded to a computer database, stored against the machine and measuring point, tagged with date, time, speed and load, building a historical trend file.
**Evaluating:** the software processes the signal using a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to produce a frequency spectrum; since different faults excite characteristic frequencies (imbalance at 1× shaft speed, misalignment at 2×, bearing/gear defects at their own frequencies), the spectrum diagnoses the type of fault. Readings are trended against baseline signatures and pre-set alarm limits, flagging developing faults for planned attention.

answers.title: The ISM Code
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set:
The International Management Code for the Safe Operation of Ships and for Pollution Prevention, is commonly referred to as the ISM Code.

(a) Explain the objectives of ISM and how are they achieved. (6)

(b) List the emergency scenarios for which contingency plans may be developed under ISM with respect to the engine room. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Objectives of ISM and how achieved.** The ISM Code provides an international standard for the safe management and operation of ships and for pollution prevention. Objectives: ensure safety at sea; prevent human injury or loss of life; avoid damage to the environment and to property.

Achieved through the Safety Management System (SMS), which every Company must develop, implement and maintain: it sets out a safety and environmental-protection policy and documented procedures; defines levels of authority and communication (identifying the Master's overriding authority); requires appointment of a Designated Person Ashore (DPA) linking ship and top management; establishes procedures for reporting accidents, non-conformities and near-misses; requires procedures to prepare for and respond to emergencies (contingency plans and drills); provides for planned maintenance and documentation control; and is subject to verification/audit leading to a Document of Compliance (Company) and Safety Management Certificate (ship).

**(b) Engine-room emergency scenarios for contingency plans.** Engine room fire (including major fire requiring evacuation and fixed system release); main engine/propulsion failure or total loss of propulsion (and steering gear failure); total electrical failure ("blackout"); flooding of the machinery space.

answers.title: Marine Growth Prevention System (MGPS) — Impressed Current Type
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to Marine Growth Prevention Systems, which incorporate impressed current anodes fitted in the sea boxes or sea strainers of main seawater cooling water systems:

(a) explain how the system protects steel pipework against marine growth and corrosion; (6)

(b) explain how the effectiveness of the system can be ascertained; (2)

(c) state the advantages this system has over one which makes use of biocides. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) How the system protects steel pipework.** The system is fitted inside the sea chest or sea strainer, where two anodes are mounted in the flow, fed with low-voltage direct current (impressed current) which dissolves them at a controlled rate. The copper anode releases copper ions that are toxic to marine organisms even at a few parts per billion, preventing marine growth from settling, breeding or establishing anywhere downstream. The aluminium anode releases aluminium ions deposited as a thin anti-corrosive film over the steel pipework's internal surfaces.

**(b) Ascertaining effectiveness.** At the control panel, check each anode is drawing its correct current; by physical inspection when opened up, examine sea chest, strainers and coolers for absence of marine growth and corrosion; maintained seawater flow and cooler performance (no rising pressure drop) is further confirmation.

**(c) Advantages over a biocide system.** No storage, handling or discharge of hazardous chemicals; also provides corrosion protection via the aluminium anode, which a biocide system does not; automatic, continuous and self-regulating with low labour (only periodic anode renewal).

answers.title: Machinery Condition Monitoring Systems (Four-Part Variant)
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to machinery condition monitoring systems:

(a) state what is meant by machinery condition monitoring; (2)

(b) state the means available for gathering data; (3)

(c) describe how the data is used to indicate machinery condition trends; (3)

(d) explain the relevance of machinery condition monitoring to approved planned maintenance systems. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)** The continuous or periodic measurement and interpretation of selected operating parameters (vibration, temperature, oil condition, performance values) to determine a machine's actual running condition, so faults are detected early and maintenance is based on real condition rather than fixed intervals.

**(b)** Vibration measurement (accelerometers/proximity probes); lubricating-oil analysis (spectrographic, viscosity, TBN); temperature monitoring; performance/operating-parameter monitoring (pressures, flows, power, speed).

**(c)** Each reading is recorded against the machine and measuring point, tagged with date/speed/load, and trended over time against a baseline signature and alert/alarm limits. A steady reading shows healthy condition; a rising trend warns of a developing fault. This trended record is the evidence presented to Classification Society: under an accepted scheme, items shown to be in good condition can have opening-up/survey credited or deferred — supporting the Continuous Survey of Machinery (CSM).

**(d)** Condition monitoring underpins an approved Planned Maintenance System — the monitored condition decides when work is actually needed rather than purely on running hours, and where approved by class, the recorded data satisfies survey requirements under CSM, reducing survey-related downtime while maintaining full compliance.

answers.title: Checks and Procedures Prior to UMS Operations
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set: Explain the checks and procedures to be carried out prior to Unattended Machinery Space (UMS) operations. (10)
answers.answer_text:
**Alarm and call system — the heart of the answer.**
Test the engineers' alarm and alarm-transfer arrangement — confirming an unacknowledged alarm in the control room transfers to call the duty engineer.
Test the duty engineer's cabin alarm — verify the alarm sounds in the cabin of the engineer on duty.
Test the public-room/accommodation alarms — confirm the alarm also sounds in dining saloon, mess rooms and alleyways.
Set up and test the "dead-man" (engineer's safety) alarm — must be reset at intervals (typically ~30 minutes) or a full alarm is raised in the accommodation/bridge, protecting an engineer incapacitated alone in the space.
Test communications and the bridge link — confirming machinery alarms also annunciate on the bridge.

Auto slow-downs, boiler trips and quick-closing valves are part of the periodic/planned testing schedule and are not repeated before every UMS period — what matters is confirming the monitoring, alarm-transfer, call and standby/auto-start systems are functioning.

answers.title: Legal, Administrative and Technical Responsibilities of a Chief Engineer Officer
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set: Explain the legal, administrative and technical responsibilities of a Chief Engineer Officer. (10)
answers.answer_text:
**Legal (statutory) responsibilities.** Compliance with international and flag-state law (SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, ISM, ISPS, MLC, Class). Maintaining statutory machinery records — the Oil Record Book Part I, the Engine Room Log/Movement Book, the Garbage Record Book and Annex VI records, night order book and Official Log Book entries. Bunkering and fuel responsibility. Upholding valid certificates and surveys. Safety and pollution-prevention duty of care.

**Administrative responsibilities.** Management of the engineering department (watchkeeping/UMS arrangements, supervision, training). Operating the SMS in the engine room. Planned Maintenance System administration. Stores, spares and budget control. Reporting and communication with Company, Master, Class and makers.

**Technical responsibilities.** Safe and efficient operation of all machinery. Maintenance, repair and condition monitoring. Fault diagnosis and emergency decision-making. Energy efficiency and performance (SEEMP, trim/load management, IMO GHG requirements). Survey and dry-dock preparation.

answers.title: Letter/Note of Protest — Short Bunker Delivery
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set: Following bunkering operations, it is discovered that the vessel received a quantity which was short of what was stipulated in the pre-delivery document. As Chief Engineer Officer, write a Note of Protest to the Master of the bunkering vessel. (10)
answers.answer_text:
**LETTER OF PROTEST**
To: The Master, Bunker Barge/Supplying Vessel [name]
From: [Name], Chief Engineer Officer, MV [Receiving Vessel]
Subject: Protest against short delivery of marine fuel oil — Bunker Delivery Note No. [ref]

I hereby formally protest regarding the quantity supplied during today's bunkering operation. **Bunkering particulars:** commenced/completed times, grade supplied, quantity stated on the BDN. **Receiving vessel's measured figures:** soundings/ullages jointly witnessed before and after, corrected for temperature and density. **Discrepancy:** BDN quantity vs ship's measured quantity, giving the shortfall and percentage.

This shortfall exceeds any reasonable measurement tolerance. The Owners reserve all rights to claim for the value of fuel not delivered. I request the supplier's figures be made available for joint verification and that you countersign this protest. Representative samples have been drawn jointly and sealed in accordance with MARPOL Annex VI.

Built on measured evidence — before/after soundings, times, temperatures/densities used for correction, the BDN figure against the ship's figure, and the quantified shortfall — plus the professional essentials: reserving rights, requesting countersignature, noting any refusal to sign.

answers.title: Screw-Type Air Compressors
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to air compressors for general service use:

(a) explain the principle of operation of a screw type compressor; (4)

(b) explain the advantages of screw compressors over reciprocating compressors in terms of running and maintenance. (6)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Principle of operation.** A positive-displacement rotary machine compressing air using two intermeshing helical rotors — a male rotor (rounded lobes) driving a female rotor (mating flutes), turning in opposite directions in a close-clearance casing. Air is drawn in and fills the spaces (cells) between rotor flutes and casing wall; as the rotors mesh, cells are progressively closed off and carried along the rotors, the trapped volume reduced continuously, compressing the air toward the discharge port. Most machines are oil-flooded, injecting oil to seal clearances, lubricate and absorb heat of compression.

**(b) Advantages over reciprocating — running.** Continuous, pulsation-free delivery (no large receiver needed); far fewer moving parts with no reciprocating mass, so little out-of-balance vibration; high rotational speed and compact size; no valves to leak or break.

**(b) Advantages — maintenance.** Lower wear and longer intervals between overhauls (rotors run without metal-to-metal contact); simpler, quicker maintenance largely limited to oil/filter changes rather than valve grinding, ring/liner renewal.

answers.title: Bunkering Fuel Oil — Information, Loading Rate, Effect
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set:
(a) With reference to bunkering fuel oil, list the information to be supplied to the port authorities prior to commencement of bunker operations. (5)

(b) With reference to the tank being filled, state the factors that govern the bunker loading rate.(4)

(c) State a possible effect of a high bunker loading rate. (1)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Information to port authorities.** Identity and details of the vessel (name, IMO number, berth position); the intended bunkering operation (date, start time, duration, method of supply); the fuel grade(s) and quantities and intended maximum transfer rate; details of the supplier/supplying craft; confirmation of safety and pollution-prevention readiness (SOPEP in place, scuppers plugged, responsible officer identified).

**(b) Factors governing the bunker loading rate.** The capacity/number of tanks being filled and pipework/manifold size; the venting (air-escape) arrangement of the tank; the number of tanks open simultaneously and stage of filling (reduced "topping-up" rate near full); the properties of the fuel and temperature (viscosity/grade affecting line resistance).

**(c) Possible effect of a high loading rate.** Displaced air unable to escape through vents quickly enough, leading to over-pressurisation and overflow of the tank — an oil spill/pollution incident.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Bunkering Fuel Oil — Information, Loading Rate, Effect
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; part (c) (effect of high loading rate) is worth pinning down precisely -- static build-up/risk in the tank and reduced time to react to overflow/mis-valving are the usual answers expected.

answers.title: Main Thrust Block — Tilting Pad Arrangement
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to main thrust block arrangements:

(a) explain how the tilting pads assist in the formation of an oil wedge; (2)

(b) describe the actions that may be taken if upon inspection the pads are found to be:

(i) lightly scored; (2)

(ii) wiped; (2)

(c) explain how the thrust clearance may be measured, stating a typical value; (2)

(d) state the possible effects if the thrust clearance is incorrect. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) How tilting pads assist the oil wedge.** Each pad is free to tilt/pivot; as the rotating thrust collar drags oil across the pad face, the pad tilts to a small angle, forming a converging wedge-shaped gap. Oil dragged into this wedge generates a hydrodynamic pressure that lifts and supports the collar on a full oil film with no metal-to-metal contact. The pivoting freedom lets each pad self-adjust to speed, load and viscosity.

**(b)(i) Lightly scored.** Superficial — can be reconditioned in place: stoned/scraped smooth with a fine oilstone, washed and refitted. Establish and remove the cause (typically dirty/contaminated oil) by checking the LO system and filters.

**(b)(ii) Wiped.** The white-metal facing has overheated and melted/smeared — must be renewed, not repairable by stoning. Investigate and rectify the cause (oil starvation, overloading, blocked oil flow) before returning to service.

**(c) Measuring thrust clearance.** Measured with a feeler gauge between the thrust collar and pads, or a dial gauge (DTI) mounted axially while the shaft is jacked fully forward then fully aft, the total axial movement being the clearance. A typical value is ~0.3–0.5mm.

**(d) Effects if incorrect.** Too small — pads over-tight, restricting oil flow and wedge formation, causing overheating and wiping of the white metal. Too great — excessive axial float, giving fore-and-aft "hunting"/knocking, shock loading and uneven load sharing across the pads.

answers.title: Medium-Speed Auxiliary Diesel Engines — Cylinder Head Valves
answers.topic: Sewage Systems & Related Chief Engineer Duties
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to medium speed auxiliary diesel engines:

(a) explain why twin air inlet and exhaust valves are often fitted to each cylinder head; (6)

(b) explain why, in some cases, valve rotation is employed. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why twin valves are often fitted.** Medium-speed engines have very short gas-exchange time. Two smaller valves give greater total valve flow area for better breathing than one large valve; smaller, lighter individual valves reduce reciprocating mass in the valve gear, allowing accurate high-speed cam-following without valve bounce; lower thermal loading and less distortion per valve, since each runs cooler and dissipates heat better; and using two of each type allows the fuel injector to be mounted centrally for symmetrical, efficient combustion.

**(b) Why valve rotation is employed.** A rotator mechanism turns the valve slowly about its axis each time it operates. This gives even temperature distribution and reduced distortion (preventing local hot spots and burning); self-cleaning of the valve seat and face (wiping away carbon deposits — not "grinding," since the valve is not worn down); even seat and valve-gear wear (since the valve does not return to exactly the same point each time); and reduced sticking of the valve stem in its guide.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Medium-Speed Auxiliary Diesel Engines — Cylinder Head Valves
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: A popular, well-scored question despite initially looking like an odd fit for the syllabus (it falls under section 6.8, auxiliary diesel engines). Part (b) has a recurring wording issue: valve rotation is better described as self-cleaning (keeps deposits from building unevenly and promotes even seating/wear) rather than 'grinding' the valve, which examiners specifically didn't like as a description.

answers.title: Static Oily Water Separator — Separating Matrix and Polishing Pack
answers.question_as_set: Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the principle of operation of a static oily water separator that utilises a separating matrix and polishing pack. (10)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw a vertical vessel: oily water inlet into an upper gravity chamber, then down through a separating matrix, then a polishing pack, then clean water out the bottom. Show oil collecting at the top with a sensing probe, oil outlet valve, vacuum breaker, and on the discharge side: pump, OCM, and a 3-way valve to overboard/recirculation.*

A static separator has no moving parts in the separation process — it relies entirely on gravity differential and coalescence, governed by Stokes' Law: droplet rise velocity is proportional to the density difference and the square of droplet diameter, inversely proportional to viscosity.

**Stage 1 — Gravity separation (upper chamber).** Velocity is very low, so the bulk free oil (larger droplets) rises to the top and collects under the dome.

**Stage 2 — Separating matrix (first coalescer).** Water carrying finer droplets passes through an oleophilic coalescing pack; small droplets impinge, wet the surface and merge into larger droplets that detach and rise.

**Stage 3 — Polishing pack (second/fine coalescer).** A finer stage captures the remaining tightly-dispersed oil, bringing the effluent reliably below 15 ppm (MARPOL Annex I, Reg. 14).

**Oil removal and discharge control.** The oil sensing probe detects the oil layer depth and opens the oil outlet valve to drain to the sludge tank. On the discharge side, the pump is located downstream (drawing water through under suction, not pushing it through, which would emulsify the oil), followed by the OCM and a three-way valve diverting to overboard or recirculation depending on the ppm reading.

**Examiner traps:** call it a coalescer, not a filter; never put the pump before the separator; always quote 15 ppm/MARPOL Annex I/OCM/3-way valve.

answers.title: Centrifugal Separators — Superiority, Plate Flow, Overboard Control
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to centrifugal separators used for oily bilge duty:

(a) explain why centrifugal oily water separators are superior to those which rely on gravity; (3)

(b) describe, with the aid of a sketch, how flow over the centrifugal separator plates can break down emulsions by encouraging flocculation of particles and coalescence of droplets; (5)

(c) state how the bilge overboard control valve can only be operated by the Chief Engineer; (1)

(d) state a value of overboard parts per million oil content that may be set which is below the generally recommended value. (1)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why centrifugal is superior to gravity.** A centrifuge replaces gravity (g) with a centrifugal acceleration (rω²) thousands of times g. This gives: far greater separating force, driving separation of much smaller/finer droplets a gravity unit could never settle in reasonable time; much faster, near-instantaneous separation allowing a small, compact bowl to handle high throughput; and independence from a long quiescent settling period, so it is far less affected by ship motion.

**(b) How flow over the plates breaks down emulsions.**
*Sketch instructions: draw two closely-spaced plates with a parabolic velocity profile of flow between them, showing a droplet subject to two forces — viscous drag along the flow and a centrifugal "gravity" force across the gap.*

The liquid is forced through the narrow gap between adjacent plates as a thin film. A droplet experiences the viscous drag carrying it along the flow and the centrifugal force acting across the gap, driving it toward the oil side. Droplets collide and merge (flocculate/coalesce) as they migrate across the thin film, growing large enough to separate quickly under the enhanced force.

**(c) Bilge overboard control valve under Chief Engineer's control.** The overboard discharge valve is fitted with a key-operated (or coded) interlock, the key held only by the Chief Engineer, so it cannot be opened without his authority.

**(d) A value below the generally recommended value.** A set-point below the 15 ppm MARPOL limit (e.g. 10 ppm), giving a safety margin so the alarm/diversion trips before the statutory limit is reached.

answers.title: OWS Discharge Monitoring — The “White Box” and Additional Anti-Illegal-Discharge Measures
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe an oily water separator bilge content discharge monitoring system that ensures that the oil discharge content is below the recommended maximum and that logs and retains data. (8)

(b) State TWO additional measures that can be taken to ensure that no illegal pumping overboard can take place. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) OWS discharge monitoring system.** A modern system combines three elements on the separator discharge line: an oil content monitor (OCM), an automatic three-way diversion valve, and a tamper-proof data recording unit (the "white box"), coordinated by a control unit.

**Oil content monitor (OCM).** A continuous sample of treated effluent passes through a measuring cell working on an optical principle (light scattering/absorption); a light source shines through the sample and a photo-detector measures attenuation, converted to ppm. Must comply with IMO MEPC.107(49).

**Discharge/set-point logic.** Below 15 ppm, the three-way valve directs effluent overboard. At/above 15 ppm, the control unit raises an alarm and automatically switches to recirculate back to the holding tank — the overboard route is closed while content is too high. This diversion is automatic and fail-safe (loss of power/air closes the overboard route).

**Data recording — the "white box."** A tamper-proof recorder automatically logs and retains the OCM ppm reading, the valve status, date/time, and the ship's GPS position, for a minimum of 18 months in sealed, non-erasable memory the operator cannot alter — downloadable for PSC/flag-state inspection.

**(b) Two additional measures against illegal discharge**
Locked/sealed overboard valve under the sole control of the Chief Engineer — a key- or coded interlock so it cannot be opened without authority, with any operation recorded.
Blanking/sealing of bypass connections and recording in the Oil Record Book — any flanges that could bypass the OWS/OCM are blanked and numbered-sealed, with every discharge operation, seal number and tank sounding entered in the ORB Part I.

answers.title: Bilge Water Processing Unit — Operation, Maintenance, Monitoring
answers.question_as_set: Describe in detail the operation, maintenance and monitoring of a bilge water processing unit to ensure compliance with the current MARPOL convention on the discharge of oily bilge water. (10)
answers.answer_text:
**Operation.** The unit treats oily bilge water in stages to below the MARPOL Annex I 15 ppm limit. The pump is on the discharge side, drawing water through under suction rather than pushing it (which would emulsify the oil). Bulk free oil rises and collects under the dome by gravity; water then passes through the coalescing separating matrix and polishing pack; accumulated oil is drained via the oil outlet valve, and treated water passes the OCM before the three-way valve sends it overboard or recirculates it.

**Maintenance.** Coalescer/polishing elements — monitor differential pressure; a rising ΔP indicates fouling; backflush, clean or renew at maker's intervals. OCM cell — keep clean (oil film/sludge/bubbles give false readings), calibrate/zero-span check regularly. Solenoid/three-way valve — verify it actuates freely and fails safe to recirculation. Vacuum breaker, sample valves, relief valve — check clear and functioning.

**Monitoring.** The OCM (optical cell, MEPC.107(49)) drives the alarm/diversion logic. The tamper-proof "white box" logs ppm, valve status, date/time and GPS position for a minimum of 18 months. Administrative controls: overboard valve locked under the Chief Engineer's control; bypass connections blanked and sealed; every operation entered in the Oil Record Book Part I.

**Trap:** the question asks for three things — operation, maintenance and monitoring. Describing the separator alone caps the mark at partial credit; maintenance and monitoring carry the greater weight.

answers.title: Static OWS — Operation with Pump on Discharge Side
answers.question_as_set: Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the operation of a static Oily Water Separator which conforms to current MARPOL regulations and utilises a pump on the discharge side of the separator. (10)
answers.answer_text:
Same underlying content as Q1 above, with the emphasis specifically on the pump being on the discharge (downstream) side of the vessel.

Because the pump is on the discharge side, the unit operates under suction — water is drawn through rather than pushed in. A pump placed before the separator would shear and agitate the oil into a fine, stable emulsion the coalescer struggles to break; drawing water through under low-velocity suction keeps oil droplets intact and easy to separate. The rest of the operation (gravity chamber, separating matrix, polishing pack, oil sensing probe and outlet valve, OCM and 3-way valve) follows as in Q1.

answers.title: Static Oily Water Separators — Pump Selection, Separation Mechanism, Fluid Properties
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to static oily water separators, explain EACH of the following:

(a) why the supply pump should be carefully selected and matched to the separator; (2)

(b) how the separator achieves effective separation; (4)

(c) how the physical properties of each of the fluids to be separated affects the rate and effectiveness of separation. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why the supply pump must be carefully selected.** A pump that shears or agitates the mixture (e.g. a centrifugal pump pushing oily water into the separator) will emulsify the oil into a fine, stable dispersion that the coalescer cannot break. A gentle, low-shear pump (or the pump located on the discharge/suction side) preserves droplet size so gravity and coalescence can work.

**(b) How the separator achieves effective separation.** Gravity settling gives residence time for bulk free oil to rise (Stokes' Law). The coalescing separating matrix merges finer dispersed droplets on its oleophilic surface until buoyant enough to rise. The polishing pack is a finer second coalescing stage bringing the effluent below 15 ppm.

**(c) How physical properties affect rate and effectiveness**
Density difference — the driving force; the greater the difference, the faster oil rises. Heating lowers oil density, increasing the difference.
Viscosity — rise velocity is inversely proportional to viscosity; a viscous oil resists movement and coalescence. Heating cuts viscosity dramatically, aiding separation.
Surface/interfacial tension — governs how readily droplets coalesce; detergents/surfactants lower interfacial tension, stabilising a fine emulsion that resists separation.
Buoyancy — the net upward force on a droplet; because volume rises with the cube of diameter while drag rises only with diameter, larger droplets rise much faster — the reason coalescence (growing droplets) makes separation work.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Static Oily Water Separators — Pump Selection, Separation Mechanism, Fluid Properties
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Parts (a) and (b) are handled well, but part (c) exposes a real gap -- candidates default to discussing the DENSITY difference between oil and water and rarely mention VISCOSITY, despite viscosity (of both the oil and any emulsion) being just as significant to separation rate and effectiveness.

answers.title: Hydraulic Oil Reservoir Functions; High Oil Temperature Tripping
answers.question_as_set:
(a) In deck machinery hydraulic systems, state the functions of the hydraulic oil reservoir, making reference to the volume of the hydraulic fluid in the system. (6)

(b) State FOUR reasons for machinery tripping out on high oil temperature during operation. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Functions of the hydraulic oil reservoir**
Stores the system's working volume plus reserve, so the level still covers the suction when actuators are fully extended and the pump never draws air.
Allows for thermal expansion and contraction without overflowing or uncovering the suction.
De-aeration — large surface area and dwell time (commonly 3–5 times pump delivery per minute) let entrained air escape before recirculation.
Settling of contaminants and water — dwell time lets solids/water settle to a sloped sump for draining; baffles separate return from suction.
Cooling/heat dissipation — the oil volume and reservoir surface act as a thermal reservoir.
Maintains pump suction head and provides make-up for minor leakage.

**(b) Four reasons for tripping on high oil temperature**
Cooler fault/loss of cooling — fouled cooler, low cooling-water flow, failed cooling-water pump.
Low oil level/insufficient volume — shorter circulation time reduces de-aeration and cooling.
Internal leakage/worn components — worn pump, valves or seals leak high-pressure oil internally, converting pressure energy to heat.
Relief valve passing or set too low, or system overload — oil continuously dumping across the relief valve generates heat.

answers.title: Deck Machinery Hydraulic System (Sketch) + Electric vs Hydraulic Advantages
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to deck machinery:

(a) sketch a line diagram showing the layout and components of a hydraulic system with a variable delivery, pressure compensated pump and accumulator, suitable for the operation of deck machinery; (5)

(b) discuss the advantages of using electrically driven machinery over hydraulically driven winches and windlasses. (5)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw a sump/reservoir with suction strainer feeding a variable-delivery, pressure-compensated pump (swash-plate symbol with compensator), through a check valve to a pressure line with a relief valve back to sump, a pressure-line filter, an accumulator on the pressure line, a 3-way hand-operated spring-return directional control valve feeding a double-acting load (motor/ram), with a branch "to other load," and a return line through a return filter back to the sump.*

The pump's pressure compensator senses delivery pressure and reduces the swash angle to near-zero stroke when the set pressure is reached, so it delivers only the flow the system demands; the accumulator then maintains pressure for standby.

**(b) Advantages of electric over hydraulic deck machinery**
No risk of oil pollution — no high-pressure hydraulic oil at deck level, no leak/spill risk overboard.
Higher efficiency, lower running cost — avoids the compounded losses of a hydraulic system and standby power-pack losses.
Less maintenance and no oil system — no power pack, high-pressure piping, hoses or hydraulic filters to maintain.
Better, more precise control — AC variable-frequency drives give fine speed control, regenerative braking and built-in condition-monitoring data.
Cleaner, simpler installation — no long high-pressure piping runs, no cold-weather oil viscosity problems.

Balancing note: hydraulics remain common for their inherent overload protection (relief valve), high power-to-weight ratio, and explosion-safety with no arcing.

answers.title: Deck Machinery Hydraulic System (Sketch) + Operation of the System
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a line diagram showing the layout and components of a hydraulic system with a variable delivery, pressure compensated pump and accumulator, suitable for the operation of deck machinery. (5)

(b) Describe the operation of the system sketched in part (a). (5)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)** As per Q9's sketch above.

**(b) Operation.** The variable-delivery pump draws oil from the sump through the suction strainer and delivers it through the check valve into the pressure line. The compensator senses delivery pressure and adjusts the swash-plate angle to match output to demand; when demand stops and pressure reaches the set value, the compensator destrokes the pump to near-zero flow, so the pump only makes up leakage rather than continuously dumping full flow over the relief valve.

The check valve prevents stored pressure leaking back through the destroked pump. The accumulator holds the system charged while destroked, supplies peak/transient flow demands faster than the pump can stroke up, and absorbs pressure shocks. Operating the directional control valve directs oil to the load; releasing it lets the spring return the valve to neutral (fail-safe). The relief valve protects against overpressure (e.g. a stalled actuator); spent oil returns through the return filter to the sump for de-aeration, settling and cooling.

answers.title: Hydraulic Oil Contamination — Types, Effects, Monitoring
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to hydraulic deck machinery and cargo handling systems:

(a) state FOUR possible types of contamination of the oil, describing how the contamination may have occurred; (4)

(b) state FOUR possible effects of oil contamination on the system; (4)

(c) state how the system oil may be monitored for contamination. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Four types of contamination and how they occur**
Water — condensation in the reservoir, worn seals/glands, leaking coolers, or seawater/rainwater ingress through damaged rod seals.
Solid particles/dirt — grit or weld scale left during manufacture/repair, a defective air breather, or ingress past worn ram-rod wiper seals.
Wear metal — generated internally by wear of pump components, valve spools, bearings and gears.
Air/aeration — drawn in through a low oil level uncovering the suction, a leaking suction-side joint, or insufficient de-aeration time.

**(b) Four effects of oil contamination**
Increased wear and component damage — abrasive solids and wear metal score pistons, spools and seals.
Corrosion — water and acidic oxidation products corrode internal surfaces.
Sluggish, spongy or erratic control — entrained air/water make the oil compressible.
Valve sticking/blockage and filter clogging — particles jam spool valves and block orifices.

**(c) Monitoring for contamination.** Regular sampling and laboratory analysis (water content, viscosity, TAN, particle/wear-metal spectrographic analysis). Onboard checks — visual/crackle test for water, return/pressure filter ΔP indicator, and magnetic plug inspection for wear metal.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Hydraulic Oil Contamination — Types, Effects, Monitoring

answers.title: Fuel Oil Viscosity — Necessity, Measurement Methods, Control Action
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to fuel oil viscosity:

(a) explain why correct fuel oil viscosity is necessary; (2)

(b) describe TWO methods for the measurement of viscosity that are suitable for the inclusion into a pneumatic or electronic control system; (6)

(c) state, with reasons, a control action for a viscosity controller. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why correct viscosity is necessary.** Viscosity controls atomisation at the injector. Too high (oil too cold) — poor atomisation, after-burning, carbon/soot deposits, loss of power/efficiency. Too low (oil too hot) — poor spray penetration, loss of the lubricating film in the fuel pump/injector, seizure/scuffing risk. Correct viscosity (~10–15 cSt at the injector) is set by controlling fuel temperature.

**(b) Two on-line viscosity measuring methods**
**1. Capillary/differential-pressure type.** A constant-displacement gear pump forces a fixed flow through a fixed-bore capillary tube; by Poiseuille's law, the pressure drop across the tube is directly proportional to viscosity. A differential-pressure transducer gives a continuous pneumatic or electronic signal.
**2. Oscillating/vibrating-element (torsional) type.** A probe with a vibrating element immersed in the fuel is driven at its resonant frequency; viscous drag damps the oscillation, and the power needed to maintain constant amplitude is proportional to viscosity, converted to a continuous 4–20mA output.

**(c) Control action, with reasons.** The controller acts on the fuel heater steam/electrical supply valve: if viscosity is above set point (too cold/thick), it opens the heater valve to raise temperature; if below set point (too hot/thin), it closes the valve. A proportional + integral (PI) action holds viscosity accurately with no offset as load and fuel grade change — viscosity, not temperature, is controlled directly since different fuel grades reach the target viscosity at different temperatures.

answers.title: Hydrocarbon Tanks — Flammability Terms and Safe Atmosphere
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to tanks containing hydrocarbon liquids and vapours:

(a) define EACH of the following terms:

(i) explosive limits; (2)

(ii) vapour pressure; (2)

(iii) flash point. (2)

(b) explain how the atmosphere in cargo tanks containing varying percentages of flammable gas can be maintained in a safe condition at all times. (4)
answers.answer_text:
Same underlying content as the Fire Safety topic's hydrocarbon tanks question (Q8 there) — reproduced here since this reference guide answers it under OWS/Hydraulics/Fuel Oil as well.

**(a)(i) Explosive limits.** LEL/UEL bound the flammable range of hydrocarbon-vapour-in-air concentration.
**(a)(ii) Vapour pressure.** The pressure exerted by a liquid's vapour at equilibrium in an enclosed space at a given temperature; rises with temperature.
**(a)(iii) Flash point.** The lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapour to momentarily flash when an ignition source is applied.

**(b) Maintaining a safe tank atmosphere.** Keep the atmosphere out of the flammable range by controlling oxygen rather than hydrocarbon content: inert gas reduces oxygen below ~5–8%, so no mixture can support combustion whatever the hydrocarbon percentage. Maintain a slight positive IG pressure; purge with inert gas before ventilating to air (never ventilate a hydrocarbon-rich tank directly with air, which would pass through the flammable range).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Hydrocarbon Tanks — Flammability Terms and Safe Atmosphere
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Very poorly answered -- most candidates show little grasp of basic hydrocarbon flammability terms (explosive limits, vapour pressure, flash point) or how a tank atmosphere with varying flammable-gas percentage is kept safe (inerting outside the flammable range, not just ventilating).

answers.title: Bunker Line Pinhole Leak — Immediate Actions and Permanent Repair
answers.question_as_set:
During bunkering operations, a section of deck bunker line starts leaking fuel oil from a pinhole at the mid section of the pipe.

(a) As Chief Engineer Officer, state the immediate actions to be taken to avoid a potential pollution incident; (4)

(b) Explain how a permanent repair could be made, stating any precautions to be taken and any further inspections that would be required. (6)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Immediate actions**
Stop bunkering immediately — signal the barge/shore to stop pumping and shut valves to isolate and depressurise the section.
Contain the spill — plug scuppers, deploy the SOPEP spill kit and save-alls.
Raise the alarm/inform — notify the duty officer and Master, muster the spill response team per SOPEP/SMPEP.
Transfer/relieve the line — drain remaining oil from the section, clean up spilled oil retaining it for disposal.

**(b) Permanent repair, precautions and inspections.** A pinhole indicates wall thinning/corrosion — a clamp or weld over the hole is not a permanent fix. Ship's staff renew the affected section: isolate, drain and gas-free the line; cut out the defective section and fabricate a replacement spool of correct material/bore/thickness; weld by a qualified welder, then **pressure-test the new pipe before fitting**; fit with new gaskets and pressure-test the joint in situ.

**Precautions:** hot work permit and fire precautions, gas-free certificate, correct welding procedure and qualified welder.

**Further inspections:** inspect the rest of the bunker pipework — a pinhole from corrosion strongly suggests the remainder is in similar condition, so carry out ultrasonic wall-thickness measurement along the line, especially at low points and bends, renewing any further thin sections found.

answers.title: Fuel with High Pour Point — Test and Measures to Enable Use
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to fuel with high pour point:

(a) describe test that may be carried out; (4)

(b) state the measure to be taken to enable the ship to use the fuel. (6)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Pour point test.** A sample is placed in a standard test jar with a thermometer, first heated to dissolve any wax, then cooled steadily in stages. At each 3°C interval the jar is tilted horizontally for ~5 seconds to check whether the surface moves. Cooling continues until no movement is observed; the pour point is recorded as 3°C above that no-flow temperature.

**(b) Measures to enable use of the fuel.** Keep the fuel above its pour point at every stage: maintain bunker tank temperature (heating coils) at least ~10°C above the pour point; heat-trace and lag transfer lines so fuel doesn't chill/gel in exposed pipe runs; heat settling and service tanks; heat before the purifier for correct separating temperature; final heating at the booster heater to injection viscosity (~10–15 cSt). Avoid cold pockets/dead legs by keeping fuel circulating and flushing lines through with hot fuel when stopping.

answers.title: Microbacterial Infestation — Systems Affected, Conditions, Detection
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to microbacterial infestation:

(a) list the engine room systems that may be affected by this type of contamination; (2)

(b) explain the conditions required for bacteria to evolve; (6)

(c) describe how the presence of microbial contamination could be detected. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Systems affected.** Fuel oil systems (especially distillate/diesel storage tanks); lubricating oil systems; hydraulic oil systems; fresh water/cooling water systems.

**(b) Conditions required for bacteria to evolve.** Water (the essential requirement, especially free water at the oil/water interface); a food source (hydrocarbons plus trace nutrients); a suitable temperature (roughly 20–40°C, exactly the range of bunker/settling/service tanks); oxygen for aerobic types, or oxygen-depleted pockets for anaerobic types (e.g. sulphate-reducing bacteria producing H2S); and stagnant/undisturbed conditions and time for colonies to establish.

**(c) Detecting microbial contamination.** Sampling and laboratory testing — dip-slide/culture kits or laboratory microbiological analysis of a tank-bottom sample. Physical/operational signs — rapid filter blocking, dark slimy sludge at the oil-water interface, increased water content and acidity, unusual smell, evidence of corrosion/pitting.

answers.title: Auxiliary Diesel Engine LO Sample Results — Causes and Greatest Concern
answers.question_as_set:
(a) State the possible causes for EACH of the following auxiliary diesel engine lubricating oil sample results:

(i) high acidity; (2)

(ii) high sediment content; (2)

(iii) excessive water content; (2)

(iv) fuel dilution. (2)

(b) Explain which of the results in part (a) would give greatest concern. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(i) High acidity.** Oxidation/degradation of the oil (overheating, aeration, old oil); acidic combustion products from fuel sulphur blowing past the pistons, depleting alkalinity (TBN).

**(ii) High sediment content.** Wear debris and carbon/oxidation products from normal/abnormal wear; dirt ingress and additive breakdown, plus a failing purifier or filter.

**(iii) Excessive water content.** Cooling-water leakage into the crankcase (leaking liner seals, cooler tubes); condensation from cool/intermittent operation or purifier malfunction.

**(iv) Fuel dilution.** Leaking fuel injection equipment (dripping injectors, HP pump glands); poor/incomplete combustion (faulty atomisation, prolonged idling).

**(b) Greatest concern.** Excessive water content (iii) generally gives the greatest concern — it promotes rapid corrosion, destroys the lubricating film and can lead to bearing wipe/failure, accelerates oil degradation, and if from a cooling-water leak signals a developing mechanical defect that will worsen.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Auxiliary Diesel Engine LO Sample Results — Causes and Greatest Concern

answers.title: Modern Shaft Torsion Meter; Torque/Speed & Hull Efficiency
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the principle of operation of a modern shaft torsion meter. (8)

(b) Explain why it is important in terms of hull efficiency to measure and compare shaft torque and speed. (2)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw a split-ring/collar clamped around the shaft carrying four strain gauges bonded at 45° to the axis, connected as a Wheatstone bridge. Show a stationary pickup reading the rotating collar (inductive coupling or telemetry), feeding a display unit.*

**Principle.** When the shaft transmits torque, it twists, producing shear stress that manifests as principal tensile and compressive strains at 45° to the shaft axis. Four strain gauges bonded at 45° form a full Wheatstone bridge — two sensing tension, two compression — giving doubled sensitivity, automatic temperature compensation, and cancellation of bending/axial thrust strains so the bridge responds to torsion only.

**Construction and operation.** As torque is applied, gauges in tension increase resistance and those in compression decrease, unbalancing the bridge; output voltage is directly proportional to torque. The gauges and bridge electronics are carried on a split-ring clamped around the shaft, signal transmitted across the rotating-to-stationary gap by inductive (rotary transformer) coupling or radio telemetry — no slip rings in modern meters. The stationary pickup also incorporates a speed sensor. The display shows torque, speed, and shaft power computed as P = 2πNT.

**(b) Importance for hull efficiency.** Under MARPOL Annex VI, EEDI and SEEMP require ships to demonstrate and continually improve energy efficiency. Shaft torque and speed give delivered shaft power (P = 2πNT); comparing this against ship speed and baseline (sea trial) data quantifies true propulsive efficiency. A rise in torque/power for the same ship speed reveals hull or propeller fouling, enabling informed decisions on hull cleaning and voyage optimisation.

answers.title: Propeller Slip — Definition, Calculation & Affecting Conditions
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Define propeller slip, explaining how it is calculated. (2)

(b) State, with reasons, FOUR conditions which will affect the propeller slip. (8)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)** Propeller slip is the difference between the theoretical distance the propeller should advance (pitch × revolutions) and the actual distance the ship travels, expressed as a percentage of the theoretical distance: Slip% = [(P×N − V×t) / (P×N)] × 100.

**(b) Four conditions affecting slip, with reasons**
1. Hull fouling/increased roughness — increases resistance, so actual distance falls for the same revolutions, increasing slip.
2. Weather and sea conditions — head wind/seas increase resistance and reduce propeller efficiency (propeller racing near the surface), increasing slip; a following sea can reduce or reverse it.
3. Draught, trim and displacement — a deeply laden ship has greater resistance, reducing speed for given RPM; in ballast the propeller may ventilate, losing thrust and increasing slip.
4. Propeller surface condition/damage — fouling, roughness or cavitation erosion disturbs flow over the blades, reducing efficiency and increasing slip even with unchanged revolutions and pitch.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Propeller Slip — Definition, Calculation & Affecting Conditions
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Part (a) (define slip) causes the most trouble despite being worth only 2 marks. Part (b) demands FOUR conditions WITH REASONS -- a bare word like 'fouling' or 'bad weather' earns nothing without explaining the mechanism (e.g. fouling increases resistance so the propeller can't achieve its theoretical advance speed at the same rpm).
