answers.title: Air-Type Radial Lip Stern Tube Seal (Pollution Prevention)
answers.question_as_set: Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the principle of operation of a radial lip stern tube sealing arrangement for an oil filled stern tube, which incorporates an air space and is designed to prevent pollution. (10)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw an aft seal with lip seals #1-#3 facing aft (seawater) and forward (oil), separated by a pressurised air chamber, an air control unit feeding the chamber, a forward seal tank, LO tank and a drain tank monitoring leakage.*

An air-type (void space) seal interposes a pressurised air chamber between the seawater seals and the oil seals, so oil and seawater are never in direct contact across a single lip.

**Air supply.** Control air is fed continuously into the void space at a small constant flow (~40–50 L/min), the regulator maintaining pressure slightly above ambient seawater pressure, following draught changes.

**Pollution prevention.** Since chamber pressure slightly exceeds sea pressure, any leakage across the aft lip seals is a harmless trickle of air bubbling outward — not oil; seawater cannot pass inward against the air pressure.

**Drain/monitoring.** The bottom of the air chamber connects to a drain tank in the engine room with a sight/level alarm: water indicates aft seawater-seal wear, oil indicates aft oil-seal wear — giving early warning without pollution occurring.

answers.title: Power Transmission Through Shafting; Coupling Bolt Stresses; Hydraulic Bolt Sketch
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain how power is transmitted through main propulsion shafting. (3)

(b) State THREE operational factors that may induce high stress in shaft coupling bolts. (3)

(c) Sketch a hydraulic type of shaft coupling bolt. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) How power is transmitted.** Power is a function of torque and rotational speed (P=2πNT); the shafting transmits the engine's torque to the propeller at essentially steady speed. Shaft sections are joined by flanged couplings, torque passing across each joint by friction grip between clamped flange faces (the primary mechanism with hydraulic bolts) and/or shear/bearing of accurately fitted coupling bolts. Propeller thrust is taken out separately at the thrust block.

**(b) Three operational factors inducing high bolt stress**
1. Torsional vibration/torque fluctuations — cyclic engine firing torque, especially near a barred speed range.
2. Shock torque loadings — propeller striking ice/debris, racing in heavy weather, crash-astern manoeuvres.
3. Shaft misalignment — bearing wear-down or hull deflections bending the shaft each revolution.

**(c) Hydraulic coupling bolt sketch.**
*Sketch instructions: draw two flanges with a hollow bolt through a reamed hole, a nut, a hydraulic jack screwed onto the bolt head with a piston and oil connection.*

The hydraulic jack stretches the bolt elastically with high-pressure oil; the nut is run down hand-tight while stretched; releasing pressure leaves the bolt under accurate pre-tension, clamping the flanges so torque transmits by friction.

answers.title: Combination Seal: Wrapped Bellows Face Seal + Lip Seal
answers.question_as_set: With reference to oil filled stern tubes: describe, with the aid of a sketch, the principle of operation of a combination seal, which incorporates a wrapped bellows radial face seal and a lip seal. (10)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw rotating/stationary flat annular faces (mechanical seal) outboard, a wrapped bellows/spring assembly pressing them together, a lip seal inboard, a void space between them draining to a leakage tank, and a rope guard outboard.*

This combination seal places two sealing principles in series: a radial face seal (mechanical seal) as the primary seawater seal outboard, and a radial lip seal as the primary oil seal inboard, with a monitored void space between.

**The radial face seal.** Two optically flat annular faces rub at right angles to the shaft axis; the rotating face turns with the shaft, the stationary face is fixed to the sternframe. The wrapped bellows/spring presses the faces together, accommodates axial movement and wear, and forms the static seal and drive without a sliding static joint.

**The lip seal.** Inboard of the void space, a radial lip seal retains stern tube lubricating oil, its lip pressed onto the liner by the oil's static head.

**The void space.** Drained to a leakage tank: seawater passing the face seal drains harmlessly inboard; oil weeping past the lip seal collects in the same tank rather than reaching the sea. Monitoring the tank's contents (oil or water) reveals which seal is deteriorating.

answers.title: Muff (SKF OK) Type Propeller Shaft Coupling
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a muff type propeller shaft coupling. (5)

(b) Describe how this type of coupling is connected. (5)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw two plain shaft ends butted together, a thin tapered inner sleeve spanning both, an alloy steel outer sleeve with matching taper fitted over it, a nut and seal ring forming a hydraulic jack, and press-up distance reference marks.*

**(b) Connection.** The plain shaft ends are aligned and butted; the tapered inner sleeve is positioned to span both equally, with the outer sleeve fitted over it. A clamping nut with seal ring forms an annular hydraulic jack; press-up oil pressure between nut and outer sleeve draws the outer sleeve up the taper of the inner sleeve, compressing the thin inner sleeve radially onto both shaft ends — torque is transmitted by friction grip alone, no keys or bolts. The press-up distance against reference marks confirms the designed grip. Separation oil is injected between the tapers during fitting to float the sleeves for smooth movement.

answers.title: Tilting Pad Shaft (Journal) Support Bearing
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to propeller shaft support bearings:

(a) describe, with the aid of a sketch, the operation of a tilting pad shaft bearing, indicating how the oil pressure is distributed; (5)

(b) explain why this type of bearing evolved, stating its advantages over plain bearings. (5)
answers.answer_text:
This is a tilting pad JOURNAL (shaft support) bearing, not the Michell thrust bearing — the sketch must show a radial arrangement.

*Sketch instructions: draw a shaft supported by three separate pivoted pads around the lower half of the journal, each with its own lobed pressure profile shown as a dashed curve rising from the leading edge, peaking near the trailing edge, and falling to zero at the pad exit.*

**(a) Operation.** As the shaft rotates, oil is dragged toward the leading edge of each pad; being free to pivot, the pad tilts to form a convergent wedge-shaped oil gap. Oil drawn into the wedge generates hydrodynamic pressure that lifts and supports the shaft with full fluid-film lubrication. Each pad develops its own pressure wedge; the shaft is supported by several separate pressure peaks rather than one single hump. Each pad is mounted on a spherical seat, letting it align axially with shaft slope or deflection.

**(b) Why evolved — advantages.** Multiple pads increase the number of oil wedges, giving greater overall load-carrying capacity, allowing shorter bearings and greater spacing. The self-adjusting tilt accommodates alignment changes from hull deflection or wear-down that a rigid plain bush cannot follow without edge-loading. Load distribution across pads reduces maximum oil film temperature per pad.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Tilting Pad Shaft (Journal) Support Bearing
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; the mark-earning point for tilting-pad bearings is that each pad can pivot to form its own optimal oil wedge angle regardless of load/speed changes, giving more even pressure distribution and better performance at varying loads than a plain fixed-profile bearing -- that adaptability, not just 'more oil film,' is the advantage to state.

answers.title: Keyless Propeller — Hydraulic (Wet) Fit & Withdrawal
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to a keyless propeller designed for hydraulic (wet) fit and withdrawal:

(a) describe, with the aid of a sketch, how the propeller is fitted to the tail shaft; (6)

(b) state TWO advantages compared to a dry fit; (2)

(c) explain how the thrust is transmitted without the use of a key and keyway. (2)
answers.answer_text:
This is the oil injection (wet) fit — not the Pilgrim nut dry fit and not a muff coupling.

*Sketch instructions: draw the tapered tail shaft, propeller hub with injection points connected to high-pressure hoses, a hydraulic nut, and a dial gauge measuring push-up.*

**(a)** The propeller boss has a plain tapered bore with circumferential oil distribution grooves fed through radial drillings. The propeller is pushed onto the taper to a firm seating; a hydraulic nut is fitted behind the hub. High-pressure oil injected into the grooves at the taper interface floats the hub on a pressurised oil film, almost eliminating friction. Oil pressure to the hydraulic nut then advances the propeller axially up the taper to a specified push-up distance on the dial gauge. The injection oil is released first (boss grips the cone with full designed interference), then the hydraulic nut pressure.

**(b) Two advantages vs dry fit.** No heating required, accurate repeatable grip achieved cold; easy controlled removal by re-injecting oil to float the joint, without heat or heavy pulling gear.

**(c) How thrust is transmitted.** Purely by friction: the push-up leaves the boss stretched elastically around the shaft cone, producing high radial contact pressure whose product with contact area and coefficient of friction gives a friction force far exceeding that needed to transmit torque and thrust with a safety margin.

answers.title: Tunnel Type Bow Thrusters — Multiple Units; Prime Movers & Transmission
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to tunnel type bow thrusters:

(a) explain why some vessels are fitted with more than one bow thruster; (2)

(b) discuss the options available in terms of prime mover and transmission systems. (8)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why more than one thruster.** Greater total thrust requirement — large vessels with high windage need more side thrust than one practicable tunnel can deliver. Redundancy and operational availability — ships depending on thrusters for berthing without tugs fit multiple units so one failure doesn't prevent safe manoeuvring.

**(b) Prime mover and transmission options**
1. Electric motor drive (most common) — a constant-speed AC motor drives the impeller through bevel gears, either with a Controllable Pitch Propeller (fast, stepless response) or a variable-speed drive with Fixed Pitch Propeller (simpler, robust propeller, costly converter).
2. Hydraulic motor drive — a power pack supplies a hydraulic motor at the tunnel unit; stepless reversible control, but lower transmission efficiency and more maintenance.
3. Direct diesel engine drive — a dedicated diesel drives the unit through a clutch, independent of the ship's electrical load, but with engine maintenance and slower response.

answers.title: Hydraulic Jacking to Check Bearing Loads; Load/Lift Graph
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to main propulsion shaft systems:

(a) describe a method of hydraulic jacking to check bearing loads; (5)

(b) sketch the Bearing Load versus Shaft Lift Dial Gauge Reading graph obtained by the method described in part (a), annotating the graph and how the characteristic of bearing load is obtained. (5)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Method.** A calibrated hydraulic jack is placed under the shaft close to the bearing; a dial gauge on the bearing housing reads shaft lift. Oil pressure is applied in increments, recording jack load and lift at each step; once the shaft lifts clear (limited to ~0.5mm, not until it touches the top of the bearing), the relationship becomes a straight line. The pressure is then released in increments, recording readings on the way down as well — friction gives a hysteresis loop between raising and lowering curves. The test is repeated at a defined ship condition.

**(b) The graph.**
*Sketch instructions: plot shaft lift (mm, vertical) against jack load (bar, horizontal). Draw a raising curve (initially flat/curved, becoming straight once the shaft lifts clear) and a lowering curve lying to the left of it due to jack friction. Extrapolate the straight portions of both back to zero lift, and draw the mean line between the two intercepts.*

The mean of the two straight-line extrapolations to zero lift gives the true jack load at which the bearing is just unloaded (friction errors cancelling); multiplied by a jack-position correction factor, this gives the bearing load.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Hydraulic Jacking to Check Bearing Loads; Load/Lift Graph
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Part (a) has a specific recurring gap: candidates forget that the shaft is jacked in BOTH directions -- raised AND lowered -- with both sets of readings recorded and plotted, not just jacked up until contact with the top of the bearing.

answers.title: Stern Tube Bearings: White Metal Failure; Merits of Non-Metallic Bearings
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to stern tube bearings:

(a) explain why white metal lined bearings are susceptible to failure; (5)

(b) outline the merits of non metallic bearings. (5)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why white metal is susceptible to failure.** Edge loading from the overhung propeller concentrates load at the aft bearing end. Low melting point/poor high-temperature strength means any oil-film loss (slow turning, loss of lubrication) causes wiping. Dependence on a perfect hydrodynamic film means low RPM (turning gear, slow steaming) risks boundary contact and damage. Water contamination from seal wear destroys the film and corrodes the white metal. Fatigue and bonding failure from cyclic loading can crack the lining.

**(b) Merits of non-metallic bearings.** Seawater lubrication — zero oil pollution, no oil seal to fail. Tolerance of contamination and poor lubrication — resilient polymer surfaces allow abrasive particles to embed/pass without seizure. Resilience and vibration damping — conforms to slight misalignment. Simplicity and reduced maintenance — no oil system, header tanks or oil analysis. Corrosion immunity — the material itself does not corrode in seawater.

answers.title: Hydraulic Coupling Bolt — Sketch, Advantages, Stresses
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a hydraulic type of shaft coupling bolt. (4)

(b) State the advantages of the arrangement in part (a) compared to conventional bolts. (3)

(c) State THREE operational factors that may induce high stress in shaft coupling bolts. (3)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)** As per Q4's sketch above.

**(b) Advantages compared to conventional bolts.** Accurate, repeatable pre-tension set directly by hydraulic pressure × piston area, evenly shared around the flange. No torsional or surface damage during tightening (bolt stretched axially, not twisted). Quick, easy and safe fitting/removal even after years in service — no drifts or flame cutting of seized bolts.

**(c)** As per Q4's three factors above (torsional vibration, shock torque loadings, shaft misalignment).

answers.title: Shaft Alignment Check Without Removing Coupling Bolts; Misalignment Effects
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe a method of checking main transmission shaft alignment which does not involve the removal of shaft coupling bolts. (5)

(b) State why the shaft alignment should be checked when the ship is afloat in a light ship condition. (1)

(c) A shaft system is found to be excessively misaligned so as to cause serious bending of the shaft. State what effect this could have on EACH of the following:

(i) the shaft coupling bolts; (1)

(ii) the shaft bearings. (1)

(d) State, with reasons, which of the effects in part (c) would cause the most concern. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) The bearing load (jack-up) method.** With couplings still bolted, alignment is verified by measuring the load each bearing carries and comparing with the calculated design value — as per Q10's jacking method, taken at each bearing in turn and compared against the alignment calculation.

**(b) Why check afloat in light ship condition.** The alignment must be verified in the condition for which it was calculated, with representative hull deflections: afloat (dry dock blocking distorts the hull), light ship giving the reference condition typically representing the worst case for alignment.

**(c)(i) Effect on coupling bolts.** The bend rotates with each revolution, subjecting the bolts to cyclic bending/tensile stress superimposed on pre-tension — leading to fatigue failure.

**(c)(ii) Effect on shaft bearings.** The shaft bears hard on the edges of individual bearings (edge loading), overloading some and unloading others, causing overheating and wiping.

**(d) Greatest concern.** The effect on coupling bolts is of greater concern — bearing damage develops progressively and reveals itself through rising temperatures, but bolt fatigue is cumulative, hidden and gives no warning; sudden fracture could part the coupling at sea with complete loss of propulsion.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Shaft Alignment Check Without Removing Coupling Bolts; Misalignment Effects
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Part (a) catches some candidates describing CRANKSHAFT deflection checks instead of the main transmission SHAFT alignment method actually asked for -- these are different procedures on different components.

answers.title: Power Transmission & Improved Coupling Bolt Design
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain how power is transmitted through main shafting. (2)

(b) State FOUR operational factors that may induce high stress in coupling bolts. (4)

(c) Sketch a coupling bolt of improved design. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)** As per Q4's power transmission explanation above.

**(b) Four operational factors**
1. Torsional vibration/torque fluctuations.
2. Shock torque loadings (ice, debris, crash-astern).
3. Propeller racing in heavy weather (repeated emergence/re-immersion).
4. Shaft misalignment (bearing wear-down, hull deflections).

**(c) Improved design sketch.** The hydraulically tensioned coupling bolt (as per Q4/Q12), tensioned by stretching hydraulically rather than by torque or flogging, giving accurate even pre-tension with no torsional stress and easy removal. (The older centre-rod type — a hollow bolt with a central rod heated/stretched to tension it — is also acceptable.)

answers.title: Podded Propulsion (360°): Advantages & Suited Vessel Types
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to vessels fitted with podded propulsion systems capable of being rotated through 360°:

(a) state the advantages claimed over conventional shafting and steering arrangements; (6)

(b) state, with reasons, the type of vessels that are most suited to this means of propulsion. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Advantages over conventional shafting/steering**
Superior manoeuvrability — full thrust directed through any angle, no reliance on a rudder deflecting the race.
Elimination of shafting, rudder and stern gear — no line shafting, stern tube sealing or rudder maintenance.
Space and design freedom — propulsion motor outside the hull frees machinery space.
Improved hydrodynamic efficiency — the pod propeller works in a clean wake, reducing appendage drag.
Reduced noise and vibration — no gearbox, even wake inflow.
Redundancy and operational flexibility with electric drive.

**(b) Vessel types most suited**
Cruise ships/large passenger vessels — already diesel-electric, need manoeuvrability and low noise.
Icebreakers/ice-class vessels — can direct full thrust in any direction and run astern-first through ice.
Ferries on tight schedules — frequent berthing without tugs.
DP vessels (offshore support, drill ships) — rapidly variable thrust in any direction for station-keeping.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Podded Propulsion (360°): Advantages & Suited Vessel Types
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Generally well attempted, but a recurring digression is candidates going off-topic to describe Controllable Pitch Propeller (CPP) systems, or describing the PROPELLER on a fixed shaft rotating 360 degrees -- podded propulsion means the whole propulsion pod (motor plus propeller) rotates, not just the blades or a CPP hub.

answers.title: Propeller Cavitation: Definition & Detrimental Effects
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to propeller cavitation:

(a) define cavitation; (2)

(b) describe FOUR detrimental effects of propeller cavitation. (8)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Definition.** Cavitation is the formation and subsequent collapse of vapour-filled cavities in the water at the propeller blades. Regions of high-velocity flow (chiefly on the suction face) experience a local pressure drop; where pressure falls below the water's vapour pressure, vapour cavities form, then collapse violently when carried into higher-pressure regions.

**(b) Four detrimental effects**
1. Erosion of blade material — cavity collapse produces intense local impact pressures, hammering the surface and tearing out particles, leaving spongy, pitted erosion.
2. Loss of thrust and efficiency — a vapour sheet blankets part of the blade, limiting lift; thrust breaks down while revolutions remain, slip increases and fuel consumption rises.
3. Noise and vibration — broadband underwater noise and fluctuating pressure impulses exciting hull and aft-end vibration.
4. Damage to adjacent components — rudder, stern frame and A-brackets suffer erosion; bent/eroded blades unbalance the propeller, accelerating stern tube bearing/seal wear.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Propeller Cavitation: Definition & Detrimental Effects
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Consistently good answers -- no recurring trap noted for this occurrence.

answers.title: Podded vs Azimuthing Thrusters; Pusher/Tractor; Tandem Pods
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to podded thrusters for main propulsion:

(a) distinguish between podded and azimuthing thrusters; (4)

(b) explain the meaning of thruster and tractor propellers, stating ONE advantage of tractor units;

(c) explain what is meant by tandem podded thrusters. (2) (4)
answers.answer_text:
Both pods and azimuthing thrusters steer through 360° — neither is fixed. The true distinction is where the motor is and how drive is transmitted.

**(a)** Azimuthing thruster — prime mover inside the hull, power transmitted mechanically down a steerable leg via shafts and bevel gears (Z-drive or L-drive); power limited by gear capacity. Podded thruster — the propulsion motor is inside the submerged pod itself, coupled directly to the propeller shaft, no gearing; only electrical power passes down through the slewing arrangement, permitting much higher power and efficiency.

**(b) Thruster (pusher) vs tractor.** Pusher — propeller at the aft end, working in the wake of the pod body. Tractor — propeller at the forward end, pulling the unit, meeting clean water ahead of the pod. Advantage of tractor: undisturbed inflow gives higher efficiency and reduced cavitation/vibration/noise.

**(c) Tandem podded thrusters.** A tandem pod carries two propellers — one pulling forward, one pushing aft — on the same pod, sharing total power/thrust so each is more lightly loaded, allowing greater total power on one unit with reduced cavitation.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Podded vs Azimuthing Thrusters; Pusher/Tractor; Tandem Pods
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Reasonably well answered, but a specific misconception recurs: candidates state that podded thrusters are FIXED/non-steerable, when steerability (360 degrees, like an azimuthing thruster) is actually one of their defining features -- the real distinction from azimuthing thrusters is where the prime mover sits (inside the pod vs inside the hull with mechanical drive down the leg).

answers.title: Shaft Alignment: Objectives, Conditions & Fair Curve Alignment
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to propeller shaft alignment:

(a) state the objectives of a satisfactory alignment; (3)

(b) state the conditions that must be met to achieve satisfactory alignment; (3)

(c) explain what is meant by fair curve alignment. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Objectives.** To distribute the total shafting weight among all bearings so each carries an acceptable load. To keep bending stresses and cyclic stresses at couplings within safe limits, avoiding fatigue. To ensure these conditions are maintained throughout the range of service conditions (loaded/ballast, hot/cold, hull deflections).

**(b) Conditions to be met.** Each bearing must carry load within its permissible band (no unloaded or overloaded bearings). Relative slope between shaft and bearing must be acceptable, particularly at the aft stern tube bearing. Alignment must remain acceptable under all operating conditions (hull deflections, thermal rise, wear-down).

**(c) Fair curve alignment.** A loaded shaft naturally deflects into a smooth elastic curve under its own weight and the overhung propeller. Fair curve alignment is the modern method that accepts this curvature: the shafting is treated as a continuous elastic beam, and calculation determines the vertical offset at which each bearing must be set so the shaft, resting on all bearings, lies along its natural deflected curve — each bearing carrying its intended load share, with acceptable bending stresses throughout.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Shaft Alignment: Objectives, Conditions & Fair Curve Alignment
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Poorly answered overall. Part (a) is mostly missed because candidates describe the EFFECTS OF MISALIGNMENT instead of the actual OBJECTIVES of satisfactory alignment (even bearing load distribution, avoiding excessive bending stress, maintaining acceptable bearing reaction margins). Part (c) (fair curve alignment) is very weakly understood -- most candidates just describe the jacking arrangement used to measure bearing loads without explaining the fair-curve CONCEPT itself (the shaft forming a smooth, gently curving line through all bearings under its own weight and thermal/hull-deflection conditions, rather than a straight line).

answers.title: Chief Engineer's Report — Stern Tube Oil Loss to Sea
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer on board a vessel which has lost 50 litres of lubricating oil from the stern tube system to sea overnight, write a report to the Superintendent Engineer outlining the actions taken to rectify the leakage and any other further recommendations. (10)
answers.answer_text:
The oil is stated to have gone TO SEA — this is a pollution incident with statutory reporting obligations. Claiming "it went to the bilge instead" scores zero; the answer must show both the practical engineering response and reporting knowledge.

**Model report structure:**
**1. Incident summary** — header tank level fall identified, soundings confirming loss to sea via the aft seal, no abnormal bearing temperatures, slight sheen observed.
**2. Immediate actions taken** — Master informed immediately; SOPEP/SMPEP pollution report transmitted to coastal State, flag Administration, Company (DPA); Oil Record Book Part I entry recording the discharge, signed by Chief Engineer and Master; header tank gravity head reduced to the minimum safe value to lower differential pressure and stem leakage; shaft RPM reduced; leakage rate assessed by hourly soundings; void space drained and checked to identify the failing seal; oil samples drawn for analysis; spare/standby seal ring activated where the design permits.
**3. Cause (preliminary)** — wear/damage of the aft seal lip rings, possibly aggravated by fishing line debris; confirmation requires diver inspection.
**4. Recommendations** — diver inspection and seal renewal at next port; replenishment of stern tube oil and consideration of an Environmentally Acceptable Lubricant (EAL); Class advised as applicable; SMS non-conformity report for fleet circulation.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Chief Engineer's Report — Stern Tube Oil Loss to Sea
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: A cautionary pattern across repeat sittings: many candidates take the path of least resistance and answer as if the oil stayed in the bilge (no pollution, no real incident to report), even when the question explicitly states the oil was lost TO SEA -- doing so scores zero regardless of how well-written the rest of the report is, since it ignores the actual pollution incident the question describes.

answers.title: Outboard Radial Lip Seal: Sketch & In-Situ Replacement (Vulcanising)
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch an outboard radial lip seal as fitted to an oil lubricated stern tube. (5)

(b) Explain the procedure for replacing the seal sketched in part (a) without removing the tailshaft. (5)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw the shaft with a chrome-steel/ceramic-coated liner, a seal housing bolted to the stern frame in split casing rings, four radial lip seal rings (#0-#3) with outer rings facing aft (seawater) and inner rings facing forward (oil), each pressed onto the liner by a garter spring.*

**(b) Replacing the seal without removing the tail shaft.** Access is gained in dry dock, or afloat by trimming/heeling to bring the seal clear, or using divers with a cofferdam. The header tank is drained down, the rope guard removed, and the shaft locked against turning. The split casing rings are unbolted to expose the old seal rings, which are cut through and removed; the liner is inspected for grooving.

**The key point:** since the shaft remains in place, a new endless seal ring cannot be slid over the propeller. Each new seal ring is supplied as an open ring, wrapped around the liner, and its ends joined in situ by hot vulcanising (bonding) — scarf-cut ends, bonding solution applied, clamped in a heated press at the specified temperature and time, then dressed smooth to restore an endless ring.

The bonded ring is seated with its garter spring, the split casing rings re-assembled, and the assembly pressure/leak tested before the header tank is refilled and the rope guard refitted.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Outboard Radial Lip Seal: Sketch & In-Situ Replacement (Vulcanising)
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Part (a) (sketch) is reliably strong, typically scoring 4-5 of the 5 marks; part (b) is weak -- candidates give generic stock answers rather than actually describing the in-situ replacement PROCEDURE, in particular the vulcanising (or equivalent) process that allows a new seal to be fitted and bonded without drawing the tail shaft.

answers.title: Fully Automatic DX System — LP Switch & HP Switch Faults
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a diagrammatic arrangement of a fully automatic direct expansion domestic refrigeration system. (6)

(b) Explain the operation of the Low Pressure switch. (2)

(c) State, with reasons, TWO possible faults that could cause the High Pressure switch to operate. (2)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw two rooms (e.g. meat room and veg room) each with a solenoid valve and TEV, a back pressure valve on the warmer room's suction, LP/HP switches sensing compressor suction and discharge, an oil separator, condenser with relief valve, drier and sight glass. Annotate room temperatures (e.g. meat room −10°C, veg room +4°C).*

**(b) LP switch operation.** The LP switch senses compressor suction pressure and provides automatic start/stop control. When all room thermostats are satisfied, their solenoids close, the compressor pumps down the low side, and suction pressure falls; at the cut-out setting the switch opens and stops the compressor. When a room warms up, its solenoid re-opens, suction pressure rises, and at the cut-in setting the switch closes and restarts the compressor. The differential between cut-in and cut-out prevents short cycling.

**(c) Two faults causing the HP switch to operate, with reasons**
Loss of condenser cooling water (failed pump, blocked suction) — heat of condensation cannot be rejected, so discharge pressure rises rapidly.
Fouled/scaled condenser tubes — reduced heat transfer raises condensing temperature and pressure.

Other acceptable: air/incondensable gases in the system; overcharge of refrigerant. Never say "faulty HP switch" — it must be a system fault.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Fully Automatic DX System — LP Switch & HP Switch Faults
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Strong sketches for part (a), but part (b) commonly stops halfway: candidates say the LP switch cuts the compressor OUT on falling pressure but omit that it also cuts back IN when pressure rises again -- both directions need stating. Part (c) needs reasons attached to each fault, and 'a faulty HP switch' is not itself an accepted answer -- it has to be an actual system fault (e.g. SW cooling failure, air in the condenser, overcharge) that causes the switch to trip.

answers.title: Undercooling & the Liquid–Suction Heat Exchanger
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to refrigeration systems:

(a) explain why undercooling of the refrigerant at the condenser outlet is desirable; (3)

(b) describe, with the aid of a sketch, how a heat exchanger could be incorporated in the circuit to enhance undercooling; (5)

(c) explain the possible consequences of the refrigerant having a dryness fraction at the compressor suction. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Why undercooling is desirable.** Increased refrigerating effect — liquid enters the expansion valve with lower enthalpy, so less flashes to vapour, giving more liquid in the evaporator per kg circulated. Prevents flash gas in the liquid line. Ensures solid liquid reaches the expansion valve.

**(b) Liquid-suction heat exchanger.**
*Sketch instructions: draw warm liquid from the condenser outlet in counterflow against cold suction vapour from the evaporator outlet, in a shell-and-coil or tube-in-tube arrangement.*

Warm liquid leaving the condenser flows through one side; cold vapour leaving the evaporator flows through the other in counterflow. Heat transfers through the tube wall from liquid to vapour — true heat exchange, not flash cooling. The liquid is subcooled before the expansion valve; the suction vapour is superheated, protecting against liquid carry-over.

**Trap:** an open flash economiser is just a vessel with no heat-transfer surface (cooling by partial evaporation) — it is not a heat exchanger and scores nothing.

**(c) Consequences of a dryness fraction at compressor suction.** Liquid slugging/mechanical damage — incompressible liquid droplets can cause broken valve plates, damaged pistons. Loss of lubrication — liquid entering the crankcase washes oil from cylinder walls and dilutes the sump oil.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Undercooling & the Liquid–Suction Heat Exchanger
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Part (a) is handled well, sometimes using a graph to support the explanation. Part (b) is where most marks are lost: a genuine heat exchanger needs TWO separate fluid streams (one being heated, one being cooled) -- an arrangement using a second expansion valve/flash-off stage instead of a true two-flow heat exchanger doesn't meet the definition, and the heat exchanger must be positioned to use the cooler liquid line (not warm gas before the condenser) to subcool the warmer liquid leaving the condenser.

answers.title: Superheat & Undercooling on the Pressure–Enthalpy Diagram
answers.question_as_set:
(a) With reference to a vapour compression refrigeration plant, explain why EACH of the following conditions are desirable:

(i) superheating at the compressor suction; (3)

(ii) undercooling at the condenser outlet. (3)

(b) Describe, with the aid of a Pressure-Enthalpy diagram, how the evaporator cooling load is affected by the conditions stated in part (a). (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Why superheating is desirable.** Protects the compressor from liquid carry-over (no liquid slugging, no oil dilution). Confirms full use of the evaporator (all liquid evaporated). Enables TEV control, which regulates by maintaining a set degree of superheat.

**(a)(ii) Why undercooling is desirable.** Increased refrigerating effect (lower enthalpy at the expansion valve). Prevents flash gas in the liquid line. Ensures solid liquid at the expansion valve.

**(b) Effect on cooling load, with P-h diagram.**
*Sketch instructions: draw the basic cycle (1-2 compression, 2-3 condensation, 3-4 expansion at constant enthalpy, 4-1 evaporation). Show subcooling moving point 3 left to 3' (and 4 to 4' correspondingly), and superheat moving point 1 right to 1'.*

The refrigerating effect per kg is the width of the evaporation line (h1−h4). With subcooling, h4 falls, increasing the refrigerating effect with no increase in compressor work — a genuine COP gain. With useful superheat (gained within the cooled space), h1 rises, adding to the refrigerating effect; superheat gained outside the cooled space adds nothing useful, only increasing compressor work.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Superheat & Undercooling on the Pressure–Enthalpy Diagram
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Part (a) is fine, but part (b) exposes weak P-h diagram literacy -- many candidates can't sketch even a simple Pressure-Enthalpy diagram or connect superheat/undercooling to the resulting change in evaporator cooling load (extended vaporisation length / increased refrigerating effect), despite this being a frequently recurring question.

(i) North West Europe in winter; (2)

(ii) Arabian Gulf in summer; (2)

(c) state, with reasons, FOUR locations within the accommodation that conditioned air must not be recirculated. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Comfort zone boundaries.** Approximately 21°C to 27°C dry bulb, 30% to 70% RH, controlled toward the centre (~22–25°C, 50% RH).

**(b)(i) NW Europe winter.** Cold, low-moisture outside air is heated (dropping RH well below comfort band), then humidified (dry steam/water spray), then reheated as necessary.

**(b)(ii) Arabian Gulf summer.** Hot, very humid air is cooled below its dew point (dehumidification, condensate drains away), leaving the coil cool and near-saturated, then slightly reheated to bring RH down into the comfort band. *(Never say the air is humidified after cooling — it is already near-saturated.)*

**(c) Four locations where conditioned air must not be recirculated**
Galley — cooking odours, grease, smoke.
Sanitary spaces — offensive odours and bacteria.
Ship's hospital — infectious organisms.
Laundry/drying rooms — high moisture, lint, detergent fumes.

occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Reasonably good overall; the main weak spot is sketch quality for the psychrometric/comfort-zone points rather than the written content.

answers.title: Purpose of Components — Thermostat, TEV, HP Cut-out, Safety Head, Unloader
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to a vapour compression refrigeration plant, explain the purpose of EACH of the following:

(a) room thermostat; (2)

(b) expansion valve; (2)

(c) high pressure cut out; (2)

(d) safety head; (2)

(e) unloader. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Room thermostat.** Senses room temperature and opens/closes the liquid-line solenoid valve to give automatic independent control of each room.

**(b) Expansion valve.** Reduces pressure from condenser to evaporator pressure at constant enthalpy, and regulates flow to maintain a set superheat at the evaporator outlet.

**(c) High pressure cut out.** A safety device sensing discharge pressure, stopping the compressor before a dangerous pressure ruptures a component; normally hand-reset.

**(d) Safety head.** Protects a reciprocating compressor against liquid slugging — the cylinder head/discharge valve seat is spring-loaded and lifts to relieve excessive pressure from a liquid slug, then re-seats automatically.

**(e) Unloader.** A capacity control device that holds cylinder suction valves open so those cylinders idle, matching compressor capacity to cooling demand in steps and reducing starting torque.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Purpose of Components — Thermostat, TEV, HP Cut-out, Safety Head, Unloader
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; a common trap in similar 'purpose of components' questions is describing HOW a component works rather than WHY it's fitted (its purpose) -- keep each answer to purpose/function, not full operating detail.

answers.title: Refrigerant Faults — Air, Oil, Moisture, Undercharge, Overcharge
answers.question_as_set:
In a vapour compression refrigeration system, state how EACH of the following faults are indicated and how they are remedied:

(a) air in the refrigerant; (2)

(b) oil in the refrigerant; (2)

(c) moisture in the refrigerant; (2)

(d) undercharge of the refrigerant; (2)

(e) overcharge of the refrigerant. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Air.** Indication: high discharge pressure (air's partial pressure adds to refrigerant pressure). Remedy: purge from the condenser top with cooling water running.

**(b) Oil.** Indication: reduced cooling effect (oil coats evaporator surfaces), falling sump level. Remedy: drain oil from evaporator, overhaul the discharge oil separator.

**(c) Moisture.** Indication: icing-up of the expansion valve (intermittent cooling, recovers when warmed). Remedy: renew the drier cartridge; in bad cases evacuate and recharge dry.

**(d) Undercharge.** Indication: bubbles in the sight glass, low suction/discharge pressures. Remedy: find and repair the leak first, then recharge.

**(e) Overcharge.** Indication: high discharge pressure (excess liquid floods condenser tubes), high receiver level. Remedy: remove excess charge to a recovery cylinder.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Refrigerant Faults — Air, Oil, Moisture, Undercharge, Overcharge
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Mostly well answered; the one flagged issue is candidates drifting toward fire-fighting/emergency response content rather than staying on refrigerant-fault indication and remedy, which is what the question actually asks for.

answers.title: Provision Plant Sketch & Sequence of Events on Demand
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a diagrammatic arrangement of a fully automatic provision refrigeration system incorporating a number of cold rooms. (5)

(b) Explain the sequence of events from a demand for refrigerating effect in a cold room until the room has reached its desired temperature. (5)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)** As per Q1's sketch, extended to multiple rooms with individual solenoid/TEV per room, back pressure valve, oil separator, drier and sight glass.

**(b) Sequence of events**
1. Room temperature rises above the thermostat set point.
2. The thermostat energises the solenoid valve, which opens.
3. Refrigerant flows through the TEV to the evaporator and boils, absorbing heat.
4. Suction pressure rises; at the LP switch's cut-in setting, the LP switch starts the compressor (not the thermostat directly).
5. Normal running — compressor draws vapour, compresses and discharges through the oil separator to the condenser; liquid passes via the drier and sight glass.
6. Room reaches desired temperature; the thermostat de-energises the solenoid, which closes.
7. Pump-down — the compressor continues, clearing refrigerant from the evaporator, until suction pressure reaches the LP cut-out and the compressor stops.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Provision Plant Sketch & Sequence of Events on Demand
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: The sketch in part (a) is usually good, but part (b) drifts into describing how the individual COMPONENTS work rather than the actual SEQUENCE OF EVENTS asked for. A specific, recurring error is stating the solenoid valve opens when room temperature FALLS (it's the opposite -- rising room temperature is what triggers the thermostat, opens the solenoid, and starts the sequence toward the compressor running) -- the answer needs to be a chronological story from rising temperature through to the room reaching its set point again.

answers.title: Comfort Zone Definition, Objectives & Recirculation (II)
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to a ship's air conditioning plant:

(a) define the term comfort zone; (2)

(b) state the objectives of maintaining the conditioned air within the comfort zone; (3)

(c) state, with reasons, FIVE areas from which the conditioned air must not be recirculated. (5)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Comfort zone.** The area on the psychrometric chart, bounded by temperature and RH limits, within which most people feel comfortable — the four boundary points approximately 21°C/30%RH, 21°C/70%RH, 27°C/30%RH, 27°C/70%RH.

**(b) Objectives, stated as positive aims.** Comfort, health and wellbeing of crew/passengers. Efficiency and safety of the crew (fatigue and heat stress degrade alertness). Protection of the accommodation and equipment (humidity limits preventing condensation/corrosion or excessive dryness).

**(c) Five areas not to recirculate, with reasons**
Galley, sanitary spaces, ship's hospital, laundry/drying rooms (as per Q4), plus pantries — food odours and heat from hot presses.

These must all be spaces that ARE supplied with conditioned air in the first place — machinery spaces, paint lockers, holds etc. are wrong answers since conditioned air is never sent there.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Comfort Zone Definition, Objectives & Recirculation (II)
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: A genuinely confused topic across sittings. Part (a) needs actual temperature/humidity VALUES at the comfort-zone boundary points, not just a description. Part (b) asks for the OBJECTIVES of staying in the comfort zone (occupant comfort, health, productivity) -- many candidates instead describe symptoms of getting it WRONG (dry throat, sweating, mould), which is the opposite of what's asked. Part (c) is a location question -- conditioned air is never supplied to machinery spaces, cargo holds, chain lockers or paint lockers in the first place, so naming those as 'recirculation exclusions' is wrong; the correct list is spaces like hospital/sick bay, galley and laundry, where air must not be recirculated back into the general system.

answers.title: AHU Block Diagram & Prevention of Bacterial Growth
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a block diagram of a fully automated air conditioning system for accommodation spaces, annotating the relevant temperatures and relative humidities throughout the system. (7)

(b) Describe how bacteria are prevented from multiplying to a harmful level in an air conditioning system. (3)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw a central AHU: outside air and recirculated air mixing at dampers, through a filter, over a cooling coil, past a heating coil and steam humidifier, driven by a supply fan through zone reheat coils to the conditioned spaces, with a return trunking loop. Annotate state points e.g. outside air 35°C/40%RH, recirculated air 23°C/55%RH, mixed air 28°C/48%RH, supply air 16°C/85%RH, delivered 23°C/55%RH.*

Annotating each state point and labelling every component is what scores full marks — an unannotated block diagram loses most of them.

**(b) Preventing bacterial growth.** Eliminate standing water — drain trays kept clear and self-draining. Use dry steam for humidification rather than water sprays, avoiding the warm-water reservoir bacteria colonise. Regular cleaning/renewal of filters and biocide treatment of coils/trays.

answers.title: DX System Sketch & FIVE Thermodynamic Properties of a Refrigerant
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a diagrammatic arrangement of a fully automatic direct expansion domestic refrigeration system. (5)

(b) State, with reasons, FIVE desirable thermodynamic properties of a refrigerant. (5)
answers.answer_text:
Four plain boxes (compressor/condenser/expansion valve/evaporator) scores zero at management level. Full marks need LP/HP cut-outs, oil separator, condenser relief valve, drier, sight glass, solenoid + thermostat, TEV adjacent to its cold room, and annotated room temperatures.

**(b) Five thermodynamic properties, with reasons**
High latent heat of vaporisation — smaller mass flow for the required refrigerating effect.
Low specific volume of suction vapour — smaller compressor displacement for a given duty.
Evaporating pressure above atmospheric — leakage is outward and detectable, not inward (air/moisture ingress).
Moderate condensing pressure — lighter scantlings, less compression work.
Critical temperature well above condensing temperature — ensures the refrigerant can actually be condensed.

Trap: COP is a ratio (a result), not a thermodynamic property; "non-toxic/cheap/environmentally friendly" are desirable but not thermodynamic.

answers.title: Compressor Lubrication — Synthetic Oils, Carry-over, Oil Separator
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to the lubrication of refrigeration compressors:

(a) state the advantage of using fully synthetic oils; (2)

(b) explain why oil may be carried over from the compressor; (3)

(c) describe a device which returns oil from the compressor discharge to the compressor sump; (3)

(d) state TWO reasons why an accumulation of oil in the evaporator is undesirable. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Advantage of fully synthetic oils.** Excellent miscibility with modern refrigerants and chemical stability across the working temperature range; very low wax content and pour point, so they don't deposit wax in cold parts of the system as mineral oils can.

**(b) Why oil is carried over.** Normal cylinder lubrication mist swept out with discharge gas; refrigerant dissolved in crankcase oil boiling out on start-up (oil foaming); mechanical wear or overfilling.

**(c) Oil separator.** A vessel in the discharge line: hot gas enters and impinges on baffle plates, the velocity drop and direction change throwing oil droplets out of the gas stream; oil collects at the bottom, and a float-operated needle valve returns it to the crankcase using the discharge-to-suction pressure difference, while cleaned gas continues to the condenser.

**(d) Two reasons oil accumulation in the evaporator is undesirable.** Reduced heat transfer (insulating film on tubes). Loss of compressor lubrication (oil missing from the sump risks bearing wear/seizure).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Compressor Lubrication — Synthetic Oils, Carry-over, Oil Separator
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; part (c) (device returning oil to the sump) should describe an actual oil separator (gas velocity reduced, oil droplets coalesce and drain back via a float-controlled return line), not just 'an oil separator is fitted' without describing its operating principle.

answers.title: Comfort Zone Boundary Points (Trott & Welch) & Location Control
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to ships air conditioning plants:

(a) state the temperatures and relative humidities at EACH of the points that are regarded as the boundaries of the comfort zone; (2)

(b) explain how the temperatures and relative humidities could be maintained within the comfort zone when the ship is in EACH of the following locations:

(i) North West Europe in winter; (2)

(ii) Arabian Gulf in summer; (2)

(c) state, with reasons, FOUR locations within the accommodation that conditioned air must not be recirculated. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Boundary points (per Trott & Welch).** Approximately 18°C at 72% RH, 22°C at 32% RH, 24°C at 72% RH, and 27°C at 32% RH — the envelope sloping so a lower temperature is needed for comfort at higher humidity.

**(b)(i) NW Europe winter.** Minimum fresh air mixed with warm recirculated air to conserve heat; the mixed air is heated, humidified with dry steam, and reheated as required.

**(b)(ii) Arabian Gulf summer.** Hot, humid outside air mixed with recirculated air (already ~23°C/55%RH); cooled below dew point (dehumidification), then reheated to the supply condition — no humidification needed since the air already holds ample moisture.

answers.title: Fault Diagnosis — Pressure, Cycling, Cooling Failure, Noise
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to a domestic refrigeration plant, state TWO causes of EACH of the following conditions, stating how EACH cause may be rectified:

(a) excessive pressure; (2)

(b) low pressure at evaporator suction; (2)

(c) compressor cycling; (2)

(d) compressor running for long periods but not lowering the temperature in the cold rooms; (2)

(e) compressor operating noisily. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Excessive pressure.** Loss of condenser cooling water — restore flow. Air/incondensable gases — purge from the condenser.

**(b) Low suction pressure.** Undercharge (leak) — repair and recharge. Restricted/blocked expansion valve or drier (icing, dirt) — renew drier, clean valve.

**(c) Compressor cycling.** Undercharge — repair leak, recharge. LP switch differential too narrow — widen the cut-in/cut-out differential.

**(d) Running long but not cooling.** Evaporator heavily frosted/iced (insulating the coil) — defrost. Oil accumulated in the evaporator — drain oil, overhaul the oil separator.

**(e) Noisy operation.** Liquid/oil slugging — throttle the suction valve, correct the TEV setting/overcharge. Worn bearings/gudgeon pins/big ends — overhaul the compressor.

answers.title: AC Faults — Trunking, Drains, Capacity Control & Legionnaires' Disease
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to ships' air conditioning systems:

(a) state the effects of EACH of the following faults:

(i) corroded return air trunkings; (2)

(ii) blocked evaporator drains; (2)

(iii) defective capacity control. (2)

(b) state the main health hazard that may arise in the air conditioning plant, stating the conditions that need to arise and the measures that should be taken to prevent this occurring. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Corroded return air trunking.** Ambient air (e.g. from a machinery space the trunking passes through) leaks in and dilutes the return air, altering its temperature/humidity; the plant must then work harder, increasing load and losing control of the conditioned space.

**(a)(ii) Blocked evaporator drains.** Condensate cannot drain, so the tray floods: water carries over into the supply air, and stagnant standing water becomes a breeding ground for Legionella.

**(a)(iii) Defective capacity control.** The plant can no longer modulate output to match load — either overcooling with short-cycling, or failing to meet demand on a hot day, so the spaces drift outside the comfort zone.

**(b) Main health hazard.** Legionnaires' disease, caused by Legionella pneumophila inhaled in aerosolised water droplets. Conditions required: stagnant water; warm temperature (~20–45°C); a nutrient source (sludge, scale, debris); and a means of aerosolising the water. Prevention: eliminate standing water; keep the system clean and disinfected; use dry steam rather than water-spray humidification; periodic biocide treatment.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: AC Faults — Trunking, Drains, Capacity Control & Legionnaires' Disease
occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: Part (a)(i) produces some very wide-of-the-mark answers -- corroded return-air trunking allowing rust into the system gets linked to implausible health effects (choking, oxygen depletion, CO2 formation) rather than the actual mechanism: the correct answer is that the fault lets ambient (unconditioned) air leak INTO the return duct, diluting the conditioned air and reducing the system's effective cooling/dehumidifying capacity -- and even candidates who identify the dilution effect often fail to follow through to what that does to the plant's performance.

answers.title: Steering Gear Checks on Taking Over a Vessel Without Handover
answers.question_as_set: As Chief Engineer Officer appointed to a newly acquired older vessel, compile a list of all the checks that would be required of the ship's steering gear and associated equipment, given that no hand over from the previous owners had taken place. (10)
answers.answer_text:
**1. Documentation and records review.** Maker's manuals and schematics; Class certificates and survey status; planned maintenance records and defect history; steering gear test logbook; spare parts inventory verified against actual stock; confirm operating/changeover instructions posted on the bridge and steering flat (SOLAS requirement).

**2. Steering flat — visual inspection.** Cleanliness, lighting, access/escape routes; communications between bridge and steering flat tested; check for oil leaks at rams, glands and hoses; security of foundations and absence of corrosion.

**3. Hydraulic system.** Oil level in reservoirs and replenishment tank (capable of recharging at least one system, with low-level alarm); take an oil sample for analysis since condition history is unknown; filter condition; verify relief/shock valve settings against maker's figures; position of isolating valves.

**4. Power units, pumps and electrical supply.** Confirm two power units; megger test the motor windings; two separate supply circuits plus emergency source connection; verify motor protection (short-circuit, overload/loss-of-phase alarms, no automatic overload trip); running indicators and power-failure alarms on the bridge.

**5. Operational tests (SOLAS).** Main gear 35°-35° (and 35°-30°) in ≤28 seconds; auxiliary 15°-15° in ≤60 seconds; test all remote controls and changeover procedures; check rudder angle indicators; test emergency power supply.

**6. Alarms and emergency arrangements.** Test low oil level, low pressure, hydraulic lock and power-failure alarms; verify automatic isolating arrangements; carry out an emergency steering drill.

**7. Crew familiarisation.** Brief and drill watchkeepers and engineers on the layout, changeover and emergency operation, since none of the present crew has prior knowledge of this installation.

**Key idea:** "no handover" means independent verification (oil sampling, megger tests, checking actual valve settings and spares) rather than relying on records alone.

answers.title: Steering Gear Regulations; Pipe Coupling Failure & Single Failure Concept
answers.question_as_set:
(a) State the regulations pertaining to the main and auxiliary steering gear with reference to EACH of the following:

(i) rudder angle and time of operation; (2)

(ii) electrical supply. (3)

(b) With reference to a hydraulic steering gear, explain EACH of the following:

(i) the factors that may contribute to the failure of a hydraulic pipe coupling; (2)

(ii) what is meant by the single failure concept. (3)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)(i) Rudder angle and time.** Main gear: 35° one side to 35° the other, and 35° to 30°, in not more than 28 seconds at deepest draught and maximum ahead service speed. Auxiliary: 15° to 15° in not more than 60 seconds, at deepest draught and half maximum ahead service speed or 7 knots, whichever is greater.

**(a)(ii) Electrical supply.** Two exclusive circuits fed directly from the main switchboard (one may run via the emergency switchboard), run separately as far as practicable. Short-circuit protection and overload alarm for each circuit/motor (audible and visual, e.g. on the bridge); no automatic overload trip; loss-of-phase alarm; running indicators on the bridge and at the main machinery control position.

**(b)(i) Factors contributing to pipe coupling failure.** Vibration fatiguing the joint; pressure surges/shock loading from the rudder in heavy weather; corrosion; ageing seals/O-rings; incorrect assembly; wrong-specification materials; inadequate pipe support.

**(b)(ii) Single failure concept.** No single failure in the steering gear should result in total loss of steering capability. A failure (burst pipe, oil loss, one power unit failing) must be detectable and isolable, leaving the remaining components able to maintain steering. For tankers/gas carriers of 10,000 GT and up, steering capability must be regained within 45 seconds of a single failure, achieved through duplicated power units, isolatable piping, and low-level/low-pressure alarms.

answers.title: Compensated Control System for an Active Fin Stabiliser
answers.question_as_set: Describe, with the aid of a block diagram, a compensated control system for an active fin stabilisation unit. (10)
answers.answer_text:
Active fin stabilisers reduce roll by projecting fins into the water flow and tilting them to an angle of attack, generating a hydrodynamic lift that produces a righting moment. Because lift depends on the square of ship speed, the system is only effective when the ship is making way.

*Sketch instructions: draw a gyro unit (sensing roll) feeding a compensating unit (angle + rate + acceleration terms) to a comparator (demand vs actual fin position feedback), through an amplifier to a hydraulic unit (servo valve + ram), driving the fin, which acts on the ship in the seaway subject to wave disturbance, with the ship's resulting roll sensed again by the gyro (outer loop) and fin position fed back to the comparator (inner loop).*

A system responding only to roll angle is unsatisfactory — at maximum roll the ship is momentarily stationary and about to roll back on its own, so angle-only correction applies force at the wrong moment. The compensated (three-term) system combines roll angle, roll velocity (the main damping term) and roll acceleration (providing anticipatory lead to cancel system lags):

demanded fin angle ∝ (k1×roll angle) + (k2×roll velocity) + (k3×roll acceleration)

The demanded fin angle is compared with actual fin position feedback (inner loop); any error drives the hydraulic actuator to reposition the fin. The ship's resulting roll is sensed again by the gyro (outer/master loop), and the cycle repeats. The unit also includes a fin-angle limiter, speed compensation, and provision for manual control and fin housing in harbour.

answers.title: Active Fin Stabilisers — Preference, Suitability & Partial Damping
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to activated fin stabilisers, explain EACH of the following:

(a) why such units are preferred to passive tanks in large vessels; (3)

(b) why these units are preferred for passenger and fast cargo ships; (3)

(c) why partial, rather than maximum damping of ship movement in heavy weather, is advisable for reasons other than overstressing the fin stocks and activating gear. (4)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Fins vs passive tanks in large vessels.** Fin lift is proportional to the square of speed and to fin area; a large, fast vessel has ample speed and hull length for fins of adequate area, developing a large stabilising moment for comparatively little weight and space. A passive tank would need an enormous water mass to match this, costing space, deadweight and raising the centre of gravity.

**(b) Fins for passenger and fast cargo ships.** These ships operate at high, steady speeds — exactly where fins are most effective. The anticipatory response (sensing angle, velocity, acceleration) holds roll to small angles, giving passenger comfort and protecting cargo, while allowing speed to be maintained in a seaway.

**(c) Why partial rather than maximum damping.** In heavy weather, irregular waves mean the ship's roll is no longer smooth and predictable; a system driven hard for maximum correction can apply its force out of phase with the actual roll, reinforcing rather than opposing it. A ship held rigidly upright also loses its natural ability to "give" to the sea, increasing hull and fin stresses. Removing all roll forces the fins to work continuously near their stall angle, where lift becomes unpredictable. Partial damping keeps the fins in phase, lets the ship ride naturally, and avoids stall.

answers.title: Partial vs Maximum Damping — Simplified Explanation
answers.answer_text:
A more concise restatement of Q4(c) above, for use where the question is asked on its own.

First, in heavy weather the waves are irregular, so the roll is not a smooth, predictable motion; a system driven hard to cancel it completely can apply its corrective force out of step with the actual roll, pushing the ship the same way it is already rolling and making things worse. Second, a ship allowed to roll a little can "give" to the waves and ride them easily, whereas one held bolt upright resists the full wave force directly into the hull and fins. Third, removing all roll forces the fins to work continuously near their stall angle, where a sudden loss of lift makes them unreliable exactly when needed most. Partial damping keeps the fins in phase, lets the ship ride naturally, and keeps the fins clear of stall.

answers.title: Rotary Vane Steering Gear — Circuit, Leak Operation, Advantages
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a rotary vane steering and hydraulic circuit showing 2 x 50% units and the directional control valves. (6)

(b) Describe how the system in part (a) can still operate should an oil leak occur. (2)

(c) State the advantages of rotary vane compared to four ram steering gear. (2)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw the rotary vane actuator on the rudder stock with shock/relief valves either side, isolating valves, two independent 50% power units each with its own pump, motor, directional control valve (D.C.V.) and reservoir, and a common storage tank with a low-level alarm.*

**(a)** The rotary vane actuator is keyed directly to the rudder stock: a rotor with vanes turns between fixed stator vanes, oil pumped into one set of chambers turning the rudder one way, the other set turning it the other way. Each 50% power unit has its own fixed-delivery pump and reversing directional control valve; both units together give full slewing speed, either alone gives half speed.

**(b) Operation with an oil leak.** The two power units are completely independent. A low-level alarm on the affected reservoir gives early warning; the faulty unit or leaking section is isolated by closing its isolating valves, stopping further loss. The sound 50% unit continues supplying the actuator, so steering is maintained at reduced rate — the single-failure principle in action.

**(c) Advantages over four-ram gear.** Far more compact and lighter (torque applied directly to the stock, no rams/crossheads/tiller/Rapson-slide linkage); fewer moving parts and less maintenance; constant torque throughout the rudder angle (a four-ram's torque varies with angle); readily gives larger rudder angles; uses less oil; runs more smoothly and quietly.

answers.title: Hydraulic Steering Gear — Couplings, Locking, Isolation, Single Failure
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to a hydraulic steering gear, explain EACH of the following:

(a) the factors that may contribute to the failure of a hydraulic pipe coupling; (2)

(b) why it is of the utmost importance that in the event of a hydraulic system failure that the rudder is locked and isolation of the affected area is achieved as soon as possible; (2)

(c) the problems that may occur when locking the rudder in heavy weather; (2)

(d) why hydraulic locking is preferable to mechanical means; (2)

(e) what is meant by the single failure concept. (2)
answers.answer_text:
**(a)** As per Q2(b)(i) above — vibration, pressure surges, corrosion, ageing seals, incorrect assembly, inadequate support.

**(b) Why locking and isolation are urgent.** A hydraulic failure removes the gear's ability to hold the rudder, so water forces will swing it hard over, leaving the ship both unable to steer and turning uncontrollably — a serious hazard in traffic. Locking keeps the rudder on a safe heading during repairs; rapid isolation stops continued oil loss, conserving enough for the sound unit and confining the fault.

**(c) Problems locking in heavy weather.** Wave and slamming loads are resisted entirely by the locking arrangement and rudder stock instead of being relieved by the gear, risking overstressing or damage; getting the rudder to the desired position and holding it accurately amidships is also difficult with heavy seas constantly forcing it one way and the other.

**(d) Why hydraulic locking is preferable.** Trapping oil on both sides of the rams/vanes holds the rudder on an incompressible but still slightly "giving" oil column that can absorb shock through relief/shock valves, cushioning wave loads. It is quick to apply and release from the steering gear itself. A mechanical lock (clamp/pin) applies a rigid, unyielding restraint that transmits full shock loading into the structure and takes longer to fit/remove.

**(e) Single failure concept.** As per Q2(b)(ii) above.

answers.title: Reading a Rotary Vane Circuit Diagram (Component Identification)
answers.answer_text:
The rotary vane actuator: the stator (outer housing) is bolted to the ship's structure with fixed vanes projecting inward; the rotor, keyed directly to the rudder stock, carries the rotor vanes, dividing the housing into working chambers connected by oil ports.

Two 50% power units, each with its own motor-driven pump: both together give full slewing rate, either alone gives half speed. Direction valves (reversing directional control valves), one per pump, set whether the rudder goes port or starboard. An isolation valve between the actuator and power units allows a failed section to be shut off. Shock valves near the actuator relieve sudden pressure surges from wave impact; relief valves at the pumps protect against sustained overpressure. The reservoir supplies the pumps and receives returns.

**Operation.** Each pump delivers through its direction valve into one set of chambers, turning the rudder stock; displaced oil from the opposite chambers returns to tank. Reversing the direction valve reverses the rudder. The isolation valve satisfies the single-failure principle by letting a defective branch be shut off.

answers.title: Rotary Vane — Continued Operation on a Leak (Standalone)
answers.answer_text: Same content as Q6(b) above: the two independent 50% units, low-level alarm detection, isolation of the leaking section, and continued operation at reduced rate on the sound unit — with shock valves still protecting the actuator throughout.

answers.title: Four-Ram Steering Gear — Five Ram/Valve Combinations
answers.question_as_set: Sketch a hydraulic circuit for a FOUR ram steering gear that allows FIVE different ram combinations to be used, identifying EACH ram and valve combination. (10)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw four rams on the tiller (upper pair 1&2, lower pair 3&4) with isolating valves V1-V4, pair bypass valves BU/BL, two reversible variable-delivery pumps P1/P2 each with a pump isolating valve IP1/IP2, and a make-up tank with low-level alarm.*

Pressurising the left cylinders (1&3) turns the rudder one way, the right cylinders (2&4) the other. The five combinations:

**1.** P1+P2, all four rams, all valves open, bypasses closed — full speed + full torque (normal seagoing, 35–30° in 28s).
**2.** P1 only, all four rams — full torque, half speed (heavy weather / P2 down).
**3.** P2 only, all four rams — full torque, half speed (P1 isolated for maintenance).
**4.** P1+P2, upper pair only (V3/V4 closed, BL open) — full speed, half torque (light steering, fine weather).
**5.** P1 only, upper pair only — half speed, half torque (economy/standby).

In combinations 4 and 5 the lower pair is shut off and its bypass opened so it floats freely with the tiller rather than being hydraulically locked — the same valving lets a defective pump or leaking cylinder be isolated while steering continues on the remaining rams.

occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: No examiner commentary logged for this occurrence; the five combinations for a four-ram gear typically cover all four rams together, then various pairs/singles isolated via the valve arrangement -- each combination needs its specific ram(s) and valve state identified, not just the full-power configuration.

answers.title: Four-Ram Steering Gear — Combinations 6 and 7 (Lower Pair)
answers.answer_text:
**6.** P1+P2, lower pair only (V1/V2 closed, BU open) — full speed, half torque (light steering in fine weather, on the lower pair).
**7.** P1 only, lower pair only — half speed, half torque (economy/standby, on the lower pair).

Here the upper pair is isolated and its bypass opened so it travels freely with the tiller — these two combinations simply transfer the half-torque modes onto the other pair, useful when a cylinder or valve in the upper pair is defective.

answers.title: Sluggish Steering Gear After Heavy Weather
answers.question_as_set:
The steering gear operation of a vessel that recently experienced a heavy storm is found to be abnormally sluggish.

(a) State FIVE reasons for possible malfunction of the gear. (5)

(b) State the corrective actions that may be carried out at sea, that will allow the vessel to continue to the nearest port. (5)
answers.answer_text:
**(a) Five possible reasons**
Air in the hydraulic system — heavy motion plus low oil level draws in air, giving spongy, slow response.
Low oil level/loss of oil — a leak started by storm shock loading.
Relief or shock valve passing — repeated pressure surges leave it not reseating, bypassing pump delivery.
Worn or damaged pump — sustained high-pressure operation during the storm wears internals, reducing delivery.
Increased mechanical resistance or contaminated/wrong-grade oil — damage to rudder/stock bearings, a choked filter, or thickened oil.

**(b) Corrective actions at sea**
Bring the second power unit into operation to restore full delivery.
Check and replenish the oil from the storage tank.
Vent (bleed) the system at the highest points, working the gear hard-over to hard-over to expel air.
Find and isolate any leak; check and reseat/reset any passing relief/shock valves.
Clean filters, isolate any suspect pump/cylinder and continue on the sound unit; reduce speed to lower rudder load, and steer using local control if necessary while proceeding to the nearest port.

Part (b) (corrective action at sea) is also weakly answered.

answers.title: Four-Ram with Automatic Isolation Within 45 Seconds
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a four ram type steering gear comprising of two fifty per cent torque units that complies with the single failure concept and automatic isolation. (6)

(b) Describe how automatic isolation, for the hydraulic circuit sketched in part (a), is achieved within 45 seconds should leakage of system oil occur. (4)
answers.answer_text:
*Sketch instructions: draw a four-ram circuit split into two independent halves, each with its own 50% pump, sump and directional control valve, a split-lower-section header (replenishing) tank with level switches, a control valve, and an automatic isolating valve in the cross-connection between the halves.*

**(b) How automatic isolation is achieved.** Each half has its own supply and level switches in its sump (and the split header tank). If a leak develops in one half, its level switch trips, signalling the control valve, which pilots the isolating valve in the cross-connection to close automatically — separating the leaking half from the sound half and confining the fault. The bypass valve on the affected side opens so its cylinders float freely with the tiller. Because detection and response are entirely automatic, the changeover completes well within 45 seconds, and the remaining sound 50% unit continues supplying its pair of rams — satisfying the single-failure concept.

The two 50% units are independent, each with its own pump, motor, direction valve and relief valve, drawing from its own side of the sump; the actuator is served through the isolation valve.
