answers.title: Panting & pounding — causes, effects & constructional details
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain the causes and effects of panting and pounding, indicating the affected areas. (5)

(b) Describe the constructional details designed to resist panting and pounding. (5)

Marks: (a) 5 · (b) 5
answers.answer_text:
a) Panting and pounding are two distinct types of local, dynamic stresses acting on the ship's structure forward of the first collision bulkhead, primarily caused by the vessel's interaction with waves and its motion in rough seas. They are separate mechanisms — one a cyclic pressure loading, the other an impact loading — and because they are resisted by different structure they should be treated separately and not merged.

1. Panting: Panting is the in-and-out flexing of the shell plating, particularly at the fore end. Causes: It is caused by rapidly alternating water pressures on the hull as waves pass along the ship's sides and the vessel pitches (the vertical motion of the bow and stern). The loading is therefore a cyclic pressure variation arising as the ends alternately immerse and emerge while the vessel pitches, not a single blow. Affected Areas: Fore End — the primary area, specifically from the bow to the first collision bulkhead (roughly the forward 15% of the ship's length, that is approximately the forward 0.15 L in the forepeak); After End — to a lesser degree, in the aft peak area. Effects: Fatigue & Leaking (continuous flexing can lead to fatigue cracking in plating and welding); Structural Damage (separation of the hull plating from internal stiffeners and decks); Weakened Structure (severe structural deformation to side shell plating).

2. Pounding (Slamming): Pounding occurs when the ship's bow lifts out of the water in a heavy sea and then crashes down upon the water surface. Causes: High-speed motion in rough head seas, particularly when the ship is in a light or ballast condition. Affected Areas: Fore Bottom (the flat bottom plating in the forward of the ship, over approximately the forward 25–30% of the length); Fore Shoulder (the forward side shell). Pounding is thus a sudden impact load on the flat of bottom forward after it has emerged in a light or ballast trim, and not a pressure cycle. Effects: Severe Damage (dents, buckling, and rupture of the bottom plating); Structural Failure (deformed internals, floors and girders); Whipping Stresses (the sudden impact causes the entire hull girder to vibrate, creating whipping stresses, which can lead to increased stress throughout the ship and accelerated fatigue).

b) To resist panting and pounding stresses in the forepeak region where these forces are most affected, following constructional details are implemented. Each detail belongs to one of the two forces: panting is resisted by the stringers, beams and breast hooks that stiffen the shell transversely, while pounding is resisted by the heavy bottom grillage and thickened plating.

1. Panting Stringers: Triangular horizontal girders fitted on the side frames, spaced about 2m apart vertically, connecting the side frames to the collision bulkhead.

2. Panting Beams: Metal beams fitted horizontally at alternate frames, connecting the port and starboard panting stringers to stiffen the structure transversally to counteract the in-and-out flexing of the shell plating caused by panting. Where beams are not fitted, a perforated wash flat or deep beams may be used in the peaks to perform the same function.

3. Breast Hooks: Horizontal triangular plates connecting port and starboard panting stringers at the centre line at the bow, providing extra rigidity to the stem plating.

4. Increased Plating Thickness: Strengthened Shell Plating especially the bottom shell plating is significantly thickened in the forward 25% of the ship's length (pounding zone) to withstand high-impact loads.

5. Solid Plate Floors and Wash Bulkhead: Solid plate floors, fitted at every frame in the pounding region and supported by strengthened pillars/ wash bulkhead, together with intercostal side girders spaced not more than about 2.2 m apart, and reduced transverse frame spacing (reduced to not more than 700 mm), provide a robust foundation that helps absorb and distribute the forces generated. The wash bulkhead in the fore peak additionally limits free-surface movement when the peak is ballasted.

answers.title: Six degrees of motion & the structure that resists them
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe the SIX degrees of motion that a ship at sea moves in when encountering heavy weather. (6)

(b) Describe the constructional details that are designed to resist the forces exerted on a ship by the motions described in part (a). (4)

Marks: (a) 6 · (b) 4
answers.answer_text:
(a) Six Degrees of Motion a Ship Experiences in Heavy Weather The six motions divide into three translational motions — surge (longitudinal), sway (transverse) and heave

(vertical) — and three rotational motions — roll (about the longitudinal axis), pitch (about the transverse axis) and yaw (about the vertical axis).

- Surge: Forward and backward motion along the length of the ship, typically due to waves or propulsion forces.

- Heave: Vertical motion of the ship as it rises and falls with the waves.

- Sway: Lateral motion from side to side, caused by wind or wave action.

- Roll: Tilting motion from side to side around the longitudinal axis, often caused by wave action.

- Pitch: Rotational motion about the transverse axis, where the bow and stern move alternately.

- Yaw: Rotational movement around the vertical axis, changing the ship's heading due to wind or waves. A further distinction is worth stating because it governs part (b): only heave, roll and pitch have a hydrostatic restoring force, so that the ship is naturally pushed back towards equilibrium and the motion is oscillatory. Surge, sway and yaw have no restoring force and are therefore controlled by propulsion, the rudder and steering gear, and by mooring, rather than being resisted by structure. Original sketch — the six degrees of motion (preserved unaltered) Part 1, p.47

b) Constructional details that are designed to resist forces exerted on a ship by the SIX degrees of motion are;

- Rolling: Bilge keels/stabilizers/anti roll tanks are specifically engineered to handle, dissipate, or resist rolling forces.

- Yawing: Highly effective, high-aspect ratio rudder and its associated robust steering gear absorb yawing forces. Strictly, the rudder and steering gear are control devices rather than resisting structure, since yaw has no hydrostatic restoring force.

- Pitching, and Surging: High tensile steel strengthened bottom structure with stiffeners, bulbous bow, panting stringers and panting beams forward and aft absorbs the pitching and surging forces. Pitch and heave, and the slamming they cause, are resisted principally by the strengthened bottom forward and deep floors, assisted by the bulbous bow.

- Heaving and Swaying: High tensile steel strengthened double Hull, double Bottom structures absorb heaving forces. Sheer strake, bilge strake, garboard strake and keel strake designs contribute to longitudinal strength absorbing swaying forces. Sway, like surge and yaw, is controlled rather than structurally resisted; the continuous longitudinal material named here provides the hull-girder strength that carries the resulting loads.

> **Source note:** Part 1's answer describes structure as “absorbing” sway and yaw forces. Its own Model Additions correct this — those two motions, with surge, have no hydrostatic restoring force and are controlled by the rudder, propulsion and mooring. Both readings are shown above so the distinction the examiner is testing is not lost.

answers.title: Hull stresses in heavy weather & the structure that resists them
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe the stresses that the hull of an ocean going vessel is subjected to when it encounters heavy weather. (5)

(b) Explain the constructional details of ships which resist the stresses described in part (a). (5)

Marks: (a) 5 · (b) 5
answers.answer_text:
a) Stresses the hull of an ocean-going vessel is subjected to when it encounters heavy weather are; The governing design case is the longitudinal bending of the hull girder, which is the sum of the still- water bending moment and the wave bending moment — hogging when a crest is amidships and sagging when the ship sits in a trough. Acting with it are shear forces, greatest near the quarter-length points, and, in oblique seas, torsion, which is important for open-deck ships. The section modulus of the deck and bottom is sized to this combined bending moment, which is precisely why the continuous longitudinal material listed in part (b) is provided.

i) Longitudinal Stresses — Hogging: when a ship is lifted at the mid ships by a wave crest, the center of the vessel experiences upward bending, leading to tensile stresses at the deck and compressive stresses at the bottom. Sagging: when the ends are lifted by waves and the midship section sinks, it creates downward bending, resulting in compressive stresses at the deck and tensile stresses at the bottom. ii) Transverse Stresses — Racking: rolling in heavy seas induces transverse stresses that can distort the ship's structure, particularly affecting corners and joints. This stress is most significant at beam knees and tank side brackets where the rectangular cross section of the ship tries to distort into a parallelogram sideways. iii) Local Stresses — Panting: fluctuations in water pressure during wave action cause an in-and-out motion of the hull plating, particularly at the fore end. Pounding: when a ship pitches heavily, it can slam down onto waves, causing severe impacts on the forward structure. This results in high local stresses that necessitate reinforced bottom structures. iv) Water Pressure Effect: Hydrostatic pressure increases with depth (as the ship heaves) and acts perpendicularly on the ship's hull, especially below the waterline. This results in high local stresses that necessitate hull design optimization, structural strengthening, and advanced material selection.

b) Construction details which resist the stresses acting on ships are;

1. Hogging and Sagging stresses are resisted by strengthening the uppermost deck and bottom shell plating with continuous longitudinal members, so as to provide the section modulus required by the combined still- water and wave bending moment. Key structural reinforcements include thickened sheer/bilge/garboard/keel strakes, deck stringers, high-tensile steel, longitudinal bulkheads, and deep double-bottom girders.

2. Racking stresses are resisted by transverse bulkheads reinforced with large brackets, Extra-deep, strong transverse frames (web frames), Beam Knees, Deck/Bilge Brackets, rounded sheer strake, and double bottom box girder structure especially torsion boxes. The torsion boxes also carry the torsional loading imposed in oblique seas.

3. Panting and Pounding stresses are resisted by panting stringers, panting beam, reduced frame spacing (900 mm to 700 mm), deep plate floors, longitudinal/horizontal intercostal stringers supported by strengthened pillars/wash bulkhead, and Strengthened Shell Plating especially significantly thickened bottom shell plating with intercostal girders (spaced no more than 2.2 m apart).

4. Water pressure stresses are further resisted by V shaped hull, reduced fwd flared design, specialized x- stern design and ship building using robust welding techniques with a combination of longitudinal and transverse framing in addition to above design features.

> **Source note:** Part 1 twice prints “intercoastal”; corrected above to intercostal (meaning “between the ribs”), as its own Model Additions direct. Spell it correctly in the exam — it is a word markers notice.

answers.title: Five terms for hull distortion in heavy seas
answers.question_as_set:
State FIVE terms used to describe the conditions that relate to the distortion a ship's hull undergoes in heavy seas, stating in EACH case the type of stresses involved and where the stresses occur. (10)

Marks: 10
answers.answer_text:
1. Hogging — Type of Stress: Longitudinal bending stress. Location: Occurs in the midship section of the hull. When a ship is lifted at the mid ships by a wave crest, the center of the vessel experiences upward bending, leading to tensile stresses at the deck and compressive stresses at the bottom.

2. Sagging — Type of Stress: Longitudinal bending stress. Location: Occurs in the midship area. When the ends are lifted by waves and the midship section sinks, it creates downward bending, resulting in compressive stresses at the deck and tensile stresses at the bottom.

3. Racking — Type of Stress: Transverse shear stress. Location: Racking is a dynamic transverse deformation, due to transverse stresses, such as rolling or uneven wave action, where the rectangular cross- section of the ship tries to distort into a parallelogram sideways. It can lead to distortion of the transverse sections. The stress concentrates at the corners of the section — the beam knees, the tank-side brackets and the frame-to-beam connections — and is worst when the ship is rolling in a light or ballast condition.

4. Panting — Type of Stress: Localized dynamic stress. Location: Panting is the in-and-out flexing movement of the ship's shell plating due to changes in water pressure near the bow and stern as the ship pitches in heavy seas, affecting the forepeak most and the after peak to a lesser degree.

5. Whipping — Type of Stress: Longitudinal bending stress. Location: Occurs along the entire length of the hull and is a transient, high-frequency vibration of the hull girder caused by severe slamming impacts in heavy seas. The hull vibrates at its natural frequency, resulting in high-stress concentrations. More precisely it is a transient longitudinal vibratory bending of the hull girder in its two-node mode, which decays after a slam or bow-flare impact. The related condition springing — a steady, wave-excited hull vibration — is accepted by some examiners as an alternative term. Each of the five terms carries two marks, one for the stress type and one for the location, so both must be named. If preferred, pounding / slamming or pitching may be substituted for any one of the five above; all are valid conditions of hull distortion.

answers.title: Distortion effects & the structure that resists them
answers.question_as_set:
Describe EACH of the following, stating what component parts of the ship's structure help resist the effect: (a) racking (2); (b) panting (2); (c) pounding (2); (d) water pressure effect (2); (e) drydocking stresses (2).

Marks: 2 marks each part
answers.answer_text:
a) Racking: Racking is a dynamic transverse deformation, due to transverse stresses, such as rolling or uneven wave action, where the rectangular cross-section of the ship tries to distort into a parallelogram sideways. It can lead to distortion of the transverse sections. Component parts of the ship's structure, which help resist the effect are; Transverse bulkheads · Side frames · Beam knees and pillars · Tank-side brackets · Web frames · Deck transverses — the corners of the section being where racking bites hardest.

b) Panting: Panting is the in-and-out flexing movement of the ship's shell plating due to changes in water pressure near the bow and stern as the ship pitches in heavy seas. Component parts of the ship's structure, which help resist the effect are; Panting beams and stringers · Breast hooks and panting frames in the forepeak and aft peak · Deep or panting floors in the peaks · Reduced frame spacing forward.

c) Pounding: Pounding is the repetitive slamming of the ship's bow onto the water surface, especially in rough seas, leading to localized stress. It acts over the flat of bottom in the forward approximately 25–30% of the ship's length. Component parts of the ship's structure, which help resist the effect are; Reinforced bottom structure in the fore part (e.g., floors, intercostals) · Strong framing and thicker bottom shell plating in the bow area · Solid plate floors at every frame · Intercostal side girders not more than about 2.2 m apart · Increased bottom-shell thickness · Reduced frame spacing, not more than 700 mm.

d) Water Pressure Effect: Hydrostatic pressure increases with depth (as the ship heaves) and acts perpendicularly on the ship's hull, especially below the waterline. Component parts of the ship's structure, which help resist the effect are; Hull plating and stiffeners (longitudinal and frames) · Transverse bulkheads and internal framing.

e) Dry docking Stresses: Stresses imposed on the hull when a ship is supported by keel blocks and bilge blocks during dry docking. They peak at the keel during the critical period, when the stern has landed on the blocks but the ship is not yet fully supported along its length. Component parts of the ship's structure, which help resist the effect are; Keel structure (center girder, floors) · Strong transverse framing and double bottom structure · Side girders, the whole double bottom acting as a stiff grillage to spread the block reactions.

answers.title: Bulkheads, wing tanks & double-bottom purposes
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to ship construction:

(a) explain why conventional liquid carriers are divided by longitudinal bulkheads; (2)

(b) explain why ore carriers may be fitted with wing tanks; (2)

(c) state, other than the carriage of liquids, the purposes of double bottom tanks in dry cargo ships; (2)

(d) state FOUR reasons for transverse watertight bulkheads in ship construction. (4)

Marks: (a) 2 · (b) 2 · (c) 2 · (d) 4
answers.answer_text:
a) Tanker vessels are divided by longitudinal bulkheads to improve structural strength, reduce free surface effects (transverse movement of liquid), and enable the transport of multiple cargo grades. These bulkheads strengthen the hull against bending and racking, prevent excessive listing, facilitate better control of cargo weight distribution and damage stability.

b) Ore carriers are fitted with wing tanks primarily to improve stability by managing the high center of gravity associated with dense iron ore cargoes (stiff ship) and to increase structural flexibility. These tanks allow for better stability control, provide space for ballast, and can serve as protective double-hull structures, reducing risks from grounding or collision. The seakeeping reason is the headline mark. Dense ore stows low in the hold and leaves the ship excessively stiff, that is with an unnecessarily large GM and therefore a very short, violent roll period. Carrying ballast in the upper wing or topside tanks raises KG, which lengthens the roll period and eases the transverse accelerations on the structure, the cargo and the crew. Alongside this, the sloping wing-tank plating gives the hold a self-trimming hopper geometry, and the tanks form a double-skin space protecting the cargo hold in a side collision or grounding.

c) Double bottom tanks in dry cargo ships serve critical structural and safety functions beyond carrying liquids. They provide longitudinal strength, protect the hull during grounding, improve ship stability, and offer a robust foundation for cargo/machinery while enabling emergency damage control by preventing flooding of cargo holds.

d) Transverse watertight bulkheads are crucial in ship construction for maintaining structural integrity and safety. They provide essential transverse strength, subdivide the hull to prevent progressive flooding, act as fire- resistant barriers to localize blazes, and support decks.

- Subdivision for Flood Control: They divide the ship into watertight compartments, restricting flooding to one area in the event of hull damage, thus preventing the entire vessel from sinking.

- Structural Strength and Rigidity: These bulkheads act as rigid, vertical sub divisions that enhance the overall transverse strength of the hull, resist racking stresses, and maintain the ship's transverse form.

- Fire Subdivision: They act as fire-resistant partitions that limit the spread of fire from one compartment to another, enabling the crew to isolate and extinguish fires in a specific zone.

- Structural Support for Decks: They provide vertical support for the deck structure above, enhancing the ship's overall strength. Two supporting points complete the answer. The collision bulkhead and the after-peak bulkhead are themselves transverse watertight bulkheads required by SOLAS, which is the clearest illustration of the flood-control function. The number of bulkheads required is set by the floodable-length and subdivision calculation for the ship, not chosen arbitrarily.

answers.title: Container-ship strength with large hold openings
answers.question_as_set:
Explain, with the aid of a mid-ship half sectional sketch of a container ship, how strength is built into this type of vessel whilst still allowing access to the cargo holds. (10)

Marks: 10
answers.answer_text:
Original sketch — container ship mid-ship half section (preserved unaltered) Part 1, p.37 The governing problem in this ship type is torsion. Removing the deck to give the large hatch openings needed for cargo access leaves an open cross-section with very low torsional stiffness, so that oblique or quartering seas would twist and warp the hull. The purpose of the structure described below is to re-close that section and restore the torsional strength lost with the deck. Container ships maintain structural integrity, despite very large deck openings for cargo access, by utilizing high-tensile steel, a double-hull construction for torsional rigidity, and large “box-shaped wing tanks” (torsion boxes) that provide longitudinal strength. The U-shaped structure, reinforced with heavy transverse frames and a deep double bottom, compensates for the lack of deck plating. Key Structural Elements are;

- Torsion Box (Wing Tanks): The most critical element, these large box girders run longitudinally along the top edge of the side shells, providing immense torsional rigidity against twisting forces. Being closed box sections, they carry the shear flow that the missing deck can no longer carry.

- Double Hull and Double Bottom: Essential for structural strength and damage stability, providing a rigid base (double bottom) and side structure (double hull). The keel, bottom shell, tank top plating, the side shell at the top, deck stringer plates and deck longitudinal help resist longitudinal stresses.

- Longitudinal Framing: The entire structure is longitudinally framed to handle large bending moments (hogging/sagging).

- Transverse Bulkheads: Deep webs and strong transverse bulkheads are placed between cargo holds to maintain transverse strength.

- Minimized Bilge Strake: The transition from bottom to side is angled or rounded with a minimal radius to maximize cargo stowage, often eliminating traditional bilge strakes. The construction method adopted in construction of a container ship is the “Box Girder” method. The design uses Finite Element Method (FEM) to analyze and ensure the box girders can withstand the expected torsional stresses. The box girder structure helps strengthen the side structure along the hatch side together with continuous hatch coming and bulwark. At hatch end covers, transvers box section connects the box girder together forming a very rigid structure. It is this combination — closed box girders at the upper sides joined by transverse box sections at the hatch ends — that re-closes the section and restores torsional strength. The combination of longitudinal framing and double bottom construction provides enhanced stability and safety, ensuring that even with large cargo access hatches, the ship remains seaworthy. One further detail earns credit: the hatch corners are a known fatigue hot-spot because of the stress concentration at the discontinuity, so they are radiused and insert-plated with higher-grade material and checked by finite element analysis.

answers.title: Ship-construction terms (purpose & location)
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to ship construction, explain the purpose of EACH of the following, stating where EACH are located: (a) duct keel (2); (b) bilge keel (2); (c) collision bulkhead (2); (d) camber (2); (e) flare (2).

Marks: 2 marks each part
answers.answer_text:
a) Duct keel is a longitudinal, watertight tunnel built into bulk carriers and container ship's double-bottom structure, running along the centre line from the collision bulkhead to the forward engine room bulkhead. It strengthens the ship's bottom structure, surviving longitudinal stresses. It houses vital pipes for ballast, fuel, and bilge systems, allowing for easy inspection and maintenance. Its clear width is limited — commonly not more than about 2 m — so that the double bottom either side of it remains structurally effective, and it is not carried under the machinery space, where a solid centre girder is fitted instead. Being an enclosed space, entry requires the full enclosed-space-entry procedure.

b) Bilge keels are narrow fins or plates attached amidships, longitudinally along the turn of the bilge, where the bottom curves into the sides, on both sides. They work by increasing hydrodynamic resistance when the vessel rolls, creating a damping effect that reduces the amplitude of rolling motions.

c) Collision bulkhead is the foremost, heavily reinforced, transverse watertight bulkhead in a ship, extending from the bottom to the freeboard deck. Its purpose is to maintain vessel safety and buoyancy by restricting flooding from the forepeak in a head-on collision, preventing water ingress to cargo holds. Its position is set by SOLAS II-1 and the ICLL: not less than 0.05 L (or 10 m, whichever is the less) and not more than 0.08 L (or 0.05 L + 3 m) from the forward perpendicular at the load line. No openings or doors are permitted in it below the freeboard deck, and only one pipe penetration is allowed, fitted with a screw-down valve operable from above the freeboard deck.

d) Camber is the slight, parabolic, curvature (1/50 of the vessel's breadth) of a ship's exposed weather decks in the transverse (athwartship) direction, where the deck is higher at the centre line than at the sides. The classical value is therefore B/50 at midships, though modern ships often use a straight-line camber instead of a parabola. Its purpose is to allow rain or seawater from waves to drain efficiently off the weather decks and prevent accumulation. The upward curvature increases the deck's structural strength against bending, flexural loads, and longitudinal deflection, and it also offsets the visual impression that the ship is hogged.

e) Flare refers to the outward curvature of the hull's side shell plating as it rises from the waterline toward the main deck. It is essentially the widening of the hull section from bottom to top above the waterline. The highest degree of flare is located at the forward end of the ship (the bow). The outward curvature acts as a deflector, forcing water away from the deck. A flared hull increases reserve buoyancy, deck area and stability. The trade- off is that excessive flare aggravates bow-flare slamming loads in head seas. The opposite form, where the side shell curves inward as it rises, is called tumblehome. Each part carries two marks and asks two things — purpose and location — so both must be given; a purpose without a location loses half the mark.

> **Source note:** Part 1 gives the collision-bulkhead position as “between 5% and 8% of the ship's length (L) or 10 m maximum from forward”. Its own Model Additions record that this conflates two separate limits, and the corrected wording is used above.

answers.title: Bilge keels — damage prevention, testing, length
answers.question_as_set:
(a) With reference to bilge keels:

(i) describe how the design and method of attachment reduces the possibility of damage to the shell plate; (3)

(ii) state what testing must be carried out. (2)

(b) Explain why the bilge keels do not extend the full length of the vessel. (3)

Marks: (a)(i) 3 · (a)(ii) 2 · (b) 3 → 8
answers.answer_text:
a) i) Bilge keels are designed with a flexible structure, usually a bulb plate, welded to a flat bar doubler — properly called a ground bar, an intercostal flat bar — which is then attached to the shell plating via double continuous fillet welds. This design ensures that if the keel strikes an object, it tears away at the weld to the doubler without damaging or breaching the main shell plating. The essential logic is a deliberate weak link: the ground bar is continuously double-fillet welded to the shell directly over an internal longitudinal or frame, while the keel-to-ground-bar weld is made the weaker joint, so that on impact the keel shears off at that weld and the shell plating stays intact. The ground bar must always land on supported structure, so that loads are never fed into unsupported shell plating. Key design and attachment features to prevent shell damage are:

- Doubler Plate: The bilge keel is not welded directly to the shell; instead, a flat bar “doubler” is welded to the shell plating, and the keel is welded to this doubler. This provides a sacrificial buffer zone.

- Weakened Connection (Soft Nose): The weld connecting the vertical plate of the keel to the flat bar doubler is often designed to be weaker than the shell plating, acting as a breaking point.

- Internal Stiffening Alignment: The bilge keels are positioned directly in line with internal stiffeners (such as transverse frames or longitudinal) to spread loading, rather than on unsupported, flexible shell plating.

- Rounded Ends (Scallops): The ends of the bilge keels are tapered or rounded to prevent stress concentrations at the tip. The end is additionally snipped or soft-toed and aligned with internal structure, so that the termination does not create a hard spot at which fatigue cracks would initiate.

- Limiting Length: They are typically restricted to 30%-60% of the ship's length amidships, avoiding areas with high bending/twisting stresses, which reduces the chance of propagating cracks into the main hull.

(ii) Testing

The first point to make is that a solid bilge keel cannot be leak- or pressure-tested, since it encloses no volume. Its integrity is judged instead by:

- Visual Inspection: During dry docking, the entire bilge keel is inspected for any damage, cracks, or deformation.

- NDT (Non-Destructive Testing): Techniques such as ultrasonic testing or magnetic particle inspection may be employed to assess the integrity of welds and detect any defects — in practice crack testing by MPI or dye-penetrant of the welds.

- Hammer or percussion testing along the keel, to find sections that have detached from the ground bar.

- Examination of the weld toes for fatigue cracking, particularly at the ends and at any repair, carried out at dry-dock.

b) Bilge keels are designed to extend only 30% to 60% of the vessel's length, primarily in the midship region. Reasons for not extending Bilge keels to the full length include:

1. Increased Resistance and Drag: Extending the bilge keels along the full length would cause excessive frictional drag, significantly increasing fuel consumption and reducing the vessel's speed.

2. Structural Damage Risk: The bow and stern areas are more prone to damage. If extended to the full length, the bilge keels are at higher risk of being torn off due to slamming, maneuvering, or docking.

3. Optimal Effectiveness in Midship Region: The maximum roll damping occurs in the midship section, where the bilge keels have the highest velocity relative to the hull's rolling axis, making their extension to the tapered ends unnecessary.

4. Protection of the extreme dimensions: The keel must remain inside the moulded line of the bilge, so that it does not increase the vessel's extreme breadth or draught. Carrying it forward or aft, where the hull form narrows, would push it outside that line and expose it to grounding and quay contact — which is why it sits at the turn of the bilge amidships.

answers.title: Roll reduction systems
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to roll reduction systems, explain the principles of operation of EACH of the following, stating the advantages and disadvantages of EACH:

(i) Bilge keels (5)

(ii) Passive Uncontrolled Tanks (5)

Marks: (i) 5 · (ii) 5
answers.answer_text:
i) Bilge Keels: Bilge keels are narrow fins or plates attached amidships, longitudinally along the turn of the bilge, where the bottom curves into the sides, on both sides. They work by increasing hydrodynamic resistance when the vessel rolls, creating a damping effect that reduces the amplitude of rolling motions. The design usually involves flat plates or strakes that present resistance to water flow during a roll, thus helping to stabilize the vessel. Stated precisely, bilge keels are a passive damping device and the damping is produced by eddy and vortex shedding at the sharp edges of the keel: as the hull rolls, the keels are dragged through the water and shed vortices, and the energy carried away in those vortices is taken out of the rolling motion, so the roll is damped. Because the damping force depends on the velocity of the water relative to the keel, bilge keels oppose roll velocity rather than roll displacement. They therefore bite hardest at resonance, where roll velocity is greatest, and have little effect at zero speed or where there is no relative motion between hull and water. A roll-amplitude reduction of approximately 20–35% is a useful figure to quote.

Original sketch — bilge keel at turn of bilge (preserved unaltered) Part 1, p.6 Advantages:

- Low Maintenance: They require minimal maintenance compared to active stabilization systems.

- No Internal Components: Unlike fins or other stabilization systems, bilge keels do not take up space inside the hull, preserving cargo and operational areas.

- Cost-Effective: They are relatively inexpensive to install and maintain. Disadvantages:

- Increased Drag: The presence of bilge keels increases hydrodynamic resistance, which can reduce speed and fuel efficiency.

- Limited Effectiveness: While they reduce roll, bilge keels are not as effective as other stabilization methods like fins or gyroscopic stabilizers.

- Potential Damage: They can be susceptible to damage when docking or grounding as they protrude out from the hull. ii) Passive Uncontrolled Tanks: Passive uncontrolled tanks utilize the principles of fluid dynamics to reduce roll by allowing water to move freely within tanks located in the hull. As the vessel rolls, water shifts from one side of the tank to the other, creating a counteracting moment that helps stabilize the ship. This system does not require active control or mechanical components. The key marking point is the tuning principle. A passive uncontrolled tank — the free-surface or Frahm type — works because the natural period of the water oscillating in the tank is tuned to the ship's natural roll period. When correctly tuned, the moment generated by the moving water lags the roll by about 90°, so that it opposes roll velocity and gives maximum damping near resonance. Omitting the phrase “tuned to the ship's natural roll period” normally loses a mark. It follows that if the tank is mistuned, or the ship is operating far from resonance, a free-surface tank can actually worsen the roll. Note also the terminology: “passive uncontrolled” means the free-surface / Frahm type with no throttle valve, as distinct from “passive controlled”, which has a tunable air cross-over or water-duct valve that adjusts the tank's response.

Original sketch — passive (free-surface) anti-roll tank, athwartship view (preserved unaltered) Part 1, p.7 Advantages:

- Simplicity: The system is straightforward with no moving parts, leading to lower maintenance requirements and reduced failure points.

- Cost-Effective Installation: Passive tanks can be integrated into existing designs without significant modifications or costs associated with active systems.

- Increased Stability: They provide an effective means of roll reduction by utilizing the natural movement of water within the tanks. Disadvantages:

- Delayed Response Time: The effectiveness of passive tanks can be slower than active systems since they rely on fluid movement rather than immediate mechanical response.

- Reduced Stability (Free Surface Effect): The presence of a large, freely moving liquid surface inside the tanks creates a free-surface effect, which decreases the ship's metacentric height and can reduce initial stability. This loss of GM is unavoidable, precisely because the system depends on having a free surface.

- Significant Space Consumption: They occupy a large volume of the vessel's interior, often reducing usable cargo or storage space.

answers.title: Double-bottom fuel tanks — sounding pipes, air pipes & vent design
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to double bottom fuel tanks:

(a) explain why weighted cocks are fitted to the tank sounding pipes; (2)

(b) explain the purpose of air pipes; (2)

(c) state the design features incorporated on air pipe vents with respect to EACH of the following: (i) heavy weather (2); (ii) fire (2); (iii) bunkering (2).

Marks: 2 marks each part
answers.answer_text:
(a) Weighted cocks are fitted to tank sounding pipes for the following reasons:

- Preventing Water Ingress: The weighted design helps keep the cock closed when not in use, preventing water from entering the tank through the sounding pipe, which could lead to contamination of the fuel.

- Ease of Operation: When the sounding pipe is needed for measuring liquid levels, the weight allows for easy operation, ensuring that the cock can be opened and closed smoothly without requiring excessive force. The cock is a self-closing weighted cock: the weight returns it to the shut position as soon as the hand is taken off it, so the pipe cannot be left open. Describe the pipe itself as well — it runs from the tank top down to a striking plate on the tank bottom, which takes the impact of the sounding rod, it terminates at an accessible deck level at the cock, and it must be run as straight as practicable so that the rod or tape reaches the bottom.

(b) Purpose of Air Pipes:

- Pressure Equalization: They allow air to flow in and out of the tank, preventing pressure build-up or vacuum formation as fuel is pumped in or out. This ensures safe and efficient operation during filling and emptying.

- Ventilation: Air pipes help ventilate the tank, allowing any gases that may accumulate to escape, thus reducing the risk of explosive atmospheres within the tank. The sizing rule follows from the first purpose: the air-pipe cross-sectional area must be at least 1.25 times the area of the filling line, so that the vent can never become the restriction during bunkering and over- pressurise the tank.

(c) Design Features Incorporated on Air Pipe Vents

- i. Heavy Weather: Air pipes are often designed with a gooseneck shape, which helps prevent water from entering the pipe during heavy seas. The upward bend creates a barrier against wave action. The head is fitted with a float-type automatic self-closing device, which shuts if the vent is submerged by a boarding sea. Under the Load Line Convention the coaming height before the automatic closing device must be at least 760 mm on the freeboard deck and 450 mm on the superstructure deck.

- ii. Fire: Air pipes are equipped with flame arresters to prevent flames from entering the tank in case of an external fire, thereby reducing the risk of explosion due to flammable vapors inside the tank. In practice this is a corrosion-resistant flame screen fitted in the vent head, removable for cleaning.

- iii. Bunkering: For safety during bunkering operations, fuel tank air vents are fitted with suitable sized save- all trays around the base of air pipe. Vents are located at the highest point of the tank to prevent air pockets and terminate on open decks. They allow air to flow out of the tank, preventing pressure build-up as fuel is pumped in. This ensures safe and efficient bunkering. The 1.25 × filling-line area rule applies here, and the vent must terminate clear of accommodation openings and of any source of ignition. Quoting the coaming heights and the 1.25 × area rule is what lifts this part from a descriptive answer to a specification-level one.

answers.title: Construction of refrigerated spaces — insulation materials, properties & attachment
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to the construction of refrigerated spaces:

(a) state suitable materials that can be used for insulating refrigerated spaces; (2)

(b) state the properties that an insulating material should possess; (3)

(c) skech a section through a wall of a cold storage space detailing how the insulation is attached to the ship's structure. (5) “skech” is the paper's own printing slip, left as set. It appears in both sittings.

Marks: (a) 2 · (b) 3 · (c) 5
answers.answer_text:
a) Suitable materials that can be used for insulation refrigerated spaces are; (i) Cork · (ii) Fiber Glass · (iii) Mineral Wool · (iv) Foam. Modern practice is dominated by closed-cell rigid foams — polyurethane (PUF) and polyisocyanurate (PIR), often supplied as factory-bonded panels; cork, glass-fibre and mineral wool are the traditional materials. Naming a closed-cell foam by name is worth doing, because it is what is actually fitted in a modern reefer space.

b) Properties that an insulating material should process are;

- It should have low thermal conductivity.

- It should resistance to mold and vermin.

- Resistance to moisture.

- It should be non-hazardous/toxic.

- It should be non-corrosive.

- It should be noncombustible.

- It must incorporate a vapour / moisture barrier — the property most often left out, and the one that matters most.

- It must be dimensionally stable, of low water-absorption, odourless, rot- and vermin-proof, light, and fire- retardant. The vapour barrier is essential because condensation forming on the cold side and wetting the insulation destroys its insulating value: a wet insulant conducts, so the R-value collapses and the space cannot hold temperature. The sealing strips and the sheet-metal facing in the sketch below are there for exactly this purpose — they are the vapour seal, not merely a finish.

c) Cross-section of a wall of cold storage space:

Cold-storage wall section — insulation attachment to ship structure (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.12 The insulation is not fastened to the shell or the frames directly. Wood grounds are secured to the structure by lugs welded to the frames; the insulation is laid between and against the grounds, the joints are closed with sealing strips, and the whole is faced with sheet metal on the cold side, which both protects the insulant mechanically and completes the vapour seal.

answers.title: Double hulled oil tankers — mid-ship section, why they evolved & the disadvantages
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to double hulled oil tankers:

(a) sketch a mid ship cross section; (5)

(b) state the reason this type of design; (1)

(c) state FOUR disadvantages of this type of design. (4)

Marks: (a) 5 · (b) 1 · (c) 4
answers.answer_text:
Sol: a) Double-hull oil tanker — mid-ship cross section (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.10 Working outwards from the centre line the section shows the keel strake and centre girder, the double bottom with its floors, side girders and inner bottom shell, the bilge strake turning up into the side shell and the inner shell that together form the wing water ballast tanks, the longitudinal bulkhead dividing the port and starboard cargo tanks, and at deck level the deck plating, deck stringer plate and sheer strake with the horizontal girders, end brackets and plate brackets that tie the inner and outer skins together.

b) Double-hulled oil tankers evolved over a period of time to minimize massive oil spills resulting from groundings, collisions or internal tank rupturing. Following catastrophic accidents like the Exxon Valdez, international regulations (MARPOL) and US law (OPA 90) mandated this design because the extra, protective inner layer prevents cargo tank rupture during lower-impact incidents. The requirement is MARPOL Annex I, Regulation 19, which requires double-hull or equivalent construction for oil tankers, with the phase-out of existing single-hull tankers under Regulation 20. The United States driver is OPA 90, following the 1989 Exxon Valdez grounding.

c) Dis-Advantages of this type of design are;

1. Explosion and atmosphere risk in the double-hull void spaces. The narrow voids between the skins can accumulate hydrocarbon vapour leaking from the cargo tanks, and they must therefore be inerted or ventilated and routinely gas-monitored — the lesson of the Bow Mariner.

2. Increased Construction and Operational Costs.

3. Difficult Maintenance and Inspections. Access for close-up survey in the narrow ballast voids is poor, and the incidence of corrosion in them is high, so coating condition has to be maintained in the least accessible part of the ship.

4. Increased light weight of the vessel. The additional steel weight is a real penalty because it is deducted from deadweight, so for a given displacement the ship carries less cargo.

5. Reduced Stability and High Center of Gravity.

6. The cost of coating and maintaining the additional ballast spaces over the life of the ship. If only four disadvantages are wanted, give the atmosphere risk in the voids, the survey access and corrosion in the narrow ballast spaces, the steel weight lost from deadweight, and the coating and maintenance cost of the extra tanks — those four are the technically defensible set.

> **Source note:** Part 2 lists the four disadvantages as increased cost, difficult maintenance and inspection, increased light weight, and “Reduced Stability and High Center of Gravity”, and its own Model Additions box then records that the “increased light weight → reduced stability / high CG” reasoning is loosely argued and tells the candidate to lead with the void-space atmosphere risk, the survey access and corrosion, the deadweight penalty and the coating cost instead. All four original items are preserved above; the stronger items have been added and put first, and the light-weight point is re-expressed as a deadweight penalty, which is what it actually is.

answers.title: Large bulk carriers — mid-ship section & the design features that resist
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to large bulk carriers:

(a) explain how the design and operation of this type of vessel has contributed to structural failure; (5)

(b) describe the designs that have evolved to minimise the possibility of failure. (5)

Marks: (a) 5 · (b) 5
answers.answer_text:
Sol: a) Large bulk carrier — mid-ship cross section (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.32 The section is the classic single-side-skin bulker: a duct keel and double bottom tank with centre girder and floors, the hopper tank with its sloping plating and transverse ring webs carrying the load out to the bilge, the side shell with side-shell frames and longitudinals, and the topside tank with its sloping plating, vertical strake and transverse ring web running up to the strength deck and the hatch coaming. The topside and

hopper tanks are what give the section both its strength and its self-trimming geometry: the sloping plating makes the cargo flow to the centre, and the tanks themselves are the ballast capacity.

b) To minimise the possibility of failure in large bulk carriers, several key design features have evolved by Utilization of corrugated transverse bulkheads which enhances strength by effectively distributing stress during operations and at sea. Transverse watertight bulkheads between cargo holds prevent flooding from spreading, increasing survivability in emergencies. Implementing alternate hold loading helps distribute cargo weight evenly, reducing stress on the hull and maintaining stability. Water ingress alarms alert crews to rising water levels in cargo holds, enabling prompt action to prevent flooding. Adoption of double hulls provides an extra layer of protection against leaks and breaches, significantly improving safety. These features are the SOLAS Chapter XII bulk-carrier safety measures, introduced after the heavy bulk- carrier losses of the 1980s and 1990s — the Derbyshire era. Named individually they are:

- Mandatory water-ingress detection alarms in the cargo holds and in the forward spaces.

- A strengthened No.1 hold and, above all, a strengthened transverse corrugated bulkhead between Nos. 1 and 2 holds — the critical interface, because it is failure there that turns flooding of No.1 hold into progressive flooding of the ship.

- Loading-instrument verification, with restricted or alternate-hold loading, to keep shear force and bending moment inside the permissible envelope during multi-port loading and discharge.

- The move to double-side-skin construction, which removes the exposed side-shell frames and their end brackets — a known wastage and fracture site on single-side-skin ships.

answers.title: Bulk carrier — inspection of the upper topside areas as Chief Engineer
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to a bulk carrier, describe, as Chief Engineer Officer, the inspection that should be carried out on the upper topside areas. (10)

Marks: 10
answers.answer_text:
As Chief Engineer Officer on a bulk carrier, inspection of the upper topside areas is crucial for structural integrity, safety, and operational efficiency. Inspection regime focuses on mitigating corrosion, ensuring watertight integrity, and structural reliability as follows;

i) Hatch Covers and Coamings: Inspect for cracks, deformation, and wastage, especially at the corners of hatches, which are high-stress areas. ii) Watertight Integrity: Check the condition of rubber gaskets, packing, and sealing arrangements for all hatch covers. iii) Securing Devices: Ensure all hatch cleats, hinges, and quick-acting cleats are operational and well- greased. iv) Air Pipes & Sounding Pipes: Inspect the air pipes to the topside tanks for corrosion, particularly in the threads, and verify the proper functioning to prevent water ingress. Confirm in particular that the automatic (float-type) closing devices on the topside tank air pipes are free and seating — a seized or missing float is a direct route to progressive flooding of the topside tanks.

v) Deck Structures: Check for wasting or pitting on deck plating, particularly around crane foundations, pedestal mounts, and windlasses. Include the cross-deck strips between hatches and the hatch-end beams, which carry the transverse deck loading between the hatch openings. vi) Ventilation and Access: Ensure the manholes, ladders, and ventilation access to the tanks are safe, clean, and not compromised. vii) Underside of Upper Deck: Inspect for buckling or corrosion of deck stiffeners. Extend this into the topside (sloping) tank internal structure and its brackets, which is the structure this question is really about — the sloping plating, its longitudinals, the transverse ring webs and the bracket toes where they land. viii) Load line marks: Ensure the load line marks and draft marks are clearly visible and not obstructed by corrosion or paint. Confirm that the markings have not been altered and are still compliant with regulatory standards. ix) Fire Fighting System Check: Inspect the condition of fire hoses, nozzles, and sprinkler systems for readiness and compliance with regulations.

x) Lighting: Verify that emergency lighting and work lighting in the upper deck spaces are functioning. xi) The bulk-carrier-specific structure Two further items turn a general deck inspection into a bulk-carrier inspection, and both should be named. First, the transverse corrugated bulkheads and their lower stools between holds, inspected from the topside tanks and hold access — this is the classic No.1 / No.2 hold progressive-flooding failure mode, where a corroded or buckled corrugation lets flooding of one hold into the next. Second, on a single-side-skin bulker, the side- shell frames and their end brackets at the top and bottom connections, a known wastage hotspot where grab damage, alternate wetting and coating breakdown combine.

answers.title: Transverse watertight bulkheads — reasons, what constitutes one, minimum number & testing
answers.question_as_set:
(a) State FOUR reasons for transverse watertight bulkheads in ship construction. (4)

(b) State the minimum number of transverse watertight bulkheads and their location. (4)

(c) Describe how watertight bulkheads are tested. (2)

Marks: (a) 4 · (b) 4 · (c) 2
answers.answer_text:
a) Transverse watertight bulkheads in ship construction serve several critical purposes:

- Flooding Prevention: They divide the ship into separate compartments, helping to contain flooding in the event of a hull breach, limiting the spread of water and enhancing survivability.

- Structural Integrity: They contribute to the overall structural strength, helping resist bending and shear forces that occur during operations, particularly in rough seas.

- Stability Improvement: By providing additional support and reducing free surface effects, they help enhance the ship's stability.

- Fire Containment: They can serve as fire barriers, restricting the spread of fire from one compartment to another. The second printing of the same question puts the same three reasons more tightly, and this is the form to write if only three are asked for: Reasons for Fitting Transverse Watertight Bulkheads: Flood Prevention (compartmentalize the ship, limiting water ingress if the hull is breached, maintaining buoyancy and stability); Structural Integrity (provide strength, acting as pillars supporting deck and tank tops); Fire Containment (slow the spread of flames and smoke between compartments). What constitutes a watertight bulkhead A watertight bulkhead is a vertical partition within a ship designed to prevent water ingress into adjacent compartments. It must be constructed with minimal openings, able to withstand hydrostatic pressure when flooded, with reinforced plating (steel or equivalent) to ensure integrity under pressure. In practice that means plating stiffened vertically or horizontally and scantled for the design head of water — the head to the bulkhead deck — with every penetration made good: watertight doors of an approved class, cable and pipe penetrations sealed by approved glands, and no unprotected openings below the bulkhead deck.

b) The minimum number of transverse watertight bulkheads typically required includes:

- Collision Bulkhead: Located at the forward end, designed to protect against collision damage, extending from the bottom of the hull to the upper deck. Its position is set by rule: not less than 0.05 L and not more than 0.08 L abaft the forward perpendicular — in some cases 0.05 L + 3 m — which is the figure that earns the mark.

- After Peak Bulkhead: Situated at the aft end, enclosing the stern tube, extending to at least the first deck above the load waterline.

- Machinery Space Bulkheads: A watertight bulkhead is required at each end of the machinery space. Stated as a count: Minimum Number and Location: One Collision Bulkhead (forward); One Aft Peak Bulkhead (stern); One Bulkhead at Each End of the Engine Room. So for a ship with machinery amidships the minimum is typically four transverse watertight bulkheads — collision, after peak, and one at each end of the machinery space — while an aft-machinery ship needs a minimum of three, because the after-peak bulkhead and the after machinery-space bulkhead can be one and the same. Above that minimum the number required increases with ship length under the class rules, and for a ship carrying passengers it is set by the floodable-length and damage-stability calculation rather than by a count.

c) The second printing answers this as: Testing: Pressure Testing (hose simulating water pressure to check for leaks and structural integrity); Visual Inspection (for buckling or deformation); Air Leak Testing (pressurized air within a compartment to detect leaks by monitoring air escape). That list conflates two different tests under “pressure testing”, so set them out separately, because they prove different things.

- Hose Test: A hose test involves applying water pressure to check for leaks. Water is sprayed or directed onto the bulkhead's surface, ensuring that no water seeps through any joints or connections. What this proves is joint and seam tightness only — it says nothing about the strength of the bulkhead.

- Fill (head) test: the proper strength and boundary test is to fill the compartment to the head the bulkhead is designed for, so that the test reproduces the design hydrostatic head and the structure is loaded as it would be in the flooded condition.

- Air / leak test: where filling is impracticable, pressurise the compartment with air to the approved test pressure and paint the seams with a leak-indicating solution, which shows a leak as bubbles. Air Leak Testing (pressurized air within a compartment to detect leaks by monitoring air escape).

- Visual Inspection (for buckling or deformation) accompanies whichever test is used, before and after.

> **Source note:** Part 2 answers this topic twice. At p.30 part (c) is answered with the hose test alone, and its Model Additions box records that a hose test proves joint and seam tightness only, the proper strength test being a fill (head) test to the design head or an air test with leak-indicating solution. At p.48 part (d) is printed as “Pressure Testing (hose simulating water pressure to check for leaks and structural integrity)”, which the same box identifies as conflating the two tests. Both original passages are preserved above, and the two tests are set out separately with what each one actually demonstrates.

answers.title: Aluminium alloy in shipbuilding — advantages, disadvantages & welding of
answers.question_as_set:
(a) State the advantages and disadvantages of aluminium alloy in ship building. (4)

(b) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a method of welding aluminium panels. (6)

Marks: (a) 4 · (b) 6
answers.answer_text:
a) Advantage: (i) Light weight (ii) Corrosion resistance (iii) High versatility (iv) Recyclability. Dis-Advantages: (i) Softer than steel (ii) Expensive (iii) Corrodes rapidly in sea water (iv) Requires specialised welding techniques. Two further disadvantages actually govern the design: aluminium's low melting point and loss of strength in a fire, which is why an aluminium structure forming a fire division has to be insulated to the A-class standard on the basis that the core temperature must not rise to the point where the alloy loses strength; and its higher coefficient of thermal expansion than steel, roughly twice that of steel, which has to be allowed for at joints and at aluminium-to-steel connections. The corrosion behaviour needs stating correctly. Aluminium forms a self-protecting oxide film and is in general corrosion-resistant in seawater — better than mild steel. The real problem is galvanic corrosion at aluminium-to-steel joints, where the aluminium is anodic to the steel and wastes rapidly; such joints must be electrically isolated with insulating material or made through an explosion-bonded bi-metallic transition strip, so that the aluminium is welded to aluminium and the steel to steel. b) TIG (gas tungsten arc) welding (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.26 Gas tungsten arc welding is referred to as "TIG" welding. It utilizes a non-consumable tungsten electrode and separate filler metal in the form of a wire (not used for thin sections). Inert shielding gas is supplied through an annular nozzle around the tungsten electrode. It is better suited for shop fabrication than field fabrication because movement must be less than 5 mph to maintain the inert gas blanket. The consumable filler metal is

added either manually or by some mechanized process. The inert gas shielding protects the molten metal, which is cooling, and it also provides the required arc characteristics. The process may use direct current (DC), with positive or negative polarity, attached to the tungsten electrode, although in most applications the electrode is attached to the negative polarity. Alternative current (AC) is also used to produce different effects on the welding. Argon and helium are the two inert gases used for this process. Choice of gas and type of current and polarity depends on the type of material and quality of weld desired. Applied to aluminium specifically For aluminium the choice is AC TIG (or AC MIG), and the reason should be given: the cathodic half-cycle of the alternating current breaks up the tenacious oxide film, which melts at a far higher temperature than the parent metal and would otherwise remain as an inclusion in the weld. The joint must be cleaned and the oxide mechanically removed immediately before welding, and pre-heat and interpass temperature must be controlled to avoid porosity — hydrogen is very soluble in molten aluminium — and lack-of-fusion defects, aluminium's high thermal conductivity carrying heat away from the joint. Argon is the usual shielding gas; helium, or an argon-helium mixture, gives a hotter arc and deeper penetration for thicker sections.

> **Source note:** Part 2's original list gives “Corrodes rapidly in sea water” as a disadvantage, and its own Model Additions box records that this is misleading — aluminium forms a self-protecting oxide film and is generally corrosion-resistant, the real problem being galvanic corrosion at aluminium-to-steel joints. The original item is preserved above as printed and the corrected mechanism is given immediately after it, so the galvanic explanation is what gets written in the exam.

answers.title: Roll reduction — bilge keels plus TWO other methods, with advantages & disadvantages
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to roll reduction systems:

(a) explain the principle of operation of bilge keels, stating their advantages; (4)

(b) describe TWO other methods of roll reduction, stating the advantages and disadvantages of EACH system. (6)

Marks: (a) 4 · (b) 6
answers.answer_text:
a) Bilge Keels: Bilge keels are narrow fins or plates attached amidships, longitudinally along the turn of the bilge, where the bottom curves into the sides, on both sides. They work by increasing hydrodynamic resistance when the vessel rolls, creating a damping effect that reduces the amplitude of rolling motions. The design usually involves flat plates or strakes that present resistance to water flow during a roll, thus helping to stabilize the vessel. Advantages: Low Maintenance (require minimal maintenance compared to active stabilization systems) · No Internal Components (do not take up space inside the hull, preserving cargo and operational areas) · Cost- Effective (relatively inexpensive to install and maintain). They also work at any speed, including zero speed and at anchor, because the damping comes from the ship's own rolling velocity and not from forward way.

b) Other methods of roll reduction are;

i) Anti Roll Tanks: Passive uncontrolled tanks utilize the principles of fluid dynamics to reduce roll by allowing water to move freely within tanks located in the hull. As the vessel rolls, water shifts from one side of the tank to the other, creating a counteracting moment that helps stabilize the ship. This system does not require active control or mechanical components. The effect depends on the water arriving out of phase with the roll, so the tank and its cross-over duct are tuned to the ship's natural roll period; if that period changes with loading — that is, with a change of GM — the tank can become ineffective, or in the worst case can arrive in phase and amplify the roll. Advantages: Simplicity · Cost-Effective Installation · effective roll damping close to the natural roll period, and at zero speed. Disadvantages: Delayed Response Time · Reduced Stability (Free Surface Effect) · Significant Space Consumption. To those add the tuning dependence just described.

(ii) Active Fin Stabilizers: Fin stabilizers are underwater, wing-like appendages attached to both sides of a ship's hull below the waterline that reduce roll motion caused by waves. They work like wings, using sensors to tilt the fins, creating hydraulic lift that acts against the wave-induced rolling motion. When a ship rolls, sensors detect the movement and command hydraulic cylinders to tilt the fins, creating counter-acting upward or downward forces. Advantages: Superior Roll Reduction · Enhanced Safety and Comfort · Highly efficient at reducing roll at higher, cruising speeds. Disadvantages: Increased Drag and Fuel Consumption · Risk of Damage and Vulnerability · Space Limitations. And, the standard counterpoint, they are ineffective at low speed and at anchor, because a fin can only generate lift with water flowing past it. That is the comparison the question is looking for: bilge keels and passive tanks work at zero speed, fins do not; fins are far more effective than either once the ship is up to service speed.

> **Source note:** Part 2's original answer lists “Increased Stability” among the advantages of the passive anti-roll tank and “Reduced Stability (Free Surface Effect)” among its disadvantages, and its own Model Additions box records that this is contradictory and instructs that “Increased Stability” be removed: a passive tank does not increase stability, its free surface always reduces GM, and the genuine benefit is roll-amplitude damping near the natural roll period at a small GM cost. That is the one place in this entry where original wording has been changed rather than added to — the advantage now reads “effective roll damping close to the natural roll period, and at zero speed”. The disadvantage is preserved as printed.

answers.title: Watertight / weathertight doors · bilge injection valve
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain the function and location of EACH of the following:

(i) watertight doors; (3)

(ii) weathertight doors. (3)

(b) Explain why a bilge injection valve is incorporated into the main sea water system, describing how it is tested. (4)

Marks: (a)(i) 3 · (a)(ii) 3 · (b) 4
answers.answer_text:
(a) (i) Watertight doors: Watertight doors on ships are critical safety barriers designed to prevent the spread of flooding between compartments during emergencies, limiting the spread of water within the vessel and help maintain its buoyancy and stability. The defining requirement is that the door withstands a static head of water from either side without leakage, and it is designed for the pressure at its particular location, that pressure being set by the subdivision and damage-stability calculation for the ship. They are essential in any opening that compromises the watertight integrity of the ship's hull, ensuring that water does not flow between compartments during emergencies. These doors are installed below the bulkhead (freeboard) deck, in areas prone to flooding such as: Shaft tunnels · Ballast tanks · Engine room bulkheads · Pipe tunnels. ii) Weathertight Doors: Weathertight doors are designed to withstand weather conditions and prevent water from entering the vessel during heavy seas or rain. They can withstand brief submersion and provide fire and smoke containment, enhancing overall safety. The definition to give is that water will not penetrate into the ship in any sea condition — achieved by gaskets and cleats — but that the door is not designed to hold a sustained head of water, which is the essential difference from a watertight door. They are critical for maintaining the ship's integrity against environmental conditions without compromising internal safety features. These doors are installed on the freeboard (weather) deck and in superstructures, in areas subjected to adverse weather conditions such as: Main Decks · Accommodation Entrances · Navigation Bridge Entrances · Engine Room Entrance.

(b) A bilge injection valve is incorporated into the main sea water system to provide emergency bilge pumping capacity, allowing large main sea water pumps to directly remove high volumes of floodwater from the engine room in situations like collision or grounding. It is a normally closed, non-return valve, often with a red handle, connected to the suction side of the main cooling pump. Specifically it is a screw-down non-return (SDNR) valve, fitted on the suction of the largest-capacity sea-water (main circulating) pump, with a diameter typically not less than two-thirds of the main sea suction, and with the handwheel mounted high and readily accessible above the anticipated flood level. This arrangement gives the maximum possible emergency dewatering capacity for the machinery space. Testing is performed to ensure operation, through the following steps:

1. Preparation: Place a screen over the strainer at the bilge injection suction point to prevent debris from entering the pump, while ensuring the area is relatively clear. Make arrangements for the suction at the bilge injection valve.

2. Procedure: Open the bilge injection valve. Ensure the valve operates freely and the spindle is in good condition.

3. Operation: Start the main sea water pump and close the main sea chest (sea inlet) valve to create suction from the bilge.

4. Verification: Monitor the pressure gauges to ensure suction is working and check that water is being discharged overboard.

5. Completion: Once tested, close the bilge injection valve and re-open the main sea chest to restore normal cooling water flow. After successful testing record the test results in the logbook. After testing replace the seal on the valve. State the safety caution as part of the answer: the valve must never be left cracked open in service, because if the non-return element passes, the sea will flood the bilge. Confirm that it shuts tight on completion of the test.

> **Source note:** Part 1 locates the two door types “below” and “above the waterline”. Its Model Additions record that this is only loosely right; the precise boundary is the freeboard (bulkhead) deck, and that wording is used above.

answers.title: Watertight-door classification, closure & safe passage
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain the system of classification for access doors passing through watertight bulkheads of a vessel. (3)

(b) State THREE circumstances under which all watertight doors must be closed when situations are defined as potentially hazardous. (3)

(c) Explain the safety features built into the watertight door operating system to enhance safety to personnel. (4)

Marks: (a) 3 · (b) 3 · (c) 4
answers.answer_text:
a) Watertight bulkhead access doors are classified as follows:

- Type A: These doors may be left open and are to be closed only during emergencies.

- Type B: These doors should remain closed but can be opened when personnel are working in the adjacent compartment.

- Type C: These doors must remain closed at all times, only opening briefly when personnel pass through.

- Type D: These doors shall be closed before the voyage commences and shall be kept closed during navigation. That is the operational usage classification, taken from the IMO MSC.1 circular on the operation of watertight doors. Because the question could equally be read as asking about the construction classification, state both: SOLAS II-1 separately classifies watertight doors by operating type — Class 1 hinged, Class 2 hand-operated sliding, and Class 3 power-operated sliding, closeable from the bridge. Giving both schemes covers either reading of the question.

b) Circumstances under which all watertight doors must be closed when situations are defined as potentially hazardous are;

- Heavy weather conditions or where depth is less than 3 times the draught.

- Proximity to underwater hazards, port limits or compulsory pilotage waters.

- Restricted visibility, high traffic density or any other factor constituting a hazard.

c) Procedure to pass safely through a hydraulically operated watertight door;

- The door is hydraulically operated and has three operating positions, bridge control, emergency position, and local control. Locate Controls, Check Indicators, and move the local handle to the 'open' position and wait until the door is completely open.

- Before opening, confirm that the bridge master mode switch is set to “local control”. If it is set to “doors closed” — as it will be during a drill or an emergency — the door will re-close as soon as the local handle is released, which is a crushing hazard. Check both the local and the remote open/closed indicators.

- Pass quickly and safely, watching your footing using the handles provided on the door to assist in movement.

- After passing through, move the local handle to the 'close' position to close the door until the green light indicates.

- Never attempt to pass through a door while it is moving (risk of fatal crush injuries) and never stop a closing door. Emphasize the need to keep doors closed at sea for water tight integrity.

- After the explanation, physically demonstrate the operation of a hydraulically operated watertight door and ensure the crew member can operate it safely. Where the sitting instead asks for the safety features designed into the operating system, present the same material as design provisions: audible alarm before and during travel, local and bridge open/closed indicators, a hold-to-run local handle on both sides of the bulkhead, controlled closing time and closing force, and an independent power supply so the door remains operable on loss of main power.

answers.title: Watertight doors — number/size factors, operating requirements & hazards
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to watertight doors:

(a) explain the factors that affect the number and size compatible with the proper working of the ship; (3)

(b) explain the operating requirements of watertight doors below the weather deck; (3)

(c) outline the potential hazards when passing through power operated watertight doors stating how these are overcome. (4)

Marks: (a) 3 · (b) 3 · (c) 4
answers.answer_text:
(a) Factors that affect the number and size of watertight doors compatible with the proper working of the ship are;

1. Subdivision and Damage Stability Requirements (Safety Factor): A (singular) watertight door is required where a watertight bulkhead requires access through it for passage.

2. Operational Function and Access Requirements (Functional Factor): WTDs are restricted to essential access points (shaft tunnel, duct keel, passage between compartments for passengers on passenger ships). The size of the opening shall be made as small as possible.

3. Structural Strength of the Bulkhead (Structural Factor): The number and size of WTDs must be limited to allow for proper framing and structural reinforcement of the bulkhead to maintain its strength against water pressure.

b) Operating requirements of watertight doors below the weather deck are;

1. Safety and Emergency Power: WTDs must be kept closed at sea, used only for passage, and immediately closed after. WTDs should have two sources of power, including an independent, emergency power source to ensure operation during a blackout. A power-operated sliding door has its own hydraulic accumulator or independent power supply, sufficient for at least three complete open-and-close cycles against a 15° list with no main power available, corresponding to about an hour of independent operation.

2. Remote Closure & Local Control: Must be capable of being closed simultaneously from the bridge within 60 seconds, with the ship listed up to 15°. Must be operable locally from both sides of the bulkhead. The two closure times must be kept separate, and this is the most commonly lost mark on this question: the 60 seconds is the time to close all doors simultaneously from the bridge master switch, whereas an individual power-operated sliding door must close in 20 to 40 seconds with the ship upright when it is operated on its own. The bridge also carries a master mode switch, selecting “local control” or “doors closed”.

3. Alarms & Indicators: Remote, audible alarms must sound for 10 seconds before and during closure. Remote, visual, “open/closed” indicators must be present at the bridge and control station. These figures are those of SOLAS II-1 Regulations 13 and 13-1, and quoting the regulation earns credit.

c) Potential hazards when passing through power operated watertight doors are;

1. Crushing Injuries/Fatalities: The doors close with immense force, sufficient to crush bones or cause fatal injuries if a person is caught in between while it is already in motion.

2. Hand/Body Safety Risks: Sliding WTDs are often moved by hydraulic cylinders and can cause severe injuries if hands or clothing are caught in the pinch points.

3. Sudden Automatic Re-closure: If a WTD is opened locally while the master mode switch on the bridge is set to “closed” (e.g., during a drill or emergency), the door will immediately close upon release of the local handle.

4. Lack of Situational Awareness: In noisy environments, the audio-visual alarms may go unnoticed or unheard. Potential hazards could be eliminated by;

1. Adherence to alarm systems, standard operating procedure and clear signage.

2. Mandatory two-handed manual operation (hold-to-open local handle procedure).

3. Prohibition of carrying load alone and passing while door is in motion.

4. Regular training and familiarization.

> **Source note:** Part 1's part (b) quotes only the 60-second bridge closure. Its Model Additions require the 20–40 second individual door closing time to be added, and it has been folded into point 2 above.
