answers.title: Conditions of assignment of load line
answers.question_as_set:
Describe the items that should be inspected to ensure that the conditions of assignment of Load Line are satisfactorily complied with. (10)

Marks: 10
answers.answer_text:
To ensure compliance with load line assignment according to The International Convention on Load Lines, 1966 (ICLL 1966) and The UK Merchant Shipping (Load Line) Regulations 1998, inspections focus on maintaining the vessel's watertight/weathertight integrity, structural strength, and crew safety. Key items include closing appliances (hatches, doors), air pipes, ventilators, scuppers, side scuttles, cargo ports, and marking of the deck line and load lines. Critical inspection areas for load line compliance are;

i) Load Line Markings: The deck line, load line marks, and draught marks must be clearly visible, painted, and properly located, and must agree with the freeboard shown on the certificate. ii) Hatchways and Closures: All hatch covers on exposed decks must be weathertight, with secured closing appliances, tarpaulins, and securing devices. iii) Machinery Space Openings: Openings on freeboard decks must have efficient weathertight closures. Engine room skylights and fiddley openings must be in good condition. iv) Manholes and Flush Scuttles: Must be watertight and capable of being secured.

v) Ventilators and Air Pipes: All ventilators (including air pipe closing devices) must be efficient, weathertight, and capable of being closed. vi) Side Scuttles and Deadlights: Below the freeboard deck must be watertight, including checking packing for cracks. vii) Cargo Ports and Watertight Doors: All openings in the ship's side below the freeboard deck must be securely watertight. viii) Scuppers, Inlets, and Discharges: Non-return valves on overboard discharges must be functional and effective.

ix) Bulwarks and Guardrails: Must be structurally sound, secure, and maintained in good condition to protect the crew and allow drainage.

x) Structure and Stability: General structural integrity of the hull, frame, and bulkheads, along with documentation of stability, must be verified. xi) Freeing ports in bulwarks: The freeing-port area must be correct for the length of bulwark served, and the non-return flaps must be free to operate and not seized, painted up or lashed. This is a classic conditions-of- assignment item. xii) Protection of the crew and means of access: Guard rails, lifelines, gangways and walkways, and the safe access arrangements between the accommodation and the machinery space. These are expressly an ICLL condition of assignment, not merely good practice. xiii) Coaming heights and positions: Hatch, ventilator and air-pipe coamings must be of the required height for their position, distinguishing Position 1 from Position 2, together with the required companionway and door sill heights. Finally, tie the inspection back to the documents, which is what converts a list of items into a proper conditions- of-assignment answer. The assigned marks must agree with the freeboard shown on a valid Load Line Certificate; the certificate and the stability book must be checked; and it must be confirmed that no structural alteration has been made that would change the assigned freeboard. On an older, newly purchased vessel these three checks are the priority.

answers.title: Hydraulically operated folding hatch cover — operation, watertightness & security
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, how a hydraulically operated folding hatch cover opens and closes. (7)

(b) Explain how the water tightness and security of the hatch cover sketched in part (a) can be ascertained before proceeding to sea. (3)

Marks: (a) 7 · (b) 3
answers.answer_text:
Sol: (a) Hydraulically operated folding hatch cover (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.24 The Hatch cover sketched is made of a pair of covers operated by a hydraulic cylinder for opening and closing. The cylinder is connected to the first hatch cover at one end and is secured to the deck at the other end. The pressurisation and de-pressurisation of the cylinder causes the first cover to move. The first cover is connected to the second using a roller arrangement and chain track which helps in transfer of motion for opening and closing. The chain track also acts as a guide. When closing a part of the rail can be retracted so that the end wheel is lowered down causing the neoprene seal to press down on the coming rail. Read in order, then: extending the cylinder lifts the leading pair of panels about their hinge so that the two panels fold face to face and travel along the coaming top on their end wheels in the chain track, stowing vertically at the hatch end. Closing reverses it — the folded pair runs back along the track, and at the end of travel the retractable section of rail drops the end wheels so that the panels come down flat and the neoprene seal is compressed onto the coaming rail rather than being dragged along it. Wheels off the rail and the cover resting on its landing pads is what makes the seal work; the cleats then hold it there.

(b) The watertight integrity and security of a hatch cover can be done by carrying out cheks of the cleat arrangement which helps in securing the hatch on the cover. Before securing of the cleat we need to ensure the

Neoprene seal is properly seated on the coaming rail. Before proceeding to sea, and because this part carries 3 marks in its own right, go further:

- Ascertain tightness by a hose test at not less than 2 bar at the nozzle, or by an ultrasonic tightness test of the perimeter seal, which gives a quantitative reading and can be done with cargo loaded and in any weather.

- Confirm the rubber-to-compression-bar contact by chalk or witness line all round, and confirm that the compression is correct — the rubber compressed onto the bar but not over-compressed or permanently "set", since a set gasket cannot recover and will leak.

- Check that the drainage channels and the non-return drain valves in the coaming are clear, so that any water passing the first barrier drains overboard instead of into the hold.

- Verify that all cleats, cross-joint wedges and the locating and landing pads are correctly set and bearing, so that the cover cannot lift, shift or "pant" against its seal in a seaway.

> **Source note:** Part 2 reproduces this answer with “cheks” for checks and “coming rail” for coaming rail, and records both as spelling slips in its own note rather than editing the answer. They are left exactly as printed here for the same reason, since the original answer text is not altered; both words are spelled correctly everywhere else in the entry.

answers.title: Cargo hatch covers on large container ships — tightness testing, load transfer & wear
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to cargo hatch covers on large container ships:

(a) describe how they are tested for watertightness; (2)

(b) explain how the weight of the hatch and containers is transferred to the ship's structure whilst allowing for deflections of the hull in a seaway; (3)

(c) describe, with the aid of a sketch, the type and location of damage that can occur due to wear of the hatch supporting arrangements. (5)

Marks: (a) 2 · (b) 3 · (c) 5
answers.answer_text:
a) Cargo hatch cover can be tested for water tightness by Hose test. In this test, a water spray from a nozzle of 12 mm diameter is sprayed over the joint of hold and cover from a distance of 1 m to 1.5 m with a pressure of 0.5 m/sec water jet. Any leak of water inside the cargo hold will indicate a gap between the hold and the cover. The figures to quote are: nozzle bore not less than 12 mm, held not more than 1.5 m from the joint, water pressure not less than 2 bar at the nozzle, and the jet traversed slowly along the whole length of the joint. Other methods include: Chalk test (on top of bar that the hatch sealing rubber rests) · Ultrasonic testers · Inspect from inside of the closed hatch for any light penetrating. Of those, the chalk test only checks that the rubber is being compressed onto the bar — it shows the contact line, but it does not prove tightness, and it is not accepted as a tightness test. The definitive alternatives to the hose test are an ultrasonic tightness test, which is preferred at sea because it gives a quantitative leak reading, is independent of the weather and can be carried out with the hold loaded, and a pressure or vacuum test where the covers are fitted for it.

b) Weight of lift-away pontoon type hatch cover and containers is transferred to ships structure using weight bearing pads which are fitted to hatch coaming & hatch cover to relieve stress on elastomeric neoprene seal. These support pads are designed to distribute heavy loads from container stacks evenly to the vessel's deck structure. The bearing pads are not locked rigidly across the entire length; they are designed as separate, local supports that allow the hatch cover to move slightly relative to the coaming without damaging the structure during deflections of the hull in a seaway. The principle worth stating explicitly is that the load path and the sealing path are kept separate: the pads carry the vertical container load into the coaming and deck structure, while the neoprene seal carries no load at all and only has to remain in compression. Because the hull works in a seaway — hogging, sagging and twisting — the cover must be free to move a little relative to the coaming; the pads therefore locate it vertically while the stoppers take the horizontal load, and nothing is rigidly built in. c)

Hatch-cover support — weight-bearing pads, cleat, neoprene seal, coaming (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.19

1. Hatch Support Pads (Bearing Pads): Location — the interface between the hatch cover (bottom) and the hatch coaming (top). Damage — excessive wear of steel or specialty pads (elastomeric or copper alloy) due to the heavy loads of stacked containers and vessel vibration; this leads to reduced pad height, improper seating of the hatch cover, uneven distribution of weight and potential stress cracks in surrounding steelwork.

2. Hatch Cover Stoppers (Restraining Devices): Location — longitudinal and transverse stoppers fitted at the sides and ends of the hatch cover and coaming. Damage — wear and deformation of the stopper plates due to constant buffeting of the cover during ship motion, causing enlarged clearances, allowing the hatch cover to move, resulting in severe deformation of the stoppers and surrounding plate structure.

3. Hatch Cover Sealing Arrangement (Periphery): Location — the rubber gasket and the compression bar (landing bar) on the coaming. Damage — improper support causes the sealing rubber to be compressed unevenly, resulting in permanent deformation, hardening, or tearing of the seal; the compression bar itself can show localized thinning due to corrosion and friction. The three are one chain of consequences, and saying so is what earns the last mark: pads wear down, the cover sits lower, the rubber is over-compressed and takes a permanent set, the cover then works against its stoppers, and the enlarged clearances let it move further still — so worn pads are found as a leaking hatch and as cracking in the coaming steelwork, not as a pad defect.

> **Source note:** Part 2's original part (a) gives the hose test as “a pressure of 0.5 m/sec water jet”, and its own Model Additions box records that 0.5 m/sec is a velocity and not a pressure, the markable figures being a nozzle of at least 12 mm held within 1.5 m at a water pressure of at least 2 bar. The original sentence is preserved above exactly as printed and the correct set of figures follows it.

answers.title: Drainage from the external structure — scuppers, freeing ports & tanker handrails
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to drainage from a ship's external structure, explain EACH of the following:

(a) why scuppers are located in close proximity to the superstructure, whereas freeing ports are generally located at open areas of the weather deck; (3)

(b) why it is essential that scuppers and freeing ports are operational at all times; (4)

(c) why oil tankers have handrails on the main cargo deck other than for reasons of personnel safety. (3)

Marks: (a) 3 · (b) 4 · (c) 3
answers.answer_text:
a) Scuppers are located in close proximity to the superstructure to instantly drain water away from weathertight doors and vertical structures to prevent structural damage or flooding. Superstructures create corners and obstructions where water gathers, scuppers are placed there to protect entrances and deckhouses from water logging. Freeing ports are placed along open bulwarks to rapidly release large volumes of seawater from the main deck, preventing pocketing that compromises stability. These are large openings in the bulwarks intended to quickly remove massive quantities of water entered in to open areas during heavy weather, preventing the accumulation of weight on deck. Both systems are critical for maintaining stability and preventing structural damage. The distinction is one of duty. A scupper is a small drain through the deck or bulwark, piped overboard, sized to clear rain and spray continuously from a local low spot — which is why it belongs where the superstructure creates a pocket. A freeing port is a large opening at deck level in the bulwark, sized by rule against the length of the bulwark, and its duty is to clear a boarding sea in seconds — which is why it belongs on the open run of weather deck where green water actually lands.

b) It is essential that scuppers and freeing ports are operational at all times to ensure;

1. Water Drainage: Scuppers allow water that accumulates on deck to drain overboard, preventing excessive weight and potential instability.

2. Free surface effect, raising COG, and reducing freeboard: Freeing ports facilitate quick drainage of water from enclosed decks. If these systems fail, water can pool on deck, increasing free surface effect and raising COG. Accumulated water adds significant weight, reducing the vessel's freeboard.

3. Safety During Operations: During rough seas, operational scuppers help maintain a clear deck by preventing water accumulation, which could create slippery surfaces and increase the risk of accidents among crew members.

4. Compliance with Regulations: Keeping scuppers and freeing ports operational is essential by regulation 24 of International Convention on Load Lines (ILLC). Non-compliance can lead to penalties, and detention of the vessel until issues are resolved. The two arrangements sit under different regulations and should be quoted separately: scuppers, inlets and discharges are ILLC Regulation 22, freeing ports are ILLC Regulation 24. Both are conditions of assignment of the freeboard, so a defective arrangement puts the load line certificate in question and not merely the drainage.

c) Oil tankers have handrails on the main cargo deck, beyond personnel safety, for the following reasons,

i) Handrails ensure that any green seas are drained very quickly from the deck, this prevents an increase in stress on the vessel that would be produced if the extra mass of water was retained on board. ii) The use of guard rails makes a saving in construction costs, as less steel is used. iii) Large volumes of water, if retained on deck, could possibly affect the vessels stability by raised COG, free surface effect and reduced free board, and by fitting handrails this will ensure that water drains quickly. The reasoning to spell out is that open rails, fitted instead of solid bulwarks, let a shipped sea clear straight off the deck edge with nothing to hold it. A loaded tanker has very little freeboard and ships water readily, so a solid bulwark on a tanker's cargo deck would trap large volumes of water between the rails and the

tank tops. Open rails therefore prevent water trapping, remove the added weight and free surface before they can act, and remove the racking and sloshing loads that a trapped body of water would impose on the deck and the bulwark itself. Note also that the rule allowing freeing-port area to be credited as a fraction of the bulwark length does not arise where open rails are fitted, because there is no bulwark to pierce.

> **Source note:** Part 2's original part (b)4 puts both scuppers and freeing ports under ILLC Regulation 24, and its own Model Additions box records that these are different regulations — scuppers and discharges Regulation 22, freeing ports Regulation 24. The original sentence is preserved above and the split is given immediately after it. The same slip appears in the March 2019 printing of the neighbouring question and is corrected the same way in E42.

answers.title: Watertight & weathertight doors — function and location; scuppers &
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain the function and location of EACH of the following:

(i) watertight doors; (3)

(ii) weathertight doors. (3)

(b) Explain why it is essential that scuppers and freeing ports are operational at all times. (4)

Marks: (a)(i) 3 · (a)(ii) 3 · (b) 4
answers.answer_text:
Definitions first — the marks are in them Watertight means the closure withstands a design head of water from either side without leakage, and watertight closures are fitted below the bulkhead or freeboard deck. Weathertight means water will not penetrate into the ship in any sea condition, and weathertight closures are fitted at openings in exposed positions on and above the freeboard deck. The difference is a static head from either side versus no penetration from outside in the intact condition.

(a) (i) Watertight doors: Watertight doors on ships are critical safety barriers designed to prevent the spread of flooding between compartments during emergencies limiting the spread of water within the vessel and help maintain its buoyancy and stability. They are essential in any opening that compromises the watertight integrity of the ship's hull. These doors are installed below the waterline in areas prone to flooding such as: Shaft tunnels · Ballast tanks · Engine room bulkheads · Pipe tunnels.

(ii) Weathertight Doors: Weathertight doors are designed to withstand weather conditions and prevent water from entering the vessel during heavy seas or rain. They can withstand brief submersion. They do not provide a fire rating: resisting the passage of fire and smoke is the duty of an A-class or B-class fire division, and a weathertight door resists water from any direction in the intact condition and nothing else. Where a door has to do both jobs it is rated twice over, as a weathertight closure and as a fire door. These doors are installed above the waterline, in areas subjected to adverse weather conditions such as: Main Decks · Accommodation Entrances · Navigation Bridge Entrances · Engine Room Entrance.

(b) It is essential that scuppers and freeing ports are operational at all times to ensure;

1. Water Drainage: Scuppers allow water that accumulates on deck to drain overboard, preventing excessive weight and potential instability. Water logging can lead to corrosion, and structural damage.

2. Free surface effect, raising COG, and reducing freeboard: Freeing ports facilitate quick drainage of water from enclosed decks. If these systems fail, water can pool on deck, increasing free surface effect and raising COG. Accumulated water adds significant weight, reducing the vessel's freeboard. Taken together those three effects are why trapped water is dangerous out of proportion to its weight: the added weight and the raised centre of gravity reduce GM, the free surface of a body of water lying loose on deck reduces it again, and the lost freeboard reduces the reserve buoyancy and the range of stability — so in a beam sea a deck-load of trapped water can carry a ship past the point of return.

3. Safety During Operations: During rough seas or adverse weather conditions, operational scuppers help maintain a clear deck by preventing water accumulation, which could create slippery surfaces and increase the risk of accidents among crew members.

4. Compliance with Regulations: Keeping scuppers and freeing ports operational is essential by regulation 24 of International Convention on Load Lines (ILLC). Non-compliance can lead to penalties, and detention of the vessel until issues are resolved. Quote the two separately — scuppers and discharges are ILLC Regulation 22 and freeing ports are ILLC Regulation 24 — and add that both are conditions of assignment of the freeboard, so keeping them clear and operable is a condition of the load line certificate itself.

> **Source note:** two corrections from Part 2's own Model Additions box are applied above. First, the original part (a)(ii) reads “They can withstand brief submersion and provide fire and smoke containment, enhancing overall safety”; the box records that fire and smoke containment is not a function of a weathertight door and instructs that the claim be removed, so that sentence is the one place in this entry where original wording has been cut rather than added to — it now reads “They can withstand brief submersion”, with the reason for the removal given in the text. Second, the original part (b)4 puts both scuppers and freeing ports under Regulation 24; the sentence is preserved and the correct split, Regulation 22 and Regulation 24, follows it.

answers.title: Class A bulkheads & ventilation (accommodation)
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to structural fire protection in passenger ship accommodation spaces:

(a) define the meaning of Class A bulkheads, stating the requirements; (4)

(b) discuss the design of ventilation systems to prevent the spread of smoke and fire; (4)

(c) explain how the integrity of the bulkhead is retained with respect to ventilation trunkings, where A Class bulkheads have to be penetrated. (2)

Marks: (a) 4 · (b) 4 · (c) 2
answers.answer_text:
a) Class A bulkheads are structural divisions constructed of steel or equivalent material, suitably stiffened, and designed to prevent the passage of smoke and flame for a designated time during a standard fire test. Requirements for Class A Bulkheads are;

- Construction Material: Must be made of steel or equivalent non-combustible material securely stiffened to maintain structural integrity.

- Fire Integrity: Capable of preventing the passage of smoke and flame for the designated time standard fire test.

- Insulation (Thermal Performance): Must be insulated with non-combustible materials so that the average temperature on the unexposed side does not rise more than 139 °C, and the temperature at any single point (including joints) does not rise more than 180 °C within the following times: ◦ Class A-60: 60 minutes. ◦ Class A-30: 30 minutes. ◦ Class A-15: 15 minutes. ◦ Class A-0: 0 minutes. One further line is a common discriminator between a pass and a strong answer. Integrity is judged against the standard fire test (time–temperature) curve applied over 60 minutes. The suffix number — 60, 30, 15 or 0 — is the insulation period only, that is the time for which the temperature-rise criteria must be met; flame and smoke must be held for the full 60 minutes regardless of the suffix. This is also the answer to the March 2019 sitting's part (b) on the standard fire test for an A-60 division.

b) Design features of ventilation systems to prevent the spread of smoke and fire in Passenger Ship accommodation are;

- Division by Main Vertical Zones (MVZs): Ventilation systems are typically separated according to the ship's main vertical zoning. Ductwork serving one MVZ should not pass through another, or if it does, it must have robust, fire-resistant insulation to prevent heat transfer and fire spread across zone boundaries.

- Fire Dampers and Automatic Closure: Ventilation trunkings must be able to maintain the fire integrity of the bulkhead or deck through which it passes. Ducts passing through bulkhead divisions must have automatic fire dampers with manual operation facility from both sides of the bulkhead with open-closed indicator.

- Duct Material and Construction: Ducts passing through accommodation areas must be constructed of steel or equivalent non-combustible materials to ensure they do not catch fire themselves.

- Isolation and Control: Atriums shall be within enclosures formed of Class A divisions. Atriums shall be equipped with a smoke extraction system. The smoke extraction system shall be activated by the detection system and be capable of manual control. The fans shall be sized such that the entire volume within the space can be exhausted in 10 min or less.

- Smoke and Fire Containment: The ventilation system is designed to be easily controlled, allowing for the immediate shutting down of fans in the event of a fire, reducing oxygen supply and preventing the smoke from being circulated throughout accommodation.

- Location and isolation of the plant itself: Where the sitting narrows the question to air-conditioning units, supply and exhaust fans, add that AC units and fan rooms are located within their own A-class boundaries, that supply and exhaust systems are separated by main vertical zone so that no fan serves two zones, and that fans are provided with remote stops grouped at a control station outside the space served, so that ventilation can be shut down without entering the fire area. A dedicated safety centre as per SOLAS Chapter II-2, Part C, Regulation 23 manage fire doors, dampers, and detection systems to contain smoke and fire effectively.

c) Class A bulkhead integrity in passenger ship accommodation is maintained at ventilation trunkings penetrations by using steel sleeves, welding trunks directly to bulkheads, insulating them to match the bulkhead rating, or by using automatic fire dampers, ensuring the boundary prevents smoke and flame passage for 60 minutes. To maintain the integrity of the bulkhead with respect to ducts having cross-sectional area exceeding 0.02 M² must be fitted with an insulated steel sleeve unless the duct is made of steel. Ducts with cross-sectional area exceeding 0.075 M² must be fitted with automatic fire dampers with manual operation facility from both sides of the bulkhead with open-closed indicator.

> **Source note:** Part 1 writes “SOLAS Chapter II-II”; corrected above to SOLAS II-2. Note also the part-order discrepancy flagged with the question wording — in the March 2024 sitting the two sources disagree over whether the 5-mark part is the penetration integrity or the ventilation design, so both are answered in full above.

answers.title: Class A and Class B bulkheads defined; integrity at doors & ventilation
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to structural fire protection in passenger ship accommodation spaces:

(a) define the meaning of EACH of the following:

(i) Class A bulkheads; (3)

(ii) Class B bulkheads; (3)

(b) where A Class bulkheads have to be penetrated, explain how the integrity of the bulkhead is retained with respect to EACH of the following:

(i) doors; (2)

(ii) ventilation trunking. (2)

Marks: (a)(i) 3 · (a)(ii) 3 · (b)(i) 2 · (b)(ii) 2
answers.answer_text:
(a)(i) Class A Bulkheads: Class A bulkheads are structural divisions that are designed to provide high fire resistance. Constructed from steel or equivalent materials. Capable of preventing the passage of smoke and flame for a minimum of one hour during a standard fire test at 927°C. Insulated with non-combustible materials such that the average temperature on the unexposed side does not rise more than 140°C above the original temperature, and no point exceeds 180°C during the specified time. The standard fire test is not held at a single temperature: it follows the cellulosic (ISO 834) time– temperature curve, which rises to roughly 841 °C at 30 minutes and about 945 °C at 60 minutes. Class A divisions are then rated by the period for which the insulation criterion is held — A-60, A-30, A-15 and A-0 — while integrity against the passage of flame and smoke is maintained for the full 60 minutes regardless of the suffix. So an A-0 division is still a one-hour barrier to flame and smoke; what it does not do is hold the temperature rise on the far side.

(ii) Class B Bulkheads: Class B bulkheads offer moderate fire resistance and are made from approved non- combustible materials, although combustible veneers may be permitted under certain conditions. Designed to prevent the passage of flame for at least 30 minutes during a standard fire test. The average temperature on the unexposed side must not rise more than 140°C above the original temperature, and no single point can exceed 225°C within the specified time. Class B divisions are rated B-15 and B-0 by the insulation period, with integrity for the 30 minutes of the test. The three differences from Class A worth stating are: B divisions need not be steel or equivalent, their integrity period is 30 minutes rather than 60, and their single-point limit is 225 °C rather than 180 °C. (b)(i) Doors: If the bulkhead has to be penetrated by a door, it must be of the approved type. The door should be of the same material or higher Class "A" standard. The door must be fitted according to the classification requirement. The door should have closing mechanism and should have self-latching and hold back are allowed with remote activation or fusible link. Stated precisely, the door rating must match the rating of the division — an A-60 bulkhead requires an A-60 door — and the door is type-tested and approved as an assembly with its frame, hinges and securing arrangements, since a door leaf on its own proves nothing. The door must be self-closing against a 3.5° inclination and capable of remote release from a continuously manned control station, and no door in an A-class division may carry a louvre or ventilation opening.

(ii) Ventilation trunking: Ventilation trunking that is passing through bulkhead must be provided with sleeves and dampers of suitable material. The dampers should must be provided with open close indicator. In practice the trunk passes through a steel sleeve welded into the division, of the same thickness as the division, with the insulation carried across the penetration; and at an A-class boundary an automatic fire damper is fitted, arranged to fail closed, operable both automatically and by hand from either side, and provided with a position indicator showing open or shut. Where a duct passes through the boundary without a damper, it must instead be of the required thickness for a stated length either side and have no openings within the space it crosses.

> **Source note:** Part 2's original definition of a Class A bulkhead gives the standard fire test as being carried out “at 927°C”, and its own Model Additions box records that the test follows the ISO 834 cellulosic curve rather than being held at one temperature, and that 927 °C is approximately the 30-minute point on that curve. The original sentence is preserved above exactly as printed and the curve is given immediately after it. The original also uses 140 °C for the mean-temperature limit; SOLAS states 139 °C, and E18 carries that figure — either is accepted, but the two entries are not identical and the difference is noted here rather than harmonised silently.

answers.title: In-water survey of a very large carrier
answers.question_as_set:
Describe the in-water survey to classification society requirements of the underwater structure of a very large carrier. (10)

Marks: 10
answers.answer_text:
In-water survey — preparation, operation and procedure. An In Water Survey allows for inspection of a vessel's underwater parts while afloat, replacing one of the two required 5-year dry-dockings for vessels less than 15-year-old. It requires approved diving firms, clear water, good visibility, and a clean hull. Put more precisely, the survey replaces one of the two bottom inspections required within a five-year special- survey cycle; it is generally permitted for ships under 15 years of age, older ships being at the discretion of the society; and the ship must carry the IWS class notation, with an approved high-resistance coating and clearly marked draught and identification points on the hull. Preparation: To facilitate the underwater survey, plans must be submitted showing the external features of the hull below the sheer strake together with a key plan indicating the location of frames, bulkheads, weld lines, and openings. Proper identification of hull markings is required to confirm location. The survey, including procedures for viewing and reporting, must be approved in advance by the Classification Society. Cleaning: The hull plating surface to be cleaned prior to the survey by Brush Kart. It is a hydraulically operated vehicle with three brushing heads, it is drawn by a diver to clear the plating surface of all forms of marine fouling. Internal Inspection: Complementary internal examinations of tanks and spaces must be completed without revealing significant damage. Documentation: A Master's declaration of no damage, grounding, or unreported incidents must be submitted. No CoC on hull and hull structure should be pending.

Vessel Condition: The ship should be at a light draft in sheltered waters. High-resistance hull paint is required for the IWS notation. Survey Vehicle (Scan): It is a self-propelled, steerable survey vehicle fitted with the following; A long-range low light TV Camera to aid steering and check for hull distortion · A close view high-resolution color TV Camera, to give a true picture of the state of the hull coating, and for inspections of weld seams · A 35 mm still Camera · An ultrasonic probe to measure plate thickness · A depth meter and a Speed indicator · An umbilical cable from survey vehicle to survey Boat for electrical power supply to the hydraulic motor, and information transfer · Buoyancy spheres and compressed air bottle for floating of the vehicle. Survey Boat: It houses the surveyor and consists of — A control console containing monitor, Plate thickness printer, audio/video recording, and playback facility · Diver Communication System · Vehicle Control system and associated instruments. Survey Method: Certified divers use CCTV with two-way communication, allowing the surveyor to monitor, direct, and record the survey in real-time; the surveyor must witness the survey in real time, not merely review a recording afterwards. The survey vehicle is taken to the datum line by a diver. With the aid of TV monitors and using the shell expansion plan as a map, the vehicle may be guided, from the control console, over the bottom and sides of the hull by following weld-runs and other features such as inlets and tank plugs. Pictures and information are relayed back and video recorded along with plate thicknesses giving the surveyor an integrated visual record of all relevant information. Thickness gauging of suspect areas is mandatory. Divers are also used for measurement of stern tube bearing wear down, rudder bearings/pintle clearances and to inspect sea chests, valves, propeller, propeller shaft, stern seals, anodes, rudder, and rudder stock palm coupling bolts — the rudder and stern-tube wear-down measurements being mandatory items. The vehicle will also provide pictures of the stem frame, rudder, propeller, bilge, keels and hull openings. Limits of the survey: The in-water survey cannot proceed if significant damage is suspected, or if there are outstanding hull Conditions of Class; in either case the ship must be dry-docked. Outcome: The diving company submits a final report containing all recordings and measurements. The surveyor reviews the report, verifies all items are in order, and formally endorses the Class Certificate for the “Intermediate Bottom Inspection,” provided all IWS requirements are met. If significant damage is found, the surveyor may require the vessel to enter dry dock.

answers.title: Classification of ships & the notation +100A1
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to the classification of ships, explain EACH of the following:

(a) why ships are built to classification society rules; (5)

(b) the meaning of the notation Maltese Cross 100A1; (4)

(c) how a ship remains in class throughout the life of the vessel. (1)

Marks: (a) 5 · (b) 4 · (c) 1
answers.answer_text:
a) IACS ensures ships are built to the highest standards, can operate effectively and safely, comply with strict maritime and environmental regulations, and prolong their working life. Key reasons for building to classification rules are;

- Safety and Integrity Standards: Class establish comprehensive rules for the design, construction, and inspection of ships, ensuring they are structurally sound. These rules ensure the reliability of the hull, machinery, and propulsion systems, effectively mitigating risks.

- Regulatory Compliance: Ships must comply with international conventions, such as SOLAS, MARPOL, Load Line, Tonnage, and COLREGS which require adherence to the rules of a recognized classification society to operate.

- Insurance and Finance: Classification is a prerequisite for insurance companies to classify a vessel as a good risk, leading to lower insurance premiums. Banks also require this for financing, as it ensures the vessel's asset value.

- Quality Control and Certification: The construction process is monitored by surveyors to verify that the vessel is built in accordance with approved drawings and rules.

- Operational Requirements: A classification certificate proves that the ship is seaworthy, which is necessary for charterers, bankers, and for operating in various ports.

b) According to Lloyd's Register (LR) classification society standards, the notation +100A1 represents the highest-level classification for a seagoing ship. It is a steel ship built under special survey, suitable for unrestricted worldwide service, with approved equipment. Meaning of the notation is as follows;

- + (Maltese Cross): Indicates that the ship is constructed under the special survey of the Classification Society's surveyors, in compliance with their Rules and Regulations, to the satisfaction of the Committee.

- 100: Signifies that the vessel is considered suitable for sea-going service according to structural strength of a steel ship designed for unrestricted navigation. Historically the figure is Lloyd's character figure, denoting a ship built and eligible to be entered as first class (100A) in the Register for sea-going service.

- A: Confirms that the hull and its appendages have been built in accordance with the society's rules, and are maintained in good and efficient condition.

- 1: Signifies that the anchoring and mooring equipment (cables, hawsers) are in good and efficient condition and comply with the society's Rules. For full marks, add that the notation is normally followed by a service or ship-type notation — for example “Oil Tanker, ESP” — and sometimes by (E), indicating equipment to rule. Other societies use equivalent symbols for the same meaning, for example DNV's ✘1A.

c) To remain in class throughout its life, a ship must adhere to;

- Surveys and Certification: Initial, annual, intermediate, periodic, renewal and special surveys on a five- year cycle.

- Maintenance Compliance and Approval: Ensuring maintenance (PMS), repairs and upgrades are approved by LR to maintain structural and mechanical integrity.

- No overdue surveys or Conditions of Class, prompt repair of any damage affecting class, and compliance with the ISM and audit regime. Failing these, class may be suspended or withdrawn. Note the weighting in this sitting — part (c) carries only one mark, so one line is enough and the time belongs in part (a).

answers.title: Drydocking — pre-docking information & items to inspect once dry
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to drydocking a vessel:

(a) state the pre-docking information that should be given to the drydock authority; (5)

(b) list the items to be inspected once the dock is empty. (5)

Marks: (a) 5 · (b) 5
answers.answer_text:
(a) Pre-docking information that should be provided to the drydock authority are:

- Vessel's Docking Plan: Docking plan is a technical drawing prepared during a ship's design phase that details the underwater hull structure, including the keel, bilge keels, stabilizers, propellers, rudder, sea chests, ICCP anodes, Speed Log transducer, Echo Sounder transducer, cathodic protection anodes and drain plugs. It guides the shipyard on how to arrange blocks in a dry dock to securely support the vessel.

- General Arrangement Plan, Capacity Plan and Shell Expansion Plan: General Arrangement plan provides a comprehensive overview of the ship's layout. Capacity Plan is used for calculating the vessel's displacement and stability. Shell Expansion Plan shows the details of the hull plating.

- Stability Data: Provide the arrival stability condition, including Current Metacentric Height (GM), arrival drafts (forward and aft), and trim, to ensure safe docking. Soundings of all tanks, ensuring tanks are either completely full or empty to minimize free surface effects.

- Repair List: A comprehensive list of planned repairs and maintenance tasks that need to be performed during the dry dock period.

- Tank Arrangement: Information on the tank arrangement and distribution, including any ballast, FW and fuel tanks that may need to be adjusted before docking.

- The docking officer's landing data: the ship's weight and its longitudinal and vertical centres of gravity for the landing calculation, and the declared trim on landing — a small trim by the stern being preferred so that the stern lands first on the after blocks.

- Block and bilge-block plan: marked up to show every appendage, transducer, stabiliser fin, sea-chest projection or sacrificial anode that the keel and bilge blocks must clear.

- Confirmation that the ICCP system is switched off and isolated before the ship enters the dock.

b) Once the dock is dry, the immediate inspection focuses on the hull, propulsion, and appendages for damage, corrosion, and wear. Key items to be inspected immediately are;

- Hull Plating & Painting: Full inspection for corrosion, pitting, deformation, damage to paint coating, and antifouling coating condition.

- Propeller and Rudder System: Checking propeller for damage to blades, fouling, and inspecting the rope guard. Checking rudder for damage and checking rudder plug tightness.

- Sea Chests & Sea Valves: Inspect gratings and valves at sea inlets and sea chests to ensure they are clear of obstructions and secured properly, together with the condition of the internal sea-chest anodes and gratings.

- Anodes & Transducers: Inspecting sacrificial zinc anodes for wastage and ensuring ICCP anodes/ electrodes, Echo Sounder and Speed Log Transducers are in good condition.

- General Structure, Anchor & Cable: Inspection of the bow thruster tunnel, stern frame, anchor, bilge keels, and any other appendages. Ensuring all tank plugs are secured and properly sealed, against a tank- plug tally sheet recorded as plugs are removed and refitted. Add the measurements that can only be taken with the ship dry, since these are what the docking is really for: rudder pintle and stern-tube (tail-shaft) bearing wear-down by poker gauge, rudder and pintle clearances, and propeller-cone and rope-guard security.

answers.title: Overhaul of ship-side valves in dry dock
answers.question_as_set:
(a) With reference to the overhaul of a ship side valve in dry dock explain, as Chief Engineer Officer, what information should be given to the docking company prior to work commencing. (5)

(b) Describe how the valves would be overhauled stating the precautions to be taken before returning the ship to service. (5)

Marks: (a) 5 · (b) 5
answers.answer_text:
a) As Chief Engineer Officer, providing detailed information to the docking company is crucial for safe and efficient valve overhaul. Essential information includes;

- Valve Identification & Location: A comprehensive valve list (location, type, valve ID, means of closure (manual or power actuated), diameter, and flange PCD), with a marked-up plan showing sea chest positions, including their precise location with frame number.

- Scope of Work: Clearly define scope of work including cleaning, inspection, packing replacement, comprehensive overhaul, including valve seat grinding and testing.

- Material and Spares Availability: Clearly state which spares will be supplied by the ship (gaskets, nuts, studs) and what is expected from the workshop.

- Isolation and Safety Measures: Hand over a clear procedure for isolation and safety measures prior commencing the removal.

- Critical Timing: Clearly define the docking schedule, particularly the timeline for when valves must be opened for overhaul and when they must be fitted back for re-floating.

- The survey requirement: state that these are classed items and that the Classification Society surveyor must be given notice to attend, so that the yard plans the work around the surveyor's availability rather than around its own convenience.

b) Key steps of overhauling procedure include;

- Dismantling: Ensuring proper isolation, remove the valve cover, gland packing, and spindle. Remove the valve chest from the hull if necessary for extensive overhaul.

- Inspection & Cleaning: Clean all parts, remove rust/corrosion, and inspect for wastage. Check the valve seating face for damage or pitting. Lap the valve seat and disc using grinding paste to ensure a proper seal, lapping until a continuous contact band is achieved and proving it with an engineer's-blue check.

- Reassembly: Ensure all exposed steel parts are coated to prevent corrosion. Replace all worn-out studs, nuts, and joints (graphite gaskets), renewing studs to the correct grade and tightening to the specified torque. Apply anti-seize paste to threads.

- Function Test: Check the valve for smooth operation, opening, and closing properly. Conduct a hydrostatic test to ensure the valve is leak-proof at testing pressure, and record the test pressures in the dry-dock and class report. Ensure the overhaul is inspected and approved by a Classification Society surveyor.

Precautions to be taken before returning the ship to service;

- The survey and witness chain — the single most important precaution. Ship-side valves, that is sea inlets and overboard discharges below the deepest waterline, are classed items. The Classification Society surveyor should witness the opening up, the condition of the seat, the reassembly and the hydrostatic test, all before the dock is flooded. Nothing should be closed up out of sight of the surveyor.

- Positive isolation: confirm lock-off arrangements are in place while the valve is open, and that all blanks and spectacle-plate isolations are removed before the system is returned to service.

- Securing the valve: Lock the valve in the open or closed position as required, ensuring the locking washer and nut are secure. Verify that the valve operating handle is properly greased and the valve is functional before flooding the dock.

- Final tally: account for every sea connection as closed and locked before flooding, against the valve list handed over in part (a). This closes the loop and is the check that prevents a flooding incident on undocking.

answers.title: Repair of defects on a solid propeller in dry dock
answers.question_as_set:
Describe how EACH of the following defects on a solid propeller may be repaired whilst a ship is in drydock:

(a) bent blades; (2)

(b) damaged blade tips; (4)

(c) pieces of blade missing. (4)

Marks: (a) 2 · (b) 4 · (c) 4
answers.answer_text:
a) Bent blades can be hot or cold straightened using a hydraulic press or mechanical tools designed for alignment. The propeller is secured, and the bent section is carefully worked back into its original shape. Care must be taken to avoid over-stressing the material, which could lead to cracks. In practice, straightening of manganese bronze or nickel-aluminium bronze is done with local pre-heat rather than truly cold, precisely to avoid cracking. After straightening, the blade should be inspected for any signs of fatigue or damage. After repairs, the propeller must be balanced to ensure smooth operation.

b) Damaged blade tips can be repaired by metal arc welding or adding material to restore the original shape. Using appropriate materials such as cast steel/copper alloys to weld a new tip onto the existing blade. Once the new material is added, it is shaped and finished to match the profile of the other blades. After repairs, the propeller must be balanced to ensure smooth operation. The repair should comply with IACS UR W24 guidelines (welding especially below the 0.7 radius needs class approval), and post-repair non-destructive testing (NDT) is necessary to verify structural integrity.

c) When pieces of a blade are missing, the repair involves evaluation of the extent of damage and determine if the propeller can be salvaged or if it needs replacement. Blades are divided into three stress zones (A-highest, C-lowest). Welding in Zone A (near root) is strictly controlled or prohibited. Pinning the zones to radius: Zone A is the blade root and lower radii, roughly inboard of about 0.4–0.6 R on the driving face, where welding is prohibited or requires special Class approval; Zone B is the intermediate region, where welding is permitted by an approved procedure; and Zone C is the outer blade and tip, where repair is most freely allowed. If salvageable, use metal arc welding techniques to build up the missing sections with compatible materials. Either adding new metal to reconstruct the blade profile or casting a new piece to fit into the existing structure may be necessary. The repaired area must be smoothed and finished appropriately, followed by balancing the entire propeller to prevent vibrations during operation. The repair should comply with classification society approval, and post-repair non-destructive testing (NDT) is necessary to verify structural integrity. Procedural controls applying to all three repairs. State these, because they are what examiners reward: an approved welding procedure and a welder qualified for the specific bronze or alloy; controlled pre-heat and interpass temperature; stress relief after any major build-up; dye-penetrant NDT — note that the propeller is non-magnetic, so magnetic particle inspection is not used on it; and a final static balance, with dynamic balancing for high-speed installations and controllable-pitch propellers.

> **Source note:** Part 1 cites “IACS UR W24/W27”. Its Model Additions record that W24 is the propeller-repair rule and that W27 concerns stern-tube and shafting, so W24 alone is cited above.

answers.title: Dry dock specification — repair of ballast tank shell damage, and costing the repair
answers.question_as_set:
As Chief Engineer officer, write a dry dock specification for the repair of the following damage that has occurred, stating what factors have to be considered when costing the repairs. Damage to water ballast tank number 1 port wing. The shell plating 15 mm thick for approx 2 metres square has to be removed and replaced along with the relevant damaged stiffeners. (10)

Marks: 10
answers.answer_text: Scope of Work: Removal and replacement of the damaged shell plating (approximately 2 m², 15 mm thick steel), repair or replacement of damaged stiffeners, NDT inspection of adjacent areas for hidden damage, and surface preparation (cleaning, blasting, painting) to the vessel's coating system. Two items belong in the specification itself and are the ones most often left out. First, the material: state that the new plate is to be of the same grade and thickness as the original and approved by class — 15 mm to the specified steel grade — supplied with mill and material certificates, and that the repair itself is to be to a class-approved plan. Second, the welding: require an approved welding procedure specification (WPS) worked to by certified welders, with weld NDT by UT and MPI to a stated acceptance standard and the reports submitted before the tank is accepted back. Factors to Consider When Costing the Repairs: Material Costs (steel plates and stiffeners, procurement, transport, certifications); Labor Costs (labour hours based on complexity, accessibility, shipyard rates); Equipment and Tools; Additional Services (subcontracted NDT, surface prep, painting); Dry Docking Expenses; Contingency budget for unforeseen circumstances. To that list add the costs that a ballast-tank repair carries and a plate repair on open deck does not: staging and access into the tank; gas-freeing and continuous mechanical ventilation throughout, because hot work inside a wing ballast tank is simultaneously enclosed-space work and hot work and needs both permits, an attendant and continuous atmosphere monitoring; the cost of the attending class and flag surveyor; and the coating of the repaired area to the ballast-tank coating standard, which is a significant fraction of the job in a narrow wing tank. Repair Procedure: a) Preparation — schedule docking, allocate resources, obtain permits. b) Removal — cut out damaged shell plating with clean, precise edges; remove damaged stiffeners; dispose of removed materials per environmental regulations. c) Replacement — fit and weld new 15 mm plates with proper alignment and welding procedures; install new stiffeners securely welded to shell. d) NDT Inspection — ultrasonic or magnetic particle inspection of repaired and adjacent sections. e) Surface Preparation and Coating — clean and blast, apply approved coating system. f) Quality Assurance and Control — strict adherence to standards, regular inspections and testing. Within that sequence, specify that the cut-out is taken to a rectangular insert with rounded corners, that no new weld seam lands on or too close to an existing one, that the stiffeners are cut back and re-welded so that the shell butt is welded first and the stiffener connections after, and that the welding sequence is balanced to control distortion in a 15 mm plate. On completion the tank is hydrostatically tested to the design head before the coating is accepted as final. Documentation: Detailed repair report (work performed, materials used, QC measures), NDT inspection reports, coating application records (type, thickness, method), and copies of relevant certifications, permits and approvals.

answers.title: Aft end vibration on a new vessel — report to the Engineer Superintendent
answers.question_as_set:
December 2016: As Chief Engineer Officer on a new vessel which is experiencing severe aft end vibration at full service speed, write a report to the Engineer Superintendent suggesting reasons for the vibration and recommendations for further sister vessels presently under construction. (10) October 2019: As Chief Engineer Officer on a new vessel, which is experiencing severe aft end vibration at full service speed, explain the possible reasons for the vibration, and make recommendations for further sister vessels presently under construction. (10) [same content — the report format is dropped]

Marks: 10
answers.answer_text:
[The original answer is a formatted report to the Technical Superintendent. Its technical content is summarised verbatim below; the letterhead placeholders are from the original.] Written as a report, it needs a heading, an addressee, a statement of the observed symptom — severe vibration at the aft end at full service speed on a new vessel — then causes, recommendations for this ship, and recommendations for the sisters still building. Possible Causes for Aft End Vibration: a. Propeller Issues — the propeller could be imbalanced, damaged, or experiencing cavitation. b. Shaft Misalignment — misalignment between the propulsion shaft and the stern tube bearings could result in significant vibration. c. Structural Resonance — the design of the aft section (stern frame, hull, supporting structures) may be prone to resonance and harmonic amplification. d. Machinery Imbalance — imbalance or misalignment of engine, generator, or rotating equipment. e. Insufficient Damping — inadequate vibration isolation systems or ineffective shock absorbers. The cause to name explicitly, because on a new ship vibrating only at full service speed it is much the most likely, is blade-rate (blade-passing) frequency resonance. The propeller exciting frequency is shaft rpm × number of blades, and its harmonics; when that frequency coincides with a natural frequency of the aft hull structure or of the sterngear, the response is amplified and you get exactly the “resonance and harmonic amplification” described above. The driving force is normally cavitation-induced pressure pulses on the hull plating above the propeller — the propeller does not have to be defective at all, which is why the vibration appears at one speed and not at others, and why it appears on a whole class of ships rather than on one. Recommendations: a) Propeller inspection and maintenance (balance, cavitation). b) Alignment check between propulsion shaft and stern tube bearings. c) Structural analysis of the aft section to identify resonance; reinforce or modify design. d) Machinery alignment and balancing. e) Enhanced vibration damping. f) Sea trial and performance monitoring after implementing measures. For this ship, order the work by what it will settle: take a vibration survey with accelerometers at the stern, over a speed sweep, and identify the frequency and its relation to shaft rpm × blade number before anything is altered — that single measurement distinguishes blade-rate excitation from an out-of-balance propeller or a misaligned shaft. Then inspect the propeller for damage and blade-to-blade pitch error in dock, check the stern tube bearing alignment and wear-down, and only then consider stiffening. Recommendations for Sister Vessels Under Construction: a) Enhanced structural design with comprehensive structural analysis and optimization to minimise resonance in the aft section. b) Quality control during propeller installation (balancing, alignment, avoidance of cavitation). c) Standardized machinery alignment and balancing procedures. d) Vibration monitoring systems for real-time tracking. e) Lessons-learned documentation for future vessel construction projects. Four specific measures should be named for the sisters, because they are what actually shifts the problem rather than absorbing it:

- Increase the propeller tip clearance from the hull, so that the pressure pulse reaching the plating above the propeller is reduced.

- Fit a highly-skewed propeller, which spreads blade loading over a range of angular positions and softens the pressure pulse instead of delivering it as a single blow per blade.

- Change the number of blades, which moves the blade-rate frequency clear of the aft-hull natural frequencies without changing the hull at all.

- Run a finite-element vibration analysis of the aft structure at the design stage, so that the natural frequencies are known and kept away from blade rate and its harmonics before steel is cut.

answers.title: Standing orders — serious fire in the machinery spaces while in dry dock
answers.question_as_set:
When a vessel is in dry dock, the possible risks of fire in the machinery spaces are heightened due to the nature of the work being carried out. As Chief Engineer Officer, compile a set of standing orders instructing ship's staff on the actions to be taken should a serious fire occur. (10)

Marks: 10
answers.answer_text:
[The original answer is a set of standing orders under ten headings, reproduced in summary form:]

1. Immediate Response: Raise the alarm (activate nearest fire alarm, shout "FIRE!"); call for help (notify bridge and dry dock management with location and extent). 2. Evacuation Procedures: Evacuate machinery spaces and adjacent areas; proceed to the designated assembly point and report to supervisor. 3. Firefighting Equipment: Use portable extinguishers (CO2 or foam) if trained and safe; do not take risks. 4. Isolation of Equipment: Shut down machinery/electrical systems if safe; close fuel oil, lube oil and flammable liquid valves.

5. Communication Protocol: Maintain communication; report conditions and trapped personnel to emergency services. 6. Fire Control Measures: Activate fixed firefighting systems (e.g. CO2 flooding) if applicable; assist firefighters with vessel layout and hazards. 7. Post-Incident Actions: Account for personnel; do not re-enter until declared safe. 8. Training and Drills.9. Reporting Procedures.10. Safety Equipment Checks. The dry-dock specifics — where the marks actually are A generic fire drill will not score this question, because the whole point of it is that the ship in dock is not the ship at sea. The standing orders must therefore say, in terms:

- Who supplies fire-fighting water. The ship's sea suctions are out of the water and the fire main is normally isolated and often opened up for survey, and the fixed CO₂ system may be isolated for hot work, so primary fire cover is the shore or yard fire main and the dock fire party. The orders must state where the shore connection is, that a charged shore-supplied hose is rigged in the machinery space before any hot work starts, and who calls the yard brigade.

- Hot work control. No hot work without a hot-work permit, with the space gas-freed and tested, combustibles removed or protected, a continuous fire watch during the work and for a stated period after it, and boundary cooling and watch on the far side of any bulkhead or deck being worked on.

- The alarm must reach both ship and yard. Ship's alarms may be isolated during electrical work; the orders must name the alternative means of raising both crews, since a fire found by a yard worker must reach the duty engineer and a fire found by the crew must reach the dock.

- Escape routes and muster point change in dock. Access is by staging and a single brow rather than the normal gangways, lifts and internal routes may be out of service, and there may be scaffolding in the escape routes — so the orders must state the revised routes and the revised muster point, which is normally ashore on the dock side, and must require a head count against both the crew list and the yard's contractor list.

- Before CO₂ is even considered, confirm that the space can be sealed and that nobody — including yard workers who do not appear on the ship's muster — is inside it. Openings made for the docking work commonly defeat the boundary, so the release decision in dock is the Chief Engineer's with the dock master, not a routine action.

answers.title: Fatigue cracks in a ship's hull — why and where; the drydock hull inspection
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain why fatigue cracks occur in a ship's hull, stating the locations where they may be found. (3)

(b) Describe the hull inspection that should be carried out in drydock to ascertain the maintenance and repairs that may need to be carried out. (7)

Marks: (a) 3 · (b) 7
answers.answer_text:
(a) Fatigue cracks in a ship's hull occur due to the repeated cyclic loading and unloading that the structure experiences during its operational life. Ships are subjected to dynamic forces from waves, wind, and operational maneuvers, leading to fluctuating stresses that can cause material fatigue over time. The inherent properties of the materials used in the hull construction can contribute to fatigue. Poor design or inadequate structural reinforcement in critical areas can lead to stress concentrations that promote fatigue cracking. Areas where different materials are joined can experience high-stress concentrations, making them prone to fatigue cracks. Structural corners or edges where changes in geometry occur often exhibit stress risers, leading to crack initiation. The lower sections of the hull are frequently subjected to bending moments and shear forces from wave action. The mechanism to state plainly is that fatigue is driven by cyclic stress range acting at a stress concentration — the number of load cycles and the local geometry, not weakness in the steel. A ship sees of the order of 108 wave-load cycles in its life, and hull steel has no fatigue limit in a corrosive environment, so cracking starts wherever the local stress range is raised by a discontinuity and is then accelerated by corrosion pitting at that same point. Locations where they may be found The high-incidence sites, which is what the mark is for, are:

- Hatch-corner radii and the corners of deck openings — the classic site, because the deck is the most highly stressed part of the hull girder and the opening interrupts it.

- Bracket toes, and the ends and heels of longitudinals, where longitudinal material stops or changes section.

- Intersections of longitudinals with transverse webs, and the edges of lightening holes and cut-outs.

- Side-shell-frame end brackets on bulk carriers, top and bottom.

- Weld toes, and anywhere there is undercut or a poor weld profile.

- The sheer strake and bilge strake, and the ends of the bilge keel, where the keel is welded to the ground bar.

(b) A comprehensive hull inspection during drydocking is essential for identifying maintenance needs and repairs. Conduct a thorough visual examination of the entire hull surface for signs of corrosion, pitting, deformation, and other anomalies, including checking for any visible cracks or weld defects. Inspect the condition of protective coatings and paints; look for peeling, blistering, or wear that may expose the underlying metal to corrosion. Use ultrasonic gauges to measure the thickness of the hull plates at various locations to identify areas where corrosion has reduced material thickness below acceptable limits. Perform detailed inspections of critical areas such as welded joints, brackets, and supports where structural integrity is crucial; this may involve using borescopes to access hard-to-reach areas. Assess for any deformation in the hull structure due to grounding or collision impacts, including checking for hogging or sagging along the length of the ship. Open sea chests for cleaning and inspection of intake systems. Check sea valves for functionality and signs of wear or corrosion. Record all findings systematically, noting locations, severity of defects, and recommendations for repairs. Name the methods and the framework, because “inspect for cracks” does not say how. Surface cracks are found by magnetic particle inspection (MPI) or dye penetrant after the area has been cleaned to bare metal; thickness loss and embedded defects by ultrasonic testing, taken to a set gauging pattern so that readings

can be compared with the previous docking and a wastage rate established rather than a single figure. The whole exercise sits inside the class survey regime, and for tankers and bulk carriers specifically the Enhanced Survey Programme (ESP), which requires close-up survey of nominated critical areas and suspect areas, thickness measurement to a prescribed extent, and a thickness-measurement report submitted to class. The hull condition monitoring and repair plan follows from that report.

> **Source note:** Part 2's original part (a) offers “The inherent properties of the materials used in the hull construction can contribute to fatigue” among the causes, and its own Model Additions box records that the driver is stress concentration combined with cyclic stress range and not primarily material weakness. The original sentence is preserved above as printed, and the corrected emphasis is given in the paragraph that follows it, so the mechanism written in the exam is the stress-range one.

answers.title: Survey & repair of a hollow rudder
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe the survey of a hollow rudder. (7)

(b) State what repairs may need to be carried out on the rudder. (3)

Marks: (a) 7 · (b) 3
answers.answer_text:
a) A thorough survey of a hollow rudder is essential for ensuring its structural integrity and functionality. The following steps outline the procedure:

- Initial Inspection: Begin with a visual inspection of the rudder for any obvious signs of damage, such as cracks or corrosion. This includes checking the alignment of the rudder with the stern frame and the ship's centreline, and confirming that the rudder hangs true with no list of the blade.

- Water Entry Check: When the vessel is in dry dock, inspect for water ingress. Open the top and bottom plugs to see if any water leaks out; if it does, this indicates a breach in the rudder.

- Pressure Testing: Conduct a pressure test with a water head of approximately 2.45 metres to assess the rudder's watertightness. This helps identify any hidden leaks or weaknesses. Describe it correctly as an internal head test: the rudder is filled through the upper plug to the specified head — often referenced to the deepest waterline as required by class — and is then watched for a pressure drop, or for water issuing from the lower plug, either of which indicates ingress. An air or vacuum test is the common alternative where filling is impractical.

- Thickness Gauging: For older vessels or those with visible rust, perform thickness gauging on the rudder plates to measure material loss due to corrosion.

- Clearance Measurements: Measure clearances between the pintle and bush in both longitudinal and transverse directions. Standard clearances should be maintained to ensure proper function. Measure also the jumping clearance at the pintle and the rudder carrier bearing wear-down.

- Condition of Anodes: Inspect sacrificial anodes for wear and replace them if necessary to prevent corrosion.

- Percussion Testing: Use a hammer to perform percussion tests on the rudder to evaluate its condition by listening for variations in sound, which can indicate areas of weakness or delamination.

- Stock and coupling checks: Examine the condition of the stock keyway, check the coupling-bolt tightness at the rudder-stock palm, and carry out a freedom-of-movement check hard-over to hard- over.

b) Depending on the findings from the survey, repairs may be necessary as follows:

- Corrosion Treatment: Areas affected by corrosion may require treatment or replacement of affected sections of the rudder plate.

- Gouging and Re-welding: Cracks in welding seams or rudder plating are removed by grinding or gouging, followed by re-welding using approved procedures.

- Bearing Replacement: If measurements indicate excessive wear in the bearings or if clearances exceed allowable limits, replacing the bush or sleeve may be necessary.

- Straightening: Bent rudder stocks without fractures may be repaired by hot or cold straightening in an approved workshop.

- Handling Twisted Stocks: If a rudder stock is twisted by less than 10 degrees, it may be reused (possibly with a new keyway), but more severe twists require annealing or replacement.

- Controls on all repair work: all welding to a class-approved procedure with controlled pre-heat and post-heat, NDT after repair, renewal of the anodes, and a re-pressure-test before undocking, with the surveyor in attendance to witness it.

> **Source note:** Part 1's first survey item reads “checking the alignment with the vessel's mast”. Its Model Additions record this as wrong; the check is alignment with the stern frame and centreline, and that wording is used above. The head is also given as 2.46 m in Part 1 and 2.45 m in the Additions — either figure will be accepted, both being the same textbook value.

answers.title: Single vs twin propeller / rudder (wide-beam vessel)
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain why a single propeller and single rudder may not be suitable for large cargo vessels having a wide beam. (3)

(b) Explain the advantages of a twin propeller twin rudder installation in vessels with a large cargo carrying capacity. (7)

Marks: (a) 3 · (b) 7
answers.answer_text:
a) A single propeller and single rudder configuration are generally unsuitable for large cargo vessels with a wide beam due to reduced maneuverability, increased risks of operational failures, and inefficient wake flow. The root cause is the wake: a single screw on a full, wide, high-block hull sits in a very non-uniform wake field, which drives vibration, cavitation and reduced open-water efficiency, and the rudder working directly behind it is partly shadowed by the hull. Twin screws sit further outboard in cleaner flow. A further practical limit is that a single screw of the power required may demand a diameter that exceeds the available draught and immersion.

- Steering Challenges: For a very wide and large ship, a single rudder needs to be massive to produce sufficient turning forces. This results in extremely high bending moments on the rudder stock and very high hydraulic loads on the steering machinery, making the design impractical.

- Increased Drag / Lower Efficiency: Wider vessels face greater hydrodynamic resistance, limiting the effectiveness of a large single propeller.

- High Risk of Cavitation: To achieve the necessary thrust on a wide-beam, heavy-displacement vessel, a single propeller must be exceptionally large, which increases the risk of cavitation (vapor bubbles forming on blades), leading to reduced thrust, noise, and structural erosion of the blade surface.

b) A twin propeller, twin rudder installation on large cargo vessels with a large cargo carrying capacity significantly improves manoeuvrability, allowing for superior control in confined waterways, enhanced crabbing abilities, and safer navigation. It offers high redundancy, where one propeller/rudder set can compensate for failure, and enables better wake equalizing, reducing fuel consumption and vibration. The strongest points to lead with are redundancy, manoeuvring capability and the shallow-draught benefit. Key advantages include:

- Superior Manoeuvrability & Handling: The system provides better control at low speeds and improved turning ability in restricted waters, often reducing the need for tug assistance during docking.

- Enhanced Reliability and Safety: Redundant systems ensure that if one propeller or rudder fails, the vessel retains steering and propulsion capability.

- Increased Propulsive Efficiency: The twin arrangement improves wake equalizing, allowing for better efficiency, reduced fuel consumption, and lower emissions.

- Superior Low-Speed Performance: It enables easier “crabbing” (moving sideways) by utilizing differential engine thrust and rudder angles.

- Reduced Vibration and Noise: The improved flow of water to the propellers reduces vibrations throughout the ship, improving onboard comfort.

- Reduced Drag: Twin rudder systems can allow for better propeller immersion and less cavitation.

- Reduced draught requirement: two smaller-diameter propellers can absorb the same power within a restricted draught, which is the decisive advantage on a wide-beam, shallow-draught cargo vessel. Although the question awards seven marks for advantages, a complete answer notes the trade-offs: higher build and maintenance cost, additional appendage drag from the shaft brackets or bossings, and the fact that a well-designed single screw is usually more efficient per kilowatt in deep water.

> **Source note:** Part 1 lists “Improved Stability” — symmetrical thrust improving hydrostatic balance and reducing roll — among the advantages. Its own Model Additions assess that claim as weak, since twin shafts provide little roll damping, so it has been replaced above by the shallow-draught benefit. If you wish to include it, do so as a minor point and not as a headline.
