answers.title: Large fixed bladed propellers — hull fouling, clean ballast running & the light propeller
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to large fixed bladed propellers:

(a) describe, with the aid of a sketch, EACH of the following:

(i) the effect of hull fouling; (3)

(ii) operation in clean hull, ballast condition. (3)

(b) explain why fitting a light propeller may be beneficial. (4)

Marks: (a)(i) 3 · (a)(ii) 3 · (b) 4
answers.answer_text:
(a)(i) The effect of hull fouling: Hull fouling occurs when marine organisms such as barnacles and algae accumulate on the hull and propeller. This increases drag and reduces the efficiency of the propeller. When a propeller is fouled, it requires more power to achieve the same thrust, leading to decreased speed and increased fuel consumption. In propeller-law terms the fouled hull makes the propeller heavy running: the added resistance means the ship makes less speed for the same revolutions, the wake is less favourable, and the propeller therefore absorbs more torque at any given rpm. Its power-demand curve moves to the left on the power/rpm diagram, towards the torque limit, so the engine reaches its torque or thermal limit before it reaches MCR revolutions — the ship cannot make full power and full speed, exhaust temperatures and scavenge pressures rise, and the engine is overloaded if the setting is not reduced.

(ii) Operation in clean hull, ballast condition: In a clean hull condition, the propeller operates efficiently with minimal drag. The ship is typically in a balanced state, with ballast distributed evenly. The propeller achieves optimal thrust with lower power requirements, enhancing speed and fuel efficiency. Clean and in ballast is the lightest the propeller ever runs: the displacement and resistance are low, so for a given rpm the propeller absorbs less torque and its demand curve lies to the right of the design curve. The engine can then reach MCR rpm — and the overspeed limit — before it reaches full power, which is why the light-running condition is limited by revolutions rather than by torque.

Engine power (% kW) vs % RPM — clean/ballast, fouled and light-running curves about MCR (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.49 Reading the diagram: the design or loaded service curve passes through MCR. The curve to the right of it, reached with a clean hull in ballast, is the light-running line, and the curve to the left, reached with a fouled hull, in heavy weather or when towing, is the heavy-running line. The vertical line at about 104 % rpm is the speed limit and the curve above MCR is the torque and overload limit; the whole art of matching the propeller is to keep the ship's operating point inside that envelope over the whole life of the docking cycle.

(b) A light propeller improves a ship's maneuverability, especially in challenging conditions, by increasing the Light Running Margin (LRM) for better engine power during low-speed maneuvers. It also enhances fuel economy by reducing drag and optimizing engine performance. Light propellers help vessels navigate "critical speed ranges" more safely by increasing the power margin, reducing the risk of damaging vibrations. They are designed to adapt to operational challenges like hull fouling and adverse weather, ensuring full power availability when needed. Put in engine-margin terms, which is what the question is really testing: a propeller is light when it absorbs less torque for a given rpm, so its power-demand curve lies to the right — at higher rpm — of the design curve, and the engine can reach MCR revolutions and full power before it meets the torque and overload limit. The reserve between the running point and that limit is the Light Running Margin (LRM), normally specified at about 4–7 % of revolutions, and it is built in on purpose at the design stage by matching a slightly under-pitched propeller to the engine. The reason it is built in deliberately is the whole answer to part (b). A ship does not stay new: as the hull and propeller foul, and as the ship meets heavy weather or a head sea, the demand curve migrates left into heavy running. If the ship had been matched exactly on the design curve when new, it would be over the torque limit within months of leaving the yard. The LRM is the margin that lets the engine go on developing its full output, at full revolutions, through the whole fouling-and-weather range without overloading — and it is why a new ship on trials appears to be “over-revving” slightly for its power, which is correct and intended rather than a fault.

answers.title: Improving propulsion efficiency — ducted propeller (Kort nozzle) & Grim
answers.question_as_set:
Describe, with the aid of sketches, how main propulsion efficiency can be improved by the addition of EACH of the following:

(a) ducted propeller (Kort nozzle); (5)

(b) vane or Grim wheel aft of the propeller. (5)

Marks: (a) 5 · (b) 5
answers.answer_text:
(a) Ducted Propeller (Kort Nozzle): Ducted propeller / Kort nozzle (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.41 A ducted propeller, commonly known as a Kort nozzle, consists of a cylindrical duct surrounding the propeller. This design helps to streamline the flow of water around the propeller, reducing turbulence and enhancing efficiency. The duct accelerates the water flow through the propeller and reduces the effects of tip vortices. Advantages: Increased Thrust (the duct concentrates the flow); Reduced Power Consumption; Improved Maneuverability at low speeds. Disadvantages: Weight and Complexity; Cost; Potential for Cavitation if not designed properly. The mechanism is worth one more sentence, because it is what the marks are for: the duct is an aerofoil section in its own right, and the acceleration of flow through it generates a forward force on the duct itself, so the total thrust is the propeller thrust plus the duct thrust. Closing the tip gap also suppresses the tip vortices, which is where a heavily-loaded open propeller loses much of its efficiency. Be specific about when it helps. A Kort nozzle benefits heavily-loaded propellers working at low speed and high thrust — tugs, trawlers, pusher craft and dynamically positioned vessels — and it can raise bollard pull by a substantial margin. On a fast, lightly-loaded merchant ship the duct's own drag at speed cancels the gain, and can leave the ship worse off than with an open propeller, which is why ducts are not

fitted to container ships. So the answer to “how is efficiency improved” has to be qualified by the loading condition of the propeller, not given as a general improvement.

(b) Vane or Grim Wheel Aft of the Propeller: Vane / Grim wheel aft of the propeller (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.42 A vane or Grim wheel is installed behind the propeller to harness the rotational energy left in the water after it passes through the propeller. This device redirects the flow of water, recovering some of the energy that would otherwise be lost as turbulence. Advantages: Energy Recovery; Reduced Wake Turbulence; Enhanced Thrust at Low Speeds. Disadvantages: Increased Drag; Maintenance Requirements; Space Constraints. The essential point about it is that the Grim vane wheel is free-running — it is not fixed to the shaft and is not driven by the engine; it turns freely on its own bearing in the propeller slipstream, more slowly than the propeller. It is also of larger diameter than the propeller, and that is the whole design idea, because the two radii do two different jobs:

- the inner radius, inside the propeller race, acts as a turbine, driven round by the rotational (swirl) component of the slipstream and extracting energy from it;

- the larger outer radius, outside the race in undisturbed water, acts as a propeller, using that extracted energy to add thrust. So the device recovers the rotational or swirl energy that a single propeller leaves behind in its race, which is energy otherwise lost entirely, and converts it into useful thrust — gains of the order of a few per cent are claimed. Its known weakness in service is blade fatigue and blade fracture: the outer blades are long, lightly supported and pass repeatedly through the sharp velocity gradient at the edge of the propeller race, and several installations have lost blades, which is why the device has not been widely adopted.

> **Source note:** Part 2's original part (b) describes the vane wheel only as a device installed behind the propeller that redirects flow and recovers energy, and its own Model Additions box records that this is not a correct description of a Grim wheel — the essential characteristics being that it is free-running rather than fixed, and that its inner radius acts as a turbine while its larger

outer radius acts as a thrust-producing propeller. The original description is preserved above and the correct mechanism follows it.

answers.title: Twin skeg rudders — why they are fitted & the advantages on high-capacity
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain why twin skeg rudders may be fitted on some vessels. (3)

(b) Explain the advantages of a twin skeg installation in modern vessels with a large cargo carrying capacity. (7)

Marks: (a) 3 · (b) 7
answers.answer_text:
What a skeg is — define it before answering either part A skeg is a structural extension of the hull that carries or encloses the propeller shaft and supports the rudder — not an appendage bolted on, but shaped hull structure. A twin-skeg arrangement therefore puts two shafts and two propellers under a wide, shallow, full-form hull, each in its own faired skeg with its own rudder behind it. It is used on large bulk carriers, car carriers and LNG ships — beamy, high-block, draught-limited ships — where a single screw would have to be either too large in diameter for the available draught or too heavily loaded for the power being absorbed.

a) Reasons for Fitting Twin Skeg Rudders:Improved Maneuverability (two rudders allow more effective directional control, especially at low speed such as docking or narrow channels); Increased Stability (additional hydrodynamic resistance against rolling); Redundancy (if one rudder is damaged or inoperative, the other can still function). Lead, though, on the draught and loading argument, because that is the reason the arrangement exists: splitting the power between two smaller-diameter propellers allows each to be fully immersed and lightly loaded under a shallow draught, which a single propeller of the necessary diameter could not be. Redundancy is the second real reason — a twin-skeg ship has two independent propulsion trains and two independent steering gears, so a single failure does not immobilise her.

b) Advantages of a Twin Skeg Installation:Enhanced Propulsion Efficiency (improved flow of water around the propellers, reducing turbulence and drag); Reduced Draft (shallower draft than traditional single rudder systems, advantageous in shallow waters or depth-restricted ports); Improved Roll Damping (skegs help dampen rolling motions); Better Course-Keeping (improved directional stability and control in rough seas); Structural Integrity (distributes loads more evenly across the bottom structure); Less Vulnerability to Damage (two rudders further apart, reduced risk of losing both to a single incident); Flexibility in Design (naval architects can optimise the hull shape for performance while accommodating large cargo holds). Of those, the three that carry the marks on a large-capacity vessel are:

- A better and far more uniform wake field. Each propeller works in the flow behind its own faired skeg rather than in the thick, highly non-uniform wake behind a full-form single-screw stern, so propulsive efficiency is higher and the cyclic variation in blade loading is much reduced — which means less cavitation and markedly less hull vibration. On a beamy, blunt-sterned ship this is the dominant gain.

- The ability to fit two smaller-diameter propellers under a limited draught, each properly immersed and at a sensible loading, so the ship can be built with the full block coefficient and cargo capacity wanted without an unworkable propeller.

- True propulsion redundancy — two complete trains, which for a large gas carrier or car carrier is a commercial as well as a safety argument.

> **Source note:** Part 2's own Model Additions box flags “Increased stability against rolling” as a weak point — skegs add little roll damping — and advises not leading with it. Both the part (a) item and the part (b) “Improved Roll Damping” item are preserved above exactly as printed, because nothing in the original is removed; but they have been placed last in the order of merit and the wake-field, draught and redundancy arguments put first, so that an answer written from this entry opens with the strong material.

answers.title: Hollow rudder — the survey, and the effects of losing watertight integrity
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe the survey of a hollow rudder. (5)

(b) Explain the possible effects if the watertight integrity of the rudder was compromised. (5)

Marks: (a) 5 · (b) 5
answers.answer_text:
(a) A thorough survey of a hollow rudder is essential for ensuring its structural integrity and functionality. The typical procedure:

- Initial Inspection: Visual inspection for cracks or corrosion, including checking the alignment with the vessel's mast and overall appearance. The alignment actually checked is the alignment of the rudder stock and pintle axis — that the stock, the neck bearing and the pintles are co-axial and that the rudder hangs square in the stern frame — together with the jumping (lifting) clearance at the top of the rudder, which is the gap that prevents the rudder lifting off its carrier.

- Water Entry Check: In dry dock, inspect for water ingress; open the top and bottom plugs to see if water leaks out (indicating a breach).

- Pressure Testing: Pressure test with a water head of approximately 2.46 meters to assess watertightness.

- Thickness Gauging: For older vessels or those with visible rust, gauge the rudder plates to measure material loss.

- Clearance Measurements: Measure clearances between pintle and bush in longitudinal and transverse directions.

- Condition of Anodes: Inspect sacrificial anodes for wear and replace if necessary.

- Percussion Testing: Use a hammer to evaluate the rudder by listening for variations in sound indicating weakness or delamination. (b)[The original answer to (b) listed repairs — weld repairs, corrosion treatment, bearing replacement — rather than the effects of lost integrity.] The effects of the rudder losing its watertight integrity are:

- The rudder floods and its submerged weight increases greatly. A hollow rudder is buoyant by design; full of water it is not, and the whole of that added weight is carried by the rudder carrier, the neck bearing and the pintles. Bearing loads and friction rise, the steering gear has to develop higher torque to turn the rudder, and there is a real risk of overload of the steering gear or of the bearings seizing.

- Internal corrosion accelerates, and does so unseen. The inside of the rudder is not coated to the standard of the outside and carries no anodes, so seawater trapped inside wastes the internal stiffening and the plating from the inside, where no external inspection will find it. The plate can be sound on the outside and wasted through on the inside.

- A free-surface and weight effect, where the flooded volume is large — a change of trim by the stern and, with the rudder partly full, water surging inside it as the ship rolls and as the rudder is put over.

- Ice damage in freezing service. Water trapped inside the rudder that freezes expands and can split the rudder plating from within, converting a small leak into a structural failure.

- The loss of the leak test as a monitoring tool. Once the rudder is known to be flooded, the annual drain- plug check no longer tells you anything new, and the class implication is that the rudder must be opened up, the source of ingress found and repaired, and the rudder re-tested to the design head before it is accepted.

> **Source note:** two corrections from Part 2's own Model Additions box are applied above. First, part (b) as printed answers a different question — it lists repairs rather than the effects of lost watertight integrity — and Part 2 records that and supplies the effects; the bracketed record of what the original contained is preserved above and the effects are answered in full. Second, the original part (a) checks “alignment with the vessel's mast”, which Part 2 identifies as an error: rudder alignment is checked against the rudder-stock and pintle axis and the jumping clearance, not the mast. The original wording is preserved and the correct check follows it.

answers.title: Tank inspections, erosion in ballast tanks & enclosed-space entry
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to tank inspections:

(a) list SIX items that should be looked for in a tank inspection; (3)

(b) state where erosion would be found in ballast tanks; (2)

(c) write a procedure for enclosed space entry. (5)

Marks: (a) 3 · (b) 2 · (c) 5
answers.answer_text:
a) Items that should be looked for in a tank inspection;

- Structural integrity (cracks, fractures and grooving)

- General corrosion, pitting, blistering and coating condition

- Condition of Cargo Equipment

- Sacrificial anodes condition

- Internal pipework and fittings condition

- Tank openings and manholes integrity

b) Erosion in ballast tanks would be found around;

- Underneath the Bell-Mouth: Severe pitting corrosion often occurs on the bottom plating directly below the suction pipes (bell-mouth) due to high-velocity water movement and vortex action during stripping operations. Strictly this is erosion-corrosion: the protective scale or coating is mechanically swept away by the high-velocity flow, and the bare steel then corrodes.

- Bottom Plating & Suction Wells: Areas where sediment retention is high are prone to microbiologically induced corrosion.

- Areas of coating breakdown, where the paint film has already failed and the exposed steel is subject to flow.

- The waterline or part-full band — the zone that is alternately wet and dry as the tank is filled and emptied. This is the worst corrosion zone in a ballast tank and is the location most candidates omit; naming it earns the mark.

c) Enclosed Space Entry procedure according to COSWP 2025;

- Pre-Entry Planning: Conduct a risk assessment to identify potential hazards (oxygen depletion, toxic/ flammable gases, slip, trip, fall and entrapment) and implement control measures. Develop an entry plan that outlines the tasks to be performed and safety measures.

- LOTO and Atmosphere Testing: Ventilate the space thoroughly. Isolate all connecting pipelines, machinery and tag out (LOTO). Test the atmosphere using calibrated gas detectors at various levels (top, middle, bottom). Keep ventilation running during entry and re-test periodically, particularly after breaks. Entry should proceed only once the readings confirm oxygen at 20.9% by volume, and hydrocarbon and toxic gas — for example hydrogen sulphide and carbon monoxide — within their permitted limits.

- Safety Equipment: Rescue equipment (tripod, stretcher, SCBA, first aid) must be ready at the entrance with designated rescue party. Entrants must wear appropriate PPE, including personal gas monitor, harness, lifeline, safety torch and EEBD (for emergency use).

- Enclosed Space Entry Permit and Tool Box meeting: Complete an Enclosed Space Entry Permit confirming that the hazards of the job and of the space have been dealt with. Ensure all personnel involved are aware of the task, the hazards, and are competent in their job. The permit must be time-limited and re-validated after any break in the work, consistent with the requirement to re-test the atmosphere.

- Authorized Entry and Monitoring: A trained person/safety officer must be posted at the entrance to establish clear communication protocols through radio and monitor the entry process. If any person feels unwell, or if the oxygen level drops/gas alarm sounds, the space must be evacuated immediately. On completion, the space is secured, and the permit is closed.

answers.title: Anchor cable attachment & chain locker
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a method of attaching an anchor cable to a ship's structure, showing how the cable could be released in an emergency. (5)

(b) Explain how chain lockers are emptied of water and silt, stating any restrictions that may have to be observed. (3)

(c) State the dangers associated with entering a chain locker. (2)

Marks: (a) 5 · (b) 3 · (c) 2
answers.answer_text:
a) A clear sketch of attaching the bitter end of anchor cable to ships structure is given below. The bitter end of the anchor chain is released in an emergency by removing a safety pin and driving out a locking pin from the securing bracket using a dedicated emergency sledge hammer (painted in red color). The marking point in this part is that the cable must be releasable from a safe position. The bitter end is secured by a weak-link bracket or slip — for example a senhouse slip, or a clenched ring retained by a release pin — arranged so that it can be operated from outside the chain locker, normally from the deck or the compartment above. State explicitly that the release arrangement must not require anyone to enter the locker, because the chain locker is an enclosed space and entry in an emergency would be impossible. That is the point the examiner is testing, and the sketch should show the release pin and its operating position accordingly. Original sketch — bitter-end attachment to bulkhead, plan view (preserved unaltered) Part 1, p.23

(b) Chain lockers are emptied of water and silt using a dedicated drainage eductor. The eductor uses a high- velocity jet of sea water (motive water) from the fire main system, which creates a suction that draws out water, mud, and silt from the chain locker sump. The effluent is generally mixed with the motive water before being discharged overboard. As chain locker is pumped out, fire main water is sprayed into the locker to flush out any remaining sediment or mud.

Restrictions that may have to be observed while discharging chain locker effluent are;

- Anchor chain must be carefully and thoroughly washed down as it is being hauled out of the water to remove sediment and organisms.

- Rinsing or pumping out chain lockers is prohibited in port to avoid the adverse effects of non-native species introduction.

- At least once per month, the rinsing or pumping out of chain lockers must occur as far from shore as possible and, if technically feasible, the rinsing or pumping out of chain lockers must not occur in US federally- protected waters / special areas.

c) Dangers associated with entering a chain locker as per Enclosed Space Entry guidelines of COSWP 2025 are;

- Oxygen Deficiency/Asphyxiation — arising chiefly because the rusting of the chain and of the locker steel consumes the oxygen in the space, which is the cause worth naming.

- Accumulation of Toxic / Flammable Gases

- Inadequate Ventilation

- Slip, trip, fall and entrapment (especially if chains shift unexpectedly while working inside). Entry therefore requires a full enclosed-space-entry permit, with atmosphere testing, forced ventilation and a standby man posted at the access.

answers.title: Defects in the steelwork of ballast tanks — causes, areas affected &
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to defects found in the steelwork of ballast tanks:

(a) explain the factors that may cause defects in ballast tanks; (4)

(b) state, with reasons, areas most likely to be affected and how they may be indicated; (4)

(c) state methods employed to minimise damage, caused by the facors in (a). (2)

Marks: (a) 4 · (b) 4 · (c) 2
answers.answer_text:
(a) Factors That May Cause Defects:Corrosion (general corrosion, pitting, and microbial influenced corrosion (MIC), exacerbated by inadequate coating and contaminants); Poor Maintenance (failure to clean tanks or inspect/replace gaskets and seals; poorly secured manhole covers allowing water ingress); Stress Concentrations (at welds, fittings, or areas where temporary lifting devices were used during construction; repeated loading/unloading cycles causing fatigue fractures); Operational Practices (improper ballasting/ deballasting introducing excessive forces; rapid filling or emptying creating pressure surges). Underlying all of them is coating breakdown followed by alternate wetting and drying: a dedicated seawater ballast tank spends its life half full or empty, so the steel is repeatedly wetted with aerated seawater and then exposed to air, which is the most aggressive corrosion regime there is — plenty of oxygen and plenty of electrolyte, in turn.

(b) Areas Most Likely to Be Affected:Tank Bottom (bottom plating particularly susceptible to erosion and corrosion due to sediment accumulation and stagnant water; indicated by visible rust or pitting and by ultrasonic thickness measurements revealing material loss); Weld Seams (common points for stress concentration and potential failure; indicated by visible cracks or deformations, detected by visual inspection or NDT such as dye penetrant or ultrasonic testing). Four further zones should be named, with the reason in each case:

- The tank top and under-deck plating, where warm humid air condenses on the underside of a sun-heated deck and drips back — corrosion from above, in a place nobody looks at from the bottom of the tank.

- The air–water interface, the “waterline band” — the band of plating and structure at the level the ballast normally sits at. Alternating wet and dry with a plentiful oxygen supply gives the worst pitting anywhere in the tank, and it is the classic finding of a ballast tank survey.

- Horizontal surfaces that hold water — flange faces, bracket toes, the tops of stiffeners and girder faces — because water standing on a horizontal ledge never dries and the coating fails there first.

- Around heating coils, where the local temperature accelerates the reaction, and at the suction bell- mouth, where high local velocity strips the coating and the corrosion product together — erosion- corrosion.

(c) Methods to Minimise Damage:Regular Inspections and Maintenance (rigorous inspection schedule, routine checks for corrosion and structural integrity, regular cleaning to remove sediment and contaminants); Coating and Cathodic Protection (high-quality protective coatings to reduce corrosion rates; cathodic protection systems such as sacrificial anodes to mitigate galvanic corrosion). Name the standard and state how the two protections divide the work. Coatings for dedicated seawater ballast tanks are applied to the IMO PSPC — the Performance Standard for Protective Coatings — which specifies a coating system with a 15-year target useful life, together with the surface preparation, edge treatment, film thickness and inspection needed to achieve it. Coatings and anodes are then complementary, not alternatives: the coating is the primary barrier, and the anodes protect the bare steel at coating holidays, damage and breakdown. The corollary is worth stating because it is often missed — anodes only work where the steel is wet, so in a tank that is frequently empty the anodes give no protection at all for much of the time and the coating is doing the whole job.

answers.title: Ballast Water Management Convention
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to the International Convention for the Control and Management of Ships' Ballast Water and Sediments:

(a) state the aims of the Ballast Water Management Convention; (2)

(b) explain the difference between ballast water standards D-1 and D-2 (2)

(c) state, with reasons, the documentation required by ships in international traffic to manage their ballast water and sediments. (6)

Marks: (a) 2 · (b) 2 · (c) 6
answers.answer_text:
a) The International Convention for the Control and Management of Ships' Ballast Water and Sediments, 2004 aims to:

- Prevent the Spread of Invasive Species: The primary goal is to minimize the transfer of harmful aquatic organisms and pathogens through ballast water, which can disrupt marine ecosystems and lead to significant ecological and economic consequences.

- Protect Marine Environments: By regulating ballast water management practices, the convention seeks to safeguard marine biodiversity and protect coastal environments from the adverse effects of non-native species introduction.

b) Difference Between Ballast Water Standards D-1 and D-2

- D-1 Standard: This standard requires ships to perform ballast water exchange in open seas, at least 200 nautical miles away from land (50 NM for shorter voyages) and in waters at least 200 meters deep. The aim is to dilute and reduce the number of organisms in the ballast water before it is discharged. The volumetric exchange efficiency must be at least 95%, which by the flow-through method means pumping at least three times the tank volume through the tank. The 50 NM figure is the fallback provision — as far from land as practicable, but not less than 50 NM and in water not less than 200 m deep.

- D-2 Standard: Regulation D-2 of the BWM Convention mandates that ships treat ballast water to meet following discharge limits for viable organisms and indicator microbes using approved ballast water treatment systems; ◦ Organisms ≥ 50 µm: Less than 10 viable organisms per cubic metre (m³).

◦ Organisms 10 µm – 50 µm: Less than 10 viable organisms per mL. ◦ Toxicogenic Vibrio cholerae: Less than 1 CFU per 100 mL. ◦ Escherichia coli: Less than 250 CFU per 100 mL. ◦ Intestinal Enterococci: Less than 100 CFU per 100 mL. State the currency point explicitly, as it is often the key mark: D-1 is being phased out. All ships must meet the D-2 standard, normally by means of an approved ballast water management system, by the implementation dates, with full D-2 compliance required from 8 September 2024.

c) Documentation required, with reasons, by ships in international traffic to manage their ballast water and sediments are;

1. International Ballast Water Management Certificate (IBWMC): This certificate confirms that the ship complies with the Ballast Water Management Convention requirements. It is issued by RO on behalf of the flag state and specifies which standard (D-2) the ship adheres to.

2. Ballast Water Management Plan (BWMP): Each vessel must have a specific plan detailing procedures for managing ballast water, including operational guidelines for crew members. This plan must be written in a language understood by the crew and include instructions for handling sediments, reporting requirements, and emergency procedures.

3. Ballast Water Record Book (BWRB): This record book documents all ballast water operations, including when ballast water is taken on board, treated, and discharged. It must also record any unusual events or deviations from normal procedures, ensuring transparency and accountability.

4. Type Approval Certificate for BWMS: If a ship is equipped with a Ballast Water Management System (BWMS), it must have documentation proving that the system has been type-approved according to international standards.

5. Ballast Water Reporting Form (BWRF): Some ports may require this form upon arrival to ensure compliance with local regulations regarding ballast water management.

6. Additional Documents: Certificate of Calibration, Training records, Commissioning Test Report, and, in cases of exemption, documentation detailing voyages between specified ports. Following the 2020 amendments to the Convention, a BWMS must have a commissioning test with validation sampling recorded before the system may be relied upon for compliance, which is the purpose of the Commissioning Test Report listed here. Six of the ten marks are in this part and the question says “with reasons”, so every document must carry its purpose as above, not merely its name.

answers.title: IMDG hazard classes & dangerous-goods documentation
answers.question_as_set:
(a) List FIVE of the nine hazard classes of Dangerous Goods as stated in the International Maritime Dangerous Goods (IMDG) code. (5)

(b) State the documentation that must accompany any hazardous shipment, explaining the purpose of this documentation. (5)

Marks: (a) 5 · (b) 5
answers.answer_text:
a) Hazard classes of Dangerous Goods as stated in the International Maritime Dangerous Goods (IMDG) code are;

- Class 1: Explosives — divisions 1.1 to 1.6

- Class 2: Gases — 2.1 flammable, 2.2 non-flammable non-toxic, 2.3 toxic

- Class 3: Flammable Liquids

- Class 4: Flammable Solids — 4.1 flammable solids, 4.2 spontaneously combustible, 4.3 dangerous when wet

- Class 5: Oxidizing Substances and Organic Peroxides — 5.1 oxidisers, 5.2 organic peroxides

- Class 6: Toxic and Infectious Substances — 6.1 toxic, 6.2 infectious

- Class 7: Radioactive Materials

- Class 8: Corrosive Substances

- Class 9: Miscellaneous Dangerous Substances and Articles Only five classes are asked for, at one mark each, so naming five with their divisions is sufficient; listing all nine costs nothing but earns nothing extra.

b) The documentation that must accompany any hazardous shipment:

- Dangerous Goods Declaration (DGD): This is a signed declaration by the shipper confirming that the cargo is properly packed, marked, labeled, and in proper condition for carriage according to IMDG regulations. It acts as a legal document identifying the hazards, enabling the ship's crew to take appropriate precautions.

- Container/Vehicle Packing Certificate: Required when hazardous goods are loaded into a Cargo Transport Unit (CTU). It certifies that the unit was properly packed, secured, and cleaned, complying with safety standards.

- Special List or Manifest: The ship must carry a special list or manifest detailing the dangerous goods, their classification, and their precise location on board. This is required by SOLAS Chapter VII and MARPOL Annex III, and a detailed stowage plan may be carried in its place.

- Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS/SDS): It provide detailed info on physical properties, health hazards, and emergency procedures.

- Document of Compliance for the carriage of dangerous goods: the ship-side document, required by SOLAS II-2 Regulation 19, certifying that the ship's construction and equipment are suitable for carrying the classes of dangerous goods listed on it. These documents, along with the UN number, Proper Shipping Name, Class & where appropriate, the Division & Compatibility group, Description of the goods with Gross mass/volume, Transport emergency cards (TREM cards) and emergency contact information to ensure safe handling, stowage, and regulatory compliance must be handed over to the ship's master or authorized representative prior to loading. Purpose of Documentation

- Safety & Emergency Response: Enables the vessel's crew, port authorities, and emergency responders to identify the exact hazard and take appropriate action in case of spillage or accident.

- Stowage & Segregation: Ensures hazardous goods are stored in compliant locations on board, preventing dangerous reactions with incompatible goods.

- Legal Compliance: Certifies that the shipment meets international regulations, allowing it to be transported through different jurisdictions.

answers.title: Noise levels on ships
answers.question_as_set:
During sea trials, extensive noise measurements are taken in accordance with the Code of Practice for Noise Levels in Ships.

(a) State and explain the unit of sound measurement. (2)

(b) State the noise level above which personnel are required to wear ear protection. (1)

(c) Explain how a ship's crew may be made aware of the hazards posed by exposure to excessive noise. (2)

(d) Explain how the noise levels can be reduced in the design of EACH of the following: (i) diesel generators (3);

(ii) ventilation fans and trunkings (2).

Marks: (a) 2 · (b) 1 · (c) 2 · (d)(i) 3 · (d)(ii) 2
answers.answer_text:
a) The unit of sound measurement is decibel, expressed as dB(A). dB(A) (A-weighted decibels), is a unit of sound measurement that adjusts readings to match the human ear's frequency response. It filters out very low and high frequencies that people hear poorly, making it the standard unit for measuring noise.

b) Based on the Code of Safe Working Practices (COSWP 2025) for Merchant Seafarers, MLC 2006 and The IMO Code on noise levels on board ships, the noise level above which personnel are required to wear ear protection is 85 dB(A). Quote the figures from the Code on Noise Levels On Board Ships, resolution MSC.337(91), which is mandatory under SOLAS II-1 Regulation 3-12. At 85 dB(A) and above, hearing protection is mandatory and the space must be marked with warning signs; between 80 and 85 dB(A) protectors must be made available and information given to the crew; and the daily exposure limit is L = 85 dB(A). The Code's space limits are Aeq(24) manned machinery spaces not exceeding 110 dB(A) with protection worn, unmanned machinery spaces not exceeding 115 dB(A), and cabins not exceeding 60 dB(A).

c) A ship's crew can be made aware of hazards from excessive noise through a combination of mandatory regulatory compliance, safety training on PPE especially uses of earmuffs, clear warning signage, and routine inspections. These methods ensure that personnel understand the risks of noise-induced hearing loss and other health issues, such as increased fatigue and stress.

d) i) Noise levels can be reduced in the design of Diesel generators by;

- Engine/Fan Design: Use modern engines with lower noise profiles and optimized, low-noise fan blades for cooling.

- Exhaust Silencers (Mufflers): Install high-performance exhaust silencers to reduce 75% of noise generated by exhaust discharge.

- Vibration Isolation: Incorporate rubber or spring anti-vibration mounts under the engine and alternator to stop structural-borne noise.

- Resilient or double-elastic mounting of the whole generating set on a common raft with a floating floor, together with an acoustic enclosure or lagging around the unit. This is the single strongest design measure and should be named first. ii) Noise levels can be reduced in the design of Ventilation Fans and Trunkings by;

- Fan Selection and Vibration Isolation: Use high-efficiency low noise fans with aerodynamic blades to reduce source noise and install fans on anti-vibration mounts or pads to stop structure-borne noise.

- Flexible Connectors and Acoustic Duct Linings: Use flexible duct connectors between the fan and rigid trunking to prevent vibration transmission. Lining ventilation ducts with acoustic materials can absorb sound energy and reduce noise transmission through the ducting system.

- Splitter or attenuator silencers fitted in the trunking, and reduced air velocity in the ducts achieved by generous duct sizing, since noise generated at bends and grilles rises steeply with velocity.

Half the marks are in part (d), and the question asks how noise is reduced in the design — PPE and operational measures score nothing there.

answers.title: Harmonised System of Survey & Certification; the load line certificate
answers.topic: Additional Part 2 topics — not set in this window
answers.question_as_set:
a) Explain the Harmonised System of Survey & Certification (HSSC). (4)

b) With reference to the load line certificate explain what will be inspected and how these items are kept in compliance. (6)

Marks: (a) 4 · (b) 6
answers.answer_text:
a) HSSC: An IMO initiative to streamline and standardize survey and certification processes for ships. Main objectives: Efficiency (harmonizing requirements across conventions to reduce redundancy); Consistency (a consistent framework so vessels are assessed uniformly regardless of flag state); Simplification (clear guidelines reducing confusion and administrative burden); Interoperability (better cooperation between classification societies and regulatory bodies, mutual recognition of surveys and certificates). The defining mechanism has to be given, because the objectives on their own do not explain what the system actually does. HSSC sets a five-year certificate cycle for all the convention certificates, with annual, intermediate and renewal surveys aligned so that the SOLAS, MARPOL, Load Line, IOPP, Tonnage and other surveys fall together rather than at scattered dates through the year. Each is tied to a single anniversary date, and each survey may be carried out within a survey window of ±3 months about that anniversary date. That is the point of the whole scheme: one attendance instead of several, no certificate quietly expiring between dockings, and a window wide enough that surveys can be planned around the ship's trading pattern.

b) Inspection Items Related to Load Line Certificate:Hull Condition (corrosion, damage, structural integrity affecting buoyancy and stability); Load Line Marks (correctly displayed, visible, accurately reflecting assigned freeboard); Hatch Covers and Closing Appliances (watertight and in good working condition); Freeing Ports and Scuppers (unobstructed and functioning); Stability Information (up-to-date documentation); Maintenance Records (regular inspections conducted). Keeping Items in Compliance: Regular Surveys (annually or every five years); Maintenance Protocols for all load-line fittings; Documentation Updates; Training and Awareness of crew. Stated against the HSSC cycle, that means a Load Line renewal survey every five years, with an annual survey in each intervening year, each within the ±3-month window. The link that must be made explicit is that the items listed are not an arbitrary inspection list — they are precisely the conditions of assignment of the freeboard. The freeboard was assigned on the assumption that the closing appliances are weathertight, that the freeing ports and scuppers will clear water from the deck, that the guard rails and means of access protect the crew, and that the marks are correct and visible. Keeping those items in order is therefore what keeps the assigned freeboard valid, and a defect in any of them is a defect in the certificate itself and not merely a maintenance item.

answers.title: Five methods of preventing distortion of plates and frames during welded
answers.topic: Additional Part 2 topics — not set in this window
answers.question_as_set:
Sketch FIVE methods used to prevent the distortion of ships' plates and frames during major welded hull repairs in dry dock. (10)

Marks: (a) 10
answers.answer_text:
FIVE methods to prevent distortion: (1) weld both sides; (2) back-step welding; (3) skip / wandering technique; (4) toggle-plate welding; (5) sequence welding (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.43 FIVE methods to prevent distortion: (1) weld both sides; (2) back-step welding; (3) skip / wandering technique;

(4) toggle-plate welding; (5) sequence welding. Because this is a 10-mark sketch question, the sketches alone will not carry it — each one must be annotated with the principle that makes it work, and that annotation is what earns the marks:

1. Weld both sides — balanced or double-sided welding. Depositing equal weld metal either side of the plate equalises the shrinkage about the neutral axis, so the angular contraction of one side is cancelled by the other and the plate stays flat instead of pulling into a vee.

2. Back-step welding. Short runs are deposited in the reverse direction to the general direction of travel, so that each run's contraction opposes the last and the accumulated longitudinal shrinkage is broken up into short, self-cancelling lengths instead of building up along the seam.

3. Skip or wandering technique. Runs are deposited in a scattered order along the joint rather than consecutively, which spreads the heat input and avoids a local build-up of temperature — it is uneven heating that distorts, so distributing the heat distributes the strain.

4. Toggle-plate welding — tack and strongback restraint. Toggle plates, strongbacks or tack-welded bridging pieces hold the plates mechanically to the set gap and in plane while the weld cools, so the joint cannot close up or lift; they are removed and the marks dressed off afterwards.

5. Sequence welding — a balanced welding sequence. The sequence is planned to work outward from the centre of the panel or the repair, so that shrinkage is drawn toward the middle and the free edges are left free to move rather than being restrained into locked-in stress. Two further recognised methods are worth adding if more than five are wanted, or as supporting comment: pre- setting and pre-cambering, in which the plates are deliberately set out of line by the amount the weld is expected to pull them, so that the shrinkage brings the work to the correct shape; and controlled heat input — low-hydrogen consumables, the correct run size and a limited interpass temperature — since the total heat put into the joint is the ultimate driver of how much it will move.

answers.title: Propeller slip — definition, calculation & the conditions that affect it
answers.topic: Additional Part 2 topics — not set in this window
answers.question_as_set:
a) Define propeller slip, explaining how it is calculated. (2)

b) State, with reasons, FOUR conditions which will affect the propeller slip. (8)

Marks: (a) 2 · (b) 8
answers.answer_text:
a) Propeller Slip is the difference between the theoretical distance a propeller should travel in one complete revolution (based on its pitch) and the actual distance it travels through the water. Slip % = (Theoretical Speed − Actual Speed) / Theoretical Speed × 100, where Theoretical Speed is calculated from the propeller's pitch and the engine's RPM, and Actual Speed is the speed of the vessel through the water. There are two slips, and the definition should distinguish them, because they answer different questions:

- Apparent slip = (engine speed − ship's speed) / engine speed, where engine speed = pitch × rpm and the ship's speed comes from the log. It is the figure worked out in the engine room from the counter and the log, and it is the one normally meant by “slip” on a daily report.

- Real slip = (engine speed − speed of advance V ) / engine speed, where V = V(1 − w) and w is the wake a a fraction. It uses the speed of the water actually arriving at the propeller disc, which is less than the ship's speed because the propeller works inside the hull's own wake. The consequence follows from the definitions: real slip is always positive, because the propeller must always advance less than its pitch to generate thrust, whereas apparent slip can go negative — with a following current or a following sea, the ship is being carried along faster than the propeller is driving her, and the arithmetic returns a negative figure. A negative apparent slip is therefore not an error and not an impossibility; it is information about the current.

b) Conditions Affecting Propeller Slip:Hull Condition (a fouled or damaged hull increases drag, leading to higher slip); Speed of the Vessel (as speed increases, slip typically decreases); Propeller Design (diameter, pitch, and blade shape impact efficiency — larger diameter propellers generally have less slip); Environmental Conditions (wind, current, and sea state — operating against a strong current or in heavy seas increases resistance and slip). For a displacement merchant ship the four conditions to give, with the reason in each case, are:

- Hull and propeller fouling. Added resistance means the ship makes less speed for the same revolutions, so slip rises — which is exactly why slip is logged daily: a steadily rising slip on unchanged draught and weather is the standard indicator of a fouled hull and the trigger for a hull clean.

- Head seas and heavy weather. Added resistance and the loss of speed in a head sea raise slip; a following sea lowers it, and can drive apparent slip negative.

- Shallow water. The restricted flow under the hull increases resistance and changes the wake field — the shallow-water effect — and slip rises noticeably before any change in draught or weather.

- Increased draught and displacement. A deeper ship has more resistance for the same revolutions, so a loaded passage shows a higher slip than the same ship in ballast. The wake fraction is the underlying reason apparent and real slip differ at all, and it is itself a function of hull form, draught and fouling — which is why slip is a useful performance indicator rather than a fixed number.

> **Source note:** Part 2's Model Additions box for this question carries a correction reading that the “displacement vs planing mode” reasoning applies to fast planing craft and not to displacement merchant ships. No such reasoning appears anywhere in the original answer as Part 2 prints it, so the correction has nothing to attach to — like the welding-process correction recorded at E37, it appears to be a residue from an earlier draft of the answer. The discrepancy is recorded rather than resolved silently, and the substantive material that accompanies it — the four conditions that raise slip on a displacement ship, and the wake fraction as the reason the two slips differ — has been written into part (b) above. Nothing has been removed from the original.

answers.title: TBT antifouling — why it was banned, alternatives, and selecting an
answers.topic: Additional Part 2 topics — not set in this window
answers.question_as_set:
a) State why the International Maritime Organisation has banned the use of Tributyltin antifouling (T.B.T.) coatings for ship's hulls. (1)

b) State the base elements of TWO alternative coatings to T.B.T. antifouling. (2)

c) Explain the considerations in the selection of a coating for a ship's underwater surface. (7)

Marks: (a) 1 · (b) 2 · (c) 7
answers.answer_text:
a) The IMO has banned TBT antifouling coatings due to their detrimental effects on non-target marine organisms. TBT is highly toxic and causes severe ecological damage, including hormone disruption in marine species, leading to reproductive issues and population declines, and accumulates in the food chain. Name the instrument and the signature damage. The ban is imposed by the IMO AFS Convention — the International Convention on the Control of Harmful Anti-fouling Systems on Ships, 2001, which entered into force in 2008 — and the specific effect that made the case against TBT is imposex in molluscs, the development of male characteristics in females that sterilises the population, documented in the dog whelk, together with shell malformation in oysters. TBT leached from hulls at concentrations of a few nanograms per litre was enough to do it, which is why a coating on a ship became an international convention.

b) Alternatives:Copper-Based Coatings (base element: Copper — releases copper ions toxic to fouling organisms, less harmful than TBT); Biocide-Free Coatings (base element: non-toxic polymers or silicone — create a slick, low-adhesion surface that prevents attachment without leaching toxic chemicals). Stated in the terms the industry uses, the two families are copper self-polishing copolymer (SPC), in which the copper oxide biocide, usually with a co-biocide, is released at a controlled rate as the binder hydrolyses and polishes away; and foul-release silicone or fluoropolymer coatings, which are biocide-free and work by low surface energy — fouling cannot key to the surface, and what does settle is released by the water flow once the ship is under way.

c) Considerations in Selection:Environmental Impact (minimal harmful leaching, compliance with IMO regulations); Fouling Resistance (long-lasting protection against barnacles, algae, mussels); Durability and Lifespan (withstand abrasion and impacts; longer lifespan reduces reapplication); Application Process (ease of application, curing time, surface preparation); Compatibility with Existing Systems; Cost-Effectiveness; Regulatory Compliance. Two further drivers decide the choice in practice and should be given:

- Self-polishing versus hard or ablative behaviour. An SPC keeps a smooth surface and a predictable leaching rate over the docking interval; a hard coating survives abrasion and ice better but loses its release rate; an ablative wears away mechanically. The docking interval wanted — 30, 60 or 90 months — largely dictates which is specified.

- The ship's speed and activity profile. A foul-release silicone needs water flow to shed settled fouling, so it suits a fast ship on regular service and suits a slow or frequently idle ship very badly — and an idle ship fouls fastest of all, since fouling settles in still water. The trading pattern, the proportion of time at anchor and the water temperature of the trading area are therefore as much part of the selection as the coating's own properties.

answers.title: Insulated vs earthed neutral system: advantages/disadvantages + NER
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to a THREE phase electrical distribution system:

(a) explain the advantages and disadvantages of an insulated neutral system; (8)

(b) state how an earthed neutral system is earthed and the measures taken to limit the maximum earth fault current. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Insulated (unearthed) neutral system

In an insulated neutral system, the star point of the generator or transformer has no deliberate low-impedance connection to earth - the only path to earth is through the system's natural, distributed capacitance to the hull, a very high impedance path.

Advantages:
1. Continuity of supply on a single fault - since there's no deliberate low-impedance earth path, a single phase-to-earth fault doesn't create a large fault current and doesn't force an automatic trip. Propulsion, steering, and essential services can keep running with a fault present somewhere in the system.
2. Limited fault energy on the first fault - only a small capacitive charging current can flow (typically low single-digit amps on a ship's LV system), minimal risk of arc damage or fire from that first fault.
3. Time to act safely - the vessel can complete a critical manoeuvre or reach a safe location while the fault is traced and isolated methodically.

Disadvantages:
1. Voltage rise on healthy phases - the moment one phase earths, its voltage to earth collapses toward zero, but the two healthy phases rise to full line voltage relative to earth - an increase of √3 (approximately 1.73x) above normal. This sustained overvoltage continuously stresses the healthy phases' insulation for as long as the fault remains uncleared.
2. Risk of a cross-country (double) fault - if a second earth fault develops on a different phase before the first is cleared, the result is effectively a phase-to-phase short circuit through the hull.
3. Fault location takes time and system knowledge - because nothing trips automatically, engineers typically isolate sections one at a time while watching the insulation monitoring device.
4. Total reliance on the monitoring device working - the entire safety benefit depends on the insulation monitoring device being installed, functioning, and its alarm being noticed and acted on.
5. Transient overvoltages from arcing faults - an intermittent, restriking earth fault can produce voltage spikes considerably higher than the steady-state √3 rise.

(b) Earthed neutral system

The star point is connected to the ship's hull through a Neutral Earthing Resistor (NER), rather than solidly earthed. The NER is sized to limit maximum earth fault current to a controlled, low value - enough to reliably operate an earth-fault relay/alarm, but low enough to avoid the arc damage and fire risk that an uncontrolled high fault current would cause.

answers.title: Earth leakage detection (instrument type) + insulated neutral fault clearance
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain, with the aid of a sketch, the principle of operation of an earth leakage detection system of the instrument type. (6)

(b) Explain why an insulated neutral system is used extensively on board ships. (2)

(c) State, with reasons, why a single earth fault on an insulated neutral system should always be cleared as soon as possible. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Instrument-type earth leakage detection system

This system uses a sensitive centre-zero moving-coil milliammeter, connected across the system so that it continuously measures any current leaking from the phase conductors to earth through the ship's insulation resistance. Typically the meter is connected between the neutral/star point and earth (or via a network of equal high-value resistors from each phase to a common point, with the meter reading the resulting current at that point). Under healthy conditions, insulation resistance is high, so only a very small, steady leakage current flows and the meter reads near zero. If insulation deteriorates anywhere on the system, or an actual earth fault develops, the leakage current increases measurably, the meter deflects, and this triggers a visual/audible alarm.

Worth explicitly distinguishing this from the simpler earth lamp indicator method: three lamps, each connected from one phase to earth. Under healthy conditions all three glow at similar brightness. If one phase develops an earth fault, that lamp dims or goes out while the other two brighten. The earth lamp method gives only a rough visual indication; the instrument type gives an actual measured value on a meter.

(b) Why insulated neutral systems are used extensively at sea

A single earth fault does not immediately create a large fault current or force a shutdown, since there's no solid earth return path. Propulsion and essential services can continue running even with a fault present, critical at sea where an unplanned blackout is far more dangerous than a monitored, uncleared fault.

(c) Why a single earth fault must still be cleared promptly

The two healthy phases rise to full line voltage relative to earth (approximately 1.73x) for as long as the fault remains, stressing their insulation. If a second earth fault develops on a different phase before the first is cleared, the result is effectively a phase-to-phase short circuit - far more severe than either fault alone.

answers.title: Insulation resistance test + resistance/continuity tests
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain the principle of operation of an insulation resistance test, stating why the test is carried out on a regular basis. (6)

(b) Describe how EACH of the following electrical tests is carried out:

(i) resistance; (2)

(ii) continuity. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Insulation resistance (IR) test

A DC test voltage - commonly 500V for testing low-voltage equipment such as a 440V winding - is applied between the conductor under test and earth (or between separate windings), using an insulation resistance tester (Megger). The instrument measures the resulting leakage current and displays the insulation resistance in megohms. Sound insulation gives a high reading; the reading falls only if insulation has degraded through moisture ingress, contamination, or ageing. It's carried out on a regular basis because insulation deteriorates progressively - regular testing catches a downward trend early, before it develops into an earth fault or winding failure.

(b)(i) Resistance test

Measures the actual resistance of the conductor or winding itself - not its insulation - typically using a low-resistance ohmmeter or Kelvin bridge. For a three-phase machine, comparing all three phase windings checks they're balanced; an abnormally high reading on one phase points to a loose connection or partial winding fault.

(b)(ii) Continuity test

Simply confirms an unbroken electrical path exists, using a continuity tester or multimeter's buzzer setting - testing a fuse is the classic example: continuity means the fuse is intact, no continuity means it's blown.

answers.title: Insulation testing procedure + Polarisation Index
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to insulation testing of electrical equipment:

(a) state the reasons for insulation testing and why it is carried out on a regular basis; (2)

(b) describe the procedure for taking a set of insulation readings on an electric motor in-situ, stating the minimum acceptable readings; (6)

(c) explain the term Polarisation Index. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Insulation deteriorates over time from heat, moisture, oil contamination and mechanical stress. Regular testing - PMS routine, before running standby equipment, after overhaul - catches this early, before it progresses to an earth fault, allowing corrective action before failure.

(b) Procedure: isolate and lock off the motor, confirm dead with an approved voltage indicator, disconnect electronic control gear sensitive to test voltage. Select the correct test voltage (typically 500V DC for a low-voltage motor). Connect one lead to earth (motor frame) and test each phase winding to earth in turn; also test winding-to-winding if required. Take each reading after a consistent time interval (commonly 1 minute), noting ambient temperature and humidity.

Minimum acceptable reading: a practical guide is roughly 1-10 MΩ for low-voltage machines - a healthy new winding reads far higher (often several hundred MΩ), so the absolute minimum matters less than a clear downward trend against previous readings.

(c) Polarisation Index: the ratio of the insulation resistance reading at 10 minutes to the reading at 1 minute, during one continuous test. Sound, dry insulation shows resistance rising over that period as absorption currents decay, giving a PI ratio above 1 (commonly 2 or more is good). Poor/damp insulation shows little rise, giving a PI close to 1. PI reflects insulation condition independent of ambient temperature/humidity effects that distort a single-point reading.

answers.title: Self-excited A.C. generator circuit and operation
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a circuit diagram of a self excited a.c. generator. (5)

(b) Describe the operation of the circuit sketched in part (a). (5)
answers.answer_text: (a)/(b) Principle and operation: A self-excited generator supplies its own field excitation current from its own output, rather than needing a separate external DC supply or battery. The process relies on residual magnetism: a small amount of magnetism always remains in the rotor iron even when stationary. As the prime mover brings the rotor up to speed, this small residual field induces a small initial EMF in the stator windings. That small AC output is fed through a step-down transformer and rectifier bridge, producing a small DC current, delivered back to the rotor's field winding via slip rings - increasing the field strength slightly. This stronger field induces a larger stator EMF, which when rectified and fed back further increases field current again. This self-reinforcing build-up continues until the magnetic circuit begins to saturate, at which point output voltage stabilises at its rated value. No external battery or DC supply is ever needed - reliance on residual magnetism alone defines 'self-excited' as opposed to a separately-excited design.

answers.title: Automatic Voltage Regulator (AVR) using thyristors
answers.question_as_set: Describe, with the aid of a circuit diagram, the operation of an automatic voltage regulator (AVR) which employs the use of thyristors. (10)
answers.answer_text:
The AVR continuously compares the generator's actual output voltage - sensed via a voltage transformer/sensing circuit - against a fixed reference (set-point) voltage. Any difference is fed to a firing control circuit, which adjusts the point in each AC half-cycle at which the thyristors supplying the exciter/field winding are triggered (fired). Firing earlier in each half-cycle increases the average DC delivered to the field winding, increasing field current and generator output voltage; firing later reduces it. This forms a continuous closed loop - sense output voltage, compare to reference, adjust thyristor firing angle, adjust field current, adjust output voltage - correcting for load changes and keeping output voltage within a tight regulated band.

Expanded technical depth: Sensing stage - three-phase output stepped down via a voltage transformer, rectified to a DC signal proportional to true RMS voltage, sensing all three phases to detect unbalance too. Reference and comparison - sensed DC compared against a stable reference (Zener diode or IC internal reference) via an op-amp error detector, giving an error signal indicating direction and magnitude of correction needed. Firing/control stage - phase-angle control of the thyristors, giving fast response and no moving parts, which is why thyristor control replaced older carbon-pile/rotating-amplifier regulators. Field/exciter stage - controlled thyristor output supplies the exciter winding (brushless: feeds rotating exciter armature, rectified via rotating diode bridge to main rotor field; static/slip-ring: feeds main field directly via brushes). Protective functions commonly built in: volts-per-hertz (V/Hz) protection reducing the voltage reference if frequency falls, preventing core saturation/overheating; overexcitation limiting capping maximum field current; under-voltage protection signalling an alarm/trip if the AVR cannot maintain voltage despite full field current.

answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, a static excitation system for a generator. (8)

(b) Explain TWO advantages of static excitation. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Unlike a brushless system (separate small rotating exciter generator with a rotating rectifier bridge), a static excitation system draws its excitation power directly from the main generator's own output terminals via a dedicated tapping or step-down transformer. This AC supply is fed through a controlled thyristor rectifier bridge, producing DC delivered to the main rotor field winding via slip rings and brushes. 'Static' refers to the excitation equipment itself (transformer, thyristor bridge) having no moving parts, unlike a rotating exciter armature - though slip rings and brushes remain necessary since excitation current still has to cross from stationary equipment to the rotating rotor.

(b) Two advantages: (1) Faster response - excitation power drawn directly from the generator's own terminals through solid-state thyristor control, with no separate rotating exciter's time-constant, responds very quickly to a voltage error signal, directly improving voltage-dip recovery speed. (2) Simpler and more reliable - no separate rotating exciter armature or rotating rectifier assembly to maintain, though slip rings/brushes still need periodic inspection and brush replacement.

answers.title: Shaft generator using a frequency converter
answers.question_as_set: Describe, with the aid of a circuit diagram, the operation of a shaft generator that uses a frequency converter. (10)
answers.answer_text:
A shaft generator is driven directly (or via a step-up gearbox) by the ship's main propulsion shaft, generating electrical power as a byproduct of the main engine's rotation. Because the main engine runs at a speed dictated by propulsion requirements, not electrical requirements, the shaft generator's raw output frequency would vary directly with shaft speed - unacceptable for direct connection to the ship's electrical system, which needs a stable, fixed frequency.

A frequency converter solves this: the shaft generator's variable-frequency AC output is first fully rectified to DC via a rectifier bridge, completely removing the frequency variation by converting to a DC link. This DC is fed to an inverter (thyristors or IGBTs), which electronically synthesises a new, stable-frequency AC output matching the ship's standard busbar frequency, regardless of actual shaft speed or the generator's raw input frequency. This rectifier-DC link-inverter arrangement allows a shaft generator, despite running at whatever speed propulsion demands, to supply stable, standard-frequency power directly onto the ship's main switchboard, in parallel with the diesel generators if required.

answers.title: Reverse power protection: mechanical vs electronic relay + phase sensitive detector circuit
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to reverse power protection for a.c. generators operating in parallel:

(a) explain why traditional reverse power relays, operating on mechanical principles, have been replaced by electronic digital microprocessor types; (2)

(b) describe, with the aid of a sketch, a generator reverse power protection circuit that uses an electronic phase sensitive detector. (8)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Traditional mechanical relays (induction spinning-disc mechanism reacting to reversed power flow via electromagnetic torque) have moving parts subject to wear and friction, and need periodic mechanical calibration. Electronic digital/microprocessor types offer faster and more accurate detection - important since reverse power can mechanically damage the prime mover quickly - precisely adjustable trip settings, self-diagnostic capability, no moving parts to wear or stick, and digital event logging.

(b) Reverse power occurs when a generator, instead of supplying power to the busbar, begins absorbing it - its prime mover no longer providing enough torque to overcome the electrical load (mechanical fault, fuel failure, governor mis-setting while paralleled), so the machine effectively starts 'motoring,' being driven by the other generator(s) on the bus.

The protection circuit takes two signals: a voltage reference from a VT across the generator terminals, and a current signal from a CT in the generator's output. The phase-sensitive detector continuously compares the phase relationship between these two signals. In normal operation (exporting power), current sits in a normal phase relationship relative to voltage. When the generator begins absorbing power instead, current effectively reverses relative to the voltage reference - the phase angle shifts by approximately 180 degrees, since power flow itself has reversed.

When the detector senses this reverse-power phase relationship, it feeds a time-delay circuit - deliberately included so a brief transient swing during normal load changes doesn't cause a nuisance trip. Only if the reverse condition persists beyond this set delay (typically several seconds) does the relay operate, tripping the generator breaker before the reversed power flow can mechanically damage the prime mover.

answers.title: Why reverse power protection is necessary for generators in parallel
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain why it is necessary to provide reverse power protection for a.c. generators operating in parallel. (2)

(b) Sketch a generator protecting circuit. (7)

(c) Explain how the operation of the reverse power trip is tested. (1)
answers.answer_text:
If a generator's prime mover loses the ability to supply sufficient driving torque - fuel failure, mechanical fault, governor problem, or operator error reducing fuel too far - the generator doesn't simply stop, because it remains electrically connected to the other generator(s) on the same busbar. Instead, it continues to be driven, but now by the electrical system rather than by its own prime mover: it runs effectively as a synchronous motor, drawing power from the bus to keep its own shaft turning.

This is hazardous for three reasons. First, the affected prime mover - being mechanically driven while receiving no fuel or steam - can suffer real damage: a diesel engine motoring without combustion can lose proper lubrication conditions and overheat certain components; a steam turbine motoring without steam flow can overheat its blading from windage losses. Second, the other generator(s) on the system are now carrying the extra burden of driving the motoring machine, reducing their remaining spare capacity. Third, with spare capacity reduced, any subsequent load change or emergency demand has far less margin before risking a complete blackout.

Reverse power protection exists specifically to detect this condition automatically and trip the affected generator's breaker before mechanical damage occurs or the situation compounds - precisely why it's a mandatory fitted protection wherever generators run in parallel.

answers.title: Protective devices fitted to a main A.C. generator (overcurrent, negative phase sequence, loss of field, undervoltage, reverse power)
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to the protective devices fitted to a main alternating current generator, explain EACH of the following:

(a) overcurrent and short circuit protection; (2)

(b) generator negative phase sequence; (2)

(c) loss of field (excitation); (2)

(d) undervoltage; (2)

(e) reverse power. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Overcurrent and short circuit protection: inverse-time overcurrent relays (or a generator breaker with adjustable overcurrent trip settings) monitor output current via CTs. If current exceeds a preset threshold for longer than a set time delay (allowing brief starting currents to pass), the relay trips the generator breaker.

(b) Generator negative phase sequence: detects an unbalanced condition across the three output phases - a 'negative sequence' current component arising from an unbalanced load, single-phasing fault on a connected motor, or asymmetric system fault. Negative sequence current sets up a magnetic field rotating opposite to the rotor's normal rotation, inducing double-frequency eddy currents in the rotor surface and causing rapid, severe localised overheating - a risk ordinary overcurrent protection wouldn't catch, since total current might not exceed a normal threshold while still being dangerously unbalanced.

(c) Loss of field (excitation): detects loss of DC field excitation (AVR/exciter fault, slip-ring/brush failure). Without excitation the generator can't maintain synchronism and draws reactive power from the busbar to sustain a residual field, destabilising the system.

(d) Undervoltage: trips or blocks closing if generator terminal voltage falls below a set threshold - sustained low voltage risks connected motors overheating, and guards against closing onto a bus under a fault condition already suppressing voltage.

(e) Reverse power: trips the generator if it begins absorbing power from the bus (motoring) rather than supplying it, protecting the prime mover from mechanical damage.

answers.title: High winding temperature alarm: immediate/subsequent actions + cooler tube leakage protection
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to main a.c. generators:

(a) state the immediate and subsequent actions to be taken in the event of a high windings temperature alarm being activated; (8)

(b) state the feature of the windings cooler tubes that prevent damage to the windings in the event of leakage. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Immediate action: reduce load on the affected generator as far as practicable - bringing another generator online in parallel to share load if not already running - to reduce heat being generated. Confirm cooling air or water flow is actually functioning (fans running, cooling water valves open, coolers not blocked). If temperature continues rising despite reduced load and confirmed cooling flow, prepare to remove the generator from service in a controlled manner - bring a standby unit online first, reduce the affected generator's load to zero, then open its breaker - rather than waiting for an automatic trip.

Subsequent action: once safely removed from service (or if temperature stabilises and it remains running), investigate the root cause - checking cooling air filters or water strainers for blockage, checking for excessive ambient temperature in the generator space, and checking for genuine electrical causes such as overload, unbalanced load/negative phase sequence, or a developing insulation fault. The generator shouldn't return to full service until the cause is identified and corrected.

(b) The windings cooler (an air-to-water heat exchanger cooling the generator's internal ventilating air) is arranged so the cooling water side operates at a lower pressure than the air side. If a cooler tube develops a leak, this pressure differential means water tends to leak outward into the air stream/drain rather than being drawn under pressure into the winding space - protecting the windings from water ingress and consequent electrical fault.

answers.title: Paralleling of A.C. generators: synchronisation requirements, KW/Kvar sharing, damage from incorrect sync / PMS features (two verified variants of part (d))
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to the paralleling of a.c. generators:

(a) outline the requirements for synchronisation; (3)

(b) explain how KW power is shared; (2)

(c) explain how Kvar power is shared; (1)

(d) state FOUR types of damage that may be caused when machines are incorrectly synchronised. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Requirements of synchronisation: before a generator can be safely closed onto a live busbar, four conditions must be matched between the incoming generator and the busbar: (1) Same voltage; (2) Same frequency; (3) Same phase sequence (R-Y-B order, checked at commissioning, doesn't change in normal operation); (4) Phase angle in coincidence - instantaneous voltage waveforms in phase at the moment the breaker closes. Checked using a synchroscope: a rotating-pointer instrument whose speed/direction shows fast/slow relative to the busbar, and whose position shows instantaneous phase difference. The breaker is closed when the pointer is at (or just approaching) 12 o'clock, rotating slowly in the fast direction - closing slightly before exact coincidence compensates for the breaker's own closing delay.

(b) How KW power is shared: controlled by adjusting the governor setting (speed droop) of each engine. Increasing fuel/steam admission to one prime mover increases that generator's share of total KW load without affecting frequency, since the other generator's governor compensates.

(c) How Kvar power is shared: controlled by adjusting each generator's field excitation (via its AVR). Increasing field current on one generator increases the reactive power it supplies without significantly affecting shared bus voltage.

(d) Variant 1 - damage from incorrect synchronising: closing a generator onto the busbar out of synchronism can cause: deformation of the alternator's stator end-windings from electromagnetic shock force; crack propagation in the coupling, shaft, or crankshaft from sudden torque reversal; twisting/shearing of the prime mover's flexible coupling; damage to circuit breaker contacts from very high fault-like current at closure; bearing damage from sudden mechanical shock loading; loosening of foundation bolts/mountings from transient vibration.

(d) Variant 2 - PMS features in unattended mode: automatic starting and stopping of standby generators based on load demand; automatic synchronising and load sharing when bringing a new generator online; automatic load shedding of non-essential consumers on approaching overload; preferential tripping sequences protecting essential services first; monitoring/alarm functions reporting generator status to the bridge/control room during unattended periods.
