answers.title: Load sensing electronic governor controller for an A.C. generator
answers.question_as_set: Describe, with the aid of a block diagram, the operation of a load sensing electronic governor controller for an a.c. generator. (10)
answers.answer_text:
A load-sensing electronic governor continuously monitors the generator's electrical output load (via CTs on the output, combined with voltage sensing to calculate actual KW) rather than relying solely on sensing a change in engine/shaft speed after the fact. Because electrical load changes at the busbar happen essentially instantaneously, sensing load directly - rather than waiting for the resulting speed droop to be detected mechanically - allows the governor to begin adjusting fuel/steam admission before a significant speed deviation has even had time to develop, giving a faster response than older speed-only governors.

Block diagram, described: Load sensing transducer (CTs/VTs on generator output, calculating actual KW) -> signal conditioning/comparator (comparing sensed load against the engine's current fuel setting) -> electronic control unit (computing required fuel rack/valve position to match the new load) -> actuator (electric or hydraulic actuator driving the fuel rack or steam governor valve) -> prime mover, with speed feedback (from a speed pickup on the shaft) closing an outer loop to fine-tune and correct for any remaining deviation, settling the engine precisely back to its set speed/frequency once the new load is matched.

This combination - fast-acting load anticipation plus a speed feedback trim loop - gives both quick initial response to a sudden load change and accurate final speed/frequency regulation.

answers.title: Automatic starting, load sharing and stopping of generators
answers.question_as_set: Describe, with the aid of a block diagram, how automatic starting, load sharing and stopping of generators in response to load changes is effected. (10)
answers.answer_text:
Automatic starting: the Power Management System (PMS) continuously monitors total electrical load against available generating capacity. As load approaches a preset percentage of the running generator's capacity, the PMS automatically starts a standby generator, brings it up to speed, and - once at rated speed and voltage - automatically synchronises it (checking voltage, frequency, phase sequence, phase angle coincidence) before closing its breaker onto the live busbar.

Load sharing: once paralleled, KW load is shared by the PMS adjusting each engine's governor setting; Kvar (reactive) load is shared by adjusting each generator's AVR/field excitation - both automatically balanced so each generator carries a proportionate share of total load relative to its rating.

Automatic stopping: as total load falls, the PMS monitors the load that would remain if a generator were removed. Once remaining generators could safely carry the total load, the PMS unloads the generator due to be stopped (transferring its share to the others via governor/AVR adjustment), opens its breaker once its load has fallen to near zero, and allows it to run unloaded briefly for cooling before shutting down - avoiding an abrupt disconnection of a generator still carrying significant load.

Block diagram, described: Load sensing (CTs/VTs on the busbar) -> PMS logic comparing load against running capacity and preset thresholds -> start/stop signal to standby generator's automatic starting sequence -> synchronising check unit -> breaker close/open signal -> governor and AVR control for load/reactive sharing among all paralleled units.

answers.title: Automatic Power Management System features + manual fallback on PMS failure
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to automatic Power Management Systems for the control of the operation of main switchboards and generators:

(a) list the features that the Power Management System controls in order to comply with the requirements for a vessel; (7)

(b) explain how the generators and switchboard would be controlled following a failure of the Power Management System. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Features the PMS controls: (1) Automatic starting of standby generators as load rises toward a preset percentage of running capacity. (2) Automatic synchronising and paralleling - bringing a starting generator up to speed and voltage, then closing its breaker onto the live busbar once synchronised. (3) Automatic load sharing - KW via governor adjustment, Kvar via AVR/excitation adjustment. (4) Automatic stopping of a generator once remaining load can be safely carried by fewer running units. (5) Load shedding/preferential tripping of non-essential consumers as load approaches or exceeds available capacity. (6) Blackout recovery - automatic restart and resynchronising sequence following a total loss of power. (7) Monitoring and alarm functions - continuously monitoring generator and switchboard parameters, reporting to the bridge or engine control room, specifically essential for UMS compliance.

(b) Following PMS failure: control reverts to fully manual operation - the duty engineer manually starts and stops generators based on observed load, manually operates the synchronising panel (checking the synchroscope, voltage, frequency) to parallel a generator, and manually adjusts governor and AVR settings to share load. Manual monitoring and manual shedding of non-essential consumers is required if approaching overload. Critically, continuous manned attendance in the engine room becomes necessary - the vessel cannot safely continue in unattended (UMS) mode without it.

answers.answer_text:
(a) The shore power cable connects via a dedicated shore connection box through an isolating switch/breaker, with the three phases wired to the ship's main switchboard or a dedicated shore-supply busbar section. A phase sequence indicator is connected across the incoming shore supply specifically to confirm phase rotation matches what the ship's system expects, before the shore supply is actually connected. This is a fundamentally different check from paralleling two generators: since the ship's own generators are normally shut down when taking shore power, there's no dynamic voltage/frequency/phase-angle synchronising process at all - the phase sequence check is a static, pre-connection safety check.

(b) Variant 1 - consequences of incorrect connection:
(i) Wrong phase sequence: any three-phase motor would run in the wrong direction - reversing any two of three phases reverses the rotating field direction - risking serious damage to pumps, fans, or other rotating machinery running backwards.
(ii) Higher voltage: connected equipment (motors, transformers, lighting) would be over-voltaged, risking insulation breakdown and overheating.
(iii) Higher frequency: motors and frequency-dependent equipment would run faster than intended, with cooling fan performance also tied to frequency - risking overheating or mechanical overspeed damage if equipment isn't rated for the resulting altered speed and airflow.

(b) Variant 2 - shutdown procedure prior to shore changeover, both scenarios covered since the actual installation type varies:

Scenario 1 - Paralleled changeover (make before break): confirm shore power is correctly matched (voltage, frequency, phase sequence). Synchronise the shore supply onto the busbar exactly as paralleling a second generator - matching voltage, frequency, phase sequence, phase angle via the synchroscope. Gradually transfer load from the ship's generator onto shore power by reducing its governor setting toward zero output. Once carrying negligible load, open its breaker, then allow it to run unloaded briefly for cooling before shutting down the prime mover completely.

Scenario 2 - Break before make: used where switchgear isn't rated for paralleling with an unsynchronised external source. Shed or stand by non-essential loads first. Open the ship's generator breaker, briefly interrupting supply. Confirm shore power is correctly matched before closing the shore supply breaker to re-energise the busbar. Allow the disconnected generator to run unloaded briefly for cooling before shutting down.

Common to both: follow the vessel's own SMS/company procedure for exact sequencing, since this varies by installation. The underlying principle either way: never leave the busbar without a confirmed, correctly-matched supply at any point, and never shut down a generator carrying significant load without first transferring that load elsewhere.

answers.title: A.C. switchboards: protective devices, breaker failure to open, stuck breaker actions
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to a.c switchboards:

(a) state, with reasons, the protective devices that are fitted; (5)

(b) state why a breaker may fail to open under prolonged low voltage conditions; (2)

(c) explain the actions to be taken should a main generator circuit breaker stay connected despite repeated efforts to trip it off the board. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Protective devices, with reasons: Overcurrent/short-circuit protection (breaker overcurrent trip or fuses) - protects cables and busbars from thermal/mechanical damage from fault or overload current. Undervoltage protection/release - trips or blocks closing if voltage falls too low, since low voltage risks motors overheating and prevents uncontrolled reclosure once voltage is restored. Reverse power protection (generator breakers) - trips if the generator absorbs power rather than supplying it, protecting the prime mover. Earth fault protection - detects and alarms/trips on a fault to earth. Preferential trip devices - disconnect non-essential loads in a pre-set sequence as the system approaches overload, protecting continuity of essential supply.

(b) Why a breaker may fail to open under prolonged low voltage: the breaker's trip coil/mechanism relies on a solenoid needing a minimum voltage/current to develop enough magnetic force to physically operate the tripping mechanism. Under prolonged low voltage, the trip coil may not receive sufficient current to generate enough force to release the latch, so the breaker can remain stuck closed despite a trip signal.

(c) Actions if a main generator breaker stays connected despite repeated tripping attempts: reduce the generator's load manually by adjusting the governor to cut fuel/steam admission, easing the immediate risk. If another generator is running in parallel, check the synchronising/load-sharing arrangement and manage load distribution manually. If the breaker genuinely cannot be opened electrically, prepare to shut down the affected generator's prime mover directly (fuel to zero) as a last resort. Isolate and investigate the breaker mechanically once safe, and report the fault for repair.

answers.title: Protection of electrical power circuits: discrimination, fuse types, preferential tripping
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to the protection of electrical power circuits:

(a) explain discrimination, describing how it is achieved. (5)

(b) state, with reasons, the type of fuses used for protection; (3)

(c) explain preferential tripping. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Discrimination (selectivity): the principle that when a fault occurs anywhere in a distribution system, only the protective device closest to the fault should operate, isolating just the affected section while everything else remains in service. Achieved by grading the time delay and/or current setting of devices in series, so devices nearer the load operate faster (shorter delay, lower threshold) than devices further upstream. A fault on a small branch circuit trips its local device quickly; if that device fails, the next device upstream (deliberately set with a longer delay) operates as backup.

(b) HRC (High Rupturing Capacity) fuses are typically used for power circuit protection, since they can safely interrupt very high fault currents without violent rupture or dangerous arcing, and have well-defined, repeatable time/current characteristics important for reliable discrimination.

(c) Preferential tripping: an automatic, pre-arranged sequential load-shedding scheme that disconnects non-essential consumers in priority order as the system approaches overload capacity - deliberately sacrificing lower-priority loads to protect continuity of essential services rather than risk a complete blackout.

occurrences.examiner_feedback_text: A specific, genuine confusion flagged in July 2019: some candidates described discrimination AS preferential tripping. They are genuinely different mechanisms - discrimination governs which protective device responds to an actual fault, isolating only the faulted section; preferential tripping deliberately sheds non-essential load as the system nears capacity, with no fault necessarily present at all.

answers.title: Protection of electrical equipment in a distribution system + causes of electrical fires
answers.question_as_set:
(a) With reference to the protection of electrical equipment in a distribution system:

(i) state the aims of the protective devices; (3)

(ii) list the parameters that are monitored and acted upon by the protective devices. (4)

(b) State, with reasons, THREE causes of electrical fires. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a)(i) Aims: detect an abnormal condition (overcurrent, short circuit, earth fault, overload) as quickly as possible, isolate only the affected part of the circuit before damage or fire can result, protect personnel from electric shock, and maintain continuity of supply to unaffected circuits.

(a)(ii) Parameters monitored: current (overcurrent/short-circuit detection), voltage (over/undervoltage), earth leakage current (earth fault detection), temperature (thermal overload, via a thermal element or embedded sensor), and time (the deliberate time-delay characteristic used to achieve discrimination).

(b) Three causes of electrical fires, with reasons: (1) Overloaded circuits - conductors carrying current beyond rated capacity generate excess heat that can ignite surrounding insulation. (2) Poor or loose connections - a loose terminal presents higher contact resistance, generating localised heating (and sometimes arcing) that can ignite insulation or debris. (3) Damaged or degraded insulation - aged, mechanically damaged, or oil-contaminated insulation can break down, allowing a short circuit or earth fault, with associated arcing and heat presenting a direct fire risk.

answers.title: Overcurrent protection methods + inverse time characteristic
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to overcurrent protection for electrical circuits:

(a) explain THREE methods of protection, stating where EACH may be used; (6)

(b) explain, with the aid of a diagram, the meaning of the term inverse current time characteristic. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Three methods: (1) Fuses (typically HRC) - used on smaller, lower-cost circuits and as backup protection, replaced after operating. (2) MCB/MCCB - used on distribution circuits where resetting/reclosing after a transient fault without needing a replacement part is valuable. (3) Protective relays operating a circuit breaker - used on larger power circuits and generator/switchboard protection, where adjustable, selective tripping characteristics beyond a simple fuse or MCB are needed.

(b) Inverse current time characteristic: a protective device that operates faster the higher the fault current is, taking progressively longer to trip as current gets closer to its minimum pickup threshold. Shown as a graph of operating time (often logarithmic) against current (as a multiple of rated/pickup current): the curve falls steeply at first then flattens, so a small overload trips slowly (avoiding nuisance trips) while a severe fault trips almost instantly. This characteristic is specifically what allows discrimination between devices in series: a downstream device's curve is set to operate faster than the upstream device's curve for the same fault current.

answers.title: Factors influencing short-circuit severity + role of reactance
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to electrical short circuits:

(a) state, with reasons, THREE factors that will influence the severity of a short circuit; (6)

(b) explain the role of reactance when selecting protective devices. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Three factors: (1) Distance from the source (generator/transformer) - a fault closer to the source sees less cumulative circuit impedance, so more current can flow, making it more severe than an equivalent fault further downstream. (2) System fault level (source impedance/generating capacity connected) - more generating capacity in parallel, or lower source impedance, delivers higher fault current for the same fault location. (3) Type of fault - a three-phase bolted fault is generally most severe (highest current), while a single-phase-to-earth fault on an insulated neutral system produces comparatively limited current.

(b) Reactance (particularly source and cabling inductive reactance) is a major component of total circuit impedance and directly limits maximum fault current at any given point. Protective devices must be selected with a fault-current rating (breaking capacity) at least equal to the maximum prospective fault current calculable at their installation point - calculated using total impedance, including reactance, between source and that point. A device with insufficient breaking capacity risks catastrophic failure rather than safely interrupting the fault.

answers.title: Electrical system protective devices: purpose of each (overcurrent, short circuit, no-volt, reverse power, preferential tripping)
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to electrical system protective devices, explain the purpose of EACH of the following:

(a) overcurrent protection; (2)

(b) short circuit protection; (2)

(c) no-volt protection; (2)

(d) reverse power protection; (2)

(e) preferential tripping. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Overcurrent protection: protects conductors, cables and equipment from damage due to current in excess of rated capacity for a sustained period, disconnecting before resulting heat damages insulation or creates fire risk. Time-delayed, allowing brief harmless excursions.

(b) Short circuit protection: protects against a very high-magnitude fault current (direct phase-to-phase or phase-to-earth bolted fault), capable of severe near-instantaneous damage if not cleared immediately. Fast/instantaneous characteristic, little to no intentional delay.

(c) No-volt protection: prevents a machine or circuit from automatically restarting once voltage is restored after an interruption, without deliberate manual action - protecting personnel working on stopped equipment from an unexpected restart, and preventing an uncontrolled surge of multiple motors restarting simultaneously.

(d) Reverse power protection: trips the generator breaker if the machine begins absorbing power (motoring) rather than supplying it, protecting the prime mover.

(e) Preferential tripping: disconnects non-essential loads in a pre-arranged priority sequence as the system approaches overload, protecting continuity of essential supply.

answers.title: Emergency generator power supply and distribution system sketch + regulations
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a circuit diagram of an emergency generator power supply and distribution system, indicating the essential services provided at 440 volts ac, 220 volts ac and 24 volts dc. (6)

(b) State the regulations pertaining to the emergency generator. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Emergency generator -> emergency switchboard -> distribution at 440V AC directly to larger essential loads (emergency fire pump, steering gear if required, emergency lighting distribution boards) -> a step-down transformer to 220V AC for smaller essential services (lighting circuits, communication equipment, some control systems) -> a transformer/rectifier arrangement providing 24V DC for battery charging and DC essential services (navigation lights, radio/GMDSS equipment, emergency alarm/communication systems) - typically including the emergency battery itself, kept on float charge and available even if the emergency generator hasn't started.

(b) SOLAS requires the emergency source of electrical power to automatically start and be capable of supplying essential services within 45 seconds of a main power failure, with sufficient capacity for a minimum specified duration (commonly 18 or 36 hours depending on vessel type). The emergency generator and switchboard must be located above the bulkhead deck, outside machinery spaces, in a readily accessible position, separated from the main machinery space by fire-resistant boundaries.

answers.title: Emergency generator starting, connection to busbars, and load testing
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a circuit diagram showing how the emergency generator is started, connected to the emergency busbars and how the main busbars are disconnected in the event of a blackout. (6)

(b) Explain how an emergency generator is load tested to ensure that it is capable of satisfactorily delivering the full rated power. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a) On loss of main power, a voltage-sensing relay on the main busbar detects the failure and signals the emergency generator's automatic starting sequence (compressed-air or battery-electric start) to begin. Once the emergency generator reaches rated speed and voltage, an automatic changeover switch (interlocked so main and emergency supplies can never be connected together simultaneously) disconnects the emergency busbar from the dead main busbar connection and connects it instead to the emergency generator's output. The sketch needs to show: the voltage-sensing/starting-initiation relay, the starting arrangement, the emergency generator, and specifically the changeover switch mechanism between main and emergency supply - not the downstream distribution to individual services, which is a different question.

(b) Testing: run the emergency generator on load (using a dummy/test load bank, or transferring actual non-essential ship's load onto it) to confirm it can deliver full rated output without excessive voltage or frequency droop, checking automatic starting and changeover both function within the required time, run for a specified minimum duration to properly prove capability rather than just confirming the machine starts unloaded.

answers.title: Essential electrical services operable under fire conditions + cable bulkhead passage
answers.question_as_set:
(a) State FIVE essential electrical services that are able to be operable under fire conditions. (5)

(b) Explain how electric cables for the essential services in part (a) pass through bulkheads whilst maintaining gas tight and water tight integrity. (3)

(c) State the requirements for the cables which supply electrically driven emergency fire pumps.(2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Emergency lighting, the emergency fire pump, fire detection and alarm systems, public address/general alarm systems, and steering gear (where electrically powered) - all needed to fight the fire, evacuate safely, and maintain vessel control while it's happening.

(b) Cables pass through purpose-built cable transits - typically a steel frame fitted into the bulkhead penetration, packed with a fire-resistant, water- and gas-tight sealing compound (or pre-formed sealing modules) around each individual cable, maintaining the structural fire rating and watertight integrity at the penetration point. Cable glands provide additional mechanical support and sealing where cables enter equipment or junction boxes.

(c) Cables must be fire-resistant type (rated to continue functioning for a specified period even when directly exposed to fire, not merely fire-retardant), and routed away from areas most likely to be affected by a fire - specifically avoiding the main machinery space, where a fire is statistically most likely to originate and where the pump is most needed to remain functional.

answers.title: UPS (a.c. input) operation + essential services supported
answers.question_as_set:
During a complete loss of electrical power, essential vital services can be maintained by means of an Uninterruptable Power Supply (UPS).

(a) Describe, with the aid of a block diagram, the operation of an a.c. input UPS arrangement. (7)

(b) List SIX essential services that the UPS or emergency batteries may support. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a) The AC mains supply is continuously rectified to DC, which simultaneously trickle-charges a standby battery bank and feeds a DC bus. This DC is continuously fed to an inverter, which converts it back to a stable AC output supplying connected essential loads - under normal conditions, power actually flows AC mains -> rectifier -> DC bus (battery on float charge) -> inverter -> AC output, rather than the load being connected directly to mains. If AC mains fails, the rectifier's DC output disappears, but the battery bank - already on the same DC bus - seamlessly continues supplying the inverter, which continues producing AC output with no interruption at all. This is what makes it genuinely 'uninterruptable,' unlike a standby generator which takes time to start - the battery bridges power until mains is restored or a backup generator takes over.

(b) Emergency lighting, navigation lights, radio/GMDSS communication equipment, fire detection and alarm systems, steering gear control circuits, and critical propulsion monitoring/alarm systems.

answers.title: Synchronous motor and induction motor: construction and operation
answers.question_as_set:
Describe the construction and operation of EACH of the following:

(a) synchronous motor; (5)

(b) induction motor. (5)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Synchronous motor: constructionally similar to an alternator run in reverse - a wound rotor (DC field excitation via slip rings, or increasingly a brushless static/rotating exciter) sits inside a three-phase stator winding. When the stator is energised, it produces a rotating magnetic field; the DC-excited rotor's own magnetic poles lock onto and follow this field, causing the rotor to turn at exactly synchronous speed (determined purely by supply frequency and pole count) regardless of load. A synchronous motor cannot start from standstill on its own, so typically needs an auxiliary starting method - a damper/amortisseur winding acting like a squirrel cage to start it as an induction motor before the DC field is applied, or a separate starting motor.

(b) Induction motor: the stator winding, energised from the three-phase supply, produces a rotating magnetic field. The rotor - typically a squirrel cage design (solid conducting bars short-circuited at each end by end rings, no external electrical connection) - has this rotating field sweep across it, inducing currents in the rotor bars purely by electromagnetic induction. These induced currents create their own magnetic field, which interacts with the stator's rotating field to produce torque, dragging the rotor around. The rotor must always turn slightly slower than the rotating field (slip), which sustains the induced current - an induction motor never reaches true synchronous speed under load, distinguishing it from the synchronous motor above.

answers.title: Induction motor cross section + construction
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Sketch a cross section through an a.c. induction motor. (5)

(b) Describe the construction of the a.c induction motor sketched in part (a). (5)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Cross section showing the stator (outer laminated core with windings) surrounding the rotor, separated by a small air gap, mounted on a shaft supported by bearings in end shields bolted to the frame - either a side elevation (along the shaft axis) or a front/radial cross-section is acceptable.

(b) The stator consists of a laminated silicon-steel core - thin, insulated laminations reducing eddy current losses - housed in an outer cast iron or steel frame, with slots on its inner circumference holding the three-phase stator winding. The rotor (squirrel cage) sits inside, separated by the air gap, mounted on a shaft supported by bearings in end shields bolted to each end of the frame. Cooling is typically provided by a shaft-mounted fan drawing air through ventilation ducts in the frame and over the windings, with terminal boxes on the frame providing the connection point for supply cables.

answers.title: Squirrel cage rotor constructional details + double cage rotors
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, the constructional details of a squirrel cage rotor as fitted in an induction motor. (7)

(b) Explain why some rotors have a double cage. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a) The rotor core is built up from thin, insulated laminated steel sheets stacked onto the rotor shaft. Running axially through slots around the circumference are solid conducting bars - typically copper or aluminium, in smaller motors often die-cast aluminium bars and end rings formed in a single casting operation with integral cooling fins. These bars are short-circuited together at each end by continuous conducting end rings, forming a closed conducting cage - hence 'squirrel cage.' There is no external electrical connection to the rotor at all - no slip rings, no brushes - since current is induced directly into the bars by the stator's rotating magnetic field, with the end rings providing the necessary circuit path.

(b) A double-cage rotor has two separate conductor bars per slot: an outer cage with higher resistance near the rotor surface, and an inner cage with lower resistance deeper in the core. At starting (high slip, high induced frequency), current flows predominantly through the outer high-resistance cage due to a skin/reactance effect, giving high starting torque. As the motor accelerates and slip falls, current transfers progressively to the inner low-resistance cage, giving good running efficiency at normal speed - both strong starting torque and efficient running performance, a compromise a simple single-cage design can't achieve as well.

answers.title: Improving starting torque: wound rotor + double cage
answers.question_as_set:
Describe how the starting torque of electric induction motors may be improved by using EACH of the following:

(a) wound rotor; (5)

(b) double cage. (5)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Wound rotor (slip-ring) motor: instead of a squirrel cage, the rotor carries its own three-phase winding, brought out via slip rings and brushes to external variable resistors. At starting, full external resistance is inserted in series with the rotor circuit - increasing rotor circuit resistance shifts the point of maximum torque toward higher slip, closer to standstill conditions, giving a high starting torque with a correspondingly lower starting current than an equivalent squirrel cage motor started direct-on-line. As the motor accelerates, this external resistance is progressively cut out in steps (via a rotor starter/controller), shifting maximum torque back toward normal running slip, until at zero added resistance the motor runs as a standard induction motor with rotor windings short-circuited via the slip rings.

(b) Double cage: as above - the outer, higher-resistance cage dominates at starting, giving strong starting torque, but achieved entirely passively through the rotor's own construction, with no external resistors, slip rings, or controller needed at all.

answers.title: Star-delta starters: reduced voltage starting + sequence of operation
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to star delta starters used for three phase induction motors:

(a) explain in detail why this type of starter is employed; (4)

(b) explain, with the aid of a circuit diagram, the sequence of operation of a star delta starter. (6)
answers.answer_text:
(a) To reduce the very high starting current a large induction motor would otherwise draw if started direct-on-line (typically 5-7x full-load running current) - this large inrush causes excessive voltage dip on the ship's electrical system and unnecessary thermal/mechanical stress on the motor and supply cables.

(b) During the star starting phase, the motor's stator windings (normally connected in delta for running) are instead temporarily connected in star, applying roughly 58% (1/root-3) of normal line voltage across each winding. Since starting current is proportional to applied voltage, and the star connection itself further changes the current relationship, the combined effect reduces line starting current to roughly one-third of direct-on-line delta starting. Since torque is proportional to voltage squared, starting torque is also reduced to roughly one-third - meaning star-delta starting is only suitable for loads that don't need high starting torque, such as pumps or fans starting unloaded or lightly loaded.

(c) At starting, a star contactor connects the three stator winding ends together at a common star point, while a main/line contactor connects the winding starts to the three-phase supply - giving the reduced-voltage star connection. After a preset time delay, allowing the motor to accelerate to around 80-85% of full speed, the star contactor opens, and a delta contactor closes shortly after, reconnecting the same three windings in delta configuration directly across full line voltage. An electrical interlock between star and delta contactors ensures they can never close simultaneously, since that would create a direct short circuit across two winding ends.

answers.title: Direct-on-line starting consequences + electronic soft starting system
answers.question_as_set:
(a) State the consequences of using direct on line starters for comparatively large sized a.c. induction motors. (2)

(b) Describe, with the aid of a sketch, an electronic soft starting system that may be used for large sized a.c. induction motors. (8)
answers.answer_text:
(a) A very high starting current (5-7x full-load running current) causes a significant voltage dip on the ship's electrical system, affecting other connected equipment. The sudden, uncontrolled application of near-full torque at starting also imposes high mechanical shock and stress on the motor shaft, coupling, and driven load.

(b) An electronic soft starter uses a back-to-back thyristor pair (or triac) in each of the three supply lines, controlling the RMS voltage applied to the motor by varying thyristor firing angle - the same phase-angle control principle as the AVR, applied to the motor's supply rather than a generator's field. At the start, the firing angle is set so only a small fraction of each half-cycle passes, giving a low initial voltage and correspondingly low starting current and torque. Over a set ramp-up period (typically several seconds), the firing angle is progressively advanced, smoothly increasing applied voltage, current and torque in a controlled ramp. Once close to full running speed, the thyristors are fully gated on; a bypass contactor then typically closes across the thyristors to carry running current directly, avoiding continuous heat dissipation in the thyristors and improving reliability. The same arrangement can provide a controlled ramp-down (soft stop), useful for loads like pumps where sudden stopping risks damaging pressure transients.

answers.title: Synchro-converter for variable speed control of A.C. motors
answers.question_as_set: Describe, with the aid of a circuit diagram, a synchro-converter for the variable speed control of a.c. motors. (10)
answers.answer_text: A synchro-converter provides variable speed control for AC motors by allowing the motor's supply frequency itself to be varied, since a motor's synchronous speed is directly proportional to supply frequency. The ship's fixed-frequency AC supply is first rectified to DC via a rectifier bridge - the same principle as the shaft generator frequency converter, but running in the opposite direction: fixed-frequency AC in, DC link, variable-frequency AC out. This DC link feeds an inverter, whose switching devices (thyristors or IGBTs) synthesise an AC output at whatever frequency - and corresponding voltage, maintaining a constant volts-per-hertz ratio to preserve motor flux and torque capability - is needed for the desired speed. Varying the inverter's switching frequency directly and smoothly varies the motor's running speed across a wide range, without needing to physically change the motor's pole configuration - unlike simpler methods such as pole-changing motors, which only offer a few fixed speed steps.

answers.title: Overload relay types: thermal, magnetic, electronic
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to overload protection for electric motors, describe the principle of operation of EACH of the following types of overload relay:

(a) thermal; (3)

(b) magnetic; (3)

(c) electronic. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Thermal overload relay: uses a bimetallic strip - two dissimilar metals bonded together with different thermal expansion rates - heated either directly by motor current or via a heater element carrying a scaled-down proportion of it. As current rises above rated value, the strip heats and bends due to differential expansion; once bent sufficiently, it operates a trip mechanism, opening the contactor coil circuit. This gives an inherently time-delayed response roughly mimicking the motor's own thermal heating behaviour.

(b) Magnetic overload relay: uses a solenoid coil carrying motor current (directly or via a CT), whose magnetic pull on a plunger increases with current. Above a preset threshold, the magnetic force pulls the plunger through its full travel, operating a trip contact - often combined with a dashpot to give a time-current characteristic rather than a purely instantaneous trip.

(c) Electronic overload relay: uses current transformers to sense actual motor current, feeding a microprocessor-based circuit that calculates a thermal model of the motor's heating from sensed current, elapsed time, and a pre-programmed thermal time constant - tripping when this calculated model indicates the motor has reached its thermal limit. Offers more precise, adjustable settings and additional protection functions (phase loss, phase imbalance, stall, ground fault) built into one unit.

answers.answer_text:
(a) HRC (High Rupturing Capacity) fuses, chosen for their ability to safely interrupt high fault currents without violent rupture, with well-defined characteristics suited to motor circuit protection.

(b) If a running motor loses one of its three supply phases, it continues running on the remaining two phases but shows clear symptoms: increased noise, increased vibration, and a noticeable reduction in speed, since available torque drops significantly on two phases. If the motor is stopped in this condition, it will not be able to restart, since starting torque on two phases from standstill is generally insufficient.

(c) Thermistors (typically PTC type) are solid-state temperature sensors embedded directly within the motor's stator windings, at the point of expected maximum heating. As winding temperature rises, the thermistor's electrical resistance changes sharply once a threshold temperature is reached; a monitoring relay circuit detects this resistance change and trips the motor's contactor before winding insulation is damaged. Because it sits directly in the windings, it responds to actual winding temperature from any cause, not just current overload.

(d) Thermal (bimetallic) relay and magnetic (or electronic) relay.

answers.title: Insulated/earthed HV systems: tanker regulations + earth leakage detection methods
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to insulated and earthed electrical systems operating at High Voltage:

(a) state the regulations pertaining to tankers; (4)

(b) describe, with the aid of a sketch, a method to detect earth leakage in EACH of the following systems:

(i) earthed; (3)

(ii) insulated. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a) On tankers, HV electrical equipment located in or near hazardous cargo/pump room zones must be of an appropriately certified explosion-protected type - intrinsically safe, flameproof, increased safety, or pressurised - since HV arcing presents a significantly elevated ignition risk in a potentially explosive atmosphere. HV switchgear and cabling must be routed and segregated away from hazardous zones wherever practicable, and where HV equipment must be sited in or near such areas, additional measures (physical segregation, gas-detection interlocks, positive pressurisation of enclosures) are specifically required.

(b)(i) Earthed system: since the neutral is earthed via an NER, a genuine current flows to earth during a fault. Detection uses a current transformer around the neutral-to-earth connection (or a core-balance CT arrangement), feeding a relay that operates once current above a preset threshold is detected.

(b)(ii) Insulated system: since there's no deliberate earth connection, only a small capacitive leakage current results. Detection uses the instrument-type method - equal high-value resistors from each phase to a common point, feeding a sensitive milliammeter - scaled and insulated appropriately for the higher HV voltage level.

answers.title: Testing High Voltage equipment: earthing down, test voltage, procedure, IR temperature measurement
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to testing High Voltage equipment:

(a) explain why earthing down is considered essential; (2)

(b) state the operating voltage for an insulation resistance tester (meggar) suitable for 6.6 KV equipment; (1)

(c) describe how an insulation resistance test is carried out on High Voltage equipment, making reference to personnel safety; (5)

(d) explain why infra red temperature measurement is used on High Voltage equipment. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) 'Earthing down' means physically connecting HV conductors and equipment to earth via a dedicated earthing device or switch before personnel work on or test it. Even after isolating the supply and proving dead, HV equipment can retain a dangerous stored charge from its own capacitance, or could become accidentally re-energised from an unexpected back-feed. Earthing down provides a continuously visible, physically connected discharge path, guaranteeing the equipment cannot become live while work is in progress.

(b) A considerably higher test voltage than standard LV 500V - commonly around 5,000V DC for equipment of this class.

(c) Obtain a permit to work and isolate the equipment at every possible supply point, locking off each one. Prove dead using an approved high-voltage live-line tester rated specifically for the voltage involved. Apply temporary earthing-down connections to discharge any stored capacitive charge before work begins. Remove these earths specifically and only for the duration of the actual IR test itself, following a carefully controlled sequence. Connect the HV insulation tester and apply the appropriate test voltage, taking readings as required. On completion, safely discharge the equipment - typically using a discharge rod or earthing stick - then re-apply earthing-down connections until work is fully complete. Throughout, appropriate HV-rated PPE should be worn, with a second person present.

(d) It allows checking for abnormal heating - a developing loose connection, an overloaded joint, degrading insulation - entirely without touching or approaching the live HV equipment directly.

answers.title: Protection of HV A.C. motors: fuses/single phasing + RTD/thermistor temperature sensors
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to the protection of High Voltage electric a.c. motors:

(a) state the type of fuses that are fitted and how they prevent single phasing; (3)

(b) describe the operation of EACH of the following direct temperature sensors:

(i) resistance temperature device; (3)

(ii) thermistor. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a) HV motors typically use HRC fuses combined with a striker-pin (tripping pin) mechanism. When any one fuse operates, its striker pin mechanically ejects and operates a trip linkage on the associated contactor or breaker - disconnecting all three phases together, not just the phase whose fuse blew. An ordinary HRC fuse alone only protects and interrupts its own single phase - the striker-pin-to-trip-linkage arrangement, tying all three phases' disconnection together, is what genuinely prevents single phasing.

(b)(i) RTD: a precision resistance element (typically platinum, Pt100) whose resistance increases in a precisely known relationship with temperature. Embedded in the winding, a monitoring circuit continuously measures this resistance and converts it to an accurate, continuously-variable temperature reading, able to drive both an alarm and a trip at different thresholds.

(b)(ii) Thermistor: a semiconductor sensor embedded in the winding whose resistance changes sharply once a threshold temperature is reached, giving a simpler go/no-go protection signal rather than a continuously variable reading.

answers.title: Power factor, why low PF is detrimental, synchronous motor correction with phasor diagrams
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain the term power factor. (2)

(b) Explain why it is detrimental to have a low power factor. (2)

(c) Explain, with the aid of phasor diagrams, how a synchronous motor may be used to assist in power factor correction. (6)
answers.answer_text:
(a) The ratio of real power (kW, doing useful work) to apparent power (kVA, the total the supply system must actually deliver) - mathematically, PF = cos(phi), where phi is the phase angle between voltage and current. Unity power factor means all delivered power is useful; a power factor below 1 means part of the supplied current is reactive, sustaining magnetic fields in inductive loads like motors and transformers, and this reactive current still has to be generated and carried even though it performs no useful work.

(b) For a given real (kW) demand, a lower power factor means a higher apparent power - and therefore higher current - must flow through generators, cables, and switchgear to deliver that same useful power. Generators must be oversized in kVA relative to useful kW; cables and switchgear must carry the higher current, requiring larger conductors and increasing I-squared-R losses; voltage regulation is generally poorer, since more of the source's capacity is consumed by reactive current.

(c) A synchronous motor's field excitation can be deliberately over-excited beyond what's needed to maintain synchronism. When over-excited, the motor draws a leading current from the supply, rather than the lagging current a normal induction motor draws - effectively behaving as a source of leading reactive power. In a phasor diagram, a typical lagging load's current phasor sits at angle phi behind the voltage phasor, with a large reactive component. Adding an over-excited synchronous motor's leading current phasor to the system partially cancels that lagging reactive component when summed vectorially - the resulting overall system current phasor ends up at a smaller angle relative to voltage, meaning an improved, closer-to-unity system power factor.

answers.title: Hazardous area equipment types (intrinsically safe, flameproof, increased safety) + electrical tests
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain the meaning of EACH of the following types of electrical safety equipment:

(i) intrinsically safe; (2)

(ii) flameproof; (2)

(iii) increased safety. (2)

(b) State the electrical tests for equipment in hazardous areas, describing the safety precautions. (4)
answers.answer_text:
(a)(i) Intrinsically safe: equipment designed so the electrical energy available in the circuit is deliberately limited - via current-limiting resistors, safety barriers, and low-voltage/low-power design - to a level too low to ever produce an ignition-capable spark or sufficient heating, even under fault conditions.

(a)(ii) Flameproof (Exd): equipment in a robust enclosure designed so that if an internal explosion occurs, the enclosure contains it and cools the escaping gases sufficiently, through carefully machined flame-path joints, that the surrounding explosive atmosphere isn't ignited.

(a)(iii) Increased safety (Exe): equipment built with extra design margins specifically to eliminate the possibility of sparks, arcs, or excessive surface temperatures arising in normal operation - generous margins in insulation, clearances, and creepage distances, typically with no normally-arcing components inside.

(b) Insulation resistance testing and continuity testing of earth bonding are typically carried out, but not with the equipment live in the hazardous area unless the space is confirmed gas-free and covered by an electrical work permit specific to that area. A gas detector must confirm the atmosphere is free of explosive concentration before any spark-capable testing, and for flameproof equipment specifically, enclosures must be inspected for damage to the machined flame-path joints.

answers.title: Hazardous area equipment types (incl. pressurised enclosure) + pump room lighting
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Explain the meaning of EACH of the following types of electrical equipment:

(i) intrinsically safe; (2)

(ii) flameproof; (2)

(iii) increased safety; (2)

(iv) pressurised enclosure. (2)

(b) State TWO types of lighting equipment that may be installed in the pump room areas of a crude petroleum carrier. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a)(i)-(iii): as in the electrical-tests variant above.

(a)(iv) Pressurised enclosure (Exp): equipment housed in an enclosure continuously purged and maintained at a pressure slightly above the surrounding atmosphere, using clean air or inert gas, specifically to prevent surrounding explosive gas from entering at all. Since the positive internal pressure reliably excludes the external atmosphere, normally-arcing components (switchgear, contactors) can safely be housed inside - typically fitted with a pressure-loss alarm/trip to de-energise the equipment if the purge is lost.

(b) Bulkhead-mounted fittings viewed through a fixed, sealed glass port from an adjacent non-hazardous space - the light fitting itself sits entirely outside the hazardous pump room, shining through a gas-tight window. Alternatively, flameproof (Exd) or intrinsically safe fittings specifically certified for direct installation within the hazardous pump room itself, used where bulkhead-through-glass lighting can't achieve the coverage needed.

answers.title: Lithium-ion batteries: adoption, advantages/disadvantages, cell drift, thermal runaway
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to lithium-ion batteries:

(a) explain why this type of battery has been adopted for shipboard use; (4)

(b) state ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of lithium-ion batteries; (2)

(c) define EACH of the following terms:

(i) cell drift; (2)

(ii) thermal runaway. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Lithium-ion batteries offer significantly higher energy density than lead-acid or nickel-cadmium batteries - more stored energy per unit weight/volume - which matters directly for battery-hybrid and fully electric propulsion where weight and space are at a premium. They support much faster charge/discharge rates and more charge cycles before degrading, and their use in hybrid propulsion directly supports improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions, since batteries can be used to load-level engine operation and enable periods of battery-only operation.

(b) Advantage: significantly higher energy density than lead-acid. Disadvantage: genuine risk of thermal runaway if damaged, overcharged, or internally faulted, requiring more sophisticated battery management and fire-suppression arrangements.

(c)(i) Cell drift: in a series-connected battery pack, individual cells can gradually diverge in state of charge or internal characteristics over repeated cycles, even though the whole pack is charged/discharged together - requiring active cell-balancing as part of the battery management system.

(c)(ii) Thermal runaway: a self-sustaining, escalating chemical reaction within a cell - triggered by internal short-circuit, physical damage, overcharging, or excessive heat - where the cell's own internal heating accelerates the reaction further, in an uncontrolled positive-feedback cycle, potentially proceeding to cell rupture, fire, and propagation to adjacent cells.

answers.title: Alkaline (nickel-cadmium) battery cell: construction, charge/discharge, overcharge effects
answers.question_as_set:
(a) With reference to an alkaline battery cell:

(i) describe a typical cell, stating the materials used; (4)

(ii) describe the process that takes place during discharge and charge; (2)

(iii) state the effects of overcharge. (2)

(b) State the advantages of an alkaline cell compared with a lead acid cell. (2)
answers.answer_text:
(a)(i) A nickel-cadmium alkaline cell typically uses a positive electrode of nickel hydroxide/nickel oxyhydroxide, a negative electrode of cadmium, and an electrolyte of potassium hydroxide solution - an alkaline electrolyte, distinguishing this cell type from the sulphuric acid electrolyte of a lead-acid battery.

(a)(ii) During discharge, cadmium at the negative plate oxidises while nickel oxyhydroxide at the positive plate is reduced, both reactions consuming/producing hydroxide ions that remain within the electrolyte rather than changing its concentration significantly. On charge, an externally applied current drives these reactions in reverse.

(a)(iii) Sustained overcharge causes excess energy to be dissipated as gassing - decomposition of water in the electrolyte into hydrogen and oxygen gas - requiring adequate ventilation, and can lead to increased water loss requiring periodic topping up.

(b) Alkaline cells are considerably more tolerant of overcharge and deep discharge without permanent damage, have a longer overall service life, and can survive extended periods in a discharged state without the sulphation damage that would ruin a lead-acid cell - well suited to emergency/standby applications where a battery may sit unused for long periods.

answers.title: Battery systems for emergency purposes: personnel safety, storage, maintenance precautions + rate of charge
answers.question_as_set:
(a) With reference to battery systems for emergency purposes, explain the precautions that must be taken with regard to personnel safety, storage and maintenance. (7)

(b) Explain how batteries are kept at the correct rate of charge. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Personnel safety: appropriate PPE (acid/alkali-resistant gloves, eye protection), and awareness that batteries produce explosive hydrogen gas during charging - no naked flames, smoking, or spark-producing activity near batteries, particularly during and just after charging.

Storage: batteries must be kept in a dedicated, well-ventilated space specifically to disperse hydrogen gas before it can accumulate to an explosive concentration; lighting fixtures within the space must themselves be explosion-proof/non-sparking; batteries must be securely mounted or racked to prevent movement or toppling in a seaway.

Maintenance: regular checks of electrolyte level (topping up with distilled water where required), inspecting for terminal corrosion, periodic specific gravity or voltage checks to confirm state of charge and condition, confirming security of mounting and wiring.

(b) Batteries are typically maintained on continuous 'float' charge from a dedicated charger, supplying a small trickle current sufficient to offset natural self-discharge without overcharging. The charger's output is voltage-regulated, similar in principle to an AVR, adjusting automatically as needed, with a periodic higher-rate 'equalising' or 'boost' charge sometimes applied to correct any imbalance between individual cells.

answers.title: Large electrical transformers on board ships: use, efficiency, regulations, protection, maintenance
answers.question_as_set:
With reference to large electrical transformers on board ships:

(a) state where these transformers may be used; (1)

(b) state a typical efficiency range for a transformer; (1)

(c) state the regulations pertaining to transformers; (3)

(d) state the protective devices that are fitted; (2)

(e) describe the maintenance requirements. (3)
answers.answer_text:
(a) Stepping down high-voltage generation/distribution (e.g. 6.6kV or 11kV) to 440V for general ship's services, or supplying HV equipment (large bow thrusters, HV motors) directly, or for shore power connection.

(b) Very high, typically in the region of 97-99%, since large power transformers are among the most efficient electrical machines, with losses limited mainly to core (iron) and winding (copper) losses.

(c) Construction and testing to recognised standards, adequate cooling rated for the intended environment, and - specifically for continuity-of-supply reasons - requirements ensuring the transformer arrangement doesn't create a single point of failure for essential services, plus specific segregation, access, and warning requirements where HV is involved.

(d) Overcurrent/short-circuit protection on both primary and secondary sides, winding temperature monitoring with alarm and trip stages, a Buchholz relay on oil-filled types (detecting gas evolution from an internal fault), and differential protection on larger units.

(e) Regular insulation resistance testing, inspection and maintenance of cooling systems (fans, oil condition and level, radiators), visual checks for oil leaks/corrosion/loose connections, periodic testing of protective devices and alarms, and for oil-filled types, oil sampling and dissolved gas analysis to detect a developing internal fault.

answers.title: Impressed Current Cathodic Protection (ICCP) system
answers.question_as_set:
(a) Describe the principle of operation of a ships Impressed Current Cathodic Protection system. (6)

(b) State the routine maintenance that should be carried out on an Impressed Current Cathodic Protection system. (4)
answers.answer_text:
An ICCP system protects the ship's underwater steel hull from electrochemical corrosion by making the hull the cathode of a deliberately imposed electrical circuit, rather than relying on sacrificial metal being consumed. Permanently fitted anodes (typically platinised titanium or similar inert, non-consumable material) are mounted on the underwater hull, connected to a DC power supply via a control unit. A reference electrode, also mounted on the hull, continuously monitors the hull's actual electrical potential relative to seawater. The control unit compares this measured potential against a target protective potential and automatically adjusts the DC current fed to the anodes to maintain the hull at the correct protective level.

Unlike a sacrificial anode system (where zinc or aluminium anodes are consumed over time and require periodic physical replacement), ICCP anodes are essentially inert and don't consume themselves - protection current is generated electronically and adjusted continuously, giving more precise, controllable, longer-lasting protection without needing regular anode replacement in drydock.

Most misinterpreted the question as a Marine Growth Prevention System and described copper and aluminium anodes in a sea chest.' A separate March 2024 General-paper sitting corroborates the same confusion pattern from the reverse direction (an MGPS question answered as if it were ICCP).

answers.title: Constructional / structural difference between a two-stroke and
answers.answer_text:
a four-stroke engine.
Frame it as a running comparison and then explain the two big structural consequences:
the crosshead and the separated lubrication.
Feature Two-stroke (slow speed) Four-stroke (medium speed)
Working Power stroke every revolution — suction, Power stroke every second
cycle compression, power, exhaust completed in one revolution — four distinct strokes
crank rotation over two rotations
Running Crosshead type: piston rod → crosshead → Trunk-piston type: gudgeon pin
gear connecting rod, with a stuffing box and diaphragm connects the piston directly to the
separating the combustion space from the con-rod; no crosshead or diaphragm
crankcase
Lubrication Separate cylinder oil (total-loss, high BN) and One crankcase oil serves cylinders
system oil (circulating, low BN) and bearings
Scavenging Ports with a uniflow exhaust valve (or loop/cross Poppet inlet & exhaust valves in the
scavenging on older designs); needs turbo- head
blowers
Crankshaft Semi-built (shrink-fitted throws) Fully forged (one piece)
Reversing Directly reversible (fuel cam shift / electronic) Reversing gearbox, CPP, or electric
drive

Character High power, low rpm (~70–120), very high torque, Higher rpm (~500–900), lighter,
tall & heavy; drives the propeller directly compact; needs a gearbox
The reason for the crosshead in the two-stroke is that the guide force from the connecting rod's
angularity is taken by the crosshead guides, so no side thrust reaches the liner — essential for the
long strokes and continuous liner lubrication of a slow-speed engine. That same architecture is what
lets the combustion space be sealed off from the crankcase and the two oils to be kept separate.
If he presses further —
Scavenging types:uniflow (air in through liner ports, out through a central exhaust valve — best
scavenge efficiency, standard on modern MAN/WinGD), loop and cross scavenging (ports only, poorer,
older). Why direct-drive on the two-stroke? its speed matches an efficient propeller, so no gearbox
and highest overall efficiency (SFOC ~160–170 g/kWh).

answers.title: The two grades of oil in a two-stroke, and the
answers.answer_text:
difference from the four-stroke system — with TBN and SAE.
Because the combustion space and crankcase are physically separated by the stuffing box and
diaphragm, a slow-speed two-stroke uses two entirely different oils:
Cylinder oil is a total-loss oil, injected by timed lubricators/accumulators through quills onto the
liner running surface at the correct point in the stroke. It must have: a high Base Number (BN 40–
100) to neutralise the sulphuric acid formed from fuel sulphur; strong detergency to keep the piston/
ring pack clean; good load-carrying and spreadability to maintain the film. The BN is matched to
the fuel sulphur — a high-sulphur fuel needs a high-BN oil (e.g. BN 70–100), a low-sulphur fuel a
low-BN oil (BN 25–40). The feed rate is controlled by load and is typically of the order of 0.8–1.2 g/
kWh.
System oil is the circulating oil for the crosshead, main and bottom-end bearings, camshaft/chain,
and piston cooling. It has a low BN (5–10), high oxidation stability for long service life, and good
demulsibility / water-shedding so any leakage water separates in the sump and can be purified
out.
A four-stroke/medium-speed engine has a common sump, so one crankcase oil (BN ~12–40,
chosen for the fuel burnt) lubricates both cylinders and bearings and must cope with combustion
products reaching the sump.
TBN (Total Base Number) is the alkalinity reserve — the oil's capacity to neutralise acid, measured in
mg KOH/g. SAE is the viscosity grade (e.g. SAE 40/50 for cylinder oil). Cylinder oil is chosen by BN and
SAE; system oil primarily by viscosity and oxidation stability.
If he presses further —
Why match BN to sulphur? too low a BN on high-sulphur fuel → cold corrosion of the liner; too high a
BN on low-sulphur fuel → calcium/ash deposits, bore polishing and lacquering. Modern engines
with adjustable feed and BN sensing manage this automatically. How do you check it is right? monitor
the scrape-down / drain oil BN and iron content from the piston underside and adjust the feed rate.

2 Crosshead, Running Gear & Bearings

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: The two grades of oil in a two-stroke, and the

answers.title: Purpose of the crosshead.
answers.answer_text:
The crosshead does four jobs, and the surveyor wants all of them:
• Transmits the gas load from the piston rod straight down into the connecting rod top end.
• Takes the side (guide) thrust. As the con-rod swings, it tries to push the piston rod sideways;
the crosshead shoes running in the guides absorb this force, so no side thrust reaches the
liner. This is the whole reason a slow-speed engine can keep a clean, even liner and rely on a
total-loss oil film.
• Converts the reciprocating motion of the piston rod into the oscillating/semi-rotary motion of the
con-rod top end.
• Distributes piston-cooling oil up to the piston crown through the telescopic or articulated pipe,
and forms the sealed junction (with the stuffing box) between the combustion side and the
crankcase.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Purpose of the crosshead.

answers.title: Material of the crosshead guide and shoe.
answers.answer_text:
The guide is cast steel (or cast iron on some designs), rigidly bolted to the engine frame so it stays
true. The shoe running face is white-metal lined (tin-based babbitt) so it is soft, conformable and
low-friction against the guide — the white metal is the sacrificial, easily-renewable surface, exactly as
in a plain bearing.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Material of the crosshead guide and shoe.

answers.title: What is special about the crosshead bearing?
answers.answer_text:
It is the most heavily loaded bearing in the engine, and — the key point — it oscillates through
a small arc rather than rotating fully. A rotating journal drags oil round and builds a wedge-
shaped hydrodynamic film continuously; an oscillating pin cannot do that, because at the ends of the
stroke the relative velocity falls to zero and the film tends to collapse. To keep it apart the design
uses:
• A very large projected area to keep the unit load down.
• Aluminium-tin lining rather than plain white metal, for higher load-carrying capacity and fatigue
strength under the constant heavy load reversals.
• Longitudinal and circumferential oil grooves to spread oil across the whole surface.
• Oil supplied at high pressure, often with hydrostatic jacking — a separate high-pressure supply
that physically lifts the pin off the bearing during the part of the stroke where the hydrodynamic
film would otherwise fail.
If he presses further —
Why not white metal? white metal fatigues under the constant unidirectional heavy load reversals of
the crosshead; aluminium-tin has far better fatigue endurance. What is hydrostatic (jacking) oil? a
high-pressure oil supply timed to lift the pin when the load line and velocity would otherwise break the
film — it maintains separation at the "dead" points of the oscillation.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What is special about the crosshead bearing?

answers.title: Crosshead inspection — what to check and where.
answers.answer_text:
• Bearing clearance (top and bottom halves) and the condition of the aluminium-tin/white metal —
look for wiping, overheating discolouration, cracking, fretting and the oil-groove condition.
• Guide shoe clearance and white-metal face, and the guide surface itself for scoring or ridging.
• Crosshead pin surface finish and any ovality; the nip (interference) of the bearing when closed
up.
• Oil supply — that the drillings, grooves and telescopic/articulated piston-cooling pipe are clear and
flow is correct.
• Bolt tightness and locking; the stuffing box and diaphragm condition (scavenge/crankcase
separation).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Crosshead inspection — what to check and where.

answers.title: Types of crankshaft; which type on two-stroke and four-stroke and why;
answers.answer_text:
continuous grain flow.
Types: fully forged (machined from one forging), semi-built (throws forged, journals shrunk in),
fully built (webs, pins and journals all separate and shrunk together — older) and welded.
Four-stroke engines use a fully forged shaft — they are small enough to forge and machine in one
piece, which is the strongest and most compact.
Large slow-speed two-strokes use a semi-built shaft: each throw (the two webs plus the
crankpin) is forged as a single unit, and the main journals are shrink-fitted into the webs with a
heavy interference fit (the web is heated, the journal dropped in, and the grip on cooling transmits the
torque). A one-piece forging of that size is simply not practical to make or handle.
Continuous grain flow (CGF) means the throw is die-forged so that the metal's grain flow
follows the contour of the web and pin fillets, instead of being cut through by machining from a
straight billet. Because fatigue cracks start at the fillets, keeping the grain running along the shape
gives even stress distribution and much higher fatigue strength exactly where it is needed.
If he presses further —
How is the interference grip guaranteed? the shrink fit is calculated to a set interference; on
assembly the relative slip is checked with reference marks — any slip in service (from a bearing
seizure or overload) shows the joint has failed and the shaft is condemned. Why not weld? welding
introduces residual stress and HAZ defects at the most highly stressed region — shrink-fitting avoids
that.

answers.title: How do you find a crack in a crankshaft, and what are stress raisers?
answers.answer_text:
Detection:
• Visual — a fatigue crack has a bright crystalline appearance and often a witness line of fretting/
oil weep at the fillet.
• Dye penetrant (DPI) — surface-breaking cracks, works on any material.
• Magnetic particle (MPI) — surface and slightly sub-surface cracks in ferrous material; more
sensitive than DPI on steel.
• Ultrasonic — for sub-surface defects and to size a crack.
• Ongoing monitoring by crankshaft deflection and bearing temperatures/LO wear metals.

Stress raisers are geometric or surface features that concentrate stress locally and so lower the
fatigue strength — sharp corners, oil holes, keyways, fillets that are too tight, tool/machining marks,
dents, corrosion pits and scoring. The remedies are the mirror image: generous fillet radii, good
surface finish, shot-peening and cold-rolling of fillets, and keeping the shaft clean and
corrosion-free.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How do you find a crack in a crankshaft, and what are stress raisers?

answers.title: Why is crankshaft deflection important, when is it taken,
answers.answer_text:
and what if the readings are drastically out?
What it measures: as the shaft is turned, the two webs of a throw open and close very slightly; a
deflection gauge (a dial indicator between the webs) reads this opening/closing. A shaft
running in bearings that are worn, or on a distorted bedplate/hull, is not straight — and that
misalignment shows up directly as excessive web deflection.
Why it matters: a bent/misaligned shaft is fatigue-loaded at the fillets on every revolution; left
uncorrected it overloads the main bearings and can crack the crankshaft. Deflection is the cheap,
non-intrusive way to catch that early.
When taken:
• After grounding or heavy contact (hull distortion).
• Before and after dry dock — the hull relaxes/changes shape when the ship comes out of and
goes back into the water.
• After a scavenge fire, a crankcase incident, or renewing a main bearing.
• Periodically per PMS, always at the same loading condition, and compared with the sea-trial and
previous readings.
How to take it: readings at top, both sides near BDC, and bottom (bottom is taken with the con-
rod moved past); plot the maximum minus minimum against the maker's limits. Take them at a
consistent, recorded draught/temperature so readings are comparable.
Drastically-out readings mean the crankshaft is genuinely misaligned relative to the bedplate.
Investigate the main-bearing weardown first; if the bedplate/chocks have shifted, the engine may
need to be opened up, re-aligned and the bedplate re-chocked. Confirm with bearing
clearances and an alignment check (taut-wire or laser).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Why is crankshaft deflection important, when is it taken,

answers.title: Two-stroke cylinder-liner inspection — what you expect to see, wear
answers.answer_text:
rate, and deep grooves.
At a scavenge/liner inspection, measure the bore at several levels and in two planes (fore-aft and
athwartships) with a template or internal micrometer to establish wear and ovality. Look for:
• Cold corrosion in the upper zone (a matt, corroded band) — sulphuric-acid attack where the
surface is coolest.
• Scuffing / micro-seizure — bright vertical scoring from oil-film breakdown.
• Clover-leafing — wear patterns opposite the injectors/quills from over-lubrication or corrosion.
• Cat-fine (Al+Si) scoring — fine vertical scratches from abrasive particles.
• Condition of the scavenge and exhaust ports, quills and the honing pattern.

Wear rate: a healthy liner wears about 0.05–0.1 mm per 1000 running hours. The maximum
permissible wear is roughly 0.6–0.8% of the bore diameter before renewal (e.g. ~5–6 mm on a
700 mm bore).
Deep grooves: if wear/ovality are within limits, hone/deglaze to restore the cross-hatch oil-
retaining pattern. If beyond limits, or if there is cracking or bad scoring, renew the liner — and,
crucially, find and fix the cause (feed rate/BN, cooling temperature, fuel treatment) or the new liner
suffers the same fate.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Two-stroke cylinder-liner inspection — what you expect to see, wear

answers.title: Increased liner wear on one unit — possible causes.
answers.answer_text:
Split it into the three wear mechanisms — that structure impresses the surveyor:
• Corrosive: cold corrosion — a low jacket/liner temperature on that unit plus high-sulphur fuel, or
an under-based / insufficient cylinder-oil feed so the acid is not neutralised.
• Abrasive: cat fines passing to that unit (poor fuel treatment), or dirt ingress.
• Adhesive: oil-film breakdown — over- or under-lubrication, a faulty lubricator or blocked quill
on that unit, wrong feed timing.
Also unit-specific: a fuel-injection fault causing impingement, blow-by past worn rings, or a
cooling-water fault on that jacket. Investigate the lubricator, injector, ring pack and jacket
temperature for that cylinder.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Increased liner wear on one unit — possible causes.

answers.title: Main-bearing survey/removal, and causes of failure.
answers.answer_text:
Procedure: risk assessment and permit to work; engine on turning gear; isolate starting air, the
LO/priming system and the turning gear; enter the crankcase under enclosed-space entry;
support/jack the crankshaft; remove the bearing keep, side chocks and shells; inspect journal and
shells; renew as required and refit with the correct clearance and nip, torque and locking; record
everything; and take crankshaft deflections afterwards to confirm alignment.
Causes of failure:
• Oil starvation / low pressure — pump, filter, relief valve, or blocked drilling.
• Contamination — water, cat fines or wear debris in the oil breaking the film.
• Overload / shock — e.g. hydraulic lock, heavy-weather racing.
• Misalignment and an oval or tapered journal (the surveyor often wants "oval journal").
• Fatigue of the white metal, fretting of the shell backs, or wrong clearance/nip on assembly.
LO analysis (wear metals: Sn, Cu, Pb, Al) and bearing temperature monitoring give the early warning
before a wipe.
Q337 - 341. Intermediate-shaft coupling — how is torque transmitted, is it only the
bolts, keeping the shaft aligned?
The last vessel typically had a conventional flanged coupling — an integral forged flange coupled
with reamed, body-fitted (fitted) bolts. The important point the surveyor is chasing: the torque
is transmitted mainly by the friction grip between the mating flange faces, generated by the
bolt pre-tension clamping the flanges together. The fitted bolts carry the shear and locate the
shafts concentrically to keep them aligned; they are not, by themselves, transmitting the whole

torque. Some installations use a muff / SKF-OK oil-injection coupling, where an interference
sleeve is expanded hydraulically onto the shaft and grips by friction.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Main-bearing survey/removal, and causes of failure.

answers.title: Withdraw the propeller & intermediate shaft; tailshaft
answers.answer_text:
checks; wear-down; drain the oil?
Withdrawal: disconnect the couplings, remove the propeller (or free the muff coupling by oil
injection), support the shafts on rollers, break the aft seal, and withdraw the tailshaft inboard or
outboard depending on the arrangement.
Tailshaft checks: journal and liner condition; NDT (DPI/MPI) of the cone, keyway and the fillet
at the change of section — these are the fatigue hot-spots; ultrasonic for sub-surface cracks; the
taper contact (blueing) with the propeller boss; seal faces and the chrome liner; keyway condition.
Wear-down: measured at the aft stern-tube bearing with a poker (feeler) gauge through the
top plug — the shaft rests on the bottom of the bearing, so wear shows as an increased top
clearance compared with the original; the drop of the shaft is the wear-down.
Draining the oil: not required — the seals hold the oil, so the reading is taken without draining the
stern-tube system.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Withdraw the propeller & intermediate shaft; tailshaft

answers.title: Methods of checking shaft alignment; explain one; how
answers.answer_text:
do you check misalignment?
• Jacking (bearing-reaction) method: a hydraulic jack with a dial gauge and load cell lifts each
bearing in turn to build a jack-up curve; from the lift-off load the actual bearing reactions are
calculated and compared with the design. The two directions of jacking give slightly different
curves (hysteresis) which are averaged. This is the accurate way to confirm the loads are shared
correctly.
• Gap-and-sag: feeler and bridge gauge across the coupling flanges before bolting up — checks the
two shaft ends meet parallel and concentric.
• Taut/piano wire or optical/laser — the laser method is the accurate modern technique for
setting the line of the bearings.
• Crankshaft deflection indicates alignment at the engine end.
Misalignment shows up as abnormal bearing reactions, uneven bearing wear/temperatures,
and out-of-limit crankshaft deflections. If found, the cause (bearing weardown, bedplate/seating
movement, hull deflection) is corrected and the line re-set.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Methods of checking shaft alignment; explain one; how

answers.title: Intermediate bearing found heavily scored — what would you check
answers.answer_text:
for?
• Lubrication: oil supply, pressure, quality and any contamination reaching that bearing.
• Foreign / hard particles: filtration failure allowing debris to embed and score.
• Vibration / imbalance: engine or shaft imbalance and the coupling condition producing dynamic
loading.
• Misalignment: of the bearing casing/seating — and journal ovality or a poor surface finish.
Renew/re-metal the bearing, correct the root cause, and confirm alignment before running again.
