answers.title: Suspected blow-by from a unit; metal found in the sump.
answers.answer_text:
Blow-by (combustion gas leaking past the rings) shows as a rising exhaust temperature on that
unit, a fall in Pmax and Pcomp, puffing/flames at the scavenge, and a raised scavenge-fire risk.
Confirm at a scavenge inspection (broken/stuck rings, worn liner). Immediate action: reduce load,
increase cylinder lubrication to that unit, watch the scavenge temperatures, and plan to overhaul
the unit at the first opportunity.
Metal in the sump: first identify it — is it magnetic (steel: a gear, journal or ring fragment) or
non-magnetic (white metal / aluminium-tin: a bearing)? Its colour and form point to the source.
Then narrow it down and inspect the relevant bearings/running gear before restarting — running
on with unexplained metal in the sump risks a bearing failure or crankcase explosion.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Suspected blow-by from a unit; metal found in the sump.

answers.title: A bearing is past use with no spare — getting the ship to the next port;
answers.answer_text:
running through a barred speed range.
If a unit's bottom-end/con-rod cannot be run, you hang the crosshead and remove the
connecting rod for that unit so the engine can run on the remaining cylinders. The procedure: lock/
support the running gear of that unit, cut out its fuel pump, hold the exhaust valve open (or
lock it), stop cylinder lubrication to it, blank as required, and run the engine at reduced load/
rpm. Watch for critical (torsional) vibration ranges — the "barred speed range / black spots"
— because removing a cylinder changes the firing balance and the dangerous speed bands shift.
If you find yourself in a barred range: pass through it quickly rather than dwelling; if the engine
will not clear it, turn it on the turning gear or kick it in the opposite direction to move off the
critical speed. Keep increased watch on bearing temperatures and vibration throughout.
If he presses further —
Why is a barred range dangerous? it is a resonant torsional speed where the crankshaft's alternating
stress peaks — prolonged running there can crack the shaft. With a unit cut out, the excitation changes
and a new critical band may appear within the normal operating range.
3 Engine Performance & Operation

answers.title: M/E performance — the cards, the load diagram, and how you
answers.answer_text:
know the engine is at its optimum.
Explain the diagnostic tools first, then how you judge "optimum":
• Indicator / pressure card: in-cylinder pressure against stroke, taken with a mechanical indicator
or electronic PMI. It gives Pmax, Pcomp and the shape of combustion.
• Power (p–V) card: pressure against volume — the enclosed area is the indicated power of
that unit.
• Draw / light-spring card: a light spring exaggerates the low-pressure part, so you can read the
scavenge and exhaust events and the injection/combustion timing.
• Out-of-phase (Pmax vs crank angle) diagram: confirms the timing of peak pressure.

• Load diagram: the maker's envelope of power vs speed, bounded by the torque/thermal limit,
the scavenge-pressure limit, the overload limit and the layout/propeller curves — it tells you the
safe operating field.
Judging optimum running: the units are power-balanced (equal indicated powers), Pmax/Pcomp
are within limits and even, exhaust temperatures are even and within limit, T/C rpm and
scavenge pressure are normal for the load, and the SFOC matches the expected value — all corrected
to reference (ISO) ambient conditions before comparing.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: M/E performance — the cards, the load diagram, and how you

answers.title: Power card vs draw card; effect of early and late injection, and
answers.answer_text:
correction.
The power card tells you how much work the cylinder is doing (area = indicated power); the draw
card tells you when things happen (timing of injection, combustion and the gas exchange). You use
them together to balance and tune the engine.
Early injection: a high, sharp Pmax — the fuel burns too soon, giving mechanical and thermal
overload, hard, knocking running and stress on the bearings and combustion chamber.
Late injection: a low Pmax with a high exhaust temperature — the fuel is still burning during
expansion (afterburning), wasting energy, raising fuel consumption and overheating the exhaust
valve and turbocharger.
Correction: adjust the fuel-pump timing / VIT; also check the injector (opening pressure, spray
pattern), compression (rings/liner) and the fuel quality (CCAI), because poor ignition mimics late
injection.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Power card vs draw card; effect of early and late injection, and

answers.title: What is VIT and its use?
answers.answer_text:
Variable Injection Timing alters the start of injection so that Pmax is reached and held near its
maximum permissible value across the part-load range, instead of falling away as load
reduces. Because a higher Pmax at part load burns the fuel more efficiently, VIT lowers SFOC at
part load and also lets the engine compensate for fuel quality (CCAI) and ambient variation.
On mechanical jerk pumps it is done by a VIT rack/eccentric that advances the pump plunger's
effective timing; on electronically-controlled engines (MAN ME, WinGD RT-flex) it is done in software,
which also allows the timing to be optimised continuously and for different running modes (economy,
low-load, emissions).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What is VIT and its use?

answers.title: How to calculate SFOC and where you get the information; ER logbook
answers.answer_text:
parameters and why.
SFOC = fuel mass consumed per unit of power delivered (g/kWh). You need the fuel mass
flow (from a flow meter, or fuel-rack/counter calculation with the fuel density) and the power (from
the indicator cards — indicated power — or a torsion/shaft-power meter for brake power). The raw
figure is then corrected to ISO reference conditions (air temperature, pressure, charge-air coolant
temperature) and to the fuel's lower calorific value, so it can be compared like-for-like with the
shop-test/sea-trial figure.
Logbook parameters (rpm, powers, Pmax/Pcomp, exhaust temperatures, T/C rpm, scavenge
pressure, cooling/lube temps and pressures, and consumptions) are recorded to trend the
machinery's condition, support condition-based maintenance, prove operational compliance, and
provide the evidence trail for surveys, PSC and incident investigation.

4 Fuel Oil

answers.title: Fuel-oil analysis and properties — what you look for and
answers.answer_text:
why.
Go through the properties and say what each one tells you and the consequence if it is wrong:
Property Why it matters
Density & viscosity Set purifier and heating parameters; density limits purifier separation (max
~991 kg/m³ for conventional purifiers)
Water Corrosion, combustion problems, and can hide in the settling tank — drained
and purified out
Sulphur Cold corrosion and SOx compliance; sets the cylinder-oil BN
Ash, Vanadium, Hot corrosion of exhaust valves and T/C (V+Na form low-melting deposits);
Sodium manage V/Na ratio and valve temperature
Aluminium + Silicon Abrasive wear of liners, rings, pumps and injectors — must be reduced by
(cat fines) purification to <~15 ppm at the engine inlet
CCAI / CCR Ignition and combustion quality
Flash point Safety — minimum 60°C by SOLAS
Pour point Pumpability — keep tanks above it
Total sediment (TSP) Stability — risk of sludge/incompatibility

answers.title: What is CCAI, how does it affect the engine, how do you
answers.answer_text:
rectify it?
CCAI (Calculated Carbon Aromaticity Index) is a number derived from the fuel's density and
viscosity that indicates ignition quality — the more aromatic (high-density, low-viscosity) the fuel,
the higher the CCAI and the worse it ignites.
Effect: a high CCAI (above ~870) gives a long ignition delay — fuel accumulates in the cylinder
before it lights, then burns rapidly and uncontrollably. The result is hard, knocking running, high
peak pressure, afterburning, high exhaust temperatures and thermal loading of the exhaust
valve, piston and turbocharger.
Rectify:
• Adjust injection timing (VIT) to suit the poorer ignition.
• Raise the charge-air (scavenge) temperature and pressure and the jacket temperature to
promote ignition.
• Ensure good atomisation (injector condition, correct viscosity/preheat).
• Reduce load if the engine is running hard, and consider blending or changing fuel as a longer-
term fix.

Q416 - 419 / 91 / 272 / 273 / 189 / 656. Bunkering — deciding quantity, the process,
ordering, voyage calculation and changeover timing.
Quantity: voyage consumption = (distance ÷ speed) × daily consumption of M/E + A/E + boiler, plus
a reserve/safety margin (typically 5–10% plus weather allowance), minus reliable ROB, and
allowing for the compliant fuel needed in ECAs. Confirm tank capacity and free volume for the
loading temperature.
Plan with the deck department for stability, trim and hull stress — agree the tank-filling sequence
so GM stays adequate and free surface is minimised, and the hull girder is not overstressed.
Process (before / during / after):
• Before: complete the pre-bunker checklist, SOPEP ready, agree grade/quantity/rate and
maximum pressure, plug scuppers, rig drip trays and spill kit, sound tanks, brief the team, and
rig the continuous-drip sampler.
• During: monitor pressure and tank levels, take the MARPOL representative sample, watch for
water/temperature, and stay within the agreed rate; know the emergency-stop signal.
• After: sound and calculate the quantity received, check the sample, sign the BDN (letter of
protest if short or off-spec), and seal/retain the samples.
Changeover timing to an ECA: the whole service system (settling → service → injectors) must be on
compliant fuel before the boundary. Calculate the changeover start from the system volume and the
ramp rate, and log the position and time of the completed changeover.

answers.title: Mixing of bunkers — why not, and tank planning.
answers.answer_text:
Avoid mixing different bunkers because two fuels that are individually stable can be incompatible
when mixed: the asphaltenes flocculate and precipitate, producing heavy sludge that blocks filters
and purifiers and can starve the engine of fuel. So keep new bunkers in a separate tank, run a
compatibility (spot/ASTM) test before commingling, and burn down existing stock first where
practical. The tank plan should segregate grades and keep clear which tank feeds the engine.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Mixing of bunkers — why not, and tank planning.

answers.title: ECA / fuel changeover HFO ↔ LSFO/MGO — procedure,
answers.answer_text:
problems, and effect of low-sulphur fuel.
Procedure: change over gradually, ramping the fuel temperature at about 2°C per minute so the
viscosity changes slowly, and hold the correct viscosity at the injectors throughout. Start early enough
to be fully on compliant fuel before the ECA.
The danger of a sudden change is thermal shock to the fuel pumps: the plunger and barrel
expand at different rates, so a fast temperature swing causes sticking or seizure and increased
leakage. That is why the ramp rate matters.
Effects of low-sulphur / low-viscosity fuel: poor lubricity in the fuel pumps and injectors
(accelerated wear and leakage), possible viscosity too low for good atomisation, and a BN mismatch
with the cylinder oil if the feed/grade is not changed. Manage with viscosity control (a cooler may be
needed on very light fuel), the correct cylinder-oil BN/feed, and lubricity additives if required.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: ECA / fuel changeover HFO ↔ LSFO/MGO — procedure,

answers.title: Running on LSMGO but forgot the low-sulphur cylinder oil / joined with
answers.answer_text:
over-limit sulphur fuel onboard.
The cylinder-oil BN must match the fuel sulphur. Burning low-sulphur fuel with a high-BN cylinder
oil leaves a large amount of un-reacted alkaline (calcium) additive on the liner — it builds up as
hard ash/calcium deposits, causes lacquering and bore polishing, and destroys the oil's ability
to hold a film, giving increased wear. (The opposite mistake — high-sulphur fuel on a low-BN oil —
gives cold corrosion.) Action: switch to the correct low-BN cylinder oil and/or adjust the feed rate
down, and monitor the liner and drain-oil BN.
Fuel over the sulphur limit onboard: it may only be burnt with an approved equivalent
(scrubber), otherwise it must be retained for a permitted region or landed. Record the situation,
report as required, and use compliant fuel — a FONAR only applies to genuine non-availability, not to
a fuel you chose to load.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Running on LSMGO but forgot the low-sulphur cylinder oil / joined with

answers.title: Bunker received out of specification; ordered VLSFO not
answers.answer_text:
available; would you reject fuel?
Monitor throughout bunkering (continuous-drip sample, visual for water/solids). If you suspect it is
off-spec: stop or refuse the delivery, issue a letter of protest, retain the sealed MARPOL sample,
and land a sample for lab analysis. If off-spec fuel is already onboard: segregate the tank, do not
use it until the analysis clears it, inform the company and supplier, and treat/handle it per the results
(blend, land, or use with restrictions). If the ordered grade is unavailable, order the nearest compliant
grade with company agreement, or arrange supply at the next port — do not compromise on a non-
compliant fuel.

answers.title: Settling-tank temperature; what if you don't maintain fuel temperature
answers.answer_text:
per the report.
Keep the settling tank about 5°C above the fuel's pour point (and heavy fuel generally around 50–
70°C) so the fuel stays pumpable and water/sediment settle out. If the temperature is wrong: too low
→ wax formation, poor settling, blocked filters and pump problems; too high in the purifier → the
water seal breaks and separation efficiency falls. Set the heating and purifier temperature/throughput
from the fuel analysis, and always keep above the pour point in every tank the fuel passes through.
5 Lube Oil

answers.title: LO analysis report — what it gives, and
answers.answer_text:
reasons for high viscosity / high iron / high vanadium.
An LO analysis reports viscosity, TBN/TAN, water, flash point, insolubles, and wear metals (Fe,
Cu, Cr, Pb, Sn, Al) by spectrographic analysis — it is your condition-monitoring tool for catching a
developing problem before it fails.
• Viscosity increase: oxidation of the oil, contamination with heavier/residual fuel, water/
emulsion, or high insolubles (soot/oxidation products). (A viscosity decrease = dilution with
distillate fuel from a leak.)

• High iron: wear of steel components, or fretting of the frames/bedplate/tie-bolt seats — check
tie-bolt tightness and the running gear; on a two-stroke it may also mean liner/ring wear
scraping into the system oil.
• High vanadium: vanadium is a fuel marker, so its presence in the system oil means fuel-oil
ingress (leaking cooler/seal/injection) — find and stop the leak; vanadium also raises the hot-
corrosion risk.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: LO analysis report — what it gives, and

answers.title: LO tests onboard; micro-biological / bacterial attack — signs
answers.answer_text:
and treatment.
Onboard tests: viscosity (flow comparator), water (crackle test / water-finding paste), TBN (test kit),
a spot/blotter test for insolubles and dispersancy, and flash point.
Micro-biological attack — bacteria and fungi live at the oil/water interface and thrive where
water collects. Signs: a foul rotten-egg (H₂S) smell, emulsification, a drop in pH / rising acidity,
sludge, filter blockage, and corrosion of surfaces. Treatment: remove the water (purify/drain the
sump), dose an approved biocide, clean out the tank and lines, and then keep the system dry —
the water is the food source, so controlling water is the real cure.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: LO tests onboard; micro-biological / bacterial attack — signs

answers.title: Auxiliary-engine crankcase LO / fuel-oil contamination — ways it happens
answers.answer_text:
and effects on the AE.
Water contamination comes from cooler leaks, condensation or purifier faults — it emulsifies the
oil, reduces film strength, promotes corrosion and depletes additives. Fuel contamination
comes from leaking injection equipment or seals — it drops the viscosity, lowers the flash point
(a fire/explosion risk) and reduces TBN. Both lead to bearing wear and increased oil
consumption. Detect by LO analysis and a flash-point test; rectify by purifying the oil, finding
and fixing the leak, and renewing the charge if it is degraded beyond limits.
6 Turbocharger

answers.title: Turbocharger parts and materials; how are the turbine blades attached?
answers.answer_text:
Part Material & why
Turbine blades Nickel-chromium heat-resisting alloy (Nimonic / Inconel) — retains strength
and resists creep/corrosion at the high exhaust-gas temperature
Turbine disc / Heat-resisting forged alloy steel
rotor shaft
Nozzle ring Heat-resisting alloy steel — directs and accelerates the gas onto the blades
Compressor wheel Aluminium alloy or titanium — light for low inertia on the cooler air side
Casing Cast iron, with water-cooled sections on the gas side
Bearings Ball/roller (with own oil) or plain white-metal (engine oil)

Blade fixing: the blades have a fir-tree or bulb root that slides into matching serrations in the
turbine disc and is locked; the loose-fit root allows for thermal expansion and gives some
damping.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Turbocharger parts and materials; how are the turbine blades attached?

answers.title: What is turbocharger surging and what causes it?
answers.answer_text:
Surging is a momentary reversal of the air flow through the compressor: when the delivery back-
pressure momentarily exceeds the pressure the compressor can develop, the flow breaks down and
reverses, then re-establishes — heard as a loud, pulsating bang with fluctuating scavenge pressure.
Repeated surging damages the compressor and bearings.
Causes (anything that raises back-pressure or reduces gas energy):
• Fouled turbine or compressor, or a dirty air filter/silencer.
• Fouled exhaust-gas economiser or high exhaust back-pressure.
• Sudden load change / manoeuvring, or heavy weather causing propeller racing.
• Engine misfiring or a faulty fuel injector on a unit — uneven gas energy.
• Blocked or damaged nozzle ring / blades.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What is turbocharger surging and what causes it?

answers.title: Turbocharger damaged — taking the vessel to port without it.
answers.answer_text:
• Lock the rotor with the maker's locking device so it cannot windmill and cause further bearing/
blade damage.
• Fit the blanking plates at the T/C gas inlet and outlet, and blank off the compressor air outlet
so the scavenge air from the blowers cannot escape back out through the T/C air side.
• Run on the auxiliary blowers to supply scavenge air.
• Run at reduced load/rpm, with extra cylinder cooling and lubrication, increased
watchkeeping, and close monitoring of exhaust temperatures.
If all turbochargers are lost, the maker's emergency gas-bypass/blanking arrangement is used to
reach a safe port at much-reduced power. The whole point is to keep the engine running safely at low
load without the T/C rotor turning.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Turbocharger damaged — taking the vessel to port without it.

answers.title: Out of dock, engine started, turbocharger vibrating badly — action.
answers.answer_text:
Stop the engine and investigate the turbocharger — never run on with a heavily vibrating T/C.
The likely causes are rotor imbalance (fouling, a damaged or lost blade), bearing failure, or debris.
Check the rotor and bearings; if it cannot be run, lock and blank it and proceed on aux blowers at
reduced load as above. (The examiner may fish for "grounding" — but the correct first action for a
vibrating T/C is simply to stop and check the turbocharger.)

7 Boilers, Economiser & Steam

answers.title: How do you conduct a boiler survey and what
answers.answer_text:
does it include?
Shut down, cool and prepare: take the boiler off the load, allow it to cool, drain, and open up the
top doors/vents first to release any pressure or vacuum safely; ventilate and gas-free; then treat
entry as an enclosed-space entry with a permit and risk assessment.
Inspection scope:
• Water side: scale, corrosion, pitting, condition of tubes, stays and drum internals, and any oil
contamination.
• Fire / furnace side: soot, refractory/brickwork, tube cracking, bulging/overheating, and
burner condition.
• External: shell, casing, foundations and insulation.
• Mountings & fittings: safety valves, gauge glasses, feed check, blow-down, main stop, and the
level-protection devices.
After inspection: any repairs, then a hydraulic test if required, and the safety valves set in the
surveyor's presence.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How do you conduct a boiler survey and what

answers.title: Safety-valve overhaul & setting;
answers.answer_text:
accumulation test; who sets the economiser SV and when.
Overhaul: strip down, record the existing setting, measure the spring free length and condition,
lap the seat and lid, reassemble, and set the lifting pressure using a calibrated master gauge;
check the easing gear. The main boiler safety valves are set in the presence of the surveyor.
Accumulation test: with the safety valves set, close the main stop and fire at maximum; over
15 minutes the pressure must not rise more than 10% of the design (working) pressure — this proves
the valves can relieve the full evaporation of the boiler.
Economiser / EGE safety valve: the Chief Engineer is authorised to set it, and it is done
underway while steaming (steam is available then, and surveyor attendance is not required for the
EGE) — unlike the main boiler SV, which needs the surveyor. It is set slightly higher than the main
boiler valve so it does not lift first under normal conditions.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Safety-valve overhaul & setting;

answers.title: Hydraulic pressure test of a boiler; furnace inspection.
answers.answer_text:
Hydraulic test: fill the boiler completely and vent all air (air makes the test dangerous and
inaccurate), then raise the pressure slowly with a test pump to 1.5× the working pressure (per
class), hold, and inspect for leaks and any deformation. Carried out after a repair or at survey to prove
integrity.
Furnace inspection: remove soot/scale, check the refractory and brickwork, the tube plate and
tube ends for cracking or wastage, look for distortion or bulging (overheating from scale/low
water), and check burner alignment and the combustion side generally.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Hydraulic pressure test of a boiler; furnace inspection.

answers.title: Boiler water test & treatment; caustic embrittlement;
answers.answer_text:
safety features and level alarms.
Water treatment keeps the boiler water in condition to prevent scale and corrosion: maintain pH
~9.5–11, a phosphate reserve to precipitate hardness as a soft sludge, an oxygen scavenger
(hydrazine or sodium sulphite) to remove dissolved oxygen, low chlorides, and controlled TDS/
conductivity. Watch the hotwell/cascade tank for oil contamination. Tests: pH/alkalinity, phosphate,
chloride, hardness and dissolved O₂.
Caustic embrittlement is intergranular cracking at highly-stressed or riveted/seam areas where
free caustic soda (NaOH) concentrates and attacks the grain boundaries under stress. It is
prevented by coordinated phosphate treatment (so there is no free caustic) and by controlling the
Na₂SO₄ / NaOH ratio.
Safety features: two safety valves; high and low water alarms with a low-low water fuel trip;
high-steam-pressure trip; flame-failure and combustion safeguards. Level is measured remotely by
float, electrode or differential-pressure transmitters that drive the alarms and trips; at hi-hi
level the burner trips to prevent water carry-over (priming) into the steam system.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Boiler water test & treatment; caustic embrittlement;

answers.title: How does the feed pump regulate supply if running continuously; feed
answers.answer_text:
pressure for a 12-bar boiler.
With a continuously-running feed pump, drum level is held by a modulating feed-regulating valve
using single-, two- or three-element control (level, plus steam flow and feed flow for tighter control),
which throttles feed into the drum; a spill/recirculation line back to the hotwell protects the pump
against overheating at low demand. The feed pressure must exceed boiler pressure to force water in
against it — for a 12-bar boiler you would expect roughly 15–17 bar at the pump discharge to
overcome the boiler pressure plus pipeline and valve losses.
Q391 - 395. How are boiler tubes connected; a tube leaks at the flare — repair.
Tubes are secured into the tube plate by expanding (rolling) and then flaring/belling the ends,
and are sometimes seal-welded. If a tube leaks at the flare: isolate the boiler, remove the
defective tube, fit the new tube and re-flare (or re-expand) it with the flaring tool, then prove
the repair by a hydrostatic pressure test before returning the boiler to service.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How does the feed pump regulate supply if running continuously; feed

answers.title: Water at the scavenge drain (where from); economiser leak &
answers.answer_text:
running-dry; hydrogen fire; soot.
Persistent water at the scavenge drain can be tracked back to a leaking exhaust-gas economiser
(EGB) tube — water leaks into the exhaust gas and finds its way back through the uptake to the
scavenge space. (Also check the jacket, air cooler and liner.)
Economiser soot and hydrogen fire: soot deposits on the tubes, combined with low water
circulation, create a dry, overheating patch. This starts a soot fire; if the temperature climbs
high enough, the hot iron reacts with steam to release hydrogen — an "iron/hydrogen fire"
that is extremely hot and self-sustaining. Prevent it with regular soot blowing, maintaining
minimum forced circulation even at low engine load, and heeding the alarms.

Running-dry / fire response: reduce or stop the engine, maintain boundary cooling, and follow
the maker's dry-running procedure — do not put water directly onto a hydrogen fire (it feeds it);
starve it of oxygen and cool the boundaries.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Water at the scavenge drain (where from); economiser leak &

answers.title: Oil in the cascade/observation tank and boiler gauge glass — action
answers.answer_text:
(different quantities).
Oil in the feed system indicates a leak from a fuel/oil heater or heat exchanger into the
condensate. It is serious because oil bakes onto the boiler heating surfaces as an insulating layer
→ local overheating and tube failure, so it must be stopped and cleaned up.
• Small trace: dump the affected condensate, run the cascade/observation-tank oil detection
and skimming, find and isolate the leaking heater, and top up with treated feed.
• Larger quantity: stop using the contaminated feed, change to reserve feed, and consider
taking the boiler off load; if oil has actually entered the boiler, it must be boiled out/cleaned
before returning to service. Then investigate and repair the leaking exchanger.
8 Scavenge Fire, Crankcase & Restart Checks

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Oil in the cascade/observation tank and boiler gauge glass — action

answers.title: Scavenge fire — checks before restarting; effects of water in the
answers.answer_text:
scavenge space.
During a scavenge fire you reduce load/stop fuel to the affected unit(s), increase cylinder
lubrication, stop the auxiliary blowers if fitted with fire flaps, and use the fixed scavenge fire-
smothering (CO₂/steam) if provided; boundary-cool the uptakes.
Before restarting (once out and cooled): open and inspect the scavenge space, liner, rings,
ports and piston skirt for damage, distortion and cracks; clean out the burnt oil/soot; confirm the
scavenge drains are clear; and, crucially, establish the cause (blow-by, over-lubrication, poor
drainage, worn rings) and correct it. Take crankshaft deflections if the fire was severe, and restart
at reduced load with close monitoring.
Water in the scavenge space points to a jacket, air-cooler or economiser leak; it causes
corrosion, breaks the oil film and disturbs combustion — drain it, find the source, and repair.
Q931 - 936. 4/E reports a crankcase explosion at night — actions; restart if the cause
is not found?
The sequence the surveyor wants is about not causing a second, bigger explosion:
• Slow down and stop the engine, reduce load immediately — the oil-mist detector (OMD)
alarm/hot-spot is the trigger. Do not open the crankcase.
• Keep everyone clear of the relief doors.
• Stop the engine, engage the turning gear, and allow it to cool thoroughly before opening
up — opening a hot crankcase lets fresh air into an oil-mist atmosphere and can trigger a far larger
secondary explosion.
• Once cool, ventilate and inspect for the hot spot (a seized/overheated bearing, guide or gear),
the oil-mist source, and the damage.

Restart:do not restart until the cause of the hot-spot/explosion is found and rectified. In
heavy weather, if the only means of holding the engine is the turning gear, keep it engaged and do
nothing that risks the engine turning against it.
If he presses further —
Why does a crankcase explosion happen? a local hot spot vaporises lube oil into a fine white oil
mist; if it ignites you get a primary explosion, the relief doors lift, and if air is drawn back in over still-hot
surfaces a secondary explosion follows — which is the dangerous one. The OMD detects the mist
before ignition.
Q431 - 435 / 509 / 680 / 681 / 682. Assist the 2/E for a crankcase inspection / unit
overhaul — preparation, checks, running-in.
Preparation: get permission to isolate; risk assessment and permit to work; engine on turning
gear; isolate the starting air, fuel and turning-gear controls; allow the crankcase to cool;
ventilate and treat it as an enclosed-space entry (gas test, standby man, permit).
Inspect: all running gear — main, crank-pin and crosshead bearings (clearance, wiping, fretting,
oil-groove condition), guides and shoes, journals, the gear/chain drive, tie-rod tightness, oil supply
drillings, and take crankshaft deflections.
After a unit overhaul — running-in: increase cylinder lubrication, run at reduced load (e.g.
half ahead) for the maker's specified time, then take crankshaft deflections and open the
under-piston/crankcase doors to inspect before working up to full load. Documents to the surveyor for
credit: liner calibration report, piston clearances, onboard LO test, and photographs at each
stage.
9 Refrigeration & Air Conditioning

answers.title: Indications of an undercharge of refrigerant.
answers.answer_text:
• Low suction and low discharge pressure.
• Compressor runs continuously / short-cycles and the room temperature is not achieved.
• High superheat and a hunting expansion valve.
• Bubbles/flashing in the sight glass; a short frost pattern on the evaporator; a low liquid level
in the receiver.
These follow logically from "not enough refrigerant to fill the system," so you can reason them out
rather than memorise a list.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Indications of an undercharge of refrigerant.

answers.title: Moisture in the system — sources, indications, removal; where
answers.answer_text:
recorded.
Sources: air/leak ingress on the low-pressure side, poor evacuation after opening the system, or a
wet charge. Indications: ice forming at the expansion valve (freeze-up) — giving fluctuating
pressures and intermittent cooling — and, over time, acid formation and copper plating. Removal:
the drier (silica-gel/molecular-sieve) filter absorbs it in service, and after any repair the system is

evacuated (deep vacuum) to boil off moisture before recharging. Refrigerant handling and any
ODS refrigerant top-up are recorded in the ODS Record Book / IAPP documentation.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Moisture in the system — sources, indications, removal; where

answers.title: Air in the system; refrigeration tripping on HP; refer running
answers.answer_text:
continuously.
Air (non-condensables) collects at the top of the condenser, where it raises the discharge
pressure and temperature; purge it from the condenser top into a recovery bottle (never to
atmosphere).
HP trip causes: overcharge, air in the system, a dirty/choked condenser, insufficient
cooling-water flow (pump/fan/valve/blockage), or a high sea-water temperature — anything that
stops the condenser rejecting heat.
Running continuously: heat ingress from door/insulation packing faults, a frosted/blocked
expansion valve, undercharge, or a choked condenser. Check the charge, the TEV, the condenser
and the compressor safeties (HP/LP cut-outs, oil-pressure trip, relief valve).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Air in the system; refrigeration tripping on HP; refer running

answers.title: Meat room high temperature — likely cause (condenser choked),
answers.answer_text:
rectify and test.
A common cause of a high room temperature together with a high discharge pressure is a choked/
fouled condenser — it cannot reject heat, so the whole system runs hot and cannot pull the room
down. Rectify: clean the condenser tubes / restore the cooling-water flow. Test afterwards by
confirming the suction/discharge pressures and temperatures return to normal and the room
temperature falls. Test for refrigerant leakage in the condenser (refrigerant leaking into the
cooling water) with a halide or electronic leak detector, or by checking the cooling-water side for
the presence of refrigerant.

Electrical & Control
1 Generators & Voltage Generation

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Meat room high temperature — likely cause (condenser choked),

answers.title: How does a generator produce voltage?
answers.answer_text:
The fundamental principle is electromagnetic induction (Faraday's law): whenever a magnetic
field cuts a conductor, an EMF is induced. In an AC generator a rotating magnetic field (the rotor)
sweeps past the stationary stator windings, inducing the three-phase output.
On a modern brushless machine trace the chain, because that is what the examiner wants:
• A permanent-magnet pilot exciter (PMG) on the shaft generates a small AC supply.
• This feeds the AVR, which controls the current in the main exciter's stationary field.
• The main exciter's rotating armature therefore produces AC, which is rectified by the rotating
diodes mounted on the shaft.
• That DC energises the main rotor field; the spinning rotor field then induces the large three-
phase output in the main stator.
The beauty of the brushless arrangement is that there are no slip rings or brushes to maintain, and
the AVR only has to handle the small exciter-field current, not the full field current.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How does a generator produce voltage?

answers.title: Types of excitation system; the static-excitation principle.
answers.answer_text:
• Separately excited — the field is supplied from a separate DC source (older/simple).
• Self / shunt excited — the machine's own output feeds the field through a rectifier; relies on
residual magnetism to start building.
• Brushless (rotating diode) — as described above; the standard onboard because it is
maintenance-free.

• Static excitation — the generator's own output is stepped down by an excitation transformer,
rectified by a controlled thyristor (SCR) bridge, and the DC is fed back to the field through slip
rings. The AVR gates the thyristors. It gives a very fast response (excitation drawn straight from
the output, so it responds instantly to load) but it does have brushes/slip rings.
• Compound — excitation partly from output voltage and partly from load current, for load
compensation.
Q38 / 502 / 771 / 774 / 1010-1013. Residual magnetism & field flash; generator
started but no voltage; still no voltage after flashing.
Residual magnetism is the small amount of permanent magnetism retained in the exciter/pole iron
even when the machine is de-energised. When the generator is started this residual field induces a
small initial voltage, which the self-excitation circuit then amplifies and builds up to full voltage. If
the residual magnetism is lost — typically after a long lay-up — there is nothing to start the build-up
and the machine produces no voltage.
Field flash restores it: momentarily apply a DC source (a battery) across the field to re-magnetise
the poles, then let normal self-excitation take over. Disconnect the AVR first, because it is a
sensitive electronic device and the reverse current during flashing can damage its output stage.
If there is still no voltage after flashing, the excitation is reaching the field but not getting
through — suspect the rotating diodes on the rotor (open- or short-circuit). Check each diode with a
multimeter: a healthy diode conducts one way and blocks the other; a shorted or open diode is
replaced.
If he presses further —
Which way round for the battery? observe polarity to the field so you reinforce, not oppose, the
residual magnetism — wrong polarity leaves it worse. How do you know a diode is the fault and not
the AVR? if flashing restores nothing and the AVR/sensing check out, the fault is on the rotating
assembly — a shorted diode also over-loads and can burn the exciter.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Types of excitation system; the static-excitation principle.

answers.title: Explain the AVR and how it works.
answers.answer_text:
The Automatic Voltage Regulator keeps the generator terminal voltage constant as the load and
power factor vary. It senses the output voltage (via a PT/CT), compares it with a set reference,
and uses the error to adjust the excitation current to the exciter field. If the voltage sags under
load (or a lagging power factor demands more magnetising current), the AVR increases excitation
to restore it; if the voltage rises, it reduces excitation.
In effect it controls the strength of the magnetic flux by varying the excitation current.
When machines run in parallel, the AVRs also share the reactive (kVAR) load between them (by
droop or cross-current compensation), just as the governors share the real (kW) load.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Explain the AVR and how it works.

answers.title: Generator not producing voltage — actions; what is
answers.answer_text:
reactive power; effect of high reactive power.
No-voltage fault-finding (work the chain): check the AVR and its sensing supply; check/restore
residual magnetism (field flash); check the rotating diodes and exciter; check all connections
and the field circuit. Verify on a mounted voltmeter and, if that is suspect, confirm with a multimeter.

Reactive power (kVAR) arises from the phase difference between voltage and current in
inductive loads (motors, transformers). It flows back and forth doing no net useful work, but it is
essential to magnetise those loads; it is supplied by the generator's excitation.
Effect of too much reactive power: for the same real (kW) output the stator current is higher,
so there are more copper (I²R) losses and more heating, the power factor is poorer, and the
machine and prime mover are more heavily loaded. Reactive load is balanced between paralleled
generators by adjusting their excitation.
2 Synchronising & Parallel Operation

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Generator not producing voltage — actions; what is

answers.title: How do you synchronise aux generators if the synchroscope fails?
answers.answer_text:
First confirm the four synchronising conditions: equal voltage, equal frequency, the same phase
sequence, and in phase. With no synchroscope, use the lamp method across the incoming
breaker:
• Three dark-lamp method — all three lamps go dark together at the synchronising instant; close
the breaker when they are fully dark.
• Two-bright-one-dark (rotating) method — gives the direction of rotation as well, so you can
trim the incoming machine's speed; close at the correct point.
If desperate and no lamps are available, a multimeter across the incoming breaker (same phase
either side) reads the voltage difference: it falls to a minimum (near zero) as the machines come
into phase — close then.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How do you synchronise aux generators if the synchroscope fails?

answers.title: What do you see on the multimeter when synchronised, and when
answers.answer_text:
120° out?
With the meter across the same phase of the open breaker: at in-phase (synchronised) the two
voltages are equal and opposing across the breaker, so the difference is a minimum (near zero) —
the safe point to close. When the machines are 120° out of phase the vector difference is large (of
the order of the line voltage), so the meter reads high — closing there would be like a short-circuit/
out-of-phase paralleling, with a huge current surge and mechanical shock. Never close on a high
reading.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What do you see on the multimeter when synchronised, and when

answers.title: Shaft generators — changing engine speed; parallel with aux
answers.answer_text:
gens; effect of a speed change.
A shaft generator (PTO) is driven by the main engine, so its frequency follows the engine
speed. To run it in parallel with the constant-speed diesel generators, the frequency must be held
constant despite engine-speed changes — this is done through a frequency-controlled converter/
thyristor system (or a synchronous-condenser arrangement).
So if the engine speed changes while on shaft-generator supply, the converter/controller must hold
the output frequency constant; if it cannot, the frequency (and the load distribution) would
change and the machines would fall out of step. In practice, before making a large speed change you
transfer the electrical load to the diesel generators, then change speed, then bring the shaft
generator back on.

3 Motors & Starters

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Shaft generators — changing engine speed; parallel with aux

answers.title: Role of starters — DOL, star-delta, auto-transformer.
answers.answer_text:
The role of a starter is to limit the very high starting current a motor draws while still giving
enough torque to accelerate the load:
Starter Principle & use
Direct-on-line Full voltage applied at once — starting current 6–8× FLC, full starting torque. Simple;
(DOL) for small motors where the current surge is acceptable.
Star-delta Started in star (each winding sees line voltage ÷ √3), then switched to delta for
running. This cuts both the starting current and torque to one-third of DOL. For
larger motors that can start unloaded/lightly loaded.
Auto- Reduced voltage via transformer tappings — gives a better torque-per-amp ratio
transformer than star-delta at the chosen tap. For large motors needing more starting torque.
Modern alternatives are the soft-starter (thyristor ramp) and the variable-frequency drive (VFD),
which give smooth starting and speed control.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Role of starters — DOL, star-delta, auto-transformer.

answers.title: Star-delta circuit; what if it does not change over to delta?
answers.answer_text:
In a star-delta starter the six winding ends are brought out; a contactor first connects them in star,
and after a timer delay a second contactor reconnects them in delta. Because star gives 1/√3 of the
winding voltage, the starting current and torque are reduced to a third.
If it fails to change over to delta, the motor is left running in star at reduced voltage/torque. It
may fail to accelerate the load fully and will draw excess current and overheat (the overload
should trip). To run temporarily you would reduce the load so the motor can cope in star, then
investigate the fault — usually the changeover timer, the delta contactor coil/contacts, or the
control wiring.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Star-delta circuit; what if it does not change over to delta?

answers.title: What is single phasing (and steering-motor overheating from it)?
answers.answer_text:
Single phasing is the loss of one phase of a three-phase supply — a blown fuse, an open contact,
or a broken conductor. With only two phases feeding it, the motor cannot form a proper rotating field:
if stationary it will not start (it just hums and draws locked-rotor current); if already running it
continues on the two phases but draws a much higher current and overheats. This is the
classic reason a running motor such as the steering motor overheats. It is protected by a single-
phasing preventer / phase-failure relay and by properly-set overloads.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What is single phasing (and steering-motor overheating from it)?

answers.title: Motor checks; procedure to repair an electric motor; continuity
answers.answer_text:
value.
Checks: insulation resistance (megger) windings-to-earth and between phases (looking for low IR
from moisture/damage), continuity of the windings, bearing condition, air gap, terminal-box
tightness, the space heater, and correct overload settings.

Repair procedure: risk assessment and permit; isolate and lock-out/tag-out; prove dead; note
and photograph the connections so they go back correctly; discharge any stored energy; then
remove/repair. Megger before re-energising and dry out the windings if the IR is low.
Continuity of a healthy circuit is close to zero (~1 Ω or less — it is a low-resistance path). Insulation
resistance should be high (megohms) — the two tests sit at opposite ends of the scale, so don't
confuse them.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Motor checks; procedure to repair an electric motor; continuity

answers.title: Why do motors fail; compare synchronous and induction motors.
answers.answer_text:
Motor failure causes: single phasing; overload; insulation breakdown (moisture, heat, ageing,
contamination); bearing failure; and over/under-voltage.
Induction (asynchronous) Synchronous
Speed Just below synchronous (slip); varies Exactly synchronous, independent of load
slightly with load
Excitation None — field induced in the rotor Separate DC field — so power factor can be
controlled/corrected
Starting Self-starting No starting torque — needs a starting method
Use Simple, rugged, cheap — most Large, constant-speed / electric propulsion;
auxiliary drives power-factor correction

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Why do motors fail; compare synchronous and induction motors.

answers.title: How do main-propulsion synchronous motors start to turn?
answers.answer_text:
A synchronous motor has no inherent starting torque, so it must be brought up to speed by
another means: either it is run up as an induction motor using its damper (amortisseur)
windings, or — in a diesel-electric ship — a variable-frequency converter starts it from a very low
frequency and ramps up. As it approaches synchronous speed the DC field is applied and the rotor
pulls into step (synchronism). Thereafter its speed is set by the supply frequency from the
converter.
4 Protection, Discrimination & Switchboard

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How do main-propulsion synchronous motors start to turn?

answers.title: Overcurrent and discrimination; why do fuses get smaller
answers.answer_text:
toward the consumer?
Overcurrent is any current above the rated value — either an overload (moderate, sustained) or a
short-circuit (very high, instantaneous). It is cleared by fuses, overload relays and circuit-breakers
that have a time-current (inverse) characteristic: the bigger the fault, the faster they trip.
Discrimination (selectivity) is the coordination of these devices so that only the device
immediately upstream of the fault operates, isolating just the faulty branch while the rest of the
network stays live. It is achieved by grading the current and time settings — downstream
devices are set lower/faster than upstream ones.

That is exactly why the protection gets progressively smaller toward the consumer: the
smallest, fastest device is nearest the load, so on a fault it clears first, protecting the cable it feeds
and preserving supply to everything upstream. If the ratings were the same, a small fault could trip a
large upstream breaker and black out a whole section.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Overcurrent and discrimination; why do fuses get smaller

answers.title: Switchboard safeties; finding an earth fault; why multiple earths
answers.answer_text:
are dangerous.
Switchboard protection devices: overcurrent/short-circuit trips, reverse power, under/over-
voltage, under/over-frequency, preferential (load-shedding) trips, and earth-fault
indication.
Finding an earth fault (insulated system): the fault is shown by the earth-fault lamps/monitor
(one phase's lamp dims, the others brighten). Trace it by switching off circuits one at a time until
the lamps balance, isolating the faulty feeder — the usual culprits are in galley, laundry and deck
lighting (heat and moisture).
Why multiple earths are dangerous: on an insulated (IT) system a single earth fault does not trip
anything (that is the whole point — continuity of supply). But a second earth fault on a different
phase creates a short-circuit through the hull, with a large fault current and possible fire — so the
first fault must always be found and cleared promptly.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Switchboard safeties; finding an earth fault; why multiple earths

answers.title: How is reverse power tested?
answers.answer_text:
With the generator paralleled onto the bus, slowly reduce its governor/fuel setting so that
instead of supplying power it begins to take power from the bus (motoring). Confirm that the
reverse-power relay trips its breaker at the set percentage of rated power. Typical settings: diesel
prime mover ~5–15% (it takes a fair amount to motor a diesel), turbine ~2–5% (a turbine motors
easily and is more vulnerable). Reverse-power protection stops a generator that has lost its drive from
being motored, which would damage the prime mover and waste power.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How is reverse power tested?

answers.title: ACB fails — removal; arcing on contacts; checking
answers.answer_text:
a replacement breaker; unlabelled breaker; fault current on 690 V; impedance.
Removing a breaker: trip it and rack it out to the isolated position, discharge the closing springs,
apply lock-out/tag-out, and prove dead. Severe arcing/pitting on the main contacts indicates
worn or high-resistance contacts, a loose connection, or repeated heavy fault-clearing —
the contact resistance rises, generates heat, and the arcing gets worse.
Checking a replacement breaker is suitable: confirm the rated current (A), the rated
breaking capacity (kA — it must exceed the prospective short-circuit level at that board),
the rated voltage, the number of poles, and the trip settings. Then test insulation and contact
resistance, and verify the over-current trip by primary/secondary current injection before
putting it into service. Never fit an unlabelled breaker without confirming these ratings.
Fault current on a 690 V system is set by the source short-circuit level: I = MVA / (√3 × V),
fault
or calculated from the total source impedance to the fault. This is the figure the breaker's breaking
capacity must exceed.
Impedance (Z) is the total opposition to AC current flow — the combination of resistance (R) and
reactance (X): Z = √(R² + X²). Reactance is frequency-dependent (X = 2πfL), which is why AC
L
circuits behave differently from DC.

5 Emergency Generator & Blackout

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: ACB fails — removal; arcing on contacts; checking

answers.title: SOLAS regulations and construction for the
answers.answer_text:
emergency generator (ref MGN 52).
• Independent and self-contained, with its own emergency switchboard separate from the
main board.
• Located above the bulkhead/freeboard deck, outside the main machinery casing, in its own A-
class boundaried room with independent ventilation and access from the open deck.
• Its own fuel supply, with a fuel flash point >43°C, sufficient for the required duration (typically
18 h on a passenger ship, 36 h on a cargo ship — check the flag/ship type).
• Must start automatically within 45 seconds of a main-power failure, with two independent
means of starting (e.g. battery and air/hydraulic) or a 30-minute manual-start capability.
• Own lighting, a fire extinguisher in the room, and clear instructions; subject to weekly start
tests and monthly/quarterly on-load tests.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: SOLAS regulations and construction for the

answers.title: How the emergency generator starts on blackout / when the main
answers.answer_text:
generator fails; not coming on load.
On loss of the main busbar voltage, an under-voltage relay monitoring the main bus signals the
automatic starting unit, which cranks and starts the emergency generator. When it reaches the
correct voltage and frequency it closes onto the emergency switchboard and restores the
essential/emergency services. The whole sequence must complete within 45 seconds.
If it does not come on load: check the auto-start sequence and under-voltage trigger, the
starting means (battery charge/air pressure/hydraulic), fuel, the AVR/excitation and governor,
and the emergency-switchboard breaker and the changeover interlock from the main bus —
the machine may be running but failing to connect because the load-transfer contactor or interlock
has not operated.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How the emergency generator starts on blackout / when the main

answers.title: Which loads are connected to the emergency switchboard?
answers.answer_text:
The services needed for safety of life and to keep the ship under control: emergency and
escape lighting, navigation lights and aids, GMDSS/radio, one steering-gear supply, the fire pump
and fire detection, sprinkler/watertight-door power, the general alarm and internal communications,
emergency bilge, and the controls for essential machinery.
6 Shore Power & Earthing Systems

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Which loads are connected to the emergency switchboard?

answers.title: Shore-power connection — procedure and
answers.answer_text:
checks; frequency/voltage/phase mismatch.
Before connecting: verify the shore supply's voltage, frequency and phase sequence/rotation
match the ship, and check the cable insulation; connect the earth/hull-to-shore bond first.

Because the ship's generators and the shore supply are not synchronised together, the changeover is
normally a dead (blackout) changeover: take the ship's electrical load off, stop the generators, and
then energise the board from shore. This avoids any attempt to parallel two unsynchronised sources.
If frequency, voltage or phase do not match: you cannot parallel — a mismatch would cause
huge circulating currents and damage. Confirm the equipment is rated for the shore frequency (a 50
Hz shore supply on a 60 Hz ship would run motors slow and overflux transformers), and use the
dead changeover; if incompatible, do not connect.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Shore-power connection — procedure and

answers.title: The extra earth wire at the shore connection — why is it given?
answers.answer_text:
(insulated earth system)
Ships normally run an insulated (unearthed) neutral system so that a single earth fault does
not trip the supply — continuity of supply is vital at sea. The extra conductor at the shore
connection is the protective earth bond between the ship's hull and the shore earth. It ensures
the hull sits at shore-earth potential for personnel safety during the connection, without earthing
the ship's own live system (so the insulated arrangement is preserved).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: The extra earth wire at the shore connection — why is it given?

answers.title: Types of earthing systems.
answers.answer_text:
The recognised arrangements are TN (subdivided TN-S, TN-C, TN-C-S), TT and IT. Ships almost always
use an IT (insulated) system because a first earth fault only raises an alarm rather than tripping the
supply — essential where a sudden loss of power could hazard the ship. The trade-off is that earth
faults must be actively monitored and cleared before a second one occurs.
7 High Voltage & Diesel-Electric Propulsion

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Types of earthing systems.

answers.title: Why HV; HV safety precautions and working procedure;
answers.answer_text:
isolating an HV motor.
Why HV: for large power — electric propulsion, big thrusters — using a higher voltage means a lower
current for the same power, so cables and switchgear are smaller and lighter and the I²R
losses are lower. That is why cruise ships and large tankers with electric propulsion use 6.6 kV or 11
kV.
Safety / procedure to work on HV (the earthing-down point is the crucial one):
• Permission and a permit to work, a risk assessment, and limitation of access to competent
authorised persons.
• Isolation per a documented switching plan, then lock-out/tag-out, with interlocks preventing
generator start and breaker closure.
• Sanction to test before any live testing.
• Earth down: discharge the residual voltage (HV cables/machines hold a dangerous charge even
when isolated), close the neutral earthing resistor and fit earthing straps to the windings
before touching them.
• Correct PPE and procedures per COSWP / the company SMS.

Diesel-electric propulsion: the generators feed a network that supplies the propulsion motors
through converters (synchro-conversion or cyclo-conversion) which control speed; these
converters generate harmonics (distortion of the sine wave) that must be filtered, and the
propulsion electric motors (PEMs) are air- or water-cooled.
If he presses further —
Why earth down if it is already isolated? HV cables and windings retain a stored charge
(capacitance); the earthing straps drain it safely and hold it at earth so it cannot become live again
through back-feed or induction. Which harmonics are a problem? the low-order ones (5th, 7th, 11th)
cause heating and interference; they are reduced by filters and by 12-pulse/multi-pulse converter
arrangements.
8 Shaft Earthing & Thrust Block
Q775 / 1014-1017. Why is shaft earthing required; how do you know it is working;
problems if it fails?
Shaft earthing uses a slip-ring and brush (or silver-graphite brush) to bond the rotating
propeller shaft to the hull. Without it, a voltage builds up between the shaft and the hull (from the
propeller acting as a dissimilar-metal cell in sea water, and from stray currents), and this voltage
would discharge through the oil film in the bearings and thrust block. It is monitored by a
shaft-potential (millivolt) meter mounted at the earthing device; if that meter is faulty, confirm
with a multimeter.
If the earthing fails: the shaft-to-hull voltage discharges across the bearing oil films, causing
electrical pitting / spark-erosion of the bearing white metal and the thrust surfaces — a
distinctive frosted/pitted damage that ruins the bearings.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Why HV; HV safety precautions and working procedure;

answers.title: Checks on holding-down bolts; how is thrust transmitted to
answers.answer_text:
the hull (thrust block)?
Holding-down bolts: check them for tightness and for fretting/corrosion at the seating, and look
for any movement, cracked chocks or slackness — a loose thrust-block seating lets the block shift
and disturbs alignment.
Thrust block — how thrust reaches the hull: the propeller thrust is carried along the shaft to a
thrust collar forged on (or fitted to) the shaft; the collar bears against tilting white-metal thrust
pads (Michell type), which form an oil-film wedge and transmit the force into the thrust-block
housing; the housing passes it through the holding-down bolts and the seating into the ship's
structure — and that reaction on the structure is what actually drives the hull forward. There are
separate pads for ahead and astern thrust.

9 Batteries

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Checks on holding-down bolts; how is thrust transmitted to

answers.title: Lead-acid battery checks; specific gravity; lifeboat charging & trickle
answers.answer_text:
charging.
Checks: specific gravity (hydrometer, temperature-corrected), terminal voltage on load,
electrolyte level (top up with distilled water only), terminal cleanliness and greasing, ventilation of the
battery space (hydrogen evolution), and temperature.
Specific gravity: about 1.24–1.28 when fully charged, falling to around 1.11 when discharged. A cell
reading well below the others indicates a failing cell.
Trickle charging is a small continuous charge that just balances the self-discharge, keeping the
battery fully charged and ready. Its main benefit is preventing sulphation — the growth of hard
lead-sulphate crystals on the plates that occurs when a battery is left standing discharged and which
permanently reduces its capacity.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Lead-acid battery checks; specific gravity; lifeboat charging & trickle

answers.title: Checks on a lithium-ion battery.
answers.answer_text:
Li-ion cells are sealed, so there is no specific-gravity check. Monitoring is done through the
Battery Management System (BMS): individual cell voltages and cell balancing,
temperature, charge/discharge current, and state of charge. Also check ventilation/cooling, terminal
integrity, and the fire and thermal-runaway safeguards — Li-ion must never be over-charged,
over-discharged or allowed to over-heat, as a damaged cell can go into thermal runaway.
10 Hazardous-Area (Ex) Equipment

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Checks on a lithium-ion battery.

answers.title: Precautions using lamps/electrical fittings in tanker deck (hazardous) areas —
answers.answer_text:
Ex types.
On tankers, all electrical equipment in a hazardous zone must be certified for that zone, gas
group and temperature class so it cannot ignite a flammable atmosphere. The protection
concepts:
Type Protection principle
Ex d Flameproof — a robust enclosure contains any internal explosion and cools the escaping
gases below ignition temperature
Ex e Increased safety — construction that prevents arcs, sparks or hot surfaces in normal service
Ex i Intrinsically safe — the circuit energy is limited so no spark or hot surface can ignite the
gas, even under fault
Ex p Pressurised / purged — a protective gas keeps the flammable atmosphere out of the
enclosure

Ex n / Ex Non-sparking (normal running) / special protection
s
Why especially on tankers: the cargo vapours make the deck a hazardous zone, so a hand-lamp or
fitting that would be harmless in the engine room could ignite the atmosphere unless it is certified.

answers.title: What is Ex i (intrinsic safety) — the circuit-energy values?
answers.answer_text:
Intrinsically safe equipment works by limiting the electrical energy available in the circuit —
both the energy that can be stored (in capacitance/inductance) and the energy released in a spark —
to below the level that could ignite the specified gas, even under fault conditions. As a guide the
limits are of the order of ~30 V, ~50 mA, ~25 mW and ~200 µJ of stored energy. The safety comes
from circuit design and safety barriers, not from the strength of an enclosure — which is why Ex i
is used for low-power instrumentation and portable devices in the most hazardous zones.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What is Ex i (intrinsic safety) — the circuit-energy values?

answers.title: Venting arrangements — which tanks have flame-arrestor gauze, and the
answers.answer_text:
danger?
Cargo and bunker tank vents (and, where fitted, ballast-tank vents that could contain vapour) are
provided with flame-arrestor gauze/screens together with pressure/vacuum (P/V) valves. The
gauze quenches any external flame so it cannot flash back into the tank. The danger is that a
corroded, dirty or iced-over gauze blocks the vent: the tank can then be over-pressurised
during loading or drawn into vacuum during discharge, risking structural damage to the tank
top or bottom. So the gauzes must be kept clean, clear and in good condition, and the P/V valves
proven free.

Naval Architecture &
Stability
1 Buoyancy & Floatation

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Venting arrangements — which tanks have flame-arrestor gauze, and the

answers.title: What is the centre of buoyancy; how does a ship float?
answers.answer_text:
Centre of buoyancy (B) is the geometric centre (centroid) of the underwater volume of the
hull — the single point through which the whole upthrust of the displaced water acts, vertically
upward. Because it depends on the shape of the immersed volume, B moves when the ship changes
draught, trims, or heels.
How a ship floats — Archimedes' principle: a floating body displaces a volume of water whose
weight equals the weight of the body. Equilibrium needs two things: the buoyancy force
equals the weight (magnitude), and the two forces act along the same vertical line (so there is
no upsetting couple). When both hold, the ship floats at rest.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What is the centre of buoyancy; how does a ship float?

answers.title: Reserve of buoyancy; what does a two-compartment ship mean?
answers.answer_text:
Reserve of buoyancy is the volume of the intact, watertight hull above the waterline — the
buoyancy held "in reserve" that comes into play if the ship is loaded deeper or is bilged. It is provided
by the freeboard and is usually expressed as a percentage of the total volume. The Load Line
Convention exists precisely to guarantee a minimum reserve of buoyancy by fixing a minimum
freeboard.
A two-compartment ship is one designed to remain afloat and adequately stable with any
two adjacent main compartments flooded (a one-compartment ship survives one). The standard
applied depends on ship type, length and service — passenger ships carry the higher standard.

2 Transverse Stability Fundamentals

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Reserve of buoyancy; what does a two-compartment ship mean?

answers.title: What is GM; explain the metacentre.
answers.answer_text:
GM (metacentric height) is the vertical distance between the centre of gravity G and the
metacentre M, and it is the measure of a ship's initial transverse stability. A positive GM (G
below M) means the ship is stable and will right herself; a negative GM means she is unstable.
The metacentre (M): when the ship heels a small angle, B moves out to the low side; the vertical
line of buoyancy through the new B intersects the original centreline at M. For small angles
(up to ~10–15°) M is effectively a fixed point, which is why GM is a good measure of initial stability. It
is found from KM = KB + BM, where BM = I/V (the second moment of the waterplane area over the
displaced volume), and then GM = KM − KG.
If he presses further —
Stiff vs tender: a large GM gives a short rolling period — a "stiff" ship that snaps back quickly and
stresses cargo and structure; a small GM gives a long, slow roll — a "tender" ship, comfortable but with
little reserve. The rolling period T = 2πk/√(g·GM) links the two, so you can estimate GM from the roll
period. Why only small angles? beyond ~15° the waterplane shape changes and M shifts, so GM alone
no longer describes stability — you use the GZ curve.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What is GM; explain the metacentre.

answers.title: How does a ship return to upright when it rolls; difference
answers.answer_text:
between heel and list.
When the ship heels, B shifts to the immersed (low) side while G stays put. The buoyancy (acting up
through the new B) and the weight (down through G) are now offset, forming a righting couple
whose lever is GZ (the horizontal distance from G to the line of buoyancy). The righting moment W
× GZ rotates the ship back to upright — provided GM is positive. The bigger the GZ at that angle, the
stronger the return.
Heel vs list:heel is a temporary, dynamic inclination caused by an external force — wind, a turn, or
waves; it disappears when the force is removed. List is a permanent inclination caused by an off-
centre weight or a negative GM (loll); it stays until the cause is corrected.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How does a ship return to upright when it rolls; difference

answers.title: Positive GM importance; dangers of a negative GM; the GZ curve and IMO
answers.answer_text:
criteria.
A positive GM guarantees a righting moment at every small angle, so the ship is stable. But too
much or too little is a problem: a very large GM makes her stiff (violent rolling, cargo/structure
stress), a small GM makes her tender (sluggish, easily heeled). A negative GM is dangerous — she
is unstable upright and will either loll or, in the worst case, capsize.
GZ curve: a plot of the righting lever GZ against angle of heel. From it you read the maximum GZ,
the range of stability, the angle of vanishing stability, and — from the area under the curve
— the dynamic stability (the energy needed to heel her to that angle). At small angles the initial
slope equals GM (GZ = GM at 57.3°).

IMO intact-stability criteria (have these ready): area under GZ to 30° ≥ 0.055 m·rad; to 40° ≥
0.09; between 30° and 40° ≥ 0.03; GZ ≥ 0.20 m at 30°; maximum GZ at an angle ≥ 25°; and initial
GM ≥ 0.15 m.
3 Free Surface Effect & Angle of Loll

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Positive GM importance; dangers of a negative GM; the GZ curve and IMO

answers.title: Free surface effect — the mechanism, and what engineers do that
answers.answer_text:
affects G and M.
Free surface effect (FSE): when a tank is only partly full ("slack"), the liquid is free to move; as the
ship heels, that liquid runs to the low side, shifting its weight outboard. The effect is exactly as if G
had risen to a virtual position Gᵛ — a "virtual rise of G" — which reduces the effective GM and
the righting lever, even though no weight has actually been added or moved into the ship.
The loss is i × ρ / W, where i is the second moment of area of the free surface. The crucial points: it
depends on the surface area, not the depth of liquid, and it is independent of where the tank
is in the ship. It also reduces with the cube of the number of subdivisions — which is why tanks
have baffles.
Engineers cause it by running tanks slack — fuel/ballast transfers, part-full settling and service
tanks, or careless bunkering. Minimise it by keeping tanks pressed up or empty, by using the tank
subdivision/baffles, and by not having many slack tanks open at once.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Free surface effect — the mechanism, and what engineers do that

answers.title: Angle of loll; scenario — one wing tank half full, she takes a
answers.answer_text:
loll, what do you do?
Angle of loll is the angle a ship with an initially negative GM lolls over to and settles at, where the
righting lever GZ has returned to zero. She is unstable about the upright but finds a stable
equilibrium at the loll angle — and will "flop" from that angle to the same angle on the other side,
which is dangerous because any further upset can carry her over.
Correction (this is the trap the surveyor sets): the aim is to lower G and remove free surface
to restore a positive GM. Do not simply start filling the high-side tank — as GM is negative, that
added weight on the high side can accelerate her right over. Instead, top up the lowest, centreline
tanks first (or press up the low/slack tank carefully) to kill the free surface and lower G, watching
the ship's behaviour at every step; as GM turns positive she will come upright. In the wing-tank
case, the half-full wing tank is giving both an off-centre weight and free surface — press it up or
empty it to remove both.
If he presses further —
Why does filling the high side make it worse? with a negative GM the ship is already in unstable
equilibrium; adding weight high and to windward raises G further and adds an upsetting moment before
GM can recover — she can flop past the point of no return. How do you know GM is negative and
not just a list from weight? a loll flops to either side and the angle is the same both ways; a list from
an off-centre weight stays to one side.
