answers.title: How far can a ship heel before it capsizes?
answers.answer_text:
She capsizes once she is heeled beyond the angle of vanishing stability — the angle at which the
GZ curve returns to zero and the righting lever becomes negative, so instead of righting she continues
over. Its value depends on loading and hull form, but for a typical vessel it is of the order of 70°. Up to
that point there is still a positive righting lever trying to bring her back.
4 Damage Stability & Subdivision

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How far can a ship heel before it capsizes?

answers.title: What is damage stability and how is it calculated?
answers.answer_text:
Damage stability is the ability of the ship to stay afloat and remain adequately stable after
flooding of one or more compartments. It is governed by SOLAS Ch II-1, assessed two ways:
• Probabilistic method (current SOLAS): the attained subdivision index A must be ≥ the
required index R. A is built up by combining, for every conceivable damage case, the
probability of that damage occurring with the probability of surviving it — so it rewards
subdivision that actually improves survivability.
• Deterministic method (the older/basis approach): uses floodable length, the margin line
and the factor of subdivision to fix bulkhead spacing so that flooding does not immerse the
ship past the margin line.
Onboard, the mate calculates the actual damaged condition on the loading computer/loadicator
using the approved stability information, checking the residual GM, heel, and range against the
criteria.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What is damage stability and how is it calculated?

answers.title: Explain floodable length and factor of subdivision.
answers.answer_text:
Floodable length at any point along the ship is the maximum length of compartment, centred
at that point, that can be flooded without the ship sinking below the margin line (a line
drawn 76 mm below the bulkhead deck). It depends on the permeability of the space — how much
of it can actually fill with water (a store ~60%, a machinery space ~85%, a tank ~95–98%).
The factor of subdivision is a number less than one (depending on ship length and service) applied
to the floodable length to give the permissible length — which is what actually fixes how far apart
the watertight bulkheads may be. A smaller factor means closer bulkheads and a higher
subdivision standard (e.g. a passenger ship required to survive more flooded compartments).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Explain floodable length and factor of subdivision.

answers.title: Flooding one tank — effect on GM; minimum GM.
answers.answer_text:
Flooding a tank has several effects at once: it adds weight low down (bodily sinkage), it
introduces free surface, and it can shift B and change trim/heel. The net effect on GM depends on
the tank, but the free surface and the sinkage usually give a reduction in effective GM together
with a heel/trim. The lost-buoyancy method (treating the bilged space as no longer providing
buoyancy) or the added-weight method is used to work it out.
The damage-stability rules require a minimum residual GM (of the order of ≥ 0.05 m) and set limits
on the heel, the range of positive stability and the area under the residual GZ curve after
damage — the loading computer confirms these are satisfied for the damage case.

5 Watertight Integrity

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Flooding one tank — effect on GM; minimum GM.

answers.title: Watertight doors — classes, operating times; where do you find the
answers.answer_text:
information?
Watertight doors in the main subdivision are covered by SOLAS Ch II-1. Types: power-operated
sliding doors (in main transverse bulkheads below the bulkhead deck), and hinged or rolling doors
in less critical positions. Key requirements for the power sliding doors:
• They must close in about 20–40 seconds and be operable locally from both sides and
remotely from the bridge.
• Position indicators on the bridge and an audible warning before/while closing.
• An independent power/stored-energy source so they still operate on blackout; they are kept
closed at sea.
The details (locations, classes, closing arrangements) are found in the ship's stability booklet, the
capacity/GA plan and the SOLAS training manual.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Watertight doors — classes, operating times; where do you find the

answers.title: Openings in the machinery space affecting watertight integrity; funnel
answers.answer_text:
flaps.
Openings to watch (each must have an approved weathertight/watertight closing appliance):
skylights, machinery-space doors, ventilators, sounding pipes, air/vent pipes (fitted with
automatic float closures), side scuttles, and the funnel/uptake. Any of these left open in bad
weather is a downflooding path.
Funnel flaps are dampers in the boiler/engine uptakes. They are closed to keep water out in
heavy weather and can help contain or starve a fire in the uptake, and are opened for normal
running to let the exhaust/gases out.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Openings in the machinery space affecting watertight integrity; funnel

answers.title: Collision bulkhead and passenger-vessel watertight integrity.
answers.answer_text:
The collision bulkhead is the foremost watertight transverse bulkhead, positioned a set
distance abaft the forward perpendicular (broadly 0.05L to 0.08L from the FP). It has no doors
below the bulkhead deck — at most a single pipe fitted with a screw-down valve operable from
above the deck. Its purpose is to limit flooding if the bow is holed (a common collision damage).
Passenger vessels are built to higher subdivision and damage-stability standards with more
extensive watertight subdivision, to meet the greater survival requirement for the numbers of people
carried.
6 Fire Integrity — Bulkhead Classes

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Collision bulkhead and passenger-vessel watertight integrity.

answers.title: Bulkhead classes A, B, C; A-60 requirements; where are the
answers.answer_text:
A-60 divisions?
Class Requirement

A Steel or equivalent, non-combustible; must prevent the passage of flame and
(A-60/30/15/0) smoke for 60 minutes in the standard fire test, and be insulated so the average
temperature rise on the unexposed face stays ≤ 140°C (peak 180°C) for the rated
period. A-60 = 60 min insulation, A-0 = integrity only, no insulation requirement.
B (B-15/0) Non-combustible; restricts flame passage for 30 minutes, with insulation limiting the
temperature rise for 15 or 0 minutes.
C Made of non-combustible material only — no integrity or temperature-rise rating.
A-60 divisions bound the high-fire-risk and high-value spaces — machinery spaces, the CO₂
room, control stations, and the boundaries between accommodation and machinery.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Bulkhead classes A, B, C; A-60 requirements; where are the

answers.title: Who decides the bulkhead selection; what is a Category A
answers.answer_text:
machinery space?
Selection of divisions is governed by the fire-integrity tables of SOLAS Ch II-2, which specify
the required class based on the fire risk of the spaces on either side of the boundary.
Category A machinery space is a space (and its trunks) that contains internal-combustion
machinery used for main propulsion, or for other purposes where the combined power is ≥ 375
kW, or any space containing an oil-fired boiler or an oil-fuel unit. These are the highest-risk
spaces and carry the strictest requirements — fixed fire-fighting, A-60 boundaries, and extra means of
escape.
7 Load Line

answers.title: Load Line Convention — what is checked and why; what
answers.answer_text:
certificate is issued?
The International Convention on Load Lines (ICLL 1966) assigns each ship a minimum
freeboard (and therefore a maximum permissible draught) to guarantee an adequate reserve of
buoyancy and the watertight/weathertight integrity that goes with it. It issues the International
Load Line Certificate, and the hull is marked with the Plimsoll disc and the seasonal/zonal load
lines (S, W, WNA, T, F, TF).
The survey checks the load-line and deck-line marks and the conditions of assignment: the
closing appliances (hatch covers, weathertight doors, ventilators, air pipes), freeing ports, guard rails,
side scuttles, means of access and the structural strength — so that the assigned freeboard remains
valid and the ship keeps its reserve of buoyancy.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Load Line Convention — what is checked and why; what

answers.title: Conditions of assignment; weather-door test (chalk); ballast-tank
answers.answer_text:
air-vent check.
Conditions of assignment cover the structural strength, the protection of openings, guard rails,
freeing arrangements and safe crew access — everything that keeps the water out and the reserve of
buoyancy intact.
• Weathertight door test (chalk test): rub chalk on the knife-edge/coaming, close the door
onto the gasket, then open and look for a continuous chalk imprint on the gasket — a break in
the line shows a poor seal to be adjusted.
• Ballast-tank air vents: check the automatic ball/float closures in the vent heads operate
freely and seal, so they close if the deck is awash — protecting the weathertight integrity.
8 Hull Stresses

answers.title: Stresses on a bulk carrier and an oil tanker (racking, hogging, sagging …
answers.answer_text:
and the others he wants).
Divide them into static (longitudinal) and dynamic — that structure is what the examiner is after:
Stress Cause / effect
Hogging Buoyancy concentrated amidships and weight at the ends (or a wave crest
amidships) — the ship arches, putting the deck in tension and the keel in
compression.
Sagging Weight amidships, buoyancy at the ends (wave trough amidships) — she droops,
putting the deck in compression and the keel in tension.
Racking Transverse distortion of the structure as the ship rolls — resisted by the transverse
frames and bulkheads.
Panting The in-and-out "breathing" of the shell plating at the ends from the fluctuating
water pressure as the ship pitches — resisted by panting beams/stringers forward.
Pounding / Heavy impact on the forward bottom when the bow emerges and slams back in a
slamming seaway — the reason for extra bottom strengthening forward.
The overall hull-girder loads are expressed as shear force and bending moment, which the loading
computer keeps within class limits; there are also thermal stresses (from cargo/ambient
temperature) and torsional stresses (important on open-deck container ships).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Stresses on a bulk carrier and an oil tanker (racking, hogging, sagging …

answers.title: Precautions when loading cargo in a bulk carrier.
answers.answer_text:
The overriding concern is not to overstress the hull girder or the double-bottom structure —
bulk carriers have been lost to structural failure. So: follow the approved loading/deballasting
sequence, keep the bending moment and shear force within limits at every stage on the
loadicator, avoid excessive alternate-hold loading concentrations, match the loading rate to the
deballasting rate, and watch trim, stress and stability continuously. Also guard against cargo shift
and, for certain cargoes, moisture/liquefaction.

9 Trim & Stability for Drydocking

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Precautions when loading cargo in a bulk carrier.

answers.title: Why trim by the stern for docking; how are the blocks set?
answers.answer_text:
The ship is given a small trim by the stern so that when the dock is pumped down she lands on
the after keel blocks first, and then settles forward in a controlled, progressive way as the
water level drops — rather than landing all along the keel at once. The keel blocks are set to the
ship's docking plan, which is sent to the yard in advance so the blocks align with the keel and fall
under the structure and bulkheads (not under, say, a bilge keel or a sea chest).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Why trim by the stern for docking; how are the blocks set?

answers.title: Going to drydock — concerns as chief; why no slack tanks / keep
answers.answer_text:
tanks pressed up?
The central concern is the critical instant during docking. As the ship touches the blocks and the
dock continues to pump down, the blocks take an increasing share of the weight (an upthrust
P at the keel) while the waterplane area shrinks, so BM (= I/V) falls and the effective GM
reduces — a virtual loss of GM. If GM went negative before she was fully and evenly on the blocks,
she could list or slip off the blocks. The effective GM is roughly GM ≈ GM − (P × KM)/W.
v
That is why the ship must arrive upright, with adequate GM, and with no slack tanks — the
tanks are pressed up or emptied to eliminate free surface, because a free-surface loss on top of
the docking loss of GM at the worst moment is exactly what must be avoided.
If he presses further —
When is the critical instant? the moment the stern is fully landed and the ship is about to become
wholly supported — the point of least effective GM before she is safely down on the full length of blocks.
What else do you check before docking? take M/E crankshaft deflections and tank soundings at
anchor to compare after docking, and confirm the docking plan matches the block layout.

Drydocking, Survey, Hull,
Propeller & Shaft
1 Drydock Preparation & Planning

answers.title: Preparing for drydock — the timeline from ~6
answers.answer_text:
months to docking; what you send/need from the yard.
Present it as a countdown — it shows you manage the docking, not just attend it.
~6 months out: review every certificate expiry and the class survey status (CMS items, special
survey, tailshaft), list all jobs that genuinely need a dock (bottom, tailshaft, sea valves, anodes,
coating), build the DD work specification, order long-lead spares and materials, select and
book the yard, and gather the drawings.
Weeks out: firm up the work list and get quotations, arrange the third-party contractors
(propeller, coating, class-approved gauging), order the shore services, plan the tank cleaning /
gas-freeing and the deballast sequence, and clear outstanding PMS so nothing avoidable is
carried into the dock.
Sent to the yard in advance: the docking plan, the GA drawing, the shell expansion plan, the
DD work specification, the list of owner's third-party companies, and the hull-coating specification.
Services required from the yard: shore power, fire main and fire watch (the ship's own fire main is
off), fresh water, compressed air, cooling water, two gangways, lighting, sewage/effluent disposal,
and cranage/staging.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Preparing for drydock — the timeline from ~6

answers.title: Interval between drydocks; when can you get away with an
answers.answer_text:
in-water survey?
SOLAS and class require the ship's bottom to be examined twice in any five-year period, with a
maximum of 36 months between examinations, tied to the renewal-survey cycle. One of these
examinations may be an in-water (underwater) survey in lieu of docking, but only if class is
satisfied that the ship is in good condition and has:
• a 5-year antifouling scheme and a 5-year anode/ICCP scheme that keep the underwater hull
protected between dockings,
• an approved tailshaft (oil-lubricated seal + monitoring) arrangement, and
• a good coating and structural condition — and it is generally not permitted for passenger
ships.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Interval between drydocks; when can you get away with an

answers.title: Relieving the Chief with the ship going to dock / on anchorage
answers.answer_text:
one day out; condition the tanker should arrive in.
Handover / preparation: take over the certificates and survey status, ROB/bunkers,
outstanding defects and NCs, planned works and spares; finalise the work list and drawings;
plan the deballast and tank cleaning; and take M/E crankshaft deflections and tank
soundings at anchor to compare after docking.
Arrival condition: upright, a small trim by the stern, an adequate GM, no slack tanks (free
surface eliminated), gas-free where entry/hot-work is planned, and deballasted to the docking
condition — this is what protects stability through the critical instant when she lands on the blocks.
2 Dock-Bottom & Walk-Around Inspection

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Relieving the Chief with the ship going to dock / on anchorage

answers.title: Immediate inspection as soon as she is out of the water; first thing
answers.answer_text:
you want the yard to do.
As soon as the dock is drained, have the yard wash/hydro-blast the hull so the coating and any
damage can be seen. Then, crucially, take the "as-found" rudder and stern-gear clearances
before anything moves (weardown readings are only valid before the ship is disturbed), check the
rudder for water ingress (drain plug), and inspect the coating, bilge keel, sea chests and gratings.
Taking the clearances first is the point the surveyor is watching for.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Immediate inspection as soon as she is out of the water; first thing

answers.title: Take me through the dock inspection, aft to forward / full
answers.answer_text:
round once she is on the blocks.
Work methodically aft to forward and say what you look for at each:
• Propeller: cavitation erosion, cracks (root and edges, by DPI), pitting, the boss, nut and locking
plate; blade tip clearances.
• Rudder: pintle/bearing weardown and jumping clearance, rudder stock and carrier bearing,
fitted bolts (fretting), drain plug/water ingress.
• Stern tube: the seals, chrome liner, and tailshaft weardown (poker gauge).

• Bottom and sides: bilge keel, sea chests and gratings, inlets/discharges, anodes/ICCP, shell
plating (dents, corrosion, coating breakdown), the bulb bow, and the thrusters.
Corrosion hot-spots to mention: the wind-and-water (waterline) band, the boot-topping, aft near the
propeller (turbulence + galvanic effects), weld seams, and around sea chests and discharges.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Take me through the dock inspection, aft to forward / full

answers.title: Before-flooding walk-around; how is the sea-chest grating secured;
answers.answer_text:
refloat checks.
Before flooding confirm: all docking/drain plugs refitted, the rudder drain plug in, the locking
plate on the CPP propeller nut fitted, sea valves in the correct position, staging removed, and the
sea-chest gratings secured — typically with locking wire. On refloat: check for leaks/ingress,
re-check clearances, and re-take crankshaft deflections to compare with the anchor readings,
because the hull changes shape slightly as it takes the water again.
3 Hull & Shell Plating

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Before-flooding walk-around; how is the sea-chest grating secured;

answers.title: Hull-plate damage repair; where you find the plate material;
answers.answer_text:
check internally.
First assess the extent and location; for a damaged bottom/shell plate, also inspect internally for
damage to the longitudinals, frames and stiffeners — the framing behind the shell often tells
you the real severity. Crop out and renew the affected plate (or fair minor sets within limits). The shell
expansion plan — the "unrolled" drawing of the entire shell — gives the plate positions,
thickness and material grade, so the correct plate is ordered and the work planned. Any
significant structural damage is reported to class and repaired to their approval and under
survey.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Hull-plate damage repair; where you find the plate material;

answers.title: Testing a cropped-plate repair; plate thickness &
answers.answer_text:
allowable wastage; dents renew-or-cosmetic; when call class?
Testing a welded shell repair: the vacuum-box (soap-bubble) test — apply a soapy solution
over the weld and a vacuum box; a leak draws air through and shows as bubbles. Also DPI for surface
cracks and a hydrostatic test where the tank arrangement allows.
Plate thickness is gauged by a class-approved third-party firm using ultrasonics; renewal is
required when the diminution reaches the class allowable (broadly ~20–25% of original for most
members, less for critical strakes), and "substantial corrosion" is flagged before that as a watch item.
Dents: whether to renew or leave cosmetic depends on the depth, the location (a high-stress
zone amidships/bottom), any associated cracking or set-in framing, and the effect on
strength/watertightness. Call class for significant structural damage, cracked or set-in frames, or
anything affecting seaworthiness — they decide the acceptance/repair.

4 Rudder

answers.title: Rudder checks in dock; pressure test; water in
answers.answer_text:
the rudder; fitted bolts & jumping clearance.
• Pintle and bearing weardown (bottom clearance) and the jumping clearance (the vertical lift
of the rudder); rudder stock and carrier bearing.
• Fitted (reamed) bolts at the couplings/pintles for tightness and fretting; NDT the stock/pintles
as required.
• Drain plug and internal water ingress; coating and corrosion.
Pressure test: apply air/hydro to the maker's head to prove the rudder (a hollow structure) is
watertight. If it is full of water, there is a crack, a leaking weld or a defective plug — drain it, find
and repair the ingress path (crop/weld), and re-test. Water inside causes internal corrosion and
adds weight/unbalance, so it must not be ignored.
If he presses further —
Why does jumping clearance matter? too much lift means the rudder can jump on its pintle in a
seaway, hammering the bearings — it is checked and shimmed to the maker's limit. How do you test
after a rudder repair weld? re-pressure-test to the specified head and hold, checking for leaks and
pressure drop.
5 Cathodic Protection — Anodes, ICCP & Antifouling

answers.title: Sacrificial anodes — how they work, how attached,
answers.answer_text:
what to check before welding.
Sacrificial anodes (zinc or aluminium) protect the steel hull by galvanic action — being more
electronegative (anodic) than steel, they corrode preferentially, driving the hull cathodic and holding it
at a protective potential so the steel does not corrode. They are welded (or bolted) to the hull at the
corrosion-prone areas.
Before welding anodes, check the compartments adjacent to the weld area: if they are fuel-
or lube-oil tanks, plan early to empty, clean and gas-free them and prepare for hot work
(enclosed-space entry, isolation, gas testing, hot-work permit) — welding onto a plate with oil behind
it is an explosion risk.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Sacrificial anodes — how they work, how attached,

answers.title: Anode 80% wasted at 3 years / 50% wasted — action; the 3 and 5-year
answers.answer_text:
scheme.
Anodes are sized for a planned life — a 2.5-year or 5-year scheme — based on the hull area,
coating and expected current demand. 50% wasted at the mid-point of the life is on track. But
80% wasted at 3 years on a 5-year scheme means the hull is drawing more current than planned
and is becoming under-protected — investigate the cause (coating breakdown exposing more steel,
stray currents, or wrong anode mass) and renew the anodes early, increasing the number/mass
if the original scheme was inadequate.

answers.title: How does ICCP work; advantages of impressed-current
answers.answer_text:
protection.
ICCP (Impressed Current Cathodic Protection): reference electrodes (silver/silver-chloride or
zinc) sense the hull-to-sea potential and feed a controller/power unit, which drives a controlled
current through inert impressed anodes (platinised titanium / mixed-metal-oxide) to hold the hull
at its protective potential (about −800 mV to Ag/AgCl). It adjusts automatically for speed and
salinity. A dielectric shield protects the paint around the anodes, and the rudder/propeller are
bonded in (the propeller via the shaft slip-ring).
Advantages over sacrificial anodes: the protection level is controllable and continuously
monitored, it lasts much longer (nothing wastes away), gives lower hull drag, and adapts to
conditions — the trade-off is that it needs power and a functioning reference/anode/controller system
that must be checked in dock.

answers.title: How does antifouling paint work; how do you know how much to apply?
answers.answer_text:
Self-polishing copolymer (SPC) antifouling works by controlled hydrolysis at the surface: sea
water slowly reacts with the paint's binder, releasing the biocide (usually copper) at a steady rate and
continuously exposing fresh active paint, so growth is prevented and the surface stays smooth (good
for fuel economy). Modern foul-release (silicone) coatings work differently — a slick low-friction
surface that fouling cannot grip. The quantity, number of coats and film thickness come from
the coating manufacturer's specification for the chosen 3-year or 5-year scheme and the ship's
area, speed and trading pattern.
6 Propeller & CPP

answers.title: Types of propeller; how do you repair one; crack
answers.answer_text:
toward the hub; damaged blade in dock.
Types: fixed-pitch (FPP) and controllable-pitch (CPP), normally Ni-Al-bronze. The blade is divided
into severity zones (A near the root/boss, through to D at the tip) — damage in Zone A is the
most serious because it is the highest-stressed region.
Repair: minor edge/tip damage is ground and faired; cracks are welded (TIG/MIG) with a
preheat of about 150°C, then a stress-relief at 350–500°C, dressed to the profile and re-
balanced (static and dynamic). A crack toward the boss/hub (Zone A) is serious: on a CPP the
individual blade can be renewed; on a badly cracked FPP the propeller may be condemned.
Discuss with class and the maker's propeller-repair service; a replacement blade is ground to match
the worn profile of the others so the set stays balanced.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Types of propeller; how do you repair one; crack

answers.title: Working of a CPP; what pitch does it fail to; how are the
answers.answer_text:
blades secured to the boss?
CPP working: a hydraulic servo, controlled through the OD (oil-distribution) box on the shaft,
moves a piston and crosshead inside the boss, which turns each blade about its spindle to
change the pitch. This gives ahead, stop and astern thrust without reversing the engine,
allows a constant-speed shaft generator, and gives fine manoeuvring control.

Fail-safe: most systems fail to the last set pitch (if control oil is lost, the blades lock where they
are). By design others fail to zero pitch (no thrust) or to a fixed ahead pitch — each is a trade-off
(fail-to-last keeps way on but no control; fail-to-zero removes thrust so you can stop the shaft). Know
which your ship uses. The blades are bolted to the boss with fitted bolts and sealed.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Working of a CPP; what pitch does it fail to; how are the

answers.title: Loss of CPP control on the bridge; propeller clearance too large; muff
answers.answer_text:
coupling.
Loss of bridge control: transfer to ECR control; if that also fails, go to local hydraulic control at
the OD box, in constant communication with the bridge, and continue to manoeuvre from there.
Propeller (stern-tube) clearance too large compared with the previous record indicates a worn
aft stern-tube bearing — renew the bearing. A muff / SKF-OK coupling is dismantled by oil
injection: high-pressure oil is injected between the sleeve and shaft to expand the sleeve and release
the interference grip.
7 Tailshaft, Stern Tube & Seals

answers.title: When to remove the tailshaft; the tailshaft survey;
answers.answer_text:
tailshaft monitoring; how you test it.
When: at the tailshaft (special) survey — typically 5-yearly. The interval can be extended for
an oil-lubricated shaft with approved seals and a monitoring scheme (oil analysis, bearing
weardown, temperature), so that it aligns with the class renewal.
Survey / test: withdraw and clean the shaft, then inspect and NDT the cone, keyway and the
fillet at the change of section — these are the fatigue hot-spots — by dye-penetrant /
magnetic-particle, with ultrasonics for sub-surface cracks. Check the liner, journals, the taper
contact (blueing) with the propeller boss, the keyway, and the seal running surfaces (chrome liner).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: When to remove the tailshaft; the tailshaft survey;

answers.title: How do you take the wear-down; is it required to
answers.answer_text:
drain the stern-tube oil?
Wear-down is measured at the aft stern-tube bearing with a poker (feeler) gauge through the
top plug. Because the shaft rests on the bottom of the bearing, wear shows up as an increased
clearance at the top — the drop of the shaft — measured against the original recorded reading;
when it reaches the maker's limit the bush is renewed.
Draining the oil: not required. The seals retain the oil, so the reading is taken without draining the
stern-tube system.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How do you take the wear-down; is it required to

answers.title: Stern-tube seal working principle; a leak; chrome-liner wear.
answers.answer_text:
Working principle: an oil-lubricated lip-seal (Simplex-type) arrangement — several lip-seal
rings running on a chrome liner on the shaft, with lubricating oil supplied between them from a
head/gravity tank that keeps the seal-oil pressure just above the sea-water head. The aft seals
keep sea water out; the forward seals keep the stern-tube oil in.

Leak / repair: a leak is usually worn lip seals with a grooved chrome liner. Depending on the
groove depth: renew the lip seals, re-surface or renew the chrome liner, or fit a distance/
spacer ring to shift the seals so they run on an unworn part of the liner. If a pressurised seal head-
tank is leaking, reduce its pressure to cut the flow while planning the dock repair.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Stern-tube seal working principle; a leak; chrome-liner wear.

answers.title: How is the depth below the hull checked; other sensor; STW vs
answers.answer_text:
SOG?
Depth below the hull is measured by the echo sounder. Another hull sensor is the speed log.
STW (speed through the water) is measured by the log; SOG (speed over the ground) comes from
GPS. The difference between them is the effect of current/tide — important for performance
monitoring and fuel calculations (you compare fuel and power against STW, not SOG).
8 Surveys & Classification

answers.title: Classification societies; class vs statutory; what is
answers.answer_text:
CMS; what is / isn't covered by CMS?
Classification societies (LR, DNV, ABS, etc.) set and verify the standards for the ship's structure
and machinery and issue the class certificate; they also act as a Recognised Organisation (RO)
doing statutory work on behalf of the flag State against the IMO conventions.
CMS (Continuous Machinery Survey): instead of surveying all the machinery at once every five
years, the items are spread across the five-year cycle (about 20% each year). Items are
credited with reports and photographs and matching PMS entries. Certain items an approved/
qualified Chief Engineer can survey and record ("CE survey"), subject to a confirmatory
survey by class. Items not covered by CMS are those needing the surveyor's own attendance — e.g.
crankshaft, certain boiler and safety-critical items.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Classification societies; class vs statutory; what is

answers.title: How do you know when surveys are due; annual, intermediate,
answers.answer_text:
renewal survey; HSSC.
Survey status is tracked through the PMS/planning system and the certificate anniversary
dates, and class issues a survey-status report listing what is due and when. Under the
Harmonised System of Survey and Certification (HSSC), the certificates run on a common 5-
year cycle with ±3-month windows around the anniversary:
• Annual — each year, within ±3 months of the anniversary date.
• Intermediate — at the 2nd or 3rd anniversary (a more detailed check).
• Renewal / Special — the full survey at the 5-year point, which re-issues the certificate; plus the
periodical bottom/docking surveys.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How do you know when surveys are due; annual, intermediate,

answers.title: Special-survey tank inspection & hydrostatic-test danger on
answers.answer_text:
large tanks; underwater-survey preparation.
Special-survey tanks: after a close-up (internal) inspection and thickness gauging, tanks
may be hydrostatically/leak tested. The danger on a large tank is that a full head of water is an

enormous weight the structure may not be designed to carry when the surrounding tanks are empty
— it can over-stress the structure and upset the ship's stability/trim. So the test head is
controlled and the ship's stress and stability are managed while filling.
Underwater (in-water) survey preparation: lock out the propeller, thrusters and sea
valves; the hull is marked out in a grid so the divers/ROV and the attending surveyor (watching by
camera) know exactly which area is being examined and can record it against the plan.

Statutory Regime &
Certification
1 ISM Code & the SMS

answers.title: What is the ISM Code — what, why, objectives, how
answers.answer_text:
implemented?
The International Safety Management Code is made mandatory by SOLAS Chapter IX. It is the
standard for the safe management and operation of ships and for pollution prevention,
brought in after a series of accidents showed the "human element" and poor shore-ship management
were the real causes.
Objectives (learn these three): safety at sea, prevention of human injury or loss of life, and
avoidance of damage to the environment and property.
It is implemented through a documented Safety Management System (SMS) tailored to the
company and ship, covering: the safety & environmental policy; defined responsibilities and
authority; the Designated Person Ashore (DPA) (the link between ship and top management,
with direct access to the highest level); the master's responsibility and authority; resources and
personnel; shipboard operations; emergency preparedness; reporting and analysis of non-
conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences; maintenance of the ship and
equipment (Ch 10); documentation; and company verification, review and evaluation (Ch 12).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What is the ISM Code — what, why, objectives, how

answers.title: DOC and SMC — who issues, validity,
answers.answer_text:
where kept, survey cycle; interim certificates and prerequisites.
The Document of Compliance (DOC) is issued to the company (per ship type it operates) after a
successful audit; valid 5 years with an annual verification audit (within ±3 months). The Safety

Management Certificate (SMC) is issued to the ship; valid 5 years with at least one
intermediate audit between the 2nd and 3rd anniversaries. A copy of the DOC and the
original SMC are kept onboard.
Interim certificates bridge the gap for new arrangements: an interim DOC (new company, or
company taking on a new ship type) is valid up to 12 months; an interim SMC (new ship, change of
flag, or new company taking over the ship) up to 6 months. Prerequisites for the interim SMC (per Ch
14.2) include: the company holds a DOC/interim DOC covering that ship type; the SMS contains the
key elements and has been reviewed; the master and key crew are familiarised with the SMS;
instructions are provided before sailing; and a full audit is planned within the validity period.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: DOC and SMC — who issues, validity,

answers.title: NC, major NC, observation; a
answers.answer_text:
major NC raised onboard — your action; can you sail?
Non-conformity (NC): an observed situation where objective evidence shows a specified
requirement has not been met. Major NC: an identifiable deviation that poses a serious threat to
safety or the environment and needs immediate corrective action — or the absence of
effective, systematic implementation of an ISM requirement. Observation: a statement of fact,
supported by evidence, made during an audit that points to a potential improvement or a developing
weakness.
Action on a major NC: investigate the root cause, take immediate corrective action and
record it; report to the company (DPA), flag and Class. If it cannot be closed out on the spot, seek a
downgrade / accepted alternative from Class and a dispensation from flag, backed by a
corrective action plan (CAP) with a timeline. You cannot normally sail until it is rectified or a
dispensation with an agreed CAP is granted — a major NC left open can lead to withdrawal of the
DOC/SMC.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: NC, major NC, observation; a

answers.title: Master's responsibilities (an ISM element); master's
answers.answer_text:
overriding authority with an example.
ISM Ch 5 requires the company to define the master's responsibility and authority: to
implement the safety and pollution-prevention policy, motivate the crew, issue appropriate
orders and instructions clearly, verify that requirements are met, and periodically review the
SMS and report deficiencies to the company.
His overriding authority means the master has the authority and responsibility to take whatever
decision he judges necessary for the safety of the ship and the protection of the
environment, and to request the company's assistance — and neither the company nor the
owner can override that decision. Example: if, in a narrow channel, a pilot gives an instruction
the master believes is unsafe, the master may overrule the pilot; likewise the owner cannot
pressure him to sail into weather he judges unsafe.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Master's responsibilities (an ISM element); master's

answers.title: C/E's role in ISM; how do you ensure it is
answers.answer_text:
followed in the engine room / staff are familiar?
The C/E is the head of department responsible for implementing the SMS in the engine
room. In practice that means: working to the company procedures and checklists; keeping the PMS
and records current; ensuring risk assessments, permits to work and enclosed-space
procedures are used; identifying and maintaining critical equipment (Ch 10); reporting and

analysing non-conformities, near-misses and defects; managing the department's part of
internal and external audits; and controlling documentation.
Ensuring compliance and familiarity: run familiarisation checklists for joiners before they take
over duties, hold drills, toolbox talks and safety meetings, do rounds and spot-checks against
the procedures, and verify understanding rather than assume it. The chief's standing orders
reinforce the required standards.

answers.title: Critical spares and critical equipment — examples; where
answers.answer_text:
indicated?
Critical equipment is equipment whose sudden operational failure could result in a
hazardous situation — main engine, steering gear, generators, the emergency generator/fire pump,
and the emergency and safety systems. Under ISM Ch 10 these are identified and given specific
maintenance and regular testing to ensure reliability, and provision is made for alternative
arrangements if one fails.
Critical spares are the spares held onboard to keep that equipment available — e.g. steering-gear
pump/seal parts, emergency-generator starting spares, main-engine fuel-injection spares, generator
AVR/diodes. They are identified and flagged in the PMS, and their minimum stock is maintained.
2 MLC 2006

answers.title: What is MLC, its purpose; DMLC I & II; the 5 Titles;
answers.answer_text:
where found?
The Maritime Labour Convention 2006 is the ILO convention recognised as the "fourth pillar" of
the international regulatory regime, alongside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW. Its purpose is to guarantee
seafarers' rights and decent working and living conditions, and to create a level playing field
for compliant owners.
Compliance is demonstrated by the Maritime Labour Certificate together with the Declaration of
Maritime Labour Compliance: Part I sets out the flag State's requirements, and Part II the
company's measures to meet them onboard.
The five Titles: (1) minimum requirements to work (age, medical fitness, training, recruitment);
(2) conditions of employment (the SEA, wages, hours of work/rest, leave, repatriation); (3)
accommodation, recreation, food and catering; (4) health protection, medical care, welfare
and social security; (5) compliance and enforcement.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What is MLC, its purpose; DMLC I & II; the 5 Titles;

answers.title: Hours of rest / work — the requirement (STCW 2010
answers.answer_text:
Manila & MLC).
Minimum rest: at least 10 hours in any 24-hour period, split into no more than two periods,
one of which must be at least 6 hours, with not more than 14 hours between consecutive rest
periods; and at least 77 hours of rest in any 7-day period. (Equivalently, work is capped at 14 h/
24 and 72 h/7 days.) Records of daily hours of rest are kept and signed by the seafarer and the
master.

The requirement is common to MLC Title 2 and STCW 2010 (Manila). Exceptions are only for drills
and emergencies, with compensatory rest given afterwards.

answers.title: MLC and a cadet/trainee onboard — the special
answers.answer_text:
requirements.
The minimum age to work at sea is 16. Anyone under 18 is a "young seafarer" with additional
protection: no night work (with limited training exceptions), restrictions on hazardous work, and
stricter rest-hour arrangements. On joining, a cadet must be welcomed, inducted and
familiarised (sign-on, emergency duties and muster, meeting the staff, and the complaints
procedure explained), and their training conducted under the Training Record Book with proper
supervision. A valid medical certificate is required.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: MLC and a cadet/trainee onboard — the special

answers.title: MLC complaint / grievance procedure.
answers.answer_text:
Every ship must have an onboard complaint procedure. The seafarer normally raises the
complaint first with the head of department or master; if it is not resolved, it is escalated to the
company (DPA), and ultimately the seafarer may complain to the flag State or to Port State
Control. The seafarer has the right to be accompanied or represented, and there must be no
victimisation for making a complaint — that protection is itself part of MLC.
3 STCW & Manning

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: MLC complaint / grievance procedure.

answers.title: What is STCW and why is it important?
answers.answer_text:
STCW — the International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and
Watchkeeping for Seafarers, as amended by the 2010 Manila amendments — sets the
international minimum standards for seafarers' training, competence, certification and
watchkeeping, together with rest-hour and medical requirements. It is important because it
guarantees a common, verifiable level of competence across all flags, so that whoever you
sail with has met the same standard — the foundation of safe, standardised operation.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What is STCW and why is it important?

answers.title: New 2/E or ETO joins — how do you confirm he is
answers.answer_text:
qualified?
Check his Certificate of Competency (CoC) and its flag endorsement for the rank; the STCW
certificates (basic safety training, advanced fire-fighting, medical first aid/care, security awareness,
and any tanker/specialised endorsements); the medical fitness certificate; and the discharge
book for relevant sea time. For an ETO, look specifically for the STCW-approved electro-technical
officer certification. Then familiarise him to the ship before he takes over duties.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: New 2/E or ETO joins — how do you confirm he is

answers.title: Safe-manning document & UMS — conditions; when
answers.answer_text:
would you not go UMS; asking for extra hands.
The Minimum Safe Manning Document (SOLAS V/14) states the minimum crew the flag requires
for safe operation. For an E0 / UMS (unmanned machinery space) the machinery-space safety

systems must all be working — you would not allow the space to go UMS if the fire detection or
the fixed fire-fighting system is defective, the bilge (high-level) alarm is not working, or
the main-engine oil-mist detector (OMD) is out of service, because the automatic protection
that replaces the watchkeeper is then missing.
If the engine crew are genuinely overloaded you can request extra hands; you justify it with the
rest-hour records showing the work cannot be done within the limits and a risk assessment
— objective proof, not just opinion.
4 SOLAS, Load Line & BWM

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Safe-manning document & UMS — conditions; when

answers.title: What is SOLAS; its chapters; you used Ch II-1 Reg 7 — explain.
answers.answer_text:
SOLAS (Safety of Life at Sea, 1974, as amended) is the principal international convention for the
safety of merchant ships. Its chapters: I general provisions; II-1 construction — subdivision,
stability, machinery & electrical; II-2 fire protection, detection and extinction; III life-saving
appliances; IV radiocommunications (GMDSS); V safety of navigation; VI carriage of cargoes; VII
dangerous goods; VIII nuclear ships; IX management for the safe operation of ships (ISM); X
high-speed craft; XI-1 special measures to enhance safety; XI-2 special measures to enhance
maritime security (ISPS); XII additional safety measures for bulk carriers; XIII verification of
compliance; XIV polar. Chapter II-1 is where subdivision, damage stability and watertight-integrity
requirements sit.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What is SOLAS; its chapters; you used Ch II-1 Reg 7 — explain.

answers.title: Ballast Water Management — D1 vs D2; how a BWTP works;
answers.answer_text:
problems with double-hull ships.
The BWM Convention controls the transfer of harmful aquatic organisms and pathogens in ballast
water. D1 is the ballast-water exchange standard — exchange at sea, preferably >200 nm from
land in >200 m depth, achieving at least 95% volumetric exchange. D2 is the performance
(treatment) standard, met by a ballast-water treatment system that reduces viable organisms
below set limits — typically filtration plus UV, or filtration plus electro-chlorination. Ships have
transitioned from D1 to D2 as treatment systems are fitted.
Double-hull problems: the large enclosed ballast spaces are prone to corrosion and coating
breakdown, are difficult to access and inspect, and can accumulate flammable/toxic gas —
so coating maintenance and strict enclosed-space precautions are essential.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Ballast Water Management — D1 vs D2; how a BWTP works;

answers.title: Main conventions of IMO.
answers.answer_text:
SOLAS (safety of life), MARPOL (marine pollution), STCW (training/certification), MLC (labour), Load
Line / ICLL (freeboard), COLREG (collision avoidance), the Tonnage convention, the BWM
convention, and the Anti-Fouling Systems (AFS) convention — with the ISM and ISPS codes made
mandatory under SOLAS.

answers.title: List the statutory / mandatory / class certificates
answers.answer_text:
carried onboard.
Roughly twenty-plus — group them by convention to show structure:
• Registry/tonnage: Certificate of Registry, International Tonnage Certificate.
• SOLAS: Safety Construction (SAFCON), Safety Equipment, Safety Radio (or the combined
Cargo Ship Safety Certificate); Minimum Safe Manning Document; ISM (SMC + copy DOC); ISSC
(security).
• Load Line: International Load Line Certificate.
• MARPOL: IOPP, IAPP, ISPP (sewage), International Energy Efficiency (IEEC) with the NOx
Technical File; the Garbage Management Plan; SOPEP.
• MLC / BWM / AFS: Maritime Labour Certificate + DMLC, BWM Certificate, International Anti-
Fouling (IAFS) Certificate.
• Liability/insurance: the CLC (oil pollution), the Bunker Convention certificate, and P&I/
insurance; plus the Continuous Synopsis Record.

answers.title: Survey cycle for a certificate; how do you know the
answers.answer_text:
annual is due; renewal window; expired-certificate scenario.
Under HSSC the dates run on a common 5-year cycle. To find when the annual is due, work back
from the expiry (anniversary) date — not the issue date, which can move if a new certificate is
issued — and the annual is done within ±3 months of that anniversary. The renewal survey must
be completed within the 3 months before expiry, not after (if done more than 3 months early it
shortens the next cycle).
Expired-certificate scenario (issued Mar '11, revalidated May '12, no survey since): the certificate
is already expired. Check the correspondence between the master, DPA/technical
superintendent and Class for any exemption or short extension; if no exemption is in place you
would refuse to sign the articles / not sail until it is put right — that is the answer the surveyor is
looking for.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Survey cycle for a certificate; how do you know the

answers.title: Civil Liability Certificate; bunker liability; other insurance
answers.answer_text:
certificates?
The Civil Liability Certificate (CLC) provides financial security for oil-pollution damage from
cargo oil carried by a tanker. The Bunker Convention certificate provides security for pollution
damage from a ship's own bunker fuel oil (applies to all ships above a size). In addition the ship
carries P&I / third-party liability cover (including wreck removal and, for passenger ships,
passenger liability). These certificates confirm the owner can meet pollution and liability claims —
without them a ship can be detained.

6 Flag State, Port State & MAIB

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Civil Liability Certificate; bunker liability; other insurance

answers.title: Flag State; Port State Control; when inform PSC vs flag; sewage
answers.answer_text:
plant fails — whom inform?
Flag State: the State whose flag the ship flies (its State of registry) — responsible for ensuring the
ship meets the conventions, issuing (or authorising an RO to issue) the certificates, and investigating
incidents. Port State Control (PSC): the inspection of foreign ships visiting a country's ports to
verify their condition and certificates and to detain sub-standard ships — a safety net catching
what flag oversight misses.
Who to inform: defects and incidents affecting certificates/safety go to the company (DPA), the
flag State and Class; when in port, or where there is a pollution risk, the port State / nearest
coastal State is also informed. A failed sewage treatment plant: inform the company, the
nearest port State and the flag State, and observe the discharge restrictions until repaired.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Flag State; Port State Control; when inform PSC vs flag; sewage

answers.title: What do you know about PSC; how are ships graded; who
answers.answer_text:
covers Europe + Canada; types of inspection.
PSC operates through regional Memoranda of Understanding: the Paris MoU covers Europe and
Canada; the Tokyo MoU covers the Asia-Pacific; the USCG runs the US regime. Ships are given a risk
profile (high / standard / low) that sets how often they are inspected, based on about five factors:
ship type, ship age, flag-State performance, recognised-organisation (class) performance,
and company performance, together with the ship's inspection/detention history. Inspections
escalate: an initial inspection; a more detailed inspection when there are "clear grounds"; and an
expanded inspection for high-risk ship types.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What do you know about PSC; how are ships graded; who

answers.title: Accident on a UK-flag vessel — whom to inform; the MAIB; MSN 654 /
answers.answer_text:
MGN 069.
Report to the flag State (MCA) and to the MAIB. The Marine Accident Investigation Branch
investigates marine accidents to UK ships (and to foreign ships in UK waters) solely to improve
safety and prevent recurrence — not to apportion blame or liability; it publishes reports with
safety recommendations, which is why examiners like you to have read one. MSN 654 / MGN 069
are the UK Merchant Shipping Notices / Marine Guidance Notes conveying the applicable requirements
the examiner expects you to be aware of.
If he presses further —
What is the difference between an MSN, MGN and MIN? an MSN carries mandatory requirements
(backed by regulation); an MGN gives guidance/recommendations; an MIN is a short-life information
note for a target audience. What can you do if PSC is wrong in their assessment? you can request
a re-inspection and formally appeal through the flag State / the MoU's review process, with supporting
evidence.

MARPOL
1 MARPOL Overview

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Accident on a UK-flag vessel — whom to inform; the MAIB; MSN 654 /

answers.title: How many annexes does MARPOL have and what does each cover?
answers.answer_text:
Annex Subject & key items
I Oil — OWS (15 ppm), Oil Record Book, IOPP, slop/sludge, SOPEP
II Noxious liquid substances carried in bulk — categories X/Y/Z, P&A manual
III Harmful substances carried in packaged form (linked to the IMDG Code)
IV Sewage — treatment plant, ISPP, discharge distances
V Garbage — categories, Garbage Record Book & Management Plan, no-plastics rule
VI Air pollution — SOx, NOx, ODS, VOC, and ship energy efficiency (Ch 4)
MARPOL 73/78 — the 1973 convention modified by the 1978 protocol — is the main convention for
the prevention of pollution from ships, both operational and accidental.

2 Annex I — Oil

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How many annexes does MARPOL have and what does each cover?

answers.title: Annex I; the IOPP certificate and supplement; the MARPOL
answers.answer_text:
equipment fitted onboard.
Annex I controls oil pollution from machinery spaces and (on tankers) cargo/ballast operations. The
engine-room equipment it requires: the Oil Water Separator with a 15 ppm monitor and
automatic stopping/recirculating device and alarm; the Oil Record Book Part I (machinery)
(and Part II for cargo/ballast on tankers); sludge and holding/slop tanks; the standard
discharge connection; and SOPEP.
The IOPP certificate confirms compliance, and its supplement (Form A for non-tankers, Form B
for tankers) lists the actual pollution-prevention equipment fitted — OWS, ODMCS, tank
arrangements, monitoring. Machinery-space bilge discharge is only allowed en route, ≤15 ppm,
with the monitor and stopping device working, and never from the cargo or pump-room
bilges.
Q140 / 213 / 357 / 359-364 / 544 / 845. OWS — tests and what affects efficiency; OWS
not working — actions and alternatives; basis for dispensation.
How the OWS works: a first-stage gravity/coalescer separator removes the bulk of the oil, then a
fine coalescer stage; the 15 ppm oil-content monitor continuously checks the effluent and, if it
exceeds 15 ppm, an automatic three-way valve returns the flow to the bilge/holding tank and
raises an alarm.
What affects efficiency: emulsified oil (from detergents/chemicals or from shearing by a
centrifugal transfer pump), a high flow rate, low temperature, and solids/sludge fouling the
coalescer.
OWS unrepairable: inform the company, flag and Class and apply for a dispensation. The
dispensation is granted on the basis that Class proposes an acceptable alternative — typically
transfer the oily water to dedicated IOPP/holding tanks and discharge to a shore reception
facility or barge. Make the full ORB entries and issue a letter of protest if relevant.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Annex I; the IOPP certificate and supplement; the MARPOL

answers.title: Slop tank; what you do with the slops; sludge tank.
answers.answer_text:
A slop tank (on tankers) stores oily residues and dirty ballast/tank washings from the cargo
tanks; with the office's permission oily engine-room bilges may also be transferred there. The slops
are discharged to a reception facility or barge ashore, or (for tankers) handled by the load-on-
top / oil-discharge-monitoring system within the Annex I discharge criteria. The sludge tank holds
oily residues from the purifiers and filters, and is incinerated or landed ashore — all recorded in
the ORB.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Slop tank; what you do with the slops; sludge tank.

answers.title: Oil spill / oil leaked to sea — actions; where are the procedures
answers.answer_text:
(SOPEP); BDN / BIN.
Oil spill: stop the operation, contain and clean up (deploy the SOPEP locker/booms/absorbents),
sound the alarm, and report to the master, company, and the nearest coastal/port State. The
procedures, reporting requirements and contact list are in the ship's SOPEP (Shipboard Oil

Pollution Emergency Plan). Bunkering is documented by the Bunker Delivery Note (BDN) and
the retained MARPOL sample — the record of the fuel received and its sulphur content.
3 Annex V — Garbage

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Oil spill / oil leaked to sea — actions; where are the procedures

answers.title: Annex V garbage — who takes care of it; electrical
answers.answer_text:
waste; cooking oil; incinerate / sludge tank?
Annex V prohibits the discharge of most garbage at sea — all plastics are banned, and only
comminuted food waste may be discharged, and only well offshore (e.g. >3 nm comminuted, >12 nm
otherwise, subject to special-area rules). Garbage is segregated by category, recorded in the
Garbage Record Book, managed per the Garbage Management Plan, and landed to reception
facilities.
Cooking oil is a garbage category (operational waste) and is landed to a reception facility —
not tipped into the sludge tank (only oily machinery residues belong in the sludge tank).
Electrical / e-waste is a specific category to be landed ashore. Incineration onboard is permitted
only within Annex VI limits and not in port/ECA restrictions.
4 Annex VI — SOx & Scrubbers

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Annex V garbage — who takes care of it; electrical

answers.title: SOx control onboard; how do you prove the
answers.answer_text:
fuel is compliant; where the SOx rule comes from; ECA.
SOx is controlled through fuel sulphur under Reg 14: a global cap of 0.50% m/m and an ECA/
SECA limit of 0.10% — met either by burning low-sulphur fuel or by fitting an approved Exhaust
Gas Cleaning System (scrubber) as an equivalent. Compliance is proven by the BDN and the
retained MARPOL fuel sample (and, on a scrubber ship, the recorded scrubber data). In an ECA the
whole fuel system must be fully changed over before crossing the boundary, with the position
and time logged.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: SOx control onboard; how do you prove the

answers.title: Scrubber functionality — open and closed loop; emission
answers.answer_text:
limits; wash-water values.
An Exhaust Gas Cleaning System sprays alkaline water into the exhaust; the SO₂ reacts with the
alkalinity and is removed as sulphate.
• Open loop: uses sea water (its natural alkalinity neutralises the SO₂) and discharges the wash
water overboard after cleaning — simple but restricted where discharge is banned.
• Closed loop: recirculates fresh water dosed with caustic soda (NaOH), with a small bleed-off
to a holding tank and a make-up supply — used where overboard discharge is restricted.
• Hybrid: can run in either mode.

Wash-water discharge criteria:pH ≥ 6.5 (measured at the overboard, or 4 m from the discharge),
plus limits on turbidity and PAH (poly-aromatic hydrocarbons); and the SO₂/CO₂ ratio (ppm/%)
proves the equivalent sulphur level — ≤ 4.3 for 0.10% equivalence and ≤ 21.7 for 0.50% equivalence.
5 Annex VI — NOx

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Scrubber functionality — open and closed loop; emission

answers.title: What is NOx; how is it controlled;
answers.answer_text:
primary and secondary methods; the Tiers.
NOx (oxides of nitrogen) forms when the high combustion temperature makes nitrogen and
oxygen in the charge air combine — so anything that lowers the peak flame temperature reduces
NOx. It is limited under Reg 13 to Tier limits that depend on the engine's rated speed and its build
date:
• Tier I (ships built 2000+), Tier II (2011+) worldwide, and Tier III (2016+ in a NOx ECA) — Tier III
is about 80% below Tier I.
Control methods:
• Primary (in-engine): lower the peak temperature — Miller timing (early inlet closing),
retarded injection, Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR), Direct Water Injection (DWI), water-
in-fuel emulsification, and charge-air humidification.
• Secondary (after-treatment): Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) — urea/ammonia injected
over a catalyst converts NOx to nitrogen and water; this is the main way to meet Tier III.
To show a PSC inspector compliance, present the recorded SCR operating data and the NOx
Technical File.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What is NOx; how is it controlled;

answers.title: NOx Technical File — what it is, where engine
answers.answer_text:
NOx values are documented, contents.
The NOx Technical File is the maker's document — one per engine over 130 kW — that proves
the engine meets its Tier limit as tested. It records the identified components, settings and
operating parameters that affect NOx (injection timing, fuel nozzles, cam/injection profile,
turbocharger, charge-air cooling, etc.), the list of "adjustable/identifiable features," and the
onboard verification method/procedure a surveyor uses to confirm the engine is still within limits.
The certified NOx values are tied to the engine's EIAPP certificate; any change to a NOx-critical
component must keep the engine inside the file.
6 Annex VI — Certificates, ODS & VOC

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: NOx Technical File — what it is, where engine

answers.title: IAPP and EIAPP — what they are,
answers.answer_text:
requirements, what the surveyor wants at renewal.
The IAPP (International Air Pollution Prevention) certificate is issued to the ship, confirming
compliance with Annex VI; its supplement lists the equipment and carries the record of ODS, the

fuel-oil (SOx) arrangements, and the NOx compliance. The EIAPP (Engine IAPP) certificate
is issued to each engine over 130 kW at manufacture, confirming its NOx compliance, and is
backed by the NOx Technical File.
At renewal the surveyor checks the BDNs and fuel samples (SOx), the ODS record, the NOx
Technical File and the onboard NOx verification, and confirms that nothing NOx-critical has
been altered outside the file — so keep the file and the records straight and available.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: IAPP and EIAPP — what they are,

answers.title: ODS — where recorded; how would a surveyor know you
answers.answer_text:
have it; CFC/HCFC rule; emissions in Annex VI.
Ozone-Depleting Substances (ODS) — CFCs and HCFCs used in older refrigeration and fire
systems — are controlled under Reg 12: new installations containing CFCs are prohibited and
HCFCs are being phased out; deliberate emissions are banned and any handling/top-up is logged
in the ODS Record Book. A surveyor knows you carry ODS because the IAPP supplement carries
a list of the equipment and refrigerant charge. The emissions controlled by Annex VI are ODS,
NOx, SOx and VOC.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: ODS — where recorded; how would a surveyor know you

answers.title: VOC — the tanker arrangement to combat it; how it is transferred.
answers.answer_text:
Volatile Organic Compounds evaporate from crude and product cargoes. Under Reg 15, tankers
on certain trades operate a VOC Management Plan and, where the terminal requires it, a Vapour
Emission Control System (VECS): a cargo-tank vapour return line collects the vapours displaced
during loading and returns them to the terminal (by vapour recovery / vacuum), rather than
venting them — reducing emissions and hydrocarbon loss.
7 Energy Efficiency — EEDI / EEXI / SEEMP / CII

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: VOC — the tanker arrangement to combat it; how it is transferred.

answers.title: IEEC, EEDI and EEXI — the regulations for new-builds
answers.answer_text:
and existing ships.
Chapter 4 of Annex VI covers ship energy efficiency, evidenced by the International Energy
Efficiency Certificate (IEEC).
• EEDI (Energy Efficiency Design Index): a design-stage figure of CO₂ emitted per unit of
transport work (g CO₂ / tonne-mile), required for new-builds and tightened in phases — it drives
more efficient hull and machinery design.
• EEXI (Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index): the equivalent one-off design requirement
applied to existing ships, commonly met by engine or shaft power limitation (EPL/
ShaPoLi).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: IEEC, EEDI and EEXI — the regulations for new-builds

answers.title: SEEMP and CII — what they are; Part III /
answers.answer_text:
operational carbon; EEOI; what annual data goes to the administration.
The SEEMP (Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan) is the ship's operational plan for
efficiency: Part I = the efficiency measures (voyage/weather routeing, hull/propeller cleaning, trim

optimisation); Part II = the fuel-oil data-collection plan (DCS); Part III = the plan to achieve the
ship's required CII.
The CII (Carbon Intensity Indicator) is calculated from the ship's annual fuel-oil consumption
data (DCS), reported to the administration, and gives the ship a rating A to E; a ship rated D
for three years, or E, must submit a corrective action plan. The EEOI is the operational efficiency
indicator (CO₂ per tonne-mile of cargo actually carried), used for monitoring.
8 Inert Gas & the Flammability Diagram

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: SEEMP and CII — what they are; Part III /

answers.title: Inert gas — how important, how generated,
answers.answer_text:
what it contains, how you monitor O₂; the flammability diagram.
Inert gas keeps the cargo-tank atmosphere too oxygen-lean to support combustion — essential
on tankers during loading, discharge, tank cleaning and gas-freeing. Sources: boiler uptake flue
gas (cleaned and cooled in a scrubber), an inert gas generator (IGG) burning fuel in a dedicated
combustion chamber, or nitrogen (from a nitrogen generator, common on product/chemical tankers).
Flue-gas IG typically contains about 2–5% O₂, with CO₂ and mostly nitrogen. The rule is to keep the
cargo-tank oxygen ≤ 5%.
Flammability diagram: it plots hydrocarbon content against oxygen content and shows the
flammable envelope. As inert gas is added, the mixture moves along a dilution line, and once the
oxygen is below about 5–11% the mixture cannot enter the flammable zone whatever the
hydrocarbon content — which is exactly why the 5% O₂ limit is chosen.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Inert gas — how important, how generated,

answers.title: How do you monitor O₂; how do you ensure the analyser reads
answers.answer_text:
correctly; the calibration.
Oxygen is monitored by fixed and portable O₂ analysers, with a low-O₂ alarm; on tankers two
analysers are provided and must be calibrated before every inert-gas / discharge operation.
Calibration is a zero and span check: set the zero on a zero/nitrogen gas and the span on fresh
air (20.9% O₂). Alarms and trips (high O₂, low IG pressure, high scrubber-water level, high gas
temperature) protect the system; the deck water seal and non-return prevent cargo gas backing into
the machinery space.
If he presses further —
Why not just below 11% O₂? the 5% limit gives a safety margin below the "critical dilution line" and
covers pockets of higher-oxygen atmosphere and instrument error. What is the deck water seal for?
it is a one-way barrier that lets inert gas out to the tanks but stops flammable cargo gas flowing
back into the engine room / IG plant.

Auxiliaries & Safety Systems
1 Fixed Fire-Fighting — CO₂

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How do you monitor O₂; how do you ensure the analyser reads

answers.title: Types of CO₂ system; the operating principle and
answers.answer_text:
basic checks; maintenance; why the timer delay & safeties.
Types: the bottle (high-pressure) type — a bank of cylinders each holding liquid CO₂ at high
pressure; and the bulk (low-pressure) type — a single large refrigerated tank of liquid CO₂ kept at
about −18°C, common on larger ships as it saves space.
Operating principle (two-stage release): opening the cabinet trips an alarm; pilot CO₂ is
released first to sound the space alarm, trip the ventilation and close the dampers/quick-
closing valves, and start a time delay; after the delay the main bank is discharged to flood the
space and smother the fire by displacing oxygen.
Why the time delay & safeties: CO₂ is an asphyxiant, so the time delay (typically 20–30 s)
plus the audible alarm ensure the space is fully evacuated before release; two independent
controls (pilot + main) prevent accidental discharge; and a non-return in the pilot line prevents
back-flow. Maintenance: weekly external checks, annual weighing/level checks and pipe blow-
through, and 10-yearly hydrostatic testing of cylinders (or re-test if a cylinder has lost more than
10% of its charge).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Types of CO₂ system; the operating principle and

answers.title: Major engine-room fire — the procedure; how do you
answers.answer_text:
know CO₂ has released; re-entry.
Procedure: raise the alarm and muster the crew; attack the fire with portable and local means
first (and Hi-Fog if fitted). If it is beyond that: evacuate and account for every person, stop the
ventilation fans, close skylights, dampers and the quick-closing (fuel) valves, trip the

pumps, and boundary-cool the surrounding spaces. Only then, on a confirmed head-count,
release the CO₂, and keep the space sealed to let it work.
Confirming release: a pressure switch/indication and alarm on the discharge line, and the fall
in the bank/cylinder weight, confirm the CO₂ has gone in. Re-entry is only after the boundaries are
cool and stable, the space has been thoroughly ventilated and gas-freed / O₂ tested, and BA
teams enter first — never re-enter a hot, CO₂-flooded space, and never re-open it early (letting
fresh air in can re-ignite the fire).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Major engine-room fire — the procedure; how do you

answers.title: Purpose of the capillary tubes; distribution valve left closed; how do you know
answers.answer_text:
it's extinguished; checks before BA teams enter.
The capillary / pilot tubes carry the small pilot charge of CO₂ that operates the alarms, trips the
fans/dampers and pressurises the release mechanism. The distribution (directional) valve
directs the main CO₂ to the selected space — if it is left closed the gas cannot reach the space,
so confirming it is open to the correct space is essential. The fire is judged extinguished when the
boundary temperatures fall and stabilise; before BA teams enter, confirm the space is cooled,
ventilated and gas-tested (O₂/CO/flammable) and that there are no hot spots.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Purpose of the capillary tubes; distribution valve left closed; how do you know

answers.title: Hi-Fog vs CO₂; re-entry after CO₂; Halon vs CO₂; foam / hyper-
answers.answer_text:
mist.
Hi-Fog (water mist) is used first / locally: the very fine droplets flash to steam on the hot surfaces,
cooling and displacing oxygen without needing the whole space evacuated, so it can be used with
people still present. CO₂ total-flooding is the last resort — the space must be evacuated and
sealed. Re-entry after CO₂ only after cooling, full ventilation and a gas-free test.
Halon vs CO₂: Halon extinguishes chemically by breaking the combustion chain at a low
concentration and was very effective, but it is a potent ozone-depleting substance and is
banned/phased out. CO₂ works physically by smothering / oxygen displacement and is an
asphyxiant needing evacuation. Foam (deck foam on tankers, local ER foam) blankets a burning
liquid surface to exclude air and cool it.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Hi-Fog vs CO₂; re-entry after CO₂; Halon vs CO₂; foam / hyper-

answers.title: Is the local FFA operational in drydock; maintenance of the fixed
answers.answer_text:
FFA in dock; BA-compressor PMS.
In dock the ship's own fire main is usually shut down, so a yard fire main and a fire watch cover
hot work, while the ship's portable extinguishers remain available. Dock maintenance includes
CO₂ hydrostatic testing and recharging, hydrant and fire-pump servicing, foam sampling/
analysis, and detector testing — and there is a criteria for replacing the CO₂ gas if a cylinder is
out of weight. BA-compressor PMS: replace the air-purification cartridge/filter on schedule and
confirm the breathing-air quality by the periodic air-quality test/certificate — because
contaminated BA air can kill the very people relying on it.

2 Life-Saving Appliances

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Is the local FFA operational in drydock; maintenance of the fixed

answers.title: Lifeboat & davit tests — weekly to five-yearly; brake and
answers.answer_text:
load testing.
• Weekly: start and run the lifeboat engine (ahead and astern in the water where possible), and
check the equipment/inventory and the boat generally.
• Monthly: lower the boat to the embarkation deck (and launch where practicable), check the on-
load release gear, and hold an abandon-ship drill.
• Annual: a thorough examination of the boat, davit, winch and falls, and a brake test; the falls are
turned end-for-end and renewed at intervals.
• 5-yearly: a dynamic load test of the davit/winch and the on-load release gear at 1.1×
the working load, followed by re-inspection of the gear, and inspection of the davits for cracks/
distortion.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Lifeboat & davit tests — weekly to five-yearly; brake and

answers.title: Release-gear testing (freefall & davit); centrifugal brake / stop
answers.answer_text:
distance; where does the requirement come from?
The on-load release gear is tested for correct operation and its hydrostatic interlock (which
prevents on-load release until the boat is waterborne), and is overhauled/load-tested every 5
years. For a freefall boat, an operational free-fall drop is carried out at intervals (with the simulated-
launch procedure between). The winch centrifugal brake limits the lowering speed so the boat
descends at a controlled rate and the stopping distance stays within limits. The tests, intervals and
load factors come from SOLAS Ch III and the LSA Code, with the maintenance/testing regime in
MSC.1/Circ.1206.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Release-gear testing (freefall & davit); centrifugal brake / stop

answers.title: What document covers the LSA and FFA onboard; the SSE / Safety
answers.answer_text:
Equipment Certificate.
The Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate (SSE), with its Record of Equipment (Form E),
covers the ship's life-saving appliances and fire-fighting arrangements — the lifeboats/liferafts
and launching gear, the LSA inventory, the fixed and portable fire-fighting systems, fire detection, and
the means of escape. It is the certificate the surveyor uses to check that the LSA/FFA fit and inventory
match what is required.
3 Enclosed-Space Entry & Risk Assessment

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What document covers the LSA and FFA onboard; the SSE / Safety

answers.title: What is an enclosed space; the entry procedure (COSWP).
answers.answer_text:
Enclosed space: a space with limited openings for entry/exit, inadequate ventilation, and
not designed for continuous occupancy — cargo/ballast tanks, cofferdams, duct keels, chain
lockers, void spaces, sewage tanks and the like.
Entry procedure (COSWP Ch 15): carry out a risk assessment; raise a permit to work
(enclosed-space entry permit); isolate and blank the space (LOTO on connected systems);

ventilate thoroughly; test the atmosphere at several levels before and continuously during
entry; post a standby person at the entrance with communications; have a rescue plan and
equipment (BA, lifelines, EEBD) ready; limit the time and numbers inside; and re-test / re-
authorise if anything changes. Regular enclosed-space entry and rescue drills are required.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: What is an enclosed space; the entry procedure (COSWP).

answers.title: Checks on gases and their allowable limits (COSWP); a
answers.answer_text:
gas not on your detector (e.g. ammonia).
Gas-test limits before entry:oxygen 20.9% by volume (not enriched, not depleted); flammable
vapour less than 1% of the LEL; and toxic gases below their occupational exposure limit (for
example CO below ~30 ppm, H₂S below ~5 ppm). Test top, middle and bottom, as gases stratify.
A gas not on the standard multi-gas detector (for instance ammonia in a reefer space): use a
specific detector tube or a dedicated sensor for that gas — the four-gas meter (O₂, LEL, CO, H₂S)
will not read it, so you must not assume the space is safe from a clear four-gas reading alone.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Checks on gases and their allowable limits (COSWP); a

answers.title: Difference between a hazard and a risk; the elements of
answers.answer_text:
a risk assessment.
Hazard = something with the potential to cause harm (e.g. a rotating shaft, a toxic gas, a hot
surface). Risk = the combination of the likelihood of that harm occurring and its severity. A
hazard only becomes a risk when someone is exposed to it.
Risk assessment (the five steps): identify the hazards; decide who might be harmed and
how; evaluate the risk and the existing controls; add control measures following the
hierarchy (eliminate → substitute → engineering controls → administrative controls → PPE);
record the findings; and review and update the assessment, especially if the task or conditions
change.
4 Steering Gear, FW Generator & Heat Exchangers

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Difference between a hazard and a risk; the elements of

answers.title: Steering gear — reasons for sluggish movement; reasons for the steering
answers.answer_text:
motor overheating.
Sluggish movement: a leaking ram (internal/external), an open or leaking bypass valve, a
leaking relief valve (dumping pressure), air in the hydraulic system, or a low oil level — anything
that lets the hydraulic pressure/flow bleed away instead of driving the rudder.
Steering-motor overheating: single phasing (the classic answer the examiner wants), overload,
continuous running against heavy weather, misalignment of the pump/motor, or a fan/ventilation
failure. Protected by overloads and a single-phasing preventer, and there are two independent
power units so one can carry on.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Steering gear — reasons for sluggish movement; reasons for the steering

answers.title: Fresh-water production, sea to tank — regulations, treatment and
answers.answer_text:
maintenance.
A vacuum evaporator uses waste heat from the jacket cooling water to boil sea water under
vacuum at about 40–70°C (the vacuum lowers the boiling point, so low-grade heat suffices and
scaling is reduced). A demister removes brine carry-over, the vapour is condensed by sea water,
and a salinometer continuously checks the product — if salinity exceeds about 10 ppm it dumps
to bilge. For potable use the water is sterilised (UV or silver-ion) and re-mineralised, and
chlorinated.
Regulation: do not produce fresh water within about 20 nm of the coast or in polluted/
harbour water. Maintenance: clean the tubes/plates of scale, check the ejector/vacuum, service the
salinometer and the steriliser.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Fresh-water production, sea to tank — regulations, treatment and
