answers.answer_text:
tubes.
Open up and inspect for corrosion, erosion, leaks and fouling; check the sacrificial anodes,
tube ends and end-covers; and pressure-test. Individual leaking/damaged tubes may be plugged,
but once the number of plugged/blocked tubes reaches about 15–20% the heat-transfer capacity is
compromised and the tube bundle should be renewed. Plate coolers are opened, the plates and
gaskets inspected, and similar blockage/damage limits applied.

answers.title: Lifting equipment — load test & certify SWL; difference between
answers.answer_text:
SWL and WLL; maintenance.
Lifting appliances (the engine-room crane, chain blocks, davits) are proof-load tested above their
rated load, certified, and entered in the Register of Lifting Appliances (and loose gear); they
are examined thoroughly at set intervals and inspected before heavy lifts. SWL and WLL are the
same value — Working Load Limit is simply the newer term for Safe Working Load. Maintenance
covers the wire/chain condition, the brakes, limit switches, structural integrity and greasing.
If he presses further —
What proof load is applied? a factor above the SWL depending on the appliance (e.g. ~1.1–1.25× for
cranes, higher for loose gear at manufacture) — the exact factor is in the class/statutory requirement
and the certificate.

Management, Human
Element & Scenarios
1 The Chief Engineer's Role

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Lifting equipment — load test & certify SWL; difference between

answers.title: Your prime role and responsibilities as
answers.answer_text:
Chief Engineer; where do you find your duties?
The C/E is the head of the engine department, responsible to the master for the safe,
efficient and pollution-free operation and maintenance of all the machinery. Set out the
breadth:
• Safety and environment: implementing the SMS in the department, risk assessments, critical-
equipment maintenance, and MARPOL compliance.
• Technical management: planned maintenance and surveys, machinery performance, and defect
rectification.
• Resources: bunkers and fuel/lube management, spares and stores, and the department budget.
• People: training, familiarisation, appraisal and welfare of the engine crew.
• Records: the engine log, oil record book, PMS and survey records.
The duties are defined in the company SMS (the ISM roles & responsibilities), the
Seafarer's Employment Agreement under MLC, and STCW — the answer the surveyor wants is
that they are documented, not invented by the individual.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Your prime role and responsibilities as

answers.title: Documents / certificates the C/E is directly concerned with.
answers.answer_text:
Chiefly the machinery- and pollution-related items: the IOPP, IAPP and IEEC with the NOx
Technical File, the ISM SMC (engine-department procedures), the Safety Equipment (SSE)

certificate for the fixed fire-fighting, the CMS / class machinery survey status, the PMS records,
the Oil Record Book, and the machinery entries in the log — while also being aware of the full
statutory certificate set (Part 5).
2 Handover & Joining

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Documents / certificates the C/E is directly concerned with.

answers.title: Joining as C/E with only a one-hour handover — your
answers.answer_text:
main concerns.
With only an hour, prioritise the safety-critical and time-critical items and get the rest in writing to
follow up:
• Certificates and survey/audit status — anything expiring or due, and any outstanding
conditions of class.
• Outstanding defects, NCs and ongoing repairs; the status of critical equipment and the
critical spares held.
• Bunkers — ROB, quality (BDNs/samples), and the next bunkering plan; any off-spec fuel
segregated.
• Machinery condition, running hours and any operating restrictions or watch items.
• Pending audits / PSC, the standing and night orders, the budget, and any crew/welfare
matters.
Confirm the handover in writing, and where you could not cover something, note it and chase it once
aboard — the responsibility transfers to you regardless of the short handover.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Joining as C/E with only a one-hour handover — your

answers.title: Joining a vessel in cold lay-up — take me through it from home to ready-to-sail.
answers.answer_text:
Before joining: study the ship's particulars, the lay-up records and the recommissioning plan, and
identify what class recommissioning survey is needed.
On board: carry out a full inspection for corrosion and moisture; drain and dry systems; megger
the electrical machinery and dry out the windings (field-flash the generators if the residual
magnetism is lost); recommission the cooling, lube and fuel systems gradually; refill and treat
the closed circuits; test every safety and emergency system (fire detection, emergency
generator, steering, bilge); and arrange the class recommissioning survey and re-validate the
certificates before sailing.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Joining a vessel in cold lay-up — take me through it from home to ready-to-sail.

answers.title: Chief's standing orders — what would you include and why; how do you
answers.answer_text:
know they are carried out?
Standing orders are the C/E's written, permanent instructions to the engine staff. They should
cover: the watchkeeping standards expected; clear criteria for when to call the Chief (alarms,
abnormal parameters, any doubt); safety and pollution-prevention priorities; the operating
limits of critical machinery; the log and record-keeping requirements; and the immediate
actions for emergencies. Their purpose is a clear, consistent standard that everyone follows
regardless of who is on watch — which underpins ISM.

Ensuring they are carried out: review the logs and records, do rounds and spot-checks,
discuss them at safety meetings and handovers, and require the staff to read and sign them.
You lead by verifying, not assuming.
3 Human Element — Familiarisation, Appraisal & Welfare

answers.title: How do you familiarise and confirm a new 2/E, ETO
answers.answer_text:
or motorman is competent?
First confirm the paperwork — the CoC and endorsement, STCW certificates, medical fitness
and discharge book — so you know they are qualified for the rank. Then, before they take over
duties, run the familiarisation checklist: the location and operation of the critical and safety
equipment, the emergency duties and muster, the SMS procedures, and the plant peculiarities of
this ship. Confirm competence through supervised observation and by checking understanding,
and record the familiarisation. Competence is then tracked through the appraisal system over the
contract.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: How do you familiarise and confirm a new 2/E, ETO

answers.title: Appraisals; a junior engineer is not competent — what do
answers.answer_text:
you do; and if still not good after training?
Assess competence through direct observation, the records, and the formal appraisal reports.
If someone is not competent: identify exactly where the gap is, then provide additional training,
closer supervision and mentoring, and re-familiarise them on the weak areas — give them a fair
chance to improve, and record what you have done.
If, after training, he is still not up to standard: document it objectively, report to the
company (DPA), and in the meantime adjust his duties so operations stay safe (do not leave a
safety-critical role in unsafe hands). If necessary, request a relief. A cadet's progress is measured
against the Training Record Book and signed-off tasks.

answers.title: A crew member reports harassment / bullying (a female cadet, or a
answers.answer_text:
3/E bullied by the 2/E) — your actions.
Treat it seriously and confidentially from the outset. Given the sensitivity and the master's
overriding authority for shipboard discipline, hold the initial meeting with the master and
yourself, applying the company's anti-harassment / anti-bullying policy under MLC. Hear the
complainant fully; then interview the accused separately; gather the facts; and contact the
office / DPA. Throughout, support and protect the complainant from victimisation. If the
situation cannot be safely and fairly managed onboard, you may have to separate the parties or
repatriate one until it is resolved. Document every step. The key is a fair, confidential, well-
recorded process — not brushing it aside.
If he presses further —
What does MLC give the complainant? the right to a confidential onboard complaint procedure, the
right to be accompanied, and protection from victimisation — and the right to escalate to flag/PSC.

answers.title: Vessel runs aground — your action as C/E; first
answers.answer_text:
checks; important checks.
On the impact, work to the priority order — people, ship, environment:
• Sound the alarm, muster the engine room and stand by the controls; be ready to stop or
use the engine as the bridge requires.
• Check watertight integrity in the engine room — look for ingress in the ER and bilges.
• Sound all tanks, bilges and cofferdams and compare with the previous soundings to
detect a breach; advise the mate to sound the ballast tanks, holds and cofferdams.
• Check for oil pollution; if grounded in silt, shut/change over the sea suctions (mud can block
cooling) — go to the high sea suction.
• Stand the engine by for refloating; report to the master and company; and prepare for a
possible unscheduled drydock (have the docking and shell-expansion plans ready).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Vessel runs aground — your action as C/E; first

answers.title: Aground and going to use the engine to come
answers.answer_text:
off — checks before giving the engineers the engine; if a breach is found.
Before using the engine to refloat: confirm no water ingress, check the sea suctions are not
blocked by mud (change to the high suction), verify the cooling water and that the propeller/
rudder are clear, and check the M/E crankshaft deflections and bearing clearances against the
previous and sea-trial values. If the deflections are drastically out, the crankshaft is misaligned to
the bedplate/hull — the engine may need to be opened up, re-aligned and the bedplate re-chocked
before it is safe to run at power. Confirm alignment by taut-wire or laser.
If a tank is breached: prepare for a possible unscheduled drydock — keep the docking plan
and shell-expansion plan ready, continue to sound and monitor tanks, and inform flag and Class.
Plate location, thickness and material are found on the shell-expansion plan.
If he presses further —
Why take deflections after grounding? the grounding can distort the hull and bedplate, throwing the
crankshaft out of alignment — running at power on a misaligned shaft risks a bearing failure or
crankshaft crack, so you prove it is safe first. Why the high sea suction? in shallow/silty water the low
(bottom) suction draws mud, which chokes coolers and pumps — the high suction draws cleaner water.

answers.title: A running generator cannot be off-loaded — your action.
answers.answer_text:
A generator that will not shed its share of the load points to a governor / load-sharing fault rather
than an electrical-output fault. Check the speed-droop / load-sharing (kW) control and the
governor of that unit, the AVR / reactive-sharing for the kVAR side, and the prime-mover fuel
linkage/actuator. Re-balance the load by trimming the governors, investigate the faulty unit, and
if it cannot be corrected, take it off on a controlled changeover (bring the standby machine on and
transfer the load) rather than risk a reverse-power trip or a blackout.

How the AVR works (Q374/685): the Automatic Voltage Regulator senses the generator
terminal voltage, compares it with a set reference, and adjusts the excitation (field) current to
the exciter — thereby controlling the strength of the magnetic flux in the main field and
holding the terminal voltage constant as load (and power factor) change. On a brushless machine
36 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

it feeds the stationary exciter field; the exciter armature output is rectified by the rotating
rectifier (diodes) to supply the main rotor field.
Generator started but produces no voltage (Q61/372/683): the machine has lost its
residual magnetism, so there is no initial flux to build up voltage. Cure: flash the field —
momentarily apply a DC source (a battery) to the exciter field to establish flux, after which
the AVR takes over and voltage builds. If it still won't build after flashing (Q375/686):
suspect faulty rotating-rectifier diodes — check the diodes with a multimeter (forward/
reverse). Disconnect the AVR first (Q373/684): yes — it is an electronic device that can
be damaged by the flashing/reverse current, so isolate it before flashing.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: The UK statutory framework you operate under

answers.title: The ISM Code & your role as C/E
answers.answer_text:
ORIGIN & LEGAL BASIS
Full title: the International Management Code for the Safe Operation of Ships and for
Pollution Prevention. Adopted by IMO Resolution A.741(18) (1993) and made mandatory
through a new SOLAS Chapter IX, in force in two phases — 1 July 1998 (passenger ships,
tankers, bulk/gas carriers, high-speed craft ≥500 GT) and 1 July 2002 (other cargo ships and
MODUs ≥500 GT). It arose because casualty investigations (the Herald of Free Enterprise, 1987,
being the catalyst) showed the root cause of most accidents was human error and shore/ship
management failure. The Code therefore regulates how the ship is managed.
UK FLAG Given effect in the UK by the MS (International Safety Management (ISM)
Code) Regulations 2014; guidance in the associated MSN/MGN. UK DOC/SMC audits are carried
out by the MCA or its RO.
OBJECTIVES (ISM 1.2)
To ensure safety at sea, prevention of human injury or loss of life, and avoidance of
damage to the environment and to property. The Company's specific objectives: provide for
safe practices and a safe working environment; assess all identified risks and establish
appropriate safeguards; and continuously improve the safety-management skills of
personnel ashore and afloat, including emergency preparedness for both safety and
environmental protection.
6 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS OF THE SMS (1.4)
The Safety Management System must include: (i) a safety & environmental-protection policy; (ii)
instructions and procedures for safe operation and environmental protection in compliance with
international and flag-State law; (iii) defined levels of authority and lines of communication
(ship↔shore); (iv) procedures for reporting accidents and non-conformities; (v) procedures to
prepare for and respond to emergencies; (vi) procedures for internal audits and management
reviews.
THE ELEMENTS (PART A IMPLEMENTATION 1–12; PART B CERTIFICATION 13–16)
• 1 General; 2 Safety & environmental-protection policy; 3 Company responsibility & authority;
4 Designated Person(s) Ashore; 5 Master's responsibility & overriding authority; 6 Resources &
personnel (qualification, familiarisation, working language); 7 Development of plans for
shipboard operations; 8 Emergency preparedness (drills/exercises); 9 Reports & analysis of
non-conformities, accidents & hazardous occurrences (incl. near-misses); 10 Maintenance of
ship & equipment (PMS + identification/testing of critical equipment) — the element of
most direct interest to a C/E; 11 Documentation; 12 Company verification, review & evaluation
(internal audit & management review).
• 13 Certification & periodical verification; 14 Interim certification; 15 Verification; 16 Forms of
certificates.
THE DESIGNATED PERSON ASHORE (DPA)
Purpose: to ensure the safe operation of each ship and to provide a link between the
Company and those on board. The DPA has direct access to the highest level of
management, and the responsibility and authority to monitor the safety and pollution-
prevention aspects of each ship and to ensure adequate resources and shore support. As C/E I
deal with the DPA on defect/NC reporting and requests for resources and technical support.
MASTER'S OVERRIDING AUTHORITY (ELEMENT 5)
The SMS must define the Master's responsibility for implementing the SMS, motivating the crew,
issuing clear orders, verifying compliance, and reviewing the SMS/reporting deficiencies; and it
must contain a clear statement of the Master's overriding authority and responsibility to
make decisions with respect to safety and pollution prevention and to request the
Company's assistance as necessary.
CERTIFICATION, AUDITS & NON-CONFORMITIES
Item Detail
Document of Issued to the Company, specific to ship types operated; valid 5 years; annual
Compliance (DOC) verification within ±3 months of the anniversary. A copy is held on board.
Safety Issued to the ship; valid 5 years; at least one intermediate verification
Management between the 2nd and 3rd anniversary.
Certificate (SMC)
Interim DOC / Interim DOC ≤12 months (new company / new ship type); Interim SMC ≤6
SMC months, flag may extend +6 (new ship, change of flag, company new to the
ship). Ch. 14 prerequisites: DOC covers the type; key SMS elements in place; ship
surveyed; Master & crew familiarised and know their duties; full audit planned
within 3 months.
• Internal audits at intervals not exceeding 12 months; external audits by MCA/RO for
certification.
7 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

• Observation = statement of fact substantiated by objective evidence / area for improvement.
Non-conformity = objective evidence that a specified requirement is not met. Major NC =
an identifiable deviation posing a serious threat to personnel/ship safety or a serious
environmental risk requiring immediate corrective action, or a lack of effective, systematic
implementation of a Code requirement.
Action on a Major NC (e.g. raised by a PSCO/auditor): contain the hazard; inform
Master, DPA and office. A major NC stops the ship trading — it must be downgraded to an
NC by accepted corrective action (or an alternative measure agreed with Class/Flag) before
sailing, supported where needed by a short-term dispensation/exemption from the flag
State and a documented corrective-action plan addressing root cause; then close out and
verify at the next audit. Example (Q249–250): a major NC means you cannot sail until it is
downgraded and a dispensation obtained — you adopt the alternative measure stated
by Class, get the dispensation, then sail.
HOW ISM AFFECTS ME AS CHIEF ENGINEER
I own the SMS in the engine department: implement documented procedures, risk assessments
and permits; maintain the PMS and safeguard critical equipment (Ch. 10); familiarise
joining engineers before they work (Ch. 6); run effective engine-room drills (Ch. 8); report and
analyse defects, accidents, hazardous occurrences and near-misses and close out
corrective action (Ch. 9); participate in audits and management review; and work under the
Master's overriding authority while liaising with the DPA.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Who holds the DOC and who holds the SMC?” The Company holds the DOC (a copy is
kept on board); the ship holds the SMC. Both are valid 5 years.
• “How is each verified?” The DOC by an annual verification within ±3 months of the
anniversary; the SMC by at least one intermediate verification between the 2nd and 3rd
anniversary.
• “Observation, NC, major NC — the difference?” Observation = a fact/area for improvement;
NC = objective evidence a specified requirement is not met; major NC = a serious threat to
personnel/ship safety or the environment, or a systematic failure to implement the Code.
• “Can you sail with a major NC?” No — it must first be downgraded to an NC by accepted
corrective action (or an alternative agreed with Class/Flag) plus, if needed, a short-term
dispensation from the flag State; then you may sail and close out the root cause.
• “What is the DPA for?” To ensure the safe operation of each ship and provide the ship–shore
link, with direct access to the highest level of management and authority to monitor
safety/pollution and secure resources.
• “Which chapter interests a C/E most, and why?”Chapter 10 — maintenance of ship &
equipment: the PMS plus identification and testing of critical equipment.
• “What is critical equipment and where is it indicated?” Equipment whose sudden
operational failure could create a hazardous situation — steering, main engine,
emergency power, bilge, FFA, etc.; it is flagged in the PMS.
• “How do you prove the SMS actually works?” By records — completed PMS jobs, logged
drills/exercises, near-miss and NC reports with closed-out corrective actions, and satisfactory
internal (≤12-monthly) and external audits.
8 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

1.3 The Maritime Labour Convention 2006 (MLC) (consolidates Q2, 33, 264–265, 293, 445,
447, 539, 567–569, 601–604, 663–664)
STATUS & STRUCTURE
MLC 2006 (in force 20 August 2013) is the "fourth pillar" of the maritime regulatory regime
alongside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW; it consolidates ~68 earlier ILO instruments and sets
seafarers' rights to decent living and working conditions. It is built on five Titles, each with
mandatory Standards (Part A) and guidance (Part B):
• Title 1 — Minimum requirements to work on a ship: minimum age (16; night-work and
hazardous-work restrictions to 18); valid medical certificate; training & qualifications; use of
regulated recruitment/placement services.
• Title 2 — Conditions of employment: Seafarer Employment Agreement (SEA); wages;
hours of work and rest; entitlement to leave; repatriation; manning levels; career
development.
• Title 3 — Accommodation, recreation, food & catering: accommodation standards; food
and potable water; qualified cook.
• Title 4 — Health protection, medical care, welfare & social security: on-board and
ashore medical care; shipowner liability; occupational health & safety and accident prevention;
access to welfare facilities; social security.
• Title 5 — Compliance & enforcement: flag-State responsibilities, port-State control, labour-
supplying responsibilities.
CERTIFICATION & THE DMLC
Ships ≥500 GT on international voyages carry a Maritime Labour Certificate and a
Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance (DMLC). The DMLC has two parts: Part I
drawn up by the flag State, listing the 14 areas to be inspected and the national requirements;
Part II drawn up by the shipowner, setting out the measures adopted to ensure ongoing
compliance and continuous improvement between inspections. The MLC certificate is valid up to
5 years with an intermediate inspection.
Hours of rest (STCW/MLC): minimum 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in
any 7-day period; the 10 hours may be split into no more than two periods, one of at
least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive rest periods must not exceed 14 hours.
Records are kept and signed by the seafarer and Master. A grievance is raised through the
on-board complaints procedure, escalating to the Master, then the Company/DPA, then the
flag State — without prejudice to the seafarer.
UK FLAG Implemented by the MS (Maritime Labour Convention) (Minimum
Requirements for Seafarers etc.) Regulations 2014 and related SIs (medical certification,
hours, accommodation, recruitment). Hours-of-rest detail and record formats are in the associated
MSN. MCA verifies MLC compliance and issues the certificate/DMLC.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Why the fourth pillar?” It completes the framework alongside SOLAS (safety of life), MARPOL
(environment) and STCW (training) by governing seafarers' living and working conditions.
• “Name the five Titles.” (1) Minimum requirements to work; (2) Conditions of employment; (3)
Accommodation, recreation, food & catering; (4) Health, medical care, welfare & social security;
(5) Compliance & enforcement.
9 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

• “Who writes DMLC Part I and Part II?” Part I by the flag State (national requirements/areas
inspected); Part II by the shipowner (measures ensuring ongoing compliance).
• “State the rest-hour rules.” Minimum 10 h in any 24 h and 77 h in any 7-day period; the
10 h in no more than two periods, one of at least 6 h, with the interval between rest periods
not exceeding 14 h.
• “A seafarer has a grievance — the route?” The on-board complaints procedure first,
escalating to the Master, then the Company/DPA, then the flag State — with no detriment to the
seafarer.
• “What must a joining seafarer hold?” A valid SEA, medical certificate, the required STCW
certificates/endorsements, and completed familiarisation.

answers.title: Chief Engineer's standing orders & responsibilities
answers.answer_text:
• Synchronous vs induction motors (Q118/585): synchronous runs at exactly synchronous
speed, can correct power factor (over-excited), but needs excitation and isn't self-starting;
induction is simple, rugged, self-starting, cheap, but runs with slip and draws lagging reactive
power. Motor speed control (Q119): variable-frequency drive (VFD), pole-changing, rotor
resistance (wound-rotor), and — the point the examiner wanted — DC drives (Ward-
Leonard / DC generator feeding DC motor). Why motors get hot (Q623): overload,
high ambient, low/unbalanced voltage, blocked ventilation, bearing failure, single-phasing.
Impedance (Q624): the total AC opposition = the vector sum of resistance and reactance (Z
= √(R² + X²)).
• ACB removal & arcing (Q389–390): isolate and rack out the breaker following the switching
plan; severe arcing/pitting on the contacts indicates the breaker has interrupted heavy
fault currents / worn contacts / poor contact pressure. Replacement breaker (Q391–392):
check the rating (kA breaking capacity, rated current, voltage) matches; test the over-
current trip by primary/secondary current injection. Fault current on a 690 V system
(Q393): the prospective fault current = system voltage ÷ total circuit impedance (source +
cable), used to confirm the breaker's breaking capacity is adequate.
• Star-delta starter fails to change to delta (Q396): the motor stays in star, giving reduced
torque and overheating at full load; check the timer/contactor/auxiliary contacts — you can
run temporarily on reduced load until repaired.
UK FLAG HV safety (Q167/505/521): work under the Code of Safe Working Practices
(COSWP) and the company SMS: gain permission, Permit-to-Work, switching plan, isolation,
Sanction-to-Test, LOTO and interlocks. Because of residual/stored voltages even when
isolated, earth down the breaker/generator with earthing straps, and close the neutral-earth
resistor and fit earthing straps to the generator windings before working inside. Verify
dead before touching. Some ships use HV (Q395) to reduce cable size and I²R losses for large
loads (thrusters, propulsion).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Chief Engineer's standing orders & responsibilities

answers.title: UK health & safety, safety officer & safety committee
answers.answer_text:
• Reactive power (Q370/681): the power that oscillates between source and inductive/
capacitive loads (kVAr), doing no net work but needed to magnetise motors/transformers; it is
shared between paralleled alternators by excitation/AVR (droop). If reactive power is too
high (Q371/682): larger circulating current for the same real load → higher I²R losses, poorer
power factor, and increased fuel consumption of the generators, plus voltage-regulation
problems.
• CPP operation & fail-safe (Q78/88/137): pitch is set hydraulically; on control failure it
usually fails to the last set position ("fail-set"), though designs can fail to zero pitch or to
100% ahead depending on configuration — each with pros/cons. To control the vessel with the
38 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

bridge control lost (Q89/112), transfer to ECR then local control, and regulate speed by
engine RPM with constant bridge communication.
• Diesel-electric / propulsion motors (Q394–395): AC/synchronous propulsion motors are
started/controlled via power-electronic converters (synchro-converter or cyclo-converter);
these generate harmonics which distort the supply — mitigated by filters, phase-shifting
transformers and 12/24-pulse arrangements; the power-electronic modules (PEMs) are liquid/
air cooled. HV switching, COSWP PPE and permits apply.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Generator makes no voltage — why and cure?” Lost residual magnetism → flash the
field with a battery (disconnect the AVR first).
• “Still no voltage after flashing?”Faulty rotating-rectifier diodes — check with a
multimeter.
• “Synchroscope fails — how do you sync?” On the lamps (dark/rotating), or a voltmeter
across the breaker; close at the null.
• “First earth fault dangerous?” Not alone on an insulated system — but a second earth on
another phase completes a short-circuit; find the first fault fast.
• “How do you test the reverse-power trip?” Lower the incoming machine's governor until
power reverses and confirm it trips.
• “Why do fuse ratings reduce toward the consumer?”Discrimination — the device
nearest the fault trips first.
• “Replacement breaker checks/tests?” Match kA breaking capacity/rated current/
voltage; test over-current trip by current injection.
• “HV isolation before work?” PTW, switching plan, isolation, sanction-to-test, LOTO, and earth
down for residual voltages (neutral-earth resistor closed, earthing straps on windings).
• “Effect of high reactive power?” More circulating current/losses → poorer PF and higher
generator fuel consumption.
• “CPP fail-safe position?” Usually fail-set (last position); control via ECR then local,
regulating engine RPM.
Section 12 — Safety, FFA, Enclosed Space, LSA & Lifting

answers.title: The certificates carried on board
answers.answer_text:
Certificates fall into three families: statutory (from the conventions, issued by/for the flag),
class (hull & machinery, from the class society), and trade / liability (insurance-backed). A C/E
should be able to list ~20+ and say which convention each derives from.
MARPOL /
Class / Construction Safety (SOLAS) Trade / Personnel
Environmental
Certificate of Class (hull & Cargo Ship Safety IOPP + Supp; IAPP + MLC + DMLC I/II;
machinery); Cargo Ship Equipment; Cargo Supp; EIAPP (per Minimum Safe Manning
Safety Construction; Ship Safety Radio; (or engine) + NOx Tech File; Document; CLC (oil-
International Load Line + the single Cargo ISPP; IEEC; IAFS (anti- cargo liability); Bunkers
SUPP (International Load Ship Safety fouling); BWM; Sewage; Convention (bunker-oil
Line Exemption where Certificate if Garbage Mgt Plan/ liability); P&I entry;
applicable); International harmonised); SMC Record Book; Oil Record tanker-specific (P&A
Tonnage; Continuous (+DOC copy); ISSC Book Manual, Cert. of
Synopsis Record (CSR) (Ship Security) Fitness); container/DG
(Cargo Securing
Manual, IMDG docs)
UK FLAG UK statutory certificates are issued on behalf of the Government of the United
Kingdom by the MCA or its RO under the MS (Survey and Certification) Regulations. A full
up-to-date list and the survey/validity table are published in the relevant MSN. The CSR (SOLAS
XI-1) records the ship's history (flag, owner, ISM company, class) and must be kept up to date.
11 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

2.2 The Harmonised System of Survey & Certification (HSSC) and the
survey cycle (consolidates Q162, 203–205, 251–253, 307, 313, 358, 496, 643–644, 667)
Under HSSC all the major statutory certificates share a common 5-year cycle with a common
expiry date, so surveys are aligned ("harmonised") rather than each running on its own date. This
is why "all my certs expire together." The survey types:
Survey Purpose & timing
Initial Before the certificate is first issued / the ship enters service — full verification against
the requirements.
Annual General verification each year within a window of ±3 months of the anniversary
date. Endorsed on the certificate.
Intermediate A more detailed survey (in lieu of/additional to an annual) at the 2nd or 3rd
anniversary — e.g. hull/equipment items needing deeper checks.
Renewal Every 5 years — the fullest survey; a new certificate is issued. May be completed
(Special) within 3 months before expiry (not after), and the new certificate then runs from
the old expiry date so the cycle stays harmonised.
Knowing when the annual is due (a classic follow-up): work back from the
certificate's anniversary/expiry date, not from the issue date — because if a new
certificate is issued mid-cycle the issue date changes but the anniversary date does not. The
annual window is the anniversary date ±3 months; the renewal can be done up to 3
months before expiry but not after. All expiry dates are recorded in the PMS and a
dedicated original-certificate file.
2.3 Classification societies, statutory vs class survey, and Continuous
Machinery Survey (consolidates Q82, 305–307, 329–331, 356, 359, 546)
A classification society (an IACS member — LR, DNV, ABS, BV, etc.) writes rules for the design,
construction and upkeep of the hull and machinery, surveys the ship to those rules to assign and
maintain class, and — as a Recognised Organisation — often carries out statutory work for
the flag.
• Statutory survey verifies compliance with the international conventions (SOLAS/MARPOL/
Load Line/MLC) on the flag's behalf. Class survey verifies compliance with the society's own
rules to maintain class. A ship must hold both valid class and valid statutory certificates to
trade.
• Continuous Machinery Survey (CMS): instead of surveying all machinery at the 5-year
renewal, items are opened up and surveyed on a rolling ~5-year cycle, roughly one-fifth
each year. Under an approved arrangement the C/E may credit (survey) certain items
himself, the surveyor confirming at the next attendance. Not covered by C/E-credited CMS:
items requiring surveyor attendance or specialist testing, and certain safety-critical items (e.g.
certain pressure vessels, safety devices) — these are surveyed by the surveyor.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Statutory vs class survey?” Statutory = compliance with the conventions on the flag's
behalf; class = compliance with the society's own hull/machinery rules. A ship needs both valid
to trade.
12 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

• “What is a Recognised Organisation?” An IACS class society authorised by the flag State
to carry out statutory surveys and certification on its behalf.
• “Annual, intermediate, renewal — the windows?” Annual within ±3 months of the
anniversary; intermediate a deeper survey at the 2nd/3rd anniversary; renewal every 5 years,
completable up to 3 months before expiry, not after.
• “How does CMS work and what can a C/E credit?” Machinery is surveyed on a rolling ~5-
year cycle (~1/5 per year); under an approved arrangement the C/E may open up and credit
certain items, confirmed by the surveyor. Safety-critical items and those needing surveyor
attendance/specialist testing cannot be self-credited.
• “Why work back from the anniversary, not the issue date?” A mid-cycle re-issue changes
the issue date but not the anniversary/expiry, which is what governs the survey windows.

answers.title: The Load Line survey
answers.answer_text:
The International Load Line Certificate (LL 66 / 1988 Protocol) certifies the minimum
permitted freeboard, ensuring adequate reserve buoyancy and hull weathertight/watertight
integrity; valid 5 years under HSSC. The survey checks the conditions of assignment are
maintained: structural strength for the assigned draught; effective weathertight closing
appliances (hatch covers, doors, ventilators, air pipes with automatic closing devices, coaming
heights); protection of machinery openings and companionways; adequate freeing ports/
scuppers; guard rails, gangways, lifelines and safe crew access; and the correct load-line marks
(deck line, disc, seasonal marks TF/F/T/S/W/WNA).
UK FLAG Practical checks the surveyor makes and the examiner loves: the weathertight
door "chalk test" — chalk the knife-edge/gasket, close the door, and an unbroken chalk print
confirms even compression all round; and checking ballast-tank air-pipe/vent closing
appliances (ball/float type) and their gauzes/flame screens. SUPP in "Load Line certificate
with SUPP" = the exemption/supplement covering any granted exemptions. UK regs: MS
(Load Line) Regulations.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: The Load Line survey

answers.title: Safety Construction, Safety Equipment & Safety Radio surveys
answers.answer_text:
• Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate — structure, machinery and electrical
installations, and their safety (SOLAS II-1/II-2 construction aspects).
• Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate (SEQ/"SSE") — LSA (lifeboats, liferafts, davits,
launching gear), FFA (fixed and portable), navigational equipment, means of embarkation, line-
throwing, signals. It has annual, periodical and renewal surveys — the "periodical" being
the fuller inspection required between the 2nd and 3rd annual.
• Cargo Ship Safety Radio Certificate — GMDSS/radio installation.
As C/E preparing for a safety-equipment survey I ensure fixed FFA (CO /foam) pressure/
2
quantity and controls are proven, portable extinguishers serviced, fire main/pumps/emergency
fire pump tested, fire detection tested, LSA (lifeboats, davits, release gear, brakes, liferaft/HRU
service dates) ready, and all records/certificates current.
13 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

2.6 Underwater (in-water) survey & interval between drydocks (consolidates
Q360–363, 669–673)
The rule requires two bottom (drydock) surveys in any 5-year period, with the interval
between them not exceeding 36 months. However, ships with an approved In-Water Survey
(IWS) notation may substitute an underwater survey by diver for one of the drydockings,
extending the docking interval (commonly to a ~7.5-year pattern for suitable ships).
When you can "get away with" an underwater survey instead of docking: the ship
must have a high-durability antifouling and an anodes/ICCP scheme designed for
the extended interval (e.g. a 5-year-plus paint and anode scheme) so the hull/anodes
remain sound between dockings, plus suitable hull markings for the divers, clean sea chests/
gratings, and satisfactory tailshaft/rudder condition. Preparation: lock-out/tag-out of
thrusters, propeller and any suction/discharge that could injure divers; hull reference
markings so divers know which area they are surveying; and good visibility. Rudder pintle/
carrier clearances and tailshaft weardown can be taken by diver.
2.7 Port State Control (PSC) (consolidates Q280, 314–317, 605–606)
PSC is the inspection of foreign ships in a port State to verify condition, equipment and crew
comply with the international conventions — a safety net against sub-standard shipping. It is
coordinated by regional MoUs. Ships and companies are risk-profiled; deficiencies must be
rectified and serious ones can lead to detention until put right.
• Paris MoU covers Europe and Canada; other regimes include Tokyo MoU, the USCG regime,
etc.
• Ship risk profile / grading considers: ship type, age, flag performance (white/grey/black
list), RO performance, company performance, and the ship's inspection/detention history —
producing a Low / Standard / High Risk profile that sets inspection frequency.
• Types of inspection: initial (documents + general condition), more detailed (where "clear
grounds" exist), and expanded (for high-risk/older ships of certain types).
• If the PSCO's assessment is wrong, the C/E provides objective evidence/certificates on the
spot, and the company may lodge a formal appeal through the flag State / MoU.
UK FLAG In UK ports PSC is carried out by the MCA under the Paris MoU. As a flag, the UK
targets a strong Paris MoU "white list" position, so a UK ship's own performance affects its risk
profile abroad.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Why does PSC exist?” A safety net to catch sub-standard ships missed by flag/class,
verifying convention compliance in the port State.
• “Which MoU covers Europe and Canada?” The Paris MoU.
• “What sets a ship's inspection frequency?” Its risk profile from ship type, age, flag
performance (white/grey/black list), RO performance, company performance, and
inspection/detention history → Low / Standard / High Risk.
• “Name the inspection types.”Initial, more detailed (on clear grounds), and expanded
(high-risk/older ships of certain types).
• “What are 'clear grounds'?” Evidence justifying a deeper look — missing/invalid certificates,
visible defects/poor condition, an incident, or a report.
14 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

• “If the PSCO is wrong, what can you do?” Present objective evidence/certificates on the
spot; the company may lodge a formal appeal via the flag/MoU. A detention lifts only when
the deficiencies are rectified.
Section 3 — MARPOL Annex VI (Air Pollution) & Energy Efficiency

answers.title: Annex VI overview
answers.answer_text:
A loud bang and the vessel runs aground — my priorities as C/E, in coordination with the bridge:
• Stop/reduce the engine as directed, be ready to shut sea inlets (avoid drawing in sand/
silt and cooling problems), and start the emergency generator/steering if needed.
• Check watertight integrity in the engine room — the first action — and inspect for
flooding/ingress; be ready on bilge pumps.
• Sound all tanks and bilges, including cofferdams and double bottoms, and compare
with previous soundings to detect any rise (breach); advise the Mate to sound ballast/coffer
dams and check cargo holds.
• Check machinery for damage from the shock (crankshaft deflections, bearing clearances,
shaft alignment, sea-water/lube systems).
• Assess and report to Master/office/Class/flag; consider pollution risk (SOPEP) and prepare
the emergency dry-dock plan, sounding and shell-expansion plans if a breach is found
(Q418).
"5 grounding actions" (Q226): (1) sound all tanks & bilges and compare; (2) check
watertight/hull integrity and for flooding; (3) protect machinery — shut sea inlets, check
cooling, take deflections/alignment; (4) assess stability & pollution risk (free surface, SOPEP);
(5) report and plan repairs (Master/office/Class/flag, dry-dock & damage plans).
1

answers.title: SOx control — Reg 14
answers.answer_text:
• Limits: global cap 0.50% m/m sulphur (from 1 Jan 2020, "IMO 2020"); ECA/SECA limit
0.10% m/m.
• SOx ECAs: Baltic Sea, North Sea/English Channel, North American, US Caribbean — and the
Mediterranean Sea SECA from 1 May 2025.
• Compliance options: burn compliant low-sulphur fuel; use an approved Exhaust Gas
Cleaning System (scrubber / EGCS) as an equivalent; or use an alternative fuel (LNG,
methanol).
Scrubber types (Q76):
• Open loop: uses the natural alkalinity of seawater to neutralise SO ; wash-water is treated
2
and discharged overboard within limits. Simple, no reagent — but restricted/prohibited in some
ports and coastal waters.
• Closed loop: recirculates fresh water dosed with caustic soda (NaOH); a small bleed-off is
treated, and residues go to a holding tank for shore disposal — usable in zero-discharge
zones but needs reagent and tankage.
• Hybrid: switchable between modes.
Monitoring & values: compliance is proven by continuous measurement of the exhaust
SO (ppm)/CO (%) ratio (e.g. a ratio of ≤4.3 corresponds to 0.10% S equivalent; ≤21.7 to
2 2
0.50%), plus wash-water quality — pH, PAH (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons),
turbidity and nitrate. EGCS fails in an ECA (Q170): change to compliant low-sulphur
fuel if available; if not, notify Flag and Port State, record in the ORB/log, and submit a
FONAR (Fuel Oil Non-Availability Report) as evidence of best efforts — you cannot
15 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

simply continue non-compliant, and you would expect Flag/PSC to require the evidence and
possibly impose conditions.

answers.title: NOx control — Reg 13
answers.answer_text:
Reg 13 applies to marine diesel engines of output >130 kW installed on ships. NOx limits are set
by Tier and by the engine's rated speed (n, rpm) — the limit is a curve, lowest at high rpm:
Tier Build date Where it applies
Tier I On/after 1 Jan 2000 Global
Tier II On/after 1 Jan 2011 Global (~15–22% below Tier I)
Tier III On/after 1 Jan 2016 (Baltic/North Sea: 2021) NOx ECAs only (~80% below Tier I)
NOx ECAs: North American & US Caribbean (2016) and Baltic & North Sea (2021). Each engine's
NOx compliance is certified by the EIAPP certificate and demonstrated in service by the NOx
Technical File (defining components, settings, adjustable parameters and the on-board
parameter check / direct measurement / simplified measurement method). The NOx
value for a specific engine is found in its EIAPP / NOx Technical File.
NOx reduction methods — know them split into primary and secondary:
Primary (in-cylinder, lower peak temperature — NOx forms at high temperature):
Miller timing (early inlet valve closing + higher turbocharging), retarded/variable injection
timing, Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) (recirculates cooled inert exhaust to lower O /
2
temperature), Direct Water Injection (DWI), water-in-fuel emulsification, and
combustion optimisation.
Secondary (after-treatment): Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) — urea (→
ammonia) reacts with NOx over a vanadium/titania catalyst at ~300–400 °C to give N +
2
H O; the usual route to Tier III.
2

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: NOx control — Reg 13

answers.title: ODS, VOC & incineration
answers.answer_text:
• Bunker calculation / voyage planning (Q237): from the voyage distance and speed,
estimate consumption (ME + AE + boiler) with a safety margin for weather/reserve, checking
tank capacities, densities and temperature corrections, and compliance fuel for any ECA legs.
• Tank planning — why not mix (Q238): keep fuels of different grades/suppliers segregated
to avoid incompatibility/asphaltene precipitation and sludging, and to keep ECA-
compliant and non-compliant fuels separate for regulatory reasons.
• Azipod thruster / stabilizer checks (Q231/402): planned maintenance on the pod
bearings, seals, slip-rings, cooling and steering; pod LO analysis (Q403–404) for wear
metals and water — noting that a slow-developing failure may not show up early in analysis
(large-particle limitation), so combine with vibration/temperature monitoring.
• NOx Technical File / EIAPP (Q291–292/450–452): the NOx values for a specific engine are
found in the EIAPP certificate and NOx Technical File, which also records the engine's
components, adjustable settings, and the on-board verification method and any parameter
changes.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “First action on grounding?” Check watertight integrity in the engine room, then sound
all tanks/bilges and compare with previous.
• “Why compare soundings?” A rise reveals a breach/ingress.
• “Flooding in ER — where do you record?” Official Log Book (and ORB if oily), after stopping
the source and pumping out.
• “Leaking pressurised seal tank?”Reduce the pressure/head to cut the leak, plan a dock
repair.
• “Turbo vibrating after dock?”Stop and check the T/C — don't run on.
• “What must a joining 2/E have?” CoC/original ticket + flag endorsement, STCW certs,
medical, discharge book, safety certs.
• “Where are an engine's NOx values?” The EIAPP certificate / NOx Technical File.
• “Why not mix bunker grades?” Incompatibility/asphaltene sludging and to segregate ECA-
compliant fuel.

44 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

1 — Transverse section: K, B, G, M, Z and the righting lever GZ (Q39, 489)

THE THEORY
In equilibrium, weight W acts down through the centre of gravity G and an equal buoyant
force acts up through the centre of buoyancy B (the centroid of the underwater volume).
When the ship is heeled to a small angle θ by an external force, a wedge of buoyancy
emerges on the high side and an equal wedge is immersed on the low side, so B moves off
the centreline to the low side, to B1. The vertical line of buoyant force through B1 cuts
the centreline at the metacentre M. W and buoyancy are now horizontally separated and
form a couple; the horizontal distance GZ is the righting lever, and W×GZ is the righting
moment that returns the ship upright. The ship is stable while G is below M (positive GM,
positive GZ), neutral when G coincides with M, and unstable when G is above M.
HOW TO CONSTRUCT THE SKETCH
• Draw the transverse (midship) section symmetrical about a vertical centreline; put the
keel K at the bottom as the datum.
• Mark on the centreline, bottom-up: B (upright), G, and M.
• Incline the waterline for heel θ; shift buoyancy to B1 on the deeper (low) side and draw
the vertical line of buoyant force up through B1 — where it crosses the centreline is M.
• From G, drop a perpendicular onto that line; its foot is Z, and GZ is the righting lever.
Show W down through G and buoyancy up through B1.
Key relationships: KM = KB + BM, where BM = I/V (transverse second moment of
the waterplane ÷ volume of displacement); GM = KM − KG; and for small angles GZ =
GM × sinθ. A large GM gives a stiff ship (quick, jerky roll); a small positive GM a
tender ship (slow, easy roll) — both must stay within the ship's stability criteria.
45 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Where is M and how is it found?” The intersection of successive buoyancy verticals
with the centreline; KM = KB + BM, BM = I/V.
• “What makes GZ positive?”G below M.
• “GZ for small angles?”GZ = GM sinθ.
• “Stiff vs tender ship?” Large GM = stiff/jerky; small GM = tender/slow.
• “Redraw for angle of loll?”M below G (negative GM): unstable upright, heels until the
rising wedge restores a small positive GZ, then floats tenderly at the loll angle.
46 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack
2 — The GZ (righting-lever) curve (Q651)
Angleofheelθ(degrees)
WHAT THE CURVE REPRESENTS
The GZ (statical-stability) curve plots the righting lever GZ against the angle of heel for a
given loading condition. It is derived from the ship's cross curves (KN curves) of stability
for the displacement, corrected for the actual KG. It shows how the righting lever — and
hence the righting moment W×GZ — grows with heel, reaches a maximum, then falls to zero
as the deck edge immerses and buoyancy is lost from the high side.
HOW TO CONSTRUCT AND READ IT
Plot GZ (m) vertically against heel angle (degrees) horizontally.
Draw a tangent at the origin and extend it to 57.3° (1 radian); the height it reaches
equals GM — linking the initial slope to metacentric height.
Mark the maximum GZ and its angle; the range of stability (0° to where GZ returns to
zero); and the angle of vanishing stability (AVS, ~70°), beyond which the ship
capsizes.
The area under the curve to any angle is the dynamical stability — the energy
needed to heel the ship to that angle.
IMO intact-stability (weather) criteria worth quoting: GM ≥ 0.15 m; maximum
GZ occurring at ≥ 25–30°; area under the curve ≥ 0.055 m·rad to 30° and ≥ 0.09
m·rad to 40° (or the downflooding angle), with ≥ 0.03 m·rad between 30° and 40°;
and GZ ≥ 0.20 m at 30°.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
“How do you get GM off the curve?” Tangent at the origin to 57.3° = GM.
“What is the AVS?” The angle where GZ returns to zero / the end of the range (~70°).
“What does the area under the curve give?” Dynamical stability (energy to heel).
“State an IMO criterion.” Area to 30° ≥ 0.055 m·rad; GM ≥ 0.15 m; max GZ at ≥ 25°.
“Effect of raising KG?” Lowers GM and drops the whole curve → less range/area
(dangerous).

3 — Free-surface effect (virtual rise of G) (Q39, 510, 609–611)

THE MECHANISM
A partially filled (slack) tank has a free liquid surface that stays horizontal as the ship heels.
As she inclines, a wedge of liquid runs to the low side; this transfer of weight moves the
tank's own centre of gravity toward the low side and, in effect, raises the ship's effective
centre of gravity from G to a virtual position Gv. The resulting loss of GM (the free-
surface correction) reduces the righting lever at every angle, so the ship is less stable —
regardless of how full the tank is.
HOW TO CONSTRUCT THE SKETCH
• Draw a rectangular tank part-filled, upright, liquid surface horizontal, its c.g. g on the
centreline.
• Draw the same tank heeled; keep the liquid surface horizontal so a wedge shifts to the
low side, and mark the new tank c.g. g1.
• Show the ship's G rising to Gv and label the loss of GM.
The numbers: the virtual rise of G (free-surface correction) = i·ρ ÷ (V·ρ ) ≈ i/
liquid sw
V for like densities, where i = l·b³/12 is the transverse second moment of the tank's
free surface. Because it enters as breadth cubed (b³), a wide slack tank is far worse
than a narrow one — hence longitudinal subdivisions/baffles are fitted to cut b, and
free surface is minimised by pressing tanks up or running them empty and avoiding
several slack tanks at once.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Does the amount of liquid matter?” No — the loss depends on the free-surface
breadth, not the quantity.
• “Formula for the loss?”FSC = i/V, i = l·b³/12.
• “Why is breadth so important?” It enters as b³ — a wide tank is dramatically worse.
• “How do you reduce it?” Press up or empty tanks, fit baffles/subdivisions, avoid multiple
slack tanks.
• “How do engineers cause it daily?” Consuming fuel/LO and ballasting create slack
tanks.

4 — Main bearing arrangement (Q533)
Holding-downstuds&nuts

CONSTRUCTION & OPERATION
The main bearings support the crankshaft journals in the bedplate. Each is a thin-walled
steel shell in two halves — a lower shell in the bedplate saddle and an upper shell in the
keep — lined on the running face with white metal (a soft tin- or lead-based babbitt) which
is embeddable and conformable and, if overheated, wipes rather than seizing the
journal. The keep (cap) is held by two studs and nuts, hydraulically tensioned. Oil enters
under pressure through a groove/hole so that, as the journal turns, it drags oil into the
converging clearance to form a hydrodynamic wedge that lifts the journal off the
metal — the film is thinnest where the load acts.
HOW TO DRAW & WHAT TO LABEL
• Bedplate/transverse-girder housing; journal; lower and upper shells with white-
metal lining; bearing keep/cap; the two holding-down studs and nuts; and the
oil inlet/groove.
Failure — oval journal & wiped bearing (what the examiner wants):
misalignment (deflections out of limits), oil contamination/cat-fines, oil starvation or
overload break the oil film, causing metal-to-metal contact that overheats and wipes
the white metal and wears the journal oval (out-of-round). Detection: rising
bearing temperature, LO wear metals (Cu/Pb/Sn), increased clearance (feelers/bridge
gauge), and crankshaft deflections. If ignored it leads to bearing failure and a crankcase
hot-spot → oil-mist alarm / explosion risk.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Why white metal?” Soft, conformable, embeddable; wipes rather than seizing the
journal.
• “How is the oil film maintained?” A hydrodynamic wedge — journal rotation drags oil
into the converging clearance.
• “What causes an oval journal?” Misalignment/overload/oil failure breaking the film.
• “How do you detect a failing main bearing?” Bearing temperature, LO wear metals,
clearance, deflections.

5 — Hydraulic jack-nut / stud tensioning (Q224)
studstretches
Piston/ram

HPoilin(pressureP)

WHY HYDRAULIC TENSIONING IS USED
Large studs/tie-bolts (cylinder covers, main-bearing keeps, tie rods) must be tightened to an
accurate, uniform bolt load. A spanner cannot develop or measure that load reliably, and
torque is an unreliable proxy because friction varies. A hydraulic tensioner stretches
the stud directly by a known axial force, giving accurate, repeatable, simultaneous
tightening with no torsional stress in the stud.
HOW IT WORKS (WITH THE SKETCH)
• The tensioner body screws onto an extended thread on top of the stud; a piston/ram
inside is pressurised by high-pressure oil.
• Oil pressure P acts on the piston area A to give an axial pull F = P × A, which stretches
the stud elastically (arrows show the stretch).
• While held stretched, the nut is run down by hand onto the component; pressure is
then released and the stud remains tensioned to the calculated bolt load.
Setting & checking: the required oil pressure is read from the maker's table for the
target bolt load (P = F/A). Multiple tensioners are used together (e.g. all cover studs at
once) so the clamp load is even and the joint doesn't distort. On release the residual
stretch/gap is checked; over-pressurising risks yielding the stud, so the maker's
pressure must not be exceeded.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Why not just torque it?” Torque is friction-dependent and adds torsional stress;
tensioning gives a pure, accurate axial load.
• “What determines the load?”F = P × A (oil pressure × piston area), from the maker's
table.
• “How is the nut secured?” Run down by hand while stretched, then the pressure is
released.
• “Why tension several together?” For an even clamp load and to avoid distortion.

6 — AVR / brushless excitation block diagram (Q562)

HOW THE EXCITATION LOOP WORKS
A brushless AC generator uses an exciter to feed its rotating main field without brushes.
The exciter is a small AC generator on the same shaft whose field is stationary and
controlled by the AVR. The AVR continuously senses terminal voltage, compares it with
a set reference Vref, and adjusts the exciter-field current to correct any error. The
exciter's rotating armature output is rectified by the rotating rectifier (shaft-mounted
diodes) to give the DC that supplies the main rotor field. More excitation strengthens the
main-field flux and raises terminal voltage; less lowers it — so the loop holds voltage
constant as load and power factor change.
DRAWING & LABELLING
• Voltage sensing → comparator (vs Vref) → AVR amplifier → exciter field → exciter
→ rotating rectifier (diodes) → main field → generator, with the feedback line from
the output.
Fault-finding (the follow-ups): a generator that builds no voltage on start has lost
residual magnetism — flash the field with a battery to re-establish flux, after
which the AVR takes over (disconnect the AVR first, as flashing/reverse current can
damage it). If it still won't build after flashing, the rotating-rectifier diodes are likely
faulty — check them with a multimeter (forward-conducting, reverse-blocking). Loss of
AVR sensing or Vref supply also prevents build-up. Reactive load is shared between
paralleled sets by the AVRs' voltage droop.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “What does the AVR actually control?” Exciter-field current → main-field flux → terminal
voltage.
• “Why 'brushless'?” The rotating rectifier feeds the main field without brushes/slip-rings.
• “No voltage on start — cause and cure?” Lost residual magnetism → flash the field
(battery); disconnect the AVR first.
• “Still none after flashing?”Faulty rotating-rectifier diodes → check with a
multimeter.
• “How is reactive load shared?” By AVR voltage droop.

7 — Turning-gear interlock (start prevention) (Q38)

PURPOSE & OPERATION
The turning gear is an electric-motor-driven gear that slowly rotates ("barrs") the main
engine for inspection, overhaul and warming-through. Turning the engine while it could be
started on starting air would be catastrophic, so a safety interlock is fitted: a limit switch
senses when the gear is engaged and opens the engine start circuit (and blocks/
vents the starting-air pilot), so the engine cannot be started until the gear is
disengaged. An indication lamp (and usually a bridge indication) shows "turning gear
engaged."
DRAWING & TESTING
• Show the engaged limit switch in the start-interlock relay circuit, the relay contact in
the starting-air solenoid/start circuit, and the indication lamp.
• Test by attempting a start (on a blocked / air-off test) with the gear engaged and
confirming the engine will not start; prove the lamp/indication.
MSWB safeties & the reverse-power point (Q38 continued): the main-
switchboard generator protections are over-current/short-circuit (time-graded for
discrimination), reverse power, under/over-voltage, under-frequency, and
preferential (non-essential load-shedding) trips. They are tested by primary/
secondary current injection or simulation (e.g. lowering the incoming machine's
governor to prove the reverse-power trip). If the reverse-power trip fails, a
generator whose prime mover has failed will motor — drawing power from the bus,
over-speeding and overheating — so back-up protection and prompt manual tripping
are essential.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “What is the interlock for?” To prevent starting the engine on air while the turning gear
is engaged.
• “How does it work?” The engaged limit switch opens the start circuit / blocks the
starting-air pilot.
• “How do you test it?” Attempt a (blocked) start with the gear engaged — it must not
start.
• “How is reverse power tested?” Reduce the incoming machine's governor until power
reverses; the breaker must trip.

• “If reverse power fails?” The set motors (over-speeds/overheats) — trip it manually.

WHY AND WHAT IS MEASURED
The propeller shaft is carried in the aft stern-tube bearing (bush). As the bearing wears,
the shaft drops in the bush, increasing the clearance at the top — the "weardown."
Measuring and trending this clearance shows the bearing's remaining life and whether the
shaft must be drawn. The reading is taken at the top of the aft bush (the loaded bearing)
with a poker/wear-down gauge through an access point, and compared with the
original (as-fitted) and previous readings.
DRAWING & PROCEDURE
• Show the aft stern-tube bush with its bearing surface, the shaft resting low (worn) in
it, and the poker gauge inserted at the top measuring the top clearance.
• Take the reading in a repeatable condition (shaft weight taken normally); record and
compare with the datum and previous surveys to obtain the weardown.
Limits & the drain question: the maker/Class set a maximum permissible
weardown (often a few mm on white-metal oil-lubricated bearings); reaching it means
renew the bearing / draw the shaft. For an oil-lubricated stern tube you do NOT
drain the oil to take the reading — the seals retain the oil and the gauge reads
through the access point. Rising weardown, poor stern-tube LO analysis (wear metals/
water), high bearing temperature, or increasing oil consumption (seal wear) trigger
inspection/withdrawal; oil-lubricated shafts with approved seals and oil analysis run
under a TCM notation up to ~15 years.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Where and how is weardown measured?” Top of the aft bush, poker/wear-down
gauge, against the original/previous reading.
• “Do you drain the stern tube?” No, for oil-lubricated seals — the gauge reads through
the access point.
• “What is the limit?” The maker/Class maximum weardown; renew the bearing when
reached.
• “What else indicates a worn bearing?” LO wear metals/water, bearing temperature, oil
consumption (seal wear).

9 — Flammability (composition) diagram — inerting (Q199)
Oxygen%byvolume→
WHAT IT SHOWS
The flammability (composition) diagram plots the hydrocarbon content of a tank
atmosphere against its oxygen content and shows which mixtures can burn. A mixture
ignites only inside the flammable envelope, bounded by the lower flammable limit
(LFL, too lean below it) and the upper flammable limit (UFL, too rich above it). As oxygen
is reduced the flammable range narrows, and below a critical oxygen level (~11% by
volume) no hydrocarbon/air mixture is flammable at all. On tankers the atmosphere is kept
oxygen-lean by inert gas so cargo operations never enter the flammable zone.
DRAWING & THE KEY LINES
Axes: hydrocarbon % (vertical) against oxygen % (horizontal). Mark the flammable
envelope with the LFL (~1% HC) and UFL (~10% HC) on the air line (21% O ), and

flammable zone. Inerting first drives the atmosphere down the oxygen axis to < 8%
O (below the critical dilution line), so purging/gassing-up then moves along a path that
2
stays in the non-flammable region. Going from an inerted tank to fresh air must be done
only after purging hydrocarbons out, so the composition moves outside the
envelope. IG systems keep tank O typically < 5% for this reason.

“Why inert below 8%?” To keep the atmosphere out of the flammable zone with a margin
