answers.title: Energy efficiency — Chapter 4
answers.answer_text:
• EEDI (Energy Efficiency Design Index): a mandatory design-stage index (gCO per
2
capacity-mile) for new builds, tightened in phases; forces more efficient hull/engine design.
• EEXI (Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index): the equivalent one-off requirement applied
to existing ships (often met by engine power limitation / EPL).
• SEEMP (Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan): the ship-specific plan of operational
efficiency measures; now includes the mandatory CII (Carbon Intensity Indicator) — an
annual operational rating A–E, with a corrective action plan required for a D (three years) or E
rating.
• IEEC (International Energy Efficiency Certificate): certifies EEDI/EEXI/SEEMP compliance.
EEOI is the voluntary operational indicator (gCO /tonne-mile). Data is reported through the
2
IMO Data Collection System (DCS) and, for EU/EEA voyages, EU MRV.
Reducing CO (Q22) — because CO is proportional to fuel burned: speed/voyage
2 2
optimisation (slow steaming, optimum trim, weather routeing, just-in-time arrival); hull &
propeller condition (anti-fouling, hull cleaning, propeller polishing); machinery efficiency
(performance monitoring, waste-heat/EGB recovery, optimum load, reduced auxiliaries, shaft
generator); and technical/design measures (EEDI/EEXI compliance, EPL, energy-saving
devices, lower-carbon fuels). CO calculation: CO = fuel consumed × carbon factor C
2 2 F
(HFO ≈ 3.114, MDO/MGO ≈ 3.206, LNG ≈ 2.750 t CO /t fuel).
2
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “State the sulphur limits.” Global 0.50% m/m (from 1 Jan 2020); ECA 0.10% m/m.
• “Name the SOx ECAs.” Baltic, North Sea/Channel, North American, US Caribbean — and the
Mediterranean SECA from 1 May 2025.
• “Open vs closed-loop scrubber?” Open uses seawater alkalinity and discharges treated
wash-water overboard; closed recirculates NaOH-dosed freshwater with residue to a holding
tank for shore disposal; hybrid switches between them.
• “What do you monitor on a scrubber?” Exhaust SO /CO ratio (≤4.3 for 0.10% equivalent)
2 2
plus wash-water pH, PAH, turbidity, nitrate.
• “Scrubber fails in an ECA — actions?” Switch to compliant fuel if available; if not, notify
Flag & Port State, record, and submit a FONAR — you cannot continue non-compliant.
• “NOx Tiers and where does Tier III apply?” Tier I (2000), Tier II (2011, global), Tier III (2016;
Baltic/N.Sea 2021) — Tier III only in NOx ECAs.
• “Where is an engine's NOx status recorded?” The EIAPP certificate + NOx Technical
File.
• “Primary vs secondary NOx methods?” Primary lowers peak combustion temperature in-
cylinder (Miller, retarded/variable timing, EGR, DWI, water-in-fuel); secondary = SCR after-
treatment (urea→ammonia over a catalyst → N + H O).
2 2
• “What may NOT be incinerated at sea?” Annex I/II/III residues & contaminated packing,
PCBs, garbage with more than traces of heavy metals, refined products containing halogens,
and sludge not generated on board.
• “EEDI vs EEXI vs SEEMP/CII vs IEEC?” EEDI = design index (new builds); EEXI = one-off index
for existing ships (often met via EPL); SEEMP = operational plan carrying the CII A–E rating; the
IEEC certifies compliance.
17 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

Section 4 — MARPOL Annexes I–V & the BWM Convention

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Energy efficiency — Chapter 4

answers.title: MARPOL structure & conventions overview
answers.answer_text:
MARPOL 73/78 — six Annexes: I Oil; II Noxious Liquid Substances in bulk; III Harmful
substances in packaged form; IV Sewage; V Garbage; VI Air pollution. Other IMO conventions to
name confidently: SOLAS, STCW, MLC, Load Line, COLREG, BWM, AFS (anti-fouling),
Tonnage, and the liability conventions CLC & Bunkers. Under IMO sit the safety/
environmental conventions; MEPC is the Marine Environment Protection Committee that
develops MARPOL amendments.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: MARPOL structure & conventions overview

answers.title: Annex I — Oil pollution prevention
answers.answer_text:
Certified by the IOPP Certificate (+Supplement listing the ship's oil-pollution-prevention
equipment). Machinery-space bilge water may be discharged only when: en route; oil content
≤15 ppm; through approved 15 ppm oily-water separating/filtering equipment with a
15 ppm alarm and automatic stopping device (3-way valve returning oily water
inboard); and outside special areas (special-area/coastal limits are stricter). All oil transfers,
bilge/sludge disposals and OWS operations are recorded in the Oil Record Book (ORB) — Part I
(machinery space) (Part II for cargo/ballast on tankers).
OWS fails on voyage (Q107/453): stop using it; retain bilge/oily water in a holding tank;
record the defect and the retention in the ORB and log (the correct ORB code entry
for inoperative equipment); arrange repair or authorised shore reception at the next port;
inform the office/DPA. Never discharge non-compliant water. Oil spill to sea (Q434): stop
the source, raise the alarm, muster and deploy the SOPEP — contain with SOPEP-locker
equipment, notify Master/office/nearest coastal State/flag, record actions, and clean up. The
procedures are found in the ship's SOPEP (SMPEP if it also covers noxious liquids).
UK FLAG Enacted by the MS (Prevention of Oil Pollution) Regulations. A point unique to
UK flag the examiner may want (Q84): the internal visual inspection of the oily-water
separator is a required part of the UK-flag IOPP intermediate survey.
4.3 Annex II — Noxious Liquid Substances (chemical tankers) (context for tanker
certificate questions Q32, 198–200)
Applies to NLS carried in bulk. Substances are categorised X, Y, Z or OS (Other Substances) by
environmental hazard, with discharge criteria and, for the worst categories, a mandatory pre-
wash to a reception facility. Controlled by the ship's Procedures & Arrangements (P&A)
Manual, the Cargo Record Book, and certified by the Certificate of Fitness / NLS
certificate.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Annex I — Oil pollution prevention

answers.title: Annex IV — Sewage
answers.answer_text:
Certified by the ISPP Certificate (ships ≥400 GT or certified >15 persons, international
voyages). The ship must have an approved Sewage Treatment Plant (STP), a comminuting/
18 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

disinfecting system, or a holding tank. Discharge criteria (Reg 11): comminuted & disinfected
sewage not less than 3 nm from the nearest land; untreated sewage not less than 12 nm and
only when en route at ≥4 knots at a moderate rate; treated effluent from an approved STP (to
MEPC.227(64) standards) may be discharged closer per its type-approval.
Tank-entry / health hazards: raw sewage generates hydrogen sulphide (H S) — toxic,
2
flammable and olfactory-fatiguing — and causes oxygen depletion by bacterial action, plus
biological infection (E. coli, hepatitis). Any sewage/holding-tank entry is an enclosed-space
entry (RA + PTW, isolate/drain/ventilate, gas-test O 20.9%, HC <1% LEL, H S <5 ppm/CO
2 2
<25 ppm, standby man, rescue plan).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Annex IV — Sewage

answers.title: Annex V — Garbage
answers.answer_text:
Controlled by the Garbage Management Plan and recorded in the Garbage Record Book;
placards displayed. The general rule is a prohibition on discharge of all garbage into the
sea, with narrow exceptions: food waste may be discharged at distance limits (≥3 nm
comminuted, ≥12 nm not comminuted, en route), and certain cargo residues/cleaning agents
outside special areas. Special areas are far stricter.
Follow-ups (Q108): plastics — never discharged. Electrical/e-waste is a hazardous
stream, kept separate and landed ashore to a reception facility (not incinerated
indiscriminately). Old cooking oil is not put in the sludge/oily-water tank (it would
contaminate the oil system and mis-record under Annex I) — it is stored separately and
landed to reception; it should not simply be incinerated where prohibited (Reg 16 restrictions
apply).
4.6 Ballast Water Management (BWM Convention) (consolidates Q126, 287, 498)
The BWM Convention (in force 8 Sept 2017) requires management of ballast water and
sediments to prevent the transfer of invasive aquatic species, via a ship-specific BWM Plan, a
BWM Record Book, and the BWM Certificate. Two standards:
• D1 — Ballast Water Exchange standard: exchange in mid-ocean (ideally ≥200 nm from
land in water ≥200 m deep; otherwise as far as practicable ≥50 nm/≥200 m), achieving
≥95% volumetric exchange — by sequential, flow-through, or dilution methods. It dilutes/
replaces coastal organisms with open-ocean organisms less likely to survive in port.
• D2 — Ballast Water Performance standard: treat the water so the discharged organism
concentration is below set limits (e.g. <10 viable organisms ≥50 µm per m³; <10 per mL
for 10–50 µm; plus indicator microbe limits). Met by an approved Ballast Water
Management System (BWMS) — typically filtration + UV or filtration +
electrochlorination.
Under the implementation schedule all ships have moved (via their IOPP renewal dates) from D1
to the D2 standard. "A D1 ship" is one still exchanging; "a D2 ship" has a fitted, approved
treatment system.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Name the six annexes.” I Oil, II NLS, III packaged harmful substances, IV Sewage, V Garbage,
VI Air. Amendments are developed by the MEPC.
19 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

• “Machinery-bilge oil discharge criteria?”En route, ≤15 ppm, through 15 ppm
equipment with alarm and automatic stopping device, outside special areas (special-
area limits stricter).
• “OWS fails — what and where do you record?” Log the defect and the retention; make the
correct ORB entry for inoperative equipment; retain oily water and land it ashore to a
reception facility.
• “SOPEP — contents and who do you notify?” Reporting procedures, coastal-State/flag/
company contact lists, containment equipment and duties; notify Master, office, nearest
coastal State and flag.
• “Sewage discharge distances?” Comminuted & disinfected ≥3 nm; untreated ≥12 nm, en
route ≥4 kn; approved-STP effluent per type-approval.
• “Where do e-waste and old cooking oil go?” E-waste is landed ashore (hazardous, kept
separate); cooking oil is stored separately and landed — not into the sludge/oily tank.
• “D1 vs D2?” D1 = ballast exchange (≥95% volumetric, mid-ocean); D2 = treatment
performance standard met by an approved BWMS (filtration + UV or electrochlorination).
Section 5 — Fuel Oil & Lubricating Oil

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Annex V — Garbage

answers.title: Bunkering & fuel-oil analysis
answers.answer_text:
DURING BUNKERING
• Work to the bunker plan and checklist; agree grade, quantity, temperature, density and
pumping rate; confirm the SOPEP locker and scuppers are ready and the bunker manifold
has a save-all/drip tray.
• Take a continuous drip sample at the ship's manifold throughout (the MARPOL sample) plus
tank samples; monitor soundings, temperature and rate; watch for air/water in the stream
and rising tank levels to prevent overflow.
• Receive and check the Bunker Delivery Note (BDN) — states supplier, quantity, density,
viscosity, sulphur, flash point; retained 3 years, with the sealed MARPOL sample retained 12
months.
THE FUEL-OIL ANALYSIS REPORT — WHAT TO CHECK AND WHY
• Density & viscosity — set purifier gravity disc and heating/injection temperature; density
>991 kg/m³ challenges conventional purifiers (need modern/ALCAP type).
• Water & sediment (total sediment) — emulsification, combustion problems, sludge; flash
point (≥60 °C) — safety.
• Sulphur — Annex VI compliance and cylinder-oil BN matching.
• CCAI (Calculated Carbon Aromaticity Index) — ignition quality; a high CCAI (>~870)
indicates ignition delay / poor combustion, causing late/rough burning and afterburning.
• Ash, vanadium & sodium — high V (with Na) forms low-melting-point deposits causing
high-temperature corrosion of exhaust valves and turbine blading; sodium worsens it.
• Aluminium + Silicon (cat fines) — abrasive catalyst fines; must be reduced by settling and
purification to ≤15 ppm (Al+Si) at the engine inlet (ISO 8217) to avoid rapid liner/ring/
fuel-pump wear.
20 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

• Pour point, CCAI, asphaltenes/compatibility, and the ignition/combustion characteristics.
Rejecting fuel & shortfall (Q35/160): if the sample shows off-spec (water/sediment, low
flash, wrong density, high cat fines) or a quantity shortfall, stop bunkering, issue a
Letter of Protest, retain the sealed samples and inform the office/charterer; do not burn
suspect fuel until the lab result is back. Tank/temperature management: keep the
settling tank ~5–8 °C above the fuel's pour point; heat the service tank to give the
correct injection viscosity (~10–15 cSt at the injectors), monitored by a viscotherm/viscosity
controller. Retain BDN and sample; monitor by the "constant drip" method and visual
inspection through bunkering.
UK FLAG Fuel quality/sampling is governed by MARPOL Annex VI Reg 18 and the ship's fuel
specification to ISO 8217; the MARPOL sample and BDN are inspected by MCA/PSC. In-use and
on-board sulphur verification samples are also taken.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Bunkering & fuel-oil analysis

answers.title: Fuel changeover HFO ↔ LSFO/MGO & ECA operation
answers.answer_text:
Changeover (e.g. entering an ECA) must be gradual and controlled to protect the fuel-injection
equipment:
• Limit the rate of temperature change (~2 °C/min) when moving from hot HFO to cooler
distillate. Too-rapid cooling causes differential contraction and sticking/scuffing of fuel-
pump plungers and barrels and leakage; too-low viscosity causes internal leakage past
plungers, poor atomisation and possible loss of injection.
• Maintain a minimum viscosity at the pump — for very light MGO fit a fuel cooler/chiller to
keep viscosity above the pump minimum (~2 cSt).
• Expect a power/speed change: low-sulphur/distillate fuels generally have a different
(often lower) calorific value, so for the same rack the ship may lose a little power/speed —
the propeller-curve relationship shifts (Q444). Complete the changeover before the ECA
boundary and record time/position/tank quantities in the Annex VI logbook.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Fuel changeover HFO ↔ LSFO/MGO & ECA operation

answers.title: Lubricating-oil analysis, properties & wear-metal interpretation
answers.answer_text:
WHAT THE LO LAB REPORT TELLS YOU
• Viscosity — falls with fuel dilution, rises with oxidation/contamination. Flash point drop
confirms fuel dilution.
• TBN (Total Base Number) — the alkaline reserve to neutralise acids; depletes in service and
must be maintained (system oil ~5–12 BN; cylinder oil high BN matched to fuel sulphur).
• Water content — leaks/condensation → emulsification, corrosion and microbial growth.
Insolubles/soot, oxidation, nitration.
• Wear metals (spectrometric) and particle count / solid particles — the wear signature.
Interpreting wear metals: Fe (iron) = liner/frame/gear/bearing wear or fretting of
frames/bedplate/tie-bolt seatings; Cu/Pb/Sn = white-metal bearing wear; Cr = piston-
ring/liner; Al = piston or cat fines; Si = dust/cat fines. High iron content (Q524/620):
investigate fretting internally — engine frames, bedplate transverse girders and tie-bolt
21 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

tightness — as well as bearing/liner wear. Fretting corrosion appears as a reddish-brown
iron-oxide powder ("cocoa") at loaded/clamped joints, indicating relative micro-movement
and loss of nip.
Why analysis may NOT warn of imminent failure (Q404): spectrometric analysis
under-reads large particles — it best detects fine (<~5–10 µm) wear debris in
suspension. A rapidly failing bearing can shed large flakes that the spectrometer misses, so
combine LO analysis with magnetic plugs, filter/centrifuge inspection, particle
counting and bearing-temperature monitoring for a full picture.
MAINTAINING THE SUMP / LO PROPERTIES NEEDED
Run the LO purifier continuously at the correct throughput and temperature (~85–95 °C) to
remove water and insolubles; top up to maintain level and TBN. A 2-stroke system/crosshead
oil needs good oxidation stability, thermal stability, load-carrying, demulsibility (to
shed water), and detergency/dispersancy; the separate cylinder oil needs a high BN
(matched to fuel sulphur) for acid neutralisation plus spreadability and detergency.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Lubricating-oil analysis, properties & wear-metal interpretation

answers.title: Microbiological attack
answers.answer_text:
Bacteria/fungi (e.g. Cladosporium resinae) grow at the fuel/water interface in tanks. Signs:
filter/separator blockage, dark slime/sludge, tank-bottom pitting corrosion under the biofilm, a
water haze, acidity/low pH, rotten-egg (H S) odour and unstable fuel. Treatment: first remove
2
the water (drain tank bottoms, purify), then dose an approved biocide; in severe cases
mechanically clean the tank. Prevention: regular tank-bottom draining, good housekeeping,
keeping tanks dry and circulated.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Monitoring during bunkering + retention periods?” Continuous drip MARPOL sample
plus soundings/rate/temperature; retain the BDN 3 years and the sealed sample 12 months.
• “Danger of high vanadium?” With sodium it forms low-melting-point deposits causing high-
temperature corrosion of exhaust valves and turbine blading.
• “Cat-fines limit and effect?”≤15 ppm Al+Si at the engine inlet (ISO 8217); if high,
abrasive wear of liners, rings and fuel pumps.
• “When do you reject fuel?” Off-spec sample (water/sediment, low flash, wrong density, high
cat fines) or a shortfall → stop, Letter of Protest, retain sample, inform office; don't burn
until lab-confirmed.
• “Why changeover gradually?” Rapid cooling contracts fuel-pump plungers → sticking/
scuffing/leakage; too-low viscosity → internal leakage and poor atomisation.
• “White metal vs iron in the LO report?” White metal (Cu/Pb/Sn) = bearing wear; iron =
liner/frame/gear or fretting → check tie-bolt tightness and frame/bedplate.
• “Why might LO analysis miss a failing bearing?” Spectrometry under-reads large
particles; supplement with magnetic plugs, filter/centrifuge inspection, particle count and
bearing temps.
• “Microbial attack — first action?”Remove the water first, then dose an approved biocide.
22 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

Section 6 — Main Engine: Inspection, Faults & Scenarios

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Microbiological attack

answers.title: Crankcase inspection, oil-mist detection & explosion
answers.answer_text:
PURPOSE & PREPARATION
A crankcase inspection is condition monitoring of the running gear. Preparation: obtain the
bridge's permission to immobilise the engine; isolate positively — shut and lock the main
starting-air stop valve and drain the line, open the indicator cocks, engage and secure the
turning gear, isolate fuel/control-air and (as needed) cooling/LO, apply lock-out/tag-out.
Allow to cool before opening (opening a hot crankcase risks igniting oil mist). Raise a risk
assessment, PTW and enclosed-space entry permit — the crankcase is an enclosed
space: ventilate, gas-test (O 20.9%, HC <1% LEL, toxics within limits), post a standby man
2
with comms and rescue plan, use intrinsically-safe lighting only, and wear clean non-
shedding clothing.
WHAT TO INSPECT
• Main / bottom-end / crosshead bearings — wiping/extrusion of white metal, blueing/
overheating, cracking, fretting at keeps, and measured clearances (feelers/bridge gauge) vs
limits and history; crosshead guide shoes/surfaces and clearance.
• Journals & crankpins — scoring, ovality, heat marks.
• Tie rods — the examiner wants more than "check tightness": inspect nuts/palms for
slackness, fretting, elongation and security; lost tie-rod tension redistributes bedplate stress
and can crack transverse girders.
• LO telescopic/swinging pipes and securing; oil scraper/stuffing box for scavenge-oil carry-
over; balance weights and bolt locking; chain/gear drive and tensioner. Finish with crankshaft
deflections.
OIL-MIST DETECTION & THE EXPLOSION MECHANISM
An overheating part vaporises oil; the vapour recondenses in the cooler crankcase as a fine
white mist of sub-10-micron droplets. If mist reaches its lower explosive limit (~50 mg/litre
of air) and meets the ignition source (the hot spot), a primary explosion occurs; if a relief door
then lets fresh air rush back onto burning residue, a violent secondary explosion follows. The
Oil-Mist Detector (OMD) continuously samples each crankcase compartment (comparator type
compares against a reference), alarms at a set mist density and identifies the unit.
Actions on an OMD alarm / crankcase-explosion warning: reduce to slow/stop as
the bridge permits; do NOT open the crankcase (air onto a hot spot → explosion); keep
the LO pump running to cool the hot spot; allow to cool ~20–30 min+; investigate
running-gear ammeter, bearing temperatures, LO temps, and turn slowly on the
turning gear feeling for a tight/hot unit; when cool, find and rectify the hot spot before a
monitored restart. Protection fitted: spring-loaded self-closing relief/explosion doors
with flame trap and non-return (required on engines with cylinder bore >200 mm or
crankcase volume ≥0.6 m³), OMD, LO low-pressure/flow & high-temperature alarms, and
bearing-temperature monitoring.
23 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

Metal in the sump (Q71/127): identify it — white metal is soft, non-magnetic → main/
bottom-end/crosshead bearing; steel is magnetic → gearing/running gear; bronze → a
bush. Use appearance, a magnet and where it was found, then open the suspect component;
do not restart until the source and cause are established.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Crankcase inspection, oil-mist detection & explosion

answers.title: Bearing failure, hanging crosshead & running through a black spot
answers.answer_text:
A bottom-end bearing past its limit with no spare, ship must reach the next port: take the unit
out and run on reduced power — hang up the crosshead/piston (lock it at the top), remove
the con-rod bottom end, lift/blank fuel and lock the fuel pump to that unit, stop cylinder
lubrication to it, secure the running gear, and run at reduced load with close watch. Be aware of
increased vibration and altered balance.
Critical speed / "black spot": a barred RPM range where torsional vibration is dangerous.
If stopped within it, do not run in it — turn the engine on the turning gear clear of the
critical position, or kick the engine (start) in the opposite direction to move off it, then
run above/below the barred range. The barred range is shown on the tachometer.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Bearing failure, hanging crosshead & running through a black spot

answers.title: Turbocharger total failure — running without the T/C
answers.answer_text:
After a T/C failure (bearing/surge/vibration): stop and investigate. To reach a safe port with the
T/C out of action: lock the T/C rotor in position (fit the locking plate/tool), blank off the
compressor air outlet from the T/C so scavenge air from the auxiliary blowers is not lost back
through the dead turbocharger, run the auxiliary blowers continuously, run at reduced load,
provide extra cooling to the T/C casing, and increase watchkeeping (exhaust temps,
combustion, back-pressure). Monitor exhaust temperatures and combustion carefully.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Turbocharger total failure — running without the T/C

answers.title: Cylinder liner inspection, wear & lubrication
answers.answer_text:
Liner inspection (through scavenge ports and/or crankcase): look for wear (bore/ovality vs
limits), scuffing/scoring, micro-seizure, clover-leafing (corrosive wear pattern), cracks,
corrosion, port condition and lubricator quill condition, plus ring condition/collapse via a
scavenge inspection. Typical wear rate for a modern slow-speed 2-stroke is roughly 0.05–
0.10 mm per 1000 h (≈1.5–2.5 mm after 25,000 h) — investigate if higher. Cylinder
lubrication: feed rate and a high-BN cylinder oil matched to fuel sulphur to neutralise acid
and control corrosive wear; modern engines use timed/electronic dosing (e.g. Alpha/pulse
lubrication) synchronised to piston position, replacing the old mechanical lubricators (Sulzer
ZA40S / MAN 58/64 developments).
Increased liner wear on one unit — possible causes: insufficient/failed cylinder
lubrication (blocked quill, wrong feed rate, wrong BN for the sulphur), cold corrosion (low
jacket temperature/condensation), fuel cat fines, poor combustion/late injection on that
unit, ring blow-by/collapse, water leak into the cylinder, or scavenge-fire damage.
24 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Cylinder liner inspection, wear & lubrication

answers.title: Unit overhaul, class credit & running-in
answers.answer_text:
A full unit overhaul (dismantle, inspect, reassemble) requires isolation, PTW and enclosed-space
entry for crankcase work (removing piston palm/stuffing-box bolts). To get it surveyed/credited
by Class, provide the surveyor with the liner calibration report, piston & ring clearances,
running-gear clearances, the onboard LO test report, and photographs at every stage.
Running-in after overhaul: increase cylinder lubrication, run at half ahead for the time
given in the manual, take crankshaft deflections, and open the under-piston/scavenge and
crankcase doors to inspect before returning to full power. On electronic engines, use the HCU
cut-out procedure to isolate a unit's hydraulic/servo supply for fuel pump/valve work.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Unit overhaul, class credit & running-in

answers.title: Engine performance analysis
answers.answer_text:
Assess power/condition from indicator (power) cards and draw/out-of-phase cards (or
electronic PMI): derive Pmax, Pcomp, mean indicated pressure → indicated power, timing
and per-unit balance. Compare with shop-test / sea-trial / previous readings at the same load
and correct for ambient. Late ignition in all units → check fuel ignition quality (CCAI/delay),
injection timing and compression. Balance the engine via fuel index/VIT so exhaust temperatures
and Pmax are even. Present to the Superintendent as a trended performance report feeding
SEEMP monitoring. Contamination of AE fuel/LO by water (Q273) causes poor combustion,
corrosion, injector fouling and bearing wear — hence purification and water monitoring.
6.7 Scavenge fire & exhaust-gas-boiler (EGB) fires (consolidates Q36–37, 75, 275, 333–
334)
• Scavenge fire: unburnt fuel/oil in the scavenge space ignites (blow-by, poor combustion,
worn/collapsed rings). Signs: high scavenge-space and exhaust temperature on that unit, loss
of power, surging, sparks/flames at drains, paint blistering. Actions: reduce/stop as directed,
cut off fuel and cylinder oil to that unit, increase lubrication to adjacent units to
prevent seizure, close scavenge drains, let a small fire burn out; for a serious fire operate
the fixed scavenge smothering (CO /steam), cool the liner externally, and do not open
2
until cool. Afterwards inspect liner/rings/rod for damage and distortion.
• EGB soot/hydrogen fire: soot on the tubes + rising back-pressure raises ME/T/C
temperatures; a soot fire can escalate to a fierce iron/hydrogen fire (glowing tubes) that
self-reignites. Response: reduce load/stop as directed, keep water circulating — do NOT
let the EGB run dry, bypass the gas side if possible, and for a soot fire use steam/water
soot-blowing/smothering; a hydrogen fire needs copious water cooling to bring the
metal below ignition temperature. If the water side is lost (EGB "running dry"), take it off load,
circulate/bypass to avoid tube overheating (Q37). Water appearing in a scavenge drain can
trace back to an EGB/jacket tube leak (Q36).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Engine performance analysis

answers.title: Fuel timing, VIT, governor & 2-stroke vs 4-stroke
answers.answer_text:
• Injection timing: on jerk-pump engines changed by the eccentric/VIT rack (MAN 58/64
eccentric lever); on electronic engines (ME/RT-flex) adjusted in the control system (WECS/
ME-ECU). VIT (Variable Injection Timing) advances timing at part load (keeps Pmax high for
efficiency) and retards near full load (limits Pmax) — checked/adjusted in every port on ME
engines.
25 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

• Governor: senses speed (mechanical flyweights or electronic pickup) and adjusts the fuel
rack/index to hold set speed against load; droop control allows load-sharing on paralleled
gensets.
• 2-stroke vs 4-stroke (Q101): the 2-stroke fires every revolution, uses port/uniflow
scavenging, is low-speed, crosshead type, direct-coupled, high power per cylinder; the 4-stroke
fires every second revolution, has poppet valves, is higher speed, trunk-piston, and drives
auxiliaries or geared/medium-speed propulsion.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Isolation before crankcase entry?” Bridge permission; shut/lock the starting-air valve, open
indicator cocks, engage turning gear, isolate fuel/control air, LOTO; then RA + PTW +
enclosed-space permit with gas tests.
• “Why not open a hot crankcase?” Fresh air onto a hot spot can ignite oil mist → explosion;
let it cool and keep the LO pump running.
• “Explain the primary and secondary explosion.” Hot spot vaporises oil → fine mist reaching
the ~50 mg/l LEL → primary ignition; air rushing back through a relief door onto burning residue
→ a violent secondary explosion.
• “Relief-door threshold?” Engines with cylinder bore >200 mm or crankcase volume
≥0.6 m³; doors are self-closing with a flame trap and non-return.
• “White metal vs steel debris?” White metal is soft and non-magnetic → a bearing; steel is
magnetic → gearing/running gear.
• “Run to port with a failed bottom-end bearing?”Hang up the unit (lock piston up,
remove con-rod), lift/lock fuel and stop cyl. oil to it, run at reduced load, watch vibration.
• “Stuck in a black spot?” Don't run in it — turn on the turning gear clear, or kick-start in the
opposite direction, then run above/below the barred range.
• “Run without the T/C?”Lock the rotor, blank the compressor air outlet, run aux
blowers continuously, reduced load, extra cooling, increased watchkeeping.
• “One unit, high liner wear — causes?” Failed cyl. lubrication, cold corrosion, cat fines, poor
combustion/late injection, ring blow-by, or a water leak.
• “Documents to Class after a unit overhaul?” Liner calibration, piston/ring clearances,
running-gear clearances, onboard LO test report, and photos at each stage.
• “Scavenge fire vs EGB hydrogen fire?” Scavenge: cut fuel/oil to the unit, boost adjacent
lubrication, close drains, smother (CO /steam). EGB hydrogen fire: keep water circulating,
2
never run dry, cool with copious water.
Section 7 — Boilers, Steam & Feed Systems

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Fuel timing, VIT, governor & 2-stroke vs 4-stroke

answers.title: The boiler survey — preparation & inspection
answers.answer_text:
A boiler is a fired pressure vessel surveyed by Class/statutory survey covering four aspects:
water side, fire (furnace) side, external, and mountings & fittings.
PREPARATION
• Shut down and allow to cool; blow down and drain; positively isolate steam, feed, fuel and
blow-down with blanks and lock-out/tag-out.
26 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

• Raise a risk assessment and enclosed-space entry Permit-to-Work — the boiler is an
enclosed space. Open the top manhole/vent door FIRST to release any residual pressure/
steam safely, then the bottom doors; ventilate thoroughly and gas-test (O 20.9%, HC <1%
2
LEL, toxics within limits). Standby man, comms and rescue plan; allow to cool before entry
(burns/steam hazard).
INSPECTION & POSSIBLE FAULTS
• Water side: scale, corrosion, pitting, grooving, caustic cracking, condition of stays, tube
ends and ligaments, internal fittings and the low-water/scum arrangements. Faults:
overheating from scale, corrosion fatigue, cracking at stays.
• Fire/furnace side: refractory/brickwork, tube overheating/bulging/blistering, soot deposits,
burner condition, and cracks at the furnace/tube plate. Faults: flame impingement, soot fires,
refractory failure.
• External: casing, insulation, foundations, mountings for leakage/corrosion.
• Mountings & fittings: safety valves, water-level gauge glasses, feed check, main stop, blow-
down, pressure gauge, salinometer/scum valves.
Crack found on the water side (Q171): assess with the surveyor, mark it out, arrange
repair to an approved procedure (grind out/weld by a qualified welder to a WPS; a stay/
tube may be renewed). After repair, inspect, then hydraulically (hydrostatically)
pressure-test the boiler in the surveyor's presence — typically to 1.5 × design/
working pressure, holding to confirm no leakage before returning to service.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: The boiler survey — preparation & inspection

answers.title: Boiler safety valves & the economiser/EGB valve
answers.answer_text:
Overhaul: strip down; measure and record the existing setting; lap the valve and seat; inspect
and measure the spring; reassemble. Setting is done by adjusting spring compression (and, on
high-lift valves, the adjusting rings for blow-down), proven by an accumulation/float test using
a calibrated pressure gauge, in the surveyor's presence.
Setting values & the "why not the same" point (Q41): a boiler has two safety valves,
set to lift at not more than the approved working pressure — but they are not set at
the identical pressure: the first (easing) valve is set at the working pressure and the
second slightly higher (e.g. +3%), so they lift progressively and both do not slam open
together, and with the stop valve shut and both valves lifting the accumulation of
pressure must not exceed ~10% for the required duration. The economiser/EGB
safety valve is set higher than the boiler valves so it lifts independently/last.
UK FLAG Who may set them (Q131/245): the main boiler safety valves are set in the
presence of the surveyor. The economiser/EGB safety valve can be set by the C/E while
the ship is at sea / underway — the C/E is authorised to do so and a surveyor is not required
for that valve; it cannot practically be done in port on a live economiser, so it is done on the
sailing passage.
27 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Boiler safety valves & the economiser/EGB valve

answers.title: Boiler safety features, water-level monitoring & alarms
answers.answer_text:
Safety features / protective devices on a boiler:
• Two safety valves (over-pressure protection) and an easing gear.
• Water-level protection: two independent gauge glasses (direct reading); remote level
indication and alarms/trips.
• Combustion safeguards: flame-failure (photocell/flame-eye) trip, low-air/purge interlock,
low-water fuel trip, high-steam-pressure cut-out, and a purge cycle before ignition.
• Pressure gauge, feed check, main stop, blow-down, and low-low water fuel shut-off.
Remote water-level measurement (Q97/214): commonly by a differential-pressure
transmitter (measures the head of water), a conductivity/electrode probe system (e.g.
Hydrastep) giving stepped level indication, or a magnetic/float type — feeding high, low
and low-low alarms and trips. At hi-hi level the risk is water carry-over/priming into
the steam line (water hammer, damage to turbines/valves), so the alarm warns to stop
feeding/check the feed regulator. At low-low level the fuel/burner is tripped
automatically to prevent tube overheating and dry-firing.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Boiler safety features, water-level monitoring & alarms

answers.title: Feed system & feed-pressure
answers.answer_text:
Feed regulation at constant pump speed (Q99): a constant-speed feed pump delivers
roughly constant flow, so the supply to the boiler is regulated by a modulating feed-water
control valve driven by the level controller (single-, two- or three-element control), with the
excess handled by a recirculation/spill line back to the feed tank/hotwell to prevent the pump
churning/overheating at low demand. Level is thus held by throttling the feed valve while the
pump runs continuously.
Feed pressure for a 12-bar boiler (Q100/148): the feed pump discharge must exceed
boiler pressure by enough to open the feed check and overcome pipeline/regulator/
economiser losses — so for a 12 bar boiler you would expect a feed pressure of roughly 15–
17 bar (a margin of ~3–5 bar over boiler pressure). Too little margin and feed won't enter
against boiler pressure; the check valve prevents back-flow.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Which door do you open first and why?” The top manhole/vent first, to release residual
pressure/steam safely before opening the bottom doors.
• “What does a boiler survey include?” Water side, fire/furnace side, external, and mountings
& fittings.
• “You find a crack water-side — then what?” Assess with surveyor, repair to approved
procedure, then hydro-test to ~1.5 × working pressure in the surveyor's presence.
• “Are both safety valves set the same, and why not?” No — first at working pressure,
second ~3% higher so they lift progressively; accumulation with both lifting ≤~10%.
• “Who sets the boiler vs the economiser safety valve?” Boiler valves in the surveyor's
presence; the economiser/EGB valve by the C/E while underway (no surveyor required).
• “How is level measured remotely and what happens at hi-hi / lo-lo?” DP transmitter or
conductivity probe (Hydrastep); hi-hi warns of priming/carry-over, lo-lo trips the fuel/burner.
28 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

• “Feed pressure for a 12-bar boiler?” About 15–17 bar — a 3–5 bar margin to open the feed
check and beat system losses.
• “How is feed regulated if the pump runs at constant speed?” A modulating feed valve on
the level controller throttles supply, with a recirculation/spill line taking the excess.
Section 8 — Refrigeration & Air Conditioning

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Feed system & feed-pressure

answers.title: The vapour-compression cycle & common faults
answers.answer_text:
The plant works on the vapour-compression cycle: the compressor raises low-pressure
vapour to high pressure/temperature; the condenser (sea-water cooled) rejects heat and
condenses it to liquid, collected in the receiver; the expansion (thermostatic) valve throttles
it to low pressure, dropping its temperature; and the evaporator absorbs heat from the cold
space, vaporising the refrigerant, which returns to the compressor. Common refrigerants: R404A/
R134a (HFCs) and R717 (ammonia) on larger plant.
8.2 Air (non-condensables) in the system (consolidates Q30, 337)
Detection: air collects at the top of the condenser (highest point) and shows as a condenser
pressure higher than the saturation pressure corresponding to the measured
condensing temperature — i.e. the head pressure does not match the refrigerant's saturation
pressure for the seawater/ambient condition. Symptoms: high head pressure, HP tripping, poor
cooling, compressor running hot/long.
Venting/purging (Q337): stop the compressor and pump down so refrigerant is collected
in the condenser/receiver; leave the condenser cooling water running (to keep
refrigerant condensed as liquid) and let it stand so air rises to the top. Then crack the
purge/vent valve at the top of the condenser to release the non-condensable air —
ideally through an automatic air purger venting into a water bottle so any escaping
refrigerant is caught, not lost to atmosphere. Never vent refrigerant deliberately (ODS/
greenhouse control).

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: The vapour-compression cycle & common faults

answers.title: Meat room warm / condenser choked & HP trip
answers.answer_text:
Reported high temperature in the meat room — mention several possibilities (short of
refrigerant/leak, faulty TEV, iced/blocked evaporator, dirty air cooler, solenoid/thermostat fault)
but the examiner is usually driving at a choked/fouled condenser: poor heat transfer raises
condensing pressure/temperature, cuts capacity and warms the space.
Why the HP switch trips (Q336): anything raising condenser (high-side) pressure — a
choked/dirty condenser, air in the system, overcharge, insufficient or warm cooling
water, or a blocked/closed discharge — makes the head pressure rise until the HP cut-out
stops the compressor to protect it. Rectify: restore condenser heat transfer — clean/de-
scale the condenser tubes, restore full cooling-water flow, purge air, correct the charge —
then test capacity by pulling the room down and checking suction/discharge pressures and
superheat. Test for a condenser tube leak (Q95): use an electronic leak detector or
29 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

halide torch (or soap solution) around joints, and check the cooling-water side for
refrigerant (or refrigerant side for water ingress) to confirm a leaking tube.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Meat room warm / condenser choked & HP trip

answers.title: Moisture in the system, driers & oil/refrigerant miscibility
answers.answer_text:
Why moisture will not pass the TEV and "chokes" there (Q233): at the thermostatic
expansion valve the pressure drops and the temperature falls below 0 °C; any free water
freezes to ice at the valve orifice and blocks it, starving the evaporator. The symptom
is intermittent cooling — ice blocks the valve, the valve/section warms, the ice melts, flow
resumes, then it re-freezes. Cure/prevent: fit/renew a drier (silica gel / molecular sieve)
in the liquid line to absorb moisture; evacuate and dehydrate the system before charging.
Moisture also forms acids with the refrigerant (corrosion, "copper plating") and sludges the
oil.
Viscosity & mixing with other liquids (Q234): refrigerant is miscible with the
compressor lubricating oil — dissolved refrigerant lowers the oil's viscosity, reducing
its load-carrying and lubricating ability (risk of bearing wear), while oil carried round the
circuit collects in the evaporator and reduces heat-transfer if it does not return. Good oil
return and correct oil/refrigerant matching are therefore essential.
UK FLAG Refrigerant handling, top-ups and any release of ozone-depleting substances are
controlled under MARPOL Annex VI Reg 12 and recorded in the ODS Record Book; whether
the refrigerant is ozone-depleting is confirmed from the IAPP Supplement list of equipment
(Q432). UK enacts this via the MS air-pollution regulations.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “How do you know there's air in the system?” Condenser pressure higher than the
saturation pressure for the measured condensing temperature; high head pressure, HP
tripping.
• “How do you purge it?” Pump down, keep condenser cooling water on, let air rise, crack the
top-of-condenser vent / use the auto air-purger through a water bottle.
• “Meat room warm — the usual culprit?” A choked/fouled condenser (also check charge,
TEV, iced evaporator).
• “Why does it trip on HP?” High-side pressure rises — dirty condenser, air, overcharge,
insufficient/warm cooling water — HP cut-out protects the compressor.
• “Why can't moisture pass the TEV?” It freezes to ice at the valve orifice (below 0 °C)
and blocks it → intermittent cooling; cure with a drier and dehydration.
• “Effect of moisture besides icing?” Forms acids → corrosion/copper plating and oil sludging.
• “How does refrigerant affect the oil?” It is miscible and lowers oil viscosity, harming
lubrication; oil in the evaporator cuts heat transfer.
• “How do you leak-test the condenser?” Electronic leak detector/halide torch/soap, and
check the cooling-water side for refrigerant.
30 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

Section 9 — Stability & Naval Architecture
Sketch-based parts (the G/M/B/Z transverse section, the GZ curve, the tanker cross-section, and the free-surface
wedge) are held for the drawing pack; the concepts are explained in full here so the drawings only need labelling.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Moisture in the system, driers & oil/refrigerant miscibility

answers.title: Flotation, equilibrium & the key points G, B, M, K, Z
answers.answer_text:
How a ship floats (Q487): by Archimedes' Principle — the ship sinks until it displaces a
weight of water equal to its own weight; the upthrust (buoyancy) then equals the weight, acting
up through the centre of buoyancy.
How it stays upright (Q488): weight (W) acts down through the centre of gravity G;
buoyancy (B) acts up through the centre of buoyancy. When heeled, B shifts to the low side to
Z; the horizontal separation GZ is the righting lever, and W × GZ is the righting moment that
returns the ship upright.
• K — keel (reference point). B — centre of buoyancy (centroid of the underwater volume). G —
centre of gravity of the ship+contents. M — the metacentre, the point about which G
appears to swing for small angles (intersection of successive buoyancy verticals). GM — the
metacentric height = KM − KG.
• Stable equilibrium: G below M → positive GM → positive righting lever. Neutral: G at M.
Unstable: G above M → negative GM → the ship will not stay upright.
9.2 GZ (righting-lever) curve (consolidates Q651–655)
The GZ curve plots righting lever (GZ) against angle of heel. From it read: initial slope (∝ GM),
the maximum GZ and the angle at which it occurs, the range of stability, the angle of
vanishing stability (AVS) where GZ returns to zero (typically ~70–75°, not ~55° — a common
wrong guess), and the area under the curve = the dynamical stability (energy to heel the
ship). IMO intended-severe-weather criteria set minimum areas/GZ values.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Flotation, equilibrium & the key points G, B, M, K, Z

answers.title: Positive/negative GM, angle of loll & free surface
answers.answer_text:
Importance of positive GM (Q652): gives a positive righting lever so the ship returns to
upright and has adequate range/dynamical stability. Dangers of negative GM (Q653): the
ship is unstable upright — it will loll to one side and may capsize if further disturbed. Angle
of loll (Q490): with a small negative GM the ship is unstable at 0° and heels until the
rising wedge of buoyancy restores a positive GZ — it then floats steadily but tenderly at
the angle of loll, and can flop to the same angle on the other side. Correction: lower G
(do not simply ballast the low side first — that can worsen it); press up/fill slack tanks low
down on the centreline first to remove free surface and lower G, then correct any
residual list — always keeping the ship stable.
Free-surface effect (Q39/510) — what engineers cause: a partially filled ("slack") tank
lets liquid move to the low side as the ship heels; this shift of weight causes a virtual rise
in G and a loss of GM (the free-surface correction = free-surface moment ÷ displacement),
reducing stability regardless of how much liquid is in the tank. Engineers cause this every
31 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

day by consuming fuel/LO (creating slack tanks), transferring/ballasting, and
having multiple slack tanks. Minimise by keeping tanks either pressed up or empty,
avoiding multiple slack tanks, and using divisions/baffles. Two slack wing tanks (Q510) both
add free-surface loss and can create a list.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Positive/negative GM, angle of loll & free surface

answers.title: Reserve of buoyancy, subdivision, heel vs list & damage stability
answers.answer_text:
• Reserve of buoyancy: the watertight volume above the waterline — the buoyancy
available if the hull is bilged; the freeboard assigned under the Load Line Convention protects
it. A "2-compartment ship" can survive flooding of any two adjacent compartments
and still float (subdivision standard).
• Heel vs list (Q650): heel is a temporary, external inclination (wind/turn); list is a persistent
inclination from an internal cause (off-centre weight/G shift or asymmetric flooding).
• Damage/flooding (Q565/608): flooding a tank both adds weight (may lower G a little) and,
once slack, adds a large free-surface loss — net effect usually a rise in effective G and a fall
in GM, plus a list/trim. Engine-room actions affecting stability: transferring/consuming
fuel, ballasting, pressing up or slacking tanks, and bilge/flooding — all move weight and
change free surface. The ship's Damage Stability Booklet / loading manual tells the C/E
and Master how to maintain a positive GM.

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Reserve of buoyancy, subdivision, heel vs list & damage stability

answers.title: Bulkheads, watertight integrity & fire-class boundaries
answers.answer_text:
Watertight subdivision (SOLAS II-1): transverse watertight bulkheads (including the collision
bulkhead forward) and watertight doors maintain buoyancy after damage; passenger-ship
watertight integrity is stricter. Fire-integrity classes (SOLAS II-2) from the standard fire test:
Class Meaning
A- Steel/equivalent, stiffened; prevents passage of flame & smoke for 60 min; insulated so the
class average unexposed-side temperature rises ≤140 °C (and no point >180 °C) above initial for the
rated time: A-60/A-30/A-15/A-0 = 60/30/15/0 minutes of insulation (A-0 = steel only, 60-min
integrity, no insulation).
B- Non-combustible; prevents passage of flame for 30 min; insulation ratings B-15/B-0
class (temperature-rise limits for 15/0 min).
C- Non-combustible material; no integrity/insulation rating required.
class
Where A-60 is required (Q477/658): boundaries between category-A machinery
spaces and accommodation, service and control stations, around the fire-control
station and the CO room, and other high-fire-load divisions. Time factor /
2
penetrations (Q661–662): the class number is the minutes the insulation keeps the
unexposed side below the temperature limit; any penetration (cable/pipe) must be
made good to the same fire rating using approved transits/glands so the boundary's
integrity is not defeated.
32 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “How does a ship float and stay upright?” Archimedes (buoyancy = weight); righting
moment W×GZ with G below M.
• “Define GM and what makes it positive.” GM = KM − KG; positive when G is below M.
• “What is angle of loll and how do you correct it?” Steady tender angle from a small
negative GM; correct by lowering G — press up slack centreline tanks low down first,
then trim any list, keeping her stable.
• “What is free-surface effect and how do you cause it?” Slack-tank liquid shift causing a
virtual rise in G / loss of GM; caused by consuming fuel, ballasting, multiple slack tanks.
• “How far before capsize?” The angle of vanishing stability — typically ~70–75°.
• “Heel vs list?” Heel = temporary/external; list = persistent/internal weight shift.
• “What is a 2-compartment ship?” One that survives flooding of any two adjacent
compartments.
• “What does A-60 mean and where is it used?” 60 min insulation on an A-class steel
boundary; between machinery spaces and accommodation/control, around the fire-control
station and CO room. Penetrations remade to the same rating.
2
Section 10 — Drydock, Hull, Shafting, Rudder & Propeller
1

answers.title: Drydock preparation & docking condition
answers.answer_text:
Well in advance (~6 months, Q340): prepare the docking/repair specification and work
list; send the yard the docking plan, GA and shell-expansion plans, a list of 3rd-party
contractors, and the required services (fire main, shore power, cooling water, 2 gangways,
lighting, waste disposal); order long-lead spares; schedule Class/flag surveys due (tailshaft,
bottom, load line).
At anchor / just before docking (Q134/235): take tank soundings and M/E crankshaft
deflections to compare after docking, land/secure loose gear, and confirm the docking plan is
with the yard so the blocks are set to suit the ship's keel/bilge profile (Q512).
Condition to enter dock (Q399/511/182): upright, minimal trim (usually slight trim
by the stern per the docking plan), and NO slack tanks — tanks pressed up or empty
to remove free surface and keep the ship stable and predictable as she takes the blocks; the
tanker/ship should arrive clean/gas-free as required for hot work. The examiner's key phrase
for "concerns going to dock" is "no slack tanks."
1

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Drydock preparation & docking condition

answers.title: Dock-bottom / hull inspection
answers.answer_text:
Once the dock is pumped down, walk the bottom forward to aft (Q164/423):
• Shell plating — corrosion, coatings, and panting/pounding damage at the forward end;
dents/set-in plating; grounding damage.
33 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

• Sea chests, gratings, inlets/discharges and valves — clear of blockage/marine growth,
gratings sound; overboard valves and ship-side pipes overhauled while accessible.
• Anodes / ICCP, bilge keels, bulb, thrusters, and any openings/plugs.
• Rudder (jumping and pintle clearances, drain plugs for water ingress), propeller (cavitation/
erosion, tip/edge damage), tailshaft weardown (poker gauge) and stern-tube seals.
• Plate thickness (Q285): measured by ultrasonic thickness gauging against the
classification renewal (wastage) limits; excessive wastage → crop & renew.
1

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Dock-bottom / hull inspection

answers.title: Shell-plating damage, crop & renew, and testing
answers.answer_text:
Significant shell damage affects watertight integrity and structural strength → call the
Class surveyor. Assess with NDT/gauging; check internally for damage to longitudinals,
frames, stiffeners and brackets. Decide repair vs cosmetic (Q188) on the extent, location
(high-stress areas fwd), depth of set-in, and Class limits. Crop & renew to an approved
procedure, using material to the shell-expansion plan specification (grade/thickness —
where you find plate material, Q419), welded by qualified welders to a WPS.
Testing a shell/tank repair (Q398): test new welds for tightness — the examiner wants
the vacuum-box test (a box with a viewing window and soapy solution placed over the
weld; a vacuum is drawn and bubbles reveal leaks) for one-sided access, plus hydrostatic/
leak testing of the tank as applicable. Adjacent tanks must be gas-freed/cleaned and
enclosed-space permits raised before any hot work.
1

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Shell-plating damage, crop & renew, and testing

answers.title: Tailshaft, stern tube & shaft alignment
answers.answer_text:
• Weardown measurement (Q365): the aft stern-tube bearing weardown/clearance is
measured with a poker (wear-down) gauge at the top through an access point, comparing
with the original/previous reading; excessive weardown → renew the bearing.
• Draining the stern tube (Q366/676): for an oil-lubricated stern tube you generally do not
need to drain to check weardown — the seals hold the oil, and readings are taken via the
gauge without loss.
• When to draw the tailshaft (Q19): at the survey interval (conventional water-lubricated ~5
yrs; oil-lubricated with approved seals/oil analysis under a TCM notation up to ~15 yrs), or
earlier on abnormal weardown, poor oil analysis (wear metals/water), cracking/corrosion, seal
failure, grounding or propeller damage. Tailshaft monitoring (Q20): stern-tube LO analysis,
weardown/clearance trending, bearing/oil temperature and oil-consumption records, and seal
condition.
• Shaft alignment (Q47–48/420–422): confirmed by bearing clearances and alignment
checks; historically the taut-wire/piano-wire (string) method, now the laser (optical)
method which is more accurate. If deflections/readings are drastically out, the shaft is
misaligned to the bedplate/hull — the engine may need dismantling and the bedplate re-
chocking.
34 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

UK FLAG Tailshaft and bottom surveys are Class items credited on behalf of the MCA; the
extended-interval TCM notation and the two-bottom-surveys-in-5-years/36-month rule (see §2.6)
govern how often the shaft is drawn.
1

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Tailshaft, stern tube & shaft alignment

answers.title: Rudder, stern-tube seal & muff coupling
answers.answer_text:
• Rudder integrity (Q79/186): security of pintle/gudgeon and jumping clearances, pintle
clearances, rudder-carrier bearing weardown (measured internally, Q515), fretting of
coupling/fitted bolts, and NDT/MPI on the pintles and tailshaft. Hollow rudder (Q514):
check for water ingress by removing the drain plug — water indicates a crack/leaking weld; a
crack in the rudder (Q592–593) is confirmed by MPI/dye-penetrant, repaired by welding,
and the rudder pressure/leak-tested and drained on completion (Q594). Typical pintle
clearance (Q516) is small (a few mm, per makers).
• Stern-tube seal / chrome liner (Q50/241): a leaking pressurised seal tank — reduce the
tank pressure/head to reduce the leak. At dock, inspect the seal arrangement and
chrome liner wear; depending on groove depth it may be resurfaced (case-hardened), or a
distance piece removed to reposition the seal onto an unworn liner area.
• Muff (SKF/OK) coupling dismantle (Q185): the tapered sleeve is released by injecting
high-pressure oil between the sleeve and shaft to expand the muff and relieve the
interference, then the hydraulic pusher/nut backs the sleeve off the taper.
1

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Rudder, stern-tube seal & muff coupling

answers.title: Propeller & CPP, anodes/ICCP, bilge keel
answers.answer_text:
• Propeller checks (Q49/223/595): cavitation/erosion, edge/tip damage, cracks (esp. at blade
root — dye-penetrant/MPI, Q596–597), and roughness/fouling; polish to restore efficiency.
Damaged blade (Q114/181): talk to Class/technical superintendent, assess severity; minor
damage may be dressed on board, a spare blade fitted (bolted CPP), or the blade sent to a
specialist (e.g. MAN propeller repair service). If a replacement blade is fitted (Q115), grind/
dress it to match the worn profile of the other blades to keep the propeller balanced.
• CPP (Q595): check blade seals, bolt security and locking plates on the blade bolts, hub
oil for water (Q49 header-tank check), and blade-actuation gear; fail-safe covered in §11.
• Propeller clearance too large vs record (Q184/404): indicates tailshaft/bearing
weardown — investigate the aft bearing and report to Class as it affects the shaft survey.
• Anodes & ICCP (Q116/346/367): sacrificial anodes (zinc/aluminium) corrode preferentially
to protect the steel; Impressed Current Cathodic Protection (ICCP) uses reference
electrodes and an impressed DC current from inert anodes to hold the hull at a protective
potential — advantages: adjustable, long-life, fewer anodes, better drag. Anodes are welded
to the hull in dry dock (Q367); before welding, check adjacent tanks for fuel/oil and
empty/clean/gas-free them first.
• Bilge keel (Q345/598–599): a roll-damping fin welded along the bilge; inspect for cracks/
detachment — it is designed to fail at the connection rather than tear the shell, so cracks there
are expected and repaired.
35 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

1

occurrences.question_text_as_asked: Propeller & CPP, anodes/ICCP, bilge keel

answers.title: Thrust block & shaft earthing
answers.answer_text:
Thrust transmitted to the hull (Q382/693): the propeller thrust is taken by the thrust collar
acting on the thrust pads (Michell/tilting-pad type) in the thrust block, which is bolted to
the ship's structure/tank top, so the thrust passes through the pads and block into the hull to
drive the ship. Check the holding-down bolts for tightness and fretting corrosion
(Q381/692).
Shaft earthing (Q377–380/688–691): a shaft-earthing (slip-ring/brush) device bonds
the rotating shaft to the hull to drain shaft-generated electrical potentials to earth,
preventing electrolytic pitting/spark-erosion of bearings, gears and the thrust block
from circulating shaft currents. It is confirmed working by a mounted shaft-voltage
millivoltmeter (checked with a multimeter if the meter is faulty); if the earthing fails,
expect bearing/thrust-pad pitting and frosting from sparking.
Examiner drill-down — rapid fire:
• “Main concern going to dock?”No slack tanks — remove free surface; arrive upright, slight
trim by stern per the docking plan.
• “What do you send the yard in advance?” Docking plan, GA, shell-expansion plan, work list,
3rd-party list, services list.
• “How do you test a cropped-out shell repair?”Vacuum-box test on the welds, plus
hydrostatic/leak test of the tank.
• “Where do you find plate material spec?” The shell-expansion plan.
• “How is tailshaft weardown measured, and do you drain the stern tube?” With a poker
gauge at the top bearing; for oil-lubricated seals you don't need to drain.
• “How is shaft alignment checked now vs before?”Laser now, taut-wire/string
previously; drastically-out readings → misalignment/re-chock.
• “Replacement propeller blade — what do you do?”Grind it to match the worn profile
of the others to keep balance.
• “ICCP vs anodes — advantage?” ICCP is adjustable, long-life, fewer anodes, less drag;
anodes are welded on in dock (check adjacent tanks first).
• “Why shaft earthing, and how do you know it works?” Drains shaft currents to prevent
bearing/gear/thrust pitting; a mounted shaft-voltage meter confirms it.

answers.title: Switchboard protection, reverse power & earth faults
answers.answer_text:
• Protection devices: over-current/short-circuit (with time delay for discrimination),
reverse-power, under/over-voltage, under-frequency, preferential trips (non-essential loads
shed first), and earth-fault indication.
• Reverse-power trip (Q38/132): protects the alternator from motoring if its prime mover
fails; tested by reducing the incoming machine's governor/fuel until power reverses
and confirming the breaker trips at the set reverse-power value.
• Discrimination / fuses getting smaller toward the consumer (Q586–587): protection is
graded so the device nearest the fault trips first, leaving the rest of the system live —
hence ratings reduce from the switchboard out to the final consumer.
Earth-fault finding on an insulated (unearthed) system (Q64/133): the earth-fault
lamps/monitor show a fault; localise by switching off circuits one at a time (or using an
37 C/E Orals — Master Guide + Drawing Pack

insulation tester) — most likely in damp/high-use locations: galley, laundry, deck
lighting, refrigerated stores. Why multiple earths are dangerous: the first earth fault
on an insulated system is not itself dangerous (no current path), but a second earth fault
on another phase completes a circuit, causing a short-circuit/fire and defeating the
safety of the insulated system — so the first earth must be found and cleared promptly.

answers.title: Enclosed-space entry, gas tests & inert gas
answers.answer_text:
Procedure (COSWP Ch. 15 / SOLAS): identify it as an enclosed space; risk assessment and
enclosed-space entry Permit-to-Work; isolate (blank/lock all lines, LOTO), drain and
ventilate continuously; test the atmosphere from outside at all levels; authorise entry only
within limits; post a standby man with comms and a rescue plan, resuscitation and lifting
equipment; wear appropriate PPE; log entry/exit. Rescue & medical treatment of a casualty is
never by an unprotected rescuer — use BA and the rescue team.
Gas-test limits (per COSWP, Q531/632–633): Oxygen 20.9% (never enter on depleted/
enriched); flammable/hydrocarbon <1% of the LEL; toxic gases within occupational
limits — e.g. CO <25–30 ppm, H S <5 ppm. If a gas is not on the multi-gas meter (e.g.
2
ammonia, Q631), use a dedicated detector tube/sensor for that gas. Re-test regularly
during occupation.
Inert gas (tankers, Q198–199): the IG system (flue-gas or inert-gas generator, scrubbed and
delivered via deck seal, non-return and P/V arrangements) keeps cargo tanks below the
flammable limit by reducing O (typically <5%/≤8%). The flammability diagram (Q199)
2
plots hydrocarbon % vs O %; the flammable envelope is bounded by the LFL/UFL and the
2
critical dilution line — inerting moves the tank condition to the O -lean, non-flammable region
2
so that gassing-up/purging avoids passing through the flammable zone.

answers.title: Lifting gear & SWL
answers.answer_text:
Load-test & certify (Q473): lifting appliances are proof-load tested (an over-load, e.g. cranes
to 25% over up to certain SWLs, sliding scales for larger) by a competent person, then thoroughly
examined and issued a register/certificate of test and examination; the Safe Working
Load (SWL) is marked. SWL vs WLL (Q635): Working Load Limit (WLL) is the
manufacturer's rated maximum for the item; SWL is the maximum the competent person
allows in the given configuration — historically distinct, though modern terminology often
treats them as the same. Maintenance (Q474): periodic thorough examination (typically 12-
monthly), greasing, wire/chain/hook inspection, brake and limit-switch checks; engine-room crane
safeties: overload cut-out, limit switches, brake, emergency stop.
